sentences: In many French villages, small businesses are closing one after another.
The bakery, the grocery store, the café: once at the heart of local life, they are gradually disappearing.
The reasons are well known.
Supermarkets, often located outside of towns, offer lower prices.
In addition, online shopping allows people to order everything without leaving their homes.
One might think it's just a simple economic problem.
However, the issue is deeper.
When the last bakery closes, it's not just a store that disappears.
It's a place where residents used to meet, talk, and know each other.
Some municipalities are reacting.
They help shopkeepers set up, or open stores managed by the village itself.
Nothing guarantees that these efforts will be enough.
But they at least show that many refuse to watch their town center die without taking action.

Artificial intelligence succeeds where a lot of information needs to be processed quickly.
It still fails when it comes to understanding a human situation, showing creativity, or making a difficult decision.

The real question may not be whether the machine will replace us, but what we will choose to entrust to it.

sentences: With phones and laptops, the line between work and private life has become blurred.
You can now receive a work message at any time, even in the evening or on weekends.
To address this issue, France introduced what is called the 'right to disconnect.'
The idea is simple: an employee is not obliged to respond to messages outside of their working hours.
On paper, this measure seems excellent.
In reality, things are more complicated.
Many people continue to check their emails in the evening, out of habit or fear of falling behind.
A law can establish a principle, but it doesn't easily change behaviors.
Companies also need to genuinely encourage their employees to disconnect.
As long as responding quickly is seen as a sign of seriousness, this right will remain, for many, a nice idea that is difficult to implement.

sentences: Should we live in the city or in the countryside?
This age-old question comes up regularly, especially since many people have rethought their way of life.
The city offers obvious advantages: work, transportation, culture, and social interactions.
Everything is close, and everything moves quickly.
But this energy comes at a cost.
Housing is expensive and often small, the air is less clean, and the noise never really stops.
The countryside, on the other hand, promises calm, space, and a more direct connection with nature.
However, it also has its challenges.
Without a car, getting around is difficult, and some services are far away.
There is no universal answer.
What works for one person may not work for another.
Perhaps what matters most is not the place itself, but the fit between that place and the life one truly wants to lead.
Abroad, you can find French restaurants in almost every major city.
However, what is served there doesn't always resemble what a French person would eat at home.
The dishes are often adapted to local tastes.
A recipe can become sweeter, spicier, or heartier, depending on the country.
Some purists are outraged: for them, it's almost a betrayal.
However, one can see things differently.
A cuisine that travels is a living cuisine.
As it moves from one country to another, a dish transforms, mixes with other traditions, and sometimes gives birth to something new.
After all, French cuisine itself has developed over the centuries by borrowing products and ideas from elsewhere.
Therefore, it is not necessary for a dish to remain identical for it to have value.
What matters is perhaps less the fidelity to a recipe than the pleasure one experiences at the table.

sentences: Professional sports have never generated as much money as they do today.
The best players earn huge sums, and the major clubs are increasingly resembling real businesses.
This evolution has positive aspects.
Thanks to this money, competitions are better organized, the stadiums are more modern, and the spectacle is more impressive.
Many young people dream of becoming athletes, and some succeed.
However, not everything is that simple.
When money dominates, passion sometimes takes a back seat.
We see clubs buying players at impossible prices, while small teams struggle to survive.
It's legitimate to wonder how far this can go.
The risk is that sports become a mere product, where only the financial result matters.
The challenge in the coming years will undoubtedly be to maintain balance: to benefit from this money without forgetting what originally makes sports so beautiful.

sentences: When we hear the word 'microbe,' we immediately think of disease.
However, the vast majority of microorganisms around us are not harmful, and many are even essential to us.
Our bodies host billions of bacteria, particularly in the intestines.
Far from harming us, they help us digest, defend against certain diseases, and stay healthy.
In recent years, scientists have been closely studying them.
They have discovered that the balance of these bacteria plays a much larger role than we previously believed.
This knowledge changes our perspective on cleanliness.
Washing remains obviously important.
But wanting to disinfect everything all the time can backfire, as it also destroys good bacteria.
Therefore, we should not be afraid of microbes in general.
The real issue is not to eliminate all of them, but to learn to live with them in a proper balance.

sentences: People often think that only one language is spoken in France: French.
In reality, the country has many regional languages, such as Breton, Occitan, Corsican, or Alsatian.
For a long time, these languages were discouraged, especially in schools.
Children were asked to speak only French, and many families stopped passing down their grandparents' language.
As a result, today, most of these languages are fragile.
Some are only spoken by elderly people and are at risk of disappearing in the coming decades.
However, an opposite movement exists.
Some schools offer instruction in these languages, and young parents choose to enroll their children in them.
Singers and writers keep them alive in different ways.
Saving a language is never easy, as it's not enough to study it: it must be spoken daily.
But as long as people care about it, nothing is really lost.

sentences: When you turn on the tap, water flows effortlessly, and it's easy to forget that it's a limited resource.
Across the planet, fresh water, the kind we can drink, makes up a very small part of all the existing water.
For a long time, in wealthy countries, this resource was considered almost infinite.
But things are changing.
Droughts are becoming more frequent, and some regions lack water at certain times of the year.
Agriculture, industry, and cities consume enormous quantities of it.
It wouldn't be reasonable to continue as if nothing were happening.
Reducing waste is possible at all levels: fixing leaks, watering less, choosing crops suited to the climate.
There is still time to act, but only if we take the problem seriously right now.
Water seems ordinary precisely because it is essential; perhaps that's why we protect it too little.

To my great surprise, I felt lighter.
A less cluttered home is also, in a way, a calmer mind.
I don't believe, however, that we should fall into excess.
Living almost with nothing is not an ideal in itself.
Minimalism may not be a trend or a philosophy, but a very simple question: what do I really need to be happy?

sentences: Among all sports, there is one that is often overlooked because it seems too simple: walking.
No need for equipment, a subscription, or any special talent.
All you have to do is put one foot in front of the other.
However, its benefits are real.
Walking regularly is good for the heart, helps keep you fit, and reduces stress.
Unlike more intense sports, walking carries almost no risk and is suitable for all ages.
It also has an advantage that other activities lack: you can easily incorporate it into your day.
Getting off one stop early, taking the stairs, going for a short walk after lunch — these actions add up.
Walking finally offers a rare time: the time when you do nothing but think or simply observe your surroundings.
So, it’s not necessary to run a marathon to take care of yourself.
Sometimes, all you need to do is walk.

The weather is very nice.

Dad was proud.
News from the neighborhood: there’s a new family in your house.

He’s nice.

And you?
How is your new city?
Your new friends?
Tell me everything.

sentences: It's autumn, my favorite season.
The trees are changing color.
This afternoon, I'm walking in the big park.
The leaves are no longer green.
They are red, orange, yellow, brown.
The big tree by the lake is completely golden.
Why are the leaves changing color?
My daughter is asking me the question.
In summer, the leaves are green.
In autumn, the days become short and cold.
The tree is preparing for winter.
Before falling, the leaves show their other colors.
The leaves fall gently.
The ground is a carpet of colors.
Under our feet, it makes a pleasant sound.
Further away, children are playing in the leaves.
The park keeper makes big piles, and the children jump in them.
My daughter fills her pockets: brown chestnuts, a golden leaf, a gray feather.
At home, we put the leaves in a book.
The air is fresh.
I'm wearing my first sweater of the year.
Today, the park is celebrating.
Autumn is an artist.

sentences: That morning, everything started off badly.
My alarm didn't go off.
When I opened my eyes, it was half past seven.
My train was leaving at eight o'clock for an important meeting in Lyon.
I jumped out of bed.
No shower, no breakfast.
I got dressed in three minutes.
In the street, I ran like an athlete.
I arrived at the station at eight oh one.
One minute!
I saw my train leaving.
I shouted and waved my arms.
It left anyway.
I sat down on a bench, furious.
The next train was leaving in an hour.
I called my client to reschedule the meeting.
He was very understanding.
Next to me, an old lady was waiting too.
She smiled: "Did you miss your train?
Me too.
Come, I'll buy you a coffee.
This lady was named Jeanne.
She was going to see her granddaughter in Lyon.
We talked about everything, and the hour passed very quickly.
On the train, we traveled together.
My meeting went well.
Since that day, I prepare my things the night before.
But I sometimes think of Jeanne: a missed train is not always a disaster.
Sometimes, it's a meeting.
Last month, I made a big decision: I adopted a cat.
My apartment was too quiet, too empty.
One Saturday morning, I finally went to the animal shelter.
There, there were many cats.
A volunteer guided me between the cages.
And then I saw him: a little gray cat, sitting at the back of his cage.
He wasn't moving.
He was just looking at me, with big green eyes.
He had been found in the street and he was afraid of people.
"He needs someone patient," said the volunteer.
I chose him.
At home, I named him Gribouille.
The first week was difficult.
He was hiding under the bed all day and he hardly ate anything.
I followed the volunteer's advice.
I never forced him.
I spoke to him softly, I left his food near the bed, and I waited.
On the eighth day, a surprise: Gribouille jumped onto the couch, next to me.
I didn't move.
After ten minutes, he closed his eyes and he purred.
A small victory that made me very happy.
Today, a month later, Gribouille sleeps on my bed and he waits for me behind the door in the evening.
When I come home from work, he runs towards me meowing.
My apartment is no longer quiet and empty.
It is alive.
Thank you, Gribouille.

sentences: In my building, there are about thirty residents.
For years, I didn't know anyone.
We would cross paths in the stairwell, say hello, and that was it.
But every year, in June, there is the neighbors' party.
It's a tradition in France: one evening, the neighbors get together to eat.
This year, I finally decided to participate.
Everyone had to bring something.
I made an apple pie, using my mother's recipe.
I was a little nervous.
At seven o'clock, I went down to the courtyard with my pie.
There were already tables and string lights.
A lady welcomed me: "Ah, you are the man from the third floor!"
I'm Yvonne, from the first floor.
Yvonne has lived in the building for thirty years.
The table was full of delicious things: a rice salad, couscous, quiches, cakes.
A student played the guitar.
And my pie?
A total success!
"It's the best pie of the evening," Yvonne said.
We ate, talked, and laughed until midnight.
I learned that my neighbor from the landing is named Karim and that he loves football, like me.
We're going to watch the next match together.
Before, I would just say hello to my neighbors.
Now, I know their first names and their stories.
It only took one evening and one apple pie.

sentences: Last summer, my friends suggested an outing: a free outdoor concert in the big city park.
I said yes right away.
We arrived around seven o'clock to find a good spot.
The park was already full of people.
We laid our blanket on the grass.
In the meantime, we had a picnic.
Everyone had brought something: bread, cheese, fruit, a lemon cake.
Children were running everywhere, and an old man was already dancing by himself, even before the music.
The sun slowly set behind the trees.
The sky turned orange, then pink, then purple.
And when night fell, the musicians came on stage.
From the first song, I understood why people love outdoor concerts.
The music rose into the sky with the lights.
People were singing and dancing on the grass.
My best friend, who never dances, danced all evening!
During a soft song, I lay down on the blanket, the stars above me.
I thought: this is it, the happiness of summer.
The concert ended around eleven o'clock.
We walked home, our heads full of music.
This summer, the band is coming back.
This time, I'm the one bringing the lemon cake.

sentences: In October, in front of my house, the swallows gather on the power lines.
There are dozens of them, then hundreds.
And then, one morning, they are no longer there.
Gone.
Where do they go?
Very far: to Africa, across the sea.
Every autumn, millions of birds leave Europe and fly south.
This great journey is called migration.
Why do they leave?
Because of food.
Swallows eat insects, and in winter, here, the insects disappear.
So the birds go where it's warm.
The journey is incredible and dangerous.
Some birds fly thousands of kilometers, over the sea and mountains.
Many travel in groups: it's safer, and the young learn the route with the adults.
But the most amazing thing is the return.
In spring, the swallows come back, and often they find exactly the same nest as the year before!
Without a map, without a phone.
Scientists think they use the sun, the stars, and the Earth's magnetic field.
So in spring, when the first swallows arrive in your sky, think of their journey.
These little birds weighing twenty grams come back from Africa, and they may have been born under your roof.

sentences: For my thirty-fourth birthday, I treated myself to a surprising gift: a skateboard.
My friends laughed.
"A skateboard?
At your age?
" When I was a teenager, I dreamed of doing it, but I never dared.
This year, it's now or never.
On the first day, at the park, I was very nervous.
I put one foot on the board.
It moved.
I put my second foot on, and I fell, like a sack of potatoes.
For two weeks, it was difficult.
I fell every day and I had bruises.
Several times, I thought about quitting.
And then I met Théo, ten years old, who skates like a champion.
One day, he came over: "Sir, you are looking at your feet.
You need to look far ahead.
And bend your knees, otherwise you will fall.
Théo's advice changed everything.
Every Saturday, my little teacher gave me a new lesson.
In exchange, I bought him an orange juice.
Last month, the big moment arrived: I crossed the whole park without falling, with the wind on my face.
Théo applauded.
I was as proud as a child.
I will never be a champion.
I still fall, but every Saturday, I make a little progress.
There is no age to learn.
There are just knees to bend and a bit of courage to find.

sentences: Six months ago, my rent became too expensive for me alone.
The solution: find a roommate.
I placed an ad, and I chose Marc, a thirty-year-old nurse, calm and smiling.
We didn't know each other at all, and I was a bit worried.
The first few weeks were complicated.
Marc works early at the hospital: he gets up at five-thirty.
As for me, I go to bed at one in the morning.
In the kitchen, it was the same: he likes to tidy everything up right away, and I left my dishes 'for later.'
One evening, Marc suggested to me: 'Shall we have a coffee and talk?'
We talked honestly.
Then we wrote down a few simple rules on a sheet of paper stuck to the fridge: silence after ten p.m., dishes done the same day, cleaning on Saturday.
A piece of paper changed everything.
And little by little, we became friends.
On Sundays, we cook together.
Marc taught me his lasagna recipe, and he even accompanied me to the doctor when I was sick.
Last month, my mother came over for dinner.
When leaving, she said to me: 'You found a good roommate.'
No, mom.
I found something better: a friend.

sentences: Last Saturday, I did an experiment: a whole day without my phone.
No messages, no photos, no videos.
Nothing.
The idea came from a number: my phone showed me my screen time for the week.
Four hours a day!
I was shocked.
On Friday evening, I turned off my phone and put it in a drawer.
Saturday morning was strange.
At breakfast, my hand was looking for my phone out of habit.
On the bus, everyone was looking at their screens; I was looking at the city.
I saw new things in my own street.
The hardest part?
The little empty moments, like waiting in line at the bakery.
Usually, I fill these moments with my screen.
On Saturday, I just experienced them.
At first, it was uncomfortable.
Then, it became relaxing.
In the afternoon, I did forgotten things.
I read forty pages of a novel in one go.
I called my grandmother from the old landline; we talked for an hour, and she was so happy.
In the evening, I noticed something strange: the day felt long and full.
Usually, my Saturdays go by in a flash.
On Sunday morning, I turned my phone back on.
Verdict: twenty-three messages, and none were urgent.
Since then, I've kept a rule: on Saturday mornings, the phone stays in the drawer until noon.
It's a good start.

sentences: It all started with a remark from my daughter Camille, who is eight years old, during an ecology lesson: "Dad, why do we throw the peels in the trash?
The teacher says we can make compost.
" Good question.
I didn't have a good answer.
So, last year, we started.
I set up a compost bin at the back of the garden.
Honestly, I had doubts: I imagined terrible smells.
The rule is simple.
In the compost, we put the peels, coffee grounds, eggshells, and dead leaves.
We don't put meat, fish, or cheese.
Camille is the compost boss and empties the small bucket every evening.
And what about bad smells?
Surprise: there aren't any.
Well-made compost smells like the forest, not the trash.
The secret is the mix, and you need to stir it from time to time.
In the bin, an invisible army is at work: earthworms, insects, and microscopic fungi.
Camille calls them "our little workers."
After several months, the magic was there: beautiful black, soft, and rich soil.
Gardeners call it "black gold."
In the spring, we gave it to our tomatoes.
The result: delicious tomatoes, and a trash can that shrank by a third!
Our peels feed the garden, and the garden feeds us.
The circle is complete, as Camille's teacher says.

sentences: During the spring break, my parents announced the day's plan: a visit to a castle by the Loire.
My sister Inès sighed very loudly.
"A castle?
More history?
" Dad smiled: "Wait and see.
The castle appeared at the end of a tree-lined path.
Even Inès said "wow."
Round towers, pointed roofs, white walls reflecting in the river.
Our guide, Mr. Perrin, knew a thousand stories.
In the great hall, he showed us the huge fireplace: "Here, they used to roast a whole beef for the king's feasts.
" Inès was listening, her eyes wide open.
She even asked three questions!
Everyone's favorite moment: the spiral staircase of the great tower.
One hundred thirty-seven steps!
At the top, the view was amazing: the Loire, the vineyards, the small villages.
After the castle, we visited the gardens.
Mom took a hundred photos.
Dad took a nap on a bench, "to admire the castle's sky."
At the shop, Inès bought a book about the castles of the Loire.
Our Inès, who hates history!
In the car, she read the whole way.
That evening, Dad winked at me.
History isn't boring.
It's poorly told sometimes.
Thank you, Mr. Perrin.

sentences: Last night, at seven o'clock.
I come home from work, tired.
In front of my door, I put my hand in my right pocket.
No keys.
Left pocket.
Nothing.
The pockets of my coat.
Empty.
A little moment of panic begins.
I put my bag on the ground and empty it completely on the landing.
But no keys.
My neighbor passes by and looks at me, sitting in the middle of my things.
"Is everything okay?"
"Very well, Mrs. Morel."
Let's think.
I retrace my day in reverse.
This morning, I locked the door, so I had my keys.
Then: the bus, the office, the bakery at noon, coffee with Julien.
First call: the office.
Nothing.
Second call: the bakery.
"Keys?"
"No, sorry."
My hope decreases.
Third call: the café.
"Le Petit Zinc, good evening!"
I describe my keys: a red keychain, in the shape of a fish.
The waiter laughs: "Yes, it's here, on the table near the window!"
I think I shouted with joy.
Twenty minutes later, the waiter gives me my keys with a big smile.
"It happens every day, you know."
I leave him a good tip.
Today, I installed a red hook near my door.
Now, the keys have a home.

sentences: A year ago, I downloaded an app and wrote in my notebook: "Goal: speak Spanish."
"Why Spanish?"
A dream of traveling to Andalusia, and a Madrid colleague, Carmen.
The beginning was a lesson in humility.
In the first weeks, I mixed everything up.
I said "I am tired" instead of "I am happy."
One evening in November, feeling discouraged, I almost gave up.
It was Carmen who saved me, with a simple piece of advice: "Stop the long Sunday sessions.
Do ten minutes a day."
She was right.
A year later, I have hardly ever missed a day.
I also found my own methods.
I listen to Spanish songs and look up the lyrics.
I watch cartoons: they speak slowly, it's perfect.
And on Fridays, Carmen and I only speak in Spanish.
And then, in May, the trip.
Seville, at last.
In a café, I ordered in Spanish, chatted with the waiter about football, understood his jokes.
As I was leaving, I had a huge smile.
I still make a lot of mistakes.
Last week, I told Carmen that I had "eaten a door" instead of soup.
She still laughs about it.
But mistakes are not the enemy.
Silence is.
Year two: goal Andalusia, extended version.
And maybe, after that, Italian?

sentences: When I told my mother that I was moving in with roommates at thirty-two, she fell silent with concern on the phone.
But really...
you had your own apartment!
For her generation, living with others after finishing studies feels like a step backwards, almost a failure.
Yet, more and more adults are making this choice, often without regrets.
The first reason is obviously financial.
In big cities, rents have gone crazy.
My twenty-five square meter studio cost me almost half of my salary.
Today, I pay a third less for a room in a large, bright apartment, with a living room where you can really invite friends, a proper kitchen, and even a balcony.
With the same budget, sharing a place offers a quality of life that a studio can never provide.
But reducing shared living to just a financial issue would be a mistake.
What surprised me the most in my old studio was the evening silence.
It's not said enough: living alone can be heavy.
Coming home and telling someone about your day, sharing an impromptu meal, watching a movie with three people on a Tuesday night — these little things change the color of a week.
Of course, not everything is idyllic.
You have to deal with the habits of others: dirty dishes lying around, loud music, surprise guests.
We have learned to talk about it before tensions rise, and we have set a few simple rules.
Shared living is a school of compromise, and at thirty, you actually experience it better than at twenty: you know your limits, you dare to express them, and you more easily respect those of others.
Finally, there are the pleasant surprises.
Léa, my roommate, has become a close friend.
Simon introduced me to climbing.
Our Sunday night dinners have become an institution that no one wants to miss.
My mother eventually came over for lunch.
As she was leaving, she whispered to me: "It's true that this apartment is nice.
And your roommates are nice, too."
Coming from her, that's a total victory.
Living with roommates at thirty is not a regression.
Sometimes, it's simply a smarter — and warmer — way to live in the city.

sentences: Ten years ago, many announced the death of radio.
Young people no longer listened to it; television and the internet had won.
And yet, radio did not die out: it reinvented itself in another form.
Today, millions of people listen to podcasts every day, these audio shows that you download and listen to whenever you want.
The first advantage of podcasts is their freedom.
Unlike traditional radio, there are no more schedules.
The show waits for you, not the other way around.
You can pause, rewind, or speed up.
This flexibility perfectly matches our fragmented lives, where free time comes in small bits.
The second advantage is that it frees up your eyes and hands.
You listen to a podcast while cooking, ironing, driving, or running.
Moments that were once empty or boring become moments of learning or escape.
My daily tram ride, for example, has become my appointment with a history show.
Twenty minutes of waiting turned into twenty minutes of pleasure.
We also need to talk about variety.
There are podcasts on absolutely everything: philosophy, crime, parenting, gardening, economics, and listeners' love stories.
Professional shows sit alongside amateur creations recorded in a bedroom.
This diversity would be impossible on traditional radio, limited by its programming schedules.
But the real secret of podcasts might be elsewhere: in the intimacy of the voice.
Listening to someone through headphones is like having them close to you.
No images, no sets, just a voice that speaks to you.
Many listeners develop a strange bond with their favorite hosts: you feel like you know these people, like you're meeting friends each week.
Some worry: by constantly having our ears occupied, are we losing silence, daydreaming, and fertile boredom?
The question is worth asking.
As always, it's all a matter of balance.
If you've never tried it, the instructions are simple: choose a topic you’re passionate about, search, and listen.
The first episode is rarely the right one; the third one often hooks you.
Radio is not dead.
It has slipped into our pockets, and it has never been better.

sentences: Okay, one last episode and then I'm going to bed.
Who has never said this phrase, only to betray it immediately?
It's one o'clock in the morning, the screen asks, 'Watch the next episode?'
and our finger clicks almost by itself.
Series have become the main pastime for millions of people.
This success deserves our attention.
First, a series offers what cinema cannot: time.
A film has to tell everything in two hours.
A series, on the other hand, has ten, twenty, sometimes a hundred hours.
Characters can evolve slowly, change, and surprise us.
We see them age, love, fail, and start over.
After a few seasons, they are no longer just characters: they are acquaintances.
Some viewers cry at the end of a series as one cries at a farewell.
It's not ridiculous; it's a sign that a long story creates deep connections.
Next, we must acknowledge the skill of the creators.
The end of each episode is crafted to leave us in suspense: a revelation, a danger, a door that opens.
This old trick of serialization already existed in 19th-century novels, published chapter by chapter in newspapers.
The difference is that in the past, you had to wait a week.
Today, the next part is just three seconds away.
Our patience doesn't stand a chance anymore.
Series have also become a common language.
At the office, at a dinner, they replace the weather in conversations.
Talking about them means belonging to a community; comparing theories about what happens next has become a collective game.
Should we be worried about all this?
A little, perhaps.
Entire evenings consumed by a screen, shortened sleep, books left closed: a series is a pleasure that easily takes up all the space.
I myself devoured a whole season in a rainy weekend, and I remember the strange feeling of Sunday night — that mix of satisfaction and lost time.
The solution is certainly not to stop watching series, which are among the great creations of our time.
It's more modest: to decide beforehand how many episodes we will watch.
And sometimes, to have the heroic courage to turn it off in the middle of the suspense.
The main character will survive until tomorrow.
So will we.

sentences: Coffee has a tumultuous medical history.
In the 1980s, it was blamed for all sorts of ailments: bad for the heart, bad for the stomach, bad for the nerves.
Then the tide turned, and articles began to praise its almost miraculous benefits.
So, is it poison or a remedy?
As often happens with health matters, the truth is less dramatic and more interesting.
What does science say today?
The large studies conducted on hundreds of thousands of people are rather reassuring.
Moderate consumption — two to four cups a day — does not increase heart risks for most people.
Some research even suggests protective effects against several diseases.
However, caution is warranted: these studies show statistical links, not absolute proof.
Coffee drinkers may have other habits that explain part of the results.
What we understand well, however, is the mechanism of caffeine.
In our brain, a substance called adenosine accumulates throughout the day and gradually makes us want to sleep.
Caffeine resembles this molecule and takes its place, like someone sitting in your chair.
As a result, the signal of fatigue no longer gets through.
We are not less tired — we simply don't feel it anymore.
The nuance is important.
This is also why evening coffee is a bad idea for many people.
Caffeine stays in the body for a long time: half of it is still there five or six hours after the cup.
An espresso at five o'clock still works against your sleep at ten o'clock.
And poor sleep makes you tired, and fatigue leads you to drink more coffee the next day.
The classic vicious circle.
Finally, it should be noted that we are very unequal when it comes to caffeine.
Some break it down quickly and sleep very well after a late coffee; others still feel the effects of a cup drunk at noon.
This difference is largely genetic.
The only true expert on your coffee is therefore your own body.
In summary: if you love coffee, drink it without guilt, preferably before mid-afternoon, and without exceeding what suits you.
Beware of headlines, in either direction.
And remember that the best coffee is the one you take the time to savor — ideally with someone.

sentences: Every Sunday morning, I go for a walk for an hour in the forest that borders my town.
It's neither a sport nor serious hiking: I walk slowly, without a goal, without a watch.
And every Sunday, the same little miracle happens: I enter the woods with tense shoulders and a full head, and I come out feeling light.
For a long time, I thought it was just a personal impression.
Science says otherwise.
Since the 1980s, researchers, first in Japan, have been seriously studying the effects of the forest on our health.
The results are remarkable.
After a walk in the forest, blood pressure drops, heart rate slows down, and cortisol levels — the main stress hormone — decrease significantly.
The comparison is striking: a walk of the same duration in the city does not produce the same effects.
So it's not just the walk that does us good; it's the forest itself.
How can we explain this?
Several explanations complement each other.
First, there’s what the forest takes away from us: the noise of traffic, advertising screens, constant demands.
Our attention, exhausted by the city, can finally rest.
Scientists talk about 'soft attention': looking at the light between the leaves or listening to a bird requires no effort, unlike the constant vigilance demanded by urban life.
There’s also what the forest gives us.
Trees release natural compounds into the air, and some studies suggest that breathing them in could boost our immune defenses.
These studies still need confirmation, but they are fascinating: the forest is, literally, a healing air.
The Japanese have given a lovely name to this practice: shinrin-yoku, or 'forest bathing.'
The idea is not to cover miles, but to immerse oneself.
Walk slowly.
Stop often.
Touch a tree bark, listen to the wind, breathe deeply.
Leave the phone at the bottom of the bag — or better yet, at home.
One might argue that not everyone has a forest at their doorstep.
That's true, but the effect also exists, albeit more modestly, in a large park, along a river, or under the trees of an avenue.
The principle remains the same: regularly provide your brain with an environment for which it was designed.
We have spent most of our history among trees.
Going back for an hour a week is not escaping the modern world.
It's simply returning home for a moment.

sentences: It's one of the most famous health rules in the world: you should drink two liters of water a day, which is about eight glasses.
Apps track our glasses, graduated bottles encourage us hour by hour, and many people feel guilty for not managing to do it.
But where does this number actually come from?
Its origin is more unclear than we think.
A recommendation from the 1940s in the United States is often cited, which indeed mentioned about two and a half liters of water per day.
But the same sentence specified that a large part of this water already comes from our food.
This second half of the sentence was forgotten along the way, and only the round number survived.
This is the fate of many health advice: the nuance disappears, the slogan remains.
Because it's a fact: we eat water as much as we drink it.
A cucumber or a tomato contains more than ninety percent.
A soup, a yogurt, an orange, and even bread contribute their share.
Tea and coffee count too, contrary to a stubborn misconception: their effect on urine is far too weak to cancel out the water they contain.
Our actual needs vary greatly.
A tall person running in the summer sun does not have the same needs as a petite person sitting in an air-conditioned office.
The climate, physical activity, diet, age: everything comes into play.
Giving a single number for everyone doesn't make much sense.
The good news is that we have a remarkable measuring tool: thirst.
This mechanism, refined by millions of years of evolution, kicks in as soon as the body starts to lack water.
For the vast majority of healthy people, drinking when you're thirsty is more than enough.
A complementary indicator, not very poetic but reliable: the color of urine.
Clear, everything is fine; dark, drink more.
There are of course exceptions.
Older people feel less thirsty and need to remember to drink, especially during a heatwave.
Athletes and some sick individuals have specific needs.
But for others, there's no need to carry a giant bottle everywhere or to count your glasses anxiously.
Drink when you're thirsty, eat fruits and vegetables, and trust your body.
It's been doing this job for a very long time.

sentences: Between twenty-five and thirty-five, my physical activity was limited to running after the bus.
Work, fatigue, and evening series: I always had a great excuse.
I kept telling myself, 'I'll get back to it next month' — and those next months piled up for ten years.
The trigger came from a mundane scene.
While climbing four flights of stairs with my groceries, on the day the elevator was out of order, I arrived out of breath as if I had just run a marathon.
At thirty-five, four flights of stairs brought me to my knees.
That evening, I decided to get back to it.
For real.
My first attempt was an instructive disaster.
Full of enthusiasm, I put on my old sneakers and went out to run 'like before.'
I lasted twelve minutes.
The next three days, I discovered muscles I didn't even know existed, simply because they hurt.
My motivation died along with my soreness, and the sneakers went back into the closet for two months.
It was a doctor friend who explained my mistake: 'You want to make up for ten years in a week.
Your heart is ready to progress quickly, but your tendons and joints need months.
Start ridiculously small.
' Ridiculously small.
Those words changed everything.
Second attempt, new method: twenty minutes of brisk walking, twice a week.
It was almost too easy — and that was exactly the goal.
It's impossible to find an excuse against twenty minutes.
After a month, I moved to three sessions alternating walking and slow running.
Then running gradually replaced walking.
A year later, the results exceeded everything I hoped for.
I run for forty-five minutes without suffering, three times a week.
I sleep deeply, whereas I used to wake up every night.
My back, which had troubled me for years at the office, has calmed down.
And the four flights?
I climb them while talking on the phone.
If you find yourself in the same situation I was in, here’s what I wish I had heard earlier.
Start smaller than your pride would like.
Aim for consistency, not performance: two sessions completed are better than five sessions dreamed of.
Expect a dip in motivation around the third week — it passes.
And find pleasure in the activity itself, otherwise you won't last.
The body surprisingly forgives years of neglect.
It only asks that you return to it with patience.

sentences: Not long ago, admitting that you dressed in thrift stores would cause a bit of an awkward silence.
Second-hand clothes were for those who had no other choice, and people didn't talk about it much.
Twenty years later, the turnaround is complete: second-hand has become proud, visible, almost chic.
Resale apps have millions of users, thrift stores are opening in nice neighborhoods, and teenagers compare their finds like trophies.
How can such a turnaround be explained?
The first reason lies in the wallet.
Second-hand clothes often cost three to five times less than new ones.
For families, for students, for pretty much everyone in reality, the argument is undeniable: why pay sixty euros for something that costs fifteen, barely worn?
The second reason is ecological, and it weighs more and more heavily.
The clothing industry is one of the most polluting in the world.
Making a simple pair of jeans requires thousands of liters of water, chemicals, and transport across several continents.
Yet a large part of these clothes are hardly worn before being thrown away.
Buying second-hand is about extending the life of what already exists — the simplest ecological gesture there is: producing nothing new.
But it would be wrong to reduce second-hand to a reasonable calculation.
There is also, and perhaps above all, the pleasure.
The pleasure of the hunt: rummaging, searching, stumbling upon a gem.
Unlike a regular store, where the same sweater comes in ten sizes and three colors, a thrift store offers each piece in only one copy.
Finding the perfect jacket in your size is a small miracle, and small miracles make people happy.
You come home with a unique piece and a story to tell.
However, a paradox must be pointed out.
The ease of online resale leads some to buy more new items, thinking they will resell them later.
Second-hand then becomes an accomplice to accelerated consumption, exactly the opposite of its promise.
Buying ten second-hand clothes, of which eight will sit in the closet, is not ecological either.
The real question remains the same as before: do I need this piece of clothing, and will I really wear it?
If the answer is yes, then second-hand is a double good deal: for the budget and for the planet.
And if you also enjoy it, what's the problem?

sentences: Eat local!
The advice is everywhere: at markets, in magazines, in the mouths of politicians.
The idea seems to be common sense: a food that travels less pollutes less.
Buying tomatoes from the local producer instead of those that travel across Europe by truck obviously seems more ecological.
And yet, the reality is more subtle — and more interesting.
Let's start with what is true.
The short supply chain has undeniable advantages.
It supports local farmers, who receive a fairer share of the price.
It guarantees fresher products, picked riper, and often better.
It keeps rural areas alive and maintains local know-how.
These reasons are more than enough to defend the Saturday market.
But on the strict climate front, things get complicated.
Because transport, contrary to what we believe, represents only a small part of the carbon footprint of our food — often less than ten percent.
The essential part happens elsewhere: in the way we produce.
A telling example: the tomato.
A tomato grown next to you, but in the middle of winter in a gas-heated greenhouse, can emit several times more carbon than a tomato from Spain grown under the simple sun and transported by truck.
The journey of a thousand kilometers weighs less than the heating of the greenhouse.
"Local" does not automatically mean "clean": it all depends on the season and the method.
Similarly, a lamb raised outdoors on the other side of the world and arriving by boat — the most economical mode of transport — can compete, in carbon balance, with meat produced intensively nearby.
The boat transports tons of goods for very little emissions per kilo.
It's the airplane that is disastrous: so be cautious with fragile and exotic products that travel by air.
What should we take away from all this, concretely?
First, that the season matters more than the distance.
The most accurate reasoning can be summed up in one formula: local AND in season.
The June strawberry from your region, yes; the January strawberry, no — whether it comes from far away or from a nearby greenhouse.
Next, that the contents of the plate weigh more than its origin.
Reducing meat a bit has more effect on the climate than any hunt for kilometers.
Eating local remains a great idea — for the taste, for the producers, for the joy of the market.
We just need to add a calendar to it.

sentences: Modern sports have become talkative.
Apps publish our routes, clubs organize group outings, and social networks display everyone's performances.
Running has become a social activity, measured, compared, and commented on.
That's perfectly fine — for those it motivates.
But I would like to defend here the other path, mine: that of the solitary runner.
When I tell running friends that I always run alone, I often see a hint of pity in their eyes.
Poor thing, he hasn't found anyone.
That's a misunderstanding: solitude is not something I endure, it's what I seek.
Running alone is first and foremost total freedom.
I leave when I want, where I want.
If I feel good, I extend the route without asking anyone's opinion; if my legs are heavy, I slow down without apologizing.
There is no pace to follow, no conversation to maintain, no level to prove.
The group always imposes a negotiation; solitude imposes nothing.
It's also a rare moment of mental silence.
My life, like everyone else's, is saturated with demands: messages, meetings, notifications, decisions.
During an hour of running, all of that stops.
In the first few minutes, the day's thoughts still swirl.
Then, kilometer after kilometer, they settle like dust after a car passes.
What remains is the breath, the rhythm of the steps, the landscape that unfolds.
Some call this meditation.
I don't like big words: I would simply say that I hear my thoughts again.
It's actually while running that my best ideas come to me.
Problems that had been blocking me for days sometimes resolve themselves around a bend.
It's not magic: the mind, finally freed from urgency, quietly does its foundational work.
I will add a confession: running alone has reconciled me with slowness.
Without an audience, there's no need to put on a show.
Some days, I jog barely faster than a hurried walker, and that's just fine.
My watch knows my times; it has the delicacy to keep them to itself.
I'm not saying that the group doesn't have its joys — the competition, the encouragement, the post-run coffee.
I sometimes enjoy it with pleasure.
But if you've never run alone, without music, without a companion, and without a goal, try it once.
You might discover, like me, that this appointment with yourself is the most faithful of all.

sentences: Last night, after a tough day at work, I sat down on the couch with a sigh.
My dog, who was playing in the garden, immediately came over and rested his head on my knees.
Coincidence?
Habit?
Or did he really 'understand' me?
This question is one that all pet owners ask themselves.
And for about twenty years, science has been taking it seriously.
Let's start with the dog, the most studied animal.
The results are impressive.
An average dog can learn to recognize several dozen words; some exceptional dogs, trained by researchers, can distinguish several hundred.
But vocabulary is just the visible part.
The real talent of the dog lies elsewhere: it reads our emotions.
Experiments have shown that dogs can tell the difference between a happy human face and an angry one, even in simple photos.
They are also sensitive to the tone of voice: the same words, spoken cheerfully or harshly, do not elicit the same reaction at all.
This talent is no coincidence.
Dogs have been living with us for tens of thousands of years.
During all this time, the dogs that understood humans best were the best fed and protected.
Generation after generation, evolution has created a specialist of the human species.
And what about the cat?
Its case is more amusing.
For a long time, people believed it understood nothing — or didn't want to understand anything.
Recent studies tell a different story.
The cat perfectly recognizes its name: Japanese researchers demonstrated this by observing the ears and heads of cats listening to different words.
The cat also distinguishes its owner's voice from that of a stranger.
Simply put, it doesn't always see the point in responding.
Understanding and obeying are two different things — and the cat has chosen its side.
However, we must be honest about the limits.
Our animals do not understand our sentences the way we do.
When I tell my dog, 'we're going to the park after lunch,' he catches 'park' and the rest gets lost.
Grammar, abstract ideas, the past, and the future remain beyond their reach, as far as we know.
But is that so important?
My dog doesn't understand my sentences; he understands my sighs, my silences, my joy, and my fatigue.
Communication doesn't always happen through words.
Last night, on the couch, the question didn't even arise.
He understood perfectly.

sentences: Last year, my friends canceled our joint vacation at the last minute.
I had already taken my leave and booked my tickets to Portugal.
Two options: stay home sulking, or go anyway.
Alone.
At thirty-one, I had never traveled alone in my life.
I took the plane with a knot in my stomach.
I might as well admit it right away: the first forty-eight hours were tough.
On the first evening in Lisbon, I entered a restaurant and said the phrase that scared me the most: 'A table for one, please.'
I was convinced that everyone was looking at me with pity.
I ate quickly, my eyes on my phone, and went back early.
But by the second day, something started to change.
I got up whenever I wanted.
I spent two whole hours in a tile museum that would have bored all my friends.
I changed my plans three times in the same day, on a whim, without negotiating with anyone.
I had never known such total freedom.
In a group, every decision is a compromise; alone, every desire is a plan.
And then there were the encounters.
It's the great paradox of solo travel: you're almost never alone.
When you travel in a group, you stay in your bubble.
Alone, you become approachable — and you dare to approach.
An old lady told me the story of her neighborhood on a bench in Porto.
German hikers adopted me for a day of walking.
One evening, in a hostel, we found ourselves six people from five different nationalities, cooking together.
I also learned things about myself.
With no one to decide for me, I discovered what I really liked — not what the group liked.
In the evening, I wrote a few lines in a notebook.
Rereading those pages today makes me smile: you can see, day by day, fear turning into confidence.
On the last evening, in the same type of restaurant as the first day, I asked for my table for one with a big smile.
I ate slowly, without my phone, watching the street.
Traveling alone didn't just let me visit Portugal.
It introduced me to someone I didn't know well: myself.
I came back different — a little freer, a little more open.
My friends are already asking me where we're going next year.
I haven't told them yet that I'm considering going alone again.

sentences: Try this test: the next time you wait for the bus, look around you.
How many people are just looking at the street?
None, or almost none.
All eyes are down on a screen.
Even the slightest empty minute is quickly filled.
Without realizing it, we have made something disappear from our lives: boredom.
Good riddance, you might say.
Boredom has never had a good reputation.
Doing nothing, in our culture, is wasting time.
You have to be productive, active, efficient — and when you're not working, you should at least 'enjoy' yourself, which is still a form of activity.
Someone who stares at the ceiling is seen as lazy.
And yet.
Researchers studying the brain have made an interesting discovery: when we do 'nothing', our brain doesn't stop at all.
It enters a particular mode that scientists call the 'default network'.
It's precisely in this mode that it sorts memories, makes connections between ideas, and imagines the future.
In other words: it's when we do nothing that our ideas are formed.
Experience confirms this even without a laboratory.
Where do your best ideas come to you?
Rarely in front of the computer, while fully concentrating.
Almost always in the shower, while walking, or looking out the window of a train.
These moments have one thing in common: the mind is free there, with no task to accomplish.
Archimedes, it is said, had his idea in the bath — not at his desk.
Children also teach us a lesson.
Let a child be bored, resist the urge to suggest an activity, and observe.
After a phase of complaints — 'I'm so bored' — they always end up inventing something: a game, a story, a fort.
Boredom is the starting point of imagination.
By filling every minute of our children’s time, and our own, we eliminate this starting point.
So, what to do — or rather, what not to do?
I started a small exercise, almost ridiculously simple: every day, ten minutes sitting, without a phone, without a book, without music.
Just looking out the window.
The first few days were surprisingly uncomfortable; my hand reached for the phone on its own.
Then calm came, and with it, thoughts I never had time to have.
I'm not saying you should be bored all day.
I'm saying that a little emptiness, in a life that is too full, is not wasted time.
It might be the best time spent in the day.

sentences: For years, I was the person who always says yes.
Did a colleague need help finishing a report?
Yes.
Was a friend moving on Saturday?
Yes.
One more meeting, one more favor, one more evening while I dreamed of my couch?
Yes, yes, yes.
I was proud of this reputation: people could count on me.
Always.
The problem is that this medal had a downside that I refused to see.
I was exhausted.
My weekends belonged to others.
My own projects — sports, reading, that photography course I had been talking about for three years — were always postponed due to lack of time.
And above all, an unpleasant feeling was growing in me: a kind of quiet anger towards those I was helping.
Yet they hadn't done anything to me; they asked, I said yes.
The anger should have been directed at the only real culprit: me.
The trigger came one Sunday evening.
I had spent the whole weekend helping three different people, and I realized that I hadn't had an hour for myself.
Not one.
Sitting in my kitchen, I understood a very simple phrase that changed everything: every yes said to others is a no said to oneself.
My calendar was full of yes; my life was full of no.
Learning to refuse was harder than expected.
The first no cost me a night of reflection — for a simple evening I didn't want to spend.
I was afraid of disappointing, of coming across as selfish, of losing friends.
I discovered three things that helped me a lot.
First, you can say no without justifying yourself for ten minutes.
"Thank you for thinking of me, but I won't be able to" is a complete sentence.
The more you explain, the more you apologize, the more you give the impression that you're seeking permission.
Next, you can suggest something else when you really want to: "I can't help you on Saturday, but I'm free Wednesday evening."
The no becomes a choice, not a rejection.
Finally — and this was the real surprise — people accept it very well.
No one got angry.
No one stopped calling me.
My friendships even improved in quality: when I say yes now, it's a real yes, joyful, whole, without hidden anger.
I still say yes often.
Helping others remains a pleasure.
But it has become a decision, more than a reflex.
And my Saturdays, sometimes, are finally mine.

sentences: When I left to study in Lyon, my parents couldn't help me much.
Between my small scholarship and a few hours of work on Saturdays, I had about two hundred euros a month for everything else once the rent was paid: food, transportation, living.
Two hundred euros.
I smile when I think back on it, but at the time, I had to learn.
Quickly.
The first lesson was cooking.
A student who eats out, even sandwiches, burns through their budget in ten days — I found that out in the first month, along with the end-of-month panic that comes with it.
So I learned to cook, armed with a second-hand book and my grandmother's advice over the phone.

I discovered a whole new world: seasonal vegetables that cost three times less, dried legumes — lentils, chickpeas, beans — filling and almost free, the big pot on Sundays that provides four meals for the week.
My star dish, lentil curry, cost less than a euro per serving.
Ten years later, I still cook it.
The second lesson was more subtle: the small invisible expenses.
I noted down absolutely everything I spent for a month.
The result amazed me.
Coffee from the machine, snacking, little purchases that seemed insignificant: when added up, they exceeded my food budget!
It wasn't the big expenses that were ruining me, it was the tiny ones.
Since that discovery, I record my expenses for one week each quarter, just to check where the money goes.
It always slips away through the small holes.
The third lesson is the most valuable: free things.
Deprived of cinema, concerts, and restaurants, I explored what costs nothing — and the list is long.
Museums on the first Sunday of the month.
The library, this free palace.
Picnics in the park instead of on terraces.
Game nights at each other's places, with everyone bringing something.
These tight years left me with a paradox: I have never had so little money, and rarely such a rich social life.
Today, my situation is comfortable, and I don't romanticize poverty: I also remember the anxious end-of-months and postponed dental care.
But those years taught me to separate two questions that advertising tries to mix up: do I want it, or do I need it?
Desire fades.
Need, on the other hand, is surprisingly small.
It's a gesture we make five to ten times a day, one that we were already doing in our mother's womb, and one that we share with cats, fish, and crocodiles.
A gesture so ordinary that no one thinks about it — until someone asks the question: by the way, why do we yawn?
And there, surprise: science itself has no definitive answer.
The most well-known explanation is also the most false.
We still sometimes learn it in school: we yawn to take in more oxygen into our bodies.
The idea seems logical — this big inhale, this open mouth...
Unfortunately for it, it has been tested, and it doesn't hold up.
Researchers had volunteers breathe air that was more or less rich in oxygen: the number of yawns didn't change.
The oxygen hypothesis is dead, even if it continues to circulate in conversations.
So, what are the serious leads?
The strongest one today is thermal: yawning would serve to cool the brain.
Like a computer, our brain heats up when it works, and it functions better at the right temperature.
The big jaw movement and the air inhaled would cool the blood that rises to the head.
Several observations support this: we yawn more when the temperature around us rises, and putting a cold pack on our forehead reduces the urge to yawn.
That's also why we yawn at moments of transition — waking up, falling asleep, boredom: all moments when the brain changes its state.
But the most fascinating part is the contagion.
You already know this: seeing someone yawn makes you want to yawn.
Hearing a yawn is enough.
Reading a text about yawning is enough — and I imagine you have already yawned since the beginning of this article.
This contagion is not trivial: it is linked to empathy.
Studies show that we 'catch' yawns from our loved ones more easily than those from strangers.
Young children, whose empathy is still developing, are not sensitive to it.
And your dog, after thousands of years of living with us, can catch your yawns — the only known animal to cross the species boundary in this way.
A gesture millions of years old, present before birth, contagious just by reading, and still mysterious: yawning is a beautiful lesson in humility for science.
So, how many times have you yawned while reading this?
Don't apologize.
It's proof that you are human — and probably someone empathetic.

sentences: In the 2000s, the prediction seemed obvious: with consoles, computers, and soon phones, board games were set to join video cassettes in the museum of lost pastimes.
Twenty years later, the verdict is in — and the opposite has happened.
Board games are experiencing a golden age.
Sales are breaking records year after year, game cafés are opening in every major city, and the Cannes festival...
of board games attracts tens of thousands of visitors.
What happened?
First, the board game itself has changed.
Forget the memories of endless games and dusty rules.
A new generation of creators — because there are real game authors whose names appear on the boxes — has invented shorter, smarter, and more beautiful games.
Cooperative games, where all players win or lose together, perfect for families tired of arguments.
Party games that make you burst out laughing in five minutes.
Mystery games that you only play once, like watching a movie.
Today, there is a game for every person, every duration, every mood.
But the quality of the games doesn't explain everything.
If we are coming back to the tables, it is also, specifically, because of screens.
After whole days spent behind a computer, then evenings each on their phone, many feel the same lack: being truly together.
Board games offer exactly that.
During a game, we look each other in the eye, we bluff, we negotiate, we laugh, we tease gently.
Try to cheat at cards over video conference: it's not the same.
I have an example at home.
Last year, we established 'game Fridays': phones in a basket at the entrance, pizza, and two or three games.
At first, our friends came out of curiosity.
Now, they book their Fridays weeks in advance, and woe to us if we cancel.
The most sought-after moment of the week is the one where there’s nothing to watch.
It would be wrong to sharply oppose screens and boards: many players enjoy both, and excellent video games can also be played together.
But the success of board games sends a clear signal about our times.
Technology has given us everything, except one thing: a good reason to sit around a table, face to face, for an hour.
It only took a cardboard box.

sentences: The first time I came across a group of Nordic walkers in my park, I admit, I smiled.
About ten people were walking energetically with ski poles — in the middle of June, with not a snowflake in sight.
It looked like a joke, or a strange trend from elsewhere.
I was wrong to smile, and this article is my way of acknowledging that.
Where does this practice come from?
From Finland, as its name suggests.
In the 1930s, Finnish cross-country skiers were looking for a way to train in the summer, without snow.
They kept the poles and left the skis.
The method was refined, specific poles were created, and Nordic walking became a sport in its own right, now practiced by millions of people in Europe.
But why on earth walk with poles?
That's the whole difference from ordinary walking.
When we walk normally, our arms swing for nothing: all the work comes from the legs.
With the poles, each step is accompanied by a push from the arms.
As a result: the shoulders, arms, chest, and back join in.
Experts estimate that Nordic walking engages about eighty percent of the body's muscles, compared to barely half for regular walking.
You burn significantly more energy — without realizing it, because the effort is distributed across the whole body.
The other big advantage is the gentleness.
Unlike running, there is no impact with each step: the joints — knees, hips, ankles — are spared, and the poles even relieve some of the body weight.
That's why this sport is suitable for almost everyone: recovering athletes, elderly people, complete beginners, overweight individuals.
Everyone moves at their own pace, and the group adapts.
Last month, pushed by my neighbor — seventy years old and with calves of steel — I finally tried it.
Immediate lesson in humility: the technique doesn't come naturally.
For twenty minutes, my arms and legs refused to coordinate, under the amused gaze of the group.
Then the movement came, natural, fluid, almost hypnotic.
An hour later, I was warm all over, my mind clear, and I had signed up for the following Saturday.
Moral: beware of sports that make you smile.
They are often the ones that last.
And if you come across a group of pole walkers in your park, don't smile too quickly.
In a month, it might be you.

sentences: Let's pause for a moment to consider the strangeness of what we do every night.
For about a third of our lives, we stop eating, reproducing, and defending ourselves.
We lose consciousness, immobile and unprotected, at the mercy of the first danger.
From a survival perspective, sleep is madness.
If evolution, which ruthlessly eliminates anything unnecessary or costly, has preserved this behavior in all animals, from worms to dolphins, it must serve absolutely vital functions.
Which ones?
Science has only recently lifted the veil, and the picture it paints is astonishing.
For a long time, sleep was believed to be passive: the 'disconnected' body would simply rest, and that was that.
This image has now been swept away.
At night, the brain does not shut down; it works with an intensity sometimes greater than when we are awake, but on different tasks.
The most fascinating of these concerns memory.
During sleep, the brain replays the experiences of the day, sorts the essential from the trivial, and transfers important memories to long-term storage.
It is literally at night that we learn what we experienced during the day.
Experiments show this unambiguously: with equal effort, those who sleep after learning retain significantly better than those who stay awake.
The student who sacrifices his night before the exam deprives himself of the very tool that engraves his revisions.
Even more spectacular: the discovery, in the 2010s, of a true cleaning system for the brain.
During deep sleep, the space between nerve cells expands, and a fluid comes to flush out the waste accumulated during the day — including certain proteins associated with neurodegenerative diseases.
In sleeping, the brain essentially does its housekeeping.
Housekeeping that is impossible to do while it is running at full speed, just as you wouldn't clean a street in the middle of traffic.
These discoveries illuminate the damage caused by lack of sleep, which has long been underestimated.
Prolonged deprivation affects not only mood and concentration; it harms memory, immunity, emotion regulation, and increases the risks of many diseases.
A society that treats sleep as lost time, which is cut back to be 'productive,' is therefore making a serious miscalculation.
And yet — and this is where humility is necessary — the essential still eludes us.
No one really knows why we dream, nor what purpose these absurd stories our minds create every night serve.
Hypotheses abound, but none have unanimous support.
At the heart of the most universal experience there is, a mystery remains intact.
What science clearly establishes, on the other hand, is this: sleeping is not being absent from the world.
It is accomplishing, in the shadows, a task without which being awake itself would become impossible.

sentences: A year ago, in a small bookstore, I bought a black notebook on a whim.
That very evening, I wrote a few lines about my day.
I didn't yet know that I had just started the most enduring habit of my adult life.
Three hundred sixty-five evenings later, the black notebook is full, its successor is well underway, and I want to explain why I continue.
First, let's clear up some misunderstandings.
Keeping a journal is not about writing memoirs, creating literature, or sharing burning secrets.
My journal is completely mundane: what I did, who I saw, what annoyed or pleased me.
Five minutes, ten on big nights.
No one will read it, and that's exactly what makes it possible: without a reader, there's no style to polish, no image to defend.
We write as we think.
The first effect surprised me with its speed: writing calms.
On frustrating evenings, putting things on paper makes them shrink.
An argument, a worry, an office annoyance: as long as they spin in your head, they grow; once written down, they take their real size, often modest.
Psychologists have studied the phenomenon — putting words to emotions helps the brain process them — but you don't need a study to feel it.
It's physical.
You close the notebook feeling lighter than when you opened it.
The second effect is slower, deeper: the journal teaches you to observe.
When you know you'll write tonight, you experience your day differently.
You notice the amusing detail, the phrase heard on the bus, the unusual light on the building across the street — because you'll need something to note.
Writing doesn't just record life: it makes you more attentive to life.
My days haven't changed; my perspective has.
And then there's rereading.
It's the delayed gift of the journal.

Rereading an ordinary Tuesday from a year ago is a strange and moving experience: I had completely forgotten that day, and here it is again, with its rain, its laughter, and its little problem now resolved.
Without the notebook, that Tuesday would no longer exist anywhere.
We forget the essentials of our own lives; a few lines are enough to save pieces of it.
If you feel like it, the instructions can be summed up in three rules.
A notebook that you like.
A fixed moment — the evening, in bed, works well.
And no demands: two lines are enough, empty days can just say 'nothing to report.'
That's it.
The rest — calm, attention, memory — comes naturally, page after page.

sentences: In my day, we would stand up when an adult entered; we would say hello, madam; we didn't interrupt.
How many times have you heard this refrain?
It has crossed the centuries, remarkably stable.
Socrates, too, would have complained about the insolent youth of his time.
Every generation, upon reaching a certain age, looks at the next one and diagnoses the same deadly disease: the end of politeness.
The fact that this complaint has been repeated identically for two thousand five hundred years should make us sit up and take notice.
If politeness really disappeared with each generation, there would have been nothing left of it long ago.
Yet it is still here.
So it doesn't die: it shifts.
For we must distinguish two things that nostalgia confuses: the forms of politeness and its principle.
The forms, yes, change, and sometimes quickly.

To uncover oneself before a lady, to kiss the hand, to use ceremonial phrases: these gestures, once mandatory, have largely disappeared, and anyone who would practice them today would seem affected rather than courteous.
Similarly, the use of 'tu' has gained ground, dress codes have relaxed, and deference towards age and rank has diminished.
Seen through these old forms, yes, the world seems impolite.
But let's look at what has replaced them, for the space has never remained empty.
Our time has invented its own demands, often more subtle and sometimes heavier than the old ones.

Today, we pay much more attention than before to not hurting anyone with our words; words that were once commonplace have become unacceptable, because we take into account people whom the old politeness superbly ignored.
We apologize for bothering, we thank in writing, we ask for permission to photograph someone.
Politeness towards women has changed in nature: fewer hands kissed, more real respect.
What we have lost in ceremony, we may have regained in consideration.
This is not to deny that there are problems.

Traffic, the anonymity of cities, the brutality of certain online exchanges create very real forms of impoliteness, and the screen, which puts a face at a distance, disinhibits rudeness that one would not dare face-to-face.
Every era has its areas of harshness.
But the idea of a general collapse does not hold up under scrutiny: it stems from that persistent illusion that beautifies the past and darkens the present.
Beneath the changing forms remains the principle: this movement by which I recognize the other, I take into account their existence, I show them that they matter.
This principle, in fact, does not date from any era and does not belong to any.
It is the discreet cement of all communal life.
One day, our grandchildren will judge our manners outdated and will mourn the politeness of 'their time' — that is, ours.
They will be wrong, just as we are.
And politeness, for its part, will continue on its way.

sentences: Close your eyes and remember a significant moment from your childhood.
The image comes back to you, clear, colorful, with its sounds and emotions.
You feel like you're replaying a recorded scene, true to reality.
This feeling is one of the great illusions of the human mind.
Because memory does not work at all like a camera that archives the past to reproduce it intact.
It works like a storyteller: with each recollection, it reconstructs the story — and in doing so, modifies it.
The work of psychologists over the past several decades leaves little doubt.
Memory is not an object stored in a drawer that you can take out unchanged.
It is a reconstruction, done in the moment, based on fragments.
The brain retains a few central elements and fills in the gaps — with logic, expectations, and information acquired since.
The most troubling thing is that this reconstruction work is invisible to us: we do not feel the stitching between what was lived and what is invented.
The reconstructed memory presents itself with the same clarity, the same certainty, as the exact memory.
A researcher has demonstrated this fragility through famous experiments.
By cleverly suggesting false details to adults, she managed to make them 'remember' events that never happened: getting lost as a child in a shopping mall, spilling a bowl at a wedding.

Not only did the subjects adopt these false memories, but they also enriched them with spontaneous details, defended them emotionally, and often refused to believe, upon revelation, that they had been deceived.
We are not reliable guardians of our own history.
The consequences far exceed mere laboratory curiosity.
For a long time, the justice system treated eyewitness testimony as the ultimate proof: 'I saw it with my own eyes.'
We now know that a sincere witness, absolutely certain, can be gravely mistaken — and innocent people have been convicted based on such memories, only to be exonerated much later.

In a more everyday context, these mechanisms explain those unsolvable family disputes where everyone swears by their version: two people remember the same scene in incompatible ways, and both are acting in good faith.
Neither is lying.
Their memories have simply constructed two different narratives.
Should we then despair of our memory, considering it a fabric of inventions?
That would be an exaggeration in the other direction.
Essentially, it serves us faithfully: it retains the meaning, the main points, what matters for action.
It sacrifices the accuracy of details, but this 'unfaithfulness' may have a useful role — a flexible memory that constantly reorganizes, adapts better than a fixed recording.
The lesson is therefore not distrust, but humility.
The next time you are absolutely certain of a memory, remember that this very certainty proves nothing.
Your memory is a talented storyteller.
It does not seek to deceive you; it is simply doing its job, which has never been to tell the whole truth.
Listen closely, right now.
Even in what you believe to be calm, a background noise surrounds you: the hum of a device, the distant murmur of traffic, an engine, a voice.
In a big city, complete silence hardly ever exists.
We are immersed in noise from morning to night, and often at night, to the point that we no longer hear it.
This deafness to noise may be the problem: by getting used to it, we have stopped measuring what it costs us.
However, this cost is real and documented.
Noise is not just a temporary nuisance; it is a health hazard, which health authorities now classify among the major urban pollutants.
Prolonged exposure to noise raises blood pressure, disrupts sleep even when we think we have adapted, and keeps the body in a state of constant tension.
The mechanism is ancient: our body, inherited from times when a sudden noise signaled danger, reacts to sound with a discreet but constant alert.
We no longer startle consciously, but our body remains on high alert.
Noise tires us without our knowledge.
The effect on the mind is just as profound.
Concentration requires filtering, constantly, a mass of distracting sounds, and this filtering is exhausting.
Studies show that reading, memorization, and reasoning deteriorate in a noisy environment — this is particularly evident among children educated near busy roads.
Thinking requires a certain peace; noise gnaws at our mental resources even before we begin.
That is why silence, once commonplace, has become a luxury — in almost economic terms.
Now we must pay or go far away to obtain it: hotel rooms 'in peace' sold at a higher price, retreats in remote locations, expensive noise-canceling headphones.
Silence has joined clean air and dark nights in the category of goods that were once free and are now rare.
This scarcity speaks volumes about what our development has, unwittingly, destroyed.
But we must avoid a misunderstanding.
The silence in question here is not the total absence of sound, which would be grim.
A 'silent' forest rustles with a thousand sounds — the wind, a bird, water.
Those sounds do not tire; they soothe.
What exhausts us is human noise, mechanical, incessant, and meaningless.
And the true silence sought is not just acoustic: it is an inner space, a pause in the flow of demands, where the mind can finally rest and reconnect.
We will not give up cities, nor the joyful exchange of voices, laughter, and music, which also contribute to the richness of life.
But recognizing the value of silence, giving it a place — a few minutes, a location, a moment — is not fleeing the world.
It is simply stopping the noise from deciding for us the state of our body and mind.

sentences: Our time has made speed a cardinal virtue.
Everything must go faster: meals, transportation, exchanges, careers.
A message demands an immediate response; a queue becomes a small suffering; a page that takes two seconds to load frustrates us.
We measure the value of things by their speed, and slowness has become, at best, a weakness, at worst, a fault.
It is against this rarely questioned obviousness that a discreet movement has emerged, born in Italy at the end of the 1980s, around a simple idea: what if we are going too fast?
We would be wrong to see it as a mere whim of nostalgic privileged people.
Certainly, slowing down often requires a certain comfort, and it would be indecent to preach slowness to those juggling jobs to survive.
But the central idea of the movement touches on something universal, which goes beyond the question of means.
Here it is: speed destroys what it claims to give us.
Let's take a meal.
Swallowed standing up in five minutes, it fills the stomach but nourishes nothing else; we remember neither its taste nor that moment.
Taken slowly, shared, savored, the same meal becomes an experience, a pleasure, sometimes a lasting memory.
Speed may have saved time — but it has eliminated the essential, which was precisely in the time spent.
What holds for the meal holds for almost everything: a rushed conversation, a landscape crossed without seeing it, a book skimmed through.
By going faster, we do more things, and we experience less.
There is a paradox here that slowness illuminates.
We run to gain time, but this gained time, we immediately fill with other tasks.
Speed is never satisfied; the faster we go, the faster we need to go again.
We save ten minutes only to swallow them up in ten new tasks, and the feeling of lacking time, far from decreasing, worsens.
He who has always run never arrives.
Would he be mistaken, however, the one who concludes that everything must be done slowly?
Certainly.
Living in slow motion would be as absurd as living at full speed, and often impossible in the world as it is.
Well-understood slowness is not a uniform rule; it is an art of discernment.

It is not about slowing everything down, but about choosing: identifying the moments that deserve our time — a family meal, a walk, an important conversation — and protecting them from the surrounding haste.
For the rest, speed retains its rights; no one demands to daydream while paying their bills.
Ultimately, true wealth may not be about doing a lot, but about fully living the little that matters.
Slowing down is not wasting your time.
It is refusing to let your life slip by without having lived it.
