sentences: There is a cruel irony at the heart of modern tourism.
What drives millions of people to travel — the desire to discover unique, preserved places filled with beauty and history — is precisely what, as it multiplies, destroys these places.
We love Venice, so we go there; and because twenty million of us love it every year, we gradually suffocate the city we came to admire.
Mass tourism is this contradiction that has become the landscape.
That travel is a beautiful thing, no sensible person would dispute.
Moving around, meeting other ways of living, stepping out of the narrowness of one's own world: nothing has done more for the opening of minds.
The problem is therefore not traveling.
It relates to a purely quantitative phenomenon, whose effects change in nature on a large scale.
One visitor enriches a place; a million visitors, concentrated in the same alleys at the same seasons, crush it.
It's not a question of individual morality — each of these travelers is perfectly legitimate — but of accumulation.
The consequences, in the most affected cities, are now visible to all.
Residents are being driven out by rising rents, as housing is transformed into short-term rentals.
Everyday businesses — the baker, the shoemaker, the grocer — are giving way to identical souvenir shops from one city to another.
The city emptied of its inhabitants becomes a backdrop, a giant postcard that one crosses without ever living there again.
The place survives; its soul departs.
In the face of this, tentative responses are emerging.
Some cities limit the number of visitors, implement reservations, charge entry fees, or ban the largest ships.
These measures, often criticized, at least have the merit of acknowledging the problem and refusing fatalism.
However, they face a formidable difficulty: tourism supports entire regions, and one cannot close the floodgates without depriving of income those whom one claims to protect.
The balance is delicate.
But the actions of cities do not exempt us from more personal reflection.
Each of us, as travelers, has some leeway.
Is it really necessary to go to the same place as everyone else, at the same time?
Should we reduce a region to its three most photographed sites, which we 'do' in a day before leaving?

Traveling off-season, stepping away from the crowds, staying longer in one place, showing interest in less famous spots that are just waiting to be loved: these are all ways to continue discovering the world without contributing to its degradation.
Mass tourism places us in front of an uncomfortable but salutary question.
To love a place, is it to rush there with the crowd?
Or is it, sometimes, to know how to visit it differently — even to renounce it, so that it remains what we came to seek?

sentences: It was better before.
This phrase is so widespread that it seems obvious.
In the past, people were more polite, food had more flavor, summers were more beautiful, and life was simpler.
Each of us has thought or said this at some point.
This feeling, nostalgia, is universal and often sweet.
However, it deserves to be examined, as it is largely based on an illusion — an illusion created by the very functioning of our memory.
Our memory, in fact, is not an impartial historian: it is a painter that embellishes.
It preferentially retains happy moments and allows the difficulties, troubles, and little miseries of everyday life from the past to fade away.
When we talk about our childhood, we summon sunny summers, laughter, vacations — not the hours of boredom, arguments, or forgotten anxieties.
The past seems better not because it was, but because we only keep the best of it.
The 'good old days' is a work of art, crafted by forgetfulness.
To this illusion is added a bias of comparison.
We compare a past cleansed of its inconveniences to a present that we experience in all its thickness — with its concrete worries, immediate irritations, and uncertainty.
The game is not fair.
The present always has the disadvantage of being real, while the past has the charm of what is finished and neatly arranged.
No wonder, then, that it prevails.
Should we then condemn nostalgia as a mere mistake?
That would be going too far.
Psychologists who study it recognize its virtues.
Remembering fondly the loved ones, the places of our childhood, the music of an era warms the heart and gives a sense of continuity of self through time.
Nostalgia connects: it ties us to those who are no longer here, to what we have been.
Well-lived, it is a form of gratitude towards one's own history.
The trap is therefore not to feel nostalgia, but to let oneself be trapped in it.
For there exists a sterile, even dangerous nostalgia.
On the scale of a life, it leads to living turned backward, always finding the present mediocre and the future threatening, missing out on the good that the moment offers.
On the scale of a society, the illusion of a lost golden age feeds speeches that promise to 'return' to an idealized past that never existed.
Collective nostalgia, when it becomes political, can sometimes come at a very high price.
Wisdom lies, as often, in moderation and discernment.
Savor happy memories without forgetting that they are embellished.
Draw from the past sweetness and strength, not a judgment against the present.
Remember that our own 'good old days' were, at the time, an anxious and imperfect present — just like today.
And finally, remember this: in a few years, this present that we judge so dull may, in turn, become the 'good old days' that we will regret.
So, as long as it is here, let's try to inhabit it.

sentences: Few subjects spark as intense debates as the electric car.
For some, it is the savior of the planet, the end of pollution, a finally clean future.
For others, it is a vast illusion, an ecological lie disguised as progress.
As is often the case when positions harden, the truth lies in a less comfortable but fairer middle ground: the electric car is a real but partial advancement — neither a miracle nor a sham.
Let's start with its advantages, which are undeniable.
An electric car emits no exhaust gases where it drives.

In cities, where air pollution causes respiratory diseases and premature deaths, this point is far from trivial: replacing gasoline engines with electric ones would significantly improve the health of millions of city dwellers.
Moreover, it is silent, which alleviates another often overlooked urban pollution: noise.
On these two fronts, the gain is clear and immediate.
But the picture becomes more nuanced as soon as we broaden our view beyond the tailpipe.
A car is not just what it emits while driving; it is also what was needed to manufacture it.
However, the production of an electric car, particularly its battery, is very energy-intensive and requires rare metals, the extraction of which poses serious environmental and human issues.
Upon leaving the factory, an electric car already has a heavier 'carbon footprint' than a conventional one.
It only starts to be advantageous after tens of thousands of kilometers, once this debt is repaid by the absence of emissions during use.
A second, decisive caveat: an electric car is only as good as the electricity that powers it.
Charged with clean energy, it lives up to its promise.
Charged with coal-fired power, it merely shifts pollution from the street to the chimney.
Its balance sheet therefore entirely depends on how each country produces its electricity — which leads to very different assessments from one region of the world to another.
Thus, the electric car is a conditional advancement: it will be truly beneficial if electricity becomes decarbonized and if batteries become cheaper to produce and easier to recycle.
These conditions are partly being met, which invites a measured optimism rather than blind enthusiasm or outright rejection.
There remains a more troubling question that the enthusiasm for the electric car conveniently allows us to avoid.
What if the real problem isn't the type of engine, but the number of cars?
Replacing hundreds of millions of gasoline cars one by one with electric ones perpetuates a model based on individual car ownership, with its traffic jams, confiscated space, and drained resources.
Developing public transport, cycling, and cities where one can live without a car: these are often more effective solutions, but less appealing, as they cannot be sold at dealerships.
The electric car therefore deserves its place — provided we do not mistake it for what it is not: the end of the problem.
At best, it is part of the solution.

sentences: Observe the scene, so mundane that it goes unnoticed: two strangers meet, and after the name comes almost always the same question — "so what do you do for a living?"
We respond with our profession, as if it were obvious that our job summarizes our being.
"I am a doctor," "I am a teacher," "I am unemployed": the formula is revealing.
We don't say "I work as," we say "I am."
The profession is not presented as an activity, but as an identity.
This linguistic habit says a lot about the place that work has conquered in our lives.
That this place is significant is not absurd in itself.
Work occupies the largest part of our adult days; it structures time, provides income, and connects people.
A job that has meaning, where one feels useful and competent, is one of the most solid sources of satisfaction.
No one seriously dreams of a life of total idleness: prolonged boredom is a torment, and many retirees discover this with surprise.
Wanting to banish work from our lives would be as futile as it is naive.
The problem is not work itself, but its excessive grip on the idea we have of ourselves.
Reducing a person to their job is to amputate everything else.
We are also parents, friends, neighbors, music or mountain enthusiasts, curious individuals, citizens, dreamers.
None of this appears in a job title.
A human being infinitely exceeds their function, and forgetting this impoverishes first and foremost the one who forgets it about themselves.
This confusion has a cost, which is cruelly revealed at certain turning points.
What does someone feel who loses their job, if their job was their identity?
They lose not only an income, but the ground beneath their feet, the very feeling of existing.
And what do so many people discover at retirement, after a life entirely devoted to work?
That they have neglected friendships, passions, family life — everything that was supposed to "wait," and which did not wait.
They find themselves rich in time but poor in everything else.
The cult of work sometimes presents its bill very late, and it is heavy.
It is not about preaching disengagement or despising ambition, which has its nobility.
It is about not confusing a part with the whole.
Work is a part of life; it should not devour the others, nor claim the monopoly on meaning and dignity.
Perhaps we should, to start, change our questions.
Ask a stranger, no longer "what do you do?"
", but "what are you passionate about?"
", "how are you?"
We would discover people, where we previously gathered only functions.
And we would remember, in passing, that we are not what we do to earn a living.
We are what we do with our lives.

sentences: When we say the word 'nature', our imagination immediately soars far away: tropical forests, African savannas, big cats, birds in improbable colors.
That nature, spectacular and distant, captures our attention and our worries.
In doing so, we forget another nature, infinitely closer and just as threatened: the one that teems in our gardens, parks, streets, right at our feet.
Biodiversity is not just an issue of the tropics; it also plays out right at our doorstep, and there, we can take action.
For a simple garden, a bank, an old wall harbors a world of unsuspected richness.
Dozens of species of insects, birds, hedgehogs, bats, frogs, not to mention countless plants and soil microorganisms: it's a whole living fabric, each thread depending on the others.
Bees and butterflies pollinate the flowers, which our fruits depend on; birds and bats regulate the insects; worms and fungi create the very soil.
This ordinary biodiversity, invisible from being so familiar, provides services whose importance we only realize when they are lacking.
But they are starting to be lacking.
The decline is spectacular, including — and this is the most alarming part — in our temperate regions and even in cities.
Studies on insects are staggering: in certain areas of Europe, their mass has dropped by more than three-quarters in just a few decades.
Many remember windshields covered in mosquitoes after a summer drive; younger generations no longer know this phenomenon, not by luck, but because the insects have disappeared.
The causes are piling up: chemicals, the disappearance of hedges and meadows, soil artificialization, nighttime lighting that disorients and exhausts nocturnal species.
This observation could be overwhelming.
However, it has an encouraging counterpart, specific to this local biodiversity: everyone can act on it, concretely, at their own scale.
Unlike the Amazon rainforest, where an individual can do almost nothing, the garden, balcony, and yard offer immediate grounds for action.
Let a patch of grass grow freely instead of mowing it down.
Give up pesticides.
Plant local species and nectar-rich flowers.
Install a water point, a pile of wood, a shelter.
Turn off unnecessary lights at night.
These tiny gestures, multiplied by millions of gardens, create a network of refuges that can make a real difference.
It would be naive to believe that these individual initiatives alone will suffice, without ambitious policies or profound agricultural changes; it would be just as wrong to deem them trivial.
They have a double virtue: a concrete effect on local life, and an effect on ourselves.
For by welcoming wildlife into our homes, we relearn to look at it, to become attached to it, to feel responsible for it.
We stop viewing nature as a distant backdrop to be preserved 'over there' and instead recognize it as a daily presence beside us.
Protecting biodiversity is therefore not just the concern of large protected areas and international summits.
It is also, and perhaps primarily, a matter of everyday life, starting in a patch of lawn left in peace.

sentences: Money doesn't bring happiness," says popular wisdom — before adding, with a smile, "but it contributes to it."
This proverb, with its caveat, summarizes quite well our ambiguous relationship with money: we declare it secondary while organizing our lives around it.
So, what is the reality?
The question has shifted from the realm of moralists to that of researchers, who have been studying it for decades.
Their nuanced answers are more interesting than the proverb.
The first observation is clear: the lack of money does indeed lead to unhappiness.
Poverty is nothing romantic.
It brings constant stress, closes doors, deprives of care, security, and choices.
At the lowest income levels, every material improvement translates into a significant gain in well-being.

Getting out of precariousness, being able to pay bills without anxiety, providing the essentials for one's children: here, money very concretely buys happiness, or at least the absence of a heavy misfortune.
Claiming otherwise is a luxury of those who have never lacked.
The second observation, however, is more surprising.
Once basic needs are met and reasonable comfort is achieved, the curve flattens.
Earning more continues to bring something, but less and less.
Moving from a modest income to a comfortable income changes life; moving from a comfortable income to a very high income changes it surprisingly little.
Wealthy people are, on average, hardly happier than those who are simply comfortable.
Money follows a law of diminishing returns: the first euros are worth gold, the last ones, almost nothing.
Why this exhaustion?
Two very human mechanisms explain it.
The first is habituation: we become accustomed with astonishing speed to what we possess.
The dream car, the beautiful house, the long-desired object bring intense joy — which dulls in a few months, until it becomes the normal background, barely noticed, of our lives.
The second is comparison: our satisfaction depends less on what we have than on what we have compared to others.
And there is always someone richer, so the race has no finish line.
You catch up with your neighbor only to discover a new neighbor ahead.
So what remains once comfort is achieved?
Research converges on strangely ancient answers: the quality of human relationships, health, the feeling of being useful, the time available for what we love.
Significantly, money itself makes us happier when we use it for these purposes — buying time rather than objects, giving rather than hoarding, experiencing rather than accumulating things.
It's not the amount that matters, but the use.
The popular saying deserved better than a yes or no.
Money doesn't bring happiness, but its absence brings unhappiness; it is a wonderful means, and a poor end.
Confusing it with the goal rather than the tool means chasing a horizon that recedes as you advance.
Happiness, it seems, lies elsewhere — not further down the same road, but on a completely different path.

sentences: We live in a society that adores youth and fears old age.
Advertising sells rejuvenation as an ideal, wrinkles are erased in images, and people talk about 'seniors' with a mix of awkward respect and discreet pity.
In this context, aging appears as a pure loss: loss of strength, beauty, usefulness, and future.
However, this view, so widespread that it seems obvious, is largely false — or at least incomplete.
For while the aging of the body is inevitable, the way we age is not.
Aging well is possible, and it resembles less a matter of luck than an art that is learned and cultivated throughout life.
Let's start with what is true in the fear.
Yes, the body changes and declines; it's a fact that no miracle powder will abolish.
But this decline can be considerably slowed down, and above all, it does not solely determine well-being.

One can take care of their aging body — by moving regularly, eating well, maintaining strength and balance — and these efforts postpone the onset of dependence much more effectively than one might think.
Healthy aging is not just a matter of genetic luck; it is prepared for, starting in maturity, through habits.
But the most striking thing in aging research is elsewhere.
When studying the most fulfilled elderly people, one discovers that they are not necessarily the most vigorous or healthiest.
The body is not the decisive factor for happiness in old age.

What distinguishes those who age happily are elements of another order: the richness of their social connections, the maintenance of curiosity and projects, the feeling of still being useful, the ability to find meaning at this stage of life rather than enduring it as a long wait.
Conversely, the great enemy of old age has a name, and it is not illness: it is loneliness.
Social isolation harms health as much as many physical ailments; it accelerates both physical and mental decline.
Societies and families that keep their elders in the fabric of relationships, who engage with them, listen to them, and integrate them, offer them the best remedy — and often the most neglected.

Aging, therefore, is an art that requires attention to two things: taking care of one's body without making it an obsession, and above all cultivating what does not age within us — curiosity, affection, the desire to learn and to pass on, the capacity for wonder.
Those who continue to learn, meet, take an interest, and create go through old age while keeping the essential alive.
One last truth emerges, a bit dizzying: the way we will age is not decided at seventy, but throughout our lives.
The friendships we maintain, the passions we nurture, the relationship we establish with the passing of time — all of this slowly prepares the elderly person we will become.
Aging well does not start in old age.
It starts now.

sentences: In the act of traveling, there is something irrational that our habits prevent us from seeing.
We work hard, we save money, and then we spend that money to leave a comfortable home to sleep elsewhere, often in worse conditions, at the cost of fatigue, waiting in lines, and discomfort.
We pay to lose our bearings.
From a distance, this behavior seems strange.
It must therefore respond to a deep need.
Which one?
The most immediate answer is escape.
Escaping routine, first — that dull weariness of daily life, where the days resemble each other to the point of blending together.
Travel breaks the repetition; it reintroduces the unexpected, novelty, and surprise, sensations that ordinary life, through regularity, ends up stifling.
This is no small matter: many people live an entire year for two weeks that will be etched in memory, precisely because they break the mold.
Travel is a condensed version of life, where the daily routine can sometimes feel like a diluted existence.
But to limit it to escape would be to miss the essential, because travel is not just a subtraction — it is also an addition.
By discovering other countries, we mainly discover other ways of being human: different ways of eating, greeting, working, and perceiving time, family, and happiness.
This encounter has a precious and subtle effect: it puts our own habits into perspective.
What we took for the natural order of things — our schedules, our codes, our certainties — turns out to be just one possibility among others.

Travel may be the best remedy against narrow-mindedness: it's hard to believe that your way of living is the only right one when you've seen, with your own eyes, a thousand different ways to live well.
Finally, there is a more intimate dimension that we are less willing to admit.
Travel not only makes us meet others; it also helps us meet ourselves.
Torn from our bearings, deprived of the familiar gaze that fixes us in a role, we find ourselves acting differently.
The shy person dares to speak to strangers; the hurried one takes their time; we discover ourselves to be braver, more curious, or more fragile than we thought.
Far from home, without our usual audience, we are a little more ourselves — or we glimpse another possible self.
That's why so many people return from a trip with the feeling, hard to explain, that they have changed.
Then a troubling question remains.
If travel is primarily valuable for the inner journey it produces, do we really need to go to the ends of the earth to achieve it?
Some have noted with irony: you can travel across continents without seeing anything, locked in your habits and your phone, and conversely, you can rediscover your own city with fresh eyes.
True travel may not be about kilometers, but about openness — this ability to open up, to be amazed, to let oneself be moved.
"We travel to see the world," they say.
That's true, but incomplete.
We also travel, and above all, to see ourselves in a different light, and to return — because we must return — a little different from the person who left.

sentences: There is a fact that is often cited without realizing its strangeness: no known human culture, at any time, has lived without music.
All societies sing, create rhythms, make instruments, and dance.
However, music, unlike language or tool-making, provides no obvious advantage for survival: you don't feed on a melody, and you don't defend yourself with a rhythm.
So why is this apparently useless activity so universal, and why does it exert a power over us that no other form of art can match?
This question intrigues scientists, and the answers they are beginning to outline are fascinating.
Brain imaging has first revealed a remarkable thing: there is no 'music center' in the brain.
Listening to a piece, on the contrary, activates a vast and distributed network — the areas of sound, of course, but also those of memory, movement, and especially emotions and reward.
This explains phenomena that everyone knows from experience.
Why does a song irresistibly make us want to move?
Because music activates the motor circuits, as if the body is preparing to dance even before we decide to.
Why does a melody bring back, intact, a memory from twenty years ago?
Because it is deeply linked to memory — to the point that it reaches patients who have almost forgotten everything, in whom a song from their youth suddenly revives their gaze and words.
The most mysterious aspect remains the link with emotion.
How can simple vibrations of air, organized according to certain rules, move us to tears?
One clue lies in the notion of expectation.

Our brain, without our knowing it, constantly anticipates the progression of music; and pleasure arises from the subtle interplay between what it predicts and what occurs — an expected resolution that soothes, a surprise that captivates.
The skilled composer plays on our expectations like an instrument.
Music moves us because it secretly dialogues with our mind's incessant predictions.
These discoveries have concrete implications, beyond mere curiosity.
Today, music is used in medicine — to alleviate pain, assist rehabilitation after a brain injury, and reach patients whom words can no longer reach.
Moreover, learning to play an instrument in childhood seems to leave lasting traces: studies suggest benefits for concentration, memory, and even certain language abilities.
Music is not just a pleasure; it shapes the brain that practices it.
Should we, then, explain everything?
Many mysteries still resist, and it is not certain that science will ever fully elucidate why a sequence of sounds can move us.
But there is a beautiful lesson here: understanding the mechanisms does not abolish emotion.
Knowing how a rainbow works does not diminish its beauty; knowing the circuits of music does not take away the thrill it provides.
We do not need to understand music for it to touch us.
But discovering how deeply it is embedded in our brain adds yet another reason to marvel at this old companion of humanity.

sentences: In just about fifteen years, a behavior unprecedented in human history has become so commonplace that we no longer notice it: publicly sharing moments of our lives.
A meal, a trip, a growing child, a morning thought — everything is photographed, commented on, and shared with dozens, hundreds, sometimes thousands of people.
This gesture, which our grandparents would have found incomprehensible, now seems completely natural to us.
Each post is, however, a small decision about our private life, a decision we now make dozens of times a week, almost without thinking.
It's worth reflecting on.
Let's acknowledge right away what is valuable about this sharing, as condemning it outright would be unfair and incorrect.

It helps maintain connections that distance would have once strained: following the life of a friend who moved abroad, watching the children of a distant cousin grow up, feeling close despite the miles.
It also offers the simple joy of sharing what we love, celebrating happiness, and finding a community around a passion.
Many draw support from it in difficult times.
That's no small thing.
But it would be wise to pause before posting, if only to become aware of two realities that habit obscures.
The first is permanence.
What we put online escapes us immediately and forever.
An image can be copied, saved, and resurfaced years later, in a context we hadn't anticipated — by an employer, by a stranger, by a grown child.
The carelessness of a moment can become a lasting trace.
We publish in the present; the internet, however, retains it for a future we know nothing about.
The second reality, even more delicate, concerns others.
Sharing a scene often means sharing people who haven't asked for it: friends in a group photo, and especially children.
A child cannot consent to having their face, moments, and clumsiness exposed to thousands of eyes and archived forever.
Deciding for them is to take control of a private life that is not ours.
This question, long ignored, is just beginning to be asked seriously, and it's uncertain whether the generation thus exposed will be grateful to us.
Should we conclude that we should hide everything, retreat into secrecy, ban all images?
Certainly not — that would be swinging from one extreme to another.
The issue is not to choose between showing everything and hiding everything, but to regain some discernment where automation reigns.
We should ask ourselves, before posting: does this really concern everyone?
Are others involved without having wanted to be?
Do I want this to still exist in ten years?
Moreover, in keeping certain moments to ourselves, there is not a lack of sincerity, but perhaps the opposite.
Not exposing everything means recognizing that a moment fully lived is enough in itself, that it doesn't need an audience to be real.
The most precious moments are sometimes those we do not share — those we are content to live.
In a world that pushes us to show everything, deciding to keep part of our life for ourselves and our loved ones is not hiding.
It's protecting what is most valuable.

The shops remain open.
The residents can walk in the street without cars.
The children can play.
The bus does not go through the street on Saturday.
It stops in front of the train station.
The street will open again to cars on Sunday morning.

sentences: They are being encountered more and more often, or we hear about them: these city dwellers who, one day, drop everything to move to the countryside.
A couple taking over a small farm, a family exchanging their apartment for a house with a garden, an office worker leaving their desk to raise goats.
This movement, once marginal, has grown, fueled by the desire for another life.
It deserves to be viewed without the usual two extremes: neither the naive idealization nor the sneering of those who predict failure.
The desire that drives these people is perfectly understandable, and even healthy.
Modern urban life, with its frantic pace, constant noise, overcrowding, polluted air, and nature reduced to a few lined-up trees, creates a diffuse fatigue that many suffer from without naming it.
In contrast, the countryside glimmers with everything that is lacking: space, silence, calm, direct contact with living things, a more concrete and slower relationship with time and the seasons.
Dreaming of cultivating one's garden, seeing the sky in all its vastness, hearing something other than engines is not a whim; it is responding to a real need that the city often no longer satisfies.
However, it would be naive, and sometimes cruel, to portray this return to the land as a long, peaceful dream.
The reality is harsh.

Cultivating, raising, producing requires considerable physical work, with no set hours or vacations, subject to the climate, diseases, and markets — all things that cannot be controlled and quickly remind the new country dweller how demanding nature is up close, despite its beauty from afar.
To the harshness of the work are added isolation, distance from services, and the difficulty of being accepted by a local community that was not necessarily expecting these newcomers.
Many, after a few years, give up and leave, exhausted and disillusioned.
Others, it must be said, finally find the life that suits them, and would not return for anything in the world.
The return to the land is neither a fairy tale nor a mistake: it is a difficult gamble, which succeeds for some and breaks others.
But beyond individual trajectories, this movement says something broader about our time, and perhaps that is its main interest.

In an increasingly fast, virtual, dematerialized world — where so many jobs consist of moving symbols on a screen, where food and objects arrive without knowing from where — there is a rising thirst for the concrete, the real, the tangible.
Growing what we eat, working with our hands, seeing the immediate result of our effort: this desire responds to a lack created by modernity.
Whether or not we move to the countryside, this need concerns us all.
Moreover, it is not necessary to leave everything behind to listen to it.
A planted balcony, a shared garden, a few hours of manual work, a little time devoted to slow and concrete things: everyone can, in their own way, respond to this thirst without upheaving their life.
The return to the land, taken seriously, is not just the choice of a few.
It is a signal that our time sends us, and it deserves to be listened to: that of a need for the real that progress, through abstraction, has left unanswered.

No one seriously defends the idea of producing even more waste.
However, its implementation is likely to be less straightforward than a simple awareness poster.
Installing communal composters requires space, maintenance, and residents willing to change their habits.
Repair workshops, on the other hand, require facilities, trained volunteers, and real visibility.
Environmental organizations therefore welcome the overall direction while calling for clearer resources.
They fear that the wealthier municipalities will progress quickly, while others will remain with good intentions.
Several rural mayors also raise the issue of transportation: in a village, getting to a repair workshop may require a car.

The city hall is also trying to take action.

sentences: The city hall is launching a consultation to choose the next streets to green.
Residents can indicate the places to plant trees, create strips of land, or install larger planters.
The initiative addresses a well-identified urgency: during heat waves, the concrete streets become stifling.
Trees provide shade, retain some rainwater, and make public spaces more pleasant.
But planting in the city is never just a decorative gesture.
It requires relocating utilities, sometimes removing parking spaces, and accepting that the street will change in use.
That's where the debate begins.
Some residents are asking for more trees in front of schools and bus stops.
Others fear losing parking spaces for their cars or seeing the sidewalks cluttered.
Merchants, for their part, want to be involved in the choice of streets, as the work can disrupt their business.
The consultation won't resolve all tensions, but it can make the trade-offs more visible.
Adapting the city to the climate involves concrete choices, sometimes modest, rarely neutral.

sentences: At nineteen, I found my first job: a sales assistant in a small bookstore.
On the first day, I was very nervous.
I didn't know anyone and I wasn't exactly sure what my tasks were.
My boss, Madame Leroy, welcomed me with a big smile.
"Don't worry," she said to me.
Everyone starts somewhere.
" She introduced me to my two colleagues, Karim and Julie, who had been working in the bookstore for several years.
At first, my tasks were simple: organizing the books, helping customers, and managing the cash register.
Karim patiently explained everything to me.
When I made a mistake, he didn't make fun of me; he showed me how to do better.
The job wasn't always easy.
Some days, there were a lot of customers and I came home tired.
But I learned something new every week, and little by little, I gained confidence.
At the end of the month, I received my first paycheck.
It wasn't much, but I was proud: it was my money, earned through my work.
I invited my colleagues for a coffee to thank them.
Today, I no longer work in that bookstore.
But I will never forget that first job.
I learned an important thing there: a good boss and kind colleagues make all the difference.

sentences: Before getting a job, you often have to go through a stressful step: the job interview.
I had my first interview two years ago, and I still remember my hands shaking.
To apply, I had sent my resume and a cover letter.
A few days later, the company called me to offer a meeting.
I was happy, but also very worried.
How should I introduce myself?
What should I say?
What should I wear?
A friend who had already hired people gave me some advice.
"The boss isn't looking for someone perfect," he explained to me.
He wants to know if you are motivated, honest, and if you will work well with your future colleagues.
On the day of the interview, I arrived early.
The recruiter asked me a lot of questions: about my studies, my skills, my strengths, and my weaknesses.
The hardest one was: "Why do you want this position?"
I answered honestly, in my own words.
At the end, she asked me if I had any questions.
I had prepared two; this shows that you are really interested in the job.
A week later, good news: I got hired!
Since then, I have had other interviews, and I still feel a bit nervous.
But I understood that it’s not an exam: it’s simply a conversation between two people who are trying to get to know each other.

sentences: We spend about a third of our lives sleeping.
Yet, many people sleep poorly and wake up tired.
Sleep is important: it's during the night that the body rests and regains its energy.
When we don't sleep enough, everything becomes more difficult.
We have trouble concentrating, we're in a bad mood, and even the smallest task requires a lot of effort.
Fatigue builds up day after day.
So, how can we sleep better?
There are a few simple habits.
First, it's better to go to bed and wake up at the same time, even on weekends.
The body likes regularity.
Next, we need to prepare for the night.
In the evening, we avoid coffee and screens, because the light from the phone prevents the brain from getting ready for sleep.
A quiet, slightly cool, and dark room helps a lot.
Finally, we shouldn't stay in bed when we can't sleep.
If sleep doesn't come after twenty minutes, it's better to get up, read a few pages, and then go back to bed.
Sleeping well is not a luxury: it's a necessity.
A good night gives energy for the whole day.
Taking care of your sleep means taking care of everything else.

sentences: In the past, a small job was often a summer job for a student.
Today, more and more adults are living solely from these small jobs.
This is called 'the gig economy.'
What is it about?
Delivering meals by bike, walking dogs, driving passengers, cleaning for individuals: these are simple tasks that are often found through an app on your phone.
There's no need to go through a long interview or send a resume: you sign up, and you start working.
The big advantage is freedom.
You don't have a boss watching every minute.
You choose your hours: you can work in the morning, in the evening, or only on weekends.
For a parent or a student, this flexibility is valuable.
You are, in a way, your own boss.
But there is a price to pay.
These jobs are often precarious: the pay is not guaranteed, and it changes from week to week.
There is no stable contract, no security in case of illness.
When you are self-employed, no one takes care of you.
The gig economy therefore raises a difficult question for the future of work.
Should we prefer freedom and flexibility, or the security of a traditional job?
The answer is not simple.
What is certain is that the world of work is changing quickly, and these small jobs are no longer so small.

sentences: Eating healthily is complicated and expensive.
This idea is very common, but it's false.
In reality, eating well relies on a few simple habits, and it gives the body the energy it needs.
The first rule is easy: eat more vegetables and fruits.
They are full of vitamins, they are inexpensive, especially when in season, and they fill you up without tiring the body.
In every meal, half of the plate should be vegetables.
The second rule concerns sugar.
Today, we eat way too much sugar, often without realizing it: in sodas, cakes, but also in products that don't taste sweet.
Sugar gives a quick burst of energy, followed by a big crash an hour later.
It's better to avoid it and drink water.
The third rule is perhaps the most important: cook for yourself.
When you prepare your meal, you know what you're eating.
You don't need to be a great chef: a soup, a salad, a pasta dish with vegetables, it's simple and balanced.
Eating healthily doesn't mean depriving yourself of everything.
You can treat yourself from time to time.
The important thing is the daily habit.
The body, like a car, works better with good fuel.

sentences: To stay healthy, you need to move.
But be careful: that doesn't mean running a marathon or spending hours in a gym.
Moving a little every day is already enough to do a lot of good for the body.
The problem with modern life is that we sit all day: sitting at work, sitting in the car, sitting in front of the television.
However, the human body is not made for immobility.
Without exercise, the muscles weaken and energy decreases.
The good news is that a little regular effort is better than a big effort now and then.
Walking for twenty minutes a day, taking the stairs instead of the elevator, getting off the bus one stop earlier: these small habits make a real difference.
The heart works, the muscles wake up, and you feel fitter.
Moving is not only good for the body; it's also good for your mood.
After a walk, even a short one, you often feel calmer and in a better mood.
Mental fatigue from the day decreases.
The secret is to choose an activity you enjoy: walking, dancing, cycling, gardening.
When an activity is a pleasure, you repeat it effortlessly.
And it's regularity, more than intensity, that keeps the body healthy for life.

sentences: Stress is a part of modern life.
Work, money, family, world news: there are plenty of reasons to feel under pressure.
A little stress is normal, and even useful.
But too much stress, for too long, wears out the body and mind.
When we are stressed, the body reacts: the heart beats faster, the muscles tense up, and we sleep poorly.
We become irritable and have less energy.
If this state lasts, it can harm our health.
It is therefore important to learn to manage stress.
The first thing to do is simple: breathe.
When we feel overwhelmed, a few slow, deep breaths already calm the body.
Closing our eyes, inhaling gently, exhaling slowly: it costs nothing and really helps.
We also need to know how to take breaks.
We often believe that we have to work without stopping to be effective.
That's false.
A short break to walk, drink tea, or look out the window allows the mind to relax and unwind.
Finally, stress and sleep are linked.
A tired person handles pressure less well.
Protecting our nights is also about protecting our calm.
We cannot eliminate all the stress from our lives.
But we can learn to live better with it by listening to our bodies and giving ourselves a few real moments of calm each day.

The doctor asks questions, examines the body, and tries to understand the cause of the problem.
It's important to be honest and explain everything, even the details that seem embarrassing.
After the examination, the doctor explains what we have and suggests a treatment.
Often, he gives a prescription: a list of medications to buy at the pharmacy.
It's important to follow his advice carefully and to take the treatment until the end, even when we feel better, to truly heal.
But the role of the doctor is not just to treat the sick.
It is also to help them stay healthy.
This is what we call prevention.
A regular visit allows us to spot a problem before it becomes serious.
"An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure," says the proverb, and this is particularly true for health.
Taking care of your body also means accepting to consult, without waiting until the last moment.
The doctor is not an enemy: he is an ally for a longer and healthier life.

sentences: The word 'budget' doesn't inspire enthusiasm.
It brings to mind boring spreadsheets, calculations, and the idea of deprivation.
However, creating a budget isn't a punishment: it's one of the best ways to live more peacefully with your money.
The principle is simple.
A budget is a comparison between what comes in and what goes out: on one side, the income, meaning the money you earn; on the other side, the expenses, meaning the money you spend.
As long as you don't do this calculation, you're moving forward a bit blindly.
The first step is to write down, for a month, absolutely all your expenses.
The exercise is often a surprise.
You discover that the big expenses — rent, bills — aren't the only ones that weigh heavily.
It's mainly the small daily expenses, when added up, that make the money disappear: a coffee here, a purchase there, a forgotten subscription.
Once you have these numbers in front of you, you can take action.
It's not about cutting everything out, but about making choices.
What do I really want to spend on?
What doesn't bring me any pleasure, really?
Managing your money means deciding for yourself rather than enduring the end of the month.
A good budget also includes a portion for saving, even if it's small.
Setting aside a little each month, even before spending, changes everything.
This reserve allows you to handle an unexpected event — a broken appliance, a surprise bill — without panicking or going into debt.
It would be naive to think that a budget solves all problems: when income is too low, no spreadsheet is enough.
But for most people, the real problem isn't earning more; it's knowing where the money goes.
And this clarity, curiously, doesn't make life sadder.
It brings something valuable: peace of mind.

sentences: Buy now, pay later.
This promise is everywhere: in stores, online, at the end of our online purchases.
Consumer credit has made almost everything immediately accessible, without having to wait to save up.
It's convenient, sometimes useful, but it's also a trap that many people fall into.
The principle of credit is simple: a bank or a store lends you money for a purchase, and you pay it back little by little, each month.
The problem is that this money isn't free.
In exchange for the loan, you have to pay interest.
In other words, the item bought on credit ends up costing more — sometimes much more — than its displayed price.
The danger comes from the ease of it.
Since you don't pay right away, you feel like the expense is small: "only thirty euros a month."
But these small monthly payments add up.
You take out a loan for a sofa, another for a phone, another for a vacation, and soon a large part of your salary goes each month to repayments.
That's how you end up in debt without even realizing it.
Credit isn't bad in itself.
Borrowing can make sense for an important and lasting project, like housing, or in case of a real necessity.
But you should always ask yourself the same question before signing: am I borrowing for a real need, or just because I don't have the patience to save?
The wisest rule can be summed up in one sentence: never go into debt for a fleeting pleasure.
The sofa will be old long before the debt is paid off, and you'll continue to pay for an item you no longer enjoy.
In the face of advertising that pushes you to consume right away, the old habit of waiting and saving is often the most rewarding — and the most peaceful.

sentences: On Wednesday afternoon, it was raining heavily.
My son Léo was watching the rain through the window, a bit disappointed: no football today.
Suddenly, he asked me, "Dad, where does all this water come from?" I proposed a deal: I'll explain it to you, and then we'll make crepes.
The story of rain is a great journey.
It starts far from here, at the sea.
The sun heats the water of the sea, lakes, and rivers.
When the water gets hot, some of it rises into the air, invisible.
This invisible water is called steam.
"Like above the pot?" Léo asked.
Exactly!
The steam rises high into the sky.
Up there, it's cold.
So the steam turns into tiny drops.
Millions of drops gather and form...
"A cloud!" Léo shouted.
Well done!
The wind pushes the clouds over the cities and mountains.
The drops grow larger, the cloud becomes gray and heavy.
And when it is too heavy, the drops fall.
That's the rain.
Then, the rainwater enters the ground, finds the rivers, and the rivers return to the sea.
And it all starts again!
This journey is called the water cycle.
Léo looked at the rain with new eyes.
"So the rain is the sea that travels."
And now, the crepes.
I promise, it's a promise.

sentences: Why learn dates, poems, and multiplication tables when all of that can be found in three seconds in our pocket? This argument is heard everywhere, and it's not foolish.
It even reflects a valid intuition of our time: at a moment when an infinite library fits in a phone, human memory seems to have lost its job.
However, upon closer examination, this quick conclusion seems to rest on a deep misunderstanding of what it means to think.
First, let's acknowledge what is true about the argument.
It would be absurd to make a student memorize a directory or a list that a machine can instantly retrieve.

For a long time, schools have confused instruction with recitation, and they were partly right to move away from that to develop analysis, critical thinking, and the ability to search for and sort information.
A brain turned into a simple hard drive is a waste; on this point, opponents of 'learning by heart' have made a valid point.
But they make a crucial confusion: they believe that one can think without knowing anything, think in a vacuum, reason about content that one would go and look for as needed.
But that is false, and cognitive sciences clearly confirm it.
To understand new information, one must attach it to knowledge already present in the mind.
Read an article on a subject you know nothing about: the words flow by, but nothing sticks, due to a lack of hooks to hang the meaning on.
In contrast, the expert reads the same text and grasps every nuance because their internal knowledge provides the context.
Stored knowledge is not the enemy of reflection: it is its condition.
We do not think despite what we know; we think with it.
There’s more.
Constantly consulting a screen has a hidden cost.

Every interruption to check a piece of information breaks the thread of reasoning; the mind that has to search for everything never has enough materials available to establish quick links, those sudden connections from which ideas emerge.
The scholar who has a thousand facts from their field 'in mind' sees connections invisible to someone who has to look for them one by one.
Creativity feeds on what is immediately there, in the mind, ready to combine.
Finally, there’s what the utilitarian argument completely overlooks: some knowledge serves no purpose, and that is precisely its value.
A poem learned in childhood accompanies us throughout life, returning on a night of sadness or happiness, connecting us to those who knew it before us.
Knowledge is not just a tool; it is also companionship, shared culture, a part of ourselves that no screen will ever replace.
The right question is therefore not 'memory or reflection?' — a false opposition — but 'what is worth knowing by heart?'.
To this question, each era must respond anew.
Ours would be wrong to answer 'nothing'.

sentences: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day. You know the saying; your parents already knew it.
It has the solidity of a proverb and the authority of a law.
Here's a tricky question: where does it come from?
Partly...
from advertisements by cereal manufacturers in the early twentieth century.
The most effective slogans end up sounding like science.
That doesn't mean the saying is false — but it invites us to take a closer look.
What does research say, exactly?
More nuanced things than the proverb.
Yes, a good breakfast has real benefits, especially for certain people.
After a night of fasting, the body and brain appreciate an energy boost.
For children and adolescents, studies are quite clear: those who eat breakfast in the morning concentrate better in class during the morning.
For a schoolchild, skipping breakfast is rarely a good idea.
But for adults, the obligation doesn't hold.
Contrary to popular belief, skipping breakfast doesn't make you gain weight and doesn't 'block' your metabolism: serious studies have found no catastrophic effects.
Millions of people simply aren't hungry in the morning, and forcing them to eat makes no sense.
The body generally knows what it's doing.
The real rule is disappointingly simple: if you're hungry in the morning, eat; if not, don't.
The most interesting question isn't actually 'should we have breakfast?' but 'what should we put on our plate?'.
Because not all breakfasts are equal, and the most common is probably the worst: sugary cereals, fruit juice, white bread, and jam.
A meal almost entirely made up of sugar.
It causes a quick energy spike...
followed by a drop just as quick.
It's the famous 'mid-morning slump' at ten-thirty, with cravings and concentration down.
Your sugary breakfast has betrayed you.
The solution is known: proteins and fibers.
An egg, plain yogurt, cheese, whole grain bread, a handful of nuts, a whole fruit rather than juice.
This type of meal releases its energy slowly and keeps you going until lunch, without roller coasters.
So, the most important meal of the day?
Let's say instead: a meal like any other — neither sacred nor mandatory, but deserving better than sugary boxed products.
The most important thing, after all, might simply be to start the day without lying to yourself about what's in the bowl.

sentences: There is something in laughter that should surprise us even more.
This is a behavior shared by all the peoples of the Earth, without exception, regardless of language and culture.
A behavior present in infants long before they can speak, and one that we also find in our primate cousins.
A behavior, above all, that we do not control: we cannot laugh on command, and we struggle to stop laughing when we get the giggles.
Laughter bursts out of us, almost despite ourselves.
What is this thing that is so human and so little controlled?
The first surprise, when we study it, is that laughter has very little to do with humor.
We imagine it triggered by jokes; observation tells a different story.
By listening to ordinary conversations, researchers found that the vast majority of laughs do not follow any joke.
They punctuate mundane phrases, accompany reunions, emphasize agreement, and fill silences.
We laugh much more at 'there you are at last!' than at the best punchline.
Laughter is not primarily a reaction to something funny; it is a social signal.
This is its deepest key: laughter is made for others.
One fact proves it better than anything else: we laugh much more in company than when we are alone.
In front of the same movie, alone, we smile; surrounded by friends, we burst out laughing.
Laughter is up to thirty times more frequent in groups.
It is not a judgment on a funny situation, but a bond woven between people.
Laughing together is a way of saying, without a word: we share the same perspective, we are on the same side, you are one of us.
Long before language, our ancestors likely already had this means of sealing group belonging.
This social function also explains the more troubling laughs that the idealized view often conveniently forgets.
We laugh to include, but also, sometimes, to exclude: mocking laughter designates those who are outside the circle.
We laugh out of embarrassment, out of nervousness, in moments that are far from cheerful.
Laughter is not always innocent; it is a powerful relational tool, capable of both the best and the cruelest.
On the body, its effects are real, though sometimes exaggerated by the trend of 'laughter as therapy.'
Laughter relaxes muscles, releases tension, and provides temporary well-being.
To see it as a miracle cure would be naive; to consider it negligible would be foolish.
Let’s say it feels good, without claiming that it heals.
Many questions remain open, and laughter retains a part of mystery that science has not dispelled.
But perhaps it is not necessary to explain everything.
Knowing that this strange sound that escapes us is, at its core, one of our oldest ways of saying 'we are together' is enough to see it differently.
The next time you laugh with someone, think about it for a moment: you are not just reacting to something funny.
You are, unknowingly, performing a gesture of connection as old as humanity.

sentences: Few questions cause as much anxiety and guilt among parents as the issue of screens.
Should they be banned?
Should they be limited?
From what age, and for how long?
Between alarmist articles that describe a generation in peril and those who shrug it off by reminding us that 'every generation demonizes its novelty,' parents struggle to find their way.
Let's try to clarify things by separating what research establishes from what it does not say.
On one point, the data is solid: for very young children, before the age of two or three, excessive screen time is harmful.
At this age, the brain develops through interaction with the real world and with people: manipulating objects, hearing speech, exchanging glances and smiles.
Time spent in front of a screen is time taken away from these irreplaceable experiences, and several studies link early excessive exposure to delays in language and concentration.
For toddlers, the caution in recommendations — as little as possible — is based on solid grounds.
But as soon as we move past early childhood, the question becomes murky, and this is where public debate often goes wrong.
Because 'screens' do not exist: there are only radically different uses.

Putting in the same category a child who passively watches endless videos, another who calls their grandparents, a third who learns to code or draws on a tablet, and a fourth who plays online with friends makes no sense.
The 'screen time' counter, so convenient, is a crude measure that adds together incomparable things.
The real question is not just how much time, but what, at what age, and with whom.
This last point — with whom — is crucial and too often overlooked.
The same program watched alone in silence, or watched with an adult who comments, explains, and extends the conversation, does not have the same effect at all.
In the latter case, the screen becomes a medium for exchange rather than a substitute for relationships.
It's not the object that matters most; it's what happens around it.
We must also place the screen within the context of a child's entire life.
The problem is not so much what the screen provides but what it replaces when it takes up too much space: shortened sleep, free play, fertile boredom, physical activity, and friendships in person.
A child who reads, runs, plays, sleeps well, and sees friends can watch a screen without harm; danger arises when the screen pushes everything else out.
Finally, example weighs more than rules.
It's hard to convince a teenager to look up from their phone when their parents have their noses in theirs at the table.
Children imitate what we do, not what we say.
The reasonable response is therefore neither panic nor indifference, but attention.
Not just 'how many hours?' as the only compass, but 'what content, at what age, replacing what, and under whose gaze?'.
It's more demanding than a simple rule.
It's also much fairer.

sentences: We often imagine that saving means depriving oneself: giving up pleasures, counting every penny, and leading a sad life.
This is a mistake.
The people who save most effectively are not necessarily the stingiest; they are the ones who know how to distinguish between a desire and a need.
The difference seems obvious, but it isn't in real life.
A need is what is necessary: having a place to live, eating, getting around.
A desire is what would feel good in the moment: the latest phone, one more piece of clothing, an item seen in an advertisement.
The problem is that modern marketing constantly works to turn our desires into needs.
It convinces us that we cannot live without what we didn't even know we needed yesterday.
Resisting this trap doesn't require iron willpower, but a few simple habits.
The most effective one is to wait.
When faced with a desire to buy, we give ourselves a few days before deciding.
Very often, the desire disappears on its own: we had confused a fleeting wish with a real need.
The money saved this way does not represent any sacrifice, since we don't regret what we didn't buy.
Another key is to ask the right question.
Not 'Can I afford it?', but 'What value will this purchase really bring me?'.
Some expenses, even significant ones, enrich life: a trip, a book, a shared meal.
Others, once the excitement has faded, leave just one more object in a closet.
Saving intelligently, therefore, is not about saying no to everything.
It's about saying yes to what matters and no to what doesn't.
Seen this way, saving stops being a deprivation and becomes a form of freedom: the freedom to no longer spend by reflex and to keep our money for what truly has value for us.

sentences: For ten years, Thomas worked the same job: an accountant in a large company.
The salary was good, the job was stable, but he was bored.
Every day, the same tasks, the same routine.
One morning, he realized that he no longer wanted to get up to go to work.
Changing careers after thirty-five is not easy.
It's even a real risk.
Thomas was earning a good living; by changing, he might earn less, at least at first.
"You're crazy," some colleagues told him.
But others encouraged him: "At least you're trying."
Thomas had dreamed for a long time of working with wood.
So he decided to retrain and become a carpenter.
To do this, he took a course for a year.
Going back to school at his age, with younger students, required courage.
But he dared.
Today, Thomas earns a little less money than before, and his days are more physically tiring.
Yet, he has never been so happy.
In the evening, he looks at the furniture he has made with his own hands, and he feels a real pride.
Of course, retraining is not possible for everyone, and it doesn't always succeed.
But Thomas's story raises a good question: is it better to have a comfortable job that bores us, or a more challenging job that has meaning for us?

sentences: The objection arises with every spectacular launch, with every announcement of a mission to Mars, and it has the force of obviousness: how can we justify spending fortunes on space exploration when so many problems remain unsolved on Earth?
Hunger, poverty, illness, climate: the list of urgent issues on Earth is long, and spending billions to send robots to contemplate distant rocks may seem, at best, a whim, and at worst, an indecency.
The argument deserves to be taken seriously — and it is by taking it seriously that we discover it is weaker than it appears.
The first response, the most down-to-earth: space exploration is not money thrown into the void.
A considerable part of the technologies that equip our daily lives has originated, directly or indirectly, from space research.

The weather forecasts that save lives, the location systems that guide our movements, a host of advances in medicine, materials, and miniaturized electronics: all these applications stem from the efforts made to go into space.
The history of technology teaches a constant lesson: fundamental research, seemingly useless, almost always leads to unforeseen and valuable applications.
Giving up exploration in the name of immediate utility means depriving ourselves of future utilities that we cannot foresee.
The second response, less expected: space teaches us to know Earth.

It is from space that we monitor the climate, the state of forests, the melting of ice, the health of oceans; without satellites, our understanding of climate change — this very urgency that is opposed to space — would be infinitely poorer.
It is also from space that humanity saw, for the first time, its entire planet: a small blue and fragile marble, suspended in the dark, with no visible borders.
This image, brought back by the first missions, has permanently changed our view of ourselves and nurtured the emerging ecological awareness.
Paradoxically, moving away from Earth has taught us to love and protect it.
There remains a third dimension, harder to quantify, and yet perhaps the most important.

Seeking to know where we come from, whether there is life elsewhere, what this universe we are part of is: this desire to understand is not a superfluous luxury, it is one of the deepest traits of our humanity.
It is this desire that drove our ancestors to cross oceans, to map continents, to uncover the secrets of the atom and of life.

A humanity that would give up exploration, that would completely retreat into managing its immediate problems, would lose something essential — that part of dream and curiosity without which none of the great advances would have taken place.
Should we then accept everything in the name of space?
No, and the objection retains its share of truth as a safeguard.
The billionaires who indulge in orbital rides, the militarization of space, the race to plant flags for mere glory: all of this is legitimately critiquable.
The question is not 'space, yes or no?', but 'what space, for what purpose, and at what cost?'.
An exploration in service of knowledge and the common good has nothing to do with the space tourism of the very rich.
Space will not solve hunger or poverty, and those who oppose it to urgent earthly issues are right to refuse that it serves as an escape.
But if well designed, it is not the enemy of these causes: it can sometimes be an unexpected ally.
Continuing to look up at the sky, as long as we never forget the Earth beneath our feet, is not an escape.
It is faithful to what we have always been: a species that, to move forward, has always needed a horizon.

sentences: Climate change is everywhere in the news, often amidst passionate debates and complicated figures.
However, the basic mechanism is surprisingly simple, and understanding it helps to move beyond slogans.
Let's try to explain it calmly, without jargon.
It all starts with a natural phenomenon that is, in fact, essential: the greenhouse effect.
Around the Earth, the atmosphere contains certain gases that trap some of the sun's heat, like a blanket.
Without them, the planet would be frozen and life impossible.
So the problem is not the greenhouse effect itself, but its intensity.
For the past two centuries, human activity has been adding enormous quantities of these gases to the atmosphere.
By burning coal, oil, and gas to produce energy, we release carbon dioxide emissions.
The blanket thickens, trapping more heat, and the average temperature of the planet rises.
This is what we call global warming.
An increase of one or two degrees may seem tiny; after all, the temperature changes much more than that between morning and afternoon.
But here we are talking about a global average, and at this scale, a few degrees are enough to upset everything: melting ice, rising sea levels, droughts, and more violent storms.
The climate is not just becoming 'warmer'; it is becoming more unstable.
Regarding the causes, the scientific community is now almost unanimous: this rapid warming is indeed of human origin.
The serious debate is no longer about 'if', but about 'how much' and what we decide to do.
Understanding this alone doesn't solve anything, and it can even be overwhelming given the scale of the problem.
But it is a necessary starting point.
We cannot act intelligently in the face of a threat we do not understand.
And the good news is that the same activities that caused the problem can, if transformed, be part of the solution.

sentences: There is a subject that people are less willing to talk about than politics, religion, or even their private lives: money.
Asking someone how much they earn is considered rude in many cultures.
Money is the last great taboo.
But is this silence really a good thing?
The reasons for this discomfort are old and deep.
Talking about one's salary risks being judged: if you're too rich, you seem pretentious; if you're too poor, you feel ashamed.
It also exposes you to comparison, that subtle poison that turns neighbors into rivals.
So, out of caution, people prefer to remain silent, and this discretion is passed down from generation to generation as a rule of good manners.
However, this taboo has a cost, and it doesn't always benefit those who stay silent.
In the workplace, for example, silence about salaries mainly benefits employers: when no one knows what others earn, it becomes harder to notice injustice or negotiate.
Transparency, on the other hand, allows for comparison and sometimes corrects differences that have no reason to exist.
Silence also weighs heavily in private life.
How many couples avoid the topic until the day a hidden debt or secret spending causes a real crisis?
How many families tear apart, upon the death of a loved one, for having never calmly addressed these issues?
Not talking about money doesn't make money problems disappear; it simply allows them to grow in the shadows.
Of course, it's not about flaunting your bank account at the first meeting.
But it would be healthy to be able to talk about money more freely with those who matter: your family, your partner, your close colleagues.
Bringing up the subject honestly requires a bit of courage and a lot of trust.
In return, it avoids many misunderstandings, and often many injustices.
The real taboo, in the end, may not be money itself, but the fear of what it reveals about us.

sentences: We spend a large part of our lives exchanging time for money: this is, at its core, the very definition of work.
We sell our hours, our days, our years, in exchange for a salary.
But we often forget that this exchange can also work the other way: money, when used wisely, allows us to buy back time.
And perhaps that is its greatest power.
Let's think about what we are really buying when we spend.
An object, often; but sometimes something much more valuable.

Paying someone to clean, taking a more expensive but faster train, buying a ready-made meal on a tired evening: in all these cases, we are not really paying for a thing, we are paying for time and energy saved.
Research on happiness confirms this: spending money to gain time makes us, on average, happier than spending the same amount on objects.
Yet, we rarely make this calculation.
We accept long journeys to save a few euros, we spend hours repairing things ourselves that a professional would fix in an instant, out of principle or habit.
We treat our money with care and our time with neglect — while time, in contrast, can never be refunded.
You can always regain lost money; a lost day is lost forever.
This does not mean that we should pay for everything to do nothing, nor that free time is always better spent than work.
Repairing an object yourself can be a pleasure; chosen slowness has its value.
The real question is not 'what is the price?', but 'what does this money buy me in terms of time and peace of mind, and what will I do with that time?'.
Learning to see money as a means to buy time, and not just things, changes the way we spend it.
We stop chasing after the latest trendy item to simply ask ourselves: what do I need to live the days I want to live?
To this question, money is no longer a goal, but a tool — and the time it frees up becomes true wealth.

sentences: Each inhabitant of a wealthy country throws away, on average, nearly half a ton of waste per year.
Put together, this waste forms an invisible mountain that we prefer not to look at: once the trash is taken out, the problem seems to disappear.
But it doesn't disappear; it just moves.
Where does our waste go?
Some of it is burned, which in turn produces emissions.
Another part ends up in enormous landfills, where certain materials, like plastic, will take centuries to decompose.
Finally, a portion is recycled — but much less than we think.
Sorting our waste is a useful gesture, and we must continue to do it; but recycling has its limits.
It costs energy, and many items simply cannot be recycled.
That's why specialists remind us of an uncomfortable truth: the best waste is the one we don't produce.
Before recycling, we should primarily reduce.
However, our way of life is going in the opposite direction.
We consume more and more items, often packaged multiple times, often designed to be thrown away quickly.
Waste is not an accident of the system; it is part of it.
What can we do, concretely?
On an individual scale, a few habits significantly reduce our waste: refusing unnecessary packaging, buying in bulk, repairing instead of replacing, avoiding single-use items.
These actions alone will not save the planet — we shouldn't fool ourselves.
But they change our perspective, and they send a signal.
For the real lever is broader.
It is the companies that decide on packaging, and the governments that set the rules.
A citizen who reduces their waste is also a consumer and a voter who pushes, in their own way, in the right direction.
The mountain of our waste is not a fatality: it is the result of billions of small decisions, and these decisions can change.

sentences: We use energy at every moment, almost without thinking about it: to light our homes, to heat ourselves, to move around, and to power our devices.
All it takes is to press a button.
But behind this ordinary action lies an essential, and rarely asked, question: where does this energy actually come from?
Because not all sources are equal, far from it.
For two centuries, most of our energy has come from fossil fuels: coal, oil, and gas.
They have a huge advantage — they are powerful and easy to use — but a major drawback: burning them releases enormous gas emissions, which are the main contributors to global warming.
Moreover, these resources are not infinite; one day, they will run out.
In the face of this dual problem, renewable energies are developing.
As their name suggests, they do not run out: solar energy captures sunlight, wind energy uses the wind, and others harness the water from rivers.
Their great merit is that they produce energy with almost no pollution.
Their limitations are real too: the sun does not shine at night, the wind does not always blow, and we must therefore learn to store this energy and balance the grid.
The transition from one model to another is one of the greatest challenges of our time.
It is complicated, costly, and no one claims it will be easy.
Changing the way an entire country produces its energy does not happen in just a few years.
This question goes far beyond our individual actions: turning off a light is a good habit, but the key decisions are made at the level of countries and companies, in the choices they make today.
However, understanding where our energy comes from is not useless.
An informed citizen makes better choices, supports better decisions, and stops believing that electricity comes, as if by magic, from the wall socket.
Behind every switch, there is a societal choice.

sentences: When we think about protecting the environment, we often imagine sorting waste or renewable energy.
We forget a more discreet but essential cause: the way we consume.
Because every item we buy requires energy, water, and raw materials to be made, long before it reaches our hands.
Reducing our consumption is therefore one of the most effective actions — and one of the most difficult.
The problem has a name: overconsumption.
We are buying more than ever, often items designed not to last.

A piece of clothing worn three times and then forgotten, a device that breaks down just after the warranty and can't be repaired, a phone replaced even though the old one was still working: this disposable model has become the norm.
It enriches the industry, but it depletes the planet and fills our landfills.
Consuming differently doesn't mean buying nothing, which would be unrealistic.
It means buying better and less.
A few simple principles are enough to change things.
First, ask yourself if you really need the item before buying it.
Then, prioritize quality: a solid and repairable item costs more upfront, but lasts for years, and is therefore cheaper in the long run — for us as well as for the environment.
Finally, rediscover second-hand: buying used is giving a second life to an item that already exists, without making a new one.
However, this change faces a powerful force: marketing, which tirelessly works to make us desire new things.
Fashion itself is based on this logic: what was perfect last year suddenly becomes 'outdated.'
Resisting this pressure requires a certain freedom of mind — the freedom not to let advertising dictate our needs.
Consuming more responsibly is not a sacrifice, and it is also not the only solution to the ecological problem.
But it is a choice that makes sense, and it has an unexpected advantage: it also lightens our lives.
Fewer items mean less clutter, less spending, and fewer things to organize and maintain.
By taking care of the planet, we often end up taking care of ourselves.

sentences: Sorting waste, turning off the light when leaving a room, taking the bike instead of the car: we are often told that every little action counts for the planet.
But is that really true?
In the face of a problem as immense as climate change, are our individual efforts not insignificant?
The question is uncomfortable, and it deserves more than a simple answer.
Let's start with the objection, because it is serious.
If we add up all the emissions in the world, the portion that each individual can reduce through their daily actions is tiny.
While one person carefully saves water, a single factory, a single flight, or a single political decision can instantly negate the efforts of millions.
Worse still: by focusing on small actions, we risk forgetting what really matters.
Some large companies are actually quite happy to promote this idea, as it shifts the responsibility onto the consumer and leaves them off the hook.
Should we conclude that our actions are useless?
That would be jumping to conclusions, and it would be dangerous.
First, because these actions have a value that is not just mathematical.
Someone who changes their habits also changes their perspective: they become more attentive, more consistent, and harder to convince that 'nothing can be done.'
Next, because behaviors are contagious.
A habit, when it spreads, ends up changing the norms of an entire society, and then the decisions of those who govern us.
The real trap would be to choose between the two.

Pitting individual action against collective action is a false choice, and a choice that paralyzes: those who expect everything from governments do nothing themselves, and those who rely solely on small actions become discouraged when they discover their limits.
Yet the two feed off each other.
A citizen who acts in their life is also the one who votes, who talks to those around them, and who pushes companies and states to take action.
So, does one single action suffice?
No, obviously.
But framing the question this way is already a mistake.
The individual action was never meant to be enough; it is a starting point, not an end.
It matters not because it saves the planet on its own, but because it keeps us moving, and because nothing great, on a collective scale, has ever started without individuals deciding to act.

I waited.

A man was withdrawing money.

She put the box on a scale.

Two or three weeks was too long for the birthday.

In the end, I chose express.

Five centimeters?
Fifteen?

I almost fell asleep.
Then, she started cutting.
I watched the hair fall to the floor.
A lot of hair.

very nice, thank you."

But in the evening, my husband said: "You look younger!"
