sentences: On Tuesday, at the supermarket, my bank card didn't work.
I had a full cart and there were four people behind me.
The cashier tried twice.
"Card declined," said the machine.
I was very embarrassed.
Fortunately, I had some cash in my bag.
I was able to pay.
But I didn't understand why.
I was sure I had money in my account.
In the evening, I checked online.
My account was fine.
So what was the problem?
I called my bank.
I waited fifteen minutes with horrible music.
Then a voice said: "All our lines are busy.
Please call back later." And it hung up!
I was annoyed.
The next morning, I went straight to the agency.
I waited ten minutes, then an advisor saw me.
I explained the problem to him.
He looked at his computer for a minute.
"Ah, I see.
Your card expired at the end of last month.
We sent you a new card three weeks ago."
A new card?
I hadn't received anything.
Then I thought and understood.
There was an envelope from the bank on my desk at home.
I had never opened it.
The advisor smiled.
"It happens often, you know."
In the evening, I opened the envelope.
My new card was inside.
Last week, I forgot my umbrella on the tram.

On Thursday morning, I went there.
The office was small.
There was no one there, except for an employee behind a counter.
"Hello, I lost an umbrella on the tram Monday evening."
"Which line?"
"Line B."
He wrote something down, then he disappeared into a room behind him.
While he was searching, I looked through the open door.
That room was amazing!

I started at seven o'clock and finished at four o'clock, six days a week.
It was tiring.

Others were difficult: they complained about everything, and sometimes they spoke to me badly.

I looked at the paper for five minutes.
It was my money, earned through my work.
This job wasn't my dream.

sentences: I have lived in the same village for forty years, and I have had a garden for almost as long.
Like many gardeners, I write everything down in a notebook: the dates of sowing, the first tomato, the first frost, the last rain of summer.

What I saw is very clear.
In the 1980s, I used to plant my tomatoes around May fifteenth.
Today, I plant them at the end of April.
The first frost of autumn used to arrive around October twentieth.
Now, it often arrives in November.
Summers are drier.
Before, I used to water twice a week in July.
For the past five years, I water almost every day.
Some plants no longer grow well here.
Others, which came from the south, now grow very well.
I am not a scientist.
I only talk about my garden.

sentences: After eight years in a small house, I moved into an apartment building on the third floor.

sentences: In my family, we never talked about our feelings.

I told him that I wished I had talked more when I was little.

sentences: Behind our building, there had been an empty lot for years.
No one took care of it.
There was tall grass, some papers, and an old broken chair.
One day, the young man from the fourth floor had an idea.
During the neighbors' meeting, he proposed turning this lot into a shared garden.
At first, many people were against it.
"Who will take care of it?" "It will cost money."
But he had prepared his project well.
He explained that the town hall provided assistance, and he suggested starting small: six vegetable plots.
After a long discussion, we voted yes, just barely.
We started in April.
There were seven of us at the beginning: the young man, me, the elderly couple from the first floor, the family from the second, and Mrs. Renard, who complained but came every Saturday.
We cleaned the lot, brought in soil, and built the wooden plots.
Each family takes care of one plot, but we all water together.
This summer, we harvested tomatoes, zucchinis, salads, and a lot of herbs.
But the most interesting part isn't the vegetables.
Before, I knew three neighbors.
Now, I know twelve.
And Mrs. Renard hardly complains anymore.

sentences: On Tuesday morning, I woke up and immediately realized that something was wrong.
I had a headache, a sore throat, and I felt cold.
I took my temperature: thirty-eight point eight degrees.
I had a fever.
My first reaction was to get ready anyway to go to work.
I had an important meeting.
I got up, then I had to sit down.
I felt dizzy.
So I called the office to say that I wasn't coming.
In the afternoon, I called my doctor.
He saw me at five o'clock.
He examined me, then he said: "It's the flu.
There is no magic treatment.
You need to rest, drink a lot, and wait."
He gave me a medicine for the fever and a three-day sick leave.
Those three days were long.
I slept a lot, sometimes twelve hours a night.
I wasn't hungry.
I watched series without really following them.
On Friday, I felt a bit better.
On Monday, I was able to go back to work.
My colleague said to me: "You did well to stay home.
Last time, you came sick and half the office got sick too." She was right.

sentences: Three months ago, I hurt my back.
It happened stupidly, while carrying a box of books.
I bent my back instead of bending my legs.
I felt a sudden pain, like an electric shock, and I couldn't move for a few seconds.
The next day, it was worse.
I couldn't put on my socks by myself.
My doctor examined me and reassured me: it wasn't serious.
"You have a blocked muscle.
It will take one or two weeks."
He gave me medication and a surprising piece of advice: "Don't stay in bed.
Move gently."
I thought you had to rest completely.
He explained the opposite to me: staying lying down too long made the problem worse.
He also sent me to a physiotherapist.
The physiotherapist showed me simple exercises to do every morning.
But above all, he asked me questions about my daily life.
How many hours did I spend sitting?
About nine hours a day.
"That's the real problem," he said.
"The box was just the last straw.
Your back is weak because it never moves."
Since then, I've changed two things.
I get up every hour at the office, and I walk for twenty minutes each day.
I no longer have back pain.

sentences: My brother Thomas smoked for twenty years.
He started at sixteen and he smoked about a pack a day.
He had already tried to quit four times.
Each time, he lasted two or three weeks, then he started again.
Last year, something changed.
Our father had a heart problem and he spent a week in the hospital.
Thomas was silent for a long time after that visit.
Then he told me, 'This time, I'm quitting for good.'
But he did one thing differently: he asked for help.
Before, he always tried alone.
He went to see his doctor, who offered him patches.
He also joined a group of people who were quitting at the same time.
The first weeks were very hard.
He was nervous, he slept poorly.
He called me several times in the evening, just to talk.
He also changed his habits.
Before, he always smoked with his morning coffee, so he stopped having his coffee in the same place.
After a month, it was easier.
After three months, he was going up the stairs without being out of breath.
It's now been fourteen months.
He told me recently, 'The first four times, I tried alone.
The fifth time, I accepted to be helped.'

sentences: In my company, we have a medical check-up every two years.
It's mandatory, and I used to think it was pointless.
In February, it was my turn.
I went there without thinking about it, between two meetings.
The nurse first took the usual measurements: weight, height, and vision.
Then she took my blood pressure.
She noted the number, then she did it again five minutes later, without saying anything.
"Is there a problem?" I asked.
"Your blood pressure is a bit high.
It's not serious, but it's not ideal."
I was surprised.
I'm forty-two years old, I'm not in bad health, I don't smoke.
Then, the occupational doctor asked me a lot of questions.
"Do you sleep well?"
"How much coffee do you drink?"
My answers were honest: six hours of sleep, five or six coffees a day, and yes, I've been stressed for six months.
He told me: "None of this is dramatic.
But all of this together, over the years, can become a problem."
He didn't give me any medication.
He advised me to see my doctor in three months and to start with one thing: reduce coffee.
I went from six coffees to two.
Three months later, my blood pressure was normal.
Now, I no longer find this check-up pointless.

sentences: Last September, I signed up for a volleyball club.
I hadn't played since high school, twenty years ago.
It all started at the associations forum in town.
Every year in September, all the clubs set up a booth.
I passed by the volleyball booth almost by chance.
A woman smiled at me and asked, 'Do you play?'
'I played a long time ago.'
'We have a recreational group on Tuesday evenings.
No level required.
Come try it out, the first time is free.'
I hesitated all week.
Then I went to the first training session.
It was a disaster.
I missed almost all the balls.
After twenty minutes, I was out of breath and sore all over.
During the break, I thought, 'I won't come back.'
But a player came to talk to me.
She told me she had started two years earlier, in the same state as me.
'In the first month, we are terrible.
It's normal.
After that, it gets better.'
I came back the following week.
Then the next one.
Today, eight months later, I still play poorly.
But I miss fewer balls, and Tuesday evenings have become an appointment I never miss.

sentences: Every Saturday morning, I go to watch my son Léo play football.
He is nine years old and he plays for our neighborhood club.
The match starts at ten o'clock.
We need to be there at a quarter past nine, so we leave early.
On the edge of the field, there are about twenty parents.
In winter, it is really cold and we stand for a long time.
I really enjoy these mornings.
The children play with a lot of energy and little organization.
They all run towards the ball at the same time.
But there is a problem on the edge of the field: some parents shout too much.
One father, in particular, constantly yells at his son: "Pass!
Run!
But what are you doing?" The boy is eight years old and he looks down every time.
Last Saturday, the coach stopped the match for a minute.
He turned to the parents and said calmly:
"They are children.
They play to have fun.
Please let them play."
There was a great silence.
After that, the match continued, and it was much more enjoyable.
Léo scored a goal.
His team lost four to two.
In the car, he said to me: "It was good today."

sentences: After two years without sports, I started running again in March.
My first attempt last year had been a failure.
I had started too fast and for too long.
I had run for thirty minutes on the first day, and my legs had hurt for a week.
This time, I read some advice before starting.
They all said the same thing: start much more slowly than you think.
So I followed a very simple program for beginners.
The first week: one minute of running, then two minutes of walking, eight times.
That seems ridiculous.
It was even a bit embarrassing: I passed people who were really running.
But I wasn't in pain, and I came back three days later.
The second week: two minutes of running, two of walking.
Each week, I increased a little.
Some weeks, I didn't make progress, and that was okay.
After eight weeks, I ran for twenty minutes without stopping.
After four months, forty minutes.
Today, I run three times a week.
I'm not fast.
I don't compete.
But I sleep better and I'm calmer.
What has changed is not my motivation: it's my patience.

sentences: I started collecting vinyl records five years ago.
Today, I have about two hundred.
It all started at my parents' house.
While clearing out the attic, I found a box with my father's records: jazz and French songs.
I bought an old second-hand turntable, and I listened to these records one Sunday afternoon.
It surprised me.
The sound wasn't perfect, there were some little noises, but the listening experience was different.
With a vinyl record, you can't skip from one song to another in a second.
You have to get up, turn the record over.
You listen to the whole album, in order.
Since then, I've been looking for records everywhere: flea markets, second-hand shops, small thrift stores.
It's a pleasure in two parts.
First the search: you look at hundreds of covers, often finding nothing.
Then, sometimes, the discovery.
Last month, at a flea market, I found an album I had been looking for for two years.
It cost three euros.
I was so happy that the seller laughed.
My friends sometimes tell me: 'You can listen to everything for free on the internet.' That's true.
But it's not the same thing.
On Sunday evenings, I put on a record, and I do nothing else.

sentences: For two years, I have been part of a book club.
We meet once a month, on the first Thursday, at the city library.
There are eight of us.
The youngest is twenty-three, and the oldest is seventy-eight.
Outside of the club, we have almost nothing in common.
The principle is simple: we choose a book together, everyone reads it during the month, and we talk about it.
What I like the most is reading books that I would never have chosen myself.
For two years, I have read science fiction, poetry, and even a history book.
Some books I didn't like at all.
But even those were interesting to discuss.
The most surprising thing is the difference between us.
We read the same book, and we do not read the same book.
Last month, we read a novel about a family.
For me, the main character was selfish.
For Sylvie, he was brave.
We discussed for forty minutes.
No one changed their mind, and that wasn't the goal.
At the end, the librarian always tells us: 'We have to close!' So we continue outside, on the sidewalk, for another ten minutes.

sentences: My phone was six years old.
For a phone, that's very old.
For a few months, it had problems: the battery lasted only four hours, it was getting slow, and some apps no longer worked.
I didn't want to buy a new one.
I first tried to get it repaired.
I went to a repair shop.
The technician looked at my phone for ten minutes.
"I can change the battery: seventy euros.
But the real problem is the system.
This model hasn't received updates for a year."
He explained to me that without updates, the phone becomes less secure, and some apps stop working.
"You can keep it for a few more months, but not for years."
I found that absurd.
The device was working, not perfectly, but it was working.
It's not the machine that was dead: it's the software that had abandoned it.
I finally bought a refurbished phone, that is to say, a repaired and checked second-hand phone.
It cost me two hundred thirty euros instead of six hundred for a new one.
It's two years old, but it still receives updates for three more years.
I dropped off my old phone in a recycling bin.
I hope to keep this one for six years too.

sentences: Six months ago, I looked at the statistics on my phone.
The number shocked me: I was receiving an average of two hundred notifications a day.
Two hundred!
That's about one interruption every five minutes, all day long.
There was everything: messages, emails, store apps, games, news.
Many of them were useless.
The problem wasn't just the noise.
It was the attention.
Every time my phone vibrated, I lost track of what I was doing.
One evening, during dinner, my daughter said to me: "Mom, you look at your phone all the time."
She was right, and it made me ashamed.
So I did something simple.
I opened the settings and turned off almost all notifications.
I only kept calls, messages from my family, and my work app.
The first few days were strange.
I looked at my phone for no reason, almost like a reflex.
Then, after a week, something changed.
I was calmer.
I read whole pages without stopping.
I didn't miss anything important in six months.
News still comes in.

sentences: Last month, my father almost lost a lot of money because of a phone scam.
A man called him on a Tuesday afternoon.
He said he worked at my father's bank, in the security department.
He knew my father's name, the name of his bank, and even his address.
He spoke politely and calmly.
He explained that a suspicious transaction had just been detected: someone was trying to withdraw one thousand eight hundred euros.
We needed to act right away.
He asked my father to confirm his card number and to provide the code received by SMS.
My father was worried.
The man spoke quickly and kept repeating that it was urgent.
But just before giving the code, my father remembered one thing: a real bank never asks for a code over the phone.
So he said, "I'm going to hang up and call my bank myself."
The man immediately changed his tone and became aggressive.
My father hung up.
He called his bank using the number written on his card.
There was no suspicious transaction, of course.
Urgency is the main weapon of these scammers.
They don't want us to think.
Since then, my father has a rule: he always hangs up and calls back himself.

sentences: For two years, I've been working from home three days a week.
On Tuesdays and Thursdays, I go to the office.
At first, I was very happy.
No more commuting: I was saving an hour and a half each day.
I could sleep a little longer.
I also noticed that I worked better on certain tasks.
At the office, people interrupted me all the time.
At home, I could concentrate without being disturbed.
But after a few months, problems appeared.
The first problem was space.
My apartment is small.
I worked at the kitchen table, the same table where I ate in the evening.
The second problem was time.
Without commuting, there was no clear limit anymore.
I started at eight o'clock and was still checking my messages at nine o'clock.
The third problem was loneliness.
Some days, I didn't talk to anyone face to face.
So I changed several things.

sentences: At seventy-two years old, my mother bought a tablet.
She wanted to see her grandchildren on video because they live far away.
I offered to teach her.
I thought it would be quick.
I was completely wrong.
On the first day, we spent two hours on things I thought were obvious.
How to turn on the device.
How to touch the screen, not too hard and not too long.
I realized that I wasn't explaining well.
I was using words like 'app' or 'menu' without defining them.
For me, it was natural; for her, it was a foreign language.
I also noticed something else: she was scared.
Scared of pressing in the wrong place, of breaking everything.
So I told her a phrase that helped a lot: 'You can't break anything.
If you make a mistake, we can fix it in thirty seconds.'
After that, she dared to try on her own.
We did something useful: we wrote a little notebook.
At each step, she wrote down the instructions in her own words.
This notebook is still useful to her.
It took about two months.
Today, she calls her grandchildren on video by herself, sends photos, and reads the news online.
Last week, she called me to show me something I didn't know how to do.

sentences: One evening in May, around ten o'clock, I heard a noise in the garden.
I took a lamp and went outside.
Under the hedge, there was a hedgehog.
It curled up right away and didn't move again.
I quickly went back inside so as not to disturb it, but I was happy.
I had never seen a hedgehog at my home.
The next day, I looked for information.
Hedgehogs are becoming increasingly rare in France.
Their numbers have decreased a lot over the past thirty years.
The reasons are many: roads, chemical products, and especially overly tidy gardens.
A hedgehog needs dead leaves and wild corners to sleep and eat.
So I changed a few habits.
First, I stopped using products against slugs.
These products also kill the animals that eat them.
And the hedgehog eats slugs: it's a free gardener.
Then, I left a corner of the garden untouched, with leaves and branches.
Finally, I made a small hole at the bottom of my fence.
This may seem strange, but hedgehogs walk one or two kilometers at night.
If all the gardens are closed, they can no longer move around.
This summer, I saw the hedgehog four times.
One evening, there were two.

sentences: I live in the city, on the fourth floor.
I don't have a garden, just a three-square-meter balcony.
Last year, I decided to transform it to help the insects.
The idea came from an article: the number of insects has dropped a lot in Europe.
Without insects, there is no pollination, and without pollination, there are almost no fruits or vegetables.
I thought a balcony would be useless.
A neighbor, who works in a nature association, told me the opposite: in the city, every flowering balcony helps the insects that cross the city.
I started by changing my plants.
Before, I used to buy pretty flowers but without any interest for the bees.
Some modern flowers produce almost no nectar.
My neighbor advised me to get simple plants: lavender, thyme, sage, and marigolds.
These are easy plants that require little water.
Then, I stopped using any chemical products.
Finally, I put a small dish of water with pebbles, so the insects can drink without drowning.
The results were quick.
By June, there were bees every day on the lavender.
In July, I saw three different butterflies.
It's not much.
But in the morning, with my coffee, I watch my balcony at work.

sentences: I have been walking in the same forest for thirty years.
As a child, I used to go there with my father.
Today, I go there with my children.
It's an ordinary forest, twenty minutes from home.
There are oaks, beeches, a few pines, and a small stream.
This forest has changed a lot, but it takes time to notice.
The stream, first.
When I was little, there was water all year round.
We played in it during the summer.
For the past six or seven years, it has been dry from July to September.
Next, the trees.
Many beeches are sick.
Their leaves turn brown too early, starting in August.
A forest ranger explained to me that beeches don't like dry summers: their roots don't go deep enough.
"In fifty years, he told me, there will be no more beeches here.
They are already planting other trees that come from the south."
There are also new things.
Birds and insects that lived further south have arrived in our area.
My children, however, don't see any of this.
For them, this forest is normal.
This is what troubles me the most: each generation thinks that the world it discovers is normal.
So I tell them about the stream.

sentences: Two years ago, we decided to adopt a dog.
My children wanted a puppy, of course.
But at the shelter, the volunteer explained an important thing to us.
Puppies find a family in a few days.
Older dogs, on the other hand, sometimes stay for years.
"Everyone wants puppies," she said.
"However, a seven-year-old dog is often easier: he is calm and already knows the rules."
We met Oscar, a seven-year-old dog.
His owner had moved into a retirement home and could no longer keep him.
Oscar had been at the shelter for eleven months.
He didn't run towards us like the young dogs.
He stayed seated and looked at us calmly.
We chose him.
The first month was difficult.
He didn't eat much and slept near the door, as if he were waiting for someone.
The vet told us to be patient: an older dog has a history, and it takes time.
Little by little, Oscar changed his spot.
He moved from the door to the living room rug, then to the couch.
Today, he is nine years old.
He walks slowly and sleeps a lot.
But every evening, he comes to rest his head on my daughter's lap.

sentences: It's December, and like every year, I'm thinking about next year.
This time, I want to do things differently.
Usually, I make a long list in January: exercise, eat better, read more, learn Spanish, tidy up the house, save money.

Too many projects at the same time is like having no project at all.
So this year, I've chosen only three things.
First, I'm going to sign up for an accounting course.
My job is going to change, and I will need this knowledge.
The classes start in February, on Tuesday evenings, for four months.
Next, I'm going to go on a trip with my sister.
We've been talking about it for six years, without ever doing it.

This market is different from usual markets: all the sellers are producers from the region, within a radius of forty kilometers.

sentences: In English, there is only one word: 'you.'
In French, you have to choose between 'tu' and 'vous.'
For my English friend Tom, this is one of the most difficult things.
The general rule seems simple.
You say 'tu' to family, friends, and close colleagues.
You say 'vous' to strangers and in official situations.
But in real life, it's much more complicated.
Tom told me about several mistakes.
One day, he used 'tu' with a sixty-year-old man in a store.
The man seemed surprised and cold.
In France, using 'tu' with an older stranger can seem rude.
Another time, it was the opposite.
He used 'vous' with a friend his age for two hours.
In the end, the other guy said to him while laughing: 'We can use 'tu,' you know!'
The rules also change depending on the environment.
In some companies, everyone uses 'tu,' even the director.
In others, you use 'vous' with your boss for twenty years.
I gave Tom a simple piece of advice: when you don't know, start with 'vous.'
There is a magic phrase: 'Can we use 'tu'?' It's often the oldest person who suggests it.
Tom learned it by heart.

sentences: When Tom arrived in France to work, several things surprised him.
The first one is the holidays.
In France, all employees have at least five weeks of paid leave per year.
Many companies even give a little more.
In the United Kingdom, the legal minimum is about four weeks, including public holidays.
The second surprise is the legal working time: thirty-five hours per week.
That doesn't mean that no one works more.
But beyond that, those are overtime hours, which must be paid or compensated.
The third surprise concerns evening emails.
In his previous job in London, Tom received messages at ten o'clock in the evening and he would reply to them.
It was normal.
In France, there has been a 'right to disconnect' since 2017.
Companies must respect their employees' rest time outside of working hours.
The first time Tom sent a message on a Sunday, a colleague replied to him on Monday morning: 'On Sundays, I don't read my messages.'
Tom took it badly at first.
Then he understood that it wasn't a criticism.
Today, he turns off his computer at six o'clock.
'It's the best habit that France has given me,' he says.

sentences: The first time Tom went to the doctor in France, he didn't understand anything.
In the UK, with the NHS, you don't pay for the consultation.
You make an appointment, see the doctor, and leave without paying.
In France, the system is different.
At the end of the consultation, the doctor asks for payment: about thirty euros for a general practitioner.
Tom was very surprised.
He thought that healthcare was free in France too.
In reality, it is not free: it is reimbursed.
After the consultation, Social Security reimburses about seventy percent of the price.
A complementary insurance, the 'mutuelle', often reimburses the rest.
With the Vitale card, everything is done automatically.
Tom found this system complicated.
But he noticed one advantage.
In France, you can make an appointment quickly, often in two or three days.
You can also freely choose your doctor.
"Back home," he said, "I sometimes waited three weeks for an appointment."
Each system has its strengths and weaknesses.
The British system is simpler: nothing to pay, nothing to claim.
The French system is faster, but it requires money in advance.
Tom now has a Vitale card and a mutuelle.
"It took me a year to understand," he said.
"Now, it's fine."

sentences: There is a cultural difference that Tom often talks about: the way of queuing.
In the United Kingdom, the queue is almost sacred.
People naturally stand one behind the other.
Cutting in front of someone is considered very serious.
In France, the queue exists too, of course.
But it is often less straight and less strict.
At the bakery, for example, people tend to form a small group.
The first time, Tom found it chaotic.
He thought that no one knew who had arrived first.
Then he observed, and he understood that he was wrong.
People know perfectly well whose turn it is.
They watch each other, and often someone says: 'It's your turn, madam, I believe.'
There is an important rule to know.
In a small shop, you have to ask: 'Who is the last?' This question solves everything, without a straight line.
Tom took a while to learn it.
At first, he politely stayed near the door, and people entered after him and went ahead.
He waited without being served.
'No one was dishonest,' he says now.
'It's just that I hadn't said I was there.'
Two cultures, two methods.
In both cases, the idea is the same: everyone takes their turn.

sentences: In most major French cities, finding housing has become the main problem for residents.
Housing now accounts for about a third of a household's budget, and often much more for young people and single individuals.
How did we get here?
Several factors have added up.
First, the population of cities has increased, while the number of housing units has not kept pace.
When demand exceeds supply, prices go up: it's mechanical.
Next, the size of households has changed.
Fifty years ago, an apartment housed an average of three people; today, it's just over two.
This means more housing is needed for the same population.
Finally, in very touristy cities, part of the housing stock has shifted to short-term rentals, which are more profitable for owners.
Apartments that once housed residents now welcome travelers.
The consequences are concrete.
People who work in the city no longer live there: they move thirty or forty kilometers away and spend two hours a day commuting.
Certain essential jobs — nurses, teachers, municipal employees — are becoming hard to fill due to a lack of affordable housing.
What can be done?
No single solution is enough.
Building more is necessary, but it's slow and sometimes unpopular.
Regulating rents, as several cities do, protects tenants but doesn't create housing.
Limiting short-term rentals helps in the most affected neighborhoods.
What is certain is that this issue doesn't only concern those who are poorly housed.
A city where only the wealthiest can live will eventually lose what makes it function.

sentences: I have lived in a big city for twelve years.
People often ask me if I like it, and I never manage to answer simply.
The truth is that the city gives a lot and takes a lot.
Let's start with what it gives.
Choice, first.
There are jobs, and not just a few: thousands, in very different fields.
When I wanted to change careers, I didn't need to move.
In my parents' village, it was impossible.
There is also culture.
A concert on a Tuesday night, an exhibition on a Sunday, a cinema showing films that no one knows.
I don't take advantage of it every week, far from it.
But knowing that it's possible changes something.
Finally, there's anonymity.
In a village, everyone knows what you are doing.
In the city, no one is watching you.
Depending on the person, it's either freedom or solitude.
Now, what it takes.
The noise, first, which never really stops.
The price, next: I pay for thirty-eight square meters what my brother pays for a house with a garden.
And fatigue, above all.
Crowded transport, queues, rushed people: everything requires a little effort, and these little efforts add up.
So, should we stay or leave?
I believe the question is poorly posed.
What matters is knowing what we came to find.
As for me, I came for work and for opportunities.
As long as I benefit from it, the city makes sense.
The day I pay this rent without getting anything in return, I will know it's time to leave.

sentences: In recent years, many French cities have been planting trees at a rate not seen in a long time.
It's not just a matter of aesthetics.
The first reason is heat.
Cities are significantly hotter than the surrounding countryside — sometimes by five to ten degrees during summer nights.
Concrete and asphalt absorb heat all day and release it at night.
This phenomenon is called the 'urban heat island'.
Trees act in two ways.
They provide shade, which is obvious.
But more importantly, they cool the air by evaporating water through their leaves, somewhat like a natural misting system.
A well-planted street can be three to six degrees cooler than a bare street.
During a heatwave, this difference is not just a comfort: it can be vital for elderly people.
The second reason concerns water.
When it rains heavily in a fully paved city, the water goes nowhere and the sewers overflow.
Planted soils absorb some of this water and reduce flooding.
Finally, there is a less measurable but real effect.
Several studies show that the presence of trees reduces stress and improves the well-being of residents.
Green neighborhoods are, on average, areas where people go out more.
All of this requires choices.
A tree in the city is expensive to plant and maintain, and sometimes parking spaces need to be removed to make room for it.
These debates are often heated in city council.
But a tree planted today will be beneficial for sixty years.

sentences: A few months ago, I had to work nights for three weeks.
I discovered a city I didn't know.
Between midnight and five in the morning, the city doesn't sleep: it changes its inhabitants.
Around one o'clock, it's still people who are going out.
The streets around the bars are lively, sometimes noisy.
Taxis are waiting.
Then, little by little, calm settles in.
Starting at three o'clock, another population appears.
They are invisible during the day, yet they keep everything else running.
First, the bakers.
In the bakery, the light has been on since two in the morning.
The bread we will buy at seven o'clock is already baking.
Next, the cleaning staff.
They enter the offices and train stations when everyone has left.
In the morning, we find clean places without ever seeing who cleaned them.
There are also the caregivers in hospitals, the drivers who deliver to stores, the workers who repair the subway tracks during the few hours it doesn't run.
What struck me the most was the relative silence.
You hear things you never hear: the sound of a shutter, a bird at four-thirty, your own footsteps.
When I returned to a normal rhythm, I kept one habit.
In the morning, at the bakery, I look at the person behind the counter and wonder what time they started.

sentences: One day, I will leave the city. Many city dwellers say this.
Some actually do it.
It's interesting to listen to what they say afterwards.
The reasons for leaving often look similar: the cost of housing, fatigue, noise, the desire for a garden, and sometimes the birth of a child.
The possibility of remote work has made this project realistic for people who, in the past, wouldn't have been able to consider it.
Those who succeed in their move almost always mention the same factors.
First, they chose a place they already knew, where they had family or friends.
Arriving somewhere without knowing anyone is much more difficult than one might think.
Then, they checked the practical aspects before leaving: internet coverage, the distance to school, the doctor, and the supermarket.
These details seem secondary from an apartment in the city; they shape daily life in the countryside.
Finally, they got involved in local life — the sports club, the events committee, the school.
Those who stay among themselves, without ever participating, often feel isolated after a year.
Those who return to the city mention three things: isolation, dependence on the car for even the smallest trips, and their teenagers' boredom.
So there isn't a universally correct answer.
The real question isn't 'city or countryside?', but 'what am I fleeing from, and what am I looking for?'.
Those who leave just to escape are rarely satisfied.

sentences: A few years ago, I used to travel in a certain way: trying to see as much as possible in the least amount of time.
Five cities in seven days, three museums a day, a checklist.
I would come back exhausted, with seven hundred photos and strangely blurry memories.
I would confuse the churches.
I couldn't remember in which city I had eaten a specific dish.
For the past three years, I've been doing the opposite: spending the entire stay in just one city, or even just one neighborhood.
The change has been deeper than expected.
When you stay in the same place for several days, you stop being a rushed visitor.
You have the same coffee in the morning, and by the third day, the waitress recognizes you.
You understand the rhythm of the place: what time the streets fill up, which day is market day, where the locals actually go to eat.
You also have time for off days, which is valuable.
It's raining?
That's okay, there are still four days left.
In a tight schedule, a rainy day ruins everything.
This way of traveling has another advantage, which is less personal.
Staying longer in the same place reduces travel, thus lowering emissions related to travel, and the money spent benefits the local economy more than the transport companies.
I'm not claiming that this is the only good method.
A first trip to a country sometimes justifies moving around a lot.
But I no longer count the cities I've visited.
I count the places where I've ended up feeling a bit at home.

sentences: Before each trip, I learn about twenty words in the language of the country.
Not complicated phrases: hello, thank you, please, excuse me, yes, no, how much, where is, I don't understand, goodbye.
It takes about two hours in total.
And the effect is disproportionate.
The first time I noticed this was in Greece.
I had learned 'hello' and 'thank you' on the plane.
In a small grocery store, I used them awkwardly, with a certainly terrible accent.
The shopkeeper, who spoke English, immediately changed his attitude.
He smiled, corrected my pronunciation while laughing, and offered me a fruit.
Why such a difference for two words?
I believe the reason is simple.
These words don't really serve to communicate: English would have been enough.
They serve to say something else: 'I know I am in your country, and I am making an effort.'
It's a form of politeness, and politeness has always been more of a signal than information.
The opposite is also true.
A traveler who arrives and immediately speaks English, assuming that everyone understands him, sends a message too — even if he doesn't realize it.
I don't speak any of the languages of the countries I have visited correctly.
I don't claim otherwise.
But I have never regretted those two hours.
And even years later, I still sometimes remember the word 'thank you' in Hungarian.

sentences: In the 2000s, night trains almost disappeared from Europe.
In France, most lines were closed between 2000 and 2017.
They were expensive, the equipment was aging, and low-cost airlines offered unbeatable tickets.
In recent years, the trend has reversed.
Several lines have reopened, and others are announced, in France as well as in Austria, Sweden, or Germany.
Why this return?
The most obvious reason is ecological.
A train journey emits significantly less greenhouse gas on average than the same journey by plane.
For distances of six hundred to one thousand five hundred kilometers, the night train becomes a credible alternative.
But there is also a practical argument, often underestimated.
A night train does not take time away from the day: you board in the evening, sleep, and arrive in the morning.
No airport to reach, no check-in two hours beforehand, no hotel night to pay for.
When compared honestly, the actual time difference is smaller than it seems.
The challenges remain numerous.
Rolling stock is expensive, and it takes years to build.
Tracks are used at night for maintenance.
Finally, it is difficult to make these lines profitable without public support.
Comfort, on the other hand, has improved: the new cars offer smaller compartments, sometimes individual, very different from the six-person couchettes of the past.
I took a night train last year.
I slept poorly, I admit.
But I woke up in another region, without having lost a single day.

sentences: Tourism supports entire regions.
In France, it accounts for about eight percent of the economy and hundreds of thousands of jobs.
No serious person suggests doing without it.
However, in some cities, the relationship between residents and visitors has become strained.
The problem is not tourism itself: it's its concentration.
Visitors arrive at the same places, during the same months, and often at the same times.
A narrow street that comfortably accommodates fifty people becomes unlivable with five hundred.
The consequences are well documented.
Housing is being transformed into more profitable short-term rentals, which drives up rents for residents.
Shops are changing: the hardware store and the cobbler are giving way to souvenir shops.
Little by little, the city center stops being a place to live and becomes a backdrop.
Several European cities have started to react.
Some limit the number of authorized cruises.
Others strictly regulate tourist rentals or impose a higher tourist tax.
Some very fragile natural sites now require a mandatory reservation.
These measures are criticized, sometimes by the residents themselves, because many depend on tourism.
Finding balance is difficult.
As travelers, we do have a small margin of action.

Coming off-season, avoiding the same three sites that everyone photographs, staying in a hotel rather than in an apartment taken off the rental market: these choices have a real effect when they multiply.
Loving a place is not just about wanting to see it.
It’s also about accepting that it continues to belong to those who live there.

sentences: For a long time, I brought back objects from my travels.
Small statues, decorated boxes, fridge magnets.
Almost all of them ended up in a drawer, and I would be unable to say which country half of them comes from.
What has remained, however, are things I hadn't planned to bring back.
Habits, first.
Since a stay in Spain, I have dinner later and I walk after the meal.
Since a trip to Japan, I take off my shoes when I enter my home, and I now find it strange to do otherwise.
These gestures entered my life without me deciding them.
Tastes, next.
I discovered a spice mix in a Moroccan market that I had never used.
I still buy it today, six years later, in a grocery store in my neighborhood.
And above all, a way of seeing.
It's harder to explain.
Living a few days in a place where the obvious things are not the same — the schedules, the role of family, the way of talking in the street — has a lasting effect.
You come back finding your own habits a little less natural.
This might be the true benefit of travel: not what you have seen, but what you stop considering as obvious.
Today, I hardly buy souvenirs anymore.
On the other hand, I write a few lines every evening.
This notebook is the only object I bring back, and it's the only one I reopen.

sentences: We talk a lot about investment and quite a bit less about something more basic: precautionary savings, which means having a reserve of money available immediately in case of unexpected events.
The idea is nothing spectacular.
It's not about making your money grow, but about being able to absorb a shock: a broken car, a device to replace, a month with less income.
Its main interest is not financial, in fact.
It is strategic.
A person without a reserve suffers from unexpected events.
If their washing machine breaks down, they have to either go into debt at a high rate, accept the first available solution, or do without the machine.
None of these options is good, and all of them end up being expensive in the long run.
A person who has a reserve, even a modest one, can instead take the time to compare, wait for a cheaper repair, or refuse an unfavorable loan.
This is what specialists sometimes call 'the cost of poverty': being short on money forces you to make choices that, in fact, end up costing more.
How much should you set aside?
The advice varies, often between one and three months of regular expenses.
But this figure discourages a lot of people, who give up before they even start.
However, the essential point is elsewhere.
A reserve of five hundred euros already changes a lot of everyday situations.
The best advice I ever received was very simple: set aside a small amount automatically on payday, before spending anything.
What you don't see go by doesn't hurt.

sentences: Forty years ago, people repaired things.
A toaster, a television, a washing machine: there was a repairman in every neighborhood, and replacing a working appliance would have seemed absurd.
Today, the situation has reversed.
Getting something repaired often costs almost as much as buying new, and sometimes even more.
Several reasons explain this shift.
First, the price of manufactured goods has dropped significantly, while the cost of human labor has increased.
An hour of labor can exceed the value of the appliance.
Next, the design has changed.
Many products are assembled with glue rather than screws, making them difficult to open without breaking.
Some spare parts are not sold separately, or they disappear a few years after being marketed.
Finally, software plays an increasing role.
A perfectly functional device can become unusable simply because it no longer receives updates.
However, things are changing.
France has introduced a 'repairability index' displayed on certain products, along with a repair bonus that covers part of the cost.
European law is gradually requiring the availability of spare parts.
At the same time, 'repair cafés' have emerged: volunteers help people repair things for free, teaching them to do it themselves.
I went there once with a vacuum cleaner that wasn't working.
The problem was a piece of fabric stuck in it.
The repair took twelve minutes.
I almost threw away a two hundred euro appliance.

sentences: Last month, I did an exercise that I recommend to everyone: I went through twelve months of bank statements, line by line, looking only for recurring payments.
I found eleven active subscriptions.
I was actually using four of them.
There were two video services, one of which I hadn't opened in eight months.
A sports app I subscribed to in January, during a moment of enthusiasm, and used three times.
An online storage space that I had forgotten about.
A digital magazine.
A warranty on a device that I no longer owned.
The total came to seventy-three euros a month, which is nearly nine hundred euros a year.
What struck me was not the amount: it was not having noticed it.
The subscription model relies precisely on this.
Each amount is deliberately modest, below the threshold where we react.
The deduction is automatic, so it's invisible.
And there is no moment of decision: we don't choose to pay, we only choose to cancel — which requires active effort.
Companies know this perfectly well.
That's why it often takes three clicks to sign up and many more to cancel.
I canceled seven subscriptions.
The process took about forty minutes in total.
Forty minutes for six hundred euros a year: that's probably the best hourly rate of my life.
Since then, I've adopted a rule.
Every year, in January, I review my statements.
And I cancel anything I can't justify out loud.

sentences: A few years ago, I bought a pair of shoes for thirty euros.
They lasted seven months.
I bought a similar pair, then another one.
A friend then explained a very simple calculation to me that changed the way I shop: the cost per use.
Thirty euros for seven months of daily wear comes to about fourteen cents a day.
A pair that costs one hundred twenty euros and lasts five years amounts to seven cents.
So the 'expensive' pair actually costs half as much.
This reasoning doesn't apply everywhere, and it shouldn't be made an absolute rule.
A high price does not guarantee quality at all: in many sectors, you mainly pay for a brand.
So you need to look at the manufacturing, the warranty, and the possibility of repairs.
It also assumes you have the money upfront, which is far from the case for everyone.
Not being able to buy durable items and having to constantly replace them is one of the most concrete ways that a lack of money is costly.
But when the choice is available, the useful question is not 'how much does it cost?'.
It is: 'how long will it last, and can I get it repaired?'
I have applied this logic to only a few items: shoes, a coat, a pot, a bag.
They cost me more at the start.
I still have all of them.
And curiously, I pay more attention to them.
We take better care of what we don't plan to replace.

sentences: It's easy to blame yourself for your lack of willpower in front of a phone.
This forgets that these apps are designed, by entire teams, to capture attention for as long as possible.
The main mechanism has a name: variable reward.
When you pull down the news feed, you don't know what you're going to find — nothing interesting, or something exciting.
This uncertainty is exactly the principle of slot machines, and the brain reacts very strongly to it.
A predictable reward becomes boring; an unpredictable reward keeps you engaged.
Other elements are added: infinite scrolling, which removes any natural stopping point; the automatic playback of the next video; notifications, which create an interruption that's hard to ignore.
None of these techniques are an accident.
They are measured, tested, optimized.
The result is measurable: the average screen time exceeds three hours a day in most European countries.
It's not just three hours wasted, because part of it is useful.
But very few people, when honestly asked, say they chose this time.
What to do?
The effective advice doesn't rely on willpower, but on friction.
Turning off non-essential notifications removes interruptions.
Putting the most captivating apps in a folder, out of the home screen, adds two gestures — which is often enough.
Leaving the phone in another room at night is more effective than any resolution.
The idea is not to demonize these tools, which provide immense services.
It's to restore a more balanced relationship: that we decide when to engage, not the other way around.

sentences: In France, most administrative procedures are now done online: declaring income, requesting assistance, renewing a document, making a medical appointment.
For the majority of people, this is progress: faster, available at any time, without waiting in line.
But a significant part of the population faces real difficulties.
We talk about illiteracy in digital technology, or digital exclusion.
According to estimates, several million people are affected in France.
We spontaneously imagine elderly people, and they indeed make up a significant portion.
But it would be a mistake to stop there.
There are also people who do not have suitable equipment: a smartphone does not replace a computer for filling out a complex form or uploading documents.
There are those who live in areas where the connection is still poor.
There are those who find it difficult to read administrative French — a language that is already complicated on paper and does not improve on screen.
And there are simply those who are blocked by the fear of making mistakes: many procedures do not allow you to go back.
The consequences are serious.
A significant percentage of people give up rights they are entitled to, due to their inability to complete the procedure.
Solutions exist: 'France Services' in the regions, digital mediators, and maintaining physical and telephone support.
But these measures require a clear political choice: to consider that support is part of the service, and not a cost to be reduced.
An administration accessible only online is not accessible to everyone.

sentences: Artificial intelligence is very much in the news, with spectacular promises and concerns.
It's useful to look at what it already does, concretely, in an ordinary day.
It is present when a translation app turns a photographed menu into understandable text.
When a navigation service recalculates a route taking traffic into account.
When a phone finds all the photos where the same person appears.
When a messaging service filters out unwanted emails.
These uses have a common point: the machine recognizes patterns in huge amounts of data.
That's what it does very well.
The more recent tools, capable of writing a text or answering a question, work on a similar principle.
They have learned, from a very large number of texts, which words probably follow which others.
This explains both their fluency and their main flaw.
Because these systems don't 'know' anything in the sense we understand.
They produce the most plausible sequence, which is not the same as the most true.
They can therefore confidently assert false information, invent a reference, or get a date wrong without ever hesitating.
This confidence is precisely the trap: we spontaneously associate a confident tone with reliability.
The reasonable use that emerges is quite simple.
These tools are useful for drafting, rephrasing, translating, summarizing, and suggesting ideas.
They do not replace verification, especially when it comes to facts, figures, or important decisions.
In other words: a quick assistant, never a source.

sentences: The question arises in almost every family, usually around the age of ten or eleven: should we give a phone to our child?
It is often poorly framed, as it mixes two very different things: having a phone and having full access to the internet and social networks.
A simple phone, which allows calling and sending messages, meets the practical need that motivates most parents: to reach their child when they come home alone from school or go to a friend's house.
This need is real.
A connected smartphone is something else.
It provides access to content designed to capture attention, to monetized games, and to spaces where the child can be exposed to difficult messages or images.
The available data suggests caution, without dramatizing.

What worries specialists the most is not moderate use, but two specific situations: access to social networks before adolescence, and having the phone in the bedroom at night, which significantly reduces sleep time.
Sleep may be the strongest argument, because it is measurable and its effects on mood, concentration, and academic performance are well established.
In practice, families that manage best are neither the strictest nor the most permissive.
They are the ones that set clear rules, discussed, and especially applied to adults as well.
It is difficult to require a teenager to leave their phone out of the bedroom if their parents are dining with theirs at the table.
Consistency is more convincing than prohibition.

sentences: The French meal — an appetizer, a main course, cheese, and a dessert, enjoyed together and without rushing — has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage since 2010.
This recognition surprised some: can a way of eating really be classified?
The argument was, however, precise.
What was distinguished was not French cuisine, but the ritual: the set table, the order of the dishes, the act of eating together, and talking about what one is eating.
Has this ritual disappeared?
The numbers tell a nuanced story.
On one hand, it has clearly shortened.
The weekday lunch now lasts about thirty minutes on average, compared to much longer forty years ago.
Many employees eat in front of a screen, and sandwiches have taken on a considerable role.
The number of dishes has also decreased: few families serve four courses during the week.
On the other hand, something resists with real strength.
Compared to its neighbors, France maintains remarkably synchronized meal times: at one o'clock, a large part of the country eats at the same moment.
The meal remains predominantly a collective practice, seated and at the table.
And on weekends, the long meal reappears, especially on Sundays.
What has changed is not so much the value placed on the meal, but the space that work allows it during the week.
It would be excessive to talk about disappearance.
It is more accurate to say that the meal has become more concentrated: less frequent, but still important when it occurs.

sentences: When data collection is mentioned, a common response is, 'I have nothing to hide.'
This comes from an understandable intuition, but it is based on a misunderstanding.
The question is not whether we have secrets.
It is about what the accumulation of perfectly harmless details reveals.
Taken separately, these elements say nothing.
The time at which we connect.
Daily commutes.
The searches conducted.
Purchases, pauses, hesitations before clicking.
When gathered, they paint a very precise picture: work schedules, a probable state of health, family situation, beliefs, financial capacity, and sometimes a moment of vulnerability.
This profile has value, and that is why it is created.
Its uses are not all concerning — a better-suited service can sometimes be pleasant.
But some raise real questions: prices that vary according to the buyer's profile, credit offers targeted at people in difficulty, political ads addressed differently based on presumed sensitivities.
Another problem is the duration.
What is collected today can be kept for a long time and interpreted later in a context that no one anticipates.
European law offers real protections: consent, right of access, right to erasure.
They are useful, but rarely used, as the interfaces make refusal tedious.
A few simple actions reduce collection: refusing non-essential cookies, limiting app permissions, using a more protective browser.
None of this is paranoia.
It is simply about deciding who, whether us or someone else, knows our habits best.

sentences: Ask the question at the table: where does this chicken come from?
What about these tomatoes?
What about this cheese?
Few people can answer precisely.
This is not a criticism.
Modern supply chains are long and intentionally discreet.
Labels help, but not as much as we think.
"Made in France" means that the processing took place in France, not necessarily that the ingredients come from there.
A French biscuit can contain wheat, sugar, and oil from three different continents.
For meat, the origin is better defined, but the label can distinguish the place of birth, raising, and slaughter — which are not always the same.
Should we then try to know everything?
That would be exhausting and a bit vain.
A few simple guidelines are often enough.
The first is the season.
A seasonal product has rarely traveled far or grown in a heated greenhouse.
It is generally cheaper, better, and more energy-efficient.
The second is the degree of processing.
The more ingredients a product has, the harder it becomes to trace its origin.
The third is the circuit.
Buying directly from a producer does not guarantee quality, but it at least allows you to ask the question — and get an answer.
There is finally a less practical interest.
Knowing that an apple takes months to ripen, that cheese requires aging, and that a chicken takes several weeks to grow changes the way we view its price.
What we call "expensive" sometimes seems less so when we know what it entails.

sentences: We like to think that our purchases are thoughtful: we compare, we evaluate, we decide.
Behavioral economics research tells a different story.
Let's take a common example.
In a store, an item is displayed as '€80 instead of €120.'
Our brain doesn't really remember the price: it remembers the difference.
We feel like we've saved forty euros, even though we've spent eighty.
The reference price serves as an anchor, and it is often chosen precisely for that reason.
Another well-known mechanism: the pain of payment.
Paying in cash physically makes you notice the expense.
Paying contactlessly, in one second, makes it almost invisible.
Several studies show that we spend more when the act of paying is less concrete.
Payments in installments amplify the effect even more: 'four times twenty-five euros' seems smaller than one hundred euros, even though it's the same amount.
Finally, there's artificial scarcity.
'Only two left in stock,' 'offer valid today': these messages trigger an ancient reaction, the fear of missing out.
They don't inform us; they pressure us.
Understanding this doesn't make anyone completely rational.
These mechanisms work even when we know about them.

But we can set up a few simple safeguards: wait twenty-four hours before any unplanned purchase, look at the final price rather than the discount, and ask ourselves not 'is this a good deal?' but 'would I have wanted it at the normal price?'
This last question, asked honestly, often reduces the desire.
It's not deprivation.
It's simply taking back the decision.

sentences: According to estimates from the United Nations, nearly a third of the food produced in the world is never consumed.
This figure is hard to believe, yet it is well documented.
Waste does not occur in the same way depending on the countries.
In low-income countries, losses mainly happen before sale: poor storage conditions, slow transport, lack of a cold chain.
Food spoils before it arrives.
In wealthy countries, it's the opposite.
Most of the waste occurs at the end of the chain, in distribution and especially at home.
In France, it is estimated that each person throws away about thirty kilograms of food per year, including a portion that is still packaged.
The domestic causes are trivial: we buy too much, we forget what is at the back of the refrigerator, we cook portions that are too large, we confuse two date labels.
This confusion deserves to be clarified.
"To be consumed until" relates to safety: after this date, the product can be dangerous.
"To be consumed preferably before" relates to quality: the product remains consumable, it just loses some taste or texture.
Tons of rice, pasta, and perfectly good canned goods are thrown away because of this misunderstanding.
What works, in practice, comes down to a few things: planning meals for the week, making a list, putting older products in front, and considering leftovers as a planned meal rather than just scraps.
French law now prohibits large stores from throwing away consumable unsold goods; they must give them away.
This is a step forward.
But the main issue still lies in our kitchens.

sentences: The debate about meat is often presented in binary terms: to eat it or not eat it at all.
This opposition makes the discussion difficult, while the data suggest a more modest conclusion.
From an environmental perspective, the orders of magnitude are clear.
Livestock farming accounts for a significant portion of greenhouse gas emissions related to food, as well as considerable use of land and water.
But not all meats are equal: the gap between beef and poultry is much larger than the gap between poultry and certain plant products.
From a health standpoint, official recommendations do not call for elimination.
They advise limiting red meat and especially processed meats, without excluding other sources.
There is also a social dimension that is rarely mentioned.
Meat holds a strong symbolic place in many cultures, including in France: it marks festive meals, hospitality, and generosity.
Ignoring this leads to moralizing discourse that mainly produces resistance.

That’s why the approach that works best, in studies as well as in cafeterias, is not very spectacular: reduce frequency rather than ban, improve the quality of what is served, and offer genuinely good alternatives.
A poorly prepared vegetarian dish convinces no one.
A good vegetarian dish is chosen without thinking about it.
Personally, I have gone from eating meat almost every day to two or three times a week.
I spend the same amount because I buy better.
And I have never felt deprived.

sentences: Many adults make the same observation: it is significantly harder to make new friends at thirty-five than at eighteen.
This is often explained by personality — people have supposedly become less open and more difficult.
The explanation is probably elsewhere, and it is more reassuring.
Sociologists identify three conditions that promote the formation of a friendship: repeated proximity, unplanned interactions, and an environment that encourages lowering one's guard a bit.
At school or university, these three conditions are constantly present, without any effort.
You see the same people every day, you run into each other without planning it, and you share a common situation.
In adulthood, they almost all disappear.
You often see your colleagues, but in a professional setting that limits what you show of yourself.
Meetings become planned: you have to suggest a date, postpone it, reorganize.
And the unexpected, which creates connections, becomes rare.
This diagnosis has the advantage of being actionable.
If friendships arise from repetition, then what works is regular activity: a weekly class, a sports club, a community engagement, a choir.
Not because the activity matters, but because it recreates frequency.
A single dinner rarely produces a friendship.
Twelve sessions of the same activity often do.
The other lever is less comfortable: you have to dare to propose.
In adulthood, someone has to make the first move, and everyone is waiting for the other to do it.
It's not intrusive.
In most cases, the person opposite is simply relieved.

sentences: In France, about one in three households consists of a single person.
This proportion has doubled in fifty years, and it continues to rise.
This figure is often commented on in a worried tone.
It deserves to be examined more calmly, as it mixes two different realities.
Living alone is a housing situation.
It is sometimes chosen and appreciated: freedom, calm, absence of daily compromises.
Many people living alone have a rich social life.
Isolation is something else.
It is the absence of regular relationships and support, and it can perfectly exist within a couple or a family.
This distinction is important because the documented health effects concern isolation, not the fact of living alone.
Research is quite convergent: prolonged isolation increases cardiovascular risks, promotes depression, and in some studies, compares to well-known risk factors like smoking.
The most affected populations are not always those we imagine.
Widowed elderly people, yes.
But also young adults who have just arrived in a city, and caregivers who look after a sick relative and have no time for themselves.
Effective responses do not consist of telling people to 'go out more.'
They create opportunities: associations, neighborhood activities, community gardens, third places, organized visits.
What makes these initiatives effective is regularity.
A one-time event is not enough.
Living alone is therefore neither good nor bad in itself.
What matters is the number of people who would notice your absence.

sentences: There is a contemporary paradox: never before has cooking been so present in the media, and never has the time spent cooking been so low.
Cooking shows attract millions of viewers.
Recipes circulate in video by the thousands.
However, the time spent daily on meal preparation has significantly decreased over the past fifty years, and the share of prepared dishes in purchases has greatly increased.
Watching someone cook is not the same as cooking.
This evolution can be easily explained: longer days, commutes, and an abundant and cheap supply of ready-made meals.
It would be unfair to see this as laziness.
But it has concrete consequences.
The first is financial.
Cooking with raw ingredients remains significantly cheaper, assuming comparable quality.
The second is nutritional.
Industrial dishes contain, on average, more salt, sugar, and additives, not out of malice, but because they need to be preserved and appeal immediately.
The third is a form of autonomy.
Knowing how to cook means being able to eat well on a budget, improvise with what you have, and not be entirely dependent on what the industry offers.
However, this is not a rare talent.
Five or six techniques are enough to cover the essentials: boiling eggs, sautéing onions, cooking starches, roasting vegetables, making a vinaigrette, and preparing a soup.
With this, you can manage months of meals.
This is not gastronomy, and that is not the goal.
It is simply about knowing how to feed oneself.

sentences: There comes a time, hard to pinpoint, when the relationship with your parents starts to change.
It's not a one-time event: it's a buildup of small signs.
An overlooked medical appointment.
An unpaid bill.
A conversation where you repeat the same thing three times.
A minor fall, but one that raises concern.
Most families react late, and there are good reasons for that.
Bringing up the topic means acknowledging a decline, something neither parents nor children want to do.
So, they postpone it until an emergency forces decisions to be made in a rush — often under the worst possible conditions.
People who have gone through this period almost always give the same advice: talk about it beforehand.
Not to organize everything, but to know some answers.
Where do your parents want to live if they can no longer stay alone?
Who should decide if they can no longer do so?
Where are the important documents located?
Who is the primary care physician?
These conversations are easier when they are hypothetical.
They become almost impossible in the hospital, on a Sunday evening.
There is a second point, less practical but just as real: guilt.
Many caregivers feel they never do enough, no matter how much time they give.
This guilt is exhausting, and it often leads caregivers to neglect their own health.
Taking care of a parent over several years means you need to still be standing at the end.
Asking for help is not giving up.
It's the condition for holding on.

sentences: We have more means of communication than any previous generation.
Messages, photos, free video calls to the other side of the world: everything is technically possible.
And yet, long-distance friendships continue to fade away, often without arguments and without any decision.
This paradox is partly explained by the nature of these tools.
They are excellent for brief and frequent contact: a photo, a reaction, a three-word message.
They are much less suited to what really builds a relationship, namely a long conversation without a specific goal.
However, we easily confuse the two.
Seeing someone's posts regularly gives the impression of keeping in touch.
In reality, we follow their life without ever talking to them.
The feeling of closeness increases while the relationship, on the other hand, deteriorates.
What works, according to those who maintain long-distance friendships over the years, comes down to two things.
The first is the chosen regularity.
A fixed appointment — the first Sunday of the month, a thirty-minute call — holds up much better than the good intention of calling each other 'soon.'
Without a date, time passes and awkwardness sets in.
The second is accepting that the relationship changes form.
A long-distance friendship cannot be what it was when we saw each other every week.
Wanting to find exactly the same thing mostly leads to disappointment.
I have a friend in Canada for six years.
We talk every other Sunday morning.
It's not much.
But it's written in both our calendars, and that's probably why it lasts.

sentences: People often imagine that a successful relationship is one without conflict.
Research conducted on couples over several decades suggests the opposite: it's not the frequency of disagreements that distinguishes lasting relationships, but how they unfold.
Certain patterns consistently appear in relationships that deteriorate.
The first is global criticism.
There is an important difference between 'you didn't do the dishes' and 'you never do anything.'
The first statement refers to a fact; the second refers to the person, and it almost necessarily invites a defense.
The second is contempt: hurtful irony, a condescending tone, eyes rolled to the sky.
This is the most negative signal identified in this research.
The third is withdrawal: not responding, leaving the room, giving up.
This ends the argument without resolving anything, and the problem reappears unchanged.

In contrast, effective exchanges share a few characteristics: they start gently, they focus on a specific behavior, they allow each person the opportunity to acknowledge a point, and they accept pauses when the tone rises.
A frequently mentioned detail: when one of the two becomes too tense to listen, the discussion can no longer progress.
A twenty-minute interruption, announced and followed by a return, changes everything.
None of this is unique to couples.
The same principles apply among friends, colleagues, and between parents and children.
It's not the disagreement that damages relationships.
It's the way we handle it, and especially how we end it.

sentences: There is a common confusion in ecological discussions: people put gestures with effects that differ by a factor of one hundred on the same level.
Turning off the light when leaving a room is a good habit.
But in terms of emissions, it cannot be compared to a long-haul flight.
The available analyses provide fairly stable orders of magnitude for a European household.
What weighs the most are, in no particular order: air travel, the daily use of a personal car, heating a poorly insulated home, and food — particularly red meat.
What weighs significantly less includes: plastic bags, straws, letting tap water run for a few seconds, and lighting.
This does not mean that small gestures are useless.
They have a value of habit and consistency, and some have other benefits — plastic pollution is a real problem, even if its climate impact is low.

But it is discouraging, and a bit unfair, to place a disproportionate guilt on households for marginal gestures, while structural decisions — such as housing insulation, transport options, and urban planning — largely depend on public policies and businesses.
The practical conclusion is rather liberating.

It's better to focus your efforts on two or three truly important levers — reducing air travel, insulating your home, changing how you move around daily, adjusting your diet — rather than spreading yourself thin over twenty micro-gestures.
And there is one last lever, often forgotten: the voice.
A citizen who votes, writes, or supports a local project carries more weight than perfectly sorting their waste.

sentences: It is estimated that several million French homes are considered to be "thermal sieves": poorly insulated, expensive to heat, uncomfortable in winter, and increasingly unbearable in summer.
The topic seems technical.
In reality, it is as much a social issue as an ecological one.
Heating accounts for a significant share of emissions related to housing, and buildings are one of the main sources of emissions in the country.
Reducing heating needs is therefore a major lever.
But the most immediate effect concerns the residents themselves.
Living in a poorly insulated home means paying more to be less well heated.
It is often the most modest households that occupy these homes, especially in rental situations.
This is referred to as "energy poverty": having to choose between heating properly and other essential expenses.
Why is renovation progressing slowly?
First, because it is expensive: a complete renovation costs tens of thousands of euros.
There are aids available, but the applications are complex and you often have to pay upfront.
Then, because the owner is not always the one who pays for heating.
A landlord has no direct financial incentive to insulate a property for which they do not pay the bills.
Finally, because the work is extensive and the number of trained craftsmen remains insufficient.
Measures have been taken, including the gradual ban on renting the least efficient homes.
These measures raise legitimate debates: if poorly implemented, they can reduce the rental supply.
But leaving millions of households in homes that are expensive to heat is not a viable policy either.

sentences: I'm too old to learn that." This phrase is one of the most common, and one of the least accurate.
The adult brain retains a capacity for learning throughout life.
This phenomenon has a name, brain plasticity, and it is well established: connections reorganize based on what one practices, at thirty as well as at seventy.
That doesn't mean there are no differences.
Some things are indeed easier when young, especially acquiring a perfect accent in a foreign language.

But adults have real and underestimated advantages: they understand structures, make connections with what they already know, choose their methods, and know why they are learning — a chosen motivation is better than an imposed one.
What mainly changes are the conditions.
An adult has less time, more fatigue, and much more fear of looking foolish.
This fear is probably the main obstacle, well before age.
Research on learning provides some solid principles that are valid at any age.
Spaced repetition beats massed repetition: three times twenty minutes in a week is better than one hour on Sunday.
Testing oneself is more effective than rereading.
Trying to remember, even without succeeding, anchors more than just reviewing the text.
Finally, moderate difficulty is useful: what is too easy teaches nothing.
So the question is not whether one can still learn.
It is whether one accepts being bad for a few weeks.

sentences: The term 'eco-anxiety' has recently appeared in public debate.
It refers to the worry, sometimes deep, felt in response to climate change and environmental degradation.
Several international surveys indicate that a significant portion of young people report feeling anxious, and a notable fraction says it affects their daily lives, even their future plans.
We need to be cautious with these figures, but the phenomenon is real and documented.
The first thing to say is that this is not an illness.
Worrying about a documented danger is a rational reaction.
To treat this anxiety as a simple individual disorder would be to ask people to misperceive reality.
That said, anxiety that paralyzes is not helpful to anyone, neither to the person nor to the cause.
What psychologists working on this subject report is quite consistent.

What exacerbates the feeling of helplessness: the continuous consumption of catastrophic information without the possibility of acting, and isolation — experiencing this worry alone, surrounded by people who do not talk about it.

Another helpful element: distinguishing what we can act on from what we cannot.
No one can solve global climate issues alone.
But almost everyone can do something somewhere, with others.
