sentences: Many people today are noticing the same thing, a bit worried: they can no longer concentrate like they used to.
Reading a book for an hour, following a long argument, staying absorbed in a single task without giving in to the urge to check one's phone — what used to be taken for granted now seems difficult.
This is not an isolated impression; it is a widely shared experience, and it deserves to be taken seriously.
First, we must dismiss an overly simple explanation, one that would blame a weakening of individuals.
Our brains haven't changed in twenty years.
What has changed is the environment in which they operate.
We now live under an unending stream of distractions: notifications, messages, alerts, content that constantly demands our attention.
However, attention, by its nature, is built over time and continuity, precisely what these interruptions destroy.
Every interruption has a cost that we underestimate.
When our attention is diverted, even for a few seconds, it then takes effort and time to get back on track.
Multiply these breaks by the dozens of times they occur each day, and you get a mind that never really settles, jumping from one thing to another without ever diving in.
This is sometimes called 'continuous partial attention': we are a bit everywhere, and fully nowhere.
The consequences go beyond mere discomfort.
Deep thinking — the kind that allows us to understand a complex idea, to create, to truly reflect — requires sustained concentration.
A culture that would make this concentration rare would, in turn, make deep thinking rarer.
It's not just our comfort that is at stake, but our collective ability to think.
The good news is that concentration can be retrained.
Like a muscle, it strengthens through exercise: setting aside screen-free time, reading long texts again, accepting boredom instead of fleeing from it immediately.
None of this is spectacular, and nothing is immediate.
But the effort is worth it.
Regaining one's ability to concentrate is not just about working better; it's about reclaiming control over one's own mind.

sentences: We have seen that 'free' services come at the cost of our attention.
They also come at another cost, something even more intimate: our personal data.
Every search, every purchase, every movement, every message leaves a trace, and these traces, when gathered, create a disturbingly precise portrait.
This portrait has value, and it is partly what we give up in exchange for free services.
For a long time, this concern has been brushed aside with a phrase: 'I have nothing to hide.' The argument seems sensible; however, it is fragile.
The protection of privacy has never been about hiding faults, but about maintaining a space that belongs only to oneself.
Closing the door to one's room is not an admission of a guilty secret; it is the exercise of a basic freedom.
Yet it is precisely this door that the massive collection of data tends to keep open permanently.
Moreover, the objection of 'nothing to hide' assumes that this data will never be used against us.
Nothing guarantees that.
A seemingly innocuous piece of information today can become compromising tomorrow, if laws change or if power shifts.
Data collected for a specific purpose can be diverted to another.
Entrusting one's traces is to make a bet on the future, a bet whose terms we do not control.
Finally, we must go beyond just the individual perspective.

Even if everyone, for their own sake, willingly accepted this exchange, the accumulation of our data gives a few companies considerable power: the power to predict our behaviors, to shape our choices, and sometimes to influence our opinions.
This power does not only concern the individuals who have, apparently, consented; it weighs on society as a whole.
Defending privacy is therefore not a whim of people who have something to hide.
It is defending a condition of freedom, for oneself and for others.
The free services offered to us come at a price, and this price is not only personal: it is, ultimately, political.

sentences: After measuring the power of the devices that capture our attention, one question remains: what to do?
Simply "making an effort" is not enough, as we've seen, since the game is uneven.
Regaining control of our attention is not just a matter of willpower; it requires organization, method, and no illusions.
The first principle is to modify your environment rather than rely on your discipline.
Our willpower is a limited resource that quickly gets depleted; it's pointless to call on it at every moment.
It's better to act upstream: turn off notifications, remove the most captivating apps from your phone, and physically distance the screen during work or meals.
You can't resist a temptation you don't encounter.
The second principle is to rehabilitate boredom.
We've gotten into the habit of filling every little void — a queue, a journey, a break — by immediately grabbing our phone.
However, these empty moments have value: it's often in boredom that the mind wanders, reflects, and invents.
By systematically filling them, we deprive ourselves of precious time.
Accepting to be bored sometimes is to give the mind back a space that had been taken from it.
The third principle is to deliberately cultivate long attention.
Just as a flood of interruptions weakens it, regular practice strengthens it.

Reading an entire book, listening to a piece of music without doing anything else, walking without headphones: these seemingly modest practices retrain a faculty that the surrounding world tends to atrophy.
Finally, it's important to approach all of this without guilt.
The goal is not to give up digital tools, which provide immense services, nor to judge ourselves harshly for every slip.
It's about restoring a more equitable balance of power, where we decide our attention, not machines designed to capture it.
Our attention is what we have that is most precious: it is through it that we connect with the world, with others, and with ourselves.
Defending it is not a whim; it is to safeguard the very fabric of our inner life.

sentences: Never before has humanity had access to so much information.
At any hour, from anywhere, we can know what is happening on the other side of the world, almost in real time.
This abundance should make us exceptionally well-informed citizens.
However, nothing is less certain, and it may even be that the opposite is true.
The first problem lies in the volume.
A continuous stream of information does not allow time to digest it.
Barely have we grasped one event before another pushes it aside, then another still.
This succession creates the illusion of following the world, while it prevents us from understanding it.
Understanding requires perspective, connections, and context — everything that speed forbids.
The second problem lies in the nature of what captures our attention.
In a saturated space, only the most striking content floats to the surface: the dramatic, the scandalous, the shocking.
Not because they are the most important, but because they catch the eye.
Thus, a distorted image of the world forms, where the exceptional seems ordinary and where slow, yet decisive, changes remain invisible due to their lack of spectacle.
A third problem, more insidious, concerns our emotions.
Continuous information keeps us in a state of permanent alertness, mixing anxiety, anger, and helplessness.
However, a constantly agitated mind judges poorly.
Overwhelmed by anxiety-inducing news over which we have no control, we often end up feeling overwhelmed without any action resulting from it.
Should we then cut ourselves off from current events?
That would be a reverse error, as staying informed remains a duty in a democracy.
The solution is not to know less, but to know differently.
It is better to read a few in-depth analyses than to swallow dozens of brief articles; it is better to choose our moments of information than to endure a constant flow.
Truly staying informed requires an effort that the ease of continuous flow makes us forget.
Being exposed to information is not the same as understanding it, and confusing the two means believing oneself to be enlightened while merely flailing in the dark.

sentences: One can live for thirty years in a city without ever feeling that it belongs to us.
We work there, we sleep there, we move around there, but we pass through it more than we inhabit it.
This feeling, very common in contemporary large cities, raises a question that is far from obvious: what does it take to feel at home in a place, and not just to reside there?
The answer partly lies in public space.

A city is not just an addition of housing and offices; it is also made up of streets, squares, gardens, benches — all those places that do not belong to anyone in particular and thus, in a sense, belong to everyone.
This is where the feeling of belonging is played out.
Where public space is welcoming, we linger, we meet, we weave those tenuous connections that make a neighborhood feel like our own.
Where it shrinks, we just pass through.
However, this common space is today weakened.
It is shrinking under the pressure of cars, commerce, and sometimes fear.
We design places for consumption, not for staying without buying anything.
We multiply the measures that discourage sitting, lingering, or simply being there.
Little by little, the city stops offering places where one can exist for free, and with them disappears a part of what made it livable.
Feeling at home also implies having a say in one's living environment.
However, the decisions that shape a city — what is built there, what is demolished — often escape the residents.
They are rarely asked for their opinion, and when they are, it is sometimes just for show.
How can one appropriate a place that one has not helped to shape, and that can change overnight without our input?

sentences: The scenario is repeating itself in many cities, and it has something troubling about it.
A neighborhood that was once modest, even neglected, is starting to change.
Cafés are opening, old buildings are being renovated, and wealthier residents are moving in, attracted by the charm and still affordable prices.
The neighborhood is becoming more beautiful and gaining a reputation.
And as it becomes desirable, those who have lived there forever can no longer afford to stay.
This phenomenon, often referred to by a word borrowed from English, 'gentrification', has a double face.
On one hand, it's hard to regret that a degraded neighborhood is being renovated, better maintained, safer, and better served.
Such improvements are, in themselves, welcome, and no one seriously wishes for neighborhoods to remain poor to preserve their 'authenticity'.
On the other hand, these transformations have a human cost that is too often overlooked.
As rents rise, the original residents — often the most modest — are forced to leave, driven out not by force but by price.
They are replaced without being formally evicted, which makes the injustice less visible, but no less real.
A neighborhood can thus become more beautiful while emptying of those who had made it vibrant.
What is lost is not just housing, but a web of relationships: the shopkeepers we knew, long-time neighbors, the habits patiently woven.
One does not just move out of an apartment; one is torn away from a world.
And those who arrive, however well-intentioned they may be, inherit a place whose soul has partly fled with its former inhabitants.
Should we then give up on improving poor neighborhoods?
Certainly not.
But we can do it differently, ensuring that renovations first benefit those who live there, rather than replacing them.
This requires protected housing, rent control, and a political will not to abandon residents to the sole laws of the market.
For a just city does not simply beautify its neighborhoods: it ensures that those who have inhabited them can remain.

sentences: There is a paradox unique to big cities: it is often there, surrounded by millions of human beings, that one feels the most alone.
Every day, we pass by hundreds of faces without knowing any of them.
We live just a few meters away from neighbors whose names we don't know.

This solitude in the midst of the crowd is one of the characteristic experiences of urban life, and it fuels a recurring criticism: big cities make people cold, indifferent, and strangers to one another.
This criticism is not without foundation.
In a village, everyone knows everyone, and this familiarity creates a natural mutual aid, a safety net of solidarity.
In the big city, this safety net becomes stretched.
One can go through a hardship without anyone noticing, fall ill without anyone caring.
Urban anonymity does have a shadowy side, and it would be dishonest to deny it.
But it would be just as unfair to focus only on the dark side, because this anonymity is also a form of freedom.
In the village where everyone knows each other, everyone observes each other, and the gaze of others can sometimes weigh heavily.
Those who don't fit the mold, who live differently, who want to escape a past or a reputation, find in the anonymity of the city a space to breathe.
One can be oneself there without having to explain, change one's life without the whole village commenting on it.
That is why big cities have so often attracted those whom their original environment stifled.
The artist, the outsider, the one who loves differently, the one who wants to start over: all have seen in the city not a human desert, but a promise of emancipation.
The indifference of others, so harsh when one suffers, becomes beneficial when one simply wants to live without being judged.
The anonymity of cities is therefore neither an absolute evil nor an absolute good; it is both depending on the moment in life one is in.

The challenge is not to eliminate it — one cannot know millions of people — but to create, within the vast anonymous city, small circles of familiarity: a building where people greet each other, a neighborhood where one has their bearings.
The freedom of the unknown, tempered by the warmth of a few chosen connections.

sentences: We are promised the 'smart city': a city filled with sensors, capable of continuously measuring traffic, energy consumption, air quality, pedestrian flows, and adjusting its operations accordingly.
Traffic lights that adapt to traffic, lighting that adjusts to presence, optimized transport: the idea is appealing, and its promises of efficiency are not illusory.
Well designed, such a city could waste less and function better.
However, behind this technically appealing vision lies a question that enthusiasm often forgets: a city that measures everything is also a city that monitors everything.
The same sensors that optimize traffic can track people's movements.
The same data that improves a service can be used to control, profile, and predict behaviors.
The line between an efficient city and a surveillance city is thinner than one might think.
We must therefore ask who holds this data and for what purposes.
Too often, the infrastructure of the smart city is designed and operated by private companies, which gain valuable knowledge about the residents.
In exchange for a few conveniences, they find themselves constantly observed, often without having wanted or even understood it.
The city, an ideal common space, risks becoming a vast capture device, to the benefit of a few.
Another concern relates to democracy.
When a city is managed by algorithms, who decides their rules?
Software that allocates resources, directs investments, or prioritizes needs actually wields political power.
Moreover, this power escapes public debate: we do not vote for an algorithm, and we even struggle to understand how it works.
Technical efficiency then tends to replace collective choice.
None of this condemns the idea of a smarter city.
Technology can provide real services, as long as it remains a means and not an end.
But this requires us to ask the right questions from the outset: who controls the data, for what purpose, under what democratic oversight?
A city is not smart because it measures everything; it is smart when it puts technology at the service of those who inhabit it, and not the other way around.

sentences: Noise may be the most underestimated form of pollution in urban life.
Traffic, construction sites, sirens, machines, amplified voices: the city produces a constant background noise that we eventually stop paying attention to.
Not that it has disappeared, but because we have gotten used to it.
However, this habit is deceptive: even when we no longer listen to it, noise continues to affect us.
Research on this topic is compelling.
Prolonged exposure to noise not only causes temporary discomfort; it affects sleep, raises tension, and maintains a state of stress of which we are not even aware.
The body reacts to the din even if the mind believes it is ignoring it.
Silence is therefore not just a luxury for sensitive souls; it is a condition of health, just like air or water.
The problem is that silence, in our cities, has become an unevenly distributed luxury.
Those who can afford it settle in quiet neighborhoods, soundproof their homes, and escape on weekends to peaceful places.
The others endure, with no escape, the continuous rumble of major roads and poorly soundproofed housing.
Calm, once available to everyone, is thus tending to become a privilege that money can buy.
Restoring a place for silence in the city is, however, not out of reach.
This involves concrete choices: limiting speed and thus noise from traffic, greening the streets, creating calm zones, and demanding better sound insulation for homes.
None of these measures are spectacular, but their cumulative effect would profoundly transform the daily experience of millions of residents.
We must especially stop viewing noise as an inevitability of urban life, a nuisance to which we should simply adapt.
The din is not an unavoidable characteristic of cities; it is the result of choices—of planning, transport, construction—that other choices could correct.
Demanding silence is not fleeing the city or dreaming of an impossible countryside calm.
It is asking that urban life, so dense and vibrant, also allows for spaces where we can finally hear ourselves think.

sentences: Eating was for a long time one of the simplest acts of existence: we ate what we had, what the region produced, what the season offered.
In just a few decades, this act has strangely become complicated.
Every meal now seems to raise questions: is it good for my health?
for the planet?
for the animals?
for the producers?
What was once obvious has become a field of concerns and sometimes guilt.
This complexity is not imaginary; it reflects a new reality.

Today we know what we didn't know yesterday: the impact of our diet on the climate, the conditions in which animals are raised, the effects of certain products on our bodies, the difficulties of the agricultural world.
This knowledge is progress, but it has a downside: it burdens each bite with a moral weight that previous generations did not know.
The risk is twofold.
On one hand, there is a convenient indifference, which consists of wanting to know nothing in order to keep eating without thinking.
On the other hand, there is a constant anxiety, which turns every meal into a dilemma and ultimately spoils a pleasure that is essential.
Between blindness and obsession, it is not always easy to find a way.
We must first recognize that few choices are perfect.
The ideal food — healthy, ecological, ethical, accessible, tasty — practically never exists.
Eating is almost always about dealing with contradictory constraints: what is good for health is not always affordable, what is ecological is not always available.
Demanding perfection means condemning oneself to failure and guilt.
A more reasonable attitude would be to aim for better rather than perfect.
Reduce, without necessarily eliminating; prioritize, without completely forbidding oneself; inform oneself, without becoming paralyzed.
Small changes maintained over time are better than a brief and heroic strictness.
Finally, it is important not to forget what a meal is also: a pleasure, a moment of sharing, a cultural heritage.
By making food too much about calculations and rules, we risk forgetting that it is primarily one of the great joys of living.
Eating with awareness, yes; eating with anxiety, certainly not.

sentences: This is a figure that should make us stop: about a third of the food produced in the world is never eaten.
It is lost or thrown away at some point in its journey, from the farm to the plate.
In a world where millions of people still suffer from hunger, and where food production heavily impacts the environment, such waste is truly scandalous.
We first need to understand where this waste occurs, as the responsibilities are shared.
Some of the losses happen very early, in the fields and during transport: damaged crops, fruits discarded because they are not the right size, goods lost due to lack of preservation methods.
Another part occurs in stores, where items approaching their expiration date or those that do not sell are thrown away.
Finally, the last part happens at home, in our kitchens, where we buy too much, forget, and let things spoil.
What strikes you about this waste is its absurdity.
It does not result from a shortage, but rather from a poorly managed abundance.
We do not throw away food because we lack it, but because we have too much and treat it as something worthless.
Absurd aesthetic standards lead to the rejection of perfectly edible vegetables; a too-strict reading of dates causes good products to be thrown away.
The good news is that none of these causes are insurmountable.
Unlike other environmental issues that require deep transformations, the fight against waste often relies on common sense and organization.

Redistributing unsold goods, revising appearance standards, clarifying dates, better planning purchases: these are all concrete measures, already successfully tested, that require no sacrifice, only attention.
On an individual level, a few simple habits are enough to significantly reduce one's own waste: buying according to real needs, using leftovers, trusting your senses rather than a date.
Nothing heroic, just a basic respect for what food represents.
Food waste may be one of the few major problems that could be largely solved without sacrifice, simply by stopping to treat as waste what has required so much land, water, and labor.
In short, we just need to remember the value of what we throw away.
Few food-related questions stir up as much passion as that of meat.
It touches on deep habits, childhood memories, a certain idea of a meal, and just bringing it up can sometimes be irritating.
However, it deserves to be examined calmly, distinguishing the arguments rather than getting heated.
Three main reasons support reducing our meat consumption.
The first is ecological: livestock farming, especially of large animals, significantly contributes to emissions responsible for global warming and requires considerable amounts of land and water.
The second is health-related: excessive consumption of meat, particularly processed meat, is associated with various health issues.
The third is ethical: the conditions in which many animals are raised rightly disturb a growing number of consciences.
These arguments are serious, and it would be dishonest to dismiss them.
But we must also avoid two symmetrical extremes.
The first would be to deny these realities and change nothing about one's habits.
The second, conversely, would be to make the issue a moral absolute, dividing the world into the virtuous and the guilty, and shaming anyone who still eats meat.
The truth is that 'eating less meat' does not mean 'never eating it again.'
Between a daily plate of meat and total abandonment, there is a vast middle ground where most reasonable solutions lie.

Reducing frequency, choosing higher quality and better-produced meat, making it an occasion rather than a habit: these changes, modest on an individual scale, would have a considerable effect if widely adopted.
We must also recognize the real obstacles.
Changing one's diet requires time, knowledge, and sometimes resources.
We cannot expect the same efforts from someone who cooks without constraints and someone who is already struggling to feed themselves.
Making meat reduction a purely individual matter, without considering these inequalities, would be unjust.
The question is therefore not whether one is 'for' or 'against' meat, as if it were a camp to choose.
It is about how much, which kind, how often — questions of measure, not dogma.
And in this regard, everyone can progress at their own pace, without giving up all at once or blinding themselves to the issues.

sentences: A recipe is never just a list of ingredients and actions.
It carries within it a story, that of a region, a family, a time.

The dish that a grandmother passes on to her grandchildren is not just food: it is a fragment of memory, a connection to those who cooked it before, a way to preserve a bit of what, without it, would disappear.
In this sense, cooking is a heritage, but a particular heritage: alive, fragile, that only exists as long as it is practiced.
This is what distinguishes it from a monument or a painting.
A cathedral remains even if no one looks at it; a recipe, on the other hand, dies as soon as we stop making it.
It is not preserved in a museum, but in hands that repeat actions, in a transmission that plays out from one generation to the next.
Break this chain, and a whole body of knowledge vanishes, often without us realizing it until it’s too late.
However, this transmission is now under threat.
Time is lacking, lifestyles have changed, and it has become so easy to buy ready-made that we cook less and less.
What’s the point of learning a dish that takes a long time to prepare when you can, in just a few minutes, get an equivalent?
The question seems reasonable, but it overlooks what is lost in the exchange: not just a flavor, but a know-how and the connection it carried.
It is not about condemning convenience, nor about insisting that everyone spend hours at the stove.
Modern life has its constraints, and one can legitimately rely, sometimes, on ease.
But it would be a shame to let this domestic art completely disappear, on the pretext that it is no longer necessary.
For what is no longer necessary is not therefore without value.
Cooking for oneself, passing on a recipe, learning a dish from one's family: these modest actions maintain a precious link with the past and with others.
They remind us that eating is not just a function, but a culture.
Preserving this living heritage requires neither law nor museum: only that, from time to time, someone takes the time to do and to show.

sentences: Among all the rituals that once structured daily life, the shared meal is one of the last to endure.
Meeting at a fixed time, around the same table, to eat together: this seemingly mundane gesture is also one of the few moments when a family or community truly comes together.
However, this ritual, long taken for granted, is gradually unraveling, and it's worth considering what is at stake in this slow dissolution.
The causes are well known.
Schedules have become desynchronized: everyone eats when they can, according to their timetable.
Screens have made their way to the table, capturing the gazes that once met.
Individual food, eaten alone and in haste, has gained ground over shared dishes.
Little by little, the meal is ceasing to be a moment of gathering and is becoming a simple function, carried out by each person on their own.
What is being lost in this evolution is not insignificant.
The shared meal is not just about food; it is a space for conversation, transmission, and connection.
It is often here that news is exchanged, where children learn to listen and speak, and where, day after day, the invisible threads that connect family members are woven.
Eliminate this moment, and you do not just remove a dinner: you take away one of the main supports of communal life.
Studies on the subject confirm this intuition.
Where meals are regularly shared, family bonds are stronger, and children themselves benefit in many ways.

Not that the meal has magical virtues, but because it creates what modern life offers increasingly rarely: a regular, predictable time where we are simply together, with no other purpose than to be there.
Preserving this ritual does not require great means, just a decision: to treat the shared meal as an important appointment, and not as a variable adjustment.
Turning off screens, waiting for one another, making dinner a protected moment: these modest choices are often enough to save what, once lost, is hard to regain.
In a world that scatters our lives, the shared meal remains one of the last places where we can gather every day.
It would be a strange poverty to let it disappear through simple neglect.

sentences: A discreet but significant social fact marks our time: never before have so many people lived alone.
In large cities, single-person households have become one of the most common ways of life.
This phenomenon, historically unprecedented on this scale, provokes contradictory reactions: some see it as progress, while others view it as a worrying symptom.
The truth, as often, resists easy conclusions.
On one hand, living alone is also a sign of newfound freedom.
For centuries, few could afford it: people lived with family out of economic necessity, and prolonged singleness was often endured rather than chosen.
The fact that so many people can live alone today is a testament to an autonomy — material, social, personal — that did not exist before.
Many live alone because they want to, and they find a space to be fully themselves.
On the other hand, this evolution comes with a very real risk: isolation.
Living alone does not necessarily mean being alone, but the two sometimes overlap.
Without the daily connections that communal living once imposed, some slide, almost without noticing, into a solitude they did not choose.
The danger is all the greater because it is silent: one can gradually isolate themselves without anyone noticing.
We must therefore be wary of both symmetrical discourses.
Those who blissfully celebrate the solitary lifestyle forget that human beings remain social animals, who need others to thrive.
Those who lament a collapse of connection forget that living alone can be a happy choice, and that forced marriage of the past was far from paradise.
What the rise of solitary living reveals most of all is a new challenge: since we no longer live automatically surrounded, we must now build our social circles more deliberately.
The connections that communal living provided effortlessly, everyone must now cultivate: maintained friendships, vibrant neighborhoods, shared commitments.
Living alone is therefore neither a blessing nor a curse in itself; it all depends on what one makes of it, and especially on the connections one weaves beyond their own home.
Chosen solitude can be a wealth; imposed solitude remains a trial.
The whole difference lies in this little word: choose.

sentences: Sometimes, it only takes a detail to reveal a profound change.
Researchers have observed that the mere presence of a phone placed on a table, even when it is turned off and face down, is enough to alter the quality of a conversation.
Exchanges become more superficial, and the participants confide less, as if the object, by its mere presence, reminds us that an elsewhere is always available.
This observation, seemingly trivial, says a lot about what constant connectivity does to our relationships.
The mechanism is subtle.
Our deepest conversations require full attention and a certain vulnerability: one must feel listened to in order to dare to open up.
However, the presence of a screen, always ready to grab our attention, introduces a latent distraction.
Even when we are not looking at it, we know it is there, and this diffuse awareness is enough to hold back, shorten, and prevent the exchange from going deep.
In addition, there is a broader transformation of our relational habits.
We multiply brief contacts — a message, a reaction, a notification — at the expense of long and attentive exchanges.
We are constantly connected to dozens of people, but rarely fully present to the one in front of us.
The quantity of our interactions has exploded; their depth, however, has diminished.
We should not give in to the easy nostalgia for a golden age of conversation that may never have existed.
Screens also connect us to those who are far away and provide immense services.
The problem is not the technology itself, but the way it becomes a permanent third party, present even in our most intimate moments.
The solution does not lie in a dramatic rejection, but in a few simple and deliberate gestures: putting away your phone during a meal, a moment of sharing, or a significant time.
Creating, during the day, protected spaces where we are truly present, fully there for the other person.
For what we risk losing, due to partial presence, is not trivial: it is that quality of attention that truly connects us in a conversation.
Being fully present with someone has paradoxically become one of the rarest gifts we can offer.

sentences: It has never been easier to meet someone.
Apps put thousands of potential partners at our fingertips, which we can sort, compare, and contact with a simple gesture.
In theory, this abundance should make love more accessible than ever.
In practice, many report the opposite: they have never had so many choices, nor found it so difficult to form attachments.
This paradox deserves our attention.
The first effect of unlimited choice is to change our perspective on others.
Faced with an apparently endless offer, each person we meet becomes just one option among others, compared to those that might follow.
Why invest in an imperfect relationship when a more attractive profile seems just a gesture away?
This logic, borrowed from consumerism, clashes with what love requires: patience, commitment, and acceptance of imperfections.
The second effect is more subtle.
By choosing too much, we end up not knowing how to choose.
Psychology has shown that, beyond a certain threshold, an abundance of options does not liberate: it paralyzes.
We hesitate, we procrastinate, we always keep a door open, for fear of giving up something better.
And by wanting to reserve the best for ourselves, we often miss out on the good.
This is not about condemning these tools, which have also allowed countless couples to form, and which help those whom life has not brought together.
The problem is not the tool, but the mindset it encourages: that of the consumer who compares, never quite satisfied, always in search of the ideal option that, by definition, does not exist.
Loving perhaps requires, at its core, the opposite of what unlimited choice promises.
Not finding the perfect person among an infinity of possibilities, but deciding to commit to a real person, with their flaws, and to build something with them rather than continuing to search.
Commitment is not the end of freedom; it may be its deepest use.
In a world that constantly invites us to keep all our options open, truly choosing someone — and giving up, for them, all the others — has become an act almost counter to the current trend.
Perhaps this is what gives it, today more than ever, its value.

sentences: Many people experience this as they get older, without always daring to admit it: it becomes harder to make real friends.
Friendships from childhood and youth were formed almost effortlessly, supported by the daily proximity of school or studies.
In adulthood, this ease disappears, and one discovers that friendship, far from being automatic, now requires an attention that one never had to give it before.
The reasons for this are concrete.
Adult life scatters: we move, change jobs, start families, and free time becomes scarce.
The opportunities for regular meetings, which used to spark friendships without us thinking about it, become rare.
However, friendship needs time and repetition: you don't become close to someone you only see occasionally.
What used to be woven simply through the force of habit now requires intentional maintenance.
This evolution explains a discreet but widespread phenomenon: the slow disappearance of friendships that mattered.
Not due to quarrels or disagreements, but simply through neglect.
We don't argue; we gradually stop seeing each other.
Connections don't break suddenly; they unravel due to lack of maintenance, like a garden that one has stopped tending.
Recognizing this is not despairing; on the contrary, it's liberating.
For if adult friendship no longer arises on its own, it can still be built, provided one dedicates intention to it.
Proposing, following up, setting regular appointments, being the one to take the first step: these somewhat voluntary gestures are the price of friendship in adulthood.
They may seem artificial to those who long for the spontaneous bonds of the past, but they are, in reality, a form of loyalty.
One must also accept that not all friendships are meant to last, and that some fade naturally, without us having to feel guilty.
The important thing is not to hold on to everyone, but to nurture what truly matters.
Adult friendship may be less easy than that of youth, but it is no less precious — and the very fact that it requires effort gives it, in a sense, more value.
What we deliberately choose to cultivate is often worth more than what was simply given to us.

sentences: Few institutions have changed as much, in such a short time, as the family.
The model that seemed so obvious just a few decades ago — a married couple for life, surrounded by their children — is now just one form among many.
Blended families, single-parent families, childless families, uniting same-sex couples: the diversity of configurations is now the norm.
In the face of this transformation, a concern arises: are we witnessing the decline, or even the disappearance, of the family?
This fear is based on a misunderstanding.
What is declining is not the family, but a particular form of family, historically situated, that we had come to see as the only possible one.
However, history shows that the family has always varied according to the times and places.
The model we believed to be eternal was itself just a moment in a long evolution.
So, what we are observing is not the end of the family, but a new metamorphosis.
What remains, across all these forms, is the essential function of the family: to provide a lasting bond, a place of belonging, and support in the face of life's challenges.
That this bond takes on new forms does not make it any less real.
A child raised with love by a single parent, or by two same-sex parents, does not lack a family; they simply have one that does not resemble the image of the past.
It would be naive to deny that these changes also pose difficulties.
Blended families must invent bonds without an established model; isolated parents bear a heavy burden alone; the reference points, less obvious, must be constructed rather than received.
Recognizing the richness of these new forms does not mean ignoring the challenges they present.
But the essential point may lie elsewhere.
What makes a family has never been conformity to a model, but the quality of the bonds that unite its members: attention, loyalty, love that withstands the test of time.
In this light, a family that does not resemble any image of the past can be a fully-fledged family, and a family that appears conventional may only have the appearance of one.
The family is not disappearing; it is reinventing itself, as it always has.
And as long as human beings need to be loved and supported by others over time, it will continue to exist, in a thousand forms.

sentences: Technology is neutral; it all depends on how we use it." This phrase, repeated a thousand times, has a reassuring quality: it places the responsibility entirely on the user and absolves the tool itself.
A knife can cut bread or harm; it is not the knife that decides.
The idea seems sensible.
However, upon closer inspection, it is largely insufficient.
For while every technology allows for multiple uses, it does not allow them all equally.
Each tool makes some actions easy and others difficult; it inclines, it directs, it suggests.
A car does not force anyone to drive fast, but it makes speed possible and desirable in a way that a bicycle does not.
A social network does not compel anyone to compare themselves to others, but it is designed in such a way that comparison becomes almost inevitable.
The tool does not decide for us, but it is also not indifferent to what we do with it.
We can go further.
Some technologies carry effects within them that go beyond any individual use.
The automobile, by becoming widespread, did not just transport people: it reshaped cities, dispersed living spaces, transformed our lifestyles.
No one had decided this; it is the tool itself that, by its own logic, has shaped the world around it.
To claim it was 'neutral' is to ignore this power of transformation.
Recognizing this does not mean holding technology responsible for everything, nor does it absolve individuals.
We remain free in our uses, and this freedom is real.
But it operates within a framework that the tool has already, in part, set up.
Ignoring this framework is to believe oneself freer than one is, and to become blind to the forces that shape our behaviors.
The issue is important, as it concerns how we conceive of technologies themselves.
If we accept that they are not neutral, then it becomes legitimate to ask, even before adopting them, what uses they favor and what effects they produce.
The question is no longer just 'how will I use it?', but 'what will this tool do to me, and to us?'.
Believing technology is neutral is to give up judging it.
However, the tools we give ourselves shape us in return, and it is better to know this before they change us.

sentences: For a long time, we reassured ourselves by thinking that machines would only replace repetitive and physical tasks, leaving humans with the monopoly on intelligence, creativity, and judgment.
This boundary, which we believed to be solid, has begun to waver.
Programs write texts, produce images, analyze documents, and hold conversations.
Activities that we considered exclusively human are now, in part, automatable.
How can we think about this upheaval without succumbing to either panic or blindness?
We must first dismiss two equally misleading narratives.
The first predicts a catastrophe: machines will do everything, human work will disappear, and mass unemployment is inevitable.
The second promises a paradise: technology will free us from menial tasks and leave us with the best.
History suggests that reality will be more nuanced, and especially more unequal, than these opposing prophecies claim.
What we can reasonably anticipate is a profound transformation, rather than a simple disappearance of work.
Some tasks will be automated, others will emerge, and many jobs will be less eliminated than redefined.
Past experience shows that new techniques destroy jobs but create others, often unpredictably.
However, nothing guarantees that this will be painless, nor that the jobs lost and created will concern the same people.
This is where the real issue lies, often overlooked in the debate.
The problem is not so much automation itself as the way its benefits and costs will be distributed.
If productivity gains enrich a minority while others lose their jobs without prospects, technology will have worsened inequalities.
If, on the contrary, these gains are shared and supported — through training, protection, and job distribution — it can benefit the greatest number.
In other words, the consequences of artificial intelligence are not inscribed in the technology itself; they will depend on collective choices.
It is not the machine that will decide whether it liberates or impoverishes us, but the society that employs it and how it organizes its effects.
In the face of these transformations, the right attitude is neither resignation nor naive enthusiasm, but vigilance.
A powerful technology is never good or bad in itself; it all depends on what we make of it, together.

sentences: In the face of climate change, a question often arises, often tinged with discouragement: what's the point?
What weight can my gesture, so modest, have in the face of such a vast problem?
I sort my waste, I reduce my consumption, while entire industries continue to pollute massively.
Isn't it ridiculous, even hypocritical?
This question is legitimate, and it deserves an honest answer that neither resorts to guilt nor offers empty reassurances.
We must first acknowledge a grain of truth in the doubt.
Yes, on a planetary scale, an individual's gesture is tiny.
No, sorting our waste alone will not be enough to solve the climate crisis.

Those who let others believe that responsibility rests entirely on consumers are making a mistake, and sometimes an act of dishonesty: they divert attention from the collective and industrial decisions that truly weigh heavily.
But drawing the conclusion from this observation that our gestures are useless would be another error, symmetrical and just as convenient.
For this conclusion, in reality, is quite convenient: it provides a perfect excuse to change nothing.
"Since it’s useless, we might as well continue as before." The feeling of powerlessness then becomes a comfortable justification for inaction.
However, our gestures matter for several reasons.
First, because when added together, the behaviors of millions of people actually begin to weigh.
Then, because our individual actions are not isolated: they influence those around us, shape norms, and make some changes desirable while rendering others shameful.
Someone who changes their way of living does not only change their own impact; they slightly shift what seems normal.
Finally, and perhaps most importantly, there is a link between our actions and our beliefs.
It's difficult to demand deep changes while refusing to make any oneself.
Our gestures, even modest ones, commit us, lend credibility to our demands, and transform us into coherent citizens rather than powerless spectators.
The real answer is therefore not to choose between individual action and collective action, as if one excludes the other.
It is to understand that they mutually nourish each other.
Changing one’s life without ever influencing collective decisions would be insufficient; demanding collective changes without ever changing anything in one’s life would be lacking in credibility.
The two go hand in hand, and it is their conjunction that alone can hope to make a difference.
To capture our attention, digital platforms primarily show us what is likely to please us.

This logic, seemingly benevolent, has a consequence that is often underestimated: by continually presenting us with what reinforces our tastes and opinions, it tends to trap us in a bubble, where we only encounter a reflection of ourselves.
This phenomenon, often referred to as 'filter bubbles', deserves our understanding of its mechanisms and implications.
The principle is simple.
An algorithm observes what we linger on, what we approve of, what we share, and offers us more of the same.
In doing so, it does not seek to inform us, but to satisfy us, because a satisfied user stays connected longer.
What satisfies us is not what contradicts us, but what reassures us.
Little by little, without our wanting it, our horizon shrinks to what resembles us.
The effects of this shrinking are concerning.
By only encountering opinions similar to our own, we end up believing they are universal, and we consider any differing viewpoint as absurd.
Our convictions, never confronted with contradiction, harden.
Others, whose reasons we no longer hear, become foreign to us, even incomprehensible.
Thus, between groups that no longer communicate, chasms deepen that threaten communal life.
Because a democracy requires a shared space where citizens with different views can meet, debate, and at least understand each other a little.
If everyone lives in their own bubble, exposed to a different version of reality, this common space disintegrates.
We no longer debate; we hurl insults, each convinced that the other is acting in bad faith.
The fragmentation of information threatens, in the long run, the very possibility of deliberating together.
What can we do in the face of this risk?
Platforms certainly have a responsibility, and we can demand more transparency and diversity from them.
But it is also up to each individual to resist their own bubble: to deliberately seek out different viewpoints, to engage with varied sources, to be wary of the comfort of only hearing what we like.
Stepping out of one's bubble requires effort, as it is more pleasant to be right than to be contradicted.
But it is at this price that we remain capable of understanding the world as it is, and not as an algorithm has decided to show us.

sentences: We feel like we freely choose what we watch.
We open an app, scroll, and click here rather than there.

However, this feeling of freedom masks a more complex reality: what we see has first been sorted, prioritized, and selected by systems that we do not control and that, most often, we do not understand.
Behind the apparent spontaneity of our choices, invisible decisions guide our gaze.
These decisions are far from trivial.
On major platforms, what appears first, what is highlighted, and what remains buried, results from rules designed by a few companies.
These rules determine which information reaches us, which opinions gain visibility, which voices are amplified, and which are silenced.
It is immense power, all the more formidable because it operates discreetly, without us perceiving it as power.
This power raises unprecedented democratic questions.
In a society, the way information circulates is never neutral: it shapes what citizens know, believe, and discuss.

Now this role, once held by institutions that were at least partially subject to public debate, is today largely exercised by private actors, driven by their own interests and largely escaping collective control.
A few companies effectively decide what billions of people see and do not see.
The problem is exacerbated by opacity.
The criteria that govern these choices are rarely made public; they are protected like industrial secrets.
We therefore endure decisions whose principles we are unaware of, unable to know why certain content is shown to us and why others are hidden.
This opacity makes any control, any criticism, almost impossible: one cannot discuss what one does not know.
What can we do in the face of this situation?
The first necessity is to become aware of it, because we do not distrust a power that we cannot see.
The second is to demand transparency: those who organize the circulation of information on such a large scale should be held accountable for the rules they apply.
The third is to refuse to rely on a single source and to deliberately diversify what informs us.
We believe we are looking at the world; most often, we are looking at what others have chosen to show us.
Knowledge does not make us entirely free, but it is the beginning of all freedom.

sentences: Being reachable everywhere, at any time, was initially presented as an achievement: never cut off from the world, always within reach of those we love, never lost.
This promise has largely been fulfilled.

But it has come with an unforeseen downside: if we can always be reached, we are also always reachable, and this constant availability, initially experienced as freedom, gradually reveals itself to be a form of servitude.
The shift occurred imperceptibly.
What was once possible has become expected, then mandatory.
Not responding quickly to a message is now seen as negligence, even rudeness.
We feel compelled to stay connected, to check, to react, as if the whole world demands our presence at all times.
The technology that was supposed to liberate us has chained us to an unending expectation.
What we lose in this perpetual availability is something precious: the right to be unreachable at times.
The right to step away from the flow, to withdraw, to be there for no one other than those who are truly around us.
This right, which our ancestors exercised without even thinking about it — because no one could reach them — has become a rare commodity that we must now consciously defend.
It's not about demonizing tools that provide immense services, nor about dreaming of an impossible return to a disconnected world.
It's about restoring a balance, distinguishing between what is a real necessity and what is merely a habit or social pressure.
Almost nothing, in truth, requires immediate attention; the constant urgency is most often an illusion we maintain ourselves.
Regaining the right to disconnect requires concrete decisions: screen-free periods, moments when we turn off, rules we set for ourselves and uphold in front of others.
This takes a certain courage, as we must accept disappointing expectations that have become excessive.
But it is at this price that we regain control of our time, instead of being its servant.
Being reachable is a convenience; being able not to be is a freedom.
In a world that confuses the two, preserving the latter has become an ordinary yet essential act of resistance.

sentences: The climate crisis reveals a deep weakness in our societies: their difficulty in thinking and acting for the long term.
The efforts we are being asked to make today will only bear fruit in decades, and will mainly benefit generations we will never know.
However, acting now for a distant future, at the cost of immediate sacrifices, goes against powerful trends, both individual and collective.
On an individual scale, our minds are such that they give much more weight to the present than to the future.
Immediate satisfaction attracts us more than a distant benefit, even if it is greater.
This trait, undoubtedly useful to our distant ancestors, whose survival depended on day-to-day existence, works against us in the face of threats whose effects unfold over generations.
We know the danger, but it seems abstract, distant, and easy to push off to later.
On a collective scale, the obstacles are no less significant.
Political leaders are elected for short terms and judged on immediate results.
Devoting resources to a problem whose benefits will only appear long after they have left holds little appeal for them.
The markets, for their part, value quick returns and care little for a horizon that extends beyond a few years.
Our institutions, as a whole, are built for the short term.
This shortsightedness is not a fatality; rather, it is a challenge to be met.
Other eras, other cultures, have been able to think beyond their own existence.
Those who planted trees whose shade they would never see, or built cathedrals they would not see completed, acted for a future that transcended them.
This capacity exists within us; it is a matter of reviving it.
Achieving this requires transforming our relationship with time.
This involves education, which can teach us to project ourselves beyond the immediate.
This involves rethought institutions, capable of representing the interests of future generations in present decisions.
This finally involves a narrative: that of a responsibility that connects us to those who will come after us, just as we are connected to those who preceded us.
Thinking long term is not natural; it is a conquest, a discipline, almost a virtue.
The climate crisis forces us to acquire it.
Perhaps this is, in the end, one of the few benefits it could bring us: forcing us to finally become the guardians of a future that transcends us.

sentences: In the face of the scale of the ecological crisis, two opposing attitudes lead to the same result: inaction.
The first is denial, which refuses to see the problem or minimizes its severity, thus allowing nothing to change.
The second is despair, which judges the situation to be so hopeless that any effort seems futile, and it too leads to giving up.
Between these two dead ends, is there room for another attitude, a hope that is both clear-sighted and active?
Despair deserves to be taken seriously, as it is not absurd.
The news is often alarming, progress is slow, and resistance is strong.
In light of this observation, discouragement is a comprehensible reaction, and it would be futile to deny it with forced optimism.
A hope that refuses to face reality would merely be a polite form of denial.
However, despair has a decisive flaw: it is mistaken about the nature of the future.
It assumes that the worst is certain, while nothing is.
The future is not written; it depends, precisely, on what we will do.
To declare the game lost in advance is to contribute to losing it, by demobilizing those who could still act.
The paradox of despair is that it produces what it merely claims to observe.
This is where another hope becomes possible, provided we understand it well.
It is not about naively believing that everything will turn out fine, nor about reassuring oneself at little cost.
It is about recognizing that nothing is set in stone, and that this very uncertainty is a reason to act.
Since the future depends on our actions, every effort matters, not because it guarantees victory, but because it weighs on an outcome that is still open.
That hope is not a prediction; it is a choice, and almost a responsibility.
One could even say that hope, understood this way, is not a prerequisite for action, but its fruit.
It is not because we hope that we act; it is often by acting that we regain hope.
Those who engage, in their own way, almost all testify to this reversal: action, by giving meaning and control, dissipates the overwhelm that inaction maintains.
Reasonable hope is therefore neither blind optimism nor disguised resignation.
It is the conviction that, with the future remaining uncertain, it is worth fighting to influence it.
Not because we are sure to win, but because we are not sure to lose — and that is already a sufficient reason.

sentences: Ecology is all well and good, but it's a luxury for the rich. This objection, often expressed with a hint of bitterness, highlights a reality that would be dishonest to ignore.
How can we ask someone who struggles to make ends meet to care about the planet?
The changes we advocate — consuming better, traveling differently, choosing more virtuous products — often come at a cost, and that cost primarily affects those who have the least.
The issue of social justice runs through the entire ecological question, and forgetting it would be a mistake.
There is some truth in this objection, and environmental advocates would be wrong to dismiss it.
Too many ecological discourses, delivered by comfortable people, ignore the constraints faced by those who have no choice.

To blame someone for taking their car to work, when no public transport serves their village and they can't afford a clean vehicle, is not only unjust: it's politically absurd, as it turns those who we need against ecology.
But the idea that ecology is a luxury also relies on a misleading reversal.
Because it is precisely the most modest who suffer the most from environmental degradation.
They are the ones who live in the most polluted areas, who endure the harshest heatwaves, floods, and rising energy and food prices.
Climate change is not a concern for aesthetes; it is a threat that primarily strikes the most vulnerable.
In this sense, ecology is not the enemy of the poor, but their most direct interest.
The real problem is therefore not choosing between the end of the month and the end of the world, as a common saying summarizes.
It is about rejecting this false dilemma.
An ecology that would worsen inequalities would be doomed to failure, as it would provoke rejection.
But a social justice that ignores the environment would condemn the most disadvantaged to the first disasters.
The two demands do not oppose each other; they must be held together.

Specifically, this means that the ecological transition must be just: that its costs do not burden the most vulnerable, that alternatives are made accessible to everyone, and that the effort required is proportionate to each person's means.
An ecology that is not social condemns itself; a social policy that is not ecological prepares for worse injustices.
Ecology is a luxury only when it is poorly conceived.
Well thought out, it is, on the contrary, what primarily protects those who have the least.

sentences: We spontaneously associate reducing consumption with impoverishment, as if living with fewer possessions necessarily means living worse.
This equation seems obvious; however, it is based on a particular belief, unique to our time, that happiness depends on the quantity of things we own and consume.
Yet this belief, upon examination, proves to be more fragile than it appears.
It is not a matter of denying that meeting material needs is essential.
Lacking the essentials — food, shelter, healthcare — is true poverty, and it would be indecent to downplay it.
No sensible person claims that deprivation brings happiness.
The question is not there; it concerns what happens once the essentials are secured.
And on this point, observations converge: beyond a certain threshold, accumulating possessions hardly increases well-being.
This observation can be explained by a well-known mechanism.
We quickly get used to what we acquire.
The long-desired object, once obtained, quickly ceases to bring us joy, and a new desire takes its place.
This endless race — desiring, obtaining, getting used to it, desiring again — keeps us in a state of permanent dissatisfaction, where each acquisition only briefly alleviates a renewed lack.
Consuming more does not fill this lack; it maintains it.
From this perspective, consuming less might not be impoverishment, but rather liberation.
Breaking free from the logic of accumulation means escaping an exhausting race, regaining time, money, and attention for what truly matters.
For what makes lives rich — relationships, commitment, creativity, nature, free time — is hardly bought, and the obsession with possessing often distracts us from it.
We must be careful here of an opposite trap: turning sobriety into a new guilt-inducing morality or romanticizing lack.
Living with less only makes sense if the essentials are secured, and it would be cruel to preach frugality to those who already suffer deprivation.
Happy sobriety is a choice; imposed, it is nothing but misery.
But for those who have enough, the question deserves to be asked without prejudice: what if living better is not about having more, but about desiring differently?
Consuming less is only impoverishment if one has first confused wealth with an abundance of things.

sentences: We spend a considerable part of our childhood and youth at school.
However, if we were asked about what we learned there, many pieces of knowledge would surprisingly be forgotten.
The dates, formulas, and rules that we patiently memorized have mostly vanished.
This somewhat troubling observation leads to a radical question: do we really learn at school, and if so, what exactly?
One might be tempted to conclude that school fails, since so much of its content is forgotten.
But this conclusion is based on a narrow understanding of what learning means.
Reducing education to the accumulation of knowledge misses the essential point.
For what remains, years later, is not the list of accumulated knowledge, but something deeper and more lasting.
What remains, first of all, are ways of thinking.
Learning to read a text, to follow a reasoning, to solve a problem, to doubt a statement: these skills, once acquired, are not forgotten like a date.
They have become incorporated, becoming ways of approaching the world.
We forget the content of a math class; we often retain, without realizing it, the rigor it helped to develop.
What remains next is a relationship to knowledge.
School, when it succeeds, does not just transmit knowledge: it teaches how to learn, awakens curiosity, and shows that one can understand what seemed obscure.
This confidence in one's own ability to grasp the world may be the most precious legacy, as it allows one to continue learning long after leaving the school benches.
What remains, finally, are encounters and openings.

A teacher who has instilled a passion for a subject, a book that has revealed a world, an idea that has transformed a way of seeing: these moments shape a life more surely than a thousand forgotten lessons.
School is not just a place where one accumulates; it is a place where one can be awakened.
Recognizing this does not exempt us from questioning what school transmits and how it does so.
But this shifts the question.
The goal of education is not to fill heads with knowledge destined to fade; it is to form minds capable of thinking, understanding, and continuing to learn.
By this measure, what is forgotten is not what matters most.

sentences: From childhood, we are taught to fear mistakes.
At school, it is punished with a bad grade; in life, it is a source of shame.
We come to see it as a failure, something to be avoided at all costs.
However, this view, as widespread as it may be, is based on a deep misunderstanding.
Far from being just the enemy of learning, mistakes are often its very condition.
Let's think about how we actually learn anything.
We try, we make mistakes, we understand why, we correct, we start again.
The child learning to walk falls countless times; the one learning a language makes mistakes before speaking correctly.
At no point are these mistakes failures: they are the necessary steps of progress.
Without them, no real learning would be possible, because it is precisely by confronting our limits that we push them back.
Research confirms this intuition.
We learn better and more durably when we have first fumbled, struggled, and failed, than when we passively receive a ready-made solution.
The effort that precedes the mistake, and the understanding that follows its correction, engraves knowledge much more deeply than a lesson absorbed without difficulty.
Mistakes are not a regrettable accident on the path; they are the path itself.
So why do we fear them so much?
Because we have been shaped by a culture that punishes them instead of exploiting them.
By punishing mistakes rather than using them, we teach people not to stop making them, but to be afraid to try.
However, those who fear making mistakes dare less, try less, and ultimately learn less.
The fear of mistakes thus produces the exact opposite of what it claims to achieve.
Changing our relationship with mistakes would have considerable effects, far beyond school.
In work, in creation, in research, advances almost always arise from a succession of overcome failures.
Environments that allow mistakes, that treat them as information rather than faults, are those where the most invention and progress occur.
Conversely, the fear of making mistakes sterilizes.
It is not about celebrating mistakes for their own sake, nor about being satisfied with our faults.
It is about stopping the demonization of mistakes, to see what they really are: not the failure of learning, but its most faithful instrument.
Those who never accept making mistakes condemn themselves, in reality, to never truly learn.

sentences: Since any information is now available in an instant, a question arises: what is the point of memorizing anything at all?
Why remember dates, facts, and knowledge if our phones provide them on demand?
This question, made inevitable by permanent access to knowledge, deserves more than a hasty answer, as it touches on the very nature of thought.
The argument in favor of assumed forgetfulness seems appealing.
What is the use of burdening your memory with easily accessible data?
Isn't it better to keep the mind free, available for thinking rather than for remembering?
After all, no one regrets not memorizing phone numbers anymore.
Delegating the burden of memorization to machines seems like progress, freeing us for more noble tasks.
This argument, however, overlooks something essential.
Thinking does not consist of manipulating external information; it requires having knowledge already integrated within oneself.
We do not reflect with what we can consult, but with what we know.
To understand a new situation, establish a connection, or have an intuition, knowledge must be present in the mind, ready to combine.
An empty mind, which would have to consult everything, would not think; it would only search.
Memory is not a simple warehouse of information, separate from intelligence.
It is one of the materials of intelligence.
Ideas arise from the connection of knowledge we possess; creativity itself often consists of linking distant pieces of knowledge.
However, we can only connect what we have in mind.
Completely externalizing our memory would mean depriving ourselves of the very material with which we think.
It is not about memorizing everything, nor about considering memorization as an end in itself.
Easy access to information is a real advancement, and freeing the mind from certain burdens is nothing to regret.
But we must distinguish what we can safely delegate to machines from what must remain within us.
Fundamental knowledge in a field, the kind that allows for understanding and reasoning, cannot be delegated without impoverishing thought itself.
The real question is therefore not about choosing between memorizing and consulting, but about knowing what to keep within ourselves and what to entrust to the outside.
A mind that would retain nothing would not be a liberated mind; it would be a dispossessed mind, incapable of thinking without support.
Remembering remains, in the age of available information, a condition of thought.

sentences: What does it mean to be healthy?
The most common answer is to say: not being sick.
According to this view, health would be a default state, one that we possess as long as no illness disturbs it.
This definition, seemingly obvious, is surprisingly poor, and it prevents us from properly thinking about what fundamentally constitutes a healthy life.
Reducing health to the absence of illness means defining it negatively, by what it is not.
But we can sense that health is more than that.
Two people can have no declared illness and be in very different states: one full of energy, the other exhausted; one calm, the other plagued by anxiety.
Neither is 'sick' in the strict sense, and yet one is doing well while the other is not.
Health, evidently, cannot be confined to merely the absence of pathology.
That is why a richer definition has been proposed, which sees health as a complete state of physical, mental, and social well-being.
This formulation has its flaws — such a complete state may never be fully achieved — but it has the merit of broadening our perspective.
It reminds us that health involves the body, but also the mind and social connections, and we cannot reduce it to just one of these aspects.
This broader conception has practical consequences.
If health is not just the absence of illness, then taking care of it does not only mean treating what is wrong, but also nurturing what is right.
Moving, sleeping, maintaining relationships, finding meaning, managing stress: all these dimensions are fully part of health, even though none appear on a prescription.
Taking care of oneself is more than just treating oneself.
However, we must be cautious of excess.
Making health an ideal of 'complete well-being' risks turning it into a permanent obligation, a demand to always be at our best.
But no one is at their best all the time, and feeling guilty for not achieving a perfect state would be a new form of distress.
Health is not a performance to achieve, but a balance to seek, always imperfectly.
Understanding that health goes beyond the absence of illness means stopping waiting to be sick to care about it.
It is recognizing that it is built every day, in the ordinary gestures of life, and not only at the doctor’s when something goes wrong.

alignments.english: This formulation has its flaws — such a complete state may never be fully achieved — but it has the merit of broadening our perspective.

alignments.french: Elle rappelle que la santé engage le corps, mais aussi l'esprit et les liens sociaux, et qu'on ne saurait la réduire à l'un de ces aspects.
alignments.english: It reminds us that health involves the body, but also the mind and social connections, and we cannot reduce it to just one of these aspects.

alignments.french: Cette conception élargie a des conséquences pratiques.
alignments.english: This broader conception has practical consequences.

alignments.french: Si la santé n'est pas seulement l'absence de maladie, alors s'en occuper ne consiste pas seulement à soigner ce qui va mal, mais à cultiver ce qui va bien.
alignments.english: If health is not just the absence of illness, then taking care of it does not only mean treating what is wrong, but also nurturing what is right.

alignments.french: Bouger, dormir, entretenir des relations, trouver du sens, gérer son stress : autant de dimensions qui relèvent pleinement de la santé, bien qu'aucune ne figure sur une ordonnance.
alignments.english: Moving, sleeping, maintaining relationships, finding meaning, managing stress: all these dimensions are fully part of health, even though none appear on a prescription.

alignments.french: Prendre soin de soi, c'est plus que se soigner.
alignments.english: Taking care of oneself is more than just treating oneself.

alignments.french: Il faut néanmoins se garder d'un excès.
alignments.english: However, we must be cautious of excess.

alignments.french: Faire de la santé un idéal de « bien-être complet » risque de la transformer en obligation permanente, en injonction à être toujours au mieux de sa forme.
alignments.english: Making health an ideal of 'complete well-being' risks turning it into a permanent obligation, a demand to always be at our best.

alignments.french: Or personne ne l'est en permanence, et culpabiliser de ne pas atteindre un état parfait serait une nouvelle forme de mal-être.
alignments.english: But no one is at their best all the time, and feeling guilty for not achieving a perfect state would be a new form of distress.

alignments.french: La santé n'est pas une performance à réussir, mais un équilibre à chercher, toujours imparfaitement.
alignments.english: Health is not a performance to achieve, but a balance to seek, always imperfectly.

alignments.french: Comprendre que la santé dépasse l'absence de maladie, c'est cesser d'attendre d'être malade pour s'en soucier.
alignments.english: Understanding that health goes beyond the absence of illness means stopping waiting to be sick to care about it.

alignments.french: C'est reconnaître qu'elle se construit chaque jour, dans les gestes ordinaires d'une vie, et non seulement chez le médecin quand quelque chose ne va plus.
alignments.english: It is recognizing that it is built every day, in the ordinary gestures of life, and not only at the doctor’s when something goes wrong.

sentences: We have inherited a view of learning that associates it with a specific period of life: childhood and youth.
One would learn at school, then, once the diploma is obtained, enter the working world, with learning behind them.
This view, convenient for a long time, is now doubly outdated: due to the necessities of a rapidly changing world, and because of what we now know about how the mind works.
The first reason is practical.
In a world where knowledge, techniques, and jobs are constantly evolving, stopping learning once and for all is no longer feasible.
What we learned in our youth becomes outdated, new skills become necessary, jobs appear while others disappear.
Continuing to learn is no longer a luxury or a passion reserved for a few; it is a condition for staying relevant in a changing world.
But reducing lifelong learning to this economic necessity would mean missing the essential.
For learning throughout life is not just a constraint to endure; it is also one of the great sources of vitality in existence.
Discovering, understanding, and progressing in a new field provides deep satisfaction at any age.
The mind that continues to learn remains alive, curious, and open; the one that stops gradually closes in.
Research on the brain supports this idea.
Contrary to a persistent belief, the ability to learn does not disappear with youth.
The brain retains, until an advanced age, a remarkable ability to transform itself, create new connections, and adapt.
Learning later may sometimes require more effort, but it remains entirely possible, and this very exercise helps preserve the sharpness of the mind over the years.
However, one must overcome a few internal obstacles.
The first is the belief that one is 'too old' to learn, a belief that, by discouraging attempts, proves itself.
The second is the fear of starting over, of being a beginner, of making mistakes — this fear of error which, again, hinders learning.
Accepting to be clumsy, to not know, to progress slowly is the modest price of any new learning.
Learning throughout life is therefore not just an obligation imposed by the times; it is a way to remain fully alive.
The mind, like the body, is maintained through exercise, and the day one stops learning may be the day one begins, slowly, to age.
