sentences: A long-standing debate in education revolves around an opposition: should we prioritize understanding or memorization?
On one side, there are those who criticize rote learning, this mechanical recitation of poorly digested knowledge.
On the other side, there are those who lament that students no longer know anything and confuse understanding with a vague impression.
This opposition, while it contains a grain of truth, is actually based on a false dilemma.
Those who criticize memorization are right about one thing: reciting is not understanding.
One can perfectly repeat a formula without grasping its meaning, state a rule without knowing how to apply it.
Knowledge that is purely memorized, unconnected, and not understood remains inert: it is useless, forgotten quickly, and gives the illusion of knowledge that isn't real.
In this regard, the distrust of rote learning is justified.
But the opposite stance — understanding without needing to memorize — is equally misleading.
For one never understands in a vacuum.
Understanding requires prior knowledge to which new discoveries can be linked.
To understand a text, one must know the words; to grasp an idea, one must have other ideas that illuminate it.
Claiming to develop understanding without transmitting knowledge is like wanting to build without materials.
A mind that knows nothing understands nothing, lacking the connections to relate to what it encounters.
In truth, understanding and memorization do not oppose each other; they mutually support one another.
We remember better what we have understood, as meaning gives knowledge a place and coherence that fix it.
And we understand better when we already possess a foundation of knowledge, as understanding feeds on what we know.
Far from being enemies, memory and understanding are two sides of the same learning process.
The false dilemma arises from confusing poor memorization — mechanical, isolated, without understanding — with memorization in general.
However, there is another way to retain: the one that accompanies understanding, which fixes knowledge we have grasped and which, in turn, will allow us to understand new things.
This kind of memory is not the enemy of intelligence; it is one of its foundations.
The question is therefore not about choosing between understanding and memorization, as if one must sacrifice one for the other.
It is about retaining while understanding, and understanding thanks to what we have retained.
Separating the two condemns one to either empty knowledge or understanding without substance.

sentences: Among all the body's needs, sleep is undoubtedly the one we treat with the most nonchalance.
We often boast about sleeping little, we cut back on our nights to work or have fun, and we see sleep as wasted time that it would almost be virtuous to reduce.
This attitude, however widespread it may be, is based on a profound misunderstanding of what sleep really is and what it accomplishes.
For sleeping is not doing nothing.
While we sleep, our body is far from inactive: it repairs itself, consolidates memory, regulates emotions, maintains immune defenses, and eliminates waste accumulated in the brain.
Sleep is not an interruption of life, but one of its essential processes, as vital as food.
Neglecting it is not saving time; it is sabotaging an essential task.
The consequences of chronic sleep deprivation are considerable, and research continues to clarify its extent.
Mentally, it impairs concentration, judgment, mood, and memory.
Physically, it is associated with an increased risk of many diseases.
A mind and body deprived of sleep function poorly, even when the person suffering from it, accustomed to their state, no longer realizes it.
For the lack of sleep is deceptive in that it makes us poor judges of our own abilities.
How then can we explain that we mistreat it to such an extent?
Partly because its effects are delayed and invisible: a night too short does not have immediate consequences, and one can be under the illusion for a long time about their ability to 'hold on.'
Partly also because our culture values activity and despises rest, as if sleeping were an admission of weakness or laziness.
We sacrifice our sleep on the altar of productivity, which paradoxically suffers as a result.
Rehabilitating sleep therefore requires a change in perspective.
It is not a favor we grant our body when we have the leisure, but a fundamental need that must be respected.
This involves concrete actions — regular schedules, a calm and dark room, a distance from screens in the evening — but above all a conviction: that the time spent sleeping is never wasted time.
Sleeping well is not a luxury or laziness; it is one of the most basic conditions for a healthy life.
By neglecting our sleep, we are neglecting ourselves.

sentences: We live surrounded by images of bodies.
On screens, in advertising, on social media, idealized silhouettes constantly parade: slim, firm, young, and flawless.
This flood of images, historically unprecedented in its scale, does not fail to affect how each person perceives their own body.
And this effect, studies confirm, is most often negative.
The mechanism is that of comparison.
By constantly seeing idealized bodies, we take these images as the norm, and our own body, judged by this standard, always seems insufficient.
What we compare, however, is not comparable: the images around us are selected, retouched, staged, while our body appears to us in its ordinary reality.
We measure ourselves against a perfection that does not exist, and we inevitably find ourselves lacking.
This constant comparison has a real cost.
Dissatisfaction, shame, obsession with control, and sometimes serious eating disorders: bodily distress, particularly widespread among the young, is far from trivial.
It is not a mere vanity, but a suffering that can invade one's entire life, robbing those who experience it of a part of their self-esteem.
We must also recognize how arbitrary and changeable these norms are.
What is presented today as the ideal body is not universal: other eras and cultures have valued entirely different silhouettes.
The current ideal is not a truth of nature, but a social construct, shaped notably by commercial interests.
For we must not forget: a significant part of this dissatisfaction is deliberately maintained because it drives sales.
Recognizing this is not enough to free oneself from it, but it helps to gain perspective.
Understanding that these images are manipulated, that these norms are arbitrary, and that this distress is partly manufactured is the beginning of loosening their grip.
We can also choose what we look at, turn away from sources that fuel comparison, and seek more diverse and authentic representations of real bodies.
The body is not primarily an object to be displayed, a product to conform to a norm.
It is what we live through, experience, and act with.
Reconnecting with this truth — inhabiting one's body rather than judging it — may be the first step towards a peace that no perfect image will ever provide.

sentences: If someone breaks a leg, they consult without hesitation, receive treatment, and no one finds fault with that.

But if that same person suffers from anxiety, depression, or another mental disorder, everything becomes more complicated: shame gets involved, silence settles in, and seeking help, when it happens, often occurs late and reluctantly.
This difference in treatment between physical ailments and mental ones is one of the most persistent injustices in our relationship with health.
Where does this difference come from?
Partly from a long history of misunderstanding and prejudice.
For centuries, mental disorders have been misunderstood, surrounded by fear, associated with moral weakness, madness, and something shameful.
These representations, although declining, have not disappeared.

Many continue to believe, more or less consciously, that a mental disorder is a lack of willpower, that one just needs to 'pull themselves together' to feel better — as if one could cure depression solely through sheer willpower.
This belief is not only false but also dangerous.
Mental disorders are not weaknesses of character; they are real conditions that have their causes, mechanisms, and treatments, just like physical illnesses.
To impose a requirement of willpower is to add guilt to suffering and to divert those who suffer from the care that could help them.
Silence and shame literally kill by preventing people from asking for help.
It is therefore necessary to affirm an obvious truth that has been ignored for too long: mental health is a component of health, no more shameful and no less serious than physical health.
Suffering in your mind is no more dishonorable than suffering in your body, and seeking help is not an admission of weakness but an act of common sense and courage.
Consulting for a mental issue should be as natural as consulting for a physical issue.
Things are, fortunately, evolving.
People are talking more, understanding better, voices are gradually being freed, and public figures are daring to share their own struggles, helping to reduce shame.
This movement, still fragile, is heading in the right direction: it is slowly bringing the treatment of mental ailments closer to that of physical ailments.
Healing the mind like the body: this simple phrase summarizes the progress that still needs to be made.
As long as this is not an obvious truth for everyone, people will continue to suffer in silence, afraid to ask for help that would be readily given for any visible injury.

sentences: Money doesn't bring happiness," says the proverb, to which a cynic readily adds, "but it contributes to it.
Behind this worn exchange lies a real question, to which modern research provides a more nuanced answer than a simple yes or no.
For money does indeed have a real relationship with happiness, but this relationship is neither what the proverb suggests nor what the cynic implies.
Let's start with what is firmly established: up to a certain point, money does indeed contribute to well-being.
For those who lack the essentials, an additional income changes everything.

Escaping poverty, being able to feed oneself, have a roof over one's head, receive medical care, and stop living in fear of tomorrow: at this level, money buys not happiness itself, but the end of a very concrete misery.
To claim otherwise, from the comfort of an easy life, is indecent.
But the link transforms as one rises.
Beyond the threshold where essential needs are met, each additional gain brings less and less well-being.
Doubling an already comfortable income does not double satisfaction; the effect diminishes until it becomes almost imperceptible.
Money, after a certain point, obeys a law of diminishing returns: it still matters, but less and less.
Why this exhaustion?
Partly due to the habituation already mentioned: we quickly get used to what we acquire, and the new comfort rapidly becomes the norm, ceasing to bring us joy.
Partly also because, once the essentials are secured, what makes happiness—relationships, meaning, health, time—cannot be bought.
You can buy a beautiful house, but not the affection of those who live in it.
There is something even more troubling: the way we earn and spend money matters more than the amount itself.
A demanding job that pays well can harm the happiness it claims to serve.
And research shows that we derive more satisfaction from spending on experiences or for others than from accumulating possessions.
It's not just how much we have, but what we do with it that matters.
The honest answer to the old question is therefore nuanced.
Money does not bring happiness, but its absence brings misery; it contributes, but less and less; it matters, but less than how we use it.
To despise it would be naive; to expect happiness from it would be just as naive.

sentences: We commonly judge the value of something by its price.
What is expensive seems precious to us, while what is cheap seems advantageous.
This convenient reflex, however, rests on a confusion: the price of something does not reflect its true cost.
Often, the displayed price reflects only a part of what the item truly cost, with the rest being borne by others, elsewhere, without appearing on the receipt.
Let's take a product sold at a very low price.
This attractive price can hide very real but invisible costs: underpaid workers who made it, an environment degraded by its production, depleted resources, and damages deferred to the future.
These costs exist; it's just that the buyer does not pay them directly.
Economists talk about 'externalized' costs: pushed outside the price, borne by society, by nature, by future generations.
A low price is therefore not a true saving; it is a shifting of the cost onto those who cannot defend themselves.
Conversely, a high price does not guarantee that something is truly 'worth' what it costs.
A portion of the price may not compensate for quality, but for an image, a brand, or artificial scarcity.
Paying a high price does not always mean paying for value; sometimes it is paying for prestige, or simply for the satisfaction of having paid a lot.
The price, indeed, is a misleading guide.
Understanding this transforms the way we view consumption.
It invites us to ask, behind each price, what the real cost is: who produced it, under what conditions, and with what consequences?
These questions do not always have easy answers, and we cannot investigate every purchase.
But just having these questions in mind is enough to make us less naive, less quick to confuse cheapness with advantage.
This awareness also has a collective significance.
If prices told the truth — if they included the costs currently externalized — many harmful products would be more expensive, and many virtuous products would be more competitive.
Ensuring that prices reflect real costs is one of the major challenges of a fairer and more sustainable economy, even if it faces immense resistance.
The price is therefore only partial information, and sometimes misleading.
Behind the displayed figures lies a more complex reality that is worth learning to see.
For what we do not pay, someone, somewhere, pays on our behalf.

sentences: Modern medicine performs wonders.
It repairs severely damaged bodies, operates with incredible precision, and cures diseases that were once fatal.
This healing power is one of the great achievements of our time, and it would be ungrateful to underestimate it.
However, this medicine excels mainly at intervening once the disease has taken hold; it is much less attentive to what could prevent it from appearing.
Yet it is perhaps in prevention that the essential lies.
The idea is nothing new: it's better to prevent than to cure.
Preventing a disease from occurring is always better than having to treat it, both for the individual, spared from suffering, and for society, spared from the cost.
A considerable share of the diseases that weigh most heavily today could be avoided, or at least delayed, through lifestyle changes and early screening.
The potential for prevention is immense and largely untapped.
So why do we neglect it?
Several reasons come together.
The first relates to the very nature of prevention: its successes are invisible.
We never see the disease that never occurred, while a spectacular recovery is noticeable.
It is more gratifying, and more valued, to save a patient than to discreetly prevent them from becoming one.
Curative medicine shines; prevention works in the shadows.
The second reason is economic.
Our healthcare systems are largely organized to treat diseases, not to prevent them: we pay for the act of care much more than for the advice that would have made it unnecessary.
Prevention, lacking the same recognition, remains the poor relation of the system, despite the speeches that celebrate it.
The third reason, finally, relates to ourselves.
Preventing means acting today for a distant and uncertain benefit, which our minds, as we have seen, resist.
It is easier to put off protective efforts, even if it means having to seek treatment later.
Prevention clashes with our inclination for the immediate.
Rebalancing care and prevention does not mean giving up one for the other; both are necessary.
It is about stopping the wait for disease to act, and recognizing prevention's rightful place — in our healthcare systems as well as in our lives.
For the greatest healing is the one we never needed.

sentences: It is often said that we should listen to what people do rather than what they say.
This is especially true when it comes to money.
Our discussions about our values can be misleading, but our spending rarely lies: it often reveals better than our words what we truly value.
Looking at where our money goes is like looking at ourselves in a sometimes surprising mirror.
Everyone willingly states what matters to them: family, health, culture, others.
But does an honest examination of our spending always confirm these statements?
Sometimes we claim to value something while actually dedicating neither money nor time to it, while we spend freely on what we profess to disdain.
This gap between proclaimed values and lived values is mercilessly highlighted by money.
This observation is not a moral judgment; rather, it is a tool for clarity.
Examining our spending is not about feeling guilty, but about getting to know ourselves.
By concretely seeing where our money goes, we discover our actual priorities, those that govern our daily choices, beyond the intentions we display.
And it sometimes happens that this discovery is uncomfortable, as it reveals a gap between the life we lead and the one we wish to lead.
This exercise then opens up a possibility: that of realigning our spending with our values.
If I notice that I spend a lot on what matters little to me, and little on what truly matters, I can correct my course.
Spending consciously does not necessarily mean spending less; it means spending in accordance with what we care about.
A budget, from this perspective, is not an accounting constraint, but the concrete expression of a set of priorities.
We must guard against a trap here: the one that believes everything boils down to money.
Many precious things cannot be bought, and a life is not merely the sum of its expenses.
But in a world where money is the means to so many things, the way we use it remains a faithful indicator of who we are.
Asking myself 'where does my money go?' is therefore indirectly asking 'what really matters to me?'
The answer, inscribed in our statements more surely than in our speeches, deserves to be faced.

sentences: Here is a seemingly naive yet profound question: when do we have enough?
At what point can we say that we own, earn, or consume sufficiently, and that it is no longer necessary to want more?
This question is one that everyone should ask themselves; however, almost no one does, and our entire world seems designed so that we never ask it.
For the very idea of 'enough' goes against a deep logic of our economy, which is based on perpetual growth and an ever-rekindled desire.
Everything around us invites us to want more: more goods, more income, more comfort, more experiences.
Advertising, the example of others, and our own habituation conspire to continually push back the threshold of what seems sufficient.
As soon as we reach one goal, another one arises, and the notion of 'enough' recedes as we move forward.
This endless race is exhausting, and even absurd.
If the threshold of 'enough' perpetually recedes, it will never be reached, and we are condemned to a permanent dissatisfaction, regardless of the abundance we enjoy.
One can thus possess a lot and feel deprived, earn more and more, yet never be satisfied.
The lack, then, no longer comes from what we are missing, but from our inability to recognize that we have enough.
Asking the question of 'enough' thus introduces a break in this logic.
It asserts that there is a point beyond which wanting more adds nothing essential, except the burden of desire.

Defining one's 'enough' is not about resigning oneself or giving up all ambition; it is about giving oneself a chance to be satisfied one day, instead of endlessly chasing a horizon that keeps shifting.
However, we must avoid a misunderstanding.
Talking about 'enough' only makes sense for those who already have the essentials.
For someone who lacks the essentials, it would be indecent to preach moderation: their problem is not having too much, but too little.
The question of 'enough' is directed at those, many in affluent societies, who have long surpassed the threshold of real needs without ever realizing it.
Knowing how to say 'that's enough' is perhaps one of the rarest and most precious freedoms of our time.
In a world that thrives on our insatiability, recognizing that we have enough is almost an act of resistance — and undoubtedly one of the conditions for a peaceful life.

sentences: Credit is one of the great conveniences of modern life.
It allows us to acquire today what we could only afford after years of saving: a home, a car, an education.
By spreading payments over time, it makes projects accessible that would otherwise remain out of reach.
In this regard, it is a valuable tool, and it would be absurd to condemn it outright.
But this same tool, if not properly managed, can turn into a form of servitude.
The mechanism is insidious.
Borrowing means committing your future: tomorrow's income is already allocated to repaying what you've consumed today.
As long as this commitment remains measured, it is not concerning.
But when it accumulates, when repayments consume an increasing share of income, debt stops being a means and becomes a burden.
You no longer work to live, but to repay; you are no longer free in your choices, chained to deadlines you dread.
This shift is all the more dangerous because it is encouraged.
Everything in our environment pushes us to consume immediately and pay later.
Credit is offered everywhere, presented as easy, painless, almost free — until the interests, patiently accumulated, reveal their true weight.
The most vulnerable are the first victims of this ease, drawn into costly loans that worsen, rather than resolve, their difficulties.
We must therefore distinguish between two uses of debt, as different as possible.
There is chosen debt, measured, put to the service of a project that builds the future: borrowing to secure housing or education can be a reasonable investment.
And there is incurred debt, which finances immediate consumption at the expense of the future, and which gradually traps you in a spiral.
The first can liberate; the second enslaves.

Protecting oneself against bad debt requires a few simple principles: only borrow what you can repay without distress, be wary of easy and costly loans, and distinguish between momentary desire and real need.
This especially requires resisting a culture that makes debt a habit and patience a weakness.
The question is therefore not to ban credit, but to remain its master rather than its servant.
A loan for the service of a project is a tool of freedom; a debt that governs life is its opposite.
The whole difference lies in this reversal, which is better to prevent than to endure.

sentences: In front of a landscape, a monument, or a scene that moves us, our first gesture is almost always the same: we take out a camera and we photograph.
This reflex, which has become universal, seems innocent, even useful — isn't it about keeping a record of what we experience?
However, a question deserves to be asked: by constantly photographing what we see, do we still really see it?
Disturbing research suggests that photographing a scene can, paradoxically, harm the memory we have of it.
When we entrust the camera with the task of retaining, our attention relaxes, as if we are offloading the effort of memorizing onto it.
We then look less intensely, confident that the image will preserve for us what we haven't really taken the time to contemplate.
Photography, which is supposed to fix memories, risks impoverishing them instead.
There's more.
The act of photographing interposes a screen between us and what we are experiencing.
Preoccupied with framing, adjusting, and capturing the right angle, we cease to be fully present at the scene; we treat it as an image to capture rather than a moment to live.
The direct, immediate experience fades behind its reproduction.
We bring back thousands of snapshots, and sometimes very few genuinely felt memories.
This phenomenon worsens when photography is no longer intended for us, but for others.
Photographing to show, to publish, to prove that we were there transforms the experience into a spectacle.
We no longer look at a place for itself, but for the image we will take from it; we choose what we see based on what will 'look good'.
The elsewhere becomes a backdrop, and the journey, a collection of images intended for the gaze of others.
Should we then give up photographing?
That would be excessive, as the image also has its virtues: it can revive a memory, prolong an emotion, share a beauty.
The problem is not photography itself, but its automatism, which makes us capture before we have looked.
We can photograph differently: less, better, after having first contemplated.
Perhaps we should, in front of what moves us, resist the first reflex and start by looking — really, for a long time, without a camera.
Then, only afterwards, decide if we want to keep an image of it.
For no photograph will ever replace what we haven't taken the time to see.

sentences: Never before in history have humans traveled as much.
What was once the privilege of a few has become a mass practice: we travel far, often, and for little money.
This democratization of travel is, in many ways, a blessing.
And yet, a troubling question arises: by traveling so much, are we really traveling in the full sense of the word?
For a long time, traveling was something other than just moving from one place to another.
It was about exposing oneself to the unknown, allowing oneself to be transformed by encountering another place, and returning a little different from the person who left.
Travel implied a certain slowness, an element of the unexpected, and an effort to understand.
It took time to reach a place, time to inhabit it, and time to be changed by it.
It is from this experience that the enrichment we expect from travel was born.
Mass tourism has, in part, dissolved this experience.
We now rush through places, ticking off sites like we’re filling out a checklist, bringing back images more than lived memories.
The destinations themselves, shaped for this quick consumption, offer the same amenities everywhere, so much so that one can travel around the world without ever leaving a familiar setting.
We see a lot; we meet few.
Even more disturbing is that our way of traveling transforms, and often degrades, what we come to seek.
The most popular places empty of their inhabitants, turn into backdrops for visitors, and lose the very authenticity that made them appealing.
The traveler unwittingly destroys the object of their desire: by being seen so much, some places cease to be what we came to see.
Should we then give up travel, or reserve it once again for a few privileged people?
That would be an unfair and sad conclusion.
The problem is not traveling, but the way we do it.
We can travel differently: perhaps not as far, but for longer; not as quickly, but more attentively; seeking not to consume places, but to understand them and allow ourselves to be surprised.
Truly traveling is not a matter of distance or the number of countries visited.
It is a matter of inner disposition: the one that accepts being disoriented, slowed down, and changed.
By this measure, one can travel around the world without ever really traveling, and travel deeply just a few hours from home.
Ultimately, it all depends not on where we go, but on how we look at it.

sentences: There was a time when cities competed for tourists, seeing them as a source of prosperity.
Today, some of them complain, on the contrary, about having too many.
Residents are protesting against the influx of visitors, municipalities are trying to limit it, and a new word has emerged to describe this phenomenon: 'overtourism.'

This reversal, seemingly paradoxical, reveals a reality that the tourist enthusiasm had long masked: beyond a certain threshold, tourism stops benefiting the places that host it and starts to destroy them.
The effects of this saturation are concrete.
In the most visited cities, housing is being transformed into tourist accommodations, pushing out residents due to rising rents.
Local shops are giving way to souvenir stores.
The streets, overcrowded, become impassable for those who live there.
Little by little, the city empties of its residents and its own life, turning into a backdrop for passing visitors.
It survives economically, but dies as a place to live.
The paradox is that this process ultimately ruins what attracted visitors in the first place.
People come to these cities for their charm, authenticity, and unique life; but the very influx of visitors destroys that charm and life.
In the end, all that remains is a shell, perhaps beautiful, but emptied of its substance — a place that one visits without being able to encounter anything other than other visitors.
Why is this problem so difficult to solve?
Because tourism is profitable, and the interests that depend on it are powerful.
Limiting the number of visitors means giving up immediate revenue, which few are willing to do.
Moreover, each actor, taken in isolation, has an interest in benefiting from the windfall, even if it harms the whole.
No visitor feels responsible for a saturation to which they believe they contribute only in a minimal way.

Solutions do exist, however, even if they face these resistances: limiting the number of visitors, regulating tourist accommodations, protecting residents' housing, and distributing flows over time and space.
None of them are simple; all require prioritizing the interests of the places and those who inhabit them over immediate profit.
Overtourism, at its core, holds up a mirror to us.
It shows what happens when a place is treated as a mere resource to exploit, without regard for those who live there.
And it reminds us of a truth that travelers often forget: the places we love to visit are primarily the homes of others.

sentences: We set off, or so we think, to discover the elsewhere: different landscapes, different customs, different ways of living.
And it's true that travel allows us to discover all of this.
But its deepest effect may lie elsewhere: by confronting us with other ways of being, it reveals to us, in return, our own way of being, which we had until then taken for the only natural one.
The stranger is a mirror, and it's often ourselves that we end up seeing in it.
The mechanism is subtle.
As long as we only know our own world, we do not perceive it as one possibility among others, but as the very evidence.
Our habits, our values, our ways of eating, greeting, conceiving time or family seem self-evident to us, because we have never seen that they could be different.
It is by discovering that elsewhere people do, think, and live differently that we simultaneously discover that our own ways are not inevitable.
This revelation can be destabilizing, and that is its virtue.
Seeing that others organize their existence on different principles, and do not live any worse for it, shakes our certainties.
What we took for natural turns out to be cultural; what we believed to be universal is revealed to be particular.
Travel, in this sense, is a lesson in humility: it teaches us that our way of seeing the world is just one way among others, neither the only one nor necessarily the best.
But this confrontation can also be a lesson in recognition.
By discovering other ways of living, we do not necessarily give up our own; sometimes, we rediscover them, understand them better, and appreciate their value that habit had hidden from us.
We return from afar, seeing our own home with fresh eyes, finally able to appreciate or question what we no longer even noticed.
That is why true travel requires a particular disposition: that of being open to questioning.
The traveler who judges everything by the standard of their own habits, who finds what differs from them 'strange' or 'backward', will see in the stranger only a deviation from their norm.
They are not really traveling: they are carrying their world with them.
Traveling, on the contrary, is to accept, for a time, to see with other eyes.
The greatest benefit of travel may therefore not be what it allows us to discover about the world, but what it helps us discover about ourselves.
We set off in search of the elsewhere; we return with a bit more clarity about ourselves.
The stranger, indeed, is the best of mirrors.

sentences: Here is a question that we rarely dare to ask, as it seems so naive: what is the purpose of art?
A painting does not feed anyone, a symphony does not cure any disease, and a poem has never built a house.
Measured by the standard of utility, art seems perfectly superfluous.
And yet, no human society, however poor or threatened it may be, has ever chosen to do without it.
This contradiction — the apparent uselessness of art and its stubborn universality — deserves our attention.
The answer may lie in the question itself, or rather in its presupposition.
Asking what art 'is for' judges it according to the logic of utility, that of means toward an end.
However, art precisely escapes this logic.
It serves no purpose other than itself; it is not a means, but an end.
Like love, like friendship, like contemplation, it belongs to those experiences that are valuable in themselves, not for what they might lead to.
Their 'uselessness' is not a flaw: it is a sign that they touch on something beyond mere survival.
For human beings do not settle for mere survival.

Once their vital needs are met, they experience other demands, less immediate but no less profound: to give meaning to their existence, to express what they feel, to understand their condition, to experience beauty.
Art responds to these demands.
It expresses what ordinary language cannot convey, gives form to confused emotions, and allows us to share what we thought was uncommunicable.
In this sense, it serves no purpose, but it addresses everything in us that goes beyond simple necessity.
Art also has this unique power to make us experience what we will never live.
Through a novel, we inhabit another life; through a painting, we see through other eyes; through music, we feel what another person felt, centuries apart.
Art thus broadens our experience well beyond the narrow limits of our individual existence.
It connects us to others, to the dead as well as the living, in a community of emotions and meaning.
We must guard against two opposing errors here.
The first would be to disdain art as a superfluous luxury, good for times of abundance.
The second would be to turn it into a religion, to sanctify it to the point of making it intimidating, reserved for a few initiates.
Art is neither a useless ornament nor a reserved cult; it is a fundamental human need, as old as humanity itself, and accessible, in a thousand forms, to everyone.
What is the purpose of art?
None, if we understand by that a practical utility.
Everything, if we understand that a purely useful life would not be a human life.
Art does not help us to live; it is a part of what makes life worth living.

sentences: Long-distance travel, which we have come to see as enriching, now faces a difficult objection to dismiss: it pollutes, and heavily.
Air travel, in particular, is among the most intense ways to emit the gases responsible for global warming.
A round trip to the other side of the world can, by itself, weigh as much as months of efforts elsewhere.
In light of this observation, a new sense of guilt has spread among travelers.
Is it justified, and should it make us give up traveling?
We must first acknowledge the reality of the dilemma, without avoiding it.
On one hand, travel has real value: it opens the mind, brings people closer, and fosters understanding between cultures — all that we have mentioned.
On the other hand, it has a no less real environmental cost, which weighs on an already threatened climate.
These two truths are equally valid, and it is their tension that makes the question uncomfortable.
To claim that travel has no cost, or that it is not worth any cost, would also be dishonest.
Guilt, however, is a rather unhelpful response.

It gnaws without guiding, and easily turns into its opposite: by constantly feeling guilty without changing behavior, one ends up resigning to it, or outright rejecting a demand perceived as moralizing.
Individual guilt, moreover, distracts attention from collective responsibilities, which are far more decisive.
Feeling guilty neither warms nor cools the planet; only actions matter.
A more just response would be to think in terms of moderation, not fault.
Not 'do I have the right to travel?', but 'how can I travel more reasonably?'
Traveling less often, but for longer; favoring closer destinations reached by less polluting means; making long-distance travel a thoughtful exception rather than a mechanical habit.
These choices do not eliminate the dilemma, but they mitigate it, preserving the essence of what travel brings while reducing its cost.
We must also reject a common hypocrisy: the one that places all responsibility on individuals while leaving intact the structures that make alternatives difficult.
As long as trains cost more than planes, and as long as low-pollution transport remains slow and rare, it will be unfair to blame each person for their constrained choices.
The question of travel here intersects with the broader issue of a transition that must be collective to be fair.
Should we therefore feel guilty about flying?
No, if guilt leads to nothing.
Yes, however, to question, to moderate, to choose with awareness.
Travel is neither a right without cost nor a sin to atone for, but a precious good that we must learn to use more judiciously.

sentences: When faced with a work that confounds us — an abstract painting, complex music, an obscure poem — a question often arises, tinged with a slight discomfort: must we understand it to appreciate it?
Many feel excluded from art because they do not 'understand,' as if prior knowledge were necessary to have the right to feel.
This widespread belief deserves examination, as it rests on a questionable conception of what it means to appreciate a work.
There is some truth in the idea that knowledge enriches experience.
Knowing the context of a work, the intentions of its author, the codes of its time often allows us to perceive dimensions that would otherwise remain invisible.
An ancient religious painting is better appreciated by those who know its symbols; sophisticated music is enjoyed differently when one grasps its structure.
In this sense, understanding deepens pleasure, and ignorance can deprive us of much.
But making understanding a prerequisite for appreciation would be a mistake.
For many works touch us even before we understand them, and sometimes without us ever fully understanding them.
Music moves us without us knowing why; a poem grips us before we have unraveled its meaning; a painting holds us simply by its presence.
This immediate emotion, prior to any explanation, is a form of full and complete appreciation that does not need to be justified by knowledge.
There is even something precious in this direct encounter, unmediated by commentary.
It reminds us that art speaks first to our sensitivity, not to erudition; that it addresses something in us that precedes reasoning.
Reducing appreciation to understanding would mean forgetting this sensitive part and transforming our relationship with art into an intellectual exercise reserved for those who know.
The danger of the belief that 'one must understand' is precisely here: it discourages, it intimidates, it distances from art those who, lacking knowledge, no longer dare to feel.
It turns what should be a free encounter into an exam that one fears failing.
How many give up on entering a museum or listening to demanding work, convinced that 'it's not for them'?
The truth is more welcoming: one can appreciate without understanding everything, feel without knowing how to explain, be touched without being able to justify it.
Knowledge can come later, deepen, enrich — and it is worth it.
But it is not the toll to pay to have the right to emotion.
When faced with a work, the first thing to do is not to understand; it is to allow oneself to be touched.

sentences: "There’s no arguing about tastes and colors," says popular wisdom.
Everyone has their own preferences, which are equally valid, and it would be futile — even pretentious — to judge the tastes of others.
This idea, which seems to promote tolerance, deserves to be questioned.
For while it contains a grain of truth, it also hides a more disturbing one: is everything really equal when it comes to taste?
First, let’s acknowledge what this saying gets right.
Our tastes are partly irreducibly personal, shaped by our history, our sensitivity, and our memories.
No one can prove to me that I should like one piece of music over another, and it’s absurd to try to impose one’s preferences as truths.
In this sense, tastes are not up for debate: they are experienced, and no one has the right to dictate to another what they should feel.
But to stop there would be too simple.
For if all tastes were strictly equivalent, some consequences would be hard to accept.
Should we say that a profound work and a crude production are equal, just because each has its fans?
That the judgment of a connoisseur, who has long engaged with an art, is no more valuable than that of an ignorant person?
The idea that "everything is equal" leads to these conclusions, which clash with our experience.
There is a difference between taste as mere preference and taste as discernment.
The former is purely subjective: I like it or I don’t, and that’s not up for discussion.
The latter is cultivated, refined, and educated: as one engages with an art, one learns to perceive nuances, qualities, and depths that were not initially visible.
This kind of taste is not arbitrary; it rests on acquired familiarity, and for that reason, it can be discussed, argued about, and transmitted.
Recognizing this is not elitist, provided one does not confuse discernment with disdain.
Saying that some judgments are more enlightened than others does not mean looking down on those who enjoy simple things; it merely asserts that taste can deepen, and that it’s worth cultivating.
Someone who has learned to appreciate complex music does not have a "better" taste as a person; they have a more developed taste, which opens up richer pleasures.
In summary, taste can both be discussed and not discussed, depending on what one means by that.
As raw preference, it escapes discussion; as cultivated discernment, it invites it.
Between the relativism that levels everything and the arrogance that scorns, there is room for a more just attitude: to respect everyone’s tastes while believing it’s worth educating one’s own.

sentences: A book is bought, a film is sold, a song is monetized.
Culture, clearly, is also an economy: it employs, it generates revenue, it is exchanged in substantial markets.
Should we conclude that a work is a product like any other, subject to the same laws as any merchandise?
The question is not merely theoretical: the answer we give affects how a society treats its artistic creation.
On one hand, it would be naive to deny the economic dimension of culture.
Artists need to make a living, works have production costs, and their distribution requires resources.
To claim that art is above any material consideration would reflect a comfortable idealism, often held by those who do not have to make a living from it.
A work indeed has economic value, and ignoring this does a disservice to both creators and the public.
But reducing culture to its only market dimension, treating it exactly like any product, poses a serious danger.
For if we judge a work solely by its commercial success, we end up producing only what sells best, to the detriment of what has value without necessarily reaching a wide audience.
The logic of the market favors what immediately pleases the greatest number, not what is demanding, new, or disturbing.
Left to its own devices, it would impoverish creation by eliminating everything that does not immediately find its market.
That is why most societies have believed that culture should not be left solely to the laws of commerce.
They have established protections, supports, exceptions: subsidies, regulated prices, creation aids, public institutions.
These measures are based on a conviction: culture is not a commodity like any other, because it fulfills a function that the market alone cannot ensure.
It transmits a heritage, nourishes debate, shapes minds, expresses what a society holds most profound.
This conviction is not without tensions or abuses, and we can discuss the forms that support for culture should take.
But the principle remains: a work is not just a commodity, because its value is not measured solely by what it brings in.
A book that hardly sells can be immensely valuable; a commercial success may have no lasting significance.
The market measures one thing; cultural value is another.
Treating culture as an ordinary commodity would thus mean forgetting what makes it precious.

Not that it should be removed from any economy — that is impossible and would not be desirable — but because it needs protection from a logic that, if left alone, would reduce it to what sells, sacrificing what is valuable.

sentences: The past is the past: it won't come back, and we can't change anything about it.
So why insist on studying it, teaching history, and going over events and figures that have long since disappeared?
This objection, often raised by those who find history boring, is not without merit.
Answering it requires us to clarify what we really expect from knowledge of the past.
One common response suggests that the past teaches us, that history is a 'master of life', and that by studying it we would avoid repeating our ancestors' mistakes.
This idea contains a grain of truth, but it is fragile.
For the past never repeats itself exactly, and the lessons we claim to draw from it are often contradictory or misleading.
History does not provide ready-made recipes; it does not mechanically tell us what to do.
Those who knew it best did not always avoid the worst mistakes.
The true usefulness of history lies elsewhere, in deeper insights.
Knowing the past is primarily about understanding ourselves.
We are the heirs of a long chain of events that have shaped the world we live in: our laws, our borders, our languages, our institutions, and even our conflicts come from far away.
Ignoring this history means living in a present without depth, unable to understand why things are the way they are.
History gives depth and meaning to the present.
Knowing the past also means learning that the world has not always been as it is, and that it could be different.
Nothing is more precious than this lesson.
What we take for natural, eternal, and unchanging, history shows us as the product of a process, something that has begun and could end.
It frees us from the illusion that the present is the only possible world, and thus enables us to transform it.
Finally, there is a distinctly human dimension in studying the past.
Reflecting on those who came before us, on their hopes, their sufferings, their struggles, extends our humanity beyond the narrow limits of our own time.
It is to acknowledge a debt to those who built the world we inherit, and a responsibility to those who will inherit ours.
History places us in a chain that transcends us.
So what is the purpose of knowing the past?
Not to draw recipes from it, but to understand where we come from, to realize that things can change, and to connect with what precedes us.
A people without memory is like an amnesiac man: he no longer knows who he is.
That is why, although we cannot change the past, it is so important not to forget it.

sentences: Every year, countless works are created — books, films, music, paintings.
Most will be forgotten within a few years; some will barely survive their author.
And a few, rare ones, will endure through the centuries, read, seen, and listened to long after the world that witnessed their birth has disappeared.
What distinguishes these enduring works, those we call 'classics'?
The answer is less obvious than it seems, and it involves both merit and chance.
We would like to believe that the works that last are simply the best, and that time carries out a fair selection, preserving only what deserves it.
This comforting idea contains a grain of truth: the works that stand the test of time often have a depth, richness, and quality of craftsmanship that set them apart.
There is something in them that is broad enough or just enough to continue to resonate with very different eras from their own.
Their survival is not without reason.
But reducing longevity to mere merit would ignore the significant role of chance and circumstances.
Many remarkable works have been lost or forgotten, not due to a lack of value, but by accident: a destroyed manuscript, a poorly defended author, an unfavorable trend.

Conversely, some works owe their survival to factors unrelated to their quality: the prestige of their author, the support of institutions, their inclusion in school curricula, or simply the luck of having been preserved.
The selection of time is not as fair as one might wish.
There is more.
What we call a 'classic' is not just a work that has lasted; it is also a work that we have collectively chosen to make last.
Each era reconsiders the legacy it receives, rediscovering forgotten works while abandoning others once thought immortal.
The canon of significant works is not fixed; it is constantly reshaped by the sensitivities, values, and struggles of each time.
What we regard as an eternal masterpiece is also the product of a judgment that could change.
This element of arbitrariness should not lead to relativism, to the idea that everything is equally valid and that longevity is purely random.
For while chance plays a large role, it does not account for everything: a work lacking quality does not last long, no matter what favor it initially enjoys.
Merit alone is not enough to ensure survival, but it is often a prerequisite.
Time does not always keep the best, but it eventually discards what has nothing to say.
Why do some works endure through time?
Through a mix of intrinsic value, favorable circumstances, and continually renewed collective choices.
Neither pure merit nor pure chance: both are intertwined.
This should make us both demanding of what we create and humble before what we judge — for we never quite know what the future will hold for us.

sentences: What makes a multitude of individuals, often very different, feel like members of the same nation?
Neither just territory, nor just language, nor just laws are enough to explain this.
What unites a people is also, and perhaps above all, a narrative: a common story they tell about their origins, their trials, their glories, and their purpose.
Nations hold together through these shared narratives as much as through their borders.
This national narrative serves a real and valuable function.
It creates a sense of belonging, connects strangers in an imagined community, and gives individuals the feeling of participating in something that transcends and precedes them.
Without this narrative link, a nation would be nothing more than a juxtaposition of individuals with nothing in common.
Foundational narratives, celebrated heroes, and commemorated great moments weave this invisible solidarity without which no lasting communal life is possible.
But these narratives have an inherent flaw: they simplify, embellish, and sometimes distort.
To unite, a national narrative tends to smooth over rough edges, magnify glories, and silence shames, presenting as a natural truth what was the product of chance and violence.
It transforms a complex and often troubled history into a coherent and flattering narrative.
In doing so, it strays from the truth and can become a myth that blinds more than it enlightens.
The danger arises when this narrative, instead of simply uniting, begins to exclude and oppose.
For a national narrative can also be constructed against others: by designating enemies, glorifying its own superiority, and fostering contempt or hatred for those who are not part of it.
History shows the disasters that can result from perverted national narratives, when a people tells itself a story of greatness and purity that justifies aggression or exclusion.
The narrative that unites can also arm.
Should we then renounce all national narratives in the name of historical truth alone?
That would be both impossible and dangerous.
Impossible, because no community can do without a narrative; dangerous, because the void left would quickly be filled by cruder narratives.
The issue is not to eliminate the narrative, but to demand it be more honest: capable of uniting without lying, of founding a belonging without denying complexity, of being proud without being blind.
An adult nation is one that can tell itself a true story, with its glories and its faults, and still find a way to hold together.
This is a difficult balance, always threatened, between the myth that unites and the truth that liberates.
But it is under this condition that a common narrative can gather the living without arming them against others.

alignments.english: It creates a sense of belonging, connects strangers in an imagined community, and gives individuals the feeling of participating in something that transcends and precedes them.

alignments.french: Sans ce lien narratif, une nation ne serait qu'une juxtaposition d'individus sans rien de commun.
alignments.english: Without this narrative link, a nation would be nothing more than a juxtaposition of individuals with nothing in common.

alignments.french: Les récits fondateurs, les héros célébrés, les grands moments commémorés tissent cette solidarité invisible sans laquelle aucune vie commune durable n'est possible.
alignments.english: Foundational narratives, celebrated heroes, and commemorated great moments weave this invisible solidarity without which no lasting communal life is possible.

alignments.french: Mais ces récits ont un défaut inhérent : ils simplifient, embellissent, et parfois falsifient.
alignments.english: But these narratives have an inherent flaw: they simplify, embellish, and sometimes distort.

alignments.french: Pour unir, un récit national tend à lisser les aspérités, à magnifier les gloires et à taire les hontes, à présenter comme une évidence naturelle ce qui fut le produit de hasards et de violences.
alignments.english: To unite, a national narrative tends to smooth over rough edges, magnify glories, and silence shames, presenting as a natural truth what was the product of chance and violence.

alignments.french: Il transforme une histoire complexe et souvent trouble en un récit cohérent et flatteur.
alignments.english: It transforms a complex and often troubled history into a coherent and flattering narrative.

alignments.french: Ce faisant, il s'éloigne de la vérité, et peut devenir un mythe qui aveugle plus qu'il n'éclaire.
alignments.english: In doing so, it strays from the truth and can become a myth that blinds more than it enlightens.

alignments.french: Le danger apparaît lorsque ce récit, au lieu de simplement unir, se met à exclure et à opposer.
alignments.english: The danger arises when this narrative, instead of simply uniting, begins to exclude and oppose.

alignments.french: Car un récit national peut aussi se construire contre d'autres : en désignant des ennemis, en glorifiant sa propre supériorité, en nourrissant le mépris ou la haine de ceux qui n'en font pas partie.
alignments.english: For a national narrative can also be constructed against others: by designating enemies, glorifying its own superiority, and fostering contempt or hatred for those who are not part of it.

alignments.french: L'histoire montre à quels désastres peuvent mener les récits nationaux dévoyés, quand un peuple se raconte une histoire de grandeur et de pureté qui justifie l'agression ou l'exclusion.
alignments.english: History shows the disasters that can result from perverted national narratives, when a people tells itself a story of greatness and purity that justifies aggression or exclusion.

alignments.french: Le récit qui unit peut aussi armer.
alignments.english: The narrative that unites can also arm.

alignments.french: Faut-il alors renoncer à tout récit national, au nom de la seule vérité historique ?
alignments.english: Should we then renounce all national narratives in the name of historical truth alone?

alignments.french: Ce serait à la fois impossible et dangereux.
alignments.english: That would be both impossible and dangerous.

alignments.french: Impossible, car aucune communauté ne se passe de récit ; dangereux, car le vide laissé serait aussitôt comblé par des récits plus grossiers.
alignments.english: Impossible, because no community can do without a narrative; dangerous, because the void left would quickly be filled by cruder narratives.

alignments.french: L'enjeu n'est pas de supprimer le récit, mais de le vouloir plus honnête : capable d'unir sans mentir, de fonder une appartenance sans nier la complexité, d'être fier sans être aveugle.
alignments.english: The issue is not to eliminate the narrative, but to demand it be more honest: capable of uniting without lying, of founding a belonging without denying complexity, of being proud without being blind.

alignments.french: Une nation adulte est celle qui peut se raconter une histoire vraie, avec ses grandeurs et ses fautes, et y trouver malgré tout de quoi tenir ensemble.
alignments.english: An adult nation is one that can tell itself a true story, with its glories and its faults, and still find a way to hold together.

alignments.french: C'est là un équilibre difficile, toujours menacé, entre le mythe qui unit et la vérité qui libère.
alignments.english: This is a difficult balance, always threatened, between the myth that unites and the truth that liberates.

alignments.french: Mais c'est à cette condition qu'un récit commun peut rassembler les vivants sans les armer contre d'autres.
alignments.english: But it is under this condition that a common narrative can gather the living without arming them against others.

sentences: Societies, like individuals, have a memory.
They remember certain events, commemorate others, erect monuments, celebrate dates, and pass down stories.

But this collective memory, far from being a simple reflection of the past, results from choices: some things are retained, others are forgotten, certain episodes are highlighted while others are silenced.
What a people's memory retains is therefore nothing neutral; it is a stake, and often a battleground.
For a nation's past is never simple, nor solely glorious.
It contains dark pages as well as proud ones: conquests and defeats, greatness and crimes.
However, a society cannot keep everything present with the same intensity.
It selects, prioritizes, highlights certain memories, and leaves others in the shadows.
This selection reflects what it wants to be, the image it has of itself, and sometimes what it prefers not to see.
This selective memory plays out in each generation.
What was celebrated yesterday can be questioned today; figures once honored are contested, events long silenced resurface and demand recognition.

The debates over statues, commemorations, and street names, which stir so many countries, are not trivial disputes: they concern what a society chooses to celebrate or condemn, thus what it is and wants to become.
The battle is fought over the past, but the stake is the present.
These memory conflicts are often painful, and it would be tempting to want to soothe them by decreeing a convenient forgetfulness: 'let's not stir up the past.'
But this forgetfulness comes at a price.

Silencing the crimes of the past, refusing to acknowledge the inflicted suffering, deprives the victims and their descendants of the recognition they need, and allows wounds to fester for lack of being named.
A memory that only retains the glorious does not soothe; it represses, and what is repressed eventually resurfaces.
Conversely, a memory obsessed only with faults, unable to also recognize what was great, would fall into sterile self-criticism.
The issue is not to choose between pride and shame, but to hold together the whole truth: greatness and crimes, without complacency or denial.
An adult memory is one that can face its past in all its complexity.
The way a people remembers says a lot about its maturity.
Taking responsibility for its past, including its dark areas, without indulging in it or denying it, is a sign of a confident society.
For one does not build oneself on a lie, however flattering, but on the truth, however difficult.

sentences: A difficult question runs through our relationship with the past: can we judge those who came before us by our own values?
When we discover that admired figures committed or tolerated what seems unacceptable to us today, how should we react?
Should we condemn them in the name of our principles, or excuse them on the grounds that they were of their time?
The question does not have a simple answer, and the two extreme positions turn out, upon examination, to be equally unsatisfactory.
The first position is to judge the past without leniency, to apply our current values to those who lived in the past, and to condemn without appeal what offends us.
This attitude has a moral requirement: it refuses to turn a blind eye to real injustices on the pretext that they are old.
But it has a major flaw: it is anachronistic.
It blames people of the past for not sharing ideas that did not yet exist, for not seeing what no one, or almost no one, could see at the time.
It judges without understanding, from a position of easy superiority.
The second, opposite position is to excuse everything in the name of context: 'they were of their time,' it is said, as if that were enough to absolve them.
This attitude has a sense of historical nuance: it reminds us that people of the past thought within a framework that was not ours.

But when taken to extremes, it becomes a comfortable relativism that forbids any judgment, and ultimately admits that nothing, ever, could be condemned, since everything could be explained by its time.
If everything is excusable, then the worst is too.
Between these two dead ends, a fairer path is to distinguish between understanding and approving.
We can understand why people of the past thought and acted as they did, place their actions in context, and measure what they could or could not conceive — without approving what remains condemnable.
Understanding is not excusing; it is refusing lazy judgment while retaining the ability to judge.
We can recognize that an injustice was an injustice, while taking into account the blindness of the time.
This distinction also allows for a form of humility.
For if we judge harshly the blindness of our ancestors, we should remember that we too have our blind spots, which future generations may judge with the same severity.
Today, we likely tolerate things that will one day seem scandalous.
Judging the past should therefore make us not arrogant, but clear-sighted about our own time.
Judging the past with today's eyes is thus both necessary and perilous.
Necessary, because to renounce all judgment would be to renounce morality; perilous, because judging without understanding is unjust.
Wisdom consists in holding both: understanding without absolving, judging without believing oneself superior.
And never to forget that we will, in turn, be judged.

sentences: “To remember so that it does not happen again.” This phrase, often repeated regarding the great tragedies of history, expresses a deep conviction: the memory of past horrors would protect us against their return.
It is in the name of this idea that we maintain the memory of massacres, that we visit places of horror, that we pass on to younger generations the story of the worst.
But this conviction, noble as it may be, deserves to be examined with clarity.
Does memory really suffice to prevent the worst from happening again?
The idea is based on a seductive reasoning: if people know what certain ideas, certain hatreds, and certain cowardices have led to, they will be able to recognize and reject them.
Memory would thus be a vigilance, an immunity acquired at the cost of past misfortunes.
And it is true that ignorance of the past encourages its repetition: a people who knows nothing of the disasters of history would be more exposed to repeating the same path.
In this respect, memory is indeed a protection, and forgetting is a danger.
However, history itself invites us not to overestimate this power.
For atrocities have been repeated even when the memory of previous ones was vivid.
Knowing the past has not always prevented repetition, and we have seen educated societies succumb to horror once again.
Memory alone does not provide immunity.
It can even, if misdirected, foster new resentments, sustain old hatreds, and serve to justify new violence in the name of past wounds.
Memory is not always on the side of peace.
This is because memory can take very different forms.
Remembering as a victim, to nurture a grudge, does not have the same effect as remembering to understand.
A memory that merely rehashes emotion, without an effort to understand, offers poor protection: it stirs without enlightening.
What truly protects is less the raw memory than what we make of it: understanding how the worst was possible, what mechanisms led to it, and what ordinary cowardices allowed it.
Simply remembering the facts is not enough; we must draw intelligence from them.
Memory is therefore a protection only under certain conditions.
It must be accompanied by understanding, aimed at recognizing the mechanisms of evil rather than just mourning the victims, and it should illuminate the present rather than confine us to the past.
An intelligent memory looks less backward than forward: it scrutinizes the present to detect the signs of what it knows.
To remember so as not to repeat: yes, but only if we truly remember, that is, if we understand.
Memory is not an automatic guarantee; it is a vigilance to be maintained, a task always to be resumed.
It only protects us if we make it work, not if we let it lie dormant in commemorations.

sentences: Sometimes, to discredit science, a decisive criticism is heard: it changes its mind.
What it asserted yesterday, it corrects today; its certainties from one era are contradicted by the next.
How can we trust it, then, if it contradicts itself like this?
This common criticism, however, is based on a profound misunderstanding.
For what is presented as a weakness is, in reality, the very strength of science, and what distinguishes it from everything that claims to know without ever questioning itself.
Let’s understand well what 'changing one's mind' means in science.
It does not mean yielding to whim or fashion, but revising one's conclusions in light of new facts.
When an observation contradicts a theory, the scientist does not stubbornly defend their theory against the facts; they modify it or abandon it for a better one.
This ability to correct oneself is not a flaw of scientific knowledge: it is its principle.
Science progresses precisely because it accepts being wrong and rectifying.
What should concern us, then, is not a science that corrects itself, but a knowledge that would never correct itself.
A doctrine that claims to hold a definitive truth, insensitive to any objection or contrary fact, would not be more reliable: it would be dogmatic.

In the face of a complex and partly unknown reality, unwavering certainty is suspect, and the ability to doubt, revise, and admit one’s error is, on the contrary, the mark of an honest relationship with the truth.
Doubt is not the enemy of knowledge; it is its guardian.
It is this methodical doubt that makes science reliable, despite its errors — or rather thanks to its way of dealing with them.
No scientific assertion is safe from being revised one day; all are, by principle, provisional, open to criticism and the test of facts.
This absence of definitive certainty, which may seem a weakness, is what allows science to approach, correction after correction, a progressively more accurate understanding.
What is solid in it is not eternal truths, but a method that learns from its mistakes.
However, one must guard against a misunderstanding.
That science corrects itself does not mean that anything goes, nor that its current conclusions deserve no trust on the grounds that they might change.
A theory that has been thoroughly tested, confirmed by countless observations, deserves our trust, even if the future may refine it.
Because science is revisable, one cannot conclude that its results are without value: that would confuse caution with lazy skepticism.
Doubt, when properly understood, does not weaken science; it is its foundation.
To distrust what never doubts, to trust what accepts correction: this is perhaps the most valuable lesson that science can impart to us, far beyond its results.
For this willingness to revise one’s beliefs in light of the facts is not only a scientific method; it is an intellectual virtue that our debates often sorely lack.

sentences: No one can know everything or verify everything by themselves.
On the vast majority of topics, we are forced to rely on those who know: doctors, scientists, engineers, specialists of all kinds.
This trust in experts is inevitable and even reasonable: it would be absurd to claim to judge everything based solely on one's own opinion.
But it raises a delicate question: who to trust, and to what extent?
For experts are not infallible; they can make mistakes and sometimes contradict each other.
Let's start by dismissing two attitudes that are equally convenient and equally false.
The first is blind submission: believing an expert at their word simply because they are presented as such, without ever questioning.

The second is systematic distrust: rejecting the words of experts by principle, in the name of 'I form my own opinion,' which, due to a lack of expertise, is often just a poorly informed opinion disguised as independence of thought.
Between credulity and rejection, we must seek a more just path.
This path is based on a few guidelines.
First, competence is not general but specialized: an expert is only reliable in their own field.
An eminent scholar in one discipline has no more authority on another subject than anyone else.
Being wary of those who speak confidently outside their area of expertise is a healthy first reflex.
Notoriety is not competence, and the title of expert is only valid in the field where it was earned.
Next, we must distinguish between agreement and disagreement among experts.

When, on a question, the vast majority of specialists agree after years of work, that agreement constitutes the best available knowledge, and contradicting it based solely on one's intuition is unreasonable.
When, on the contrary, experts are genuinely divided, caution is necessary, and no one can claim to decide in the name of science.
Confusing a marginal disagreement with a genuine controversy, or presenting a consensus as merely an opinion, are two common ways to deceive.
Finally, we must question interests.
An expert is not a pure intellect: they can be influenced by what funds them, by their convictions, by the interests they serve.
This does not disqualify them — a funded researcher can be right — but it calls for vigilance, especially when their conclusions conveniently align with the interests of those who pay them.
Looking into who is speaking, and on whose behalf, is part of informed judgment.

Trusting experts is therefore neither an abdication nor naivety, provided it is done with discernment: respecting competence in its field, following solid consensus, remaining cautious in the face of disagreements, and questioning interests.
Thus, one can trust those who know without renouncing their own judgment — for true judgment does not consist of knowing everything oneself, but of reasonably knowing whom to trust.

sentences: Chance exists, but our minds struggle to accept it.
When faced with events that are purely due to chance, we stubbornly seek meaning, a cause, or an intention.
We see shapes in the cloud of coincidences, signs in what is merely random, and trends in what is just fluctuation.

This difficulty in accepting chance, in recognizing it for what it is, is not trivial: it distorts our judgment in a thousand ways, and understanding chance is one of the most useful and counterintuitive things that reason can learn.
Where does this resistance come from?
Surely from a deep tendency to seek explanations everywhere.
Seeing causes and intentions has been an advantage for our ancestors: it was better to imagine a predator behind a noise than to ignore a real danger.
This reflex, valuable in the face of threats, misleads us when it comes to chance: it makes us attribute meaning to what has none, to discern a will where there are only coincidences.
We are, in a way, wired to reject chance.
This refusal produces characteristic errors.
After a series of coincidences, we believe in a link that does not exist.
In the face of a sequence of results, we imagine a regularity, a 'series', where only chance operates.
We are surprised by coincidences that, statistically, were almost certain to occur one day, given such a large number of occasions.
We draw conclusions from a small number of cases, forgetting that a small sample fluctuates greatly.
All these errors have a common root: our inability to conceive what chance actually produces.
Understanding chance, then, is first and foremost about accepting a disturbing idea: many things happen without reason, without a determined cause, without intention.
A striking coincidence may be just a coincidence; a success or a failure may owe much to chance; a series may have no meaning.
Recognizing the role of chance does not mean giving up on understanding the world; it means understanding that a part of the world inherently escapes any explanation in terms of causes or intentions.
This understanding has concrete virtues.
It makes us more cautious in the face of coincidences, more modest in our successes as well as our failures, and more resistant to the illusions that exploit our difficulty with chance.
It protects against those who, playing on this tendency, sell us imaginary causes, miracle remedies, and misleading explanations of what is merely fluctuation.
Knowing how to recognize chance is to safeguard oneself against a host of errors and manipulations.
Finally, understanding chance is a form of wisdom.
It is accepting that we do not control everything, that chance plays a role in our lives that we prefer to ignore, that not everything has a hidden meaning.
This clarity may seem austere; it is also liberating.
For recognizing the role of chance is to stop desperately searching for meaning where there is none, and to focus our intelligence where it can truly understand.

sentences: Science has transformed the world and our understanding of it with unparalleled power.
It has uncovered mysteries that were once thought to be unfathomable, healed ailments that were believed to be fatal, revealed the vastness of the universe and the intimacy of matter.
In light of so many successes, it is tempting to believe that it could answer all questions, and that what it cannot establish is not worth taking seriously.
This confidence, however, deserves to be nuanced: science can do a lot, but it cannot do everything, and confusing its limits with those of knowledge would be a mistake.
What science can do, it does better than any other approach: describe and explain the world as it is.

How celestial bodies move, what bodies are made of, how species evolve, what causes diseases: to these questions, and to countless others, science provides proven answers, constantly verified and corrected.
Its strength lies precisely there: in a method that subjects every assertion to the test of facts, and grants its trust only to what withstands scrutiny.
But this very strength outlines its limits.
Science answers questions about what is; it is powerless in the face of questions about what ought to be.
It can say what an action will produce, not whether that action is good or just.
It can describe life, not say what meaning to give it.
These questions — moral, existential, aesthetic — are not scientific questions, not because they are insignificant, but because they do not fall under the observation of facts.
No experiment will tell whether a life is worth living, nor what we owe to others.
We must guard against two symmetrical errors here.
The first, which could be called scientism, consists of believing that only science provides true knowledge, and dismissing any question that escapes its method as futile.
This attitude amputates existence of essential dimensions — morality, meaning, beauty — on the grounds that they cannot be measured.
The second error, the opposite, consists of using the limits of science to discredit what it establishes, as if the fact that it does not answer everything justifies doubting what it does answer.
Recognizing that science does not say everything does not in any way allow us to deny what it demonstrates.
The right attitude lies in a double respect.
Respect for science in its domain: on questions of fact, its authority is legitimate, and preferring opinion or belief to it is unreasonable.
Respect, too, for what escapes its domain: questions of meaning and value, which it cannot settle, call for other resources — philosophy, morality, experience, wisdom.
Science is an admirable tool, but a tool, not a universal oracle.
Knowing what it can do prevents us from despising it; knowing what it cannot do allows us to ask it what it cannot provide.
Between idolatry and distrust, there is room for clear-sighted confidence.
