sentences: Here is a fascinating idea, often misunderstood: the language we speak would influence our way of thinking.
According to this thesis, the words we have and the distinctions our language imposes would shape even our perception of the world.
Those who speak different languages would not simply name the same realities differently: they would, in a sense, see them differently.
This appealing idea deserves careful examination, as it is often both exaggerated and underestimated.
In its strong version, the thesis claims that language would entirely determine thought: one could only conceive what their language allows them to express.
This version is false, and experience disproves it.
We can think of things that our language does not name with a single word; we invent expressions, borrow terms, and forge new concepts.
If language completely imprisoned thought, no new ideas could arise, and translation would be impossible.
However, we translate, we create, we understand what other languages express differently.
But rejecting the strong version should not lead to denying any influence.
For in a more modest version, the thesis holds up much better.
Language does not imprison thought, but it guides it, facilitating it here and hindering it there.
A language that has a precise word for a nuance makes that nuance easier to perceive and handle; a language that requires certain distinctions makes the mind more attentive.
Without locking us in, language traces paths that are more or less convenient for thought.
Research has highlighted such effects, subtle but real.

According to the categories their language distinguishes, speakers sometimes show themselves quicker to notice certain differences, remember certain details, and organize their perception in a certain way.
These effects do not make them prisoners of their language; they simply show that by cutting the world in its own way, language slightly inclines attention and memory.
Language does not dictate thought; it nuances it.
This measured conclusion has implications that go beyond linguistics.
It suggests that speaking multiple languages means having several ways to cut the world, thus, in a sense, enriching one's thought with multiple perspectives.
It also invites vigilance: if words guide the mind, then the choice of words in public debate is never innocent.
Naming a reality in a certain way already inclines one to see it that way.
Words do not shape thought on their own, but they do not leave it intact either.

Between the myth of a language that would determine everything and the illusion of thought being completely independent of words, the truth lies in this middle ground: language is less a prison than a landscape, where some paths are easier than others, but where the mind can always carve out new ways.

sentences: At regular intervals, somewhere in the world, a language goes extinct: its last speaker dies, and with them disappears a unique way of naming the world.
This phenomenon, long ignored, is accelerating: a large portion of the languages spoken today could be gone by the end of the century.
Should we be concerned and fight to preserve them, or accept this disappearance as a natural, even desirable simplification?
The question is more delicate than it seems.
An argument often arises in favor of indifference, even of disappearance: fewer languages would mean more mutual understanding.
If everyone spoke the same few languages, wouldn't we understand each other better?
Isn't the diversity of languages, an obstacle to communication, just a relic to be surpassed?
This argument has an appearance of common sense, but it relies on a narrow conception of what a language is, reduced to a simple interchangeable tool for communication.
For a language is much more than a means of communication.
It is the repository of an entire culture, the trace of a particular way of seeing the world, of cutting it up, of feeling it.
Each language contains concepts, nuances, and expressions that exist nowhere else, and which disappear with it.
It carries literature, memory, and accumulated knowledge about a place and a history.
When a language dies, it is not just a simple duplicate that fades away; it is a world of thought that goes extinct, irreplaceable.
We can compare this loss to that of biodiversity.
Just as the disappearance of a species impoverishes all living things, the death of a language impoverishes all of humanity, which loses one of its ways of being human.
This linguistic diversity is a common heritage, of which each language is a unique fragment.
Allowing it to erode through indifference is to accept an irreversible impoverishment of human richness.
However, we must guard against an idealism that would ignore the realities.
Languages rarely die by chance: they often disappear because their speakers, under economic or social pressure, are forced to adopt another language to survive.
Therefore, we cannot defend endangered languages without caring about the fate of those who speak them.
Preserving a language against the will of its speakers would not make sense; rather, it is about giving them the means to keep it if they wish, without having to sacrifice their future.
Defending dying languages is therefore not about opposing the course of the world out of nostalgia.
It is to recognize that each language is an irreplaceable treasure, and to refuse to let it disappear through simple neglect or under pressure.
A world that spoke only a handful of languages might be more convenient; it would surely be infinitely poorer.

sentences: An age-old dispute opposes two views of language.
For some, a language must be protected, fixed by rules, defended against mistakes and borrowings that distort it; there would exist a correct form that must be preserved from corruption.

For others, a language is a living organism that belongs to those who speak it and has the right to evolve, transform, and incorporate new words; wanting to freeze it would be futile and even harmful.
This disagreement, which resurfaces with every change in the language, deserves to be examined dispassionately.
The defenders of the norm are not entirely wrong.
A language needs common rules to fulfill its primary function: to allow its speakers to understand each other.
If everyone wrote and spoke as they pleased, without a shared convention, communication would become difficult.
Grammar, spelling, and a stable vocabulary are common goods that facilitate exchange and provide access to a written heritage.
In this regard, ensuring a certain level of correctness is not pedantry, but a service to everyone.
But the proponents of evolution also have strong arguments.
Every living language changes, and this is the very sign of its vitality: only dead languages no longer move.
The language that today's guardians of the norm defend is itself the product of centuries of transformations, borrowings, and innovations that could have been denounced as mistakes in every era.
Wanting to stop this movement ignores the fact that the 'pure' language that is claimed to be defended has never existed, and what is called a mistake today may become the correct usage of tomorrow.
There is more.
A language does not belong to an academy or a few guardians, but to the multitude of those who speak it and bring it to life every day.
It is they who, through their usage, ultimately decide what is said and what is lost.
The rules follow usage more than they precede it: they record, with delay, what speakers have already adopted.
Claiming to impose a language from above against the actual usage of its speakers is to misunderstand the very nature of language.
The truth is undoubtedly that these two forces are both necessary, and that their very tension is fruitful.
The norm retains, stabilizes, transmits; usage innovates, adapts, renews.
A language left solely to the norm would freeze and distance itself from its speakers; a language left solely to usage, without any common reference point, would risk fragmenting.
It is from the balance between these two tendencies that a language both stable and alive is born.
Thus, the language does indeed belong to those who speak it, but those who speak it also have an interest in preserving its coherence.

Between the conservatism that would want to freeze everything and the laissez-faire that would abandon all rules, wisdom consists of accompanying evolution without rushing it or rejecting it — treating the language not as a monument to be kept intact, nor as a formless material, but as a living heritage that is transmitted while allowing it to change, cautiously.

sentences: We spontaneously associate communication with speech: to communicate means to speak, to say, to express oneself with words.
In this perspective, silence is merely an absence, a void, the interruption of true communication.
However, this conception is incomplete.
For silence is not just the absence of words; it is itself full of meaning, it communicates in its own way, and it plays a role in our exchanges that chatter often makes us forget.
Silence, first of all, speaks.
A silence after a question can express embarrassment, disagreement, contemplation, or refusal.
A silence shared between two close individuals conveys an understanding that no words could express better.
A silence in the face of another's suffering can be worth more than all verbal consolations.
Silence is not a gap in communication; it is a modality of it, as rich and sometimes more accurate than speech.
What we leave unsaid means as much as what we say.
Silence also has its own value, which our era tends to ignore.
We live in a world saturated with words, noise, and demands, where silence has become rare and almost suspicious.
We rush to fill it, as if it were unbearable, filling every void with music, words, and content.
Yet this silence that we flee is precisely what the mind needs to settle, reflect, and feel.
It is often in silence that the deepest thoughts are born, where the inner life unfolds that constant noise stifles.
In the very act of exchange, silence has virtues that abundant speech cannot replace.
Knowing how to be silent to truly listen, allowing the other person space to express themselves, and not filling every pause with words: this is a form of attention and respect.
Those who speak incessantly do not listen; they occupy the space, preventing the other from existing.
Silence, on the contrary, makes room for the other, and this space is the foundation of any true encounter.
There is an eloquence in attentive silence that no discourse can match.
Of course, it is not about making silence an absolute value, nor about despising speech, which remains the best means of understanding and connecting with one another.
Silence also has its shadows: it can be an escape, cowardice, or a refusal to say what should be said.
Being silent when one should speak, keeping silence in the face of injustice, is not a virtue.
Silence does not hold value in itself; it is valued for what it carries and for the moment when we choose it.
Thus, silence indeed has meaning, and even several.
Far from being the simple opposite of communication, it is an essential part of it, which our talkative culture has unlearned to hear.

Rediscovering the meaning of silence — knowing how to be silent, listen, leave space, and inhabit the voids rather than flee from them — may be a way to regain a part of what the overflow of words has made us lose.

sentences: We are naturally impressed by those who speak well.
Eloquence, mastery of words, and fluency of speech command our respect and lead us to attribute intelligence and insight to those who possess them.
This association between speaking well and thinking well is deeply ingrained in us.
But it deserves to be questioned, because the link between the quality of expression and that of thought is more uncertain than we believe, and can even, at times, be reversed.
There is, of course, a grain of truth in this association.
Clearly expressing an idea often implies having conceived it clearly; the confusion of the message frequently betrays the confusion of thought.
Knowing how to order one's words, distinguish, nuance, and argue are operations that pertain to both thought and language.
In this sense, speaking well can be a sign that one thinks well, and the effort to express oneself better is often an effort to think better.
Language and thought are linked, and working on one helps the other.
But this association has its limits, and even its pitfalls.
For eloquence is also an art that can be cultivated independently of the correctness of ideas.
One can learn to speak beautifully without saying anything, to dress hollow or false thoughts in beautiful words.
History is full of brilliant orators serving despicable causes, in superb speeches that have led to the worst misguidances.
Eloquence is a power, and like any power, it is morally neutral: it serves both truth and falsehood with the same effectiveness.
There is something even more disturbing.
Eloquence can not only mask the absence of thought but actively deceive judgment.
A skillful speech moves, seduces, and carries away, and this seduction weakens the critical mind of the listener.
We are inclined to believe what is well said, to confuse the beauty of form with the truth of content.
Manipulators know this well, as they carefully craft their rhetoric precisely to disarm our vigilance.
The charm of words can be the best ally of lies.
Conversely, a correct thought can be expressed clumsily.
Many people who think deeply express themselves without brilliance, hesitate, search for their words, and we wrongly judge them as mediocre because they lack fluency.
Thus, we risk preferring a hollow smooth talker to a clumsy but correct thinker, deceived by form at the expense of content.
The seduction of eloquence can make us unjust towards the poorly dressed truth.
Speaking well is therefore neither a guarantee nor proof of thinking well.
Sometimes it is a sign, sometimes a mask.
Wisdom consists in not being dazzled by form, in seeking the solidity of ideas beneath the words, and in being wary of our own tendency to believe what is well said.
Not to despise eloquence — which, in the service of truth, is precious — but to never confuse it with the truth that it can serve as well as betray.

sentences: The world is complicated.
The phenomena around us — social, economic, natural — often result from multiple, intertwined causes that are difficult to untangle.
However, our mind, faced with this complexity, feels uneasy and instinctively seeks to dispel it.
It prefers simple, clear explanations that reassure and are easy to remember.
This preference, quite natural, is also one of our most dangerous weaknesses, because what is simple to understand is not necessarily true.
The temptation of simple explanations takes recognizable forms.
It seeks a single cause where there are several: this problem comes from one thing, and one thing only.
It designates a convenient scapegoat: if things go wrong, it's the fault of a certain group, a certain decision, a certain person.
It reduces a complex reality to a stark opposition, to a clear narrative where good and evil, cause and effect, can be identified effortlessly.
These explanations have immense appeal: they soothe the discomfort of uncertainty and give the feeling of understanding.
This appeal explains the success of theories that claim to explain everything by a single hidden cause.
Faced with troubling events, whose real causes are diffuse and disappointing, the mind is seduced by the idea that a plan, a will, a culprit might be hiding behind everything.
Such explanations have clarity and drama on their side; they transform the bewildering disorder of reality into a satisfying narrative.
That they are false does not prevent them from being believed, because they respond to a need stronger than the concern for truth: the need to understand, or to believe we understand.
Resisting this temptation requires effort, and even a certain courage: the courage to accept complexity, to tolerate uncertainty, to acknowledge that we do not understand everything.
It is more comfortable to hold a simple and false explanation than to admit that the truth is complicated, uncertain, and perhaps partly out of reach.
Accepting not to take sides, to suspend judgment, to live with questions that have no clear answers, goes against our most natural inclination.
Yet it is at this price that we escape reassuring illusions.
This does not mean we should retreat into a paralyzing skepticism, where nothing would ever be explainable.
Not all explanations are equal, and some, although complex, are well established.
It is not about giving up understanding, but about being wary of overly easy understandings, preferring a complicated truth to a clear lie.
Simplicity can be a mark of deep thought; it is more often a sign of lazy thinking.

To challenge simple explanations is to cultivate a form of intellectual maturity: one that prefers the discomfort of the true to the comfort of the false, which accepts that the world resists our desires for clarity.
In a time when so many voices offer clear answers to complex questions, this skepticism is not a luxury; it is a necessity.

sentences: Almost everyone claims to believe in justice.
No one openly defends injustice, and "that's not fair" is among the most universal protests.
However, as soon as we try to define what a just society is, agreement falls apart.
For under the same word lie profoundly different conceptions, and disagreement about justice may be the most fundamental issue in political life.
Understanding this disagreement is key to grasping the essence of our divisions.
Let's take a seemingly simple question: how should the wealth produced by a society be distributed fairly?
One initial answer is: to each according to their merit.
It would be fair for those who work harder, take more risks, and contribute more to receive more.
Rewarding effort and talent, allowing everyone to keep the fruits of their labor: this is, for many, the very demand of justice.
According to this view, inequalities are not unjust in themselves, as long as they reflect different merits.
A second answer challenges this perspective.
Merit, it says, is not as pure as it seems: those who succeed owe much to factors beyond their control — their birth, their background, their innate talents, and luck.
Is it fair that someone who had the luck to be born into a favorable environment reaps the rewards throughout their life, while another, born into poverty, bears all the burden?
According to this conception, a just society must correct inequalities that do not result from individuals' choices but from the lottery of birth.
Justice then requires a form of redistribution.
A third answer shifts the question further.
What matters, it says, is not so much the distribution of wealth as the guarantee, for everyone, of a minimum of dignity and freedom.
A just society would be one where no one lacks the essentials, where everyone can live decently and lead the life they have reason to want, regardless of other inequalities.
The emphasis is less on equality than on a threshold below which it would be undignified to let anyone fall.
These conceptions are not mere arbitrary opinions; each is based on respectable values — freedom, equality, dignity, responsibility — all of which matter, but which come into tension.
One cannot maximize both the reward for merit and the correction of birth inequalities; it requires arbitration, and it is in this arbitration that our disagreements lie.
Those who oppose each other on justice are not, most often, one side just and the other not: they assign different weights to equally legitimate values.
Recognizing this does not resolve the disagreement, but makes it more fruitful.
It allows us to stop seeing the opponent as an enemy of justice, and to understand that they have a different conception based on other priorities.

A just society may not be one that has found the definitive formula for justice — there isn't one — but one that knows how to debate these tensions without resolving them through force, and seeks, without ever fully achieving it, a balance among all these real demands.

sentences: Among the ideas of justice, equality of opportunity enjoys almost universal prestige.
Its principle is appealing: no matter the inequalities in results, as long as everyone starts with the same chances and success depends on merit, not birth.
A race is fair, the saying goes, if everyone starts from the same line; what happens next depends on each person's effort and talent.
This idea, widely shared, deserves to be examined closely, as its implementation and sufficiency raise serious questions.
The first problem is that equality of opportunity, as it is proclaimed, is rarely achieved.
Claiming that everyone starts from the same line is, in most societies, a fiction.
A child born into a wealthy and educated environment benefits, from birth, from considerable advantages: a stimulating environment, connections, financial ease, a thousand invisible aids.
A child born into poverty faces, from the outset, obstacles that the other does not know.
Talking about equality of opportunity when the starting points are so different often amounts to illusion or hypocrisy.
Truly achieving equality of opportunity would therefore require much more than is said.
We would need to compensate for the inequalities of birth, providing everyone with an education, health, and an environment that neutralizes initial disadvantages.
This is an immense, costly task, never fully accomplished.

Those who invoke equality of opportunity to justify inequalities in results often forget that they are invoking a principle that is, in reality, not respected — and that, if it were truly respected, would upend the existing order.
But even assuming equality of opportunity is perfectly realized: would it be enough to create a just society?
Nothing is less certain.
For a perfectly fair competition still produces winners and losers, and the fate of the losers remains a question of justice.
Should we abandon to their misery those who, in a fair race, came in last?
Would a society that ensured equal chances but left the defeated without dignity or resources be just?
Equality of opportunity organizes the competition; it says nothing about the treatment of those who lose it.
There is more.
The very idea of merit, on which equality of opportunity rests, is fragile.
For talents, energy, and the capacity for work, which determine success in a fair competition, are themselves largely gifts, inherited or received, for which no one is truly the author.
Does someone who wins because they are more gifted fully deserve their victory if they did not earn their gift?
Equality of opportunity shifts the lottery of birth without abolishing it entirely.
Therefore, equality of opportunity is a precious ideal, but neither fully realized nor fully sufficient.
Precious, because a society that approaches it is better than one where everything is determined by birth.
Insufficient, because even if perfect, it leaves intact the questions of the fate of the losers and the dignity owed to all.
Justice is not limited to organizing a fair competition; it also concerns what we owe to each person, winner or loser, in a society that aims to be humane.

sentences: Every society punishes those who break its most serious rules.
Prison, fines, and various forms of punishment seem obvious, as the idea that a crime should be punished is deeply ingrained in us.
But as soon as we ask why we punish, for what purpose, the answer becomes unclear.
We expect several things from punishment at once, often contradictory, and this confusion of goals explains many of the deadlocks in our penal systems.
A first reason for punishment is to protect society.
By removing someone who has committed a serious act, we prevent them from committing others; the punishment keeps others safe.
This function is real and legitimate: a society has the right to protect itself from those who threaten it.
But it only justifies punishment for as long as the danger persists, and it says nothing about what we owe to someone who is no longer dangerous.
Punishing to protect is a logic of security, not of justice.
A second reason is to deter.
By punishing, we send a warning to everyone: this is what awaits those who transgress.
The fear of punishment would discourage potential criminals.

This deterrent function is often invoked, but its effectiveness is uncertain: the severity of penalties, experience shows, deters less than we think, because those who act rarely believe they will get caught.
And above all, punishing an individual as an example to scare others amounts to treating them as a means, which contradicts the sense of justice.
A third reason, more obscure, is to repay: the guilty must pay, suffer in return for the harm they have done, because it would be just in itself.
This idea, ancient and powerful, responds to a deep feeling — that evil calls for reparation, that impunity is unbearable.
But it is also the closest to revenge, and one might wonder if causing suffering in return adds anything to the world, or merely doubles the evil.
The line between justice that repays and revenge that satisfies is thin.
A fourth reason, finally, is to correct: punishment should aim to amend the guilty, to reintegrate them, to ensure they do not reoffend and find a place in society.
This function, the most future-oriented, is also the most demanding and the most often neglected.
A society that punishes without ever seeking to reintegrate condemns itself to produce recidivists, and fails to provide what it owes even to those who have erred: the possibility of redemption.
These four goals — to protect, to deter, to repay, to correct — coexist in our penal systems without ever fully aligning.
What serves one sometimes undermines the other: the severity that claims to deter or repay often contradicts reintegration.
Reflecting on punishment is primarily about clarifying what we expect from it, and accepting that we cannot achieve everything at once.
A society may be judged less by how it punishes than by the clarity with which it understands why it does so — and by the space it leaves, despite everything, for redemption.

sentences: The law is binding, and a society cannot function if everyone decides to obey only the laws that suit them.
This requirement is the foundation of all communal life: without a general respect for the laws, there would be disorder, where the strongest imposes their will.
However, history has seen deeply unjust laws — laws that oppressed, excluded, and allowed inhumane acts.
In the face of such laws, a formidable question arises: should one obey a law deemed unjust?
This dilemma, as old as law itself, does not admit a simple answer.
One position argues that one must always obey the law, whatever it may be, even if it means working peacefully to change it.
The argument is strong: if everyone believed they were allowed to disobey laws they consider unjust, there would be no law at all, since everyone has their own idea of justice.
Disobedience, even if well-intentioned, would open the door to general arbitrariness and the law of the strongest.
It is therefore better to obey while advocating for change, in respect of common rules.
This position has stability and order on its side.
But taken to extremes, it leads to an unsustainable conclusion: one would have to obey the worst laws, participate in the worst injustices, under the pretext that they are legal.
History shows where this absolute obedience leads: to crimes committed 'in the name of the law' by people who hid behind their duty to obey.
If legality justified everything, no law, however monstrous, could ever be disobeyed.
Yet our conscience refuses to accept that the mere fact that something is legal makes it just or obligatory.
A second position thus asserts that there is a justice superior to the law, by virtue of which one can, at times, disobey.
When a law violates the most fundamental requirements of humanity, obeying it becomes a fault, and resisting it, a duty.
It is in the name of such a conviction that men and women have disobeyed unjust laws, often at the cost of their freedom or their lives, and that we honor them today.
Their example shows that obedience is not always a virtue, nor is disobedience always a crime.
The question remains as to when disobedience is legitimate, as it cannot be based solely on our preferences.

A thought has developed around this question, that of civil disobedience, which specifies its conditions: that it concerns a serious injustice and not a mere disagreement; that disobedience is public and not clandestine; that it is non-violent; and that the one who disobeys accepts to bear the legal consequences.
Under these conditions, disobeying is not denying the law, but calling for a better law, in the name of justice.
Should we then obey unjust laws?
As a general rule, yes, because obedience to the laws is the condition of communal life, and disagreement must first seek the path of legal change.
But there is a point beyond which injustice becomes so grave that obedience itself becomes complicity.
Recognizing this point, without abusing it, is one of the heaviest responsibilities of a citizen.
The law deserves respect; justice, even more so — and knowing how to distinguish, in extreme cases, what we owe to each, is perhaps the very mark of conscience.

sentences: We tend to oppose two terms as if they referred to two distinct worlds: on one side, 'man', and on the other, 'nature'.
We talk about protecting nature, about returning to nature, as if it were an external domain, separate from us.
This way of thinking is so deeply ingrained that it seems obvious to us.
However, upon examination, this separation proves problematic, and it is not certain that it serves us well.
For in what sense would we be separated from nature?
We are living beings, made of the same matter as the rest of the living world, subject to the same biological laws, depending at every moment on air, water, and other species.
Our body is nature; our existence is woven into the web of life.
We do not hover above nature as a separate kingdom; we are a part of it, as integrally as a tree or an animal.
The opposition between man and nature contradicts this elementary fact.
Where does this stubborn separation come from, then?
From several sources.
From a long tradition that has placed man above the rest of creation, endowed with a soul or reason that would radically distinguish him.
From the development of cities, which has distanced most of us from daily contact with the living world, to the point of perceiving it as something other.
From our technical power, finally, which has given us the illusion of dominating nature, thus making us feel external to and superior over it.
This separation is a historical construct, not a given.
However, this construct is not without consequences, and many of them are unfortunate.

By thinking of ourselves as outside of nature, we have been able to treat it as a mere backdrop, a reservoir of resources to exploit without limit, without realizing that by degrading it, we are harming ourselves.
The ecological crisis is, in a sense, the repressed return of this separation: we are suddenly discovering that we were not outside, that what we inflict on nature, we inflict on ourselves.
One does not saw off the branch on which one is sitting, believing it belongs to another tree.
Should we then deny any difference between humans and the rest of the living world?
That would be an opposite excess.
We have unique capabilities — language, reflection, culture, an unparalleled power to act — which make us distinct beings, not by a separate nature, but by increased responsibility.
Recognizing our belonging to nature does not erase our specificity; it gives it its true meaning: not one of domination, but one of responsibility towards a world of which we are a part.
Rethinking our relationship with nature therefore requires overcoming the separation that has made us strangers to it.

Not to dissolve ourselves in it, nor to renounce what distinguishes us, but to recognize ourselves as what we are: a part of the living world, unique and responsible, whose fate is linked to that of the whole.
Knowing ourselves to be in nature, and not above it, may be the first step towards a more just relationship with the world.

sentences: The freedom of some ends where the freedom of others begins." This often-cited phrase seems to resolve the issue of the limits of freedom in a single word.
Everyone would be free to do what they want, as long as they do not infringe on the freedom of others.
The idea is correct in principle, and it expresses a fundamental requirement: no one has the right to crush another's freedom in the name of their own.
But as soon as we try to apply it, we realize that it shifts the difficulty more than it resolves it.
For the whole question is to know precisely where my freedom encroaches on that of others.
Let's consider simple cases: they are rare.
Hitting someone, stealing from them, coercing them: these are obvious infringements on the freedom of others, which no one contests.
But the vast majority of our actions have less direct, more diffuse effects on others, which can be debated endlessly.
My way of living, consuming, and expressing myself affects others in a thousand indirect ways.
At what point does this effect constitute an infringement on their freedom that would justify limiting mine?
The phrase does not say; it assumes resolved what is precisely the problem.
Let's take an example.
Am I free to harm my own health if it only concerns me?
One might be tempted to answer yes, in the name of my freedom over myself.
But my choices have consequences for others: for my loved ones, for a community that may have to care for me, for the example I set.
Where does what only concerns me end, and where does what concerns others begin?
The boundary, far from being clear, is the very subject of political and moral debate.
There is more.
Freedoms often conflict with each other, without any clearly infringing on the other.
My freedom of expression may clash with another's right not to be defamed; my freedom to undertake may conflict with another's freedom to live in a healthy environment.
These conflicts are not resolved by drawing a simple boundary, as they involve two equally legitimate freedoms that mutually limit each other.
It is then necessary to arbitrate, weigh, and decide which should yield, and to what extent — something the phrase is incapable of telling us.
That is why the question of the limits of freedom cannot be settled by a formula, but by ongoing deliberation.

A society must constantly decide, on a thousand subjects, where to place the boundaries: which freedoms to absolutely protect, which to limit in the name of others or the common good, how to arbitrate between rival freedoms.
These decisions are never definitive; they are re-discussed in each era, as customs and techniques change.
Thus, the beautiful phrase about the freedom of some and others is not false; it is merely the beginning of the problem, not its solution.

It reminds us of an essential principle — that my freedom is not unlimited, that it must coexist with that of others — but it leaves us with the difficult task: to draw, case by case, the boundary it merely names.
Living freely together means accepting to endlessly re-discuss this boundary, rather than believing that a phrase could fix it once and for all.

sentences: Everyone has felt it: a walk in a park, a few moments by the water, the sight of a natural landscape soothes, comforts, and does good in a way that's hard to explain.
For a long time, this well-being was thought to be a simple preference, a matter of taste.
But a growing body of research suggests that it's much more than that: contact with nature meets a real human need, and its deprivation affects us more than we believe.
Studies on this subject converge strikingly.
The presence of nature — trees, greenery, water — reduces stress, improves mood, enhances concentration, and aids recovery.
Patients who see trees from their window heal faster; residents of green neighborhoods are physically and mentally healthier than those who are deprived of them.
These measurable effects are not a figment of the imagination or mere pleasure: they relate to the very functioning of our body and mind.
How can we explain this need?
An appealing hypothesis sees it as the legacy of our long history.
For the vast majority of its existence, the human species lived at the heart of nature, which it depended on for survival.
Our mind and body have been shaped in this environment, and in a way, they remain attuned to it.
Urban life, cut off from the living world, is a recent novelty in the scale of this history, to which we may not be suited.
The well-being that nature provides would thus be a sign of an ancient harmony, while the discomfort of entirely artificial environments signals a discord.
This hypothesis, which cannot be taken as certain, sheds light on a concerning phenomenon.
As humanity urbanizes, daily contact with nature is becoming rarer, especially for the less privileged, who are crammed into concrete neighborhoods devoid of green spaces.
Children, in particular, are growing up further and further away from the living world, in a universe of screens and concrete.
If the need for nature is real, this deprivation is not trivial: it could silently contribute to the malaise in our societies.
Recognizing this need has concrete implications.
It makes access to nature not a luxury, but a component of health and well-being that should be guaranteed for all.
Greening cities, preserving and creating green spaces, bringing children closer to the living world: these choices, often treated as embellishments, then appear as necessities.
A city without nature is not only less pleasant; it is, in a sense, less human.
Finally, the need for nature reminds us of what separation from it makes us forget: that we are part of it, and that we miss it when we are cut off from it.
This well-being we feel in front of a tree or a river is not a sentimental nostalgia; it may be the sign, inscribed in us, of our belonging to the living world.

sentences: An idea that would have seemed absurd not long ago is gaining ground: granting rights to nature itself.
Here, a river is recognized as a legal person; there, a forest or a mountain acquires rights that can be defended in court.

What initially seems like a bizarre notion deserves to be taken seriously, as this evolution touches on a profound question: is nature merely a collection of things at our disposal, or can it be a subject with its own rights?
Our law, as it has developed, recognizes only two categories: people, who have rights, and things, which do not and can be owned and used.
Nature, in this framework, falls under the category of things: a river or a forest is property that can be disposed of.
One cannot harm them in a legal sense; one can only harm the human interests attached to them.
Recognizing rights for nature means breaking this division, acknowledging that a natural element can have value in itself, and not just for the use we make of it.
The argument in favor of this evolution is twofold.
First, it is practical: as long as nature is just a thing, its protection depends entirely on human will and easily yields to their interests.
Recognizing rights for it gives nature its own defense that cannot be so easily sacrificed.

Secondly, it is philosophical: perhaps it is time to acknowledge that nature has a value that is not reduced to its utility for us, and that treating it as merely a stock of resources is precisely at the root of our ecological disasters.
However, objections are not lacking.
It is argued that a river has no consciousness, no interests it can assert for itself, and that granting it rights would make little sense: it is always humans who would speak on its behalf.
There is also a fear of confusion between categories, a weakening of the very notion of rights through its extension.
Recognizing rights for a river, is it not a convenient fiction that poorly conceals that it is indeed human interests — ecological, cultural — that are being protected?
These objections are not without merit, but they do not resolve the issue.
After all, law has always operated through useful fictions: a company, an association are legal 'persons' without having consciousness, and no one is offended by this.
That nature is defended by humans speaking on its behalf does not fundamentally differ from how we defend the rights of a child or a being unable to defend itself.
The essential point may be less about perfect legal coherence than the change in perspective that such recognition brings about.
Whether nature has rights in the strict sense or not, the question itself is revealing.
It marks a growing dissatisfaction with a world where everything that is not human is merely exploitable matter.
Whether we respond with rights or other means, the challenge remains: to find the legal and moral forms of a relationship with nature that no longer reduces it to a thing.
And on this point, the mere emergence of the question is already, perhaps, a step forward.

sentences: Human influence now extends over almost the entire planet.
There are very few spaces left that we haven't transformed, exploited, or developed.
In light of this observation, a question arises: should we deliberately allow wild places to exist, free from our control and use, or should we put the entire Earth at the service of our needs?
The answer involves the idea we have of our place in the world.
A purely utilitarian view would argue that there is no reason to preserve useless spaces.
If land can nourish, produce, or provide shelter, why leave it fallow?
In this view, the wild is merely untapped potential, a waste to be corrected.
This logic, long dominant, has guided the systematic conquest of the planet, based on the idea that every undeveloped space was just waiting to be utilized.
It rests on a presupposition: that the value of a place is measured by its utility to us.
But another, deeper conception advocates for the preservation of the wild.
It first presents practical reasons: preserved natural spaces provide essential services — climate regulation, preservation of biodiversity, reserves whose full importance we have yet to grasp.
Destroying the wild undermines the very foundations of our existence, often without us realizing it.
Prudence alone demands that we preserve substantial portions of it.
But the most interesting argument is of another kind.
There is a value, it is said, in what escapes our control, in what exists independently of us and our uses.
A world entirely mastered, shaped from top to bottom by human hands, would have something stifling and impoverished about it.
The wild reminds us that there is something other than us, that we are not the only masters, and that the world is not reduced to our projects.
Knowing that there are still free places, even if we never go there, has a value that is not utilitarian.
This value of the wild connects to something of our own balance.
In the face of a fully humanized world, where everything would bear our mark, we would lose an essential point of reference: the measure of what transcends us.
The wild is a lesson in humility, a reminder of our limits, a presence of the other that prevents us from believing we are alone in the world.
Preserving it is not just about protecting ecosystems; it is about preserving a certain idea of our place, neither all-powerful nor central.
Should we then leave a place for the wild?
Yes, for reasons ranging from simple prudence to a higher demand.
Not that humanity should renounce transforming the world — it cannot and should not — but that it should know how to impose limits on itself, reserving spaces for what is not itself.
A civilization may also be judged by what it knows not to appropriate, by its ability to allow, somewhere, the world to be without it.

sentences: One of the deepest differences between France and Great Britain lies in the role they assign to the State.
In France, a lot is expected from the public authority: to protect, to organize, to guarantee education, health, and security for everyone.
In Great Britain, despite a public health system that the British are very attached to, there is more trust in individual initiative, the market, and personal responsibility.
These two attitudes, both respectable, reflect two conceptions of society.
The French tradition is marked by a long history of centralization.
For centuries, the State has played a driving role, shaping the nation, unifying the territory, and organizing collective life.
From this history has arisen a reflex: when faced with a problem, people turn to the State, expect it to act, and blame it for not doing enough.
The State is seen as the guarantor of the general interest, above individual interests, and there is a strong desire for it to provide protection that the market alone would not guarantee.
The British tradition is different.
It is more suspicious of the concentration of power, values individual autonomy, and trusts civil society and private initiative to solve many problems.
The State is perceived less as a natural protector than as a force that needs to be limited, for fear it might encroach on freedoms.
People expect individuals to take charge of themselves, not to rely primarily on the community, and see entrepreneurial spirit as a cardinal virtue.
Both visions have their strengths and weaknesses.

The French model offers extensive protection, reduces certain inequalities, and ensures a security that many envy; however, it is sometimes criticized for being burdensome, stifling initiative, and fostering excessive expectations of the State among citizens.
The British model allows more room for initiative, flexibility, and dynamism; but it is criticized for allowing inequalities to widen and for abandoning the weakest to an indifferent market.
Each model pays for its virtues with corresponding flaws.

It would be futile to decree which is superior, as they address questions on which legitimate values diverge: how much security, how much freedom; how much imposed solidarity, how much individual responsibility.
These are trade-offs, not truths, and each society decides based on its history and preferences.
The French person attached to the State and the British person attached to initiative are not wrong or right; they prioritize different goods.
Observing these two models helps us understand that there is not just one right way to organize a society, but choices that reflect values.

And it is also, for each, an opportunity to better see their own model: the French, by discovering the British attachment to autonomy, realizes what is unique about their preference for the State; the British, by discovering French protection, may question what their individualism overlooks.
Each neighbor is, for the other, a revealing mirror.

sentences: Few countries know each other as well while understanding each other so poorly as France and Great Britain.

Separated by a stretch of sea that can be crossed in a few hours, linked by a thousand years of shared history, wars, alliances, and exchanges, the two neighbors maintain a unique relationship, characterized by attraction and rivalry, fascination and mutual mockery.
Observing them together helps us understand how two such close nations could forge such different characters.
History, first and foremost, has intertwined them intimately.

There was a time when the kings of England spoke French, when the two crowns disputed the same lands, and when their destinies were so intertwined that it was not always clear how to distinguish them.
From this ancient proximity emerged a singular blend: the English language itself is filled with words from French, remnants of this shared history.
The two peoples are not strangers to each other; rather, they are old relatives who know each other too well.
And yet, what differences there are.
Where the French love principles, general ideas, and grand abstract debates, the British are wary of theories and prefer pragmatism, specific cases, and solutions that work.
Where France made its revolution and broke with its past, Great Britain preferred slow evolution, maintaining its monarchy and traditions while transforming.
These two temperaments — one more inclined towards logic and rupture, the other towards compromise and continuity — are reflected in countless aspects of life in both countries.
These differences fuel stereotypes that each side delights in maintaining.
The French readily see the British as distant, obsessed with politeness and the weather, and poor eaters; the British see the French as arrogant, undisciplined, quick to strike, and moralizers.
These caricatures, like all caricatures, distort while capturing something.
They primarily express the pleasure these two neighbors take in defining themselves against each other, each needing the other as a foil and a mirror.
For beneath the mockery often lies a secret fascination.
The French sometimes dream of British phlegm, that ability to remain calm, and that humor which diffuses everything.
The British sometimes envy the French art of living, their appreciation for good food, conversation, and pleasure without guilt.
Each finds in the other what they lack, and perhaps that is why, despite the jibes, the two peoples never tire of each other.
Understanding the relationship between France and Great Britain is therefore grasping much more than a neighborhood rivalry.
It is observing how two nations, stemming from a shared history, have taken opposite paths, and how they continue, even today, to define themselves in relation to one another.

These articles will explore some of these differences — in relation to the state, food, rules, and daily life — not to determine who is right, but to understand what each reveals about the other and about ourselves.

sentences: Our relationship with animals is full of contradictions that we rarely notice.
We cherish certain animals like family members, we are outraged by the suffering of some species, while we raise and eat others without thinking about it.
We mourn a dog and cut up a pig, without always realizing how strange this difference in treatment can be.
Questioning this inconsistency is not being sentimental; it is asking what we really owe to the sentient beings that share the world with us.
The starting point is a fact that science has firmly established: many animals are sentient beings, capable of feeling pain, fear, and undoubtedly forms of well-being.
It is no longer a sentimental hypothesis, but a fact.
Now, if a being can suffer, its suffering counts morally — this is a principle that is hard to refute.
We all admit that it is wrong to make an animal suffer unnecessarily; we therefore recognize, at least implicitly, that their suffering has value, that it obliges us to something.
But how far does this obligation go?
This is where the difficulties begin, and where our intuitions become muddled.
Should we treat all sentient animals equally, from dogs to pigs, from cats to chickens?
Logic would suggest so, but our habits refuse it.
We establish hierarchies between species that often owe more to custom, affection, or utility than to real differences in sensitivity.
The pig is no less sensitive than the dog; if we treat them so differently, it is not on the basis of a clear principle, but out of cultural habit.
Recognizing this inconsistency does not necessarily lead to a single conclusion.
Some conclude that we must stop making animals suffer and killing them for our use; others believe that we can continue to use them, but by reducing their suffering and respecting certain limits.
Between these positions, the debate is open and legitimate.
But what seems difficult to defend is the thoughtless status quo: treating sentient beings in radically opposite ways without ever questioning what justifies it.
What is certain is that the extent of the animal suffering we inflict can no longer be ignored.

The conditions in which most animals intended for our consumption are raised and slaughtered clash, when faced directly, with the very principle we recognize: that it is wrong to cause unnecessary suffering.
Whether we choose to give up this consumption or to transform it deeply, it becomes difficult to continue it while turning a blind eye.
Loving animals, how far?
The question does not call for a simple answer, but it does call for a coherent, or at least thoughtful, response.
We can no longer be satisfied with loving some and ignoring the fate of others, as if our spontaneous feelings could serve as morality.
Taking animal sensitivity seriously means accepting to question our habits and to align our actions a bit more with what, deep down, we already know.

sentences: If there is one area where the British claim uniqueness, it is certainly humor.
The term 'English humor' is one that the French themselves use, with a mix of admiration and perplexity, to describe a way of joking that partly eludes them.
This particular humor — deadpan, self-deprecation, unflappable absurdity — deserves our attention, as the way a people laughs reveals a lot about who they are.

British humor is first recognized by its taste for deadpan: saying the funniest or most absurd things without losing an unflappable seriousness, without the slightest smile, leaving it to the listener to grasp the joke.
This form confuses those who are not used to it: one does not always know whether to laugh, whether the other is joking or speaking seriously.

This is precisely where its power lies: humor arises from the gap between the seriousness of the tone and the absurdity of the content, and from the shared pleasure of perceiving it without it being highlighted.
Self-deprecation is another major trait.
Where one might seek to elevate oneself, the British prefer to make fun of themselves, downplay their successes, and turn their own flaws into a joke.
Taking oneself seriously is, in this culture, almost a faux pas; knowing how to laugh at oneself is a mark of elegance and maturity.
This self-deprecation diffuses boastfulness, but also conflict: it is difficult to quarrel with someone who first laughs at themselves.
It expresses a certain modesty, a refusal of emphasis that the British readily associate, not without malice, with their neighbors.
This humor also has a deep social function.
In a culture that values restraint and dislikes overly direct expressions of emotions, humor offers an indirect way to say what would otherwise remain unsaid.
One diffuses tension with a joke, expresses criticism through irony, and shows affection through friendly teasing.
Laughter becomes a coded language, allowing one to communicate a lot by saying little, while maintaining that modest distance that the British hold dear.
The French, whose humor certainly exists but accommodates a more direct relationship with emotions and ideas, are often taken aback by this game.
They sometimes struggle to know when someone is joking, take literally what was ironic, or are surprised that serious matters are mocked.
Conversely, the British may find the French too serious, too quick to get worked up, and insufficiently able to laugh at themselves.
Each, through the other's humor, stumbles upon a different way of inhabiting the world.
Understanding a people's humor is therefore much more than just learning to laugh at their jokes.
It is about grasping their relationship to seriousness, to emotion, to oneself, and to others.

British humor, with its calmness and self-deprecation, expresses a whole vision: that of a culture that is wary of emphasis, prefers understatement to exaggeration, and believes that one can discuss the most serious matters as long as one knows how to smile about them.

sentences: Tom, this Englishman who has gone through several of these readings, has been living in Paris for years now.
Arriving with his suitcase of clichés — arrogant, undisciplined, food-obsessed French people — he gradually saw these images crack, become more nuanced, and sometimes even turn against his own.
His experience, like that of many people living between two cultures, offers a conclusion to this journey: what does prolonged exposure to another country really teach us?
Tom's first lesson was to discover that his certainties about France said as much about England as they did about France.
By finding the French 'too' attached to the state, he measured, without ever having articulated it, how much he himself took individual autonomy for granted.
By being surprised that people take two hours for lunch, he revealed his own British relationship with time and work.
Every judgment he made about France was, implicitly, a confession about what he had believed to be universal and which was merely English.
The foreigner, once again, turned out to be a mirror.
The second lesson was more subtle.

As he understood France from the inside, Tom stopped explaining differences with value judgments — 'they do it poorly' or 'they do it better' — and began to see them as coherent responses to common questions.

The French attachment to the state was no longer, in his eyes, a weakness, but a choice that had its reasons and its costs; British individualism was no longer a given, but an option among others, with its strengths and weaknesses.
Understanding the other had cured him of believing that his own way was self-evident.
The third lesson, the deepest, was a certain discomfort, but a fruitful one.
Tom was no longer quite English, nor ever quite French; he stood in a middle ground, able to see each country through the eyes of the other, but belonging fully to neither.
This position has its melancholies: one is no longer quite at home anywhere.
But it has its riches: one gains a freedom, that of no longer being a prisoner of a single way of seeing, of being able to choose, understand, and relativize.
Living between two cultures means losing a simple belonging, but gaining a perspective.
What Tom ultimately came to understand goes beyond France and England.
Encountering another culture, when experienced deeply and not as a tourist, teaches us not only about the other: it teaches us about ourselves, revealing what we took for granted.
It frees us from the illusion that our world is the only possible one, and enables us to look at it from the outside, with a mix of attachment and critical distance.
This may be the highest meaning of this journey between two neighboring cultures.
Not to decide who, between France and Great Britain, would be right — a question without answer and without interest — but to discover, through the other, the relativity and value of what is ours.
Like Tom, anyone who takes the time to understand another people returns, in essence, better equipped to understand themselves.
And that is already, for a reader learning a foreign language, the most beautiful reason to continue.

sentences: An idea that has long been marginal is now entering the public debate: providing every citizen, unconditionally and without compensation, a guaranteed income sufficient to live.
This 'universal income' evokes passionate reactions, with some seeing it as a dangerous utopia and others considering it a necessity for the future.
Beyond the slogans, the idea deserves serious examination, as it touches on fundamental questions about work, dignity, and solidarity.
The arguments in its favor are of several kinds.
The first is related to automation: if machines permanently destroy a part of jobs, how can we ensure an income for those who will no longer find work?
A guaranteed income would provide an answer by disconnecting survival from employment.

The second argument is about dignity: by ensuring everyone a minimum unconditionally, we would eliminate the fear of tomorrow and free individuals from the constraint of having to accept any job under any conditions.
The third is about simplicity: a universal income would replace the complicated and sometimes humiliating maze of existing aids.
But the objections are no less serious.
The first is the cost: providing everyone with a sufficient income would represent a colossal sum, the financing of which raises immense difficulties.
The second relates to work: if everyone receives enough to live without working, some fear a collapse of activity, a society where production would cease.
The third is moral: is it fair to provide an income to those who could work and choose not to, risking placing the burden of their idleness on others?
These objections deserve to be taken seriously, but some are based on questionable assumptions.

The idea that people would massively stop working if they received a basic income is not confirmed by experiments conducted here and there: most continue to work, but with more freedom in their choices.

As for the fear of widespread idleness, it is based on a pessimistic view of human beings, assumed to work only under the constraint of need—a view contradicted by the widespread desire to be active and useful.
The question of financing, however, remains real, and it cannot be brushed aside.
A generous universal income would require a profound overhaul of taxation and social protection, with consequences that are difficult to predict.
That is why the debate often focuses less on the principle than on the modalities: what amount, financed how, in replacement of what.
A modest income does not have the same effects as a sufficient income to live, and one can support the idea in one version and reject it in another.

Whether one is for or against it, the debate on universal income has the merit of raising a question that the future may make unavoidable: in a society where work may no longer be enough to occupy and sustain everyone, how can we guarantee everyone a dignified existence?
The answer is not obvious, but the question itself will not be easily evaded for long.

sentences: For over a century, a promise has recurred with every technical advancement: machines will free us from work.
By taking on the hard tasks for us, they were supposed to offer us unprecedented leisure time, a life finally free from toil.
Some thinkers even predicted that our descendants would only work a few hours a day, mainly occupied with cultivating their minds.
Yet this promised paradise has never quite arrived.
Why does this promise, constantly renewed, always elude us?
We must first acknowledge what the promise has going for it.

Machines have indeed accomplished wonders: they have spared us a huge amount of exhausting work, multiplied what a human being can produce, and made possible a level of comfort that no previous era had known.
In this sense, they have freed us from countless hardships.
No one today would want to return to the exhausting work of the past, and that kind of liberation is real, significant, and achieved.
And yet, the promised free time has not followed in proportion.
Despite gigantic productivity gains, we are not working radically less than we did several decades ago, and many even feel more rushed, more overwhelmed than ever.
How can we explain this paradox?
Where have the hours that machines were supposed to give us gone?
A first answer lies in what we have done with these gains.
Rather than converting them into free time, we have, for the most part, converted them into increased production and consumption.
Machines have allowed us to produce faster; we have chosen to produce more rather than work less.
The time that technology freed up, we immediately filled with new needs, new desires, and a constantly rising standard of living.
Liberation was possible; we preferred abundance instead.
A second answer relates to distribution.
The fruits of automation have not been shared equally: they have mainly benefited some, while others continued to work hard, sometimes even harder.
The free time gained by some has sometimes come at the cost of intensified work for others.
The promise of general liberation assumed a sharing that did not take place, and without which machines free some by enslaving others.
This means that liberation through machines has never been an automatic consequence of technology, but depended on choices we did not make.
Nothing in the machines themselves condemns us to work so much; it is our social organization, our priorities, our race for consumption that determines this.
The promise could still be fulfilled — but it requires a genuine desire for free time rather than endless production growth.
Machines can free us; we just need to decide to do so.

sentences: As machines take on more and more tasks, a question arises: what will be left that only we, humans, can do?
If we can automate not only physical work but also an increasing share of intellectual tasks, where will the true value of human work lie tomorrow?
The uncertain answer may outline what the work of the future will look like.
For a long time, it was believed that the refuge of humanity would be intelligence, as opposed to strength.
But machines are proving increasingly capable of calculating, analyzing, and processing information better and faster than we can.
The realm of pure intellectual performance, which we thought was our exclusive domain, is shrinking.
It would therefore be unwise to base the value of human work on this ground, where machines catch up to us and often surpass us.
What distinguishes us lies elsewhere.
A first area where humans seem difficult to replace is in relationships.

Caring for a sick person, educating a child, assisting an elderly person, listening to someone in pain: these tasks require a presence, empathy, and attention to others that no machine can truly offer.
We can automate actions, but not the warmth of a human relationship.
However, these care and connection professions, often poorly recognized and underpaid, could very well be the ones whose value will appear most irreplaceable tomorrow.
A second area is that of true creation, not the mass production of content, but the invention of what did not exist, born from sensitivity, experience, and a unique perspective on the world.
Machines can recombine what exists; it is less certain that they can create in the strong sense, bringing forth novelty that comes from lived experience and inner depth.
The deepest part of art, thought, and innovation could remain a human territory.
A third area, finally, is that of judgment, especially when it involves values.

Deciding what is right, mediating between conflicting interests, assuming moral responsibility: these acts require not only processing information but also weighing, choosing, and being accountable for one's choices.
We can entrust calculations to a machine; it is more questionable, and perhaps dangerous, to entrust it with decisions that involve meaning and responsibility.
Those decisions should remain ours.
What emerges through these areas is a possible redefinition of human work around what is most intrinsic to us: relationships, creation, judgment, and care.
Far from being devalued, these dimensions could gain importance as the rest becomes automated.
It is also necessary for our societies to recognize and value them, instead of despising them as they often do.
The future of human work will depend less on what machines can do than on what we choose to hold as valuable.

sentences: Automation is most often analyzed in economic terms: lost jobs, costs, and retraining.

This approach is necessary, but it overlooks a more intimate, more painful dimension: what someone feels when they are replaced by a machine in a task that was their skill, their pride, and sometimes their identity.
This experience, which more and more people will face, deserves our attention, as it touches on something deep in our relationship with work.
Being replaced by a machine is not just about losing an income.
It means being told that what we did, and what we believed was valuable, can be done without us, often better and for less money.
The skills we painstakingly acquired, the mastery we were proud of, suddenly feel devalued and rendered unnecessary.
In addition to the material loss, there is a blow to self-esteem: we are not just unemployed; we feel we have become useless.
This wound, invisible in the statistics, is nevertheless one of the heaviest consequences of technological progress.
This experience is all the more difficult because our society, as we have seen, tends to define people by their work.
Those whose jobs disappear lose more than just an activity: they lose a part of what situated them in the world, what gave them a place and recognition.

And the prevailing discourse, which celebrates innovation and urges everyone to 'adapt,' often adds to the pain by coloring it with guilt, as if those who suffer from being sidelined are responsible for not keeping up.
However, we must guard against two equally futile reactions.
The first would be to want to stop technological progress to preserve every threatened job: this is neither possible nor desirable, and we have seen that machines also relieve us of many burdens.
The second would be to dismiss the suffering of those displaced by a wave of the hand, in the name of an abstract progress for which they would pay the price without anyone caring.
Between the refusal of change and indifference to its victims, there is room for another attitude.
This attitude consists of recognizing the human cost of progress and not allowing it to weigh solely on the individuals who endure it.
A society that accepts automation, because it reaps collective benefits, has a debt to those it displaces.
This debt is not settled by a simple compensation, but by real means to regain a place and dignity: genuine training, support, recognition of skills, and the creation of new valued activities.
Progress is only just if its fruits and costs are shared.
Ultimately, the experience of being replaced by a machine poses a question about the value of people.
If we are only worth what we produce, then those replaced by machines are worth nothing, and this conclusion is unbearable.

This may be the opportunity to recognize that the value of a human being is not reduced to their economic utility—a truth that would be better affirmed before machines force us to rediscover it through pain.

sentences: We often talk about automation as a natural force, a fate that imposes itself on us: machines 'will' do this, 'will' eliminate that, as if it were an inevitable phenomenon, comparable to the tide.
This way of speaking, so common, carries a dangerous illusion.
For machines do not decide anything by themselves; behind each one, there are human choices — about what we build, for what purposes, for whose benefit.
Becoming aware of these choices means refusing to accept as fate what is, in reality, a matter of decisions.
Let’s consider what is presented as the inevitable course of technology.

Whether a particular task is automated rather than another, whether the gains are used to eliminate jobs rather than to lighten everyone’s work, whether machines are designed to replace humans or to assist them: none of this is dictated by technology itself.
These are orientations taken by companies, investors, and public authorities, based on interests and priorities.
The same technical power can be put to very different ends.
This truth is crucial, as it changes everything.
If automation were a fate, we would have no choice but to resign ourselves to it or adapt.
But if it results from choices, then these choices can be discussed, contested, and directed differently.

We can decide to develop machines that assist workers rather than replace them; we can decide to share productivity gains rather than concentrate them; we can decide to protect those displaced by change.
These decisions are not predetermined; they depend on collective will.
So why is automation so often presented as inevitable?
Partly because it suits those who profit from it.
Presenting a choice as a fate removes it from debate, discourages any contestation, and makes what serves particular interests seem natural.
"There's nothing we can do, it's progress": this seemingly neutral phrase disarms those who might want a different use of technology.
The illusion of technical fate is also a way of confiscating decisions.
Resisting this illusion does not mean opposing technical progress or dreaming of stopping machines.
It means reaffirming that technology is a means to ends we must choose, and not an end that imposes itself on us.
It means asking, at every step, the questions that the illusion of fate silences: what machines do we want, for what purpose, for whose benefit, with what consequences for those they affect?
Who decides what machines do?
The answer should not be: nobody, or technology itself.
It should be: we, collectively, through assumed and debated choices.
Reclaiming these choices means refusing to be passive spectators of a future that is presented to us as already written.
For the future of work, like that of machines, is not a prediction to endure; it is a decision to be made.

sentences: When night falls and most residents head home, one thinks the city is asleep.
It is not.
Another city awakens then, different from the one during the day, populated by beings and activities that are not usually seen.
The urban night has its own life, its inhabitants, its rhythms, and exploring it means discovering a hidden side of the city, often ignored by those who only know its daytime face.
The nocturnal city is primarily one of invisible work.
While the majority sleeps, a crowd of men and women ensures the city runs: hospital caregivers, street and office cleaners, factory workers who never stop, drivers, bakers, guards.
This essential nighttime work is done in the shadows, unnoticed by those who, in the morning, will find the city clean, the transport ready, the bread warm, without wondering who made it possible.
The night reveals a whole laboring population that the day conceals.
The nocturnal city is also one of celebration and pleasure.
When work ends, others seek in the night what the day does not offer them: freedom, connection, forgetfulness, intoxication.
The nightlife spots come alive, a youth gathers there, a particular sociability unfolds, freer, sometimes more intense than that of the day.
The night has always been the time of permitted transgression, where the rules loosen, where one can be a little different from who they are during the day.
But the urban night also has its shadow.

It is the time of solitude for those who traverse it without sleep; the time of fear for those who dare not go out; the time when the most disadvantaged, the homeless, take refuge, for whom the nocturnal city is not a choice but a deprivation.
The night that liberates some exposes others, and the same darkness can be a celebration or distress depending on whether one traverses it for pleasure or necessity.
This dual nature of the urban night makes it a revealer.

What happens in the city after nightfall says a lot about what this city is: how it treats those who work at night, how it welcomes or pushes away those who inhabit it, how it lights up or abandons its dark streets.
The night paradoxically highlights what the day hides: inequalities, solitude, but also freedoms and solidarities of a city.
Looking at the city at night is therefore seeing it differently, in a truth that the day covers.
It is discovering that a city is never entirely what one believes, that it leads, in the shadows, a parallel existence, made of labor and celebration, of freedom and distress.
The city never sleeps; it only changes its face, and this nocturnal face deserves to be learned to be seen.

sentences: Our societies operate twenty-four hours a day, which means that every night, millions of people work while others sleep.
This night work, once reserved for a few professions, has expanded as life has sped up and the demand for constant availability has gained ground.
However, this night work, which we all benefit from, has a cost that is often underestimated, and it weighs heavily on those who perform it.
The first cost is physiological, and it is significant.
Our bodies are set to a day-night rhythm deeply ingrained in our biology: we are made to be active during the day and sleep at night.
Working at night and sleeping during the day goes against this internal clock, and the body pays the price.
Daytime sleep is shorter and less restorative; fatigue accumulates; and research links prolonged night work to various health issues.
Those who stay awake for us wear out their bodies in ways we do not see.
The second cost is social.
Living on a different schedule means living partly out of sync with others.
The night worker sleeps when their loved ones are awake, works when they are resting, and struggles to share meals, evenings, and moments of communal life.
Their family and social life suffers, out of tune with that of their surroundings.
They inhabit a parallel world, awake when their loved ones sleep, and this desynchronization is a form of solitude, all the more harsh because it is invisible.
What is striking is that this difficult and costly work is often done by the most modest.
Night jobs — cleaning, security, caregiving, handling, service — are among the least well-paid and least recognized.
Those who pay the highest physical and social price are rarely the ones who reap the greatest benefits.
There is a subtle injustice here: the hardship of the night often adds to the precariousness of the day, hitting the same people twice.
Recognizing this does not lead to calling for an end to all night work, part of which is essential: we will not close hospitals at night.
But it does invite us to distinguish between necessary night work and that which is not, imposed solely by the relentless pursuit of constant availability and profitability.
Some of our nighttime activity is less about a real need than about an immediate consumption demand that we could forgo without much harm.
It especially calls for better recognition, protection, and compensation for those who work at night to keep the city running.
The minimum would be not to forget their existence, to acknowledge what we owe them, and to compensate for the hardship they endure on our behalf.
For the comfort of our days relies, in part, on the sacrifice of their nights — and it would at least be fair not to ignore that.
