sentences: We willingly celebrate generosity, the virtue of those who help, give, and dedicate themselves to others.
And this celebration is justified: helping others is one of the most beautiful things a human being can do.
But we talk much less about the other side of this relationship, which is more discreet and often more difficult: that of receiving.
However, accepting help, allowing oneself to be assisted, depending on others, is sometimes more difficult than helping oneself, and this difficulty deserves our attention.
Why is it so hard to receive?
First, because of pride, or what we take for dignity.
Asking for help, admitting that we can't do it alone, showing our weakness, clashes with the desire to be strong, autonomous, and capable.
In a culture that values independence and considers self-sufficiency a virtue, needing others is almost seen as a failure, a decline.
We often prefer to suffer in silence rather than acknowledge that we need help, as if the need itself were shameful.
There is also the fear of debt.
Receiving creates an obligation, an imbalance: the one who has received feels indebted, in a position of inferiority to the one who has given.
This asymmetry is uncomfortable; it can weigh on the relationship, introducing a feeling of dependence or humiliation.
Many refuse help precisely to avoid feeling indebted, to maintain a form of equality or independence.
Receiving means accepting that we are not even, and that comes at a cost.
Yet, knowing how to receive is at least as great a virtue as knowing how to give, and perhaps rarer.
For accepting help is to humbly acknowledge one's own vulnerability, to trust the other, and to accept not being all-powerful.
It is also, paradoxically, a gift to the one who helps: by allowing them to assist us, we offer them the joy of being useful, of giving, of mattering to us.
Refusing all help, in the name of pride, deprives the other of this joy and severs the bond that the received help would have woven.
There is pride in never accepting anything.
This reflection touches on the very nature of community ties.
A community does not only consist of people who give, but of the circulation of help, where everyone takes turns helping and being helped, giving and receiving.
Those who always want to give without ever receiving place themselves above others, in a generosity that may hide a refusal of the bond of equality.
True reciprocity requires that we also accept to receive, to allow ourselves to be helped, to recognize that we need others as much as they need us.
Learning to receive is therefore, in its own way, a lesson in humility and connection.
It is to accept that we are vulnerable, interdependent beings who cannot manage alone and do not have to manage alone.
In a world that exalts autonomy and views need as a weakness, knowing how to ask for and accept help is an act of wisdom and trust.

For a life in which one would never need anyone would not be a more successful life; it would be a poorer life, cut off from what the human bond has of the deepest: the fact that we count on each other.

sentences: Solitude has a bad reputation.
People avoid it, fear it, and consider it one of life's misfortunes.
Being alone is often seen as a failure, a sign that one hasn't managed to surround oneself with others, a situation to be corrected as quickly as possible.
This fear of solitude is so widespread that many cannot stand to be alone for a moment, filling every void with presence or distraction.
However, this perspective is incomplete, as it confuses two very different things: imposed solitude and chosen solitude.
Imposed solitude, that of isolation, is indeed a suffering.
Feeling alone against one's will, deprived of desired connections, excluded from the company of others, is a real ordeal, which we have seen is becoming more common.
This type of solitude must be fought against, and nothing that follows claims otherwise.
But there exists a completely different solitude: the one we choose, seek out, and make into a space for living.
And this chosen solitude, far from being a misfortune, is one of life's greatest riches.
For chosen solitude offers what the constant presence of others does not: a return to oneself.
When surrounded all the time, constantly solicited, one ends up no longer belonging to oneself, caught up in the gaze and demands of others.
Solitude is the moment when one finds oneself, when one can think without interruption, feel without having to show it, be oneself without having to deal with others.
Many essential things — deep reflection, creation, prayer, the simple rest of the mind — require this solitude and cannot be born in the continuous noise of company.
History bears witness to this fertility of solitude.
Thinkers, artists, and sages have almost all needed moments of withdrawal, away from the world, to create and to understand.
It is not a coincidence: it is in silence and solitude that the mind gathers, that ideas mature, and that one takes the necessary distance to see clearly.
Avoiding all solitude is to deprive oneself of that inner space where the deepest work takes place, the kind that no conversation can replace.
Chosen solitude also has a virtue for life with others.
Those who know how to be alone do not depend on others to avoid boredom, to feel alive, or to fill a void; they come to others by choice, not out of a need to escape their own company.
They can thus maintain freer, healthier, and less greedy relationships.
Knowing how to be alone, paradoxically, makes one better with others: we no longer ask them to save us from ourselves.
The ability to be alone is a condition for balanced relationships.
It is therefore not about choosing between others and solitude, but about making space for both.
A life entirely focused on others, without ever returning to oneself, becomes exhausted and scattered; an entirely solitary life dries up and becomes sad.
Balance lies in the alternation: moments of true connection and moments of chosen solitude.
Rehabilitating the latter, learning to be alone without suffering, to savor silence and the return to oneself, is to reclaim a part of the richness that the fear of solitude has made us forget.

sentences: At the end of this reflection on connection and solitude, a truth emerges, confirmed by both common experience and research: in the face of life's challenges, what protects us best is not primarily material wealth or even individual strength, but other people.
Social connection, the presence of people we can rely on, is one of the most precious resources in life — and one of the most neglected.
Studies on well-being and health are remarkably convergent on this point.

The quality of a person's relationships — the depth of their connections, the presence of loved ones, the feeling of being supported — is among the most determining factors of their happiness, resilience in the face of challenges, and even their physical health and longevity.
Those who are surrounded cope better with difficulties, heal better, and live longer.
Connection is not just a source of joy; it is a true protection, as concrete as it is invisible.
It's easy to see why.

In the face of a challenge — an illness, a bereavement, a loss, a difficulty — the person who is alone faces it with all their strength, which is often insufficient; the person who is surrounded can lean on others, be supported, helped, and comforted.
Others provide material help, but especially that moral support that allows one to endure: the feeling of not being alone, of being carried, of mattering to someone.
A shared challenge is lighter than a solitary one, not because it changes in nature, but because it is no longer borne alone.
This strength of connection also applies at the level of communities and societies.
In the face of disasters, crises, and collective misfortunes, it is the most supportive societies, where the bonds are strongest, that withstand the best.
Where everyone is alone, the crisis dislocates; where people are connected, they help each other, support each other, and hold together.

The strength of a society is not only measured by its wealth or power, but by the quality of the bonds that unite its members, by their ability to face challenges together rather than each for themselves.
This observation should alert us, because we live in societies that, as we have seen, tend to break down connections: individualism, mobility, screens, and the disappearance of meeting places.
By weakening what connects us, we also weaken, often without realizing it, our collective and individual protection in the face of challenges.
We gain autonomy and freedom, but we lose resilience, support, and shared strength.
A society of isolated individuals is a more fragile society, where everyone is more exposed.
Recognizing that connection is strength means understanding that maintaining relationships, weaving and preserving bonds, is not a mere luxury, but an essential investment.

The time spent on others, the attention given to loved ones, the commitment to a community, is never time wasted: it builds the net that will support us in challenges, and that we will extend, in turn, under others.
In a world that exalts the autonomous individual, it is worth remembering this ancient truth: that our greatest strength, in the face of life's fragility, is each other.

sentences: Here is the oldest and most important of questions, the one that all others, in a way, serve: what does it mean to have a successful life?
What does it mean to live well, to lead a life that is worthwhile, one that can be said, in the end, to have been good?
Everyone asks themselves this, at least vaguely, because the answer given to it determines the direction of an entire life.
And yet, we rarely take the time to truly examine this fundamental question, as we are caught up in the tasks of existence.
The difficulty begins as soon as one tries to answer, because the possible answers are numerous and divergent.
For some, a successful life is a happy life, rich in pleasures and poor in suffering.
For others, it is a fulfilled life, where one has realized their potential, created, and left a mark.
For yet others, it is a morally good life, lived with integrity, in service to others.
Finally, for others, it is an authentic life, true to oneself, to one's choices, to one's truth.
These answers do not overlap, and one can succeed according to one while failing according to another.
This diversity could be discouraging, as if the question had no answer.
But it can be read differently: perhaps these answers each capture a part of what a successful life is, without any of them exhausting it.

Pleasure matters, but a life of empty pleasures would leave a taste of incompleteness; accomplishment matters, but success without joy or kindness would be bitter; morality matters, but virtue without any happiness would be austere; authenticity matters, but being true to a bad self would not be a success.
Perhaps a fully successful life brings together these dimensions, rather than sacrificing some for others.
One must also be wary of the answers that our time whispers to us without our having chosen them.
Our world tends to measure the success of a life by external criteria: money, status, professional success, recognition, consumption.
These criteria have a deceptive obviousness: we pursue them without ever really questioning them, as if succeeding in life meant succeeding according to those measures.
Yet nothing is less certain, and many, having reached the pinnacle of these external successes, discover that they are not enough, that they lack the essential.
Asking what a successful life is, is first about freeing oneself from ready-made answers.
There may be something more important than finding the right answer: it is to truly ask oneself the question.

For the danger is not so much in getting the answer wrong as in never reflecting, living without ever questioning what one is seeking, swept along by the current, pursuing goals that one has not chosen.
An unexamined life, said an ancient philosopher, is not worth living.
It is not that one must spend their life philosophizing; but an existence that never asks itself what it is aiming for risks missing out on itself.
These last reflections will not provide a definitive answer, for there is none that is valid for all.
But they will explore some of the big questions that lie behind the question of a successful life: happiness, meaning, the place of others, the acceptance of finitude.

Not to dictate an answer, but to help each person seek their own — for this is, at its core, a task that no one can accomplish in our place, and which gives existence, even uncertain, its gravity and its worth.

sentences: If there is one thing that human beings seem to need as much as happiness, it is meaning.
We can endure immense suffering if it has meaning, and feel overwhelmed by a comfortable life that seems empty.
Meaning is not pleasure, nor even happiness; it is the feeling that our life matters, that it has direction, value, and a reason for being.
And this need for meaning, often overlooked, may be even more fundamental than the pursuit of happiness.
We measure the importance of meaning by what happens when it is lacking.
A life devoid of meaning, even if it has everything else — comfort, pleasures, security — falls into a form of emptiness, weariness, and dull despair.

In contrast, those who have found meaning in their existence — in a cause, a faith, a work, a dedication — endure trials that would overwhelm others, drawing strength from that meaning that keeps them standing.
A thinker who had gone through the worst horrors observed this: those who survived were often those who had a reason to live, something or someone to hold on to.
Where does meaning come from?
It cannot be decreed, bought, or found ready-made.
It most often arises from a connection: the feeling of belonging to something greater than ourselves, serving a cause, being useful to others, contributing to something larger than oneself.
What gives meaning is often what takes us out of ourselves: love, commitment, creation, transmission, service.
A life entirely focused on its own interest, on its own satisfaction, rarely finds meaning; it is found in transcendence, in giving, in connection to something beyond oneself.
Meaning also arises from the coherence between what we do and what we believe.
A life has meaning when our actions align with our values, when we live according to what we hold as important, when there is no gap between what we believe and what we do.
In contrast, an existence that betrays its own values, that pursues goals it does not truly believe in, becomes devoid of meaning even if it succeeds by external standards.
Meaning relies on this integrity, on this fidelity to what we believe we should be and do.
It should be noted that meaning does not depend on circumstances as much as we think.
One can find meaning in a modest, difficult life devoid of brilliant success; and lack meaning in a life filled with achievements.
For meaning is not measured by what we have, but by how we inhabit our lives, the connections we weave, and what we dedicate ourselves to.

This is good news: meaning is not reserved for a few privileged individuals; it is, in principle, within reach of everyone, regardless of circumstances, as long as one seeks something to dedicate oneself to.
Giving meaning to one's life is therefore not a philosophical luxury, but a vital necessity, as essential as bread.
In a world that offers pleasures and distractions in abundance but struggles to provide meaning, this quest may be the most urgent of all.
Not waiting for life to have ready-made meaning, but constructing it: through what we attach ourselves to, what we dedicate ourselves to, and what we choose to serve.
For a life that has meaning can endure almost anything, while a life that lacks it cannot bear, in the end, anything at all.

sentences: Happiness has become, in our time, a kind of obligation.
We are urged to be happy, we are offered a thousand methods to achieve it, and the pursuit of happiness is made the ultimate goal of existence.
This injunction seems benevolent: who wouldn't want to be happy?
However, it contains a troubling paradox: by constantly seeking happiness and pursuing it directly, we risk precisely driving it away.
Does happiness really have to be sought, or is it one of those things that only comes to those who don't chase it?
There is something contradictory in the direct pursuit of happiness.
Constantly asking oneself 'Am I happy?', watching for one's own happiness, and making it the object of an anxious quest is often the best way not to be happy.

For this self-surveillance introduces worry and dissatisfaction: as we check if we are happy, we discover everything that is lacking, and we compare ourselves to an ideal of happiness that we never quite reach.
The injunction to be happy can thus generate its opposite: the guilt of not being happy enough, the anxiety of failing at life.
Indeed, it seems that happiness is rarely found at the end of a direct pursuit.

It comes rather as a byproduct, as a secondary effect, when we are absorbed in something other than happiness: a job that excites us, a relationship that fulfills us, a cause that transcends us, a moment of beauty.
Those who seem the happiest are not those who seek happiness the most, but those who are engaged in something that captivates them and makes them forget themselves.
Happiness is born from engagement in life, not from the anxious quest for one's own contentment.
This suggests a shift: instead of seeking happiness, seek what gives meaning and joy, and let happiness come as a byproduct.
Ask not 'What will make me happy?', but 'What is worth my commitment, to which I will dedicate my life?'

For lasting happiness does not seem to reside in the accumulation of pleasures or in self-satisfaction, but in a life filled with what is meaningful: deep relationships, an activity that absorbs us, a transcendence of self.
Happiness, in a sense, is what we find when we seek something else.
However, we must guard against a misunderstanding.
Saying that happiness should not be sought directly does not mean we should disregard it or impose an austere life of sacrifice.
It means that the path to happiness comes indirectly, through what we attach ourselves to and what we do, rather than through an obsession with our own state.
Caring for what matters — our connections, our activities, our relationship with the world — is more fruitful than scrutinizing our happiness.
We do not pick happiness by focusing on it; we encounter it by moving towards something else.
Happiness is therefore sought, but not like an object that can be grasped.
It is sought indirectly, by building a life that is worth living, rich in meaning and connections, and by renouncing the anxious obsession with our own contentment.
Perhaps wisdom consists less in pursuing happiness than in making it possible, and then knowing how to welcome it when it comes — without forcing it to stay or panicking over its absences.
For a life that demands to be happy at all costs is a life that often condemns itself to not being happy.

sentences: There is an ancient distinction, at the heart of many wisdoms, whose simplicity hides depth: among the things that affect us, some depend on us, and others do not.
This distinction, which thinkers from Antiquity placed at the foundation of a good life, remains strikingly relevant.
For a large part of our suffering comes from the fact that we confuse them: we exhaust ourselves trying to change what does not depend on us, and neglect what does depend on us.
What depends on us?
Not external events, the behavior of others, the past, illness, death, the thousand circumstances that escape our will.
But our own judgments, our choices, our efforts, the way we react to what happens to us.
Here is the division: outside, a vast domain that we do not control; inside, a smaller but real domain, that of our attitude, which we can influence.
Wisdom begins by recognizing this boundary and ceasing to cross it in imagination.
For a major source of torment is wanting what does not depend on us.
We rebel against what is, we are consumed by an irreparable past, we want to control the uncontrollable, change others, bend events to our desires.
This struggle against the inevitable is lost from the start, and it exhausts us without changing anything.
You cannot bring back the dead, you cannot redo the past, you cannot force others to be what they are not.
Wanting these things is to condemn oneself to a sterile suffering.
Accepting what we cannot change is neither resignation nor passivity.
It is not giving up on acting, nor accepting everything with indifference.
It is to lucidly recognize the limits of our power, to concentrate our energy where it can make a difference, rather than wasting it where it cannot.
In the face of what does not depend on us, acceptance; in the face of what does depend on us, action and effort.
This distribution, far from weakening, makes us stronger: we stop fighting in vain, to act effectively where we have influence.
This wisdom applies even to the limits of existence.
There are evils that we cannot avoid, losses that we cannot repair, a finitude that we cannot abolish.
Against them, rebellion is futile, and acceptance, not bitter resignation but serene recognition, is the only path to peace.

Accepting that we cannot do everything, that we are mortal, vulnerable, dependent, is not a defeat; it is the condition for a peaceful existence, which has stopped fighting against reality to learn to live with it.
Distinguishing what depends on us from what does not is thus a key to a good life.

It frees us from two errors: the illusion of omnipotence, which wants to control everything and breaks against reality; and the feeling of powerlessness, which believes it can do nothing and gives up acting where it could.
Between the two, there is the right measure: to act with all our energy on what depends on us, to accept with serenity what does not.
A part of wisdom — and of peace — lies in this distinction, easy to state, difficult to live, but which illuminates an entire existence.

sentences: We are the being that knows it will die.
This awareness, which we may share with no one else, is one of the strangest and heaviest aspects of the human condition.
We live knowing that we will die, that everything we do, love, and build will come to an end.
One might think that this awareness is merely a source of anxiety, a burden from which it would be better to turn away.
But it is also, when properly considered, what can give life its depth and value.
This final text of a whole journey deserves to be reflected upon.
The most common temptation is to flee from this awareness, to live as if we do not have to die.
Our time excels in this avoidance: it hides death, pushes it out of sight, surrounds it with silence, and constantly distracts us so we do not think about it.
This flight is understandable — the thought of death is difficult — but it comes at a price.
By refusing to confront our finitude, we often live in a kind of illusion, as if we had infinite time, postponing what is essential, wasting days we believe are countless.
The forgetting of death fosters a certain unconsciousness of life.
For, paradoxically, it is the awareness of death that can give life all its value.
If we lived forever, nothing would be urgent, nothing would be pressing, each moment could be postponed indefinitely; time, unlimited, would lose its value.
It is because our days are numbered that they are precious, that each moment is unique and will not return, that our choices carry weight.
Finitude, far from making life absurd, may be what makes it intense.
What is rare and finite has value; what is infinite and unlimited no longer does.
The awareness of death, when well received, is thus a teacher of life.
It reminds us of what truly matters, distinguishes the essential from the trivial, and frees us from the vanities that consume us.
In the face of the thought of our end, we stop fretting over trivialities, we measure the value of loved ones, of the present time, of simple things.
Many wisdoms have made meditation on death not a morbid exercise, but a path to a more just, clearer, and fuller life.
To remember that we will die is to remember to live.
This awareness can even soothe us, rather than distress us.
Accepting our finitude, ceasing to flee or deny it, is making peace with the condition that is ours.
Those who have faced death often testify to a new serenity, a capacity to savor life that they did not have before.
Not because they fear nothing anymore, but because having accepted the end, they are finally free to fully live the time that remains.
The acceptance of death can be the condition for a truly vibrant life.
Thus ends this long journey, on the highest of questions.
Living knowing that we will die is not a curse to be avoided, but perhaps the very foundation of a conscious and fulfilling life.
This awareness invites us not to postpone the essential, to cherish what is, to give meaning and depth to our counted days.
It reminds anyone learning a language, as well as anyone else, that time is precious, that nothing is guaranteed, and that it is worth living each day as if it mattered — for, in truth, it does.
This is perhaps the oldest and simplest of wisdoms: since life is brief, it is all the more important to live it well.

sentences: We take debate for granted, almost as a natural backdrop of democratic life.
We forget that it is actually a late and precarious achievement, resting on such demanding conditions that it is more surprising that it exists than that it is fragile.

For debating, in the fullest sense, does not mean merely allowing opposing opinions to coexist in the same space; it means accepting to subject one's convictions to the test of contradiction, in the hope that something more true or more just will emerge.
Such a disposition is not spontaneous; it even goes against our deepest inclinations.
The first condition of debate is indeed the most improbable: to recognize that the person who contradicts us has an equal legitimacy to our own.
Nothing naturally inclines us to this.
We tend to hold our convictions as obvious, and thus explain others' disagreement by their ignorance, bad faith, or interests.
Debating requires us to suspend this reflex, to admit that the other may think differently for reasons they believe, just as we do, are good.
Without this presumption of legitimacy, there is no debate, only the confrontation of camps that mutually deny each other the right to speak.
The second condition is the existence of shared facts.
A genuine debate requires common ground, a foundation of realities that the opponents recognize together, and on which their disagreement can unfold.
Where each has their own facts, where reality itself becomes a subject of dispute, debate loses its ground: we no longer discuss interpretations of a common world, we inhabit separate worlds.
This is why the dislocation of the factual foundation — this impression that 'everyone has their truth' — is not a detail, but a threat to the very possibility of deliberation.
The third condition relates to a rare inner disposition: to accept that one could be wrong.
Anyone who enters a debate holding their conclusion as a given is not debating; they are pleading.
Authentic debate carries a risk, that of being convinced, of having to revise one's views, of leaving the exchange different from how one entered it.

This consented vulnerability is the hallmark of true debate, and its most difficult requirement, as it clashes with our attachment to our own opinions, which we experience less as hypotheses than as possessions, even as parts of ourselves.
That these conditions are so demanding explains the fragility of debate, and the ease with which it degrades into its opposite.

It is enough for just one to be lacking — for one to deny the opponent's legitimacy, for the factual foundation to dissolve, for no one to accept that they could be wrong — for deliberation to give way to invective, propaganda, and a war of camps.
Moreover, these three conditions are today simultaneously under attack, which should concern us more than the content of any particular debate.
Understanding debate as a fragile civilization, rather than as an acquired right, changes the way we view it.
This invites us to see it not as a right that merely needs to be proclaimed, but as a delicate practice that must be maintained, protected, and relearned.
A society does not suddenly stop debating overnight; it gradually loses the capacity as the conditions that made it possible unravel.
And when a people has unlearned how to debate, they are left with only paths to resolve their disagreements that history has shown to be costly.

sentences: Transparency has become a moral requirement of our time, to the point that it seems almost scandalous to question it.
It is demanded everywhere: in political life, in businesses, in institutions, and even in private relationships.
What is hidden becomes suspicious; what refuses to show itself seems to have something to conceal.
This aspiration has obvious virtues: it combats the secrecy of the powerful, the opacity that protects abuses, and the arbitrariness that thrives in the shadows.
And yet, we must have the courage to ask whether transparency, elevated to an absolute, does not turn against what it claims to serve.
For total transparency has a cost that its prestige makes us forget.
A society where everything should be visible, where nothing could remain out of sight, would be an unlivable society.
Thought itself needs a space of retreat where it can form before being exposed, where it can explore, make mistakes, and mature.
Demanding that everything be immediately public is to prohibit this work in the shadows, without which nothing profound can be developed.
A leader whose every hesitation, every doubt, and every internal deliberation would be exposed could no longer think freely; they could only conform, in advance, to what the gaze expects.
There is more.
Transparency, presented as a guarantee of truth, often produces the opposite.
When everything is likely to be seen, everyone monitors themselves, stages themselves, and calculates their words and actions based on the presumed gaze.
Total visibility does not foster authenticity, but performance: one no longer shows who they are, but rather presents what will be well received.
Thus, transparency, far from revealing the truth of individuals, forces them into a permanent performance, substituting conformity, which arises from exposure, for sincerity, which needs intimacy.
This demand is also linked to a widespread distrust that it both nourishes and expresses.
Demanding unlimited transparency presupposes that no one deserves trust, that every power, every institution, and every person inherently hides some fault that must be tracked down.
However, a society cannot function without a degree of trust, that is, without accepting not to verify everything, to give credit, and to allow others a zone of shadow.
Complete transparency, by refusing this credit, undermines the bond it claims to purify: it installs suspicion where trust is needed and turns everyone into a watcher of all.
Criticizing absolute transparency does not mean defending the secrecy of the powerful or the opacity that covers abuses.
The distinction here is crucial: it is one thing to demand that those in power be held accountable, and another to want everything, in every matter, to be exposed to scrutiny.
The first demand is legitimate and beneficial; the second is a dangerous chimera.
Confusing the two, in the name of indistinct transparency, risks destroying, along with culpable opacity, the legitimate shadow that freedom, thought, and trust need.

What a free society must preserve is therefore less transparency than its proper measure: visibility where power must be held accountable, and shadow where life, thought, and intimacy must be protected.
A civilization is not judged solely by what it exposes, but by what it knows to leave in a respected twilight.
For a completely transparent world would not be a completely true world; it would be a world where no one, knowing they are always seen, would dare to be entirely themselves.

sentences: Today, it takes a certain kind of courage to embrace nuance.

In a public space divided into camps, where every issue seems to demand a binary choice, anyone who introduces a distinction, acknowledges a grain of truth in the opponent's position, and refuses to make a clear-cut decision as expected, exposes themselves to a double suspicion: being seen as lukewarm by some and as a traitor by others.
Nuance is often seen as an evasion, a lack of courage, a way of not choosing.
We must overturn this prejudice, because nuance, far from being cowardice, is one of the most demanding forms of intellectual courage.
First, let’s understand why nuance is so devalued.
In a polarized debate, the clarity of one’s camp outweighs the accuracy of the argument.
What is expected of you is not that you think correctly, but that you are clear: which side are you on?
Nuance muddles this clarity; it makes things uncertain, unclassifiable, and therefore suspect.
Those who embrace nuance do not provide the rallying cry that the group demands; they reject the simplification that allows for immediate identification of friends and enemies.
It is this rejection that is criticized, under the guise of blaming them for a lack of firmness.
However, to embrace nuance is not to hesitate or to refuse to conclude.

It is to recognize that reality is complex, that difficult questions involve contradictory considerations, that a position can be mostly correct while still having blind spots, and that the opponent can be mostly wrong while touching on some truth in one area.
Nuance is not the absence of conviction; it is conviction that has navigated complexity instead of fleeing from it.
It demands more, not less, than a clear-cut position: it requires holding together what polarization urges us to separate.
This is what makes it a form of courage.

It is easy and comfortable to unreservedly adopt your camp's position, to repeat its certainties, to share its indignations; you gain the approval of your peers, the feeling of belonging, and the relief from thinking for yourself.
Nuancing, on the contrary, means accepting to displease your own camp, exposing yourself to their reproach, and giving up the comfort of unreserved belonging.
It risks the solitude of someone who does not fully align, who maintains their freedom to judge against the pressure of the group.
This risk, many do not dare to take, and prefer the security of alignment to the discomfort of accuracy.
Moreover, nuance has a virtue that polarization destroys: it keeps the space for dialogue open.
Where clear-cut positions clash without meeting, nuance creates points of contact, acknowledges a part of reason in the other, and makes it possible to still listen to one another.
It is the opposite of a war between camps, not because it refuses to take sides, but because it takes sides without denying complexity or demonizing the opponent.
In this way, it may be the very condition for a debate that does not degenerate into confrontation — this fragile civilization that has been discussed.
Defending nuance is therefore not advocating for lukewarmness or refusing to engage.

It is a reminder that sound thinking embraces the complexity of its subject, that a solid conviction is not afraid to recognize its limitations, and that a fruitful debate requires minds capable of distinguishing rather than rallying.

In an era that rewards loud certainty and unreserved alignment, daring to embrace nuance, maintaining complexity against the pressure to simplify, and refusing to hate those we disagree with: this is what demands, today more than ever, true courage.
And perhaps it is this kind of courage, more than firmer convictions, that our debates lack the most.

sentences: We live in the certainty of being free.
We deliberate, we choose, we hold others and ourselves accountable for our actions; our entire moral and social life rests on this conviction.
And yet, an old doubt undermines it, which modern science has revived.

If every event has a cause, if the world obeys a chain of causes and effects, then our choices, which are also events, have their own causes; they result from the state of our brain, our history, and our dispositions, which themselves stem from prior causes.
Where, in this chain, can true freedom reside?
Could the feeling we have of it be nothing but an illusion?
The argument is formidable in its simplicity.
When I believe I am choosing freely, I am merely executing what the prior state of the world and myself made inevitable.
My deliberation itself, my reasons, my feeling of deciding, are the effects of causes that I do not control.

The freedom I attribute to myself would be nothing but ignorance of the causes that determine me: I believe I am free because I do not see what makes me act, like a stone that would think it is free if it were unaware of gravity.
This thesis, determinism, has for it the coherence and support of everything science teaches us about the chain of causes.
Should we then renounce freedom?
Before conceding this, it is important to examine what we mean by this word.

If being free means escaping all cause, acting without anything determining our action, then freedom is indeed impossible, and perhaps even unintelligible: an action without any cause would not be a free act, but pure chance, which is not what we seek either.
Freedom as total absence of determination is a chimera; but is that really what we mean when we say we are free?
Another conception is possible, which does not place freedom outside of causes, but within a certain way of being caused.

I am free, according to this view, not when nothing determines me, but when what determines me is myself: my own reasons, my values, my reflection, as opposed to external constraint or an impulse I suffer.

A person forced against their will is not free; someone acting under the influence of a passion that overwhelms them is hardly free; but someone who acts according to what they judge, after deliberation, to be best, is free in a real sense, even if their deliberation itself has causes.
Freedom would not be the absence of causes, but the alignment of the act with the self that performs it.
This conception does not dispel all difficulty, as one might object that this self, with its reasons and values, is the product of causes it did not choose.
The debate here cannot be settled with a single word, and it would be presumptuous to claim to close it.
But it is important to note this: even someone who theoretically persuades themselves that freedom is illusory continues, in practice, to deliberate, to choose, to hold others accountable.
They cannot live according to their thesis.

This impossibility is not proof, but it indicates that freedom, whatever one thinks of its metaphysical status, is a category we cannot rid ourselves of, inscribed at the heart of our experience and our shared life.
Perhaps the question is not whether we are free in the absolute sense — a question that might have no answer — but rather to recognize the degrees of freedom that make a real difference in our lives.

Between the person dominated by their impulses and the one who masters them, between the one who follows blindly and the one who reflects, between the slave and the free person, there are differences that no determinism erases.

Cultivating these differences, increasing within oneself the part of what acts by reason rather than by constraint, is perhaps what it means to be free: not to escape causes, but to become increasingly the cause of one's own actions.

sentences: We all recognize that we have duties to others: not to harm, to help those in danger, to keep our promises.
This ordinary morality seems obvious to us, and we believe it to be coherent.
But as soon as we examine it, it begins to falter, because it is surprisingly difficult to say how far our obligation extends, and why it stops where we make it stop.
Questioning what we owe to others reveals that our moral intuitions, so assured in appearance, rest on boundaries that nothing fully justifies.
Let's consider a simple case.

If I pass by a child drowning in a pond, and I can save him without risk, at the cost of only getting my clothes dirty, everyone will judge that I should do it, and that refraining would be monstrous.
The intuition is unanimous.
But it has consequences that we do not accept.
For if I am obliged to sacrifice something minor to save a life at my feet, why should I not be obliged to save a distant life, which I could preserve at the cost of a comparable sacrifice?
Does distance change anything about the obligation?
It is hard to argue that a child dying far from me counts less than a child dying before my eyes, and yet we live as if it were the case.
This logic, if we follow it, becomes dizzying.
It seems to imply that we would be morally obliged to give almost everything we have beyond what is necessary, as long as there are, somewhere, lives we could save.

Few of us accept this conclusion; it clashes with our feeling that a life belongs to us too, that we have the right to pursue our projects, to prefer our loved ones, to not sacrifice ourselves endlessly.
But if we reject it, we must say where and why the obligation stops — and that is where our justifications become fragile.
We readily invoke proximity: we owe more to our loved ones than to strangers.
This intuition is powerful, and it undoubtedly contains a grain of truth, as particular bonds create particular obligations.
But it cannot justify everything.
That I owe more to my children does not imply that I owe nothing to the distant child; the preference for my own can explain a hierarchy of duties, not the abolition of all obligation to others.

Between the unlimited duty that would sacrifice us entirely and the indifference that would recognize duties only to those close to us, ordinary morality occupies an intermediate position that it struggles to justify.
Perhaps we must accept that morality cannot be reduced to a single coherent principle, applied without exception.

Our obligations arise from the tension between several legitimate demands: universality, which holds that every life counts equally; partiality, which recognizes particular bonds; and the right of each person to live their own life, to not be a mere instrument of the good of others.
These demands do not easily rank in order, and moral life may consist less of applying a rule than of composing, as best as we can, between duties that pull in different directions.
What remains, at the end of this examination, is not a clear answer, but a healthy unease.
We can no longer take our moral boundaries for granted, nor believe we are off the hook with others simply because we respect ordinary morality.
Recognizing that we probably owe more than we do, without believing we are obliged to unlimited sacrifice, is to honestly inhabit the tension that constitutes moral life.

This uncomfortable clarity is better than the false tranquility of those who believe they have fulfilled all their duties — because the question of what we owe to others is not one that can be closed, but one we must learn to live with.

sentences: Indignation today enjoys a unique prestige.
To be indignant is seen as a virtue, a sign of an awakened conscience, a refusal of injustices; not being indignant is viewed as a form of complicity, a culpable indifference.
This valuation is not without foundation: indignation has historically been the driving force behind noble struggles, and the inability to be moved by evil is chilling.
However, we must dare to question this dominant stance, because while indignation can awaken thought, it can also, more often than one might think, replace it and dispense with it.
What characterizes indignation is its immediacy.
It is a reaction, an emotional movement that precedes judgment and often replaces it.
In the face of what triggers it, it does not question; it condemns.
Yet this speed, which gives it apparent strength, is also its weakness.
For the situations that call for judgment are most often complex, ambiguous, and filled with contradictory considerations.
Indignation, on the other hand, cuts through immediately, without examination, solely based on the emotion felt.
It offers the comfort of immediate moral certainty, where thought would require the slow work of nuance.
There is something more troubling.
Indignation provides a pleasure that is rarely admitted: the feeling of being on the right side.
To be indignant is to immediately place oneself in the camp of the just, against that of the guilty; it is to enjoy a moral superiority without having to earn it through any action.

This satisfaction is all the more intense because it costs nothing: one can be indignant at little expense, without acting, without reflecting, while still experiencing the gratifying feeling of one's own virtue.
Indignation then becomes a posture, a way of presenting oneself as a moral conscience, rather than a real commitment.
This drift is exacerbated by the mechanisms that currently organize public expression.
Digital platforms specifically reward what indignation produces: the lively reaction, the impulsive sharing, the emotion that spreads.
They turn indignation into a currency, a means of visibility, and encourage everyone to be indignant ever more loudly, ever more quickly, on ever more topics.

The result is an inflation of indignation that, far from sharpening awareness, exhausts and brutalizes it, turning debate into a competition of emotions where the most outraged wins over the most just.
Should we conclude that we should ban indignation, preferring a detached coldness?
That would be a symmetrical error.
Indignation has its place and legitimacy: it can be the first movement, healthy and necessary, by which a conscience rejects the unacceptable.
The problem is not that we are indignant, but that we stop there, that indignation replaces examination instead of preceding it.
Indignation that leads to thought, that then accepts to question, to nuance, to understand, remains fruitful; indignation that is self-sufficient sterilizes itself and sterilizes the debate.
The real issue is therefore to restore to indignation its proper function: that of an alert, not a verdict.
To feel the shock of evil, but not to be content with it; to let emotion call for reflection rather than close it off.
This requires resisting the ease of immediate judgment, the sweetness of moral certainty, the inclination to prefer the brilliance of indignation to the patience of thought.
In an era that elevates indignation to the highest virtue, claiming the right to think before condemning has paradoxically become an act of audacity.

sentences: Our public life is living in the era of permanent scandal.
Hardly has one controversy died down before another takes its place; each day brings its new outrage, its designated culprit, its issue to comment on.
We have become so accustomed to this regime of continuous agitation that we no longer perceive it as abnormal.
Yet it deserves to be questioned, as it produces a paradoxical effect: by turning everything into a scandal, we exhaust our very capacity to be alarmed by what truly deserves it.
The mechanism of permanent scandal follows a logic that must be understood.
In a saturated space where countless voices compete for scarce attention, scandal is what captures the gaze.
To exist, therefore, one must produce scandal, constantly create new ones, amplify their scale, and dramatize the stakes.
What would have seemed a minor incident yesterday is today a state affair; what warranted caution becomes a subject of general outrage.
The inflation of scandal is not a sign of a morally more demanding society, but of an attention economy that needs, to function, a constantly renewed emotional fuel.
This inflation has the same effect as any inflation: it devalues the currency it multiplies.
When everything is presented as scandalous, the word loses its meaning and its power.
Collective emotion, constantly solicited, becomes dulled; indignation, too often demanded, grows weary.

As a result, there is an habituation that is the opposite of vigilance: by being alarmed about everything, we end up no longer being alarmed by anything, or we reserve our indignation for what affects our side.
Permanent scandal does not make consciences more sensitive; it anesthetizes them.
This wear and tear has a serious consequence, often unnoticed.
In the clamor of interchangeable scandals, real injustices, those that would require sustained mobilization, are drowned out, treated on the same level as trivial matters blown out of proportion.
Lacking hierarchy, the serious and the trivial become confused, and indignation, dispersed over everything, no longer concentrates on anything.

Thus, permanent scandal, far from serving justice, undermines it: it consumes the moral energy of a society by squandering it on a thousand objects, instead of reserving it for causes that would justify it.
It should also be noted that this regime favors a particular form of injustice: the summary trial.
Scandal demands an immediate culprit, a swift condemnation, without the time for examination or the precautions of judgment.

Carried away by its own dynamics, collective indignation designates, condemns, and punishes before having investigated, even at the cost of ruining reputations based on accusations that no one has verified.
The speed of scandal is incompatible with the slowness of justice, and this incompatibility creates victims that the forgetfulness of the next scandal will never exonerate.
Resisting permanent scandal requires a difficult collective discipline: relearning to distinguish, to prioritize, to reserve alarm for what deserves it, and to give judgment the time it requires.
It also requires a distrust of our own appetite for scandal, of the troubling pleasure that comes from being outraged, from condemning, from participating in the hunt.
A society that knows how to be indignant less often, but more effectively, would be fairer than a society that is outraged by everything.
For the value of indignation does not lie in its frequency, but in its accuracy — and an emotion that is lavished on everything ultimately ends up being unable to defend anything.

sentences: The idea of progress is so deeply ingrained in us that we take it for granted.
We spontaneously believe that history is moving forward, that humanity, despite setbacks, is improving, and that tomorrow will be better than yesterday.
This belief shapes our relationship with time, justifies our efforts, and comforts us in our sorrows.
However, it is relatively recent in the grand scheme of history and far from being self-evident.
Questioning it is not falling into pessimism, but examining one of the most powerful assumptions of our civilization.
The idea of progress has considerable merits to defend.

In many respects, the improvement is undeniable: life expectancy has increased, physical suffering has decreased, diseases have been conquered, education has spread, and forms of cruelty that were once commonplace have become intolerable.
Anyone who would deny these advances, in the name of a nostalgia for an idealized past, would be gravely mistaken and would insult those who, in the past, died young, in pain and ignorance.
There is indeed progress, and failing to recognize it would be both a mistake and an ingratitude.
But the idea of progress, as soon as it becomes doctrine, carries illusions that must be uncovered.
The first is to believe that progress is necessary, inscribed in the very meaning of history, as if a force guaranteed it.
Nothing could be further from the truth.
Nothing assures that what has been gained cannot be lost; history knows regressions, collapses, and returns of barbarism that were thought to be behind us.
Progress, when it occurs, is the result of efforts and choices, not a law of history; to take it for granted is to stop defending it, and thus prepare for its loss.
The second illusion is to believe in unified progress, as if improvement affects all areas at once.
However, one can progress in one area and regress in another.
Technical power is increasing, but is our wisdom keeping pace?
We treat better, but we destroy our environment; we communicate more, but we may understand each other less; we know more, but do we know how to live better?
Material and technical progress, undeniable, does not guarantee moral or human progress, and it can even, by increasing our powers without increasing our wisdom, make our faults more perilous.
Confusing the different types of progress is merely self-deception.
The third illusion, more subtle, concerns the measurement of progress.
Progress towards what?
Saying that history is improving implies a criterion, an idea of what is better.
However, this criterion is not given; it depends on what we value.
A civilization that judges progress by power and wealth does not measure the same thing as one that would judge it by justice or quality of life.
The idea of progress often conceals this assumption: it presents as an objective advance what is merely a movement towards what we consider desirable.
Questioning progress means questioning our own values, which we project onto history while believing we can read a meaning that it contains.
Should we therefore abandon the idea of progress?
That would mean giving up what gives human action part of its drive: the hope of making the world better.

But we must hold it differently: not as a law of history that carries us along, but as a task that is our responsibility; not as an established fact, but as a fragile possibility; not as a unified and guaranteed movement, but as an effort that is always partial, reversible, and to be resumed.
A progress understood this way is more modest, but more true, and above all more demanding: it does not exempt us from acting, it obliges us to do so.
For if nothing guarantees that tomorrow will be better, then it depends on us to make it so.

sentences: Philosophy suffers from a particular discredit, that of activities which produce nothing tangible.

It does not build bridges, does not heal diseases, does not increase wealth; worse, it does not even seem to progress, constantly returning to the same questions that the Ancients already asked, without ever resolving them.
In a world that judges everything by its utility and yield, it appears as a relic, an intellectual luxury that is hard to justify.
And yet, no civilization worthy of the name has done without it, and its apparent uselessness might well be a sign not of its vanity, but of its depth.
First, we must dispel a misunderstanding.
Philosophy is criticized for not resolving anything, as if it had failed to do what the sciences do.
But this criticism misunderstands its nature.

Philosophy does not deal with questions that observation or calculation could settle; it specifically addresses those that elude them, those concerning meaning, value, justice, goodness, the nature of knowledge or consciousness.
These questions cannot be resolved in the manner of a scientific problem, not because they are poorly posed, but because they engage what we are and what we hold to be important.
To criticize philosophy for not definitively resolving them is to criticize it for tackling what, by nature, cannot be closed.
So what does it do, then, if it does not resolve?
It questions.
Its primary function is to challenge what seems obvious, to uncover the assumptions that govern our lives without us ever having examined them.
We live on a mass of presuppositions — about what is just, about what is valuable, about what we ought to do — that we take for granted even though they are inherited, contingent, and debatable.
Philosophy has this uncomfortable virtue of making them visible, forcing us to justify them, depriving us of the comfort of received ideas.
It does not give us answers; it enables us to ask the questions.
This function, which seems purely negative, is in reality a liberation.

For someone who has never questioned their presuppositions is not free: they endure them, they think and act according to frameworks they have not chosen, believing they are deciding when they are merely obeying invisible assumptions.
Becoming aware of these frameworks, examining them, is the beginning of freeing oneself from them, of thinking for oneself instead of thinking despite oneself.
In this sense, philosophy is not just another body of knowledge, but an emancipation: it restores to the mind a freedom that habit and conformity had stolen.
One might argue that this emancipation is a luxury, reserved for a few, with no effect on the course of the world.
This would underestimate the significance of ideas.
The conceptions we have of justice, freedom, and human nature do not remain in books: they govern our institutions, our laws, and our ways of living together.
Major political transformations have almost always been preceded and nourished by a work of thought that had, first, made thinkable what would become real.
Philosophy does not act directly, but it shapes the horizon within which action becomes possible; its apparent uselessness masks a slow and profound effectiveness.
It remains that its value is not reduced to its effects.

Philosophy responds to a need that is not of utility but of meaning: the distinctly human need to understand one's condition, to not go through existence without ever questioning what one does and why.
A life that would never ask these questions would not be less effective; it would be less fully human.
That is why philosophy, which serves no interest in the way one serves a purpose, is indispensable in the sense that everything that makes life worth examining is.
Its uselessness is not a flaw; it is a sign that it touches on what, within us, transcends the mere need to live to question the very fact of living.

sentences: The fact that the first question asked of a stranger is about their job says a lot about our era.
We define ourselves, and we define others, by work, to the point of confusing being with doing, the person with their role.
This identification seems so natural that we believe it to be universal.
However, it is a recent historical construction, specific to societies where paid work has become central to existence, and there is no guarantee that it will last.
Questioning it does not deny the importance of work, but rather rejects the idea that it should absorb our entire identity.
We must first assess what is particular about this identification.
In many societies, past or present, people primarily define themselves by their lineage, community, faith, or status, not by productive activity.
Work there is what one does to live, not what defines who one is.

The fact that a job has become, for us, the default answer to the question 'who are you?' stems from a specific history: that of the rise of a society where production has become the cardinal value, and work, the main path to social recognition.
This identification is not inherent; it is dated, situated, and therefore reversible.
It certainly has its virtues.
Work structures existence, integrates individuals into a collective, and provides a sense of being useful and recognized.
Identifying with one's job also means valuing what one does, investing pride in it, and finding a part of meaning there.

It would be somewhat hypocritical to disdain this identification from the comfort of a leisurely life: for many, work is what gives their days shape and dignity, and depriving it of its identity dimension would impoverish them.
Critiquing identity through work should not slip into disdain for work itself.
But this identification has a downside, which becomes apparent when it becomes exclusive.
If I am only my job, who am I when I lose it — due to unemployment, illness, or retirement?

The experience of those who are left by work reveals the fragility of an identity that has no other foundation: it wavers, empties, as if what has been taken from the person is not just a job, but a part of themselves.

A society that has taught its members to exist only through their function leaves them helpless as soon as that function eludes them, and prepares, as work becomes scarcer or transforms, a crisis of identity as much as of employment.
There is more.
Identification with work also serves a logic that is not innocent.

By making work the primary place of value and recognition, a society directs energies towards production, subordinates other dimensions of existence to professional activity, and casts suspicion on any life that would not be defined by work.
Those who do not produce — whether because they cannot or do not want to — are denied a part of their dignity, as if they were failing a duty to exist usefully.
This pressure, internalized, transforms work from a means into an end, and the human being into a producer who exists only as they produce.
Recognizing the constructed nature of identity through work gives us the freedom to relativize it.
Not to devalue work, which retains its importance, but to assign it its rightful place: a dimension of existence among others, not the entirety of it.
A human being is also a relative, a citizen, a curious person, a creator, a living being — roles that no job description records.

Remembering that we are not reducible to what we do to earn a living preserves, against an era that tends to forget it, a broader conception of what a person is — and allows us to maintain, for the day when work might be lacking, a foundation of identity that its loss could not take away.

sentences: There is a rare and precious state of mind that could be called the ability to think against oneself.

It involves not just defending one's beliefs, but deliberately subjecting them to the harshest scrutiny, seeking out the strongest objections that could be raised against them, and sincerely asking oneself whether one might be wrong.
This disposition goes against all our inclinations, and perhaps that's why it represents the pinnacle of intellectual honesty, and is one of the most challenging things there is.
Our inclinations indeed lead us in the opposite direction.

We spontaneously seek what confirms our beliefs, not what contradicts them; we readily accept arguments that support us, and view with suspicion those that disturb us; we associate with those who think like us and shy away from contradiction.

This deeply ingrained tendency causes our convictions, instead of being tested, to reinforce themselves, transforming into certainties that are all the more solid because they have never been challenged.
Thinking against oneself means resisting this tendency, making the unnatural effort to seek out what could disprove us.
Why impose such an effort on oneself?
Because it is the only path to a conviction that truly matters.

An opinion that has never been confronted with its objections is not a thought, but a prejudice, even if it happens to be true; it is held out of habit, belonging, or laziness, not because it has been tested.

The one who has sought the best reasons to think differently, and maintains their position despite them, holds it in a completely different way: not as an accepted dogma, but as a conclusion that has been earned.
Thinking against oneself does not weaken solid convictions; it strengthens them by discarding those that are not.
This discipline has an additional virtue: it is the best remedy for the blindness of factions.

The one who commits to seeking what their opponent might have that is valid, to formulating the opposing position in its strongest form rather than in caricature, can no longer treat those who think differently as fools or evildoers.
They discover that disagreement often rests on reasons, not merely on the stupidity or malice of the other.
Thinking against oneself is thus a school of justice towards others, as much as it is of rigor towards oneself.
However, it is not about sinking into a universal doubt that would prohibit any conviction.
Thinking against oneself is not about thinking nothing at all, nor about changing one's mind at every objection; it is about testing one's convictions, not dissolving them.
The goal is not perpetual uncertainty, but a certainty that has paid the price of examination.
After seeking out contrary reasons and weighing their strength, one can, and must, conclude — but one concludes then with full knowledge, knowing what has been set aside and why.
It is a firmness that has gone through doubt, not one that has fled from it.
Such a discipline is demanding, and no one practices it perfectly, as it requires constantly overcoming our self-esteem, our desire to be right, our attachment to who we are.
But it is the heart of any honest intellectual life, and its very rarity makes it valuable.

In an era that rewards overt certainty and unwavering allegiance, where everyone surrounds themselves with what comforts them, making the effort to think against oneself is almost an act of resistance.

It is also the mark of a truly free spirit: not the one who never doubts, nor the one who doubts everything, but the one who has the courage to ask themselves, regarding their dearest convictions, whether it might be possible that they are wrong.

sentences: We analyze work in terms of income, conditions, and time; we often forget what it involves at a deeper and more intimate level: the need for recognition.
Because what we seek in work, beyond salary, is also to be recognized — seen, valued, and considered important in the eyes of others.
This need, rarely named, nevertheless governs a large part of our relationship with work, and its absence explains many sufferings that a purely material examination would leave incomprehensible.
Recognition is a fundamentally human need, as real as material needs, even though it is invisible.
We only become subjects in the eyes of others: it is by being recognized by others that we acquire a sense of our own worth.
A being that no one would recognize, whose existence would be ignored by all, would experience itself as nothing.
This need to be recognized is not vanity; it is constitutive of our condition as social beings, who can only relate to themselves through their relationships with others.
And work is one of the major places where this need plays out.
Because work exposes us to the gaze of others in a particular way.
It makes us contribute to a common endeavor, producing something that will be judged, used, appreciated, or despised.

To be recognized in this context means to have one's contribution acknowledged, one's effort valued, and one's competence praised; it means to exist in the eyes of others as someone who matters, who contributes, who has a place.
This recognition nourishes self-esteem, gives meaning to work, and transforms a task into a source of pride.
Conversely, unrecognized, ignored, or despised work hurts in a way that no salary can compensate.
This is where a major suffering of contemporary work reveals itself, often invisible to purely economic analyses.

Many of those who suffer at work do not primarily suffer from their material conditions, but from a lack of recognition: the feeling that their effort is not seen, that their contribution does not matter, that they are interchangeable, reduced to an anonymous function.
This denial of recognition reaches the person at the deepest level, as it signifies that they are worth nothing in the eyes of those for whom they work.
One can better endure a hard but recognized job than an easy but despised one.
This dimension also sheds light on the fate reserved for certain professions.
There are essential jobs — caregiving, cleaning, helping the most vulnerable — that are among the least recognized, poorly paid, and socially devalued.
The denial of recognition then adds to the hardship and exacerbates the injustice: those who perform tasks that society cannot do without are the ones to whom it denies esteem.
Certain circumstances, by suddenly revealing the vital utility of these jobs, have brought this scandal to light — without the proclaimed recognition always translating into reality afterward.
Taking the need for recognition seriously transforms the way we think about work.

It is not enough to improve salaries and conditions, no matter how essential that is; work must also allow everyone to be recognized for their contribution, valued for their effort, and regarded as a person rather than a function.
An organization that crushes recognition, that makes people interchangeable and invisible, produces suffering even if it pays well.

Because a person at work does not only ask for a means to live; they ask to exist in the eyes of others — and this invisible need, if neglected, exacts revenge through a suffering that nothing material can soothe.

sentences: Our time has made utility a sovereign value.

An activity, a study, an expense, even a life, is justified by what it serves; what serves no purpose is suspect, summoned to account for itself, and threatened with disappearance due to lack of profitability.

This demand for utility, which seems like simple common sense, actually exerts a discreet tyranny, as it comes to measure everything by the service it renders, and devalues everything that would be valuable in itself.
However, a civilization that no longer recognizes anything but the useful would lose what precisely gives value to existence.
First, we must see that utility is, by nature, a relative criterion: one thing is useful to another, with a view to an end that transcends it.
The hammer is useful to the nail, the nail to the board, the board to the house.
But this chain of means must stop somewhere, on something that is not useful to something else, but that is valuable in itself, and for which everything else is useful.
If everything were only useful, the chain would be endless and aimless; utility itself would have no meaning, lacking an end that is not, in turn, a mere means.
Therefore, the useful requires, to have meaning, something that escapes utility.
This something is those experiences and goods that are valuable for themselves: friendship, beauty, knowledge sought for its own sake, contemplation, play, joy.
None 'serves' any purpose in the strict sense; one does not cultivate a friendship for what it brings, nor does one contemplate a landscape for its yield.
These things are ends, not means, and it is in view of them, ultimately, that everything else is organized.

To consider them useless because they serve no other purpose is to overturn the hierarchy: it is to take means for ends, and to sacrifice what is valuable for what is only valuable for something else.
Yet it is this reversal that the tyranny of the useful enacts.
It demands that beauty justify itself by its economic utility, knowledge by its applications, leisure by its function of recovery in the service of work.
Everything must serve, and what does not serve must prove that it serves nonetheless, under threat of being abolished.
Thus, a society entirely devoted to the useful ends up no longer knowing what all this serves, having lost sight of the non-useful ends for which utility had meaning.
It produces and busies itself without knowing why, as activity has become its own justification.
This drift even affects our conception of human life.
To demand that each existence justify itself by its utility is to deny that a life can be valuable in itself, independently of what it produces or yields.
This is the slope that leads to measuring beings by their output, to considering as a burden those who no longer produce, and to recognizing dignity only in useful life.
However, a life is not a means; it is, if there is something that is valuable in itself, that very something.
Reducing existence to its utility is to miss what, in it, transcends all utility.
Defending the gratuitous against the tyranny of the useful is therefore not to advocate for idleness or waste.

It is to remind us that utility is not the supreme value, but a subordinate order, which only makes sense in service of ends that, themselves, serve no purpose because they are what everything serves.

A civilization may be judged less by what it produces than by what it knows how to preserve as gratuitous: the place it gives to beauty, to disinterested thought, to bonds that yield nothing, to all that, serving no purpose, still makes life worth living.
For what has no price, in the sense that it cannot be monetized, is also what has no price in the sense that nothing is worth it.

sentences: Do what you love, and you will never work a single day in your life." This saying, repeated a thousand times, summarizes a dominant expectation: work should not only provide for us, but also inspire us; we should love our jobs, thrive in them, and find self-fulfillment.
This injunction presents itself as a liberation, a progress from the time when people worked without joy, purely out of necessity.
However, it needs to be examined closely, because beneath its benevolent appearance, the demand to love one's work may well conceal a trap.
First, let's acknowledge what this aspiration has of legitimacy.
Rejecting the idea of spending one's life on a hated task, seeking something more than a paycheck from work, aspiring to an activity that has meaning and brings joy — nothing could be healthier.
The idea that work could be loved, rather than merely endured, has freed many lives from resignation, and it would be absurd to condemn it outright.
The problem lies not in the aspiration to love one's work, but in its transformation into a norm, a duty, a general injunction.
For as soon as the love of work becomes a requirement, it turns against us.
First, it induces guilt.

Those who do not love their work — and there are many, as not all jobs are lovable — are made to feel that they have failed, that they have not found their path, that their dissatisfaction is their fault.
On top of the pain of unloved work comes the shame of not loving it, as if it were a personal flaw.
Thus, the injunction to professional happiness produces additional suffering for those who cannot meet it, which is to say, for most people.
Next, and most importantly, the demand to love one's work serves a logic that is not innocent.

For those who love their work invest more in it, without counting the cost, without demanding compensation; they accept conditions they would refuse for a job that is merely a means to an end; they confuse their personal fulfillment with the interests of their employer.
The injunction to passion can thus become a formidable instrument of exploitation, which, in the name of love for the job, secures an unlimited commitment often without fair compensation.

"Do what you love" can practically mean: "Since you love it, you won't count your hours and won't demand what you're owed." The sectors that demand the most passion are often those that pay the least.
There's more.
The ideology of love for work assumes that everyone could find a job that inspires them, as if such jobs existed in sufficient numbers for all.
However, the vast majority of tasks necessary for collective life are not exciting, and someone will have to perform them.
Claiming that everyone should love their work ignores the reality of these essential and thankless tasks, and places the burden of an unattainable ideal on those who perform them.
This is a discourse of the privileged, projecting onto everyone a possibility reserved for a few.
Perhaps we should therefore free work from this very injunction.

Not to return to the resignation of the past, but to give work a more just place: an activity that can be loved, but does not have to be; that can have meaning, without requiring it to fulfill all of existence.
One can do a job properly, and without shame, even if one does not passionately love it, by finding elsewhere — in one's relationships, passions, and life outside of work — what brings fulfillment.
This more modest conception is also freer: it frees us from the guilt of not loving, and from the exploitation that hides beneath the demanded love.
Loving one's work, when it happens, is a privilege; making it a duty is a way of binding ourselves even more closely to it — at the risk of having no life outside of it to love.
