sentences: The idea of merit is at the heart of our conception of justice.
It seems obvious that everyone should receive according to what they deserve, that effort and talent should be rewarded, and that success achieved through work is legitimate.
This idea, meritocracy, enjoys such broad consensus that it seems almost indecent to challenge it.
And yet, as soon as we examine the notion of merit, it becomes troubled, evasive, revealing fragile assumptions.
Not that merit is nothing, but it is much less clear, and much less pure, than we believe.
The difficulty begins with the origin of what constitutes merit.
We are said to deserve through our effort and our talent.
But where do our capacity for effort and our talents come from?
Talent is, for the most part, a gift: one is born gifted or not for certain things, without having any say in it.
As for the ability to make efforts, perseverance, and discipline, they themselves depend on dispositions, education, and an environment for which no one is responsible.
Does someone who is fortunate enough to be born with talents and in an environment that has nurtured their capacity for effort really deserve what comes from gifts they did not earn?
Merit, at its root, is rooted in a lottery that is far from being meritorious.

This objection, if pushed, seems to entirely dissolve merit: if everything that constitutes my success — my talents, my energy, even my will — has been given to me, what remains that is truly mine, of which I can claim merit?
There is a vertigo in that.

But we must be careful not to draw the opposite conclusion, which would abolish all responsibility and all merit: for we do indeed do something with our gifts, we cultivate them or squander them, and that part, however small it may be, is not nothing.
Merit is not a total illusion; it is simply much more limited, and much less pure, than meritocracy claims.
Now this illusion has considerable political and moral consequences.

By making people believe that success is entirely deserved, meritocracy legitimizes inequalities: if the winners have what they deserve, their position is just, and the losers have only themselves to blame.
This logic has two symmetrical perverse effects.
Among the winners, it fosters pride and contempt: convinced that they owe everything to their merit, they forget what they owe to luck, and consider themselves superior to those who have failed.
Among the losers, it fosters humiliation: in a world that proclaims that everyone has what they deserve, failure is no longer a misfortune, but a fault, a verdict on one's own worth.
This meritocratic humiliation may be one of the overlooked springs of resentment that runs through our societies.
To the old inequalities, one could at least oppose that they were unjust, undeserved; meritocracy removes this consolation by presenting inequalities as the just reflection of merits.
Those who fail are then summoned to judge themselves responsible for their fate, even deprived of the dignity of protest.
It is not surprising that such a wound engenders the anger of those who are told, in essence, that their place at the bottom of the ladder is what they deserve.
Recognizing the troubled nature of merit does not lead to renouncing any idea of responsibility or reward for effort; that would be another illusion, and an inverse injustice.

It leads to more modesty among those who succeed — who should measure what they owe to luck —, to more compassion towards those who fail, and to a society that would not make the dignity of individuals dependent solely on their success.

A clear-sighted justice regarding the limits of merit would be both more humble and more humane: it would reward effort without making it an absolute, and would never forget that behind every merit, there is a part of grace received, of which no one could take glory.

sentences: People often confuse the past and history, as if history were just the past itself, faithfully reported.
This confusion leads to many misunderstandings, because the past and history are two distinct things.
The past is what was, the complete set of events, forever out of reach.
History is what we make of that past: the narrative we construct, the selection we make, the meaning we give it.
Distinguishing between the two is not a subtlety of scholars; it is understanding that history, far from being a mere reflection of the past, is always a construction of the present.
The past, in fact, is infinite and mute.
It does not tell itself; it is a chaos of countless events, the vast majority of which have not reached us and never will.
Making history means selecting, from this ocean, a few significant facts, ordering them, connecting them, and deriving a meaning.
However, this selection, this ordering, this meaning are not given in the past itself; they are the work of the historian, and behind him, of the era that supports him.
History always responds, in part, to questions posed by the present, and retains from the past what sheds light on those questions.
That is why history is constantly being rewritten, not out of whim, but out of necessity.
Each era interrogates the past based on its own concerns, discovering what previous ones had not seen, neglecting what had occupied them.
Entire sections of the past, long ignored — the history of women, the oppressed, the defeated, everyday life — have emerged as the present has become sensitive to these realities.
It is not that the past has changed; it is that the questions we ask of it have transformed.
History is a dialogue between the present and the past, and as the present changes, the dialogue is renewed.
Should we conclude that history would be arbitrary, that anyone could recount the past as they wish?
That would be a false and dangerous conclusion.
For if history is a construction, it is not a fiction: it is grounded in facts, constrained by traces, subject to methodological rules that distinguish serious history from novels or propaganda.
You cannot make the past say just anything; documents resist, facts oppose their objectivity, and a reconstruction that contradicts them is refutable.
History is a construction, but a rigorous construction, accountable to reality — which radically separates it from myth, which does not answer to any fact.
Understanding this nature of history has important consequences.
It invites vigilance towards any narrative of the past that presents itself as pure and simple truth, while it is always an interpretation, shaped by choices and values.
It also invites us to distinguish history, subject to criticism, from the political uses of the past, which instrumentalize it in service of a cause.

A nation, a power, a group can mobilize the past to legitimize themselves, but this mobilization is not history; it is militant memory, often necessary, but should not be confused with the critical work of the historian.

Distinguishing between the past and history, therefore, is both recognizing that our relationship to the past is always constructed, situated, revisable, and refusing to conclude that it would be arbitrary.
It is to hold together two truths: that history answers questions from the present, and that it remains accountable to the facts of the past.

This double awareness is characteristic of a mature relationship to history — one that does not take a narrative for definitive truth, but also does not fall into the idea that everything is equally valid.
The past will not return; but what we make of it, the history we write from it, engages who we are and who we want to be.

sentences: Statues, these objects we once thought were inert, have become the stage for intense confrontations.
Should we topple the monuments erected in honor of figures whose past offends us — slave traders, colonizers, men from another era honored for reasons we reject today?
Or should we preserve them, in the name of history, heritage, and the refusal to erase the past?
This question, which stirs so many societies, is not as simple as the opposing camps would like it to be, and it deserves more than slogans.
Those who demand the removal of statues put forward serious arguments.
A statue is not a neutral document; it is a tribute, an honor bestowed in public space.
Erecting a statue means proposing a model, saying to everyone: here is someone worthy of admiration.
But how can we justify continuing to honor, in public squares, figures who committed or supported what we consider crimes?
For the descendants of those who were enslaved or colonized, these statues are not abstract history; they are a daily wound, the persistent celebration of their oppressors.
Maintaining them is perpetuating an honor that has become insulting.
Those who oppose the toppling also have their arguments.
Erasing the traces of a past that disturbs us, they say, is condemning ourselves to forget, and forgetting has never solved anything.
Judging the men of the past by our present values is anachronistic: they were of their time, and almost all our ancestors, by that measure, would be condemnable.
Where would we stop if we undertook to purge public space of everything that offends today's sensibilities?
Is there not, in this desire to erase, something of a rewriting of the past, a refusal to look at it as it was, with its glories and its intertwined crimes?
Both positions have their share of truth, and that is why the question is difficult.
But perhaps the opposition between preserving and destroying is poorly framed, as if these two terms exhausted the possibilities.
For there are intermediate paths, more fruitful than simple maintenance or erasure.
One can move a statue from a place of honor to a museum, where it will no longer be celebrated but explained, placed back in its context, offered for reflection rather than admiration.
One can maintain it while contextualizing it, adding elements that remind us of the dark side of the figure, transforming the monument into an opportunity to learn.
One can make it an object of critical memory, rather than a tribute or an empty space.
What matters, ultimately, is to distinguish what the statue does in public space.
As long as it reigns in glory, it honors; it is this honor that poses a problem, not the existence of the object.
The question is therefore not so much 'should we destroy or preserve?' as 'should we continue to honor?' — and to that, the answer can be no without needing to erase.
Removing a tribute is not erasing a history; it is ceasing to celebrate what should no longer be celebrated, while keeping the means to understand it.
The debate about statues, beyond the objects it concerns, touches on our relationship with the past.

It reveals that this relationship is never fixed, that it is re-discussed with each generation, and that public space, where the past is made visible, is also a place where the present asserts its values.

Neither the conservatism that would like to keep everything intact, nor the iconoclasm that would like to erase everything does justice to the complexity of the task: to assume a past in its truth, without continuing to honor what no longer deserves it.
A mature society is neither one that blindly venerates its monuments, nor one that tears them down in a frenzy, but one that knows, in front of them, how to both remember and judge.

sentences: The expression 'duty of memory' has become established to designate the obligation to remember the great tragedies of the past, particularly mass crimes, in order to honor them and prevent their recurrence.

This obligation is just and necessary: to forget the victims, to erase the crimes, would be a second injustice, and a society that knows nothing of its own abysses would be more exposed to falling back into them.
And yet, the duty of memory, elevated to an indisputable imperative, has limits and paradoxes that require the courage to examine, not to reject it, but to clarify its meaning.
The first difficulty lies in the relationship between memory and history.

Memory is not history: it is laden with emotion, directed towards the victims, guided by the duty of fidelity; history aims for understanding, context, and explanation, with the distance that this entails.
However, if the duty of memory dominates without sharing, it can come into tension with the work of the historian.
Understanding how a crime was possible, analyzing its mechanisms coldly, may seem disrespectful to the victims, even slipping into excuse.
But to renounce understanding in the name of memory is to deprive oneself precisely of what could prevent the return of the worst: for we can only prevent what we have understood.
The second difficulty lies in the selection of memory.
We cannot commemorate everything with the same intensity; memory, like history, chooses.
However, this choice is not neutral: some victims are abundantly remembered, others forgotten; some crimes occupy public space, while others remain in the shadows.

This inequality of memory can lead to painful competitions, with each group demanding equivalent recognition for its own suffering, risking an escalation where the memory of some seems to be at the expense of others.
The duty of memory, intended to unite in reflection, can thus become a ground for conflict.
The third difficulty, deeper, concerns the very effectiveness of memory.
It is assumed that remembering protects against repetition.
But history partly disproves this reassuring assumption: atrocities have recurred despite the vivid memory of previous ones, and commemoration has not always prevented new crimes.
Memory alone does not vaccinate.
Worse, a poorly directed memory can foster new resentments, sustain hatreds, and serve to justify present violence in the name of past suffering.
Remembering is not always on the side of peace; it all depends on what we do with that memory.
Should we then relativize the duty of memory?
No, but we should think of it differently.

It is not about remembering less, but about remembering better: linking memory to understanding, rather than opposing them; aiming, through the memory of the victims, for an understanding of the mechanisms that made the crime possible; making memory not a fixed cult, turned towards the past, but an active vigilance, directed towards the present.

A memory that serves only to commemorate, without enlightening or preventing, would fail its purpose; a memory that makes us attentive to the warning signs, in the present, of what it recalls from the past, would truly fulfill its role.
The duty of memory, when well understood, is therefore not the duty to reiterate, but the duty to understand in order to remain vigilant.
It does not oppose history; it calls for it.

Honoring the victims, yes, but also understanding the perpetrators, not to excuse them, but to recognize, in ordinary humanity, the possibility of the worst — for it is this recognition, more than commemorative emotion, that can arm us.
Memory without understanding is a sterile piety; understanding without memory is a culpable coldness.
It is from their union that what the duty of memory truly aims for can arise: not only to not forget, but to not repeat.

sentences: We readily imagine that words are just simple labels, neutral instruments that designate things without coloring them.
This reassuring notion is false, and its falsehood has considerable political consequences.
For naming is never an innocent act: the word we choose to designate a reality already proposes an interpretation, shapes the way we perceive it, and biases judgment even before the argument begins.
In any debate, the one who imposes their vocabulary has already, in part, won.
Let's consider the same reality described by different words.

Depending on whether we talk about 'charges' or 'contributions', 'asylum seekers' or 'illegals', 'termination of pregnancy' or 'removal of an unborn child', it’s not just the tone that changes: it’s the reality itself that appears in a different light, prompting a different reaction.
Each word carries connotations, activates associations, and suggests an evaluation.
The choice of term is not merely a dressing of thought; it is the first act that sets the stage on which everything else will play out.
This power of vocabulary explains the intensity of struggles that seem, on the surface, to be about simple words.
When one side imposes its terminology, it simultaneously imposes its way of seeing, and forces the opponent to debate in a language that is unfavorable to them.
Accepting the other’s words is already entering into their framework, reasoning according to their assumptions, and fighting on a ground they have chosen.
That’s why the most important debates often begin with a battle over the words themselves: how to name the thing we are going to discuss.
This preliminary battle, seemingly secondary, is often decisive.
There is something even more subtle.
Certain words have the power to make some realities thinkable or unthinkable.
As long as a phenomenon has no name, it remains difficult to grasp, denounce, or combat; giving it a word is to make it exist in the debate, to give it substance, and to allow it to be taken up.
Many struggles have begun with the forging of a word that finally named what everyone felt but could not express.
Conversely, the absence of a word, or the euphemism that obscures, can keep in the shadows what we prefer not to see.
Language does not merely describe the world; it decides, to some extent, what will be visible and sayable in that world.
From this power arises a common manipulation: euphemism, which softens what it names to make it acceptable.
We talk about 'collateral damage' to avoid saying deaths, 'social plan' to avoid saying layoffs, and 'strikes' to avoid saying bombings.
These words are not entirely untrue, but they anesthetize, distance us, and prevent us from feeling what the bare fact would provoke.
Euphemism is a weapon precisely because language is not neutral: it exploits the power of words to color reality, making it bearable or invisible.
Becoming aware that words are never neutral does not mean falling into a generalized suspicion where all language is manipulation.
It is to acquire vigilance: to ask ourselves, in front of the words proposed to us, what they suggest, what they hide, what framework they establish, and what interpretation they incline towards.
It is also to refuse to let others hold the monopoly on naming, to claim the right to choose one’s own words rather than submit to those imposed on us.
For to a large extent, he who controls the words controls thought — and reclaiming language is the first of freedoms.

sentences: There is a way of speaking that has turned the absence of content into an art: jargon.

It is recognized by its ability to produce a lot of words without saying anything, stringing together hollow phrases, chaining obvious statements and generalities that commit to nothing and cannot be contradicted because they mean almost nothing.
This language, long associated with authoritarian regimes and their propaganda, has spread far beyond that, permeating ordinary political, managerial, and institutional discourse.
It deserves to be examined, as its success reveals a precise and formidable function.
Jargon is primarily characterized by vagueness.
It prefers vague words to precise terms, abstractions to concrete realities, and ready-made phrases to verifiable statements.

People talk about 'dynamics,' 'synergies,' 'implementation of measures,' and 'supporting transitions' — expressions that give the impression of saying something while avoiding any claims that could be discussed or denied.
This vagueness is not a clumsiness; it serves a purpose.
It allows one to speak without committing, to occupy space without taking risks, to seem to respond without actually responding.
For this is the first utility of jargon: to avoid compromising oneself.
Saying something precise exposes one — to contradiction, reproach, and verification.
Jargon, by remaining vague, escapes these risks.
You cannot catch out someone who has said nothing verifiable; you cannot reproach someone for a failure when they have made no precise promises.
This language is an armor: it protects the user from any accountability, at the cost of a void that it masks with an abundance of words.
Its second utility is to anesthetize.
Jargon dulls vigilance; through expected phrases and conventional turns of speech, it creates a sort of humming that discourages attention.
People stop truly listening, let these words slide by without grabbing anything, and give up searching for a meaning that they do not have.
In doing so, it disarms critical thinking: one does not contest a discourse that one no longer listens to, one does not get indignant about what one has not grasped.
Jargon conveys, under the guise of harmless verbiage, the absence of any real content — and sometimes, the evasion of what one does not want to say.
One must be careful here to avoid confusion.
Not all caution in language is jargon; there are delicate subjects where nuance and restraint are legitimate, where one must weigh their words.
Jargon is distinguished from this honest caution by its intention: it does not weigh its words to say something accurate, but empties them to say nothing.
Caution seeks accuracy; jargon seeks to evade.
One refines thought, the other dissolves it.
Knowing how to distinguish them is necessary to avoid confusing rigor with emptiness.
Resisting jargon requires a demand: to ask, behind the words, what is actually being said.
What does this phrase concretely mean?
What does it assert that could be true or false?
What does it commit to?
These questions, directed at any discourse, reveal the void where it exists and sometimes force those who speak to emerge from their verbal armor.

In a democracy, this demand is a civic duty, for jargon is not just a laziness of language: it is a way of governing without accountability, of speaking to avoid being understood, of drowning under words what should be clearly stated and openly debated.

sentences: The past is never neutral in the present; it is a stake, and often a weapon.
Those in power, nations, and movements know this, as they continually mobilize it for their own benefit: to legitimize themselves, to unite a community, to identify enemies, to justify a policy.

This political use of the past, as old as power itself, deserves to be analyzed, because it often operates without our awareness, and readily confuses its ends with those of historical knowledge, which it claims while betraying.
The most common use of the past is legitimization.
A power, a regime, a nation seeks in history the titles of its existence: a glorious origin, continuity, a mission.

One establishes a narrative of origins that grounds the present, celebrates ancestors, commemorates great deeds, and places the current order within a history that seems to make it necessary and just.
This narrative is not necessarily false, but it is always selective: it retains what legitimizes and silences what disturbs, transforming a complex and often violent history into a flattering tale.
The past serves less to understand than to justify.
Another complementary use is the construction of collective identity.
For a group of individuals to feel like a community, there must be a common past, whether real or reconstructed: shared trials, glories, sufferings, heroes.
This common past creates a sense of belonging, the 'we' without which there is no community.
However, in doing so, it also creates a closure: the 'we' is defined against an 'others', and the narrative that unites some can exclude or stigmatize others.
The past mobilized to unite can thus become an instrument of division, designating hereditary enemies, rekindling grudges, justifying hatreds in the name of old wounds.
The most perverse use, finally, is the instrumentalization in service of a present cause.
The past is summoned not to enlighten, but to settle a current debate: such a historical analogy disqualifies an opponent, such a memory justifies a claim, such a precedent legitimizes an action.
The past becomes an arsenal from which everyone draws the weapons for their current battles, even if it means distorting it, simplifying it, or using it anachronistically.
Serious history, which places facts in their context and resists simplifications, then hinders this militant use, which prefers a mythified past, reduced to a few striking and manipulable images.
These uses pose a formidable problem, as they claim to be based on history while betraying it.
They invoke the past, facts, memory, but bend them to ends that are not those of knowledge.
The power that instrumentalizes history does not say that it distorts it; it claims, on the contrary, to restore the truth that others would have obscured.

Distinguishing history from its instrumentalization then becomes difficult, especially since the boundary is not always clear, and the historian themselves is not exempt from the concerns of their time.
But this difficulty should not lead to surrender: between critical work, subject to facts and method, and militant use, subject to a cause, the difference remains, and it is decisive.
In the face of the political uses of the past, the best protection is historical knowledge itself, with its demands for rigor, context, and complexity.

An informed people about its real history, in its greatness and shadows, is better able to resist the myths that others would sell them; an ignorant people, or one that knows only a flattering narrative, is at the mercy of those who manipulate the past.
That is why teaching a critical history, which teaches how to distinguish facts from their use, is not a luxury, but a democratic necessity.
For he who controls the narrative of the past shapes the present — and nothing is more dangerous than a people who knows only what they have been led to believe about their history.

sentences: We have seen that words are not neutral; they shape thought and serve power.
We still need to explore one of their deepest powers: the power to bring into existence.
For naming is not just about describing what is already there; it is sometimes about bringing into existence what, without the word, would lack substance.
This creative power of language, both liberating and perilous, deserves reflection on its ambiguities.
Let's start with its liberating aspect.
Many human realities only truly exist in the public sphere once they are named.
A nameless suffering remains diffuse, incommunicable, isolated; the one who experiences it believes they are alone, unable to share it, denounce it, or fight against it.
Giving it a name makes it exist as a recognized reality, allowing those who endure it to recognize themselves, come together, and name it to others.
Entire struggles have begun with the forging of a word that finally named a reality that everyone felt but could not articulate.
The word has given form to the formless, visibility to the invisible, and public existence to what only existed in the silence of isolated consciences.
This power of naming is thus a weapon for the oppressed as much as for the powerful.

Those who suffer an unnamed injustice are disarmed; giving them the word that names it provides them with a tool for struggle, the ability to identify what they endure, bring it into debate, and demand a remedy.
In this sense, the conquest of language, the right to name one's own experience rather than letting others name it, is an essential dimension of any emancipation.
Reclaiming words, forging those that are missing, and rejecting those imposed on us is to regain a part of power over one's own condition.
But this creative power has a downside that would be unwise to ignore.
For naming can also bring into existence divisions, categories, and oppositions that, without the word, would not have the same reality.
Designating a group, giving it a name, constitutes it as a group, sometimes pitting it against another, creating boundaries where there were only fluid differences.
The language that liberates by naming sufferings can also confine by naming identities, freezing what was fluid into categories, opposing what coexisted.
The same power that gives form to just causes can also give substance to the worst divisions.
There is something more troubling.
Naming can create the named thing through a feedback effect.
Labeling people with a certain term, confining them to a category, can end up making them become what they are said to be, as the words we use to designate beings influence what they become.

The label we attach is not always a simple observation; it can be a prophecy that contributes to its realization, shaping perceptions, expectations, behaviors, and ultimately producing the reality it claimed to describe.
The power of naming is also, in this sense, a power to shape beings.
This dual power — liberating and divisive — demands responsibility in the use of words.
Naming is never trivial: it is to bring into existence, for better or for worse.
The same act that can give voice to the voiceless can also pit groups against each other; the same word that liberates can confine.
There is no simple rule to distinguish good usage from bad, except the awareness of what one does when naming and the concern for its effects.
For words, which seem so light, are among the most powerful forces shaping the human world — and wielding the power to bring into existence requires measuring what we call into existence.

sentences: Freedom of expression is a fundamental principle of free societies and one of the most precious rights they have achieved.
However, as soon as we try to clarify its scope, difficulties arise.
Should we be able to say anything?
Are there words that a society has the right or the duty to prohibit?

This question deeply divides opinions, and simple answers, whether they come from advocates of unrestricted freedom or from those who impose numerous prohibitions, fail to grasp the complexity of the issue.
Let's start with what underpins freedom of expression, as it is often invoked without recalling the reasons behind it.

It is based on several justifications: the pursuit of truth, which assumes that ideas can be freely confronted; the autonomy of the individual, who has the right to form and express their opinions; and democratic functioning, which requires open debate.
These justifications are powerful, and they explain why freedom of expression deserves special protection, stronger than that of other freedoms.
It should not be restricted lightly, as each restriction touches upon these fundamental goods.
But these very justifications indicate limits.

If freedom of expression is valuable because it serves truth, autonomy, and democracy, then words that do not serve any of these goods and that harm them do not benefit from the same level of protection.

An explicit call to murder, defamation that destroys a reputation through lies, and incitement to violence against a group contribute nothing to the pursuit of truth or to democratic debate; they cause real harm without the benefits that justify freedom of expression.

Recognizing certain limits is therefore not a betrayal of the principle, but an understanding of it: freedom of expression protects the exchange of ideas, not every use of speech regardless of its effects.
However, this recognition of limits immediately opens up a peril, as it is terribly difficult to draw the line and tempting to extend it indefinitely.
Once it is accepted that certain harmful words can be prohibited, where do we draw the line?
The harmful is an elastic notion, which everyone willingly extends to what offends or disturbs them.
Under the pretext of protection, one might end up prohibiting any uncomfortable speech, any unpleasant criticism, any unorthodox idea, in the name of the harm they might cause.

The slope is real: from legitimate restriction to abusive restriction, one can empty freedom of expression of its substance, leaving only the freedom to say what does not disturb anyone — which means no freedom at all.
That is why wisdom in this matter consists of firmly holding two conflicting demands.
On one hand, recognizing that freedom of expression is not absolute, that it has justified limits when speech causes serious harm without serving the goods that underpin it.

On the other hand, being extremely wary of extending these limits, setting the bar very high, restricting only reluctantly and for compelling reasons, always keeping in mind that the remedy can be worse than the disease.

Freedom of expression must be defended even in its discomfort: it only makes sense if it also protects speech that displeases, shocks, or disturbs, because consensual speech has never needed protection.
There is therefore no simple answer to the question of whether we can say anything.

Neither the 'everything is allowed' that would deny the real harm that speech can cause, nor the 'we can no longer say anything' that would multiply prohibitions to the point of stifling debate, do justice to the complexity of the issue.
Freedom of expression is a difficult balance, always needing to be readjusted, between the protection of a fundamental good and the recognition of its limits.

This balance is not determined by a formula, but by a constantly renewed judgment, exercised with the constant concern of not sacrificing, under the pretext of protection, what makes a free society valuable: the possibility of also saying what disturbs.

sentences: There is a persistent misunderstanding about doubt and uncertainty in science, which fuels a significant amount of contemporary distrust towards it.
Many confuse uncertainty with ignorance and conclude that if scientists are "not sure," it means they don't know, and that their word is therefore no better than anyone else's.
This reasoning is based on a profound misconception.
For acknowledging uncertainty is not admitting ignorance; on the contrary, it is a sophisticated form of knowledge, one that understands the limits of what it asserts.
First, we must distinguish two meanings of the word "uncertainty."
There is the uncertainty of someone who knows nothing, who has no idea, who is completely in the dark: that is ignorance.

And there is the uncertainty of someone who knows a lot but precisely understands the extent of what they do not know, who can say not only what they consider established, but also with what degree of confidence, and where the gray areas begin.
This second uncertainty is not the opposite of knowledge; it is an advanced component of it.
The scholar who says, "we know this with great confidence, that with less, and we still do not know this" knows infinitely more than someone who asserts everything with equal assurance.
This measured uncertainty is even characteristic of a rigorous scientific approach.
Science does not operate on absolute certainties, but on degrees of confidence, constantly adjusted as evidence accumulates.
A scientific assertion is always accompanied, implicitly or explicitly, by an evaluation of its solidity: is it solidly established, probable, hypothetical?
This gradation is not a weakness; it is honesty and precision.
Where ideology or belief assert everything with the same confidence, science distinguishes what it knows from what it assumes, and this distinction is a superiority, not a flaw.
That is why it is misleading, and often dishonest, to exploit scientific uncertainty to disqualify what science establishes.

"Scientists do not agree," "it's just a theory," "nothing is certain": these phrases play on the confusion between the uncertainty that accompanies all rigorous knowledge and the absence of knowledge.
The fact that a theory has areas of uncertainty does not mean it is based on nothing; that a disagreement exists on fine points does not mean that the essentials are in debate.
Using the existence of a margin of uncertainty to reject a solidly established knowledge is to cynically exploit the very integrity of science against itself.

This strategy has been deliberately employed, history shows, by those who had an interest in delaying action: fostering doubt, exaggerating uncertainty, presenting a solid consensus as an open controversy, in order to paralyze under the pretext that we "might not be sure."

This manufacturing of doubt precisely exploits our misunderstanding of scientific uncertainty: by presenting it as ignorance, it turns the virtue of science — its honesty about its limits — into an argument against it.
There is no more effective defense of inaction than to demand an absolute certainty that no science can ever provide.
Understanding that doubt is not ignorance is therefore a way to guard against this manipulation.

It is to recognize that knowledge which knows its limits is better than blind certainty, that measured uncertainty is a form of rigor, and that demanding total certainty before acting is often a disguised way of refusing to act.
Science does not offer us absolute certainties, because it is honest; but it offers us the best available knowledge, along with an indication of its reliability.

Turning away from it on the grounds that it is not absolutely certain is to prefer the illusion of certainty over the reality of knowledge — and to condemn oneself, in the name of a misunderstood doubt, to being unable to believe or decide anything.

sentences: Among the most common reasoning errors, and the most consequential, is the confusion between correlation and causation.

Observing that two phenomena vary together — whether they increase or decrease in tandem — and concluding that one causes the other: this tempting shortcut is the source of countless false beliefs, erroneous decisions, and successful manipulations.
Understanding why correlation is not causation is one of the most valuable insights of rigorous thinking, and one of the most useful in everyday life.
The principle is simple to state.
That two things are correlated — that they occur together, vary in the same direction — does not establish that one is the cause of the other.
Three other explanations are always possible.
The causal relationship may be reversed: it is not A that causes B, but B that causes A.
A third factor may cause both at once, without them being directly related.
Or the correlation may be pure chance, a coincidence without significance.
In the face of any correlation, these possibilities must be ruled out before one can conclude causation, and this work is often difficult.
Examples abound, sometimes amusing, sometimes serious.

One might observe that in cities, the number of crimes increases with the number of police officers, and absurdly conclude that the police cause crime, when it is obviously crime that calls for more police: the causation is reversed.
One can observe that children with a rich vocabulary have larger feet, and imagine a link, while a third factor — age — explains both.
These examples seem obvious once stated, but the same error, in less clear cases, constantly deceives.
For in most real situations, the trap is much more subtle.

When we are presented with the idea that a certain behavior is correlated with a certain outcome — that those who do this live longer, that a certain product is associated with a certain disease — the temptation is strong to immediately conclude a cause, while the correlation could be explained by a thousand hidden factors.
Those who adopt such beneficial behavior may differ, in many other aspects, from those who do not adopt it, and it is these other differences that explain the outcome.
Untangling true causation from mere correlation requires rigorous methods, and a caution that spontaneous reasoning ignores.
This confusion is all the more dangerous because it is exploited.
Those who want to sell us a product, convince us of an idea, or make us adopt a behavior, readily wave correlations while presenting them as causalities.
"People who use this product are healthier": this statement suggests a causal link that the correlation does not prove, and that other factors could entirely explain.

Knowing how to resist these suggestions, systematically asking whether a presented correlation really establishes a cause, is an essential protection against manipulation by numbers and misinterpreted studies.
Remembering that correlation is not causation does not mean falling into a skepticism that would deny any causal link, as if one could never conclude anything.

It is to acquire a requirement: before concluding that one thing causes another, to rule out alternative explanations, to ask whether the link is real or apparent, to demand more than mere concomitance.
This requirement, which science has established as a method, is one of the most powerful tools of critical thinking.

In a world saturated with studies, statistics, and numbers brandished to convince us, knowing how to distinguish what varies together from what truly causes is now an indispensable skill — and one of the surest protections against credulity.

sentences: When faced with a possible but uncertain risk — a product that could be harmful, a technology with poorly understood effects, a threat whose magnitude is not established — should we wait for scientific certainty before acting, or take measures as soon as the danger seems plausible, even without proof?
This question, known as the "precautionary principle," is one of the most delicate of our time, as it engages our relationship with uncertainty, risk, and action.
And the definitive answers, whether one way or the other, also prove to be insufficient.
The precautionary principle, in its common formulation, encourages action in the face of a serious risk even in the absence of scientific certainty about its reality.
Its intuition is powerful: waiting for certain proof of a danger can mean waiting until it’s too late, until the harm is done and irreversible.
Some damages — ecological, health-related — are such that we cannot afford to suffer them just to confirm that they were possible.
In these cases, demanding certainty before acting amounts to betting on the absence of danger, a gamble whose consequences, in the event of an error, would be catastrophic and irreversible.
This caution has its legitimacy, and history supports it in many cases where action was delayed too long, waiting for definitive proof while the harm took hold.

In the face of serious and potentially irreversible risks, the demand for absolute certainty can be a form of irrationality disguised as rigor: it favors inaction, which is not neutral, as it allows the risk to materialize.
Acting in doubt, when the stakes are high, can be wiser than waiting for certainty that will come too late.
But the precautionary principle, taken to the extreme, turns into its opposite and becomes unreasonable.
For every action, every innovation, every product carries possible risks that can never be entirely excluded.

If we were to demand proof of the total absence of danger before allowing anything, we would do nothing: no technology, no medication, no progress would ever come to light, as none can guarantee the absolute absence of risk.

An absolute precautionary principle would paralyze all action, and this paralysis has its own cost: the benefits we forgo, the lives we do not save, the progress we prevent, are also damages, albeit invisible.
There is more.
The inaction promoted by excessive precaution is not without risk; it has its own dangers, often overlooked.
Rejecting a technology out of precaution also means depriving ourselves of its benefits and facing the risks it would have avoided.
The precaution that focuses on the risks of action, while forgetting the risks of inaction, is not true prudence: it is a bias that treats as neutral what is not.
Doing nothing is also a decision, which also entails responsibility.

Wisdom in this matter, therefore, lies neither in refusing to act without certainty nor in demanding certainty before acting, but in a nuanced evaluation: weighing the severity and probability of the risk, its reversibility or not, the costs of action as well as those of inaction, the expected benefits as well as the possible dangers.

In the face of a serious, irreversible, and plausible risk, precaution is necessary; in the face of a minor, uncertain, and reversible risk, demanding action in doubt would paralyze us without reason.
The precautionary principle is a good guide only when tempered by proportion: applied mechanically, in either direction, it leads either to recklessness or paralysis.
Deciding in uncertainty is a difficult art that cannot be reduced to any formula — and claiming that a simple rule could exempt us from it is the illusion that must first be set aside.

sentences: Our time is egalitarian, and in many ways, that's a progress.
It rejects imposed hierarchies, considers everyone equal to one another, and values everyone's right to express their opinion.
However, this egalitarian spirit, admirable in terms of rights and dignity, sometimes extends to areas where it doesn't belong: the realm of facts and knowledge.
Thus, we slide from the correct idea that all citizens are equal in dignity to the false idea that all opinions are equally valid, even on factual matters where expertise exists.
This shift, which flatters our democratic sensibility, deserves to be questioned, as it has serious consequences.
First, we must affirm an obvious truth that our time tends to obscure: on factual matters, not all opinions are equal.
The opinion of someone who has studied a subject for years, who masters the data, methods, and debates, is not worth the same as that of someone who has never thought about it.
This does not make one person superior to the other; it simply means that, on this specific subject, one knows and the other does not.
Denying this difference in the name of equality confuses the equality of persons with a supposed equality of knowledge, which does not exist.
That everyone has the right to express their opinion does not mean that all opinions are equally well-founded.
This confusion is exacerbated by a phenomenon unique to our time: universal access to information gives everyone the illusion of competence.
Having consulted a few sources and read a few articles, anyone can believe they are capable of judging issues that actually require years of study.

This illusion is all the more persistent because those who know little do not grasp the extent of what they ignore: one must already have some knowledge to perceive the complexity of a field, and the ignorant, precisely because they are ignorant, overestimate their own competence.
Thus, a distrust of experts spreads, in the name of a "I form my own opinion" that confuses the autonomy of judgment with the presumption of ignorance.
Should we then conclude that we must blindly rely on experts, and that ordinary citizens should just remain silent?
That would be falling into the opposite excess, which is equally dangerous.
For recognizing the authority of knowledge does not mean abdicating all judgment.
Experts can be wrong, be influenced by interests, or step outside their area of expertise; their words deserve respect, not submission.

Moreover, while science establishes facts, it does not decide what to do with them: choices that involve values — what to do with what science establishes — fall within the realm of democratic debate, where everyone's opinion legitimately counts.
Expertise has authority over facts, not over ends.
It is this distinction that allows us to escape the false dilemma between contempt for experts and blind submission.
On factual matters, competence has legitimate authority, and denying it in the name of equality is unreasonable.
On issues of values and collective choices, however, no expert should decide in place of citizens, and the equality of voices reasserts its rights.

Confusing these two realms — wanting experts to decide on ends, or citizens to determine facts solely by their opinion — leads to two dead ends: technocracy that disempowers citizens, or populism that scorns knowledge.
Defending the idea that, on facts, not all opinions are equal does not betray the democratic spirit; it preserves it from its own drift.

A democracy does not need citizens who all believe they are experts, but rather citizens capable of recognizing what they know and what they do not know, of trusting knowledge where it is well-founded, while maintaining their full authority over choices that pertain to values.

The equality of persons does not require the equality of knowledge; it instead demands that we distinguish, so that democratic debate is based on the best-established facts, and not on the confusion of all opinions.
Respecting knowledge does not mean renouncing one's freedom as a citizen; it means using it wisely.

sentences: There is a boundary that rigorous thinking must constantly remind us of, as it is frequently crossed: the one that separates what is from what ought to be, facts from values, science from morality.
Science, powerful as it may be, establishes what is the case; it is inherently incapable of saying, on its own, what ought to be done.
From the observation that something is, one can never deduce, through logic alone, that it ought or ought not to be.
This boundary, often overlooked, is nonetheless crucial, and its confusion is the source of serious misguidance.
Let us clearly understand what this limit means.
Science can tell us what the effects of an action are, what means allow us to achieve an end, what will happen if we do this or that.
But it cannot tell us what end we should pursue, what is worth seeking, what is right or good.
It can establish that a policy will have a certain result; it cannot establish that this result is desirable.
It can describe what human nature is; it cannot deduce how we should live from that.
Between the observation of what is and the judgment of what ought to be, there is a leap that no observation, no measurement, can bridge.
This limit is not a weakness of science, but a characteristic of the nature of questions.
Value questions are not poorly resolved factual questions that an increase in science would eventually settle; they belong to a different order.
No experiment will tell us whether freedom is better than security, whether equality should take precedence over merit, or whether a human life has infinite value.
These questions engage what we hold to be important, what we choose to value, and pertain to moral and political deliberation, not to scientific demonstration.
Science informs these choices; it does not replace them.
Overlooking this boundary leads to two symmetrical and equally dangerous errors.
The first consists of making science say what it cannot say, asking it to resolve value questions, and presenting political or moral choices as scientific conclusions.
"Science shows that we must do this": this very common phrase almost always masks a leap from fact to value, presenting a subjective choice as an objective necessity.
This confusion is all the more insidious as it dresses preferences as truths and removes from debate, under the guise of science, what should be discussed.
The second, inverse error consists of disqualifying science on the grounds that it does not say everything, rejecting what it establishes because it does not resolve value questions.

"Science cannot tell us how to live, so its authority is not superior": this reasoning confuses the two levels in the opposite direction and is often used to dismiss inconvenient facts in the name of what science does not claim to do.
That science does not say what ought to be does not weaken what it establishes about what is; it is even by respecting its limit that we best recognize its authority in its own domain.
Firmly maintaining the boundary between fact and value is therefore to do justice to both science and morality, assigning each its domain.
To science, the rigorous establishment of what is, with the authority that comes with it; to human deliberation, the judgment on what ought to be, which no knowledge can exempt us from assuming.

This distribution does not diminish science; it preserves it from uses that would distort it and protects human freedom from the temptation to offload its choices onto a supposed scientific necessity.
For deciding what we ought to do, what we want to strive for, will always remain our task and our responsibility — a task that science can illuminate, but will never take away from us.

sentences: We live in societies that proclaim equal freedom of speech for all citizens.
Everyone, in principle, has the right to express themselves, give their opinion, and participate in the debate.
However, this principle of equality masks a more complex reality: public speech, the kind that carries weight, is not equally accessible to everyone.
It has its conditions, its guardians, and its implicit hierarchies.
Questioning who really has the right to speak — not in law, but in fact — reveals one of the deepest and least visible inequalities in our societies.
The first inequality relates to access to the means of speech.
Being able to express oneself publicly requires access to platforms, media, networks, and channels that give speech its reach.
However, these means are distributed unevenly.
Some have easy access to the public sphere due to their position, profession, or network; others, no matter what they have to say, struggle to be heard beyond their immediate circle.

Formal freedom of speech, equal for all, is thus accompanied by a real inequality in the means to make it heard, which means that the same speech does not have the same resonance depending on who utters it.
The second inequality, more subtle, relates to the legitimacy granted to the speaker.
We do not give the same attention or credit to all speeches; we rank them according to who makes them.

The words of an expert, a graduate, or a notable are listened to; those of the presumed ignorant, the subordinate, or someone who lacks the proper codes are easily disqualified, regardless of their correctness.

This hierarchy of legitimacy has its rationale — it makes sense to give more credit to those who know — but it often exceeds what would justify it, excluding voices from the debate on the grounds that they do not speak the right language, do not have the right credentials, or do not master the codes of legitimate speech.
These codes, precisely, constitute a third barrier.
Public speech follows implicit rules — a certain vocabulary, a certain tone, a certain way of arguing — mastery of which is acquired through education and environment.
Those who do not possess them are disqualified not for what they say, but for the way they say it, which is deemed clumsy, inappropriate, or illegitimate.

Thus, the very form of legitimate speech creates a social sorting, effectively reserving access to the debate for those who have acquired the codes, while excluding others under the guise of a formal requirement that masks a social exclusion.

Recognizing these inequalities does not lead to denying any hierarchy of speech, as if all were equal, as if the ignorant and the knowledgeable should be equally listened to regarding what they do not know.
There is a legitimate basis for expertise, and claiming to abolish it would lead to a populism that listens to no one because it rejects any authority of knowledge.

The problem is not that hierarchies of speech exist, but that they are unjust: that they exclude what deserves to be heard in the name of form, that they confuse the legitimacy of knowledge with the privileges of a social group, and that they silence voices for bad reasons.

The question 'who has the right to speak?' does not call for the simplistic answer 'everyone equally,' which ignores legitimate differences in competence, nor the elitist answer 'only the qualified,' which masks unjust exclusions under the guise of standards.

It calls for work: to make access to speech fairer, to listen to voices that are too quickly disqualified, to distinguish the real legitimacy of knowledge from purely social barriers, and to open the debate to those who are excluded without valid reason.
A democracy is not only measured by the freedom of speech it proclaims, but by the real equality of speech it allows — and in this regard, there is still much to be done.

sentences: In front of certain works of modern and contemporary art, a reaction often arises, so frequent that it has become almost a cliché: "it's not beautiful," "it's not art," "my child could do that."
Behind these protests lies a deep and widely shared conviction: art is meant to produce beauty, and art that breaks away from beauty betrays its vocation.
This conviction, as natural as it may seem, deserves to be questioned, because the history of modern art is precisely one of a conscious break with beauty as an end, and this break had its reasons.
First, let's recall that identifying art with beauty is neither obvious nor eternal.

For centuries, Western art did indeed aim for beauty, according to established canons; but it also aimed, and sometimes primarily aimed, at other purposes: celebrating the sacred, representing power, telling stories, edifying, commemorating.
Beauty was often a means serving these purposes, not the ultimate end.

The idea that art has only the vocation to produce beauty is itself historically situated, and questioning it does not necessarily betray art, but may reconnect with a broader conception of what art can be.
Why did modern art break with beauty?
For reasons that are not merely provocative.

First, because academic beauty, through being codified, had become an empty convention, a soulless virtuosity; breaking away from it was a way to rediscover a truth that the conventional beautiful form had ultimately stifled.

Then, because the modern world, with its horrors and upheavals, could no longer be expressed in the language of beauty alone; representing war, anxiety, the absurd required breaking harmony, for a beautiful image of horror would have been a lie.
Art that renounces beauty often seeks to express what beauty cannot say.
For art can aim for something other than aesthetic pleasure.
It can seek to provoke thought, to disturb, to reveal, to make us experience what we would prefer to ignore.
A work can be powerful without being beautiful, important without being pleasant; it can seize us with its truth, its strength, its strangeness, rather than its charm.
Reducing art to the production of beauty amputates it of these other powers, demanding that it please where it could disturb.
Art that does not seek to please is not necessarily failed art; it is sometimes art that aims higher, or elsewhere, than pleasure.
Should we then give credit to all contemporary art, and consider anyone who resists it as reactionary?
That would be to fall into the opposite excess.

For the break with beauty, while it has liberated art, has also exposed it to excesses: gratuitous provocation that says nothing, obscurity that masks emptiness, imposture that dresses itself in depth.
That art is not required to be beautiful does not mean that anything goes, nor that the absence of beauty is in itself a quality.

There is art that breaks with beauty to say more, and art that dispenses with it to have nothing to say; distinguishing them requires a judgment that neither global rejection nor blind admiration can replace.
The real question is therefore not "must art be beautiful?" which cannot be answered with a simple yes or no, but "what do we expect from art?".

If we expect only pleasure from it, then art that renounces beauty will disappoint us; if we accept that it can also make us think, disturb us, reveal us, then we can welcome works that do not seek to please.
Beauty remains one of the powers of art, one of the most precious; but making it its sole mission is to overlook all that art can be otherwise.
Art that were only beautiful would, in its own way, be as poor as art that had renounced all demands.

sentences: We live in the age of infinite reproduction.
A work of art can be photographed, digitized, and distributed in millions of identical copies, accessible to everyone, everywhere, at any time.
One might think that this reproducibility would have devalued the original: why bother traveling to see a painting that can be viewed in better definition on a screen?
And yet, the opposite has happened: never have originals attracted so many crowds, and never has their value been so high.
This paradox deserves to be examined, as it reveals something profound about our relationship with authenticity.
Let's reflect on what reproduction preserves and what it loses.
A faithful reproduction retains everything that is visible in the work: the shapes, the colors, the composition.
In a sense, it provides access to the work, and this democratized access is a tremendous benefit, making art available to the greatest number of people.

But it loses something that information cannot capture: the presence of the unique object, the fact that this, precisely, is the object that the artist touched and shaped, in front of which we stand in the same space.
This presence, which the philosopher called the 'aura,' resists reproduction, because it does not depend on what the work shows, but on what it is.
What underlies this aura of the original?
First, its uniqueness and authenticity: the original is the only real object, the one that has a history, that has traversed time, that bears the mark of the hand that made it.
The reproduction, no matter how perfect, does not have this history; it is a copy without origin, detached from time and place.
In front of the original, we experience the vertigo of a real presence, the feeling of a direct contact with the creative act and with the centuries that separate us from it.
This feeling is not rational — the image is the same — but it is powerful, and it stems from the fact that we do not value only what a thing shows, but what it is.
This observation says a lot about us.
It shows that our relationship with works, and more broadly with things, is not purely informational.
We do not seek merely to see an image; we seek a connection with the real, with the authentic, with the unique.
That is why reproducibility, far from abolishing the value of the original, may have exalted it: by making images omnipresent, it has made the contact with the thing itself more precious by contrast.
The more copies abound, the more the original stands out as the only place of authentic presence.
This phenomenon goes beyond the realm of art.
In an age where everything is reproduced, simulated, and virtualized, the authentic acquires a new value, precisely because it becomes rare.
We seek the 'real' experience, the 'true' contact, the 'authentic' object, in a world saturated with reproductions and simulacra.

This quest for authenticity, so characteristic of our time, may be a reaction to widespread reproducibility: the more the world fills with copies, the more we thirst for originals, for what is unique, real, and irreplaceable.
It is not a matter of naively opposing the noble original to the contemptible copy, nor of regretting reproduction, which has democratized access to art and culture.
It is about understanding what each brings and what each loses.
Reproduction disseminates the information of the work, makes it accessible, integrates it into our lives; the original offers presence, authenticity, and contact with the real.

Both have their value, and our time, far from having to choose, enjoys both at once: it knows the works through their reproductions and rushes towards the originals to experience what no copy can provide.
This coexistence reveals that we are beings for whom real presence has a value that information, no matter how perfect, cannot replace.

sentences: Mass culture — this vast array of productions intended for the greatest number, disseminated on an industrial scale, from series to popular songs, from blockbusters to games — has long sparked a debate between two irreconcilable positions.
For some, it represents a degradation, a decline of culture, an easy entertainment that dulls the masses and stifles true creation.
For others, it is a happy democratization, finally granting access to a culture that was long reserved for an elite.
These two equally assured positions deserve to be transcended, as each captures a part of the truth while veering into excess.
The elitist critique of mass culture is not without foundation.
It is true that a significant portion of mass production follows a commercial logic that prioritizes what immediately pleases the greatest number, to the detriment of rigor, difficulty, and novelty.
It is also true that this logic tends to standardize, reproduce tried-and-true formulas, and flatter established tastes rather than elevate them.
Finally, it is true that entertainment designed to occupy without effort can dull critical thinking, divert attention from more demanding creations, and foster a habit of ease.
These critiques touch on something real, and dismissing them in the name of democracy would be blind.
But the elitist critique, taken to extremes, falls into a contempt that disqualifies it.
For it looks down on the tastes and pleasures of the vast majority, deeming them vulgar simply because they are shared.
It assumes that what pleases the majority is thereby worthless, and that true culture is the privilege of a few distinguished minds.
This stance, besides its arrogance, is false: popular culture has produced works of real value, and the fact that a work pleases many does not prove it is mediocre.
Confusing rigor with rarity, deeming everything that is shared as vulgar, turns culture into an instrument of social distinction rather than a good to be shared.
The opposite position, which unreservedly celebrates mass culture in the name of democracy, also has its share of truth and its excess.

Its truth: mass dissemination has indeed granted access to culture for populations that were previously excluded, broken the monopoly of elites, and allowed everyone to enjoy works and pleasures once reserved for a select few.
This is a real progress, and lamenting it would be a guilty nostalgia for a time when culture was a privilege.
Its excess: rejecting any hierarchy, considering all productions as equivalent, and making popularity the sole criterion of value.
For while success does not prove mediocrity, it does not prove excellence either; the number of people who love a work does not measure its value.
Moving beyond this false debate requires rejecting the alternative between elitist disdain and populist complacency.
One can acknowledge that mass culture has democratized access to culture, which is a good thing, and that it often follows a logic that impoverishes, which is a risk.
One can appreciate popular works without renouncing rigor, distinguishing within mass production what has value from what does not, without looking down on the people or flattering all their tastes.
The real question is not "Is mass culture good or bad?", but "How can we ensure that a culture accessible to all remains a demanding culture?".
For the real issue lies here: not choosing between the elite and the masses, between rigor and accessibility, but refusing to oppose them.
A culture that is demanding but reserved for a few would betray its vocation to be shared; a culture that is accessible but renounces all rigor would betray its vocation to elevate.
The ideal would be a culture that is both demanding and shared, which sacrifices neither quality for dissemination nor dissemination for quality.

This ideal is difficult, never fully achieved, but it is toward this that we must strive — rather than resigning ourselves to the false choice between a quality culture for a few and a degraded culture for all.

sentences: Machines now produce striking images, fluid texts, and pleasant music from just a few instructions.
This new capability disrupts our relationship with artistic creation and raises a question that is not only technical but also philosophical: is what these machines produce considered creation?
And if so, what remains unique to human creation?
This question, made urgent by current events, forces us to clarify what we mean by creating and perhaps reveals that we didn't understand it as well as we thought.
One initial reaction is to deny machines any true creation on the grounds that they merely recombine what already exists.
They have been fed countless human works, from which they extract patterns that they rearrange; they create nothing new, they recycle.
This argument is compelling, but it faces an objection: is human creation itself not largely recombination?
The human artist, too, is nourished by everything he has seen, heard, and learned; he does not create from nothing but rearranges inherited elements.
If recombination disqualifies the machine, we would also have to disqualify a part of human creation, which we refuse to do.
The boundary is therefore not so clear-cut.
A second approach seeks the difference not in the result but in the intention and experience.
The machine produces without wanting to express anything, without having lived anything, without any interiority being conveyed in what it does.
The human artist, on the other hand, creates to express something, based on an experience, a sensitivity, a relationship with the world; his work carries intention, lived experience, and presence.

What the machine would lack is not the ability to produce beautiful forms, but what, in human art, makes a work the trace of a consciousness, the expression of a being who has something to say because he has something to live.
This approach is stronger, but it shifts the difficulty rather than resolving it.

For if the value of art depends on the intention and experience of its creator, then it cannot be read in the work itself: two identical images, one made by a human expressing suffering, the other by a machine without intention, would have the same appearance but not the same value.
This means that what we value in art is not only what we perceive but also what we know about its origin.
A strange conclusion, which suggests that the value of art depends as much on its context — who made it, why, from what — as on its visible qualities.
Perhaps this is what the question of machines teaches us about art.

We discover, by asking it, that we do not value only the beautiful or the skillful, which the machine can produce, but the presence of a consciousness, the expression of lived experience, the connection with another human being.

What moves us in a work is not only its form but the fact that a being like us created it to say something; art is a communication between consciousnesses, and a production without consciousness, no matter how successful, lacks what gives it value.
The machine, by imitating the results of art, reveals to us that art was not only in its results.
This does not resolve all the practical questions raised by these machines, nor does it predict what they will become.
But it suggests that human creation retains something irreducible, not because the machine could not produce equally beautiful forms, but because what we seek in art is not just form.

In the face of machines that create, the question may not be whether they will replace artists, but rather to rediscover what we truly expected from art — and to recognize that what we expected fundamentally implied the presence of another like us, who, having lived, had something to tell us.

sentences: There is a form of beauty that immediately pleases, effortlessly moves us, flatters our sweetest feelings — and yet, it leaves a vague discomfort in those who pay attention to it.
This is what we call kitsch: those overly sweet images, those overly touching melodies, those performances designed to draw tears, which provide emotion without paying the price.
On the opposite side stands what we call the sublime: that which seizes us, surpasses us, troubles us while also elevating us.
Reflecting on this opposition means questioning what distinguishes authentic aesthetic emotion from its counterfeit.
What constitutes kitsch?
Not the emotion it evokes, because authentic art also moves us, but the way it evokes it and the nature of that emotion.
Kitsch produces an easy, expected, prefabricated emotion; it does not show reality, but an idealized, softened image, purged of anything that might disturb.
It gives sentiment without truth, emotion without depth, a beauty that reassures instead of questioning.
Its very sweetness is suspect, as it rests on a lie: it makes us feel a pleasant emotion while hiding everything that, in reality, would resist that sweetness.
Kitsch is an emotion that lies to itself.
This is how it differs from authentic aesthetic emotion.
A true work can be overwhelming, but it does not deceive: its emotion arises from a true relationship to reality, including its difficult aspects.
It does not spare us complexity, ambiguity, or the shadowy parts; it makes us feel something real, even at the cost of discomfort.
The emotion it provides is not flattery, but revelation; it does not comfort us in our easy feelings, it opens us up to something we did not know.
That is why it leaves not the vague discomfort of kitsch, but the feeling of having touched something essential.
The sublime pushes this difference to the extreme.
It does not seek to please, but confronts us with what surpasses us: the vastness, the power, the infinite, before which we feel our smallness.
This experience blends disturbance and elevation, fear and exhilaration; it has nothing of the sweetness of kitsch, it is almost a trial.
And yet, it enlarges us, it connects us with something greater than ourselves, it pulls us away from the smallness of our ordinary concerns.
The sublime is the opposite of kitsch: where the latter diminishes us by flattering us, the former elevates us by surpassing us.
This opposition has implications that go beyond aesthetics.
For kitsch is not just an artistic category; it is a way of relating to the world, which prefers reassuring images to complex reality, easy emotions to difficult truths.
One can live in kitsch, tell oneself an idealized life, flee everything that disturbs, prefer sweet feelings to harsh truths.
Kitsch is a constant temptation, that of settling for a beautiful deceptive image rather than confronting reality in its complexity.
Resisting it, in art as in life, means rejecting the ease of prefabricated emotion to seek a truth that, even if painful, is better than a beautiful lie.
Distinguishing kitsch from the sublime, easy emotion from true emotion, is therefore not a subtlety for aesthetes.
It is learning not to settle for what flatters, to be wary of what moves too easily, to prefer what surpasses us to what reassures us.
This demanding requirement is that of true taste, which is not the ability to enjoy beautiful things, but the ability to distinguish the authentic from its counterfeit.
And this distinction, at its core, is a demand for truth: for kitsch, beneath its sweetness, is a lie, and the sublime, beneath its disturbance, is a truth.
Choosing the latter over the former means preferring, even in emotion, the true over the convenient.

sentences: We like to believe that we are the masters of our tools: that we design them to serve our purposes, and that they remain mere instruments at our disposal.
This reassuring view is only half the truth.
For while we shape our tools, they, in turn, shape us.

The use of a technique is never without effect on the one who employs it; as we use our instruments, they alter our ways of perceiving, thinking, and acting, until they insensibly transform who we are.
This reciprocity is one of the most important, yet most overlooked, truths about our relationship with technology.
Let’s take an ancient example to measure the depth of the phenomenon.
The invention of writing was not just a simple addition of a memory tool; it transformed thought itself.
By allowing ideas to be fixed, reread, compared, and critiqued, it made possible forms of reasoning, analysis, and knowledge accumulation that did not exist in purely oral cultures.
Writing did not merely preserve thought; it changed it, giving rise to a new type of mind.
Moreover, the thinkers of the time feared that it would weaken memory — which it undoubtedly did, while also opening up other possibilities.
Every major tool operates this way: it gives and it takes away, it opens up new capacities while atrophying others.
What writing illustrates over millennia, our contemporary techniques produce before our eyes, at an accelerated pace.

The instruments that allow us to find everything instantly modify our memory and attention; those that connect us constantly transform our relationship with others and with ourselves; those that guide us everywhere alter our sense of direction and space.
Each of these tools provides a real service, but each also transforms us, developing some of our capacities while allowing others to atrophy.
We do not emerge unscathed from the use of our instruments; we emerge changed.
This transformation is all the more profound because it is invisible and involuntary.
We do not decide to be transformed by our tools; this happens without our knowledge, through repeated use, habit, and adaptation.
We believe we remain the same simply by using more efficient instruments, while in reality, these instruments reshape our mental habits, expectations, and ways of being.
The danger lies not in the tools themselves, but in our ignorance of their transformative power, which subjects us to these changes without our perceiving or choosing them.
One does not distrust what one is unaware of the effects of.
Should we conclude that we must renounce our tools, or fear them?
Not at all.

Transformation through technology is not inherently bad; it is the very condition of the human adventure, which has been built by equipping itself with instruments that have each time metamorphosed it.
Humanity is that being who transforms itself by transforming its tools, and there is no going back to a 'pure' humanity that existed before its techniques.
The problem is not that tools change us, but that we are unaware of it, and that we undergo these changes without evaluating them.

What this reciprocity demands is vigilance: to become aware that our tools shape us, to ask how they transform us, which capacities they develop and which they atrophy, and what kind of beings they make of us.
This awareness is not enough to fully control their effects, but it at least allows us to perceive, weigh, and sometimes correct them.
Consciously choosing our tools, measuring what they do to us, deliberately preserving the capacities they tend to erase: this is what a free use of technology entails.
For we cannot prevent our tools from transforming us; but we can, if we are careful, have a say in what they make of us.
