sentences: Technological progress often manifests itself as convenience: everything becomes easier, faster, and less burdensome.
What used to require effort, time, and hardship can now be done effortlessly, in an instant, without difficulty.
This promise of convenience is so obviously desirable that we hardly think to question it: who would want difficulty when ease is available?
And yet, we must dare to ask whether convenience, this seemingly flawless good, has a hidden cost, and whether everything that spares us effort truly serves us.
Let's start by acknowledging what is legitimate about convenience.
Many of the efforts that technology spares us were pure burdens, without value, and being freed from them is an undeniable progress.
No one sincerely regrets washing their clothes by hand, traveling miles for information, or painstakingly copying texts.
These hardships had no virtue; freeing ourselves from them has opened up time and energy for better things.
In these cases, convenience is a pure blessing, and denying it would be an absurd form of dolorism that confuses effort with value.
But not all efforts are mere burdens, and this is where convenience becomes ambiguous.
For some efforts have value, not despite their difficulty, but because of it.

The effort to learn builds skills; the effort to search leads to encounters with what we weren't looking for; the effort to do things ourselves provides a competence and satisfaction that the result obtained without effort does not.
When convenience spares us those efforts, it does not just serve us: it also deprives us of what effort produced.
We gain time, but we lose what the time spent brought us.
There is something more subtle.
Widespread convenience gradually makes us incapable of effort by atrophying the skills it spares us from exercising.
By getting everything effortlessly, we lose the habit and taste for effort, until the slightest obstacle seems unbearable.
Ease creates a need for ease, an increasing intolerance for anything that resists, and impatience for anything that does not come immediately.

Thus, convenience, by sparing us effort, makes us unfit for effort, and this unfitness has a cost, because many precious things — mastery, depth, perseverance — require precisely what convenience teaches us to unlearn.
That's not all.
Convenience also has a price that we do not see because it is paid elsewhere.
What is made so easy for us often relies on invisible labor, consumed resources, and costs shifted to others or to the future.
Instant delivery, immediate access, and permanent service assume entire chains of efforts and expenses that convenience hides from us.
We enjoy ease without seeing the price, which is very real, but paid out of our sight.
Convenience does not abolish effort and cost; it displaces them, makes them invisible, and shifts the burden onto others.
Recognizing the price of convenience does not mean rejecting it outright, nor advocating a return to difficulty as a virtue.

It means distinguishing between the efforts that are good to be freed from and those that were worth making, and asking ourselves, in front of each new convenience, what it spares us and what it costs us.
Sometimes it means deliberately choosing effort where it has value, preferring to do things ourselves, to search, to learn, rather than delegating everything to convenience.

In a world that elevates ease to the highest value, reserving spaces for chosen effort is not archaic; it is preserving what convenience, by sparing us too much, ultimately takes away: the ability to do, to struggle, to earn what we obtain.

sentences: Never has the world been so accessible.
Without leaving our place, we can see the most distant places, attend various events, access a vast amount of human knowledge, and connect with people on the other side of the earth.
The whole world seems to be at our fingertips, available with a gesture.
This unprecedented accessibility is an extraordinary achievement, and it would be ungrateful to underestimate it.
But it raises a question: accessing an image of the world, its representation on a screen, is it really knowing the world, experiencing it, meeting it?
We must first recognize all that this accessibility brings in reality.
Through it, knowledge that was once reserved has opened up to everyone; distant realities have become visible; separated people can connect.
Someone who once only knew their village can now embrace the world with their gaze.
It is a vast opening that has broadened everyone's horizons, broken many isolations, and made available what was previously out of reach.
To disdain this accessibility in the name of an 'authentic' experience reserved for a few privileged individuals would be a contemptible stance.
And yet, access to the representation of something is not the experience of the thing itself, and confusing the two would impoverish oneself unknowingly.
Seeing an image of a place is not the same as being there; knowing its representation is not the same as experiencing it.
Real experience engages our whole being — the body, the senses, presence, lived time — in a way that representation on a screen cannot replicate.

Standing truly in front of a mountain, in a place, beside a person, mobilizes a fullness of perception, a presence, a relationship that the image, however faithful, reduces to its only visual dimension.
The screen shows us, but it does not allow us to live.
This difference is not trivial, as it touches on the very nature of knowledge and experience.
Knowing the world through its representations means knowing it from a distance, from the outside, without the contact that alone allows us to feel.
It risks making us believe we know what we have only seen in an image, confusing information about something with the experience of that thing, mistaking the map for the territory.
However, there are dimensions of reality that can only be revealed through presence, engagement, direct experience — and which remain inaccessible to those who only know the representation.
The world at our fingertips is a world reduced to what can pass through a screen, that is to say, amputated of everything that the screen does not convey.
There is an additional, more insidious risk: that easy access to representation diverts us from real experience, giving us the illusion of it.
Why move, engage, or experience when we can see everything effortlessly on a screen?
This ease can lead to a form of passivity, where we are content to contemplate images of the world instead of living it, where mediated experience replaces direct experience.
We then risk living vicariously, spectators of a world we watch without being in it, knowing everything in image and nothing in reality.
Accessibility, by making real experience seem less necessary, could divert us from it.
It is not about opposing noble real experience to contemptible representation, nor about renouncing the accessibility that has brought so much.
It is about not confusing one with the other, maintaining awareness that seeing is not living, that the image of the world is not the world.

It is to preserve, alongside easy access to representations, the taste and practice of real experience, presence, and direct engagement; it is to remember that certain things can only be known by living them, and that the screen, however valuable for providing access, does not replace this contact with reality of which it only transmits the appearance.
The world at our fingertips is a gift; taking it for the world itself would be to confine ourselves to its representation.

alignments.english: It is to preserve, alongside easy access to representations, the taste and practice of real experience, presence, and direct engagement; it is to remember that certain things can only be known by living them, and that the screen, however valuable for providing access, does not replace this contact with reality of which it only transmits the appearance.

alignments.english: The world at our fingertips is a gift; taking it for the world itself would be to confine ourselves to its representation.

sentences: More and more, systems are making decisions for us.
They choose our path, recommend what we should watch, read, buy, and sometimes who we should meet; they guide medical, financial, and administrative decisions.
Often, they decide better than we would: faster, with more data, and fewer errors.
This increasing delegation of our decisions to systems thus appears as progress, and it is in many respects.
But it raises a question that its very effectiveness makes us forget: what happens to our judgment when we stop exercising it?
We must first recognize the real benefits of this delegation.
In many areas, the systems that decide for us spare us from mistakes, efforts, and wasted time.
They process vast amounts of information that we could not grasp, identify patterns that escape us, and avoid biases that distort our judgments.

Refusing these aids on principle, in the name of an autonomy of decision elevated to an absolute, would be unreasonable: there are decisions where it is better to rely on a reliable system than on our own fallible judgment.
Delegation is not inherently a bad thing.
But judgment, like any faculty, is maintained through practice and atrophies through idleness.
As we delegate our decisions, we stop exercising the ability to decide, and this ability, due to lack of use, weakens.
We lose the habit of weighing, choosing, and taking responsibility; we rely on others, and by relying on them, we become unable to do otherwise.

What begins as a convenience — letting the system decide because it decides better — ends as a dependency: we no longer know how to decide without it, we have unlearned the judgment we stopped exercising.
The assistance has become a crutch that we can no longer do without.
This atrophy of judgment is all the more concerning as it makes us vulnerable.
For the systems to which we delegate are not infallible, nor disinterested.
They can make mistakes, be biased, and serve interests that are not our own.

Now, one who has lost the ability to judge for themselves can no longer control the decisions made for them; they can only submit to them, unable to discern when the system is wrong or deceiving them.

The delegation that began as a gain in efficiency results in a loss of autonomy: we are at the mercy of systems that we no longer understand and can no longer contest, due to not having retained the judgment that would allow us to evaluate them.
There is something even more troubling.
By delegating our decisions, we also gradually delegate the responsibility that accompanies them.
To decide is to take responsibility; submitting to a decision made by a system is to offload that responsibility.
"It's not me, it's the system": this convenient phrase dissolves responsibility into anonymous mechanisms, where no one is accountable for anything.

Now, a society where decisions are made by systems for which no one is responsible is a society where responsibility itself evaporates, where decisions are imposed without anyone being able to hold anyone accountable.
The delegation of judgment is also a dilution of responsibility.
Preserving our judgment in the face of increasing delegation does not mean refusing all help, which would be futile and unreasonable.

It means keeping control: understanding, at least in principle, the systems we rely on; maintaining the ability to decide for ourselves, exercising it enough so that it does not atrophy; and not delegating the decisions that deeply engage our values and our lives.

For there are choices that we can safely entrust to systems, and others that must remain ours, not because we would decide better, but because deciding is part of what it means to be a free and responsible subject.
To completely renounce judgment would not only mean losing a skill; it would mean giving up a part of what makes us autonomous beings.

sentences: Inequality is at the heart of our political debates, yet we often confuse two questions that need to be distinguished: whether inequalities exist and whether they are just.
For not all inequality is necessarily an injustice, and not every reduction of inequalities is necessarily a step towards justice.

Untangling these questions is essential for thinking clearly about a topic that political passion tends to muddle, where everyone sees their own position as obvious and that of the opponent as outrageous.
Let’s start by acknowledging that there are inequalities that hardly shock our sense of justice.

The idea that someone who works harder, takes more risks, and contributes more should receive more does not seem unjust in itself; many see it as a requirement of justice, one that rewards effort and merit.
A strict equality that would treat equally someone who dedicates themselves and someone who does nothing would indeed clash with our sense of fairness.
Thus, there are inequalities that seem just, or at least acceptable, because they reflect differences we deem relevant.
However, this justification has limits that examination quickly reveals.
Real inequalities reflect only very partially merit or effort.
A large part of inequalities stems from factors for which no one is responsible: birth, environment, inheritance, innate talents, luck.
Someone born into a privileged environment benefits from advantages they did not earn; someone born into poverty suffers disadvantages for which they are not to blame.
Inequalities that result not from individuals' choices but from the lottery of birth are much harder to justify: how can it be fair that the randomness of birth determines the fate of an entire life?
Thus, a first criterion emerges to distinguish just inequalities from unjust ones: that of responsibility.

An inequality that results from individuals' free choices, their efforts, and what they are responsible for can be considered just, or at least legitimate; an inequality that arises from circumstances for which they are not responsible — birth, luck — calls for more correction.

This appealing criterion, however, does not resolve everything, as it is terribly difficult to untangle, in a trajectory, the part of choices from that of circumstances: does not someone who has 'made efforts' owe it, in part, to an education that instilled in them a taste for effort?
The boundary between what one is responsible for and what one has received is blurred, and merit, upon examination, partly dissolves into circumstances.
A second criterion concerns the effects of inequality on the most disadvantaged.

One can argue that an inequality is acceptable if it ultimately benefits everyone, including the most deprived — for example, if by rewarding the most productive, it stimulates an activity from which the poorest also benefit.
But if an inequality worsens the plight of the most disadvantaged, trapping some in misery to allow others to thrive, it becomes difficult to justify.
According to this criterion, inequality is acceptable only insofar as it serves the interest of all, not just that of the privileged at the expense of others.
These criteria do not provide a simple answer, and the debate on the justice of inequalities remains open, as it involves values that are prioritized differently according to beliefs.

But they allow us to move beyond two equally simplistic positions: one that considers all inequality just, on the grounds that it reflects merit, while it largely stems from unearned circumstances; and one that deems all inequality unjust, in the name of an egalitarianism that ignores legitimate differences.
The truth is more nuanced: some inequalities are just, others are not, and the challenge is to distinguish between them.
Refusing this distinction, in either direction, is to avoid thinking about justice in favor of a slogan.

sentences: There have always been poor people, and there always will be. This phrase, often spoken with an air of wisdom, expresses a fatalism that treats poverty as an inevitable aspect of the human condition, a natural fact against which it would be futile to fight.
This fatalism is convenient: it relieves one from taking action, it soothes the conscience, and it makes inaction seem like a form of clarity.
But it is based on a confusion and an error that must be exposed, because poverty is not the fatality that it is claimed to be.
First, we must distinguish between two concepts that fatalism confuses: absolute poverty and relative poverty.
Absolute poverty is the lack of essential needs — enough to eat, a place to live, access to healthcare, and to survive.
Relative poverty is having much less than others in a given society, without necessarily lacking the essentials.

These two realities are quite different, and fatalism mixes them up to seem more justified: "we will never eliminate all poverty" is plausible if it refers to relative poverty, which assumes that disparities are always possible; but it is false if it refers to absolute poverty, that of lacking essentials, which is not inevitable.
For absolute poverty, far from being a fatality, has significantly decreased in recent history, and there is nothing to prevent us from thinking that it could be eradicated.
Today, we produce enough to feed, house, and care for all of humanity; the persistence of misery is not due to a shortage of resources, but to their distribution.
That human beings lack essentials in a world that produces more than enough to meet everyone’s needs is not a natural fatality, but the result of organization, choices, and power dynamics.
Absolute misery is not inscribed in the nature of things; it is a problem that we could solve, and that we tolerate.
Fatalism regarding poverty thus serves a function: it transforms a solvable problem into an insurmountable fatality, thereby legitimizing inaction.
By presenting poverty as inevitable, it discourages any effort to combat it, it passes resignation off as wisdom, and it absolves a society that could do much more.

That is why this fatalism, under its guise of realism, is actually an ideology: it serves the interests of those who do not want to change the existing order, convincing everyone that there is nothing to be done.
"There’s nothing we can do" is the best ally of "I don’t want to do anything."
Recognizing that absolute poverty is not a fatality does not mean claiming that it would be easy to eradicate it, nor ignoring the complexity of the obstacles.

The distribution of resources faces powerful interests, real difficulties, and perverse effects that must be anticipated; combating poverty is not simple, and naive solutions can worsen the ills they claim to cure.
But difficulty is not impossibility, and recognizing that something is difficult is entirely different from declaring it fatal.
We can debate the means to reduce poverty; we cannot take refuge in the idea that it would be inevitable to avoid trying.
As for relative poverty and wealth disparities, the question is different and more complex, because some inequality may be inevitable, or even, within certain limits, acceptable.
But even there, the extent of disparities is not fatal: they have varied greatly across times and societies, which proves that they depend on choices and not on an unchanging nature.
That poverty, whether absolute or relative, persists is never a simple fatality; it is always, in part, the result of what we do and do not do.
The fatalism that naturalizes it is the first thing to combat, because as long as one considers a problem inevitable, one does not even seek to cure it.

sentences: Few things seem as natural as passing on to one's children what one has acquired.
Working for one's family, leaving them an inheritance, ensuring their future: this aspiration seems so obvious that we hesitate to question it.
And yet, inheritance harbors a deep contradiction with another principle we cherish, that of equal opportunity.
For what inheritance transmits is not just material goods: it conveys unearned advantages that mean children do not start life on equal footing.
This tension deserves to be confronted, however uncomfortable it may be.
The principle of equal opportunity holds that success should depend on merit, effort, personal qualities, and not on the circumstances of one's birth.
However, inheritance directly contradicts this principle.
A child who inherits a fortune, a legacy, or a network has considerable advantages that they have not earned, which are due to nothing but the chance of being born into a certain family.
Two children of equal worth, one born rich and the other poor, will not have the same chances, and this difference is entirely due to inheritance.
Thus, it perpetuates, from generation to generation, inequalities that are not justified from the standpoint of merit.

One might argue that someone who has acquired an asset has the right to dispose of it as they see fit, including passing it on to their children; prohibiting inheritance would be an infringement on freedom and property.
This argument has its strength, but it faces a difficulty: the right of the giver conflicts with the right of all other children to equal opportunity.
The freedom to bequeath creates the starting inequality for others.

It is not obvious that the first right should absolutely take precedence over the second; one could argue that society has a legitimate interest in limiting the transmission of privileges to preserve a certain equality of opportunity among newcomers.
There is something even more troubling.
Inheritance does not only transmit material goods, but a whole set of more subtle and determining advantages: education, culture, manners, relationships, codes, aspirations.
These advantages, even more than wealth, are transmitted and perpetuated, reproducing social positions from generation to generation.
Even if we were to abolish material inheritance, these immaterial inheritances would continue to deepen the inequality of opportunity.
Inheritance, in the broad sense, is the mechanism by which a society reproduces its hierarchies, ensuring that children essentially inherit their parents' position.
Should we conclude that inheritance should be abolished?
The question is more complex than what the stark positions suggest.

On one hand, unlimited inheritance perpetuates unjust inequalities and contradicts equal opportunity; on the other hand, completely prohibiting it would be both unrealistic, infringing on legitimate attachments, and powerless to eliminate the immaterial inheritances that weigh the most.

Between unlimited inheritance and its abolition, there are intermediate positions: regulating, taxing, limiting the transmission of large fortunes, while preserving ordinary inheritance; investing in education to compensate for immaterial inheritances.
These measures do not eliminate the tension, but they do mitigate it.
The essential point may be not to sweep the contradiction under the false evidence of 'it's natural.'

Recognizing that inheritance, however understandable it may be, contradicts equal opportunity, and that what we pass on to our children unfairly advantages some at the expense of others, is to refuse to accept as just what is merely customary.
One can, with full knowledge, choose to maintain a part of inheritance, weighing the values at stake; but one should not do so while pretending that there is no problem.

For behind the apparent obviousness of passing on to one's own lies one of the most powerful mechanisms for perpetuating inequalities — and confronting it is the condition for any honest judgment on the justice of our societies.

sentences: He made it all by himself." This phrase, spoken with admiration, celebrates someone who, starting from nothing, would have built his success solely through his own merits, without owing anything to anyone.
The myth of the self-made man, the man who makes himself, occupies a central place in the imagination of our societies, where it serves as a model and justification.
But this myth, as appealing as it may be, is based on an illusion that needs to be dispelled, as it has significant consequences for how we think about merit, success, and justice.
The illusion consists in believing that a success can be entirely the work of the person who experiences it, without owing anything to others or to circumstances.
Yet no success is ever purely individual.

The one who succeeds has benefited from countless conditions that he did not create: an education received, a language learned, knowledge accumulated by others, institutions that made his activity possible, a society that provided the framework for his success, and people who helped, trained, and supported him.
Even the most self-taught of entrepreneurs has used paths that he did not build, knowledge that he did not invent, a social order that he did not establish.
No one truly makes it all by themselves; every success is supported by a multitude of invisible contributions.
To this is added the considerable and denied part of luck.

The one who succeeds owes a lot to favorable circumstances for which he is not responsible: being born with certain talents, in a certain environment, at a certain time, meeting the right people, seizing the right opportunities, escaping the misfortunes that have shattered other trajectories.
This part of luck is completely erased by the myth of the self-made man, attributing to merit alone what owes so much to chance.

Yet for every person who has succeeded thanks to their efforts and luck, how many have made the same efforts without experiencing the same fortune, due to not having benefited from the same circumstances?
Why is this myth so tenacious, despite its obvious fragility?
Because it is flattering and reassuring, for both those who have succeeded and for the social order.

For those who have succeeded, it is gratifying to attribute their success to their own merit, rather than acknowledging what they owe to others and to luck; this justifies enjoying the full fruits of their success, without any debt to anyone.

For the social order, the myth justifies inequalities: if everyone is the architect of their own fate, then the rich deserve their wealth and the poor deserve their poverty, and the existing order is just.
The myth of the self-made man is thus an ideology that legitimizes inequalities by presenting them as the rightful reflection of merit.
Dispelling this myth has significant consequences.
Recognizing that no success is purely individual, that it owes a lot to others, to society, and to luck, is to acknowledge a debt.
The one who has succeeded does not only have rights over what he has acquired; he also has obligations to this society and to those others without whom he could not have achieved anything.
Success is not a due that one would have entirely deserved, but a shared fruit that calls for a contribution in return.
It is undermining the myth of the self-made man that allows for the foundation of the idea that those who have received the most should also give the most back.
It is not about denying all merit, pretending that efforts and qualities count for nothing, that everything is just chance and circumstances.
The one who succeeds has often, indeed, worked, persevered, and demonstrated real qualities, and it would be unjust to deny that.
It is about rejecting the opposite illusion, the one that attributes everything to the individual alone, forgetting everything that has supported him.
The truth lies in between: success combines merit, the contributions of others, and luck, and honesty consists in recognizing all three.
"I made it all by myself" is a lie, not because the one who says it has done nothing, but because he forgets everything without which what he has done would have amounted to nothing.

sentences: As machines become more capable, performing tasks once thought to be exclusive to humans, imitating our creations and sometimes our behaviors, an age-old question arises with new urgency: what is uniquely human about us?
For a long time, we have defined ourselves by what only we could do — calculate, reason, create, speak.
But as machines catch up to us in these areas, these definitions begin to falter, and we are forced to look elsewhere for what distinguishes us.
This search, imposed by technology, may be one of the most fruitful of our time.
We must first rid ourselves of a defensive reflex that consists of seeking our specificity in certain abilities that machines have not yet matched.
This strategy is doomed to fail, as it constantly retreats: every time we define humanity by an ability, machines eventually imitate it, and we must fall back to another.
Defining ourselves by what machines cannot yet do condemns us to perpetual redefinition and endless anxiety.
Our humanity does not reside in performance, as every performance is, in principle, imitable.
Perhaps we should look not at what we do, but at what we are and experience.

What distinguishes humans may not be a superior ability, but a way of existing: having consciousness, feeling, suffering, enjoying, giving meaning, knowing that we will die, and living in light of that knowledge.
A machine can imitate the results of our activities, but does it feel anything?
Does it have an interiority, an experience, a relationship to its own existence?
Nothing indicates that.
What would be uniquely ours is not to do this or that, but to live it, to have the experience, to exist for ourselves and not just to function.
This line of thought shifts the question in a fruitful way.
It suggests that our humanity does not depend on our functional superiority, but on our condition as conscious and vulnerable beings, capable of feeling and giving meaning.

And this condition, far from being threatened by machines, is even highlighted: by accomplishing without consciousness what we achieve by living, machines reveal to us that our value was not in the accomplishment, but in the lived experience that accompanied it.

It is not because we calculate that we are human, but because, in calculating, we experience something; the machine calculates without experiencing anything, and it is this difference, not the performance, that matters.
This reflection has practical implications, as it indicates what we should preserve and cultivate in a world of machines.

Not to compete with them in the realm of performance, where we will always be surpassed, but to deepen what is uniquely ours: the life of consciousness, the depth of experience, the capacity for meaning, and true relationships between beings who feel.

In a world where machines are increasingly doing what is functional, what will remain precious will be precisely what is not: presence, attention, shared experience, everything that pertains not to the accomplishment of a task, but to the meeting of consciousnesses.
Remaining human among machines is therefore not about clinging to a threatened superiority, nor imitating machines to avoid being left behind.
It is about cultivating what constitutes us: our condition as conscious, sensitive, mortal beings, capable of meaning and relationship.

Machines, by depriving us of our performances, may be doing us an unexpected service: forcing us to rediscover what, within us, was not reducible to a performance, and to finally cultivate it for its own sake.

The challenge is not to remain superior to machines, but to remain fully human — and this is not played out in the realm where machines catch up to us, but in the deeper realm where they do not follow us: that of lived life and felt meaning.

sentences: We talk about 'nature' as an obvious reality: what exists independently of man, the wild world opposed to the civilized world, the order of things in contrast to human artifice.
This notion seems so natural to us that we hardly think to question it.
Yet, what we call 'nature' may be less a reality than an idea, a construct of our minds that, far from being neutral, shapes our relationship with the world in sometimes misleading ways.
Questioning this concept is not an intellectual game: it governs our very ecology.
First, let’s consider the opposition between nature and man, which structures the entire notion.
This opposition assumes that man is, in some way, outside of nature, that his productions — cities, technologies, cultures — are not natural, while the rest of living beings are.
However, this separation does not hold up well under scrutiny.
Man is a living being among others, a product of evolution like all species; his productions, however complex they may be, are the work of an animal, just as a hive is the work of a bee.
Where do we draw the line between the natural and the artificial, if the artificial is itself produced by a natural being?
The opposition, upon reflection, becomes blurred.
Next, let’s consider the idea of a 'wild' nature, untouched by human presence, which we cherish as an ideal to preserve.
This intact nature, which we dream of, exists virtually nowhere and may have never existed.
The landscapes we believe to be natural are often the product of a long interaction with humans, shaped by millennia of presence, culture, and transformation.
The forest, the countryside, the spaces we consider natural bear the marks of human action; virgin nature is a myth, a projection of our imagination more than a reality to protect.
What we want to preserve is not an original state, but a certain balance that we have learned to value.
Why is it important to recognize that 'nature' is a construct?
Because this idea, taken as a reality, distorts our ecology in two opposing ways.

On one hand, it can lead us to believe that there exists an ideal nature, a pure original state that needs to be restored, which is illusory and sometimes harmful; we can destroy real balances in the name of an idealized nature that has never existed.

On the other hand, the opposition between man and nature can make us think that we are outside of it, allowed to treat it as mere scenery, while we are part of it and destroying it means destroying ourselves.
The false idea of a separate nature simultaneously feeds a dream of impossible purity and a dangerous illusion of separation.
What should we put in place of this misleading idea?
Not to deny that there is a living world, ecosystems, balances to preserve — all of this is very real and vital.
But to abandon the opposition between man and nature, to think of man as part of a living world from which he is both derived and responsible.
Not to dream of restoring a virgin nature that has never existed, but to seek to preserve and cultivate viable balances between humanity and the rest of living beings.
Ecology does not need the myth of a pure and separate nature; it needs the awareness that we are living beings among others, whose fate is linked to that of the whole.

Saying that 'nature does not exist' is therefore not to deny the reality of the living world nor the seriousness of its destruction; it is to reject an idea that, under the guise of defending it, misunderstands it.
It is to exchange the myth of an ideal and separate nature for the more accurate and demanding recognition of a community of living beings of which we are a part.
This recognition does not give us the convenience of a simple ideal to restore; it imposes on us the more complex responsibility of inhabiting a world of which we are both members and guardians.
Renouncing 'nature' as a myth may be the condition for finally taking the living world seriously as a reality.

sentences: The ecological debate is often framed as a heartbreaking dilemma: to preserve the planet, we would have to give up our comfort, our way of life, and what makes our existence enjoyable.
On one side, the survival of our environment; on the other, the comfort we cherish.

Framed this way, the dilemma seems unsolvable, as it pits two equally valued things against each other, often leading to paralysis: between the planet and comfort, most people actually choose immediate comfort while vaguely worrying about the planet.
However, this framing itself deserves to be questioned, as it may not be as inevitable as it seems.
First, let's acknowledge the truth in the dilemma.
It would be dishonest to claim that preserving our environment will require no change, no sacrifices, or no questioning of certain habits.
Our way of life in wealthy societies heavily impacts ecological balances, and maintaining it as it is simply isn't sustainable.
Those who promise that we can preserve everything without changing anything, that technology will solve everything effortlessly, are nurturing a comfortable but false illusion.
Some renunciation of unsustainable forms of comfort will be necessary, and denying this would be self-deception.
But the dilemma, as it is presented, contains several traps that need to be uncovered.
The first is confusing comfort with a particular, historically situated way of life, which is only one form of it.
What we call 'comfort'—abundant consumption, speed, accumulation—is not the only possible comfort, nor perhaps the greatest.
Other forms of well-being exist that weigh less on the planet: the comfort of slowness, relationships, free time, and a healthy environment.

Pitting the planet against comfort assumes there is only one form of comfort, the one that destroys; it forgets that giving up that kind of comfort could open the door to other forms of well-being, equally real.
The second trap is ignoring that the way of life presented as a comfort to preserve also has its costs, nuisances, and dissatisfactions.
Unrestrained consumption does not bring the happiness it promises; speed is exhausting; accumulation does not fulfill.
A part of what we call comfort is actually a tiring race, a sustained dissatisfaction, a form of alienation.
Giving up this false comfort would not only be a sacrifice for the planet; it could also be a liberation for ourselves.
The dilemma assumes that our current way of life is a pure good that we would only regret giving up; it forgets all that is burdensome about it.
The third trap, finally, is ignoring the costs of inaction, which make the dilemma misleading.

For doing nothing to preserve our comfort does not preserve our comfort: it condemns it, in the long run, to the consequences of ecological destruction, which precisely threaten this way of life and much more.
The real dilemma is not between comfort and the planet, but between a chosen change now and a forced collapse later.
Presenting inaction as maintaining comfort ignores that inaction also leads, and much more surely, to the loss of the comfort it claims to preserve.
Therefore, escaping the false dilemma does not mean denying all renunciation, but rejecting the framing that simply opposes the planet to comfort.

It is to recognize that some sacrifices are necessary, but that they can open up to other forms of well-being; that the way of life to preserve has its own costs; and that inaction preserves nothing but leads to the loss of everything.
The question is not 'should we sacrifice our comfort for the planet?', but 'what kind of life do we want that is both sustainable and desirable?'
Reformulated this way, the question no longer invites paralysis from the dilemma, but the invention of a good life that does not destroy its own conditions.
This is a task more difficult than a simple sacrifice, but also more fruitful: not giving up happiness to save the planet, but rethinking happiness so that it is compatible with it.

sentences: There are things that can be bought, and others that we believe should not be bought.
You can buy a house, but should you be able to buy a vote in elections?
You can pay for a service, but should you be able to pay for someone else to serve your prison sentence, carry your child, or give you an organ?
These questions are not economic, but moral: they concern the limits we should set on the market, on what should remain outside its reach.
And they are all the more pressing as the market today tends to expand into areas that were previously beyond its grasp.
The first argument against the unlimited expansion of the market relates to inequality.
Where everything is for sale, those who have money obtain what others cannot have; wealth inequality then translates into inequality of access to everything that matters.

As long as the market is limited to consumer goods, this inequality is bearable; but if it extends to health, justice, education, and political influence, it transforms economic inequality into inequality regarding the most essential goods.
The more the market expands, the more money becomes decisive, and the greater the impact of wealth inequalities on all aspects of existence.
Limiting the market means preventing wealth from buying everything.
But there is a second, deeper argument that does not concern inequality but the very nature of certain goods.
For putting something on the market, giving it a price, can corrupt it, distort it, and cause it to lose its intrinsic value.

Some things are valuable precisely because they cannot be bought: friendship that could be bought would no longer be friendship, honor that could be sold would no longer be honor, and the price of a reward that could be purchased would strip it of its meaning.
There are goods whose value lies in the fact that they are given, earned, received, and not bought; subjecting them to the market does not make them accessible, it destroys them as what they were.
This second argument is decisive, as it shows that the question of the limits of the market is not just a question of distributive justice, but a question about the meaning and value of things.

When we refuse to allow certain things to be bought, it is not only because it would be unequal; it is because buying them would distort them, substituting the only measure of money for their intrinsic value.

A society where everything could be bought would not only be more unequal; it would be a society where nothing would have value beyond its price, where everything would be reduced to its market value, and where the very meaning of goods that cannot be reduced to money would be lost.

That is why the question of the limits of the market is one of the most important of our time, where the market tends to overflow its traditional boundaries, to put a price on what did not have one, and to treat as commodities things that were not.
This expansion often presents itself as progress, efficiency, and freedom; but it silently operates a transformation of our values, making the market the measure of all things.

Resisting this expansion is not opposing the market in its legitimate domain, where it provides immense services; it is refusing to let it become the sole principle of organization for all human life.
Drawing the limits of the market is not a task that economics could accomplish, as it is a moral task that engages our conception of what has a price and what has a value beyond any price.
It requires us to ask, for each good, whether it can be bought and sold without harm, or if its nature demands that it escape the market.
This deliberation, never closed, is one of the responsibilities of a society that does not want to be entirely governed by money.

For the real question is not whether money can, in fact, buy everything — it increasingly can — but whether there are things it should not be able to buy, if we want to preserve what is worth more than its price in human existence.

sentences: The ecological crisis raises a new kind of moral question: do we have duties to future generations, to those who have not yet been born?
Our present actions — what we consume, destroy, and bequeath — will profoundly affect the world that those who come after us will inherit.
But these future people do not yet exist; they cannot ask us for anything, protest, or negotiate.
Can we have obligations to beings who do not exist, and if so, what are these obligations based on?
This question, seemingly abstract, governs our relationship with the future.
A first difficulty lies in the fact that future generations cannot claim any rights, since they do not exist.
We have duties, it is said, to those who have rights; but can a being that does not exist have rights?

This objection has logical force, but it clashes with a powerful intuition: it seems clear to us that bequeathing a devastated world to future generations would be a wrongdoing, that we do not have the right to enjoy the present while ruining their future.
This intuition withstands the logical objection and suggests that our duties to the future cannot be reduced to the logic of rights and claims.
So, on what basis can we found these duties?
We can first note that, while future people do not yet exist individually, it is certain that there will be future generations, and their fate depends on us.
We know that they will exist, that they will have needs, and that they will suffer or thrive depending on the world we leave for them.
This certainty may be enough to establish an obligation: not to a specific individual, but to those, whoever they may be, who will inherit our actions.

We are in the position of someone who sets a trap on a path where they know others will pass: it does not matter that they do not know who; they know that someone will suffer from their act, and that is enough to make them responsible.
We can also base these duties on the idea of continuity between generations, a chain of which we are merely one link.
We have received from our predecessors a world, knowledge, institutions, a heritage; we enjoy it without having created it.
This debt to the past calls for a symmetrical duty to the future: to pass on in turn, not to break the chain, not to squander a heritage that we only temporarily hold.
We are not absolute owners of the world, free to enjoy it until it is exhausted; we are its custodians, tasked with passing it on.
This conception, present in many traditions, grounds our duties to the future in our place within a continuity that transcends us.
The real difficulty may not be so much in establishing these duties as in feeling them.

For our obligations to the future encounter a major psychological obstacle: the distant future is abstract to us, future generations are foreign to us, and we spontaneously give much more weight to the present than to a future that will no longer concern us.
We know intellectually that we should care about the future, but we feel it poorly, and this lack of feeling paralyzes action.
The problem is not that we ignore our duties to the future, but that we struggle to feel them with enough strength to act accordingly.
Overcoming this obstacle is one of the great moral challenges of our time.

It is not enough to theoretically establish our duties to future generations; we must learn to feel them, to concretely care about a future we will not see, to expand our moral horizon beyond our own existence.
This requires a form of imagination and generosity: to care for those we will never know, to act for a world we will not enjoy, to plant trees under whose shade we will not sit.
This ability to care for the distant future is not natural; it is an achievement, almost a virtue.
But it is this virtue that may determine the fate of those who will succeed us — and the dignity of what we leave them.

sentences: In the face of the ecological crisis, a hope keeps resurfacing, appealing in its convenience: technology will save us.
Innovation, it is said, will find solutions — clean energies, efficient processes, inventions that will allow us to preserve the planet without giving up our way of life.
This techno-optimistic hope is powerful, as it spares us from painful changes: there is no need to transform our lives, we just have to wait for human ingenuity to solve the problem.
But this hope deserves critical examination, as it mixes a grain of truth with a dangerous illusion.
Let's start with the grain of truth, as it would be absurd to disdain technology.
Innovation has an essential role to play in responding to the ecological crisis, and claiming otherwise would be a posturing.
New techniques — in energy, agriculture, industry — can significantly reduce our footprint, allow us to do more with less, and open up possibilities that no mere renunciation could provide.
Refusing to use technology on principle, in the name of a return to an idealized past, would be both unrealistic and counterproductive.
Technology is part of the solution, and it needs to be developed.
But the techno-optimistic hope becomes an illusion as soon as it turns into a passive waiting for a miraculous solution that would spare us from any change.
This illusion involves several errors.

The first is to take for granted that technology will find the necessary solutions in time, while nothing guarantees it: betting our entire future on hypothetical innovations, which may not come or may come too late, is an imprudent gamble.
Hoping that technology will save us is not a strategy; it is a wish that relieves us from acting while waiting for uncertain salvation.
The second error is to ignore that technology, while solving some problems, often creates others.
History shows that technical solutions frequently have unforeseen perverse effects, shifting problems rather than eliminating them, creating new difficulties as they resolve old ones.
Relying on technology to solve everything forgets that it is itself, in part, the source of the problems we ask it to address, and that it could create new ones.
Blind faith in technology overlooks this ambivalence.
The third error, the most subtle, is that techno-optimistic hope often serves as an alibi for inaction and the maintenance of the existing order.
By promising that technology will preserve our way of life without us having to change it, it reassures, lulls, and relieves us from questioning what should be questioned.
It allows those who benefit from the current order to defend it, indefinitely postponing change in the name of a forthcoming technical salvation.
Thus, "technology will solve the problem" becomes a way of doing nothing, of continuing as before, of refusing necessary transformations.
Technical optimism, beneath its dynamic facade, can be the most effective form of conservatism.
The correct position is therefore neither the techno-optimism that expects everything from technology nor the technophobic rejection that expects nothing from it.
It is to recognize that technology is an indispensable means, but one means among others, which will not spare us from changes in behavior, organization, and way of life.

Yes, develop useful techniques; but without using them as an excuse to change nothing else, without betting our future on hypothetical solutions, without forgetting that technology itself must be guided by choices.
Technology will not save us on its own; it can help us if we also do the rest.
And it is precisely this "rest" — the changes that techno-optimistic hope invites us to evade — that is the most difficult and the most necessary.

sentences: At the end of this reflection on our relationship with the living world, a reformulation may be necessary.
We talk about 'protecting nature' as if it were about defending an external reality, an object distinct from us.
But we have seen that this separation between man and nature is misleading, that we are part of the living world, and that our fate is linked to its.

Therefore, the question may not be so much about protecting a nature of which we would be external guardians, but about learning to inhabit the world that is ours — the only one we have, the one from which we both originate and for which we are responsible.

To inhabit is not just to occupy a place, to use it, to exploit it; it is to dwell there, to take care of it, to inscribe oneself in the duration, to feel at home while respecting what precedes and transcends us.
The one who truly inhabits a place does not treat it as a resource to be exhausted, but as a home to be maintained, to which he is connected, belonging to it as much as it belongs to him.
Moving from the idea of protecting nature to that of inhabiting the Earth is a shift from an external relationship to one of belonging, from a logic of management to a logic of care.
This shift has profound consequences.

If we only 'protect nature', we remain in a position of superiority, where man, from the outside, decides to preserve or exploit an object that is foreign to him; nature remains a thing before us, which we manage according to our interests.
If we learn to 'inhabit the Earth', we recognize ourselves as part of a common world, of which we are dependent and responsible, not from above but from within.
The destruction of the living world is no longer the degradation of an external object, but an assault on our own home, on what sustains us and constitutes us.
One does not ravage the house one inhabits.
This way of inhabiting implies a transformation of our relationship with things and beings.
To inhabit is to establish connections, not only of use but of attachment, knowledge, and care, with the places, the living beings, and the balances that surround us.
It is to know one's environment, to become attached to it, to take care of it as something that matters for itself and not just for the use we make of it.

This disposition, which ancient societies often cultivated in their relationship with their territory, has been lost in a world that treats space as a mere support for activities, interchangeable and exploitable.
Relearning it would mean regaining a relationship with the world that is deeper than mere exploitation.
It is not about falling into a mysticism of the Earth, nor about renouncing any transformation of the world, because to inhabit also means to transform, cultivate, and build.
Man cannot inhabit without acting on his environment, and it would be absurd to dream of a human presence without effect.

The difference is not between transforming and not transforming, but between two ways of transforming: one that exhausts and destroys, treating the world as a reserve to be plundered, and one that maintains and cultivates, transforming the world while caring for its sustainability.
To inhabit is to transform while remaining, to act while preserving the conditions of life, to build without destroying what makes building possible.
Learning to inhabit the Earth may be the most accurate name for the ecological task.
Not to protect an external nature in the name of an imaginary purity, nor to manage resources in our best interests, but to relearn to dwell in our world as in a home of which we are part.
This task is more demanding than simple management, as it engages our way of being in the world, our relationship with things and living beings, our conception of our place.

But it is also more fruitful, as it does not only ask us to save a threatened object; it invites us to regain a relationship with the world where we would finally feel at home, not as masters who exploit, but as inhabitants who take care of the only home we have.

sentences: Who am I? The question seems so simple that we think it has already been resolved: I am me, a person identical to herself, who persists through time.
However, as soon as we reflect on it, this obviousness slips away.
For what makes me 'me', the same today as I was yesterday and will be in twenty years, while my body renews itself, my thoughts change, and I am no longer the child I once was?
On what does this identity that I so spontaneously attribute to myself rest?
This question, upon examination, turns out to be one of the deepest and most bewildering there is.
Let’s first seek what could ground personal identity.
Could it be the body?
But the body changes continuously; its cells renew themselves, it ages, transforms, to the point that the body of a child and that of an old person have almost nothing materially in common.
If I am my body, then I am not the same as I was thirty years ago, which contradicts the intuition of continuity.
The body, in perpetual renewal, provides a fragile foundation for an identity that is supposed to persist.
Could it then be consciousness, memory, this thread of memories that connects the moments of my life?
This answer is more appealing: I am the same because I remember having been, because a continuity of consciousness links my present to my past.
But it has its flaws.
My memory is patchy, selective, sometimes misleading; I have forgotten almost all of my existence, and entire parts of my past are as foreign to me as those of another.
If I am my memories, what happens to my identity for everything I have forgotten, or if I were to lose my memory?
Consciousness, too, provides an uncertain foundation.
Perhaps the mistake is to seek a fixed thing, a permanent core, a substantial 'me' that would remain identical amid change.

Some schools of thought suggest that no such core exists, that the 'me' is not a thing, but a process, a continuously changing flow of perceptions, thoughts, sensations, without a permanent substrate.
The 'me' would not be what remains identical amid change, but the name we give to this flow itself, to this dynamic continuity that has nothing fixed.
This conception, bewildering, dissolves identity by making it coincide with change itself.
Should we conclude that the 'me' is an illusion, that I am nobody, that there is no stable subject?
That would be drawing an excessive conclusion from a real difficulty.
For even if the 'me' is not a fixed thing, there is indeed a continuity, a unique perspective on the world, a story that is mine and not that of another.
This continuity may not be that of an immutable substance, but that of a narrative, a project, a perspective that maintains itself through change by integrating it.
I am not a fixed thing; I am a story that continues, an identity that is built rather than found.
This conception has liberating consequences.
If the 'me' is not a fixed core to be discovered, but a story that is built, then I am not condemned to be what I have been; I can change, become something else, rewrite my narrative.
Identity is not a given to which one must be faithful, but a work to which I am committed.
'Who am I?' therefore does not call for the discovery of a hidden essence, but for the continued invention of oneself.
We are not things that have an identity; we are beings that are made, and this absence of a fixed core, far from being a loss, is the condition of our freedom to become.

sentences: Be yourself," "stay true to yourself," "be authentic": these injunctions have become self-evident in our time, ideals that no one thinks to contest.
Being authentic, true to one's deep self, opposed to conformity and social lies, is seen as the hallmark of a successful life.

However, this ideal, as appealing as it may be, rests on assumptions that need to be examined, because it presupposes as resolved what is precisely problematic: the existence of an authentic self, already given, to which one should be faithful.

The ideal of authenticity indeed assumes that there exists, deep down in each of us, a true self, a proper nature, an authentic identity that would be our truth, as opposed to the masks we wear in society.
Being true to oneself would then mean discovering this deep self and conforming to it, against the pressures that lead us away from it.
But this image assumes that the authentic self preexists, that it is there to be discovered, like a buried treasure.
Yet we have seen that the self may not be a fixed thing, predetermined, but something that is constructed.
If that is the case, to which already existing self should one be faithful?
There is something more troubling.
The ideal of authenticity opposes the deep, authentic self to external, social influences that would lead us astray.
But is this opposition tenable?
Isn't what we call our deep self also largely the product of influences—our education, our culture, our environment, others?
What I take to be my authentic nature may be what I have received unknowingly, internalized to the point of believing it is mine.
The idea of an authentic self, free from any social influence, may be an illusion: there is no self that would preexist influences, because we are woven from them.
To want to be true to a self prior to any influence is to pursue a ghost.
Should we then reject the ideal of authenticity, seeing it as a pure illusion?
That would be too hasty, as it expresses a real and legitimate aspiration.
What it aims for, under a questionable formulation, is the rejection of alienation, of false living, of submission to the gaze of others that we have mentioned.

Being authentic, properly understood, may not be about being true to a given self, but about refusing to live in contradiction with what one believes, what one wants, what one judges to be good; it is not to renounce oneself, not to betray oneself, not to live a life that would not be one's own.
Authenticity as coherence, as a refusal of self-deception, retains all its meaning even if the 'authentic self' as a fixed thing is an illusion.
This reformulation changes everything.

If authenticity is not fidelity to a given self, but coherence between what one does and what one believes, then it is not the discovery of a nature, but a moral requirement, a way of conducting oneself.
Being true to oneself is not about exhuming a buried treasure; it is about building a coherent existence, taking responsibility for one's choices, and not living in contradiction with one's values.
The self to which one is faithful is not a prior given, but a work in progress, which fidelity itself helps to shape.
One does not find one's self; one makes it, striving not to betray it.

The ideal of authenticity, thus understood, ceases to be the impossible injunction to discover a hidden self, and becomes the difficult but sensible requirement to lead a coherent and non-alienated life.
It is not about digging within oneself to find one's truth, but about living in such a way that one can recognize oneself in what one does, not lying to oneself, not betraying oneself.
This kind of authenticity is not given; it is earned, through the effort to align one's life with one's convictions.
"Be yourself" therefore does not mean "conform to what you already are," but rather "make sure to become someone you won't be ashamed of"—which is a task, not a discovery.

sentences: Each of us belongs to a multitude of groups, cultures, and categories: a nation, a region, a family, a profession, a generation, sometimes multiple origins, multiple languages, multiple cultures.
Our identity is made up of these multiple affiliations, which overlap and intersect.
Yet, there is often pressure to reduce this multiplicity to a single identity, to compel everyone to choose 'who they really are,' as if one could only be one thing.
This reduction of identity to a single affiliation is one of the sources of many conflicts, and its logic must be questioned.
Let us first acknowledge the richness of multiple identities.

Being from a certain nation and a certain origin, speaking several languages, belonging to multiple cultures is not confusion or lack; it is a richness, an openness, the possibility of inhabiting multiple worlds and understanding various perspectives.

Those with multiple affiliations have a breadth of experience that those with only one do not; they can bridge different universes, translate one into another, and escape the confinement of a single vision.
The multiplicity of affiliations is not a problem to be solved, but a richness to be cultivated.
However, this richness is constantly threatened by the demand to choose.
Those with multiple affiliations are asked to say which one is the 'true' one, to choose their side, to align themselves.
This demand stems from a narrowed conception of identity, according to which one could only be one thing, belong to only one group, under penalty of betrayal or inauthenticity.
'You are this or that; you must choose': this injunction denies the reality of multiple identities, forcing one to mutilate who they are, to deny a part of themselves.
It transforms a richness into a heartbreaking dilemma.
This identity reduction is particularly dangerous because it is at the heart of many conflicts.

When everyone is compelled to define themselves by a single affiliation — a nation, a religion, an origin — the world is divided into exclusive, opposing groups, erasing everything that connects, everything that crosses borders, all shared affiliations.
Identity reduced to a single dimension becomes a principle of division and confrontation: I am this against those who are that.

Deadly identities, as one writer has termed them, arise precisely from this reduction, which makes one affiliation among others the entire identity, and pits people against each other in the name of this singular affiliation.
To this logic of reduction, we must oppose the recognition of complexity.
No one is reducible to just one of their affiliations; each person is made up of a unique intertwining of multiple affiliations that distinguishes them from all other members of each of their groups.
Two people from the same nation differ by a thousand other affiliations; what brings them together under a label does not exhaust who they are.

Recognizing this means refusing to confine others, as well as oneself, to a single identity; it means seeing in each person the irreducible complexity of their affiliations, rather than reducing them to the one that, in a given context, serves to oppose them.

Defending multiple identities against the demand to choose does not advocate for a vague identity without ties, but recognizes that attachment can be plural, that one can belong to multiple worlds without being disloyal to any.
It is to refuse that identity becomes a principle of exclusion and confrontation, and to make it what it can be: a richness made of multiple loyalties, a bridge rather than a wall.

In a world where deadly identity logics are awakening, where everyone is once again compelled to choose their side, affirming the legitimacy and richness of multiple identities is not only a truth about who we are; it is also, perhaps, a condition for peace.

sentences: Democracy today enjoys such prestige that it seems almost scandalous to question it: it is regarded as the best regime, the ultimate horizon of any legitimate political organization.
However, this obviousness is recent, and the most famous praise for it is strangely paradoxical: democracy is said to be the worst of regimes, except for all the others.
This formula, half-fig, half-raisin, deserves to be taken seriously, as it expresses something true about the nature of a regime that we often celebrate without fully understanding.
Let’s start with the criticisms that democracy has always faced, and which are not without merit.

It is criticized for entrusting power to the many, that is, to a majority that is not necessarily the most competent or the wisest; for making decisions dependent on public opinion, which is fickle and manipulable; for favoring demagoguery, where the people are flattered rather than served; for prioritizing the short term, since leaders depend on upcoming elections.
These criticisms, articulated since antiquity, are not absurd: democracy indeed has these weaknesses, and claiming otherwise would be blind.
The government of the many is not the government of the best, and it can make serious mistakes.
So why prefer democracy despite everything?
The answer does not lie in the fact that it would guarantee the best decisions — it does not guarantee that — but in other virtues that compensate for its weaknesses.
The first is that it allows for a change of leaders without violence.
In non-democratic regimes, getting rid of a bad leader often requires revolt or a coup, with their accompanying violence; democracy offers a peaceful way to dismiss those who govern poorly.
This ability to correct its mistakes without bloodshed is an immense virtue, which is underestimated as long as we enjoy it.
The second virtue is that democracy, by involving the governed in decisions, recognizes a dignity that other regimes deny them.
In a democracy, the citizen is not a mere subject who obeys, but a participant, whose voice matters, who has a share in the power that governs them.
This participation, however imperfect, acknowledges each person as capable of judging, deciding, and governing themselves, rather than as a minor who needs direction.
Democracy is based on a bet on the ability of ordinary people to govern themselves — a risky bet, but one that treats them as adults rather than children.
The third virtue, linked to the previous ones, is that democracy allows for dissent, criticism, debate, and thus the correction of its own mistakes.
A regime that forbids criticism locks itself into its faults, as no one can point them out; democracy, by allowing opposition and debate, gives itself the means to recognize and correct its mistakes.
It is not infallible, but it is correctable, which is better than a claimed infallibility that prohibits any questioning.
Its strength lies not in not making mistakes, but in being able to correct itself.
The paradoxical praise of democracy then makes sense.
It is not the best regime in the sense that it would guarantee the wisest decisions; in this regard, it has real weaknesses.
But it is the best in the sense that it offers what no other does: peaceful change, the dignity of the citizen, the ability to correct itself.

These virtues do not stem from its perfection, but from its very modesty: democracy is the regime that does not claim to possess truth or wisdom, and which, knowing it can make mistakes, gives itself the means to rectify.
That is why it must be defended not as a perfect regime, but as the least bad — which, in political matters where perfection does not exist, is the highest praise one can give.
We do not build ourselves alone.

The idea that we would be an autonomous 'self', forming independently of others, is an illusion: from childhood and throughout life, we construct ourselves under the gaze of others, through the way others see us, judge us, and recognize us.
This gaze of others is constitutive of who we are, and this dependence is ambivalent: it can be a blessing, a source of recognition and existence, or an alienation, a prison in which one gets lost.
Understanding this relationship is essential for thinking about identity.
Let’s first consider what the gaze of others has that is constitutive.
We become aware of ourselves largely through others: it is by being seen, named, and judged that we form an image of ourselves.
A child is shaped by the gaze of their parents; an adult is partly defined by how their surroundings perceive them.
We need to be recognized, seen, and confirmed in our existence by the gaze of others; without this recognition, our very identity wavers.
The gaze of others is therefore not a mere external addition; it contributes to making us who we are.
This dependence can be a blessing.
Being recognized, loved, and appreciated by others confirms our worth, gives us a place, and nourishes our self-esteem.
The benevolent gaze of others makes us exist, supports us, and allows us to unfold.
We need to be seen to feel real, recognized to feel worthy.

In this sense, the gaze of others is not a constraint, but a source: we build ourselves in and through mutual recognition, and this interdependence is the very fabric of our social existence and identity.
But this same gaze can become an alienation.
For by depending too much on the gaze of others, one risks losing oneself in it, existing only through it, and conforming one's being to what others expect or approve.

Those who excessively care about the image they project, who adjust their behavior based on the judgment of others, who exist only in approval, are prisoners of the gaze of others, alienated to an image that is no longer their own.
The gaze that could confirm then becomes a prison, where one disguises oneself to please, where one forgets oneself to meet expectations.
The recognition sought at all costs turns into servitude.
This alienation is exacerbated by our time, which has made self-exposure a permanent practice.

In a world where everyone constantly puts themselves on display, where one seeks approval through carefully staged images of oneself, dependence on the gaze of others reaches an unprecedented intensity.
We live under the supposed gaze of others, we adjust our existence based on the image we project, we measure our worth by the approval received.
This constant exposure, far from liberating, can trap us in an anxious quest for recognition, where we lose ourselves in the desire to be seen.
The issue is therefore not to free ourselves from the gaze of others — which is impossible and would not be desirable, as we need recognition — but to find a proper relationship to it.

This requires welcoming the recognition of others without becoming enslaved to it, taking into account the gaze of others without surrendering one's being to it, and maintaining, under the gaze, a relationship to oneself that does not depend entirely on it.
It is about existing through others without losing oneself in them, being recognized without renouncing oneself.
This difficult balance — welcoming the gaze without becoming alienated by it — is one of the conditions for an identity that is both connected to others and true to itself.
For we construct ourselves in the gaze of others, but we must not dissolve into it.

sentences: We spontaneously associate democracy with the power of the majority: what the largest number decides is democratic.
This equation, seemingly obvious, actually hides a danger that early democratic thinkers identified: the tyranny of the majority.
For the power of the largest number, if not limited, can oppress minorities and individuals just as surely as a tyrant, all in the name of the democratic principle.
Understanding this danger and the means to guard against it is essential to avoid confusing democracy with mere numerical rule.
The danger lies in the fact that a majority can, entirely legally within a democracy, oppress a minority.

If democracy were reduced to the rule that the majority decides everything, then nothing would prevent that majority from depriving a minority of its rights, persecuting it, or imposing its will without limits.
The legitimacy of the number does not guarantee the justice of the decision: a majority can want unjust, oppressive, cruel things, and the fact that it is a majority does not make them just.
Reducing democracy to the absolute power of the majority opens the door to oppression that masquerades as legitimacy.
There is something more insidious than legal oppression: the tyranny of the majority can also exert itself on minds, through the pressure of dominant opinion.
In a democratic society, the majority opinion exerts considerable force; it defines what is acceptable to think and say, and places pressure for conformity on those who deviate from it.
This kind of tyranny does not operate through law, but through the weight of collective judgment, through the fear of general disapproval, and through the silence it imposes on minority opinions.

It can stifle freedom of thought more effectively than any censorship, as it operates through each individual, in the inner thoughts of those who no longer dare to stray from what the majority thinks.
How can we guard against this double tyranny?
The answer has shaped true democracies, which are never reduced to pure majority power, but are framed by limits.

The first limit is that of fundamental rights, which are exempt from voting: certain things — essential freedoms, the dignity of individuals, the rights of minorities — cannot be abolished by any majority, no matter how large.
These inviolable rights mark a boundary that the number cannot cross; they protect the individual and the minority from the will of the majority itself.
A democracy is not just the power of the number; it is the power of the number limited by rights that escape it.
The second limit pertains to the separation of powers and the existence of counter-powers.

For a majority to not be able to do everything, power must be divided, independent institutions must be able to provide checks, and a justice system must be able to censure even majority decisions that are unjust.
These mechanisms, which limit the power of the majority, are not obstacles to democracy, but its conditions: without them, democracy would degenerate into tyranny of the number.
A true democracy is a balance between the power of the majority and the limits that prevent it from oppressing.
Recognizing the danger of the tyranny of the majority means understanding that democracy is not reduced to the rule of number, but requires limits that protect against the number itself.

It is to reject the simplistic idea that anything the majority wants is democratic, affirming instead that a democracy worthy of the name protects rights and freedoms against the very will of the majority.
This demand is today of burning relevance, where the legitimacy of the number is sometimes invoked to justify violations of minority rights or freedoms.

Reminding that the majority does not have all the rights, that democracy is also protection against it, is not anti-democratic: it is defending what distinguishes democracy from mere tyranny of the largest number.
