sentences: We venerate the truth, and rightly so: lies disgust us, sincerity seems to us a virtue, and the pursuit of truth is a noble endeavor.
However, this veneration of the truth, however legitimate it may be, encounters a difficulty that moral reflection has faced throughout time: is the truth always good to say?
Are there truths that would be better left unsaid, cases where telling the truth would do more harm than good, where the truth would conflict with other equally important values?
This question, which seems to challenge our attachment to the truth, actually requires us to clarify its meaning and limits.
We must first distinguish between telling the truth and not lying.
Not lying means not asserting what one believes to be false; telling the truth means revealing what one knows to be true.
There is a difference between these two requirements: one can refrain from lying while not telling the whole truth, by withholding certain things, by remaining silent.
The duty not to lie is stricter than the duty to say everything; one can be obliged not to assert falsehoods without being obliged to reveal all truths.

This distinction already sheds light on the question: for while it is almost always wrong to lie, it is not always mandatory to tell the whole truth, and silence, discretion, can be legitimate where lying would not be.
Let us consider cases where telling the truth seems problematic.
There is the truth that unnecessarily hurts: should one tell someone a cruel truth that would only cause them pain, without any benefit?
There is the truth that betrays a confidence, that reveals what should remain secret.
There is the truth that, when said at the wrong time, would do more harm than good, like terrible news announced without tact.
In these cases, telling the truth conflicts with other values: kindness, discretion, care for others.
And it is not obvious that the truth should always prevail, that the duty to tell the truth always takes precedence over the concern not to harm.
Should we conclude that one can sacrifice the truth in the name of other values, that it is permissible to lie to spare, to cushion, to do good?
That would be rushing to a conclusion and opening a dangerous door.
For lying, even with good intentions, has a cost: it betrays trust, it treats the other as incapable of bearing the truth, it arrogates the right to decide what others should know.
Lying 'for the good' of others is often a form of disguised contempt masquerading as benevolence, a way of treating the other as a minor who needs to be protected from the truth.
And it opens a slippery slope, where one easily convinces oneself that lying serves the good while it serves our comfort.
Distrust of lying, even well-intentioned, remains warranted.
The correct position perhaps lies in this distinction: between lying, which must be almost absolutely rejected, and silence or discretion, which can be legitimate.
One can, without lying, choose not to say a truth that would unnecessarily hurt, to keep secret what should remain so, to consider the timing and manner of conveying a difficult truth.
It is not betraying the truth to withhold it out of respect; it is betraying the truth to assert falsehood.

Wisdom regarding the truth is not about saying everything without regard for the consequences, nor about lying in the name of good, but about never asserting falsehood while knowing when to remain silent, to be considerate, to choose the timing and manner.

There is an art to telling the truth, which is neither the brutality of those who state it without regard, nor the cowardice of those who distort it, but the discernment of those who know how to express it accurately.
This reflection brings us back to what we said about the ethics of language.
Using the truth well is not just about not lying; it is also about knowing how to convey the truth accurately, at the right time, in the right way, with concern for others.
The truth is a precious good, but it is not the only one, and the art of living often consists of reconciling goods that may come into tension: truth and kindness, sincerity and care for others.
The truth is not always good to say brutally, without regard, at the wrong time; but it is almost always wrong to betray it through lies.

Between the duty not to lie, which is almost absolute, and the duty to say everything, which has exceptions, there is room for a wisdom that honors the truth without making it a weapon, that serves it without brandishing it, that never betrays it but knows when to remain silent.

sentences: I know that I know nothing." This statement, attributed to one of the greatest sages, expresses a paradox that has traversed the entire history of thought: that the highest wisdom would begin with the awareness of one's own ignorance, that true knowledge would include the knowledge of what we do not know.

At the end of this meditation on science and its limits, this statement deserves to be examined, as it gathers and crowns what has preceded it, designating a form of knowledge superior to the accumulation of facts: the clear awareness of the extent of one's ignorance.
Let us first understand this apparent paradox.
How could the knowledge of one's ignorance be a form of wisdom, even the highest?
Isn't it better to know than not to know?
The answer lies in a distinction: between the ignorant who does not know and does not know that he does not know, and the one who, knowing much, also knows the extent of what he ignores.

The former is doubly ignorant: he is ignorant, and he is unaware of his ignorance, believing himself to be knowledgeable; the latter is wiser, as he knows the limits of his knowledge and measures the extent of what eludes him.
The worst is not to be ignorant, but to be unaware that one is ignorant, to mistake one's ignorance for knowledge.
The awareness of one's ignorance is already a form of knowledge, and a valuable one: that of one's own limits.
This awareness has several virtues.

It is first and foremost the condition for all learning: for one only seeks to know what one knows one ignores; the one who believes himself knowledgeable learns no more, while the one who knows his ignorance remains open, curious, and capable of learning.
The awareness of one's ignorance is the driving force behind the desire to know, which keeps the mind in motion, in quest, awake.
The one who believes he knows closes himself off; the one who knows he does not know remains open.

That is why the greatest minds have often been those who best measured the extent of their ignorance, not out of false modesty, but out of lucidity: the more one knows, the more one measures the immensity of what one ignores, the more one discovers that acquired knowledge is merely an island in an ocean of the unknown.
This awareness is also a safeguard against the traps of false certainty.

We have seen this in relation to biases, ideology, and the limits of reason: the danger is not so much in ignorance as in believing one knows what one does not know, in mistaking one's opinions for truths, one's assumptions for self-evident facts.
The awareness of one's ignorance protects us from this presumption; it makes us cautious in our assertions, open to contradiction, capable of recognizing our mistakes.
It is the intellectual humility without which there is no honest thought, the remedy for dogmatism that takes its beliefs for knowledge.
Knowing that one does not know is to guard against the most dangerous of errors: the one that believes it holds the truth.
However, one must guard against a misunderstanding that would turn this wisdom into paralyzing skepticism, a renunciation of all knowledge.
"I know that I know nothing" does not mean that one cannot know anything, that all knowledge is equal, or that one should give up seeking the truth.
It is the opposite: it is because one knows the extent of one's ignorance that one seeks to reduce it; it is because one knows one's limits that one can push them back.
The awareness of one's ignorance is not a renunciation of knowledge, but its condition; it does not abolish the search for truth, it founds and animates it.
The wise person who knows he does not know is not the one who renounces knowledge, but the one who knows while being aware of his limits, who seeks while knowing what eludes him.
This wisdom of ignorance crowns our journey through the highest questions.

For all these reflections on language, time, the tragic, power, beauty, and science lead to the same recognition: that the deepest knowledge includes the awareness of its limits, that wisdom is not about knowing everything, but about knowing what one knows and what one ignores, measuring the extent of the mystery, and remaining open to what transcends us.

Knowing that one does not know is not an admission of failure, but the highest accomplishment of thought: the lucidity that, having learned much, measures the immensity of what remains unknown, and finds in this very measure, not discouragement, but humility, openness, and the ever-renewed desire to understand.

This may be the culmination of all wisdom, as of all learning: not the possession of completed knowledge, but the enlightened awareness of what we still have to learn, and the humility of one who, knowing much, knows above all how much he does not know.

sentences: We often conceive of morality as a set of rules: do not lie, do not steal, do not harm, keep your promises.
To be moral, in this view, would mean knowing these rules and following them; the moral person would be one who obeys the rules, while the immoral person would be one who transgresses them.
This conception has its strengths and conveniences: it provides clear guidelines, specific prohibitions, and an apparently simple criterion for right conduct.
But it may be insufficient, and we must ask whether morality really reduces to rules, or if it requires something that rules cannot capture.
Let us first acknowledge what rules have that is useful and necessary.

They provide stable reference points, valid for everyone, independent of circumstances and individuals; they protect against arbitrariness, against the rationalizations through which one justifies their faults, and against the weakness that yields to temptations.
A morality without rules, which would decide everything on a case-by-case basis according to circumstances, would risk arbitrariness, complacency, and uncertainty.
Moral rules have the virtue of establishing firm limits, prohibitions that are non-negotiable, a foundation upon which conduct can rely.
It would be naive to want a morality without any rules.
But rules also have their limits, as moral experience reveals.

First, they cannot foresee all cases; life presents situations that no rule had anticipated, cases where rules contradict each other, where applying one means violating another, and where following the rule to the letter would produce an injustice.
Should the rule 'do not lie' be followed when lying would save a life threatened by a criminal?
Difficult cases, where rules are insufficient and judgment is necessary, reveal that morality cannot be reduced to the mechanical application of rules.
Beyond rules, there needs to be a judgment that knows how to apply them, weigh them, and sometimes exceed them.
Furthermore, and more profoundly, following rules is not enough to be moral in the fullest sense.
One can respect all rules out of calculation, fear, or conformity, without any real virtue; one can refrain from lying, stealing, or harming only out of fear of consequences, without any goodness.
In contrast, true morality seems to demand more than mere adherence to rules: an inner disposition, a goodness, an attention to others, a generosity that exceeds what any rule prescribes.
The rule states what should not be done; it does not articulate positive goodness, generosity, or love for one's neighbor, which are nonetheless at the heart of moral life.
One can follow all the rules and still remain a mediocre being; one can, by sometimes transgressing the letter of a rule, demonstrate a higher goodness.
That is why a long moral tradition has emphasized not rules, but virtues, character, and inner disposition.
What matters, from this perspective, is not so much following rules as being a certain kind of person: just, good, courageous, generous, capable of discernment.
Virtue is not obedience to rules, but an acquired disposition, a way of being that inclines toward good, a character shaped by habit and education.
The virtuous person does good not because a rule commands it, but because they are so disposed; they do good with precision, in concrete situations, through a discernment that no rule can replace.
The morality of virtues shifts the focus from rules to character, from obedience to being.
The truth may lie in the complementarity of these approaches.

Rules are necessary, as reference points, as safeguards, as a foundation; but they are not sufficient, as they cannot foresee everything, nor can they replace positive goodness, nor the judgment that applies them.

Morality requires both rules and the discernment that knows how to apply them, prohibitions and the virtue that transcends them toward positive good, obedience to rules and the inner disposition that alone makes one truly moral.
Reducing morality to rules is to mutilate it, forgetting its heart, which is a certain quality of the soul; but rejecting all rules in the name of virtue alone opens the door to arbitrariness.
Moral wisdom holds both: to follow just rules, but with the discernment and goodness that exceed them — for being moral is not just about obeying, but about becoming a certain kind of being.

sentences: There is a voice within us that judges our actions, that approves or condemns, that praises or torments us: moral conscience.
This inner voice is experienced by everyone; it is the very foundation of our moral life, what makes us feel right and wrong, what makes us responsible.
But what is it, really?
Where does this voice come from, what is its authority, and should we always follow it?
These questions, which touch on the foundation of moral life, are more complex than they seem, because conscience, however precious it may be, is not an infallible oracle.
What is moral conscience?

It can be described as that inner feeling that accompanies our actions with approval or disapproval, that voice that tells us, before the act, what we should do, and afterwards, whether we acted rightly or wrongly.
It manifests itself through remorse when we have acted wrongly, through satisfaction when we have acted rightly, and through a sense of duty when we hesitate.
This voice has something imperious, something irreducible: we cannot silence it at will; it imposes itself on us, it judges us against our will.
It is in this voice that our moral dignity resides, our ability to judge ourselves, to be accountable for our actions, to distinguish right from wrong.
Where does this voice come from?
The answers vary deeply.

Some have seen it as the voice of God within us, the echo of a divine law inscribed in the heart of man; others, the voice of reason, which recognizes universal principles of good; still others, the product of our education, our culture, and the rules internalized since childhood; and finally, some see it as a disposition shaped by our social nature, our capacity for empathy, and our need to live with others.
These explanations are not necessarily mutually exclusive, and it is difficult to decide between them.

But their very diversity raises a difficulty: if conscience is partly the product of our education and culture, then it is not an infallible and universal voice, but a particular formation that can vary, make mistakes, and reflect the prejudices of its environment.
This difficulty is crucial, as it calls into question the authority of conscience.
Should we always follow our conscience?
One might be tempted to answer yes: acting against one's conscience, isn't that betraying oneself, doing what one believes to be wrong?
There is a truth in this answer: no one should act against what they firmly believe to be good, and following one's conscience is a requirement of moral integrity.
But there is also a danger: for conscience can be mistaken, poorly formed, reflect prejudices, and approve what is actually condemnable.
History is full of crimes committed in good conscience, by individuals convinced they were doing right, whose conscience, shaped by a distorted culture, ideology, or education, approved of horror.
Thus, following one's conscience does not guarantee acting rightly if that conscience is poorly formed.
From this follows an essential requirement: conscience must be enlightened, formed, educated.
It is not enough to follow one's conscience; it must also be right, informed, and capable of judging accurately.
A blind, poorly formed conscience filled with prejudices can lead to the worst acts while giving the feeling of acting rightly.
That is why moral life consists not only in following one's conscience, but also in forming it, enlightening it, examining it, and confronting it with reflection, discussion, and other viewpoints.
Conscience is not an oracle to be consulted; it is a faculty that must be cultivated, educated, and subjected to examination so that it judges accurately.
Following an unenlightened conscience can be as dangerous as not following one's conscience.
Thus, moral conscience occupies a place that is both central and paradoxical in moral life.
Central, because it is the locus of our responsibility, through which we judge and are accountable for our actions; no one should act against it, and its voice deserves respect and attention.
Paradoxical, because it is not infallible, can be mistaken, and must be formed and enlightened.

Moral wisdom consists in holding both: respecting one's conscience, not acting against what one firmly believes to be good, but also working to enlighten it, subjecting it to examination, and not treating it as an infallible oracle.

Listening to one's conscience and educating it, following it and examining it: this is the dual duty that makes moral life not mere obedience to a voice, but a demanding dialogue with a conscience that must be continually formed to be worthy of being followed.

sentences: The end justifies the means." This phrase, often quoted to be condemned, expresses one of the most troubling issues in the morality of action: can one do evil for the sake of a greater good?
Is it permissible to resort to condemnable means if the goal pursued is good, or even necessary?
This question is not academic; it arises in real action, especially in politics, where it is often claimed that one must do evil for a greater good.
Answering it requires untangling what the phrase mixes, and resisting two overly simple responses.
The first simple response is the one that unreservedly approves the phrase: yes, the end justifies the means, and if the goal is good, any means to achieve it is legitimate.
This position, often attributed to those in power, has an appearance of realism: in action, it says, one cannot afford scruples, one must be effective, and only the result matters.

But taken to its extreme, this position is monstrous: it justifies all crimes in the name of the ends they would serve, it abolishes any moral limit, and it makes the goal a universal justification for any means.

If the end really justified all means, then the worst atrocities would be permitted in the name of supposedly good goals, and history shows where this logic leads: to crimes committed in the name of brighter tomorrows, to horrors justified by the ends they were supposed to serve.

The second simple, opposite response absolutely condemns the phrase: no, the end never justifies the means, and certain acts are forbidden regardless of their consequences, no matter what good they might produce.
This position, more noble, asserts that there are limits that nothing can lift, acts that no end could justify, a dignity of the person that cannot be sacrificed for any goal.
It has on its side moral firmness, the refusal of the slope that justifies everything by the ends.

But it also encounters a difficulty: for there seem to be cases where absolutely refusing any condemnable means would lead to worse consequences, where intransigence on means would sacrifice immense goods.
Should we allow innocents to perish rather than transgress a rule?
The absolutism of means can also lead to results that are hard to accept.

Between these two positions, moral reflection has sought more nuanced paths, which recognize the complexity of the problem without yielding to either the cynicism that justifies everything or an absolutism that ignores the consequences.

One can distinguish according to the means: some are so radically contrary to dignity — torture, the murder of innocents — that no end could justify them, while others, lesser ones, can be weighed against the ends.
One can distinguish according to the ends: not all are equal, and the invoked good must be real, certain, proportional, not a distant and hypothetical pretext.

One can recognize that action sometimes involves the tragic, those situations where every choice is culpable, where one cannot act without getting their hands dirty, and where one must assume the share of evil in their action without absolving themselves.
For perhaps this is where the deepest truth about this question lies: in the recognition of the tragic nature of action.

The one who acts, especially in public affairs, is sometimes confronted with situations where every option involves evil, where one must choose the lesser evil without that lesser evil ceasing to be evil.

Lucidity then consists not in persuading oneself that the end justifies the means, erasing the fault, nor in refusing to act in the name of purity, but in assuming the share of evil in one's action while recognizing it as such.

The responsible person of action is neither the cynic who believes themselves justified by their ends, nor the pure who refuses to get their hands dirty; it is the one who, sometimes forced into dubious means, bears the weight of it without absolving themselves, who retains a sense of fault even when they believe they must commit it.
The phrase 'the end justifies the means' is therefore both false and incomplete.
False, if it means that the goal erases the nature of the means, that anything is permitted in the name of the ends; that would abolish all morality.
Incomplete, because it ignores the complexity: that some means are absolutely forbidden, that others can be weighed, that action sometimes involves the tragic.

True wisdom is neither to justify everything by the ends, nor to ignore the consequences in the name of abstract purity, but to hold together the respect for absolute limits, the weighing of consequences, and the tragic lucidity that assumes the share of evil in action without ever absolving itself.
The end does not justify the means; but it does not make them indifferent either; and acting morally, in an imperfect world, often means bearing the weight of this tearing.

sentences: We have distinguished between suffered solitude, which is suffering, and chosen solitude, which is richness.
But there is a third solitude, deeper than the other two, that no choice or company can abolish: essential solitude, which pertains to our very condition as conscious beings.
Each of us is a unique consciousness, a singular perspective on the world, confined in a sense to our own experience, which no one can fully share.

This solitude is neither a misfortune to be cured nor a good to be cultivated; it is a given of our condition that must be faced to understand what we are and what our relationships with others can or cannot be.
What does this essential solitude consist of?
It consists in the fact that each person experiences the world from their own point of view, in their own consciousness, and that this lived experience is, by nature, fundamentally incommunicable.
I cannot feel your pain as you feel it, nor can you feel mine; I cannot see the world through your eyes, nor enter your consciousness.
We can communicate, understand each other, draw closer; but there remains, at the core of each person, a lived experience that no one shares, a unique perspective that remains their own.

I am the only one who is me, the only one who feels what I feel from the inside; and this solitude, no company, no love, no communication can abolish, for it pertains to the very structure of consciousness.
This essential solitude reveals itself with particular acuity in certain experiences.
Suffering, first: the one who suffers is alone with their pain, which no one can feel in their place, however compassionate they may be.
Death, then, the ultimate trial of solitude: one dies alone, no one can die in our place nor accompany us beyond a certain threshold.
But also the most intimate experiences, the deepest thoughts, what is most personal in us, which remains, at its core, incommunicable.
There is in each person a core of solitude that nothing can break, a part of us that remains alone, regardless of our ties and surroundings.
This recognition may seem despairing, as if it condemns us to irredeemable isolation, as if others are forever inaccessible to us.
But that would be a misunderstanding of essential solitude.

For recognizing that there is in each person an incommunicable core does not mean that communication is impossible, that connections are futile, that we are locked in ourselves without access to others.
We communicate, we understand each other, we love each other, despite and through this solitude; simply, this communication does not abolish it entirely, it builds bridges over an abyss that remains.

Recognizing essential solitude does not deny the possibility of connection; it means understanding its true nature, which is not fusion but a meeting between beings who remain, at their core, distinct.
There is even something precious in this essential solitude when we understand it well.
For it is the correlate of our singularity, of our uniqueness, of what makes each person irreplaceable.

If we could completely merge into one another, fully share our experience, abolish all solitude, we would cease to be distinct individuals, unique consciousnesses; essential solitude is the price and the guarantee of our individuality.
It is what makes each person someone, a unique perspective on the world, a being who is not interchangeable.
Essential solitude is not just a limit to our relationships; it is also what underpins the value of each being as singular.
Understanding essential solitude transforms our relationship with others and with ourselves.
With ourselves, by reconciling with this part of irreducible solitude, by ceasing to experience it as a lack to be filled, by recognizing that it is the correlate of our singularity.

With others, by understanding that true connection is not the fusion that would abolish all distance, but the meeting that respects each person's solitude, the bridge thrown over the abyss that remains.
Loving others is not about abolishing their essential solitude or ours, but about recognizing and respecting that solitude while building bridges of love and understanding towards it.

The most beautiful relationship is not one that would deny essential solitude, but one that, recognizing it, unites two solitudes that respect each other — for, as a poet said, the highest love is perhaps that where two solitudes protect, limit, and greet each other.

sentences: There is a question about the nature of goodness that has long divided moral thought: is true goodness spontaneous or costly?

Must we, in order to be truly good, have goodness come naturally to us, to do it effortlessly, by inclination; or does true moral value, on the contrary, require effort, struggle against oneself, victory over one's inclinations?
This question, seemingly subtle, touches on what constitutes the moral value of an act and a being, and the opposing answers reveal two deep conceptions of morality.
One conception sees spontaneous goodness as the highest.
The one who does good naturally, effortlessly, out of a generous inclination, would be truly good; their goodness would be pure, uncalculated, unforced.

In contrast, the one who must struggle against their bad inclinations to do good would reveal, through that very struggle, that they are not truly good, that evil attracts them, and that they only do good by forcing themselves.
According to this view, accomplished virtue is that which has become second nature, which does good with ease, spontaneously, without effort or struggle.
The truly good person would be one for whom doing good is self-evident, who does not have to force themselves, whose goodness flows naturally.
This conception has its strength and beauty; it describes an ideal of accomplished virtue, where goodness has become natural.
But it faces a powerful objection, brought forth by an opposing conception.

For if spontaneous goodness is admirable, it also seems, in a sense, to lack merit: the one who does good naturally, due to a fortunate temperament, has no more merit than one who is born beautiful or intelligent; their goodness is a gift, not a conquest.

Moral merit, from this perspective, requires effort, struggle, victory over oneself: the one who does good by overcoming their contrary inclinations, by fighting against themselves, deserves more, for their goodness is a conquest, not a received gift.
Moral value would lie in effort, not in ease.
These two conceptions seem irreconcilable, yet each captures a part of the truth.

It is true that spontaneous goodness has something admirable about it, that a virtue that has become natural and easy is an accomplishment; it would be strange to prefer a goodness that is always painful, always forced, to a goodness that has become second nature.

But it is also true that effort, struggle, and victory over oneself have their own moral value, that the one who does good despite their contrary inclinations demonstrates a moral strength that the one for whom everything is easy does not have.
How can we reconcile these two truths?
Perhaps by distinguishing two moments in moral life.

At the beginning, goodness is costly: one must struggle against their inclinations, force themselves, conquer within themselves the disposition to do good; this is the time of effort, where moral value is proven in battle.
But this repeated effort can shape a disposition, a habit, a character, where doing good gradually becomes easier, more natural, until it becomes second nature.
The spontaneous goodness of the accomplished person is not then an initial gift, but the fruit of long effort, virtue conquered and made natural through practice.
What was costly becomes easy, not through a received gift, but through a completed conquest.

Thus, the two conceptions reconcile: true goodness is spontaneous, but this spontaneity is the fruit of effort; it is a gift, but a gift that one has given to oneself through the patient conquest of virtue.
This conception has both demanding and encouraging implications.
Demanding, because it refuses to exempt one from effort on the grounds that one might not be naturally good: goodness is conquered, it requires struggle, work on oneself.
Encouraging, because it affirms that this conquest is possible, that repeated effort can shape a character, transform a disposition, make easy what was difficult.
One is not born good, or one is only good to varying degrees; but one can become good through practice, habit, and self-formation.
Goodness is neither a pure gift that one has or does not have, nor a perpetual effort without hope of ease; it is a conquest that, patiently pursued, can become second nature.
Being good without effort is possible, not as a starting point, but as an outcome — the culmination of a long work on oneself that has turned painful goodness into natural goodness.
And perhaps that is the highest answer: that accomplished virtue is that which, having been conquered through effort, has become so much our own that it no longer demands it.

sentences: We interact with others, talk to them, believe we know them; and yet, one troubling question remains: can we really know others?

Do we have access to what they truly are, to their inner life, to their consciousness, or do we only ever reach appearances, behaviors, words, never penetrating that core which essential solitude renders inaccessible?
This question, a continuation of the previous one, touches on the very possibility of knowing others, and thus on the nature of our most intimate relationships.
The problem is real and profound.
I only have direct access to my own consciousness; that of others is, by nature, inaccessible from the inside.
I perceive only their body, gestures, words, expressions; their inner life, thoughts, feelings, I only know indirectly, through what they show and what I infer.
I can never verify that what I infer about their inner self corresponds to what they actually feel; there remains, between their consciousness and mine, a distance that nothing quite crosses.
In a rigorous sense, I never know others directly; I interpret them, I guess them, I reconstruct them based on what they allow me to perceive.

This difficulty has fostered skepticism about knowing others: we would be forever trapped in our own consciousness, unable to reach that of others, condemned to know only appearances behind which the inner life of others would remain forever hidden.
This position has its logical strength, but it clashes with our experience.
For we do indeed have the feeling of knowing certain beings, of understanding them, of guessing what they feel, sometimes better than they understand themselves.
Is this feeling illusory?
Or do we really reach others, despite the impossibility of direct access to their consciousness?
Perhaps we must acknowledge that knowing others, while not being impossible direct access to their consciousness, is nonetheless real, of a different nature.
We do not know others as we know ourselves, from the inside; but we know them in our own way, through meeting, frequenting, paying attention, and empathy.

By continually being around a being, observing them, communicating with them, putting ourselves in their shoes, we acquire knowledge of them that, while not access to their consciousness, is nonetheless real and sometimes profound.
This knowledge consists of interpretation, inference, and empathy; it remains fallible, uncertain, never complete; but it reaches something of the other, it is not pure illusion.
We know others not by entering their consciousness, but by meeting them, interpreting them accurately, and opening ourselves to them.
We must nonetheless recognize the limits of this knowledge, and guard against the illusion of knowing others entirely.

For even the closest, best-known being retains a part of mystery, unpredictability, and unfathomability; we never exhaust them, they can always surprise us, escape us, reveal themselves to be different from what we believed.
This irreducible part of mystery in others is not just a limit of our knowledge; it is the respect owed to their freedom, their uniqueness, and their essential solitude.

To claim to know others entirely, to confine them to the idea we have of them, is in a sense to do violence to them, denying their freedom to surprise us, their capacity to change, their inexhaustible depth.
The just knowledge of others includes the recognition of what they keep unknowable.
This conception has an ethical dimension.

For knowing others, in this respect for their mystery, is also a way of treating them justly: not to confine them to a fixed image, to remain open to what they can reveal to us, to approach them with the humility of someone who knows they never fully know them.
The worst way to treat others is to believe we know them inside and out, to reduce them to the idea we have of them, to deny their depth and freedom.

The just knowledge of others is one that seeks to understand them while respecting their mystery, that interprets them accurately while remaining open to seeing them differently, that truly reaches them while recognizing it never exhausts them.

In essence, knowing others is not about piercing their secret, but about maintaining a relationship with them where understanding and respect for the mystery come together — where we approach them without ever claiming to possess them entirely.

sentences: This winter, it hasn't snowed a single time here.
Not once.
In December, in January, in February: it was gray and damp, with temperatures of eight or ten degrees.
It rained a lot, but the water remained just water.
My children were disappointed.
My daughter asked me, "Are we going to make a snowman this year?" I replied, "We'll see." We didn't make one.
This isn't the first time.
Last winter, it snowed only one day, and the snow melted before evening.
One Sunday, we had lunch at my grandmother's.
My daughter talked to her about the snow.
My grandmother smiled, then she told stories about her childhood in the same village.
Every winter, there was snow for weeks.
My brother and I would go to school on skis because the road was closed.
My daughter looked at her with wide eyes.
Skis?
To go to school?
Every winter,” replied my grandmother.
Then she added, “Here, snow was normal.
Now, it's an event.”
In the car, my daughter was silent.
Then she asked, “Will it still snow when I am grown up?”
I didn't know what to say.

sentences: Every language names certain things and leaves others unsaid; it illuminates some areas of experience while leaving others in the dark, due to a lack of words to express them.
This silence of language, these experiences that our language does not name, raise a troubling question: does what has no name exist for us?
Does the absence of a word condemn an experience to non-existence, or does it persist, silent, waiting for the word that will reveal it?
This question, an extension of our previous reflections, touches on the most intimate relationships between language, perception, and being.
It is certain that language guides our attention, and that what it names, we perceive better.

A language that distinguishes several shades of a color, several states of an emotion, and several forms of a human relationship with specific words makes its speakers more attentive to these distinctions; conversely, what a language does not name tends to go unnoticed, blending into the indistinct.
The word, by naming, carves out experience, makes it stand out, and brings it into existence as an object of attention.
What our language does not name thus risks remaining below our conscious perception, not because it does not exist, but because nothing designates it, detaches it, or makes it noticeable.
But should we conclude that what has no name does not exist at all for us?
That would be going too far.

For we often experience things that we cannot name, confused emotions, vague perceptions, states that have no word in our language and yet are there, obscurely present, demanding a name that they do not yet have.

This experience of the unnamed — this feeling of experiencing something for which words are lacking — proves that experience can precede the word, that it exists before being named, even in the shadows of consciousness.
What has no name is therefore not nothing; it is what awaits its name, what exists in the realm of the obscure, the confused, the formless, before the word comes to reveal and articulate it.
It is here that the creative power of language is revealed.

For naming an experience that has hitherto been unnamed is not just labeling it; it is bringing it fully into existence, pulling it out of the shadows, constituting it as an object of consciousness and thought.
When a new word comes to name an experience that everyone felt but could not express, something happens: this experience, suddenly named, stands out, becomes recognizable, shareable, thinkable.
The word does not create the experience out of nothing; rather, it fulfills it, moving it from the obscure to the clear, from the private to the shared, from the sensed to the conceived.

That is why the creation of missing words is an act of immense significance: it gives full existence to what existed only partially, it makes what everyone felt in the solitude of the unnamed expressible and therefore shareable.
This revealing function of language has an ethical and political dimension that we would be wrong to overlook.

For there are sufferings, injustices, and experiences that, lacking words to name them, remain invisible, unspeakable, condemned to silence; those who endure them feel them without being able to express, denounce, or have them recognized.
To forge the word that names them is to make them exist in the common space, allowing them to be recognized and fought against.
Many struggles have begun with the conquest of a word, through the naming of a reality that the absence of a name kept in the shadows.
The silence of what has no name is not always innocent; it can be the silence imposed on what we prefer not to see, and giving it a name is then an act of justice.
Thus, what has no name occupies a singular status: neither fully existing for us nor entirely nonexistent, it lingers in the twilight of the unnamed, demanding the word that will fulfill it.
Language does not create experience out of nothing, but it reveals it, constitutes it, and brings it from the obscure to the clear.

That is why enriching a language, forging the missing words, and learning the words of another language for what one's own does not express is not just a simple vocabulary game: it is about expanding the realm of the sayable, and therefore of the thinkable, shareable, and existent.

Every word conquered from silence is a region of experience torn from the shadows — and one who learns a new language does not just gain words, but entire sections of a world that their mother tongue perhaps left in the silence of the unnamed.

sentences: We most often use the word 'ideology' to refer to the beliefs of others, those we consider false, biased, dictated by interests or prejudices: the opponent is 'ideological', while we would be clear-sighted and objective.
This polemical usage masks what ideology really is, which is much deeper and more troubling.

For ideology is not primarily what others think; it is what makes us think what we think, without our awareness, the set of representations that seem obvious to us and which, precisely because they seem obvious, escape our scrutiny.
Ideology is less a content than an environment, the very air we breathe without seeing it.
Let us understand this deeper conception of ideology.
Every society, every era, is permeated by representations that seem self-evident, shared certainties about what is normal, natural, desirable, about how things are and should be.
We do not perceive these certainties as opinions, as positions among other possible ones; we take them for reality itself, for common sense, for what goes without saying.

Yet it is precisely these that constitute ideology: not explicit convictions that one would defend, but implicit presuppositions that structure our thinking without us questioning them, because they seem too obvious to be presuppositions.
Ideology is what thinks in us before we think, the invisible framework that guides our representations.
This concept has a formidable consequence: we are all, always, caught in an ideology, even when we believe ourselves to be the most clear-sighted.
For ideology is not something we can escape simply by goodwill, by deciding to be objective; it is the very medium of our thought, which makes it possible by orienting it.

To believe that we are outside of any ideology, that we see things as they are while others are blinded by theirs, is the very mark of the deepest ideological blindness: for it is to take the obviousness of one's own ideology for reality itself.
The height of ideology is to believe oneself to be without ideology; the one who thinks they are perfectly clear-sighted is the one who does not see the framework that structures their clarity.
Should we conclude that we are irredeemably prisoners of ideology, incapable of any truth, condemned to see the world only through frameworks that blind us?
This skeptical conclusion would be excessive and paralyzing.
For if we can never place ourselves outside of any ideology, at an absolute and neutral viewpoint, we can become aware of our presuppositions, question them, relativize them, and change them.
We cannot see without a framework, but we can examine our frameworks, compare them to others, and discover their contingency.

This clarity is never total or definitive — we always remain caught in some ideology — but it is real and gradual: one can be more or less aware of their presuppositions, more or less capable of questioning them.
The freedom regarding ideology is not to free oneself absolutely from it, which is impossible, but to make it visible, to submit it to examination, and not to take it for reality itself.
How can we gain this relative clarity?
Several paths lead to it.
Confrontation with other cultures, other eras, and other ways of thinking reveals the contingency of our own certainties by showing that we can think differently.
History, which shows that what we consider natural has an origin, has been different, could be different, deconstructs our assumptions.
Encountering those who think differently, if we truly listen to them, allows us to see our own frameworks by colliding them with theirs.
All these paths have one thing in common: they displace us, pull us away from the obviousness of our point of view, and make us see from the outside what we lived from the inside as self-evident.
To detach ourselves a bit from our ideology is to learn to see ourselves through the eyes of another.
Recognizing that ideology is the air we breathe, and not just what others breathe, is therefore the beginning of possible clarity.
This frees us from the most dangerous illusion, that of believing we are outside of any ideology, and invites us to be vigilant regarding our own certainties.

This also makes us fairer towards those who think differently: for if we are all caught in some ideology, then the opponent is not the only 'ideologue' while we would be clear-sighted; we all are, and this shared condition should temper our confidence.

In a world where everyone denounces the ideology of others while believing themselves to be clear-sighted, true clarity begins with the recognition of one's own ideology—not to renounce it, which is impossible, but to stop confusing it with the truth.

sentences: Forgiveness is regarded as a great virtue, a transcendence of vengeance, a liberation for both the one who grants it and the one who receives it.
But as soon as we reflect on it, forgiveness reveals itself to be filled with formidable paradoxes.
Are there unforgivable offenses, or can everything be forgiven?
Does forgiveness have meaning if it is always owed, or does it precisely imply that it could be refused?
Must the guilty party repent in order to be forgiven, or can forgiveness be unconditional?
These questions, far from being trivial, touch on what is most profound and most difficult about forgiveness.
Let's first consider the question of unforgivable wrongs.
One position holds that everything can be forgiven, that there is no wrong that forgiveness cannot reach, and that refusing to forgive would be a failure of virtue.
This position has its grandeur: it asserts the unlimited power of forgiveness, its ability to overcome the worst.
But it faces a formidable objection: some wrongs seem so egregious that forgiving them would trivialize them, betray the victims, and erase the horror.
Can we, should we forgive extreme crimes, those that go beyond all measure?
And who could do it?
Certainly not third parties, who have not suffered the wrong; and the victims themselves, when they are no longer there to forgive, leave the wrong in a kind of irredeemable state.
It seems that there are wrongs that exceed forgiveness, not because forgiveness is limited, but because forgiving them would be an injustice to what they have destroyed.
Here we encounter a first paradox: forgiveness may only make sense in the face of what seems unforgivable.
For forgiving what is easily excusable, a minor fault, a trivial offense, is not really forgiveness; it is excusing, forgetting, letting it go.
Forgiveness in the strong sense only begins where excuses are no longer sufficient, in the face of a real, serious fault that could legitimately provoke resentment.
Forgiveness presupposes the fault, a fault that cannot be excused, and it precisely consists of not demanding the punishment that this fault would deserve, renouncing legitimate resentment.
Thus, true forgiveness is only exercised in the face of what, in a sense, does not deserve it; it is gratuitous, exceeding what is owed.
If it were always owed, it would no longer be forgiveness, but justice; it is because it could be refused that it has the value of a gift.
A second paradox concerns the condition of forgiveness.
Must the guilty party repent, acknowledge their fault, and ask for forgiveness in order to be forgiven?
This condition seems reasonable: how can one forgive someone who regrets nothing, persists in their wrongdoing, and does not ask for forgiveness?
Forgiveness granted to someone who does not repent seems futile, even complicit.
And yet, subordinating forgiveness to repentance may distort it: for then forgiveness becomes conditional, deserved, almost owed to the one who repents, and it loses its gratuitousness.
The highest, most difficult form of forgiveness might be the one granted unconditionally, without waiting for repentance, as a pure grace.
But does such unconditional forgiveness not risk trivializing the wrongdoing, freeing the guilty party from any self-reflection?
The paradox lies here: conditional forgiveness may not be true forgiveness, but unconditional forgiveness risks injustice.
These paradoxes do not have simple solutions, and it would be presumptuous to claim to resolve them.

But they reveal the profound nature of forgiveness: that it is neither a right nor an oblivion, neither justice nor complacency, but something excessive, gratuitous, and almost impossible, which only makes sense in the face of what seems to reject it.
True forgiveness is difficult precisely because it is not owed, because it is exercised in the face of what could legitimately provoke resentment, because it exceeds justice without abolishing it.

It consists neither in excusing the wrongdoing, nor in forgetting it, nor in renouncing justice, but in overcoming personal resentment, in not allowing the wrongdoing to poison indefinitely the one who has suffered it.
What remains, in light of these paradoxes, is that forgiveness, if it is possible, is a liberation, but a liberation primarily for the one who forgives.
For resentment, hatred, and the desire for revenge first poison the one who harbors them; forgiveness, by renouncing them, frees the one who grants it from the poison of their own bitterness.

Forgiveness does not erase the fault, does not bring justice, does not resurrect what has been destroyed; but it liberates the one who forgives from the grip of the wrong suffered, refusing to let the harm received continue to dominate them through resentment.
In this sense, even in the face of what seems unforgivable, a form of forgiveness can be a victory: not over the fault, which remains, but over its power to confine us in hatred.

To forgive may not be to absolve the guilty, but to free oneself — and perhaps it is in this liberation that the deepest and most accessible meaning of forgiveness lies, one that can never be an acquittal regarding certain wrongs.

sentences: Love claims to know the other like no one else does, to reach within them what others do not see, to understand them in their profound truth.
But it is also said that love is blind, that it idealizes the beloved, that it invents them according to its desire rather than seeing them as they are.
These two contradictory statements — love sees better, love is blind — express a deep paradox of love as a way of knowing others.
To love, is it to know the other better than anyone else, or to misunderstand them by adorning them with the colors of one's desire?
The question touches on what is most mysterious about love in its relationship to the truth of the beloved.
Let us first consider the thesis of blind love.
It is true that love idealizes, embellishes, and adorns the beloved with qualities they do not have or exaggerates.
The lover sees in the beloved a perfection that others do not see, attributes virtues to them, excuses their flaws, and contemplates them through the distorting prism of their desire.
This idealization is very real, and it explains the disappointments of love, when the veil is torn and the beloved appears as they are, different from the image one had of them.
In this sense, love misunderstands: it does not see the other as they are, but as desire dreams them; it invents an ideal being that is not the real being.
Love would then be the subtlest form of misunderstanding others, one that, under the guise of seeing them better, veils them behind an image.
And yet, the opposite thesis also has its truth.
For love, through the attention it gives to the beloved and the passionate interest it devotes to them, can reach in them what indifference does not see.

The one who loves observes the beloved with an intensity that no one else grants them, perceives their nuances, guesses their states, and opens up to their uniqueness with an acuity that only love provides.
In this sense, love sees better: it knows the beloved with a finer, more attentive, and deeper knowledge than the indifferent gaze.
It can perceive in the other possibilities, a beauty, a value that others do not see, not out of illusion, but through a sharper attention.
Love would then be the highest form of knowledge of others, one that, through passionate attention, reaches what indifference misses.
How can we reconcile these two truths?
Perhaps by distinguishing two forms or two moments of love.

There is a love that idealizes, that projects an image onto the other, that loves them less for what they are than for what we dream they might be; this love misrecognizes, and it is doomed to disillusion.

And there is a more mature love, which sees the other as they are, with their flaws and limitations, and loves them nonetheless, not despite their reality, but in their reality; this love knows, and it is stronger, for it has no illusions to lose.

The transition from one to the other — from the love that idealizes to the love that knows and loves the real — is perhaps the very maturation of love, what distinguishes illusory passion from true love.
There is more.
True love not only has the power to see the other as they are; it may also have the ability to help them become better, to reveal possibilities within them that they actualize under that gaze.
For being loved, being seen with that attention, that trust, that faith in what one can be, can help us to become it.
Love that sees the best in the other does not necessarily make mistakes; it can evoke what it perceives, calling the other to become what it sees in them.
In this sense, the idealization of love is not always an illusion; it can be a forward-looking vision that perceives possibilities and contributes to realizing them.
Love does not merely know the other; it participates in making them become.
Love is thus, in its relationship with others, both knowledge and misunderstanding, clarity and blindness, depending on its form and maturity.

Immature love idealizes and misunderstands; mature love sees and knows; and the highest love, perhaps, sees the other as they are while perceiving what they can become, knows their reality while believing in their possibilities.

To truly love is neither to blind oneself to the other nor to reduce them to what they are, but to know them in their truth while loving them enough to help them become the best version of themselves.

It is this conjunction of clarity and faith, of knowledge of the real and vision of the possible, that makes love neither a deceptive misunderstanding nor a cold knowledge, but the highest way to reach others: the one that sees them as they are and loves them as they could be.

sentences: Desire is the driving force of our lives: we are constantly desiring, and this tension towards what we do not have moves us, pushes us, and makes us act.
But desire seems to be linked to lack: to desire is to want what we do not have, to reach for what is missing; and this connection between desire and lack appears to condemn it to dissatisfaction.
For hardly have we obtained what we desired than desire shifts, seeks a new object, and is reborn as a lack of something else.
Desire would thus be a perpetual dissatisfaction, an endless pursuit where we are always lacking.
Is this conception, deep and ancient, the truth of desire, or can it be something other than a lack destined to never be fulfilled?
The conception of desire as lack has a long history and great strength.
It faithfully describes a common experience: that desire arises from a lack, reaches towards what is missing, and shifts as soon as it is fulfilled.
According to this view, desire is essentially dissatisfaction: we only desire what we do not have, and possessing the object of desire extinguishes desire, which immediately reappears elsewhere.
Desire would therefore be a suffering, a perpetual lack, a quest doomed to failure; and wisdom would consist in freeing oneself from it, extinguishing desire to escape the dissatisfaction it brings.
This conception, taken to its conclusion, leads to a condemnation of desire and a wisdom of detachment, which seeks peace in the extinction of desire.
However, this conception, no matter how profound it may be, may not fully capture the truth of desire.
For there are desires that do not seem to be mere lacks, desires that are more about abundance than deficiency, expressions of a fullness rather than deprivation.

The desire to create, to give, to love, is not always the lack of what one does not have; it can be the overflow of what one has, the expansion of a force, the generosity of a being that overflows from within.

The artist who desires to create, the generous person who desires to give, the lover who desires the well-being of their beloved, do not necessarily lack; they express a fullness, an inner richness that spreads.
Thus, there would be two kinds of desires: the lack-desire, which aims at what is missing, and the fullness-desire, which expresses an abundance, an overflow of life.
This distinction transforms the relationship to desire.
If every desire were a lack, wisdom would be to free oneself from it; but if there exists a fullness-desire, then desire is not only to be extinguished, it can be cultivated, directed, and fulfilled.
The desire to create, to give, to love, is not a suffering to be eliminated, but a wealth to be unfolded; it does not call for detachment, but for commitment, expression, and realization.

The question is no longer to extinguish desire, but to distinguish desires, to discern those that are an insatiable lack from those that are a creative fullness, and to direct one's life towards the latter rather than allowing oneself to be consumed by the former.
This conception also sheds light on the nature of love.
For love can be either of the two desires.

There is a love that is lack, that seeks to fill a void in the other, that loves out of need, that possesses more than it gives; this love is greedy, anxious, never satisfied, because it expects the other to fill a lack that nothing can fill.

And there is a love that is fullness, that loves out of abundance, that desires the well-being of the beloved more than possession, that gives more than it takes; this love is not lack but generosity, not greed but giving.
The difference between these two loves — the lack-love that takes and the fullness-love that gives — is perhaps the deepest there is in terms of love, and it determines its value.
Thus, desire is not necessarily condemned to lack and dissatisfaction.

If it is true that a large part of our desires are lacks destined to never be fulfilled, and that regarding them a certain wisdom of detachment holds truth, there are also desires that are fullness, overflow, generosity, and that call for not extinction but fulfillment.

The wisdom regarding desire is therefore not simply to extinguish it, but to discern and direct it: to free oneself from lack-desires that devour us without fulfilling us, and to cultivate fullness-desires that express and unfold what we have of the best.

Not to desire nothing anymore, which would mean ceasing to live, but to desire differently: less out of lack than out of fullness, less to take than to give, less to fill a void than to spread a richness.
For the highest desire may not be the one that lacks and wants to possess, but the one that overflows and wants to give.

sentences: At the end of this meditation on solitude, the knowledge of others, love, and desire, one image can bring together what we have glimpsed: that of love as the meeting of two solitudes that recognize and protect each other.
A poet wrote that love consists in this: that two solitudes protect, limit, and greet each other.

This formula, of striking depth, expresses what the highest love can be: not the abolition of each person's solitude in a fusion, but the respectful meeting of two beings who remain, at their core, distinct and alone, and who love each other precisely in this mutual recognition of their solitude.
This conception opposes a widespread image of love: that of fusion, of union which would abolish distance, make two beings one, and dissolve each person's solitude in total communion.
This image of love-fusion has its allure; it expresses the desire to escape one's solitude, to merge with the other, to no longer be two.
But it may be a delusion, and even a danger.
For fusion, if it were possible, would abolish what gives each person their value: their uniqueness, their individuality, their own being.

To want to completely merge with the other, or to absorb them into oneself, is in a sense to wish for their disappearance as a distinct being; love-fusion, taken to its extreme, is possessive, devouring, and denies the otherness of the beloved instead of respecting it.
Love as the meeting of two solitudes is something entirely different.
It does not seek to abolish distance, to merge beings, or to deny their essential solitude; it recognizes, respects, and protects it.

To love in this way is not to want to possess the other, to absorb them, to make them one's own; it is to recognize their otherness, their freedom, their solitude, and to love them in that very distance that makes them different.
Two solitudes that greet each other: each remains itself, distinct, with its mystery and freedom, and it is across this respected distance that they meet, recognize, and love each other.

This love does not fill the essential solitude — we have seen that nothing can — but it transforms it: from a solitude endured, it becomes a solitude inhabited by the presence of the other, recognized and shared.
This conception of love has profound implications for the way we love.
It invites us to respect the freedom of the beloved, not to want to possess, control, or confine them to our own idea of them; to allow them their mystery, their uniqueness, their own space.
It invites us to love the other as other, not as an extension of ourselves, a mirror, or an object to possess; to rejoice in their otherness rather than wanting to diminish it.
It invites us to that ultimate delicacy which consists of protecting the solitude of the beloved as much as our own, not to invade, to maintain the distance that allows each to remain themselves.
The greatest respect in love is perhaps that which recognizes in the beloved a being who does not belong to us, a freedom that we do not possess, a solitude that we cannot and must not abolish.
This way of loving is more demanding than the ideal of fusion, and undoubtedly rarer.
For it is easier to want to possess, absorb, and merge than to respect the otherness, to protect the distance, and to love the other in their freedom.

Fusion flatters the desire to escape oneself, to abolish one's solitude; the respect for two solitudes requires maturity, generosity, and a renunciation of possession, which are the fulfillment of love rather than its starting point.

But it is in this demand that the greatness of true love resides: not in the impossible abolition of solitude, but in its recognition and respect; not in the fusion that denies the other, but in the encounter that honors them.

Thus, the highest love is not the one that claims to abolish essential solitude, which is impossible and would deny each person's uniqueness; it is the one that, by recognizing it, transforms it into a solitude inhabited by the presence of the other, in an encounter where two distinct beings greet and protect each other across the distance that makes them different.

This conception reconciles what we have glimpsed: the essential solitude that cannot be abolished, the knowledge of others that respects their mystery, the love that sees and brings forth, the desire that gives rather than takes.

It states that the highest relationship between beings is not the fusion that denies their solitude, but the love that recognizes and honors it — two solitudes that, knowing themselves to be irreducible, nonetheless choose to meet, to protect each other, to greet each other, and find in this respectful encounter, more than in any fusion, the truth and beauty of love.

sentences: We live with the feeling that civilization is a solid achievement, an irreversible progress that has definitively pulled us away from barbarism.
Our institutions, our laws, our softened morals, and our horror of cruelty seem to us like assured conquests, a foundation we can rely on.
However, this confidence may rest on an illusion.
For what we call civilization might well be nothing more than a fragile veneer, a thin layer covering older and darker forces that can crack and unravel with disconcerting speed.
This unsettling truth has been demonstrated by history too often to be ignored.
The twentieth century, in particular, dealt a brutal blow to the idea of a civilization that is definitively acquired.

Some of the most advanced, cultured, and refined societies plunged into a barbarism that was thought to be a thing of the past within just a few years, committing or tolerating atrocities of unprecedented scale.
This shift did not come from peoples who remained savage, but from nations at the pinnacle of culture, science, and refinement.

It showed that the veneer of civilization could crack, that beneath the softened morals lay forces that circumstances could awaken, and that the civilized man and the barbarian were not two distinct species, but that the latter could resurface within the former with frightening ease.
How can we understand this fragility?
Perhaps by recognizing that civilization does not fundamentally transform human nature, but contains it, channels it, and represses it.

The impulses of violence, cruelty, and domination do not disappear under the influence of civilization; they are contained by institutions, prohibitions, customs, and education, which repress and subliminate them.
But these barriers are fragile; if they give way, due to a crisis, propaganda, or a collapse, the forces they contained can resurface.
Civilization would not be the abolition of barbarism, but its precarious containment, always threatened with rupture.
This conception, as bleak as it may be, has the merit of lucidity.
It protects us from two dangerous illusions.

The first is the naive optimism that believes civilization is permanently secured, that barbarism is a thing of the past, and that progress is irreversible; this optimism disarms, as it does not see the danger approaching, and it does not defend what it believes is assured.

The second is to believe that barbarism is the fault of others, of peoples who remain savage, and that we, the civilized, are forever preserved from it; this illusion blinds us to our own capacity to fall, to the forces that our civilization contains without abolishing them.
Recognizing the fragility of civilization means guarding against these blind spots, and thus defending it better.
For this clarity leads to a requirement: if civilization is fragile, then it must be constantly defended, maintained, and protected.
It is not an achievement that one can enjoy passively, but a conquest that must always be reclaimed, a balance that is always threatened, and dikes that must be constantly reinforced.

The institutions that contain violence, the customs that soften, the education that civilizes, the prohibitions that protect, only hold if we maintain them, if we watch over them, if we do not let them deteriorate.
Civilization does not maintain itself; it requires constant effort, vigilance from each generation, without which it can unravel.
Recognizing that civilization is a fragile veneer is therefore not yielding to pessimism or despair.
It is to gain the clarity that alone allows us to defend it.
He who believes civilization is secured does not defend it and lets it deteriorate; he who knows its fragility watches over it, protects it, and transmits it.

The awareness of fragility is not demobilizing but mobilizing: it reminds us that what we hold most precious — peace, rights, the gentleness of customs, the horror of cruelty — is never definitively secured, that it must be earned and defended in every generation, and that it can be lost if we cease to watch over it.
Civilization is a fragile heritage; and it is because it is fragile that it obliges us — to take care of it, to transmit it, to never take it for granted.
For what centuries have built, a few years can undo; and it is up to us, in each generation, to ensure that the veneer does not crack.

sentences: We like to believe that evil, great evil, the kind associated with atrocities and mass crimes, is the work of monsters, of exceptionally cruel beings, radically different from us.
This belief is reassuring: it places a clear boundary between evil and us, it makes criminals a separate species, it protects us from the unsettling thought that we too could be capable of such acts.
But this reassuring belief may be false, and one of the most disturbing lessons of recent history is that great evil is often committed not by monsters, but by ordinary men.
This truth, difficult to accept, deserves to be confronted, as it sheds harsh light on the fragility of civilization and our own.

The observation of great mass crimes has revealed a disconcerting reality: among those who committed or allowed them, a majority were not sadists, perverts, or monsters, but ordinary men — family fathers, conscientious employees, people who, under different circumstances, would have led mundane and honest lives.
They did not act out of exceptional cruelty, demonic hatred, but out of conformity, obedience, careerism, cowardice, and a lack of reflection.

The evil they committed was not commensurate with their mediocrity; it is this contrast between the enormity of the crimes and the banality of their authors that struck observers, and which has been termed the banality of evil.
This expression, often misunderstood, does not mean that evil is trivial, nor that crimes are excusable.

It refers to the fact that the perpetrators of great crimes can be ordinary men, that extreme evil can be committed by people who are not monsters, but who, under certain circumstances, influenced by certain mechanisms — obedience to authority, conformity, disempowerment, lack of reflection — become capable of the worst.

Evil does not necessarily require extraordinary wickedness; it can arise from ordinary dispositions and circumstances, from cowardice, conformity, refusal to think, which are within the reach of almost everyone.
This truth is unsettling precisely because it abolishes the reassuring boundary between evil and us.
If great evil were the work of monsters, we would be safe from it, separated from them by a difference in nature.

But if it is committed by ordinary men, under the influence of ordinary mechanisms, then we can no longer believe ourselves to be safe; we must consider that we too, in certain circumstances, could become capable of it.
This thought is unbearable, and that is why we resist it, preferring to believe that we would have remained, we, on the right side.

But this resistance is dangerous, because it is precisely by believing ourselves to be safe that we lower our guard, that we do not monitor within ourselves the dispositions that could lead to the worst.
Recognizing ordinary evil does not excuse criminals, as if their banality justified them; rather, it makes us more vigilant, towards others and towards ourselves.

It invites us to monitor within ourselves the dispositions that make evil possible: blind obedience to authority, conformity that follows the group, the shifting of responsibility onto others, the refusal to think for oneself, the cowardice that does not dare to resist.
It is these ordinary dispositions, more than any exceptional wickedness, that pave the way for the worst.

And to protect ourselves against evil is not to believe ourselves to be of a different species than its authors, but to cultivate within ourselves what resists these mechanisms: the courage to disobey the unjust, the independence that refuses conformity, the responsibility that does not shift, the thought that does not abdicate.
The lesson of ordinary evil is, paradoxically, a lesson in responsibility.

For if evil were the work of monsters, we would have nothing to do but distinguish ourselves from them; but if it can arise in any ordinary person, due to ordinary circumstances and dispositions, then vigilance is our responsibility.

Defending civilization against the barbarism that threatens it is not just about fighting external monsters; it is about monitoring the ordinary dispositions within ourselves and around us that make evil possible, cultivating courage, independence, responsibility, and thought, which alone can resist it.

Ordinary evil teaches us that the line between civilization and barbarism does not run between people, but within each of them — and that it is through each individual, with vigilance and courage, that this line is defended or lost.

sentences: Technical progress has given humanity unprecedented powers: we can transform nature, extend life, communicate instantly across the world, and also destroy on a scale once unimaginable.
These powers are constantly growing, and nothing seems to be able to limit them.
But a question arises, all the more pressing as these powers increase: does our wisdom keep pace with our powers?
Have we become, as our power has grown, wiser and more capable of using what we can do wisely?
And if that is not the case, if our powers are growing faster than our wisdom, what do we risk?
The observation is hard to refute: our technical powers have grown tremendously, but nothing indicates that our wisdom has progressed proportionately.
We are not evidently wiser, fairer, or more in control of our passions than people of the past; we have infinitely more powerful means, but we use them for purposes that are no wiser.
This is a formidable imbalance: for increased power in hands that are not wiser is more dangerous, not less, than lesser power.
The more powerful our means are, the graver our faults can be, and the more catastrophic the consequences of our lack of wisdom can be.
The imbalance between our powers and our wisdom may be the major peril of our time.
This imbalance is strikingly evident in our capacity for destruction.
Humanity has, for the first time in its history, acquired the power to destroy itself, to make the planet uninhabitable, to annihilate civilization.
This terrifying power is in the hands of a humanity that is no wiser than before, still subject to the same passions, the same blind spots, the same follies.
The fact that this unparalleled power of destruction is held by a humanity whose wisdom has not grown proportionately should fill us with concern.
We have the means to destroy ourselves, without having acquired the wisdom that would surely protect us from it.
This imbalance is also evident in our relationship with nature.

Our technical powers have given us an unprecedented ability to transform our environment, but we use it without the wisdom that would measure the consequences, preserve the balances, and safeguard the future.
We are transforming the world on a scale that exceeds our ability to foresee and control the effects, with a power that surpasses our wisdom.

The result is the ecological crisis, which may be the most visible manifestation of the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom: we can transform the planet, but we are not wise enough to do so without destroying it.
Should we conclude that we need to limit technological progress, renouncing powers that our wisdom cannot control?
This conclusion, appealing as it is, is difficult to implement, because no one can stop technological progress, and wanting to do so would be futile.
The real answer may lie elsewhere: not in the illusory limitation of powers, but in the development of wisdom, so that it catches up with our powers.
If our powers grow faster than our wisdom, the solution is not to restrain the powers, but to increase wisdom, ensuring that it grows in proportion to our strength.

This is an immense challenge, as wisdom does not progress like technology, does not accumulate, and must be reclaimed by each generation; but it is the only one that can address the imbalance that threatens us.
This challenge gives a new meaning to what we have said about wisdom, virtue, and self-formation.
For if the major peril of our time is the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom, then the development of wisdom—both individual and collective—is not a luxury, but a vital necessity.

Cultivating wisdom, prudence, self-control, a sense of limits, and responsibility towards the future is not just a matter of personal improvement; it may be the very condition for the survival of humanity, whose powers have exceeded control.

Technological progress, without progress in wisdom, leads to catastrophe; and the great challenge of our time may be to ensure that our wisdom finally catches up with our powers, before the imbalance becomes fatal.
Never has the ancient demand for wisdom been as urgent as in an age where our powers have become excessive.
