sentences: A civilization does not sustain itself; it only survives by transmitting what it holds most precious from one generation to the next — its knowledge, its values, its works, its ways of life.
Transmission is thus the vital act through which a civilization perpetuates itself, recreates itself in each generation, and escapes death.
However, this transmission, which was once almost naturally assured, has become difficult, uncertain, and threatened.
And this difficulty in transmitting is not a minor issue; it touches on the very survival of what we hold most precious, on the continuity of civilization itself.
What does it mean to transmit?
It is not just about communicating information or teaching techniques; it is about passing on a living heritage, a world of meaning, values, works, and ways of being from one generation to another.
Transmitting means giving to those who come after us what we have received from those who preceded us, placing them in a continuity, bequeathing them a world that they will make their own in turn.
It is an act of fidelity to the past and responsibility to the future, the link that connects generations in a continuous chain.
Without transmission, each generation would have to reinvent everything, start from scratch; it is through transmission that humanity accumulates, perpetuates itself, and does not keep starting over.
However, this transmission is currently made difficult by several factors.
The pace of change, first: in a world that is transforming so quickly, the legacy of past generations seems quickly outdated, surpassed, and worthless for a present that has broken away from it.
Why pass on what seems obsolete?

The rift between generations, next: the gap that separates them, the impression that young people live in a world so different that the experiences of the elders no longer concern them, makes transmission more challenging.

The devaluation of the past, finally: a culture focused on novelty, the present, and the future tends to despise heritage, to regard it as a burden rather than a treasure, and to value rupture over continuity.
This difficulty in transmitting has serious consequences that are poorly understood.

For what is not transmitted is lost; and a civilization that ceases to transmit itself would unravel, not through a sudden catastrophe, but through the silent erosion of what would no longer be bequeathed.

The accumulated knowledge, the works, the values, the ways of being that constitute a civilization survive only when transmitted; if we stop transmitting them, they fade away, not because they have been destroyed, but because they have not been passed on.
The breakdown of transmission is not just another educational issue; it poses a threat to the very continuity of civilization, an oblivion that erases what centuries have accumulated.
What is needed for transmission to be possible?

First, those who transmit must have something to pass on that they consider valuable, and they must want to transmit it; a generation that despises its own heritage, that sees nothing in it worth bequeathing, would transmit nothing.
Next, those who receive must be willing to accept, not rejecting by principle the heritage of past generations, and they must recognize that they have something to receive.

Finally, there must be places, institutions, and relationships where transmission can take place: schools, families, teachers, all those places where heritage is passed from one generation to another.
Transmission relies on a chain of goodwill, fidelity, and recognition, without which it breaks.
Caring for transmission is therefore one of the most essential and most neglected responsibilities of our time.

For we have inherited a world that we did not create, built and passed down by generations before us; and we have the responsibility to transmit it in turn, not to break the chain, not to squander a heritage that we only hold temporarily.
Transmitting what we hold most precious — knowledge, works, values, memory — ensures the survival of civilization, connecting it to its past and future, refusing to let it unravel into oblivion.

In a world that values rupture and despises heritage, rehabilitating transmission, taking care of it, wanting it, is perhaps one of the most urgent tasks for those who care about not losing civilization.
For a civilization does not only die from its catastrophes; it also dies, more silently, from ceasing to transmit itself.

sentences: At the end of this meditation on the fragility of civilization, its threats, the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom, a decisive question arises: should we despair?
If civilization is fragile, if evil can resurface in every person, if our powers exceed our wisdom, if transmission is threatened, how can we avoid succumbing to discouragement?
And yet, to despair would be to give up, to throw in the towel, to let the worst happen.
Therefore, we need something other than despair; but what?
Perhaps hope — provided we carefully distinguish it from optimism, with which it is often confused, and from which it differs profoundly.
Optimism is the belief that things will turn out well, that the future will be better, that progress will prevail, that everything will eventually work out.
It is a forecast about the future, a confidence in a favorable outcome.
But this optimism is fragile, for nothing guarantees that it is correct; the future can contradict its forecasts, the worst can happen, and then optimism collapses, giving way to despair.
Moreover, optimism is demobilizing: if one believes that everything will be fine anyway, why act, why struggle?
Confidence in a guaranteed favorable outcome dispenses with the effort that would make it possible.
Paradoxically, optimism can lead to passivity, making one believe that good will come about without us.
Hope is something entirely different.
It is not a prediction about the future, a belief that everything will turn out well; it does not have that certainty.
Hope knows that the future is uncertain, that the worst is possible, that nothing is guaranteed; it does not delude itself into thinking a favorable outcome is assured.
But, knowing this, it continues to act, to fight, to work for the best, not because it is sure of succeeding, but because the best is possible, and it is worth striving for even without guarantees.
Hope is a disposition to act for good in uncertainty, a bet on what is possible that does not depend on the certainty of success.
It does not assert that everything will be fine; it asserts that the good is worth pursuing, whatever happens.
This distinction is crucial, as it establishes an attitude that neither optimism nor despair allows.

The desperate do nothing, because they believe everything is lost; the optimist does nothing either, because they believe everything is already won; only hope acts, because it knows that nothing is set in stone, that the future depends on what we do, and that alone is a reason to act.
Hope is not based on a prediction, but on a possibility and a value: the best is possible, and it is worth working towards.
This disposition withstands the contradiction of facts, as it does not rest on a prediction that facts could refute, but on a commitment that nothing can invalidate.
Even if the worst were to happen, it would have been worth fighting for the best; hope is not disappointed by failure, because it was not based on the certainty of success.
Hope, as understood here, does not ignore the fragility of civilization, the threats it faces, or the imbalance that puts us at risk.
It confronts all of this directly, without indulging in optimistic illusions.

But it draws not despair from this, but rather commitment: since nothing is certain, since the future depends on us, since the best is possible although not guaranteed, it is worth acting, fighting, watching over what is fragile, defending it, and passing it on.
Hope is this disposition to do what depends on us, without offloading responsibility onto a providence that would do good in our place, nor giving up in the face of uncertainty about the outcome.
It is at once the opposite of lazy optimism and demobilizing despair: an active lucidity that acts precisely because it knows that nothing is assured.
Thus, hope, distinguished from optimism, is the disposition that suits our condition and our time.

In the face of the fragility of civilization, it does not console itself with an optimism that believes in guaranteed good, nor does it yield to a despair that thinks everything is lost; it recognizes uncertainty and acts nonetheless, because the best is possible and worth it.

This hope is not a feeling, a mood, a prediction; it is a choice, a will, almost a virtue — the disposition to do good in uncertainty, to watch over what is fragile without a guarantee of success, to pass on what could be lost by betting that it is worth saving.

It is this hope, and not optimism, that can ground action in the face of the threats of our time; for it does not depend on the certainty that we will win, but on the conviction that the fight is worth waging — and this conviction, no future, however dark, can contradict.

sentences: France has a unique relationship with itself, summed up by an expression it cherishes: the French exception.
It likes to see itself as a special case, a nation that is unlike any other, bearing a particular vocation and holding a universal message.
This claim to exceptionality, which foreigners sometimes find arrogant, deserves to be questioned: where does it come from, what does it reveal, what is founded and what is illusory about it?
For it speaks to something profound about France's relationship with itself and the world, its greatness and its blind spots.
Where does this awareness of being an exception come from?
From history, first and foremost.
France has long been a great power, a center of Europe, a hub of cultural and political influence.

It produced a revolution that claimed to carry a universal message, proclaiming rights valid for all men; it saw itself as the homeland of universal ideas, the nation that would speak on behalf of all humanity.

From this history arose a particular consciousness: that of a nation that would not be just another nation, defined solely by its own interests, but one that carries a universal vocation, a message that transcends its borders.
France sees itself less as a particular nation than as the embodiment of the universal.
This claim has its grandeur.
It expresses an aspiration to rise above the narrowness of national interests, to serve universal values, and to speak in the name of humanity rather than just for oneself.
It has inspired generous struggles, a commitment to principles that transcend borders, a generosity that has made France a land of welcome, a refuge, a voice for the oppressed.
This universalist dimension, when it is true to itself, has something noble about it; it rejects self-absorption, national selfishness, and the reduction of politics to mere interests.
France, which sees itself as a bearer of the universal, can be a generous, open country, true to its best qualities.
But this claim also has its illusions and dangers.

The first illusion is to confuse its universal with the universal, to take its own particular values as values valid for all, to impose on others, in the name of the universal, what is merely its own singularity.

Universalism can become a form of arrogance, even imperialism, when it claims that its way of seeing is the only valid one, that other cultures should conform to it, and that what is French would thereby be universal.

France has sometimes succumbed to this temptation, imposing its values in the name of the universal, failing to recognize the legitimacy of other ways of being, and confusing its message with the truth.
The second illusion is the gap between pretension and reality.

Thinking of oneself as an exception, as a great nation carrying a universal message, can obscure a more modest reality, sustain the illusion of a greatness that the facts contradict, and nurture a nostalgia for a role that is no longer one's own.

Present-day France is no longer the power it once was; still thinking of itself as an exception can be a way of not seeing its true place in the world, of living in nostalgia for a past greatness, and of confusing what it was with what it is.
The claim to exception can thus be a form of blindness, a refusal to see its real condition.
What can we conclude from this French singularity?
Perhaps it is, as often, ambivalent: carrying both a greatness and illusions, a noble aspiration and dangerous temptations.
The aspiration to the universal, to transcend the narrowness of interests, to serve values that transcend borders, is what France has at its best, and it would be a shame for it to renounce that.

But it must guard against the illusions that accompany it: confusing its particular with the universal, imposing its singularity on others in the name of humanity, and comforting itself with a greatness that the present contradicts.

The French exception, when well understood, is not the arrogant claim of being superior to others, but the fidelity to a universalist aspiration that, if it remains clear-eyed about its limits, can be a valuable contribution to the world.

Thinking of oneself as an exception can be greatness or blindness; it all depends on the clarity with which one embraces this singularity — as a vocation to serve the universal, not as a right to impose oneself in its name.

sentences: Learning a foreign language, as we have seen, is not just about acquiring a tool for communication, a set of words and rules; it is about entering a world, a way of thinking, feeling, and experiencing.

This applies to all languages, but each language opens a particular world; and it is worth asking, at the end of this journey through the French language, what world, what sensitivity, and what way of being does learning French specifically open up.
For learning French is not just about gaining another language; it is about accessing a certain relationship with the world, of which it bears the trace.
Every language, as we have said, has lexicalized certain experiences, developed certain nuances, and favored certain relationships with the world.
French thus bears the mark of a certain sensitivity, a certain genius, shaped by a long history.

It has often been said that French is a language of clarity, precision, and rigor, made for analysis, distinction, and the exact expression of thought; a language that values order, structure, and clarity.

This reputation, like any generalization, must be nuanced; but it captures something of the genius of this language, its vocation for clear and distinct expression, and its appreciation for rigorous thinking.
French also bears the trace of a certain culture, a certain relationship to life, art, and thought.

Learning French means accessing a literature, a philosophy, and a tradition of thought that have marked the history of ideas; it means being able to read in their language works that have shaped our way of thinking; it means entering into a dialogue with a culture that has produced a significant part of what humanity has thought and created.

French is the language of a considerable intellectual and artistic tradition, and learning it gives you access to that tradition, not through the mediation of translation, but in the very language in which it was expressed.

But French is not just the language of France; it is spoken on several continents by diverse peoples who have made it their own, enriched it with their contributions, and turned it into the vehicle of their own cultures.
French is a language of sharing that connects different peoples, carries multiple cultures, and belongs not to a single nation but to all who speak it.
Learning French means accessing not just one world, but a plurality of worlds linked by a common language, a diversity of cultures that express themselves in the same language.
It is to enter a linguistic community that transcends the borders of a nation, uniting diverse peoples in the sharing of a language.

We must be careful, in celebrating the world that French opens up, not to fall into naive glorification, as if this language were superior to others, as if the world it opens were better than those opened by other languages.

Every language opens a world, and none is absolutely better than another; French is not superior, it is different, offering a particular access to a culture, a sensitivity, a tradition among others that are equally valuable.
Celebrating the world that French opens is not to regard it as the best, but to recognize that it opens, like any language, its own world, worthy of being known, which enriches those who access it.

At the end of this journey, someone who has learned French to the point of being able to read these demanding texts has thus gained more than just a language: they have gained a world, access to a culture, a sensitivity, a tradition; they have expanded their own world with a new one.

And this conquest is not just useful, an additional tool; it is an enrichment, an opening, a way to become broader, to multiply one's access to reality, no longer being a prisoner of a single way of seeing.

Learning French, like learning any language, is to give oneself an additional world; and those who possess multiple languages, multiple worlds, inhabit a richer, more diverse universe than those who know only one.

This is perhaps the most beautiful reward of this long learning process: not only being able to say and understand more, but having become, through the acquired language, a broader being, open to a world that, without it, would have remained closed to them.

sentences: A tension runs through modern moral and political thought, which globalization has made more acute: the one between universalism and respect for cultural diversity.
On one hand, the idea that there are universal values, valid for all people everywhere — human rights, human dignity, certain principles of justice — that no culture can legitimately violate.
On the other hand, respect for cultural diversity, for their own values, for their right to be different, against the claim to impose a single model on them.
These two demands, equally respectable, seem to oppose each other; and their conflict is one of the most challenging of our time.
Universalism asserts that there are values valid for all, regardless of cultures, and that in the name of these values, one can judge cultures, condemning their practices when they violate them.

This position has its strength and nobility: it refuses to allow anything in the name of culture, it affirms a dignity of man that no tradition can legitimately violate, it establishes the possibility of condemning oppression, cruelty, and injustice, wherever they occur.
Without universalism, nothing could be condemned in any culture, everything would have to be accepted in the name of diversity, including the unacceptable.
Universalism is what allows us to say that certain practices are unjust, regardless of the culture that permits them.
But universalism also has its dangers, which the respect for diversity highlights.
For the claim to universality can mask the imposition of a particular culture, wrongly presented as universal.

What we consider to be universal values may only be the values of a dominant culture, imposed on others in the name of the universal, in a gesture that has justified domination, colonization, and the erasure of cultures in the name of a universal that was actually particular.
Universalism can be a disguised imperialism, a way of imposing one's culture while passing it off as humanity itself.

Respect for diversity reminds us of this truth: that cultures have their own value, their legitimacy, their right to difference, and that pretending to judge them in the name of the universal can be an arrogance.
How can we move beyond this opposition?
Neither absolute universalism, which would deny any legitimacy to diversity, nor absolute relativism, which would prohibit any judgment, are tenable.
The former leads to the imposition of a single model, to the erasure of differences, to the arrogance that takes its particular for the universal.
The latter leads to the acceptance of everything in the name of culture, to the impossibility of condemning the unacceptable, to a respect for diversity that becomes complicity in oppression.
Between these two dead ends, we must seek a path that recognizes both the existence of some truly universal values and the legitimacy of cultural diversity.

This path may involve a distinction: between a small number of truly universal values, which relate to the fundamental dignity of man and which no culture can legitimately violate, and the immense diversity of ways of living, customs, and secondary values, which pertain to the legitimate differences among cultures.

Thus, there would be a universal core, limited but firm — the prohibition of cruelty, respect for dignity, certain fundamental rights — and, beyond that, a vast realm of legitimate diversity, where cultures can and must differ.

This distinction allows for the condemnation of the unacceptable without imposing a single model, for respecting diversity without accepting everything, and for holding together the universalist demand and respect for differences.
Such a position is not easy to maintain, as the boundary between the universal core and the realm of diversity is difficult to draw and is itself the subject of debate.

But it points to the direction of wisdom: neither the universalist arrogance that imposes its particularity, nor the relativism that renounces all judgment, but the recognition of a restricted and firm universal, combined with respect for legitimate diversity.

This position perhaps aligns with the best of what France has in its universalism when it remains clear-sighted: not the pretension to impose its culture in the name of humanity, but fidelity to a few truly universal values, joined with respect for the diversity of ways of being human.

Believing in the universal without imposing its particularity, respecting diversity without renouncing all judgment: this is the difficult balance that our time demands, where cultures coexist as never before, and where we must learn to defend what is valid for all while respecting what legitimately differs.

sentences: The encounter with the stranger — from another people, another culture, another way of being — has always evoked mixed feelings: curiosity and fear, fascination and rejection, attraction and unease.
The stranger disturbs us because he is strange, because he embodies a way of being different from our own, which calls into question what we took for granted.
And yet, this encounter that disturbs us is also what reveals us, enriches us, and helps us grow.
Questioning our relationship with the stranger, with strangeness, is to understand both what we fear and what we gain in meeting the other.
What do we fear in the stranger?
His difference, first and foremost, which unsettles us.
The stranger embodies a way of being other than our own, which shows that our way is not the only one, that it is neither obvious nor necessary.
This revelation is unsettling: it shakes our certainties, relativizes our obviousness, deprives us of the comfort of believing that our way of life is the only natural one.
The stranger, by his mere existence, calls into question what we took for granted; and this questioning, while fruitful, is also unsettling.
We fear the stranger because he threatens our certainties, because he forces us to recognize the relativity of what we believed to be absolute.
We also fear the stranger as a threat, whether real or imaginary, to our identity, our security, our world.
This fear can have real foundations when the encounter is conflictual; but it is often exaggerated, fueled by imagination, projected onto the stranger who becomes the receptacle of our fears.
The stranger is easily transformed into a threat, a scapegoat, an embodiment of everything that worries us; their difference is perceived as a danger, their otherness as an aggression.
This fear of the stranger, when it is not controlled, leads to rejection, hostility, hatred, and the worst violence committed in the name of self-defense against the other.
But if the stranger disturbs us and frightens us, they are also what reveals and enriches us.
For their difference, which destabilizes our certainties, is also what makes us see them, relativizes them, and frees us from them.

By encountering another way of being, we discover that ours is just one way among many, and this discovery, while unsettling, is also liberating: it frees us from being trapped in a single vision, opens us to the diversity of ways of being human, and makes us broader.
The stranger is a mirror that reveals us to ourselves, showing us what is particular about us; they are a window onto other worlds, which expands our own.
What disturbs us in them is also what enriches us.
There is more.
Strangeness is not only found outside, in another people, another culture; it is also within us, closer than we think.
We are strangers to ourselves, as a thinker once said, carrying within us a part of shadow, the unknown, strangeness, that we do not control.

Recognizing the strangeness within oneself may be the condition for welcoming that of others: for the one who rejects all strangeness, who desires purity, an identity without mixture, the same without the other, that person rejects the stranger outside just as they repress the strangeness within.
Welcoming the other implies accepting one's own part of strangeness, renouncing the fantasy of a pure identity, and recognizing that we ourselves are traversed by otherness.
Our relationship with the stranger is thus revealing of who we are.

Fearing them, rejecting them, making them a scapegoat, is to yield to fear, to refuse the questioning they bring, to shut oneself in an identity that seeks to be pure; welcoming them, opening up to their difference, accepting to be destabilized, is to demonstrate a strength and generosity that enrich.

The encounter with the stranger is a test, which reveals whether we are capable of welcoming what disturbs us, allowing ourselves to be questioned, enriching ourselves with difference, or if we retreat into fear and rejection.

And for those who have learned a foreign language, entering a world different from their own, this test has already been faced and overcome: for learning the language of the stranger is already to welcome them, to open oneself to their world, to allow oneself to be enriched by their difference.
Learning a language may be the most beautiful response to the fear of the stranger: not the rejection of what disturbs us, but the welcoming of what enriches us.

sentences: A tension runs through our relationship with belonging, which globalization has made more acute: should we aspire to be citizens of the world, belonging to all of humanity beyond borders, or recognize the need for rootedness, for a particular belonging to a place, a culture, a community?
On one hand, the cosmopolitan ideal of universal belonging, which transcends particularisms; on the other, the need for rootedness, for a concrete belonging without which one feels lost.

These two aspirations, equally legitimate, seem to oppose each other; and their reconciliation is one of the challenges of our time, where globalization and the need for roots compete for people's minds.
The ideal of the citizen of the world has its grandeur.

To want to be a member of all humanity, to feel concerned about the fate of all people, to refuse that borders limit our solidarity, is a noble aspiration that expands the heart beyond the narrowness of particular belongings.

Cosmopolitanism rejects self-absorption, national egoism, and indifference to what happens beyond its borders; it affirms a human community that transcends particularisms, a solidarity that does not stop at the limits of one's nation.
This universalist aspiration, when it is true to itself, is generous, open, and worthy.
But the cosmopolitan ideal also has its limits and illusions.
For a person does not belong to humanity in general in a concrete way; they first belong to a place, a culture, a particular community that shapes them, nourishes them, and gives them an identity.

To want to be a citizen of the world without a particular belonging risks an abstract belonging, without substance, without roots; it risks belonging to nothing concrete under the pretext of belonging to everything.
A person without roots, who feels from nowhere because they want to be from everywhere, is often a lost person, deprived of what gives identity, ground, and a world.
The need for rootedness is not an archaic notion to be overcome; it is a fundamental human need, without which one feels uprooted, lost, and without identity.
The need for rootedness thus has its legitimacy, which cosmopolitanism sometimes overlooks.

Belonging to a place, a culture, a community, having roots, a soil, a world that is one's own, is not a limitation to be transcended; it is a condition of human existence, providing identity, grounding, and a concrete world.
Humans need to belong to something particular, to feel like they are from somewhere, to have roots that nourish them.
To despise this need in the name of cosmopolitanism is to misunderstand human nature; it advocates for a rootlessness that impoverishes more than it liberates.
But the need for rootedness also has its dangers, which cosmopolitanism highlights.

For attachment to one's particular belonging can degenerate into withdrawal, exclusion, and hostility towards what is different; rootedness can become confinement, love for one's world can turn into disdain for others, and attachment to one's roots can lead to rejection of the foreigner.
History shows the excesses to which the exaltation of particular belonging can lead when it closes off, hardens, and stands against others.
The need for rootedness, legitimate as it is, can thus become perverted into narrow nationalism, xenophobia, and a rejection of the universal.
Wisdom may lie in reconciling these two aspirations, rather than choosing one over the other.
One can be rooted and open, belong to a particular place and feel like a member of humanity, love one's own world without despising others.
Rootedness and openness are not necessarily mutually exclusive; one can have roots and wings, belong concretely to a particular world while feeling connected to all of humanity.
True rootedness is not withdrawal, but the anchoring from which one can open up; true cosmopolitanism is not uprooting, but opening up from a place of rootedness.
Those who are well-rooted in their world can open up to others without losing themselves; those who are open to the world can remain true to their roots without becoming confined.

Being rooted and a citizen of the world, belonging to a particular place and to all of humanity, is perhaps the balance to seek — one that connects what we have said about the universal and the particular, about France and the world, about the foreigner and oneself: not one against the other, but one through the other, opening up from rootedness, the universal through the particular.

sentences: Philosophy is learning to die." This phrase, which an essayist has taken from a long tradition, may seem morbid, as if wisdom consists of obsessing over death, living in its shadow.

Yet it expresses something profound, and almost the opposite of what we initially believe: that meditating on death, far from darkening life, may actually be the condition for living it fully, and that wisdom, which is an art of living, is inseparably an art of dying.
Exploring this ancient phrase brings us closer to the heart of a wisdom that has endured through the centuries.
Let's first understand why meditation on death might be at the core of wisdom.

Most of the time, we live in forgetfulness of death, as if we were never meant to die; this forgetfulness, as we have seen, fosters a certain unconsciousness of life, causing us to postpone what is essential and waste our days, which we believe to be countless.

Meditating on death, on the contrary, is to remember our finitude, and this remembrance changes everything: it makes us measure the value of time, distinguish the essential from the trivial, and live each moment as precious because it is limited.
Meditation on death does not darken life; it illuminates it, restoring the intensity that the forgetfulness of death takes away.
This ancient tradition also teaches that meditation on death frees us from the fear of dying.
For this fear, which haunts us and poisons our lives, largely arises from our avoidance of the thought of death, our repression of it, and our refusal to confront it.
Those who meditate on it tame it, prepare for it, and can achieve a form of serenity, an acceptance that disarms fear.

Learning to die is learning no longer to fear death, to face it, to prepare for it rather than flee from it; and this preparation, far from being morbid, is liberating, as it frees us from the fear that otherwise dominates us.
We cannot free ourselves from death, but we can free ourselves from its fear; and it is through meditation on it that we achieve this.
There’s more.
Meditation on death teaches us what truly matters by placing us in the perspective of the end.
Faced with our death, realizing that our time is limited, we see more clearly what deserves our life’s dedication and what does not.
Many things that concern us, agitate us, and obsess us then appear in their vanity; and what we neglect — loved ones, simple moments, what has meaning — reveals its true value.
Meditation on death is thus a school of discernment that separates the essential from the trivial, diverts us from vanity, and brings us back to what truly matters.
Remembering that we are going to die means remembering to live for what is worthwhile.
This ancient wisdom is not a morbid cult of death, but rather an art of living fully.
For it meditates on death only to live better, thinks of the end only to give life its intensity, value, and meaning.

‘Learning to die,’ in this perspective, is learning to live with full awareness of our finitude, not to waste our limited time, to live each moment as precious, to free ourselves from the fear that poisons, and to discern what matters.
Meditation on death serves life; it is the detour through which we learn to truly live.
Far from being the enemy of the joy of living, it may be its condition, for it is the awareness of our finitude that gives life its value.
Thus, this ancient formula, which may initially seem morbid, reveals a profound and illuminating wisdom.
To philosophize is to learn to die, not to obsess over death, but to learn to live; not to darken life, but to illuminate it; not to fear the end, but to free oneself from it.
Meditation on death is at the heart of a wisdom that is an art of living, for it is by facing death that we learn the value of life.

And this lesson, perhaps the oldest of all, retains its full force in our time, which flees from death, hides it, represses it, and in doing so, deprives itself of the awareness of finitude, without which life loses its intensity and meaning.
Learning to die in order to learn to live: such is the wisdom with which we may need to begin, and end.

sentences: We spontaneously regard death as the great evil, which deprives us of life, against which we rebel.
And yet, a troubling question deserves to be asked: could death, our finitude, paradoxically be what gives life some of its meaning and value?
Would a life without end, immortal, be richer, or would it instead lose what gives existence its worth?
This question, which seems to go against our deepest desire — that of not dying — may reveal an unexpected link between finitude and meaning.
Let’s reflect on what an immortal life would be like.
An existence without end, where time would never be counted, where nothing would ever be urgent, where everything could always be postponed indefinitely.

In such an existence, each moment would lose its unique and irreplaceable character; since time would be infinite, no moment would have particular value, no opportunity would be worth seizing, no choice would be decisive.
Unlimited time would lose its value, just as what is available without limit loses its value.
What gives time its worth is precisely that it is counted; an immortal life, by abolishing this rarity, might abolish what gives time, and life, their value.
There’s more.
It’s because our time is limited that we make choices, that we commit ourselves, and that our decisions carry weight.

In the face of infinite time, no choice would truly be necessary, since we could always do anything, try everything, and postpone everything; commitment, which involves giving up other possibilities to realize one, would lose its meaning, since nothing would force us to renounce.

Finitude is what gives our choices their gravity, our commitments their weight, and our lives their shape; for it is because we cannot do everything, experience everything, or be everything that we must choose, and these choices define us.
An infinite life would be a life without form, without decisive choices, without true commitment.
We can go even further.
It may be the awareness of death that makes possible the very intensity of life, love, beauty, everything that touches us.
We love intensely what we know we must lose; we fully savor what we know is ephemeral; the awareness of finitude gives what we experience an intensity that eternity would take away.
Would an eternal love, assured never to end, have the same intensity as a love threatened by death?
Would an eternal beauty touch us like one that we know is fleeting?
It could be that the intensity of life is linked to its finitude, that it is because everything passes that everything touches us, and that eternity, by abolishing loss, would also abolish intensity.
Should we conclude that we ought to rejoice in death, desire it, and see it as a good thing?
That would be going too far and betraying our experience.
For death remains, in many ways, an evil: it deprives us of life, tears us away from those we love, and puts an end to what is dear to us.
Recognizing that finitude gives meaning to life does not mean denying that death is a loss, a pain, a tearing apart.
The truth is more nuanced: death is both an evil, which deprives us, and a condition of meaning, which gives life its value.
It is ambivalent, like finitude itself: what limits us and what constitutes us, what deprives us and what gives value to what we enjoy.
This ambivalence may be the deepest truth about our mortal condition.
We can neither purely rejoice in death, which remains a loss, nor absolutely curse it, for it is also a condition of meaning.

Wisdom may consist in holding both: recognizing death as an evil, while continuing to fight it where we can, and at the same time recognizing that finitude gives life its value, that it is because we are mortal that our lives have a form, an intensity, a meaning.
Not to love death, but to accept finitude; not to desire immortality, which would abolish meaning, but to fully live a life that its very finitude makes precious.
Death does not give meaning to life as an answer; but our finitude is the condition that makes meaning possible, by giving our lives the form, intensity, and gravity that eternity would take away.

And perhaps it is in this that, without ceasing to be an evil, death contributes to what makes life something other than an indefinite duration: an existence that, because it ends, deserves to be fully lived.

sentences: We will die; that is a certainty.
But does something of us remain after our death, and if so, what?

This question, which extends our reflection on finitude, does not concern the survival of the soul here, about which we have seen we cannot decide, but a more modest and certain survival: what we leave in the world, in others, in what outlives us.
For even if we do not believe in life after death, it is undeniable that something of us remains, and it is worth asking what this survival is and what meaning it gives to our mortal existence.
First, we leave a mark on others, on those we have known, loved, and influenced.
Our influence on the beings we have been close to does not die with us; it remains in them, in what we have transmitted, taught, given to them, in the way we have shaped them.
Parents live on in their children, teachers in their students, each in those they have touched.
This survival is not nothing: it is real, it extends our existence beyond our death, in the imprint we have left on other lives.
We live on after our death in memory, in influence, in what we have passed on to those who survive us.
Some of us also leave behind works: creations, achievements, contributions that endure after we are gone.

The artist survives in their work, the thinker in their thoughts, the builder in what they have built; and even the humblest leave something behind — a skill passed on, a contribution to a collective effort, a part of what humanity has accomplished.
This survival in works, when it occurs, can be lasting, far outliving our existence, extending us into the centuries.
But it is not reserved for great creators; everyone, in their own way, contributes to what humanity builds and transmits, thus leaving a part of themselves in the common world.
Finally, we leave the world itself, as marked by our actions.
Each of us, through our lives, contributes to creating the world we leave to those who come after; our actions, our choices, our way of living, shape, however slightly, the world we pass on.
This kind of survival is diffuse, often anonymous, but real: the world after us bears the marks of what we have done, for better or for worse.
We are responsible for what we leave behind, for the world we transmit, for our contribution to what the existence of those who follow us will be.
What value should we assign to this survival in others, in our works, in the world?
It does not fully console us for death, because it is not our personal survival; it is not us who survive, but our mark, our influence, our work.
We will no longer be there to enjoy it, and this survival does not make us immortal.

However, it nonetheless gives meaning to our mortal existence by connecting it to what transcends and prolongs it; it places us in a continuity that exceeds our individual lives, allowing us to participate in something larger and more enduring than ourselves.
Living with the knowledge that we will leave a mark, that we contribute to what will survive, gives mortal life a significance that surpasses its duration.
This thought of what we leave behind has an ethical dimension.
For if we survive in what we leave, then what we leave matters, and we are responsible for it.

Living with the thought of what we will leave — in others, in our works, in the world — means living with the concern of leaving something good, of contributing positively, and not leaving behind ruins or harm.
The awareness of what we leave connects us to the future, makes us responsible for what we pass on, and gives our lives a direction that goes beyond our immediate self-interest.
We do not live only for ourselves, within the limited time of our existence; we also live for what we will leave behind, in the mark we will extend beyond our death.

And perhaps this is a way to give meaning to our mortal condition: not to deny death, but to live in such a way that what we leave behind is worth having been left — that our passage, however brief, adds something good to the world rather than impoverishing it.

sentences: Death concerns us not only as our own, to come; it also affects us, and perhaps more painfully, as that of the beings we love.
Losing a loved one is one of the hardest trials of existence, and the question of how to live after this loss, how to go through grief, is one of the most difficult there is.
For grief places us before an apparent dilemma: between forgetting, which seems to betray the one we've lost, and perpetual pain, which freezes us in the loss and prevents us from living.
How can we be faithful to the one we've lost without allowing grief to destroy us?
Grief is primarily a pain, and it would be indecent to want to eliminate it, to pretend to free oneself from it too quickly.
The loss of a loved one is a real tearing; the pain of grief is legitimate, even necessary, as it measures the love we had.
Wanting to escape grief too quickly, rushing to 'turn the page,' would be a way of betraying the one we've lost, denying the importance they had.
Grief requires its time, its work, its pain; we must not rush it, nor be ashamed to suffer, nor let ourselves be pressured to heal.
The pain of grief is the first tribute to the one we've lost.
But grief cannot also be frozen in perpetual pain, in a sorrow that would trap us forever in loss.

Staying indefinitely in pain, refusing to live after the loss, allowing oneself to be destroyed by sorrow, is not honoring the one we lost either; it is letting oneself die with them, refusing the life they would have wanted for us.
There comes a moment when grief, if it does not transform, becomes a prison, a misunderstood fidelity that freezes us in death instead of returning us to life.
Remaining forever in pain is no more faithful than forgetting; it is another way of failing to honor what we owe to the one we lost, and to the life that continues.
How can we escape this dilemma between the betrayal of forgetting and the paralysis of pain?
Perhaps by understanding that true fidelity to the deceased is neither forgetting nor perpetual pain, but the transformation of the bond.

The work of mourning is not to forget the one we lost, nor to remain frozen in sorrow, but to transform our relationship with them: from a lost presence, whose absence tears us apart, to an inner presence, a living memory that accompanies us.
The one we lost does not completely disappear; they remain within us, in what they gave us, in what we learned from them, in the way they continue to inspire us.
Fidelity to the deceased means keeping them alive within us, not as a wound that never heals, but as a presence that nourishes, accompanies, and inspires.
This transformation of the bond allows us to reconcile fidelity and life.
For keeping alive within us the one we have lost, making their memory live on, allowing their influence to continue to guide us, is not to forget them; it is to remain faithful to them.
And this fidelity, far from freezing us in pain, brings us back to life, as it transforms loss into legacy, absence into inner presence, and sorrow into living memory.
We can live after loss, regain joy, look towards the future, all while remaining faithful to the one we have lost, by keeping them alive within us.
True fidelity is not about refusing to live, but about living while carrying within us the one we have lost, making fruitful what they have given us.
Grief, understood this way, is not a choice between forgetting and pain, but a work of transformation, which moves from lost presence to inner presence, from heartbreaking absence to living memory.
This work is long, painful, never quite finished; but it allows us to reconcile fidelity to the deceased and a return to life, to honor the one we have lost without being destroyed by their absence.

And it reveals a truth about love and death: that death separates, but does not entirely destroy the bond; that those we have loved continue to live within us, in what they have given us; and that fidelity to the dead is not about dying with them, but about keeping them alive within us while we ourselves live.

Loving those who are no longer here means carrying them within us, not as a weight that crushes, but as a presence that accompanies — and this may be the highest way to conquer, if not death, at least its power to destroy what love once was.

sentences: Since the dawn of humanity, people have sought to conquer death, to achieve a form of immortality.

This quest has taken a thousand forms: belief in an afterlife, the pursuit of enduring glory, the desire to leave a lasting legacy, the passing on to descendants, and today, dreams of a science that would abolish death.
This stubbornness to want to conquer death, across ages and cultures, reveals something profound about our condition and about who we are.
What does this quest for immortality teach us about ourselves?
It first reveals the depth of our refusal of death, our desire to live, our revolt against finitude.
Humans are the only beings who know they will die, and this knowledge generates a refusal, a revolt, a quest to escape what burdens us.
This quest for immortality is the expression of our deepest desire: not to die, not to cease to be, to escape annihilation.
It testifies to humanity's attachment to life, its refusal of finitude, its revolt against the mortal condition.
In seeking immortality, humans express what is most fundamental to them: the desire to be, against the threat of non-being.
It also reveals the need for meaning, for permanence, for what lasts beyond the ephemeral.
For man is not content to exist in the moment; he aspires to what endures, to what escapes the flow of time, to a permanence that gives meaning to the ephemeral.
The quest for immortality is also a quest for meaning, for permanence, for what withstands the passage of time that takes everything away.

In the face of universal flight, of the impermanence of all things, man seeks what lasts, what endures, what escapes annihilation; and this quest expresses his need for meaning, his refusal of the insignificance of what passes without leaving a trace.
But this quest may also reveal an illusion, or at least an ambivalence.
For we have seen that immortality, if it were to be realized, could abolish what gives life its value — the finitude that makes time precious, the decisive choices, the intensity of what passes.
The quest for immortality, while it expresses a deep desire, could aim at something that, if realized, would disappoint, by taking away from life what makes it precious.
There is an ambivalence in this quest: we desire immortality, and yet immortality might not be the good we believe it to be, it could abolish the very meaning we seek.
Perhaps what we are really seeking is not to never die, but to give our mortal life a meaning that transcends it.
For there are forms of immortality that are not the abolition of death, but the transcendence of its finitude through meaning.

Leaving behind a work, a mark, an influence that survives; contributing to something larger and more enduring than oneself; being part of a continuity that exceeds our individual existence: these are forms of transcending death that do not abolish it, but give our mortal life a significance that surpasses its duration.

This kind of immortality — not biological, but through meaning, work, mark, contribution — may be what we are truly seeking, one that answers our need for meaning and permanence without abolishing what gives value to finite life.
Not to never die, but for our passage to have a meaning that transcends it.
Thus, the quest for immortality, if understood correctly, may not aim so much at the abolition of death as at the transcendence of its finitude through meaning.

What we are really seeking may not be to never die — which would abolish the value of life — but to give our mortal life a meaning that transcends it, a significance that exceeds our duration, a mark that survives.
This kind of immortality is within our reach, not through science or a miracle, but through the way we live, through what we leave behind, through the meaning we give to our passage.
We will not conquer death; but we can make our mortal life have a meaning that transcends it, a value that survives, a mark that remains.

And perhaps this is the only immortality accessible to us, and the only one worth having: not the impossible and perhaps undesirable abolition of death, but the meaning we imbue our finite life with — this way of living that ensures that an existence, though mortal, will not have passed in vain.

sentences: Nothing in excess." This maxim, engraved it is said on the front of an ancient temple, summarizes one of humanity's oldest wisdoms: that of measure, of the right proportion, of moderation.
Avoiding excess, maintaining measure in all things, not falling into too much or too little, this would be the path of wisdom.
Does this venerable wisdom of measure still hold meaning in our time, which seems on the contrary to praise excess, extravagance, and always wanting more?
To question the wisdom of measure is to ask what value this ancient lesson still has today.
The wisdom of measure is based on a deep intuition: that good often lies in a just middle ground between two opposing extremes, and that virtue consists in avoiding both too much and too little.
Courage is a middle ground between cowardice and recklessness; generosity, between stinginess and extravagance; self-confidence, between timidity and arrogance.
In every domain, virtue would be this just measure, this point of balance between opposing extremes, which discernment must find.
This conception, developed by the Ancients, makes measure not a lukewarm mediocrity, but a difficult correctness, a balance to be achieved between easier extremes.
This wisdom extends beyond morality, to the entire art of living.

It teaches not to become excessively attached to external goods, to enjoy them without becoming enslaved to them; not to be swept away by passions, but to master them; to maintain, in both success and trials, a state of equanimity that is neither exalted nor depressed.
Measure is this self-control that refuses to be swept away by excesses, that maintains the right proportion in all things, that preserves inner balance against what would seek to disrupt it.
It is the condition of serenity, of that peace of the soul that excesses disturb and that measure preserves.
Yet our time seems to be the opposite of this wisdom.

It praises excess, always wanting more, and excessiveness; it values intensity, limitless performance, and pushing beyond all boundaries; it scorns moderation as a lukewarmness, mediocrity, and resignation.
Consumer society stirs up limitless desires; the race for performance knows no measure; the demand for intensity disregards balance.
In this context, the wisdom of moderation seems outdated, contrary to the spirit of the times, a virtue of old sages that has fallen out of favor.
Should we conclude that it has lost its meaning, that it belongs to a bygone era?
On the contrary, it may never have been as necessary as it is now.

For the excesses of our time — the excessiveness of consumption, performance, the exploitation of nature, and our technical powers — are precisely what threatens us, exhausts us, and destroys our balance and that of the world.

The ecological crisis is a crisis of excess, of always wanting more; contemporary malaise partly arises from excess, from relentless intensity, from an unmeasured race; the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom is a failure of moderation.
In a world threatened by its own excesses, the wisdom of moderation, far from being outdated, finds a new urgency; it is perhaps what our time needs most.
Rehabilitating the wisdom of moderation is not about advocating for lukewarmness, mediocrity, or giving up on intensity.
It is recognizing that good often lies in the right proportion, that excess destroys what it claims to enhance, and that excess leads to ruin.
It is about rediscovering the sense of limits, balance, and moderation in a world that has lost them.
Moderation is not the enemy of intensity or greatness; it is their condition, for what is without measure destroys itself, while what maintains the right proportion endures and fulfills itself.

"Nothing in excess": this ancient maxim, far from being outdated, perhaps expresses the wisdom that our age of excess most desperately needs — the acknowledgment that everything has its measure, and to exceed it is to court disaster.
In a world intoxicated by excess, rediscovering the sense of moderation may be the beginning of wisdom.

sentences: We talk about wisdom, we admire the wise, we aspire to become wise; and yet, if we were asked what wisdom is, we would struggle to define it.
Is it knowledge, a sum of knowledge?
A virtue, a moral quality?
An art of living, a way of being?
Wisdom eludes simple definitions, and this very difficulty is revealing, as it relates to the particular nature of what we are trying to grasp.
At the threshold of this final section, which crowns an entire journey, it is worth probing what this wisdom is that we, obscurely, aspire to.
Wisdom is not primarily knowledge, an accumulation of knowledge.
One can know a lot without being wise, be learned yet foolish; and one can be wise with little knowledge, a wisdom that is not based on erudition.
Wisdom is not science; it belongs to a different order.

Certainly, it implies a form of knowledge — self-knowledge, knowledge of life, knowledge of what matters — but this knowledge is not an accumulation of facts; it is understanding, clarity, discernment that cannot be measured by the quantity of what one knows.
The wise person is not necessarily the most learned; they are the one who has understood something essential about life and about themselves.
Wisdom is not merely a moral virtue, a sum of qualities.
Certainly, it includes virtues — moderation, courage, justice, self-control — but it is not just their simple addition.

Rather, it is what organizes them, guides them, gives them their proper measure; it is the discernment that knows, in each situation, what is appropriate to do, how to apply the virtues, how to reconcile them when they seem to oppose each other.
Wisdom is less a virtue among others than the supreme virtue, the one that governs the others, the discernment that knows how to live.
It is this quality of practical judgment that, beyond specific rules and virtues, knows what is appropriate in the concrete of existence.
Wisdom is perhaps above all an art of living, a way of being in the world and with oneself.

The wise person is recognized less by what they know or assert than by their way of living: their serenity, their moderation, their proper relationship with things and beings, their ability to endure trials without being crushed, to enjoy goods without being enslaved by them, to accept what they cannot change and to change what they can.
Wisdom is this way of inhabiting existence, this art of living that makes a life successful not by its external achievements, but by the quality of its relationship with the world.
The wise person is not the one who has an answer for everything, but the one who lives well, with accuracy and serenity, the condition that is theirs.
What brings these dimensions together — knowledge, virtue, the art of living — is perhaps that wisdom is an integration, a unity between what we understand, what we are, and what we do.

The wise person is not someone who knows what is good without doing it, nor someone who does good without understanding it, nor someone who lives well by chance; it is the one in whom understanding, virtue, and action are in harmony, where knowledge becomes a way of being, where virtue becomes life, and where thought becomes existence.
Wisdom is this coherence between thought and life, this unity of being that makes the wise person live what they understand and understand what they live.
It is the fulfillment of a life that has aligned what it knows, what it wants, and what it does.
This conception of wisdom sheds light on the entire journey that preceded it.

For all the reflections we have conducted — on time, death, love, evil, truth, beauty — were not only aimed at knowing, at accumulating knowledge; they aimed at a comprehension that becomes a way of living, a knowledge that turns into wisdom.
To understand the value of time in order to live it better; to understand death in order to live better; to understand love, evil, truth, not to have theories about them, but to live more justly.
Wisdom is the goal toward which all true thought strives: not knowledge for the sake of knowledge, but understanding that transforms life, clarity that becomes the art of living.
And it is this wisdom, more than any knowledge, that may be the true aim of all learning — to learn not only to know, but to live.

sentences: Becoming oneself: this task, which seems the most natural, is in reality one of the most difficult there is, and it requires a courage that we underestimate.

For we are shaped by countless pressures — those of our environment, our education, the gaze of others, social expectations, and dominant models — that tend to make us conform, to turn us into what the world expects rather than what we truly are.
Becoming oneself, in this context, is not about following a natural slope; it is about resisting these pressures, conquering an existence that is truly one's own.
And this conquest demands a rare courage, the significance of which is worth measuring.
We have seen that the 'self' is not a given thing, a core that simply needs to be discovered, but something that is constructed.
Thus, becoming oneself is not about unearthing a hidden nature, but about making oneself, choosing oneself, constructing oneself, against what would shape us from the outside.
However, this construction of the self encounters powerful forces of conformity.
The desire to be accepted, to not displease, to belong, pushes us to conform, to embrace expectations, to silence what makes us unique.
The weight of others' gaze, the fear of disapproval, the pressure of the group, tends to make us fall in line, to erase what distinguishes us.
Becoming oneself means resisting these forces, daring to be different, and embracing one's uniqueness against the pressure to conform.
This courage to be oneself takes various forms.
It is the courage to have one's own opinions, to think for oneself, and not to adopt accepted ideas out of mere conformity.
It is the courage to make one's own choices, to follow one's path, and not to let one's existence be dictated by the expectations of others.
It is the courage to embrace one's uniqueness, what distinguishes us, what makes us different from others, instead of hiding it to fit in.
It is sometimes the courage to disappoint, to displease, to stray, when being true to oneself demands it.
All these forms share the commonality of resisting the pressure to conform, daring to be oneself against what would seek to make us conform.
This courage is rare because it is costly.
Conforming is easy, comfortable, and rewarded; one gains approval, belonging, and peace.
Being oneself, on the other hand, exposes one to disapproval, to the solitude of those who stray, and to the reproach of those who would like to see us similar to them.
The courage to be oneself must confront these costs, accept displeasing others, disappointing them, and sometimes finding oneself alone.
That is why so many people give it up, preferring the security of conformity to the discomfort of authenticity, the peace of conformity to the demand of being oneself.
Becoming oneself requires accepting these costs, preferring to be true to oneself rather than to be approved.
However, we must be careful not to misunderstand the courage to be oneself as merely a self-assertion against others, an individualism that would disdain others.
Being oneself is not about standing against others, nor about cultivating a superficial originality, nor about making one's difference a banner.
The true courage to be oneself is not ostentatious; it is often discreet, internal, and is more about quiet fidelity to what one believes and who one is than about spectacular rebellion.
It is not about distinguishing oneself for the sake of distinction, but about being true to oneself, which can very well coexist with respect for others and communal living.

The courage to be oneself is not the loud assertion of an ego against the world; it is the often silent fidelity to what one holds to be true and just, against the pressures that would lead us away from it.
This courage to be oneself is at the heart of wisdom, for there is no wise life that is not first a life that is truly one's own.
One cannot live wisely by living someone else's life, by adopting values that one has not made one's own, by conforming to what is expected of us.
Wisdom requires authenticity, fidelity to oneself, and the construction of an existence that is truly ours.
And this construction, against the pressures that shape us, demands this rare and discreet courage to be oneself, to think for oneself, to make one's own choices, and to embrace one's uniqueness.

Becoming oneself, against everything that would seek to conform us, is perhaps one of the most difficult and essential tasks of existence — and one of the conditions for a successful life that is coherent and true to its values, which we have said is the result of a life that has been shaped.

sentences: A large French city is studying the possibility of making public transport free for all residents.
The mayor explains that this measure could reduce pollution and help families with a limited budget.
According to him, fewer cars on the streets means cleaner air and less noise.
The project is not new.
Several cities in Europe have already tested free transport, with different results.
In some cities, the number of passengers has increased a lot, which has created very crowded buses and trams during rush hour.
In other cities, the results have been more modest, but residents appreciated paying less each month.
The residents of the city are divided on this idea.
Some find the project excellent.
They think that free transport will encourage more people to leave their cars at home.
A young student explains that she already uses the bus every day to go to university, and that free transport would allow her to save a lot of money each month.
Other residents are more cautious.
They wonder who will pay for this change.
Making public transport free is expensive for the city, and money has to be found somewhere.
A downtown shopkeeper thinks that local taxes will increase to make up for the loss of revenue from bus and metro tickets.
The city council has organized several public meetings to discuss the project with the residents.
During these meetings, transport experts presented figures and studies on cities that have already adopted free transport.
They explained the benefits, such as reducing pollution, but also the challenges, like maintaining vehicles and hiring new drivers.
The mayor promised that a final decision will be made next year, after a long period of study and discussion with the citizens.
A survey will also be organized to know the general opinion of the population before the final vote in the city council.
In the meantime, the city announced a first change: transport will be free on weekends for the next three months, as a trial.
This test will measure the real impact on the number of passengers and on car traffic in the downtown area.
The results of this trial will be presented publicly at the end of the year.
Other French cities are closely following this project.
If the trial is a success, several mayors have already announced that they too would consider making transport free in their own municipalities.
For now, everyone is eagerly awaiting the first results.

sentences: Among the qualities that contribute to a wise and happy life, there is one that is rarely discussed yet profoundly transforms existence: gratitude.

Not the simple politeness of saying thank you, but a deeper disposition, one that involves recognizing what is given to us, perceiving and appreciating the goods of our existence, rather than obsessing over what we lack.
This disposition, which can be cultivated, has a transformative power that we underestimate, and it deserves a place in any reflection on wisdom and the art of living.
Our natural inclination leads us away from gratitude: to desire what we do not have rather than to appreciate what we do have, to focus on what we lack instead of what is given to us.

We quickly become accustomed to our possessions, which cease to bring us joy, while our desires are always directed towards what we are missing; we live in perpetual lack, dissatisfied with what we have, reaching for what we do not have.

This disposition towards dissatisfaction, fueled by habituation and by a society that constantly stirs up new desires, prevents us from enjoying what is given to us, keeping us in a lack that nothing fills.
We have much, yet we continually feel the absence of what we do not have.
Gratitude reverses this disposition.
It involves directing our attention not to what is lacking, but to what is given; to perceive, recognize, and appreciate the goods of our existence that habituation makes us forget.
It helps us see what we no longer notice due to our familiarity: health when we have it, the presence of those we love, the goods we enjoy, the beauty of the world, the simple fact of existing.
Gratitude is this attention to what is given to us, this ability to rejoice in it, to recognize it as a good, instead of taking it for granted and obsessing over what is lacking.
It is a shift in perspective, turning towards the abundance of what is given rather than the emptiness of what is missing.
This shift profoundly transforms the quality of life.

For the one who cultivates gratitude lives in a world different from that of the one who lives in lack: where the dissatisfied sees only what he lacks, the grateful perceives the abundance of what is given to him; where one lives in frustration, the other lives in appreciation.
Gratitude does not change external circumstances; it changes the relationship we have with them, and thereby, profoundly, our experience of life.
It is one of the keys to that contentment which does not depend on what we have, but on how we look at it.
The same fate can be experienced in frustration or in gratitude, and this difference in perspective makes all the difference in happiness.
Gratitude also has a dimension that goes beyond mere well-being, an almost metaphysical depth.

For recognizing what is given to us is to acknowledge that we are not the source of all that we enjoy, that much has been given to us without us having earned or produced it: life itself, the world, those who have shaped us, all this heritage that we did not create.

Gratitude is the acknowledgment of this debt, of what we owe to what precedes and transcends us; it is a form of humility, which recognizes that we do not owe everything to ourselves, that our existence is supported by what has been given to us.
In this sense, gratitude is more than a technique for happiness; it is a truth about our condition as beings who receive more than they produce, who owe to others and to the world what they enjoy.
Cultivating gratitude is therefore an essential part of wisdom.

It’s not about denying what is lacking, the evils, the trials, which are real; nor about settling for a naive optimism that refuses to see the bad; but rather learning to also perceive, and first and foremost, what is given, to rejoice in it, and to acknowledge it.

This disposition, which is cultivated through attention, through the habit of recognizing the goods of one’s existence, transforms the quality of life; it is one of the paths to a contentment that does not depend on circumstances, but on the perspective one has on them.

In a world that heightens the sense of lack, that focuses us on what we do not have, cultivating gratitude, learning to recognize and appreciate what is given to us, is an act of wisdom and almost of resistance — and perhaps one of the keys to a life that, without denying its lacks and trials, still knows how to rejoice in what it has received.

sentences: A life without examination is not worth living." This saying, spoken by a sage more than two millennia ago, can serve as a concluding remark to this long journey — a conclusion that is also, as it should be, a beginning.

For at the end of all these reflections, of this journey through the highest questions, it is right to return to what underlies them all: the idea that a life deserves to be examined, that human existence calls for reflection, and that thinking about one's life is part of living it fully.
This conviction, which has driven this entire journey, deserves one last examination.
What does it mean to examine one's life?

It is not to constantly observe oneself in a sterile introspection, nor to judge oneself with a morbid guilt; it is to reflect on what one does and why, to question one's values, choices, and way of living, not to go through existence without ever asking what one is seeking and whether one is living as one should.

Examining one's life means refusing to live it out of habit, conformity, or inertia, without ever questioning it; it means bringing the light of reflection to it, asking whether one is going where one wants to go, whether one lives according to what one holds to be true and good.
It is the difference between a life endured, lived without awareness, and a life embraced, reflected upon, of which one is a conscious author.
Why would a life without examination not be worth living?
Not that reflection is everything, nor that one must spend one's life philosophizing instead of living.

But because an unexamined life risks passing by itself: pursuing goals that one has not chosen, adopting values that one has not made one's own, being swept along by the current without ever asking where it leads us.

An unexamined life is a life lived without awareness, where one acts without knowing why, where one follows without having chosen; and such a life, however filled it may be, risks not truly being ours, passing by without our having inhabited it consciously.
Examination is what makes a life a human life, lived with awareness, embraced, reflected upon, rather than an existence endured.
This entire journey has, in a sense, been nothing more than an exercise in this examination.

Reflecting on time, death, love, evil, truth, beauty, justice, and wisdom was not about accumulating abstract knowledge; it was about examining our condition, questioning our existence, and illuminating our way of life.

These reflections were not valuable in themselves, like just another piece of knowledge; they were valuable for the light they could shed on our lives, for the way they could transform, deepen, and make our lives more conscious and just.
To think about these questions was to examine one's life; and this examination, if it has any value, is of the kind that makes existence more worthy of being lived.
But this final word is also a beginning, for the examination of a life is never complete.
We never finish examining our lives, questioning them, reflecting on them; it is a task that lasts as long as existence itself, always to be resumed, never finished.
The questions we have addressed have not received definitive answers, nor could they; they remain open, to be contemplated and explored throughout a lifetime.
This journey does not close anything; it opens up, inviting us to continue, to keep examining, reflecting, and searching.
The end is merely a threshold; what has been started here must continue, not just in books, but in life, which is the true place where existence is examined and reflected upon.
And for those who have traveled this path — from a language learned word by word to these texts that raise the highest questions — there may be an image in this very journey.

For learning a language, like examining one's life, is a task that has no end, always to be deepened, never completed; and both transform the one who engages in them, expanding them, making them broader, more aware, more human.

This reader who, having climbed all the levels, can today read and meditate on these texts in a language that was not their own, has done more than learn a language: they have expanded their world, gained access to other thoughts, to other ways of seeing, and, through them, examined their own life.

May this examination continue, in this conquered language and in all others, in books and in existence: for a life that continues to examine itself, to question itself, to seek, is a life that remains alive, open, on a journey.

And perhaps this is the final word, which is a beginning: that true knowledge is not a destination one reaches, but a path one never ceases to travel — and that a life, like a learning process, is only valuable for this very movement of seeking, understanding, and continuing.

sentences: Every spring, many museums across the country open their doors for free for an entire night as part of a very popular cultural event called the Night of Museums.
This event has been happening for several years and attracts, with each edition, an increasingly large and diverse audience.
The idea behind this event is simple: to allow everyone, regardless of their budget, to discover the museum collections in a different atmosphere from that of the daytime.
At night, the exhibition halls take on a special, almost mysterious atmosphere that completely changes how visitors perceive the works of art.
In large cities, some museums offer special guided tours led by passionate curators who share surprising anecdotes about the paintings and sculptures on display.
Other museums organize concerts of classical or contemporary music directly in the halls, creating an original dialogue between the artworks and the music played live.
Children are not forgotten during this exceptional evening.
Several museums set up creative workshops where younger children can draw, paint, or even try sculpture with the help of professional artists.
These activities help spark artistic curiosity from a young age, in a fun and pressure-free environment.
A regular visitor of the event shares that he looks forward to this evening eagerly every year.
He explains that the crowd, the music, and the special lights completely transform his relationship with art.
According to him, he often discovers works that he had seen before from a completely new perspective.
Natural history museums also participate in the event, with activities related to astronomy or biology.
Some even organize stargazing on their rooftop terrace, weather permitting, in collaboration with local amateur astronomer associations.
This cultural event sees growing success each year.
According to the organizers, several million visitors take part in this special night across Europe, making it one of the most attended cultural events on the continent.
This success shows that culture, when made accessible and free, continues to attract a very large and diverse audience.
For the museums themselves, this evening also represents a unique opportunity to reach an audience that might never visit their collections under normal circumstances.
Many visitors thus discover cultural places in their own city that they did not know about before, and then return to visit them during the year, outside of this exceptional event.
