sentences: Last night, the home team won an extraordinary match in the final seconds of the game.
The stadium had been full since early afternoon, and thousands of supporters had been waiting for this match for weeks.
The atmosphere was electric as soon as the players entered the field.
The start of the match was difficult for the home team.
The opponent scored a goal in the tenth minute, and the supporters remained silent for a long time.
The local players seemed nervous and struggled to control the ball during the first half of the match.
During the break, the coach spoke at length with his players in the locker room.
He reminded them of the importance of this match for the standings and asked them to stay calm and focused.
This speech clearly changed something, as the team returned to the field with much more energy.
When they returned from the locker room, the game completely changed.
The home players started to dominate the ball and create many scoring opportunities.
The young striker of the team, only nineteen years old, equalized the score with a powerful shot from outside the penalty area.
The stadium erupted with joy.
The match remained very tight until the last minutes.
Both teams had chances to score, but the goalkeepers made excellent saves.
Everyone thought the match would end in a draw, which would have been an honorable result for both teams.
But in stoppage time, in the ninety-third minute, the same young striker received a perfect cross and scored a beautiful header.
The stadium went wild.
The supporters cheered with joy for several minutes, and some even cried tears of happiness at this historic moment for the club.
After the match, the coach explained to the journalists that his players never gave up, even after conceding the first goal.
He also praised the young striker for his outstanding performance and announced that he would play an even more important role in the upcoming matches.
The next match will take place next Sunday, against one of the best teams in the league.
The supporters are already hoping to relive the same emotions and continue to celebrate this memorable victory in the streets of the city late into the night.
For the club, this victory is also important financially.
Winning this match allows them to stay at the top of the standings and hope for a place in European competition next season, which would bring a lot of money and visibility to the team.

sentences: Sleep is not just a simple break in our day, as one might think.
During the night, our brain actually remains very active and does essential work for our physical and mental health.
Scientists have been studying the complex mechanisms that occur while we sleep for decades.
Sleep is divided into several phases that repeat multiple times during the night.
The first phase is light sleep, during which it is easy to wake up.
Next comes a phase of deep sleep, which is essential for the body's physical recovery.
Finally, a phase called REM sleep corresponds to the time when we dream most intensely.
During deep sleep, the body repairs muscle tissues and strengthens the immune system.
It is also during this phase that growth hormone is produced in larger quantities, which explains why sleep is particularly important for growing children and adolescents.
REM sleep, for its part, plays a crucial role in memory and learning.
Researchers have shown that the brain sorts, during this phase, the information received during the day.
It strengthens important memories and eliminates information deemed unnecessary, much like cleaning up our thoughts.
Several studies have shown the negative consequences of lack of sleep on our bodies.
A person who sleeps poorly for several consecutive nights sees their concentration drop significantly.
Their ability to make decisions and solve problems is also affected.
Lack of sleep is also associated with increased irritability and mood swings.
In the long term, insufficient sleep can have more serious consequences for health.
Research has established a link between chronic lack of sleep and a higher risk of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and weight gain.
The body, deprived of sufficient rest, produces more stress-related hormones, which wears the body out over time.
In light of these findings, sleep specialists recommend that adults sleep between seven and nine hours per night, depending on individual needs.
They also advise avoiding bright screens before going to bed, as blue light disrupts the production of melatonin, the hormone that promotes sleep onset.

Establishing a regular routine, by going to bed and waking up at similar times each day, remains one of the best ways to sustainably improve sleep quality and, consequently, overall health, according to experts.

sentences: On Sunday morning, many people go to the neighborhood market.
The market starts early, at eight o'clock, and it ends at one o'clock.
There are a lot of people, especially between ten o'clock and noon.
At the market, there are many stalls.
One vendor sells fruits: apples, pears, oranges, and bananas.
Another vendor sells vegetables: tomatoes, carrots, potatoes, and zucchinis.
The vegetables are fresh and they often come from farms near the city.
There is also a bread stall.
The baker sells baguettes, country bread, and croissants.
In the morning, the smell of warm bread attracts many customers.
People often line up in front of this stall because the croissants are very popular.
A little further on, there is a cheese stand.
The seller offers many different cheeses: goat cheese, camembert, comté, and many others.
He sometimes gives small pieces for customers to taste before they buy.
Customers really enjoy this tasting moment.
The market sellers are often very friendly.
They greet customers with a smile and know their habits well.
A seller recognizes a regular customer and asks him for news about his family.
This simple and warm relationship makes the market pleasant for everyone.
Prices are written on small wooden or cardboard signs.
Customers look at the prices before choosing their products.
Sometimes, at the end of the morning, sellers lower the prices a bit to sell the last products that remain on their stand.
A family is strolling peacefully between the stalls.
The parents are choosing vegetables for Sunday dinner, while their children are curiously looking at the colorful fruits.
A child asks his mother to buy strawberries, and his mother happily agrees.
After shopping, many people stop at a café near the market.
They order a coffee or a hot chocolate and sit on the terrace to rest.
It's a simple, calm, and pleasant moment at the end of a busy morning.
The Sunday market is a true moment of life for the local residents.
Many people meet there every week, chat a bit, and enjoy this friendly atmosphere before going home to prepare lunch.

sentences: The dignity of the wife stopped the momentum of the lover and the mother.

"May I not crush this cursed race!"
he murmured; "that I disobey God, who has raised me for his punishment!"
impossible, madam, impossible!
"Edmond," said the poor mother, trying every means: "my God!
when I call you Edmond, why don't you call me Mercédès?"
Mercedes, repeated Monte-Cristo, Mercedes!
Well then!
Yes, you are right, that name is still sweet for me to say, and this is the first time, in a long time, that it has echoed so clearly from my lips.

Oh Mercedes, your name, I have pronounced it with the sighs of melancholy, with the moans of pain, with the gasp of despair; I have pronounced it, frozen by the cold, crouched on the straw of my cell; I have pronounced it, consumed by the heat, rolling on the stones of my prison.

sentences: Then, gently and almost caressing her, he ran his hand over her stomach.
She let out a sharp cry.
He stepped back, completely frightened.
Then she started to whimper, weakly at first.
A great shiver shook her shoulders, and she was becoming paler than the sheet into which her clenched fingers were sinking.
Her uneven pulse was almost imperceptible now.
Drops were oozing from her bluish face, which seemed frozen in the exhalation of a metallic vapor.
Her teeth were chattering, her wide eyes were looking vaguely around her, and to all the questions she only responded by shaking her head; she even smiled two or three times.
Little by little, her moans grew louder.
A dull scream escaped her; she claimed that she was feeling better and that she would get up shortly.
But the convulsions seized her, she exclaimed: And he looked at her with eyes of a tenderness like she had never seen.

sentences: Everyone turned towards the king's prosecutor, who, under the weight of a thousand gazes fixed on him, stepped into the courtroom, staggering, his hair disheveled and his face flushed from the pressure of his nails.

--"No, no," stammered Mr. de Villefort in a strangled voice; "no, it's unnecessary."
"No, no," stammered Mr. de Villefort in a strangled voice; "no, it's unnecessary."
I mean, shouted the king's prosecutor, that I would struggle in vain under the deadly grip that crushes me, gentlemen, I am, I admit, in the hand of vengeful God.

No evidence; there is no need for it; everything this young man has just said is true!" A dark and heavy silence, like that which precedes natural disasters, enveloped all the attendees in its leaden cloak, their hair standing on end.

What!
you are in full possession of your faculties?

Our admiration remained at its highest point.

I had never had the chance to see these animals alive and free in their natural element.

sir, said Caderousse, timidly extending one hand and wiping the sweat that was beading on his forehead with the other; oh!
sir, don't make a joke out of a man's happiness or despair!
I know what happiness is and what despair is, and I will never play with feelings for fun.
So take it, but in exchange..." "In exchange, he continued, give me that red silk purse that Mr.

sentences: The next day, they decided to organize their meetings; Emma wanted to bribe her maid with a gift; but it would have been better to find a discreet house in Yonville.
Rodolphe promised to look for one.
Throughout the winter, three or four times a week, in the dead of night, he would arrive in the garden.
Emma had deliberately taken the key from the gate, which Charles thought was lost.
To alert her, Rodolphe would throw a handful of sand against the shutters.
She would startle awake; but sometimes she had to wait, because Charles had a habit of chatting by the fire, and he never seemed to finish.
She was consumed with impatience; if her eyes could have done so, they would have made her leap out of the windows.
Finally, she would start her nighttime routine; then, she would take a book and continue reading very calmly, as if the reading amused her.
But Charles, who was in bed, called her to come to bed.
However, as the candles dazzled him, he would turn towards the wall and fall asleep.
She would escape, holding her breath, smiling, trembling, and undressed.
Rodolphe had a large coat; he wrapped her completely in it, and, putting his arm around her waist, he led her silently to the back of the garden.

sentences: Here is your path, he said, Your Excellency, you can no longer go astray now.
And here is your reward, said the traveler, offering the young shepherd some small change.
Thank you, said Luigi, withdrawing his hand; I am doing a service, I am not selling it.
But, said the traveler, who seemed accustomed to this difference between the servility of city dwellers and the pride of country folk, if you refuse a wage, at least accept a gift.
Well then, said the traveler, take these two Venetian sequins and give them to your fiancée to make a pair of earrings.
And you, then, take this dagger, said the young shepherd, you won't find one with a handle better carved from Albano to Civita-Castellana.
I accept, said the traveler; but then, I am the one who is indebted to you, because this dagger is worth more than two sequins.
For a merchant perhaps, but for me, who carved it myself, it is barely worth a piastre.
Luigi Vampa, replied the shepherd with the same air as if he had answered: Alexander, king of Macedonia.
And you?
Yes, the narrator continued, that is the name the traveler gave to Vampa as his own.

It is deserted.

I look into the sky.
Why wouldn't some of these birds, reconstructed by the immortal Cuvier, flap their wings in these heavy layers of atmosphere?

I observe the space, but the skies are as uninhabited as the shores.
All this fossil world comes alive in my imagination.
I think back to the biblical epochs of creation, long before the birth of man, when the incomplete earth could not yet suffice for him.

sentences: Follow me to the western coast of Iceland.
Can you see Reykjavik, its capital?
Yes.
Good.
Go up the countless fjords of these sea-eroded shores, and stop a little below the sixty-fifth degree of latitude.
What do you see there?
A sort of peninsula resembling a bare bone, ending in a huge kneecap.
The comparison is accurate, my boy; now, can you see anything on that kneecap?
Itself, a mountain five thousand feet high, one of the most remarkable on the island, and surely the most famous in the whole world, if its crater leads to the center of the globe.
But that's impossible!
I exclaimed, shrugging my shoulders and revolted by such a supposition.
Because this crater is obviously blocked by lava and burning rocks, and then...
I had absolutely nothing to say in response to these positive assertions; I therefore turned to the other obscurities contained in the document.
"What does this word Scartaris mean, I asked, and what do the calends of July have to do with it?" My uncle took a moment to think.
I had a brief moment of hope, but only for a moment, because soon he replied to me in these terms: "What you call obscurity is light to me.
This proves the ingenious care with which Saknussemm wanted to clarify his discovery.
The Sneffels is made up of several craters; it was therefore necessary to indicate which one leads to the center of the globe.
What did the Icelandic scholar do?

He noticed that as the calends of July approached, that is to say, towards the last days of June, one of the peaks of the mountain, the Scartaris, cast its shadow to the opening of the crater in question, and he recorded this fact in his document.
Could he have imagined a more precise indication, and once we reach the summit of the Sneffels, will it be possible for us to hesitate on the path to take?"

sentences: A loud voice shouted, "Here are some friends!" And Mathieu appeared at the threshold.
He was a sixty-year-old man, thin, with a goatee and long white mustaches.
My companion shook his hand, introduced me, and Mathieu let us into a cool kitchen that also served as his dining room.
He said, "I don't have a fancy apartment, sir.
I really like not to stray far from the food.
The pots and pans, you see, they keep me company." "Why are you coming on a Thursday?
You know very well that it's my Boss's consultation day.

I can't go out this afternoon." And, running to the door, he let out a terrible bellow: "Mélie-e-e!" which must have made the sailors of the ships going up or down the river, way down in the deep valley, look up.
"She's not happy with me, you see, because yesterday I found myself in the nineties." My neighbor started to laugh: "In the nineties, Mathieu!
How did you manage that?"
I'll tell you.
Last year, I found only twenty rows of apricot trees.
There aren't any left; but to make cider, that's all there is.
So I made a batch that I tapped yesterday.
For nectar, it's nectar; you'll hear about it.
I had Polyte here; we started having a drink, and then another, without getting enough (we could drink until tomorrow), so that, from one drink to the next, I feel a freshness in my stomach.
I said to Polyte, 'How about we have a glass of fine to warm up!' He agreed.
But that fine, it sets your body on fire, so we had to go back to the cider.
But then, from freshness to warmth and from warmth to freshness, I realize that I'm feeling quite tipsy.
Polyte was not far from a meter tall.

sentences: Everything having been agreed upon, from this day forward, the preparations for the perilous expedition were carried out quickly.
The men had bravely accepted the fact that they had six hundred miles to cover under these conditions.
Sergeant Long was in charge of the work, while Jasper Hobson, the two hunters, and Mrs.
Paulina Barnett frequently went to assess the state of the icefield.
Kalumah accompanied them most often, and his advice, based on experience, could be very useful to the lieutenant.
The departure, barring any unforeseen circumstances, was set for November 20, so there was no time to lose.
As Jasper Hobson had predicted, with the wind picking up, the temperature dropped a bit, and the mercury column registered twenty-four degrees Fahrenheit (4°, 44 degrees Celsius below zero).
The snow replaced the rain from the previous days and was hardening on the ground.
A few days of this cold, and the sliding of the sleds would become possible.
The notch, dug in front of Cape Michel, was partly filled with ice and snow, but it should not be forgotten that its calmer waters must have frozen more quickly.
What proved this well was that the waters of the sea did not present as satisfactory a state.
Ce qui le prouvait bien, c'est que les eaux de la mer ne présentaient pas un état aussi satisfaisant.
But each in turn vainly questioned the sky during this endless day; nothing appeared that could spark hope.
The last movements of the ground disappeared at sunset, whose horizontal rays stretched into long lines of fire across this flat expanse.
It was the desert.

The travelers had not covered a distance of fifteen miles, having consumed, just like the previous day, one hundred thirty cubic feet of gas to fuel the burner, and two pints of water out of eight had to be sacrificed to quench a burning thirst.
The night passed quietly, too quietly!
The doctor did not sleep.

A bit of philosophy.--A cloud on the horizon.--In the midst of a fog.--The unexpected balloon.--The signals.--Exact view of the Victoria.--The palm trees.--Traces of a caravan.--The well in the middle of the desert.
The next day, the same purity of the sky, the same stillness of the atmosphere.
The Victoria rose to a height of five hundred feet; but it barely moved noticeably to the west.
"We are in the heart of the desert," said the doctor.
Here is the vastness of sand!
What a strange spectacle!
What a peculiar arrangement of nature!
Why over there this excessive vegetation, here this extreme aridity, and this, at the same latitude, under the same rays of sun!

sentences: So, all night long, Lieutenant Hobson and his companions took care of this essential clearing.
Fire and iron kept attacking and breaking down this incoherent mass of ice.
The men wielded picks and shovels.
The women tended the fires.
Everyone had only one thought: to save Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, Madge, Kalumah, Thomas Black!
But when morning returned, these unfortunate souls had already been buried for thirty hours, in an air that was necessarily thin beneath the thick layer.
The carpenter, after the work completed during the night, thought about digging the vertical well, which was supposed to lead directly to the roof of the house.
According to his calculations, this well should measure no less than fifty feet.

The work would certainly be easy in the ice, that is to say for about twenty feet; but after that, the difficulties would be great for digging through the layer of earth and sand, which would necessarily be very loose, and which would need to be supported for at least thirty feet.
Long pieces of wood were therefore prepared for this purpose, and the drilling of the well began.
Only three men could work together on it.
The soldiers therefore had the opportunity to take turns often, and it was hoped that the digging would proceed quickly.

No bread, for example!

--Good!
Mr. Aronnax, replied the Canadian, whose teeth seemed to be sharpened like the edge of an axe, but I will eat tiger, tiger loin, if there's no other quadruped on this island.
--Whatever it is, Ned Land replied, any four-legged animal without feathers, or any two-legged animal with feathers, will be greeted by my first shot.
Don't be afraid, Mr. Aronnax, the Canadian replied, and swim strongly!
I don't need twenty-five minutes to prepare a dish my way." In just a few minutes, we were within shooting distance of the coast.
The ground was almost entirely made of coral, but some dry riverbeds, scattered with granite debris, showed that this island was formed from primordial origins.
The entire horizon was hidden behind a curtain of magnificent forests.
Huge trees, some reaching up to two hundred feet tall, were connected to each other by garlands of vines, true natural hammocks swaying in a light breeze.

They were mimosas, ficus, casuarinas, teks, hibiscus, pandanus, and palms, mixed in abundance, and under the shelter of their leafy canopy, at the base of their gigantic trunks, grew orchids, legumes, and ferns.

Long live the Nile!
Joe said, who would gladly shout long live something when he was happy.
Huge rocks were blocking the course of this mysterious river here and there.

Surrounding mountains poured down numerous torrents, foaming as they fell; the eye counted them by the hundreds.
Thin streams of water were seen bubbling up from the ground, crossing, merging, racing against each other, and all were flowing to this emerging river, which became a river after absorbing them.
"That's definitely the Nile," the doctor repeated with conviction.

I will only tell you one.

It may be that only my imagination has borne the cost of my sentimentality.
I am fifty years old.
I was young then and I was studying law.
A little sad, a little dreamy, steeped in a melancholic philosophy, I did not care much for noisy cafés, boisterous friends, or silly girls.
I would get up early; and one of my greatest pleasures was to take a solitary walk around eight in the morning in the Luxembourg nursery.
You haven't known it, have you, this nursery?

I quickly climbed to the top of the being or object that was half-submerged and served as our refuge.

no!

It produced a metallic sound upon impact, and, as incredible as it was, it seemed that, I say, it was made of bolted plates.

sentences: Amazing, magnificent, splendid!
my uncle exclaimed.
Here is all the flora from the second era of the world, from the transitional period.
Here are those humble plants from our gardens that became trees in the early centuries of the globe!
Look, Axel, admire!
Never has a botanist found himself at such a celebration!
You're right, my uncle; Providence seems to have wanted to preserve in this immense greenhouse these antediluvian plants that the wisdom of scholars has reconstructed so successfully.
You are right, my boy, it is a greenhouse; but you would be even more accurate by adding that it might also be a menagerie.
Yes, undoubtedly.
Look at this dust we're treading on, these scattered bones on the ground.
"Here is the lower jaw of the Mastodon," I said; "here are the molars of the Dinotherium, here is a femur that could only have belonged to the largest of these animals, the Megatherium.

Yes, it really is a menagerie, because these bones certainly weren't brought here by a cataclysm; the animals they belong to lived on the shores of this underground sea, in the shade of these tree-like plants.
Look, I see whole skeletons.
And yet...
I don't understand the presence of such quadrupeds in this granite cave.

sentences: While we were in that dreadful state, Mentor, as calm as he is now on this patch of grass, said to me: Do you believe, Telemachus, that your life is left to the winds and the waves?
Do you think they can make you perish without the order of the gods?
No, no; the gods decide everything.
So it is the gods, and not the sea, that you should fear.
Even if you were at the bottom of the abyss, Jupiter's hand could pull you out.
Even if you were in Olympus, seeing the stars beneath your feet, Jupiter could plunge you to the depths of the abyss or cast you into the flames of dark Tartarus.
I listened and admired this speech, which comforted me a little; but I didn't have a free enough mind to respond to him.
He did not see me: I could not see him.
We spent the whole night, trembling with cold and half-dead, without knowing where the storm was throwing us.

Finally, the winds began to calm down; and the roaring sea resembled a person who, having been long irritated, had only a remnant of turmoil and emotion, being tired of getting angry; it rumbled softly, and its waves were almost like the furrows found in a plowed field.

I hope you did that, at least?" "I know well...

sentences: Goodbye!
Goodbye, our poor polar home!” said Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, waving her hand one last time.
And everyone, with this final memory, sadly and silently took the road back.
At one o'clock, the detachment had arrived at Cape Michel, after turning around the gap that the insufficient cold of winter had been unable to close.
Until then, the difficulties of the journey had not been great, as the ground of Victoria Island had a relatively flat surface.
But it would be quite different on the ice field.

Indeed, the icefield, subjected to the enormous pressure of the northern ice floes, had undoubtedly become rugged with icebergs, hummocks, and frozen mountains, among which they would have to search continuously for passable routes, at the cost of the greatest efforts and extreme fatigue.
By evening of that day, they had advanced a few miles onto the ice field.
They had to set up their sleeping arrangements.
To do this, they proceeded in the manner of the Eskimos and the Indians of North America, digging 'snow houses' in the ice blocks.

The snow knives worked effectively and skillfully, and at eight o'clock, after a dinner of dried meats, all the staff of the trading post had slipped into these holes, which are warmer than one might be tempted to believe.

sentences: Nothing seemed changed to me.
The castle still soaked its grayish walls in the pond at the entrance of the small town; and the inn was the same, although repaired, renovated, with a more modern look.
Upon entering, I was greeted by two young Breton women of eighteen, fresh and kind, clad in their tight wool vests, wearing silver caps with large embroidered plaques on their ears.
It was around six o'clock in the evening.
I sat down to dinner and, as the owner himself hurried to serve me, fate perhaps made me say: 'Did you know the former owners of this house?
I spent about ten days here thirty years ago now.
I'm speaking to you from afar.' Then I told him the occasion for which I had stopped, how I had been held back by a friend's illness.
He didn't let me finish.
'Oh!
I remember perfectly. I was then fifteen or sixteen.
You were sleeping in the back room and your friend in the one I made mine, on the street.' It was only then that the very vivid memory of the little maid came back to me.
I asked: 'Do you remember a nice little servant your father had then, who had, if my memory serves me right, pretty blue eyes and fresh teeth?'

My silence was taken as agreement, and the descent began again.
After three hours, I still couldn't see the bottom of the chimney.
When I lifted my head, I could see its opening noticeably decreasing; its walls, due to their slight incline, were tending to come closer together, and the darkness was gradually increasing.
However, we were still descending; it seemed to me that the stones dislodged from the walls were disappearing with a duller echo and that they would soon meet the bottom of the abyss.
Since I had taken care to accurately note our rope maneuvers, I was able to get an exact account of the depth reached and the time elapsed.
We had then repeated this maneuver fourteen times, which lasted half an hour.
So that made it seven o'clock, plus fourteen quarters of an hour or three and a half hours.

The path then became easy and perfectly monotonous.

Although we were a bit tired, our health remained reassuring, and the travel pharmacy was still intact.

sentences: A fifteen-year-old lout named Isidore Duval, more simply called Zidore, took care of this invalid, giving him, during the winter, his share of oats and fodder, and had to move him four times a day in the summer to the slope where he was tied up, so that he would have plenty of fresh grass.
The animal, almost crippled, lifted his heavy legs with difficulty, swollen above the hooves and thick at the knees.
His fur, which was never brushed anymore, looked like white hair, and very long eyelashes gave his eyes a sad expression.
When Zidore took him to the grass, he had to pull on the rope, as the beast moved so slowly; and the boy, bent over and panting, cursed at it, getting frustrated at having to care for this old nag.
The people on the farm, seeing this lout's anger towards Coco, found it amusing, constantly talking about the horse to Zidore to irritate the kid.
His friends teased him.
In the village, they called him Coco-Zidore.
The boy was furious, feeling a desire to take revenge on the horse rising within him.
He was a skinny child, tall for his age, very dirty, with thick, hard, and spiky red hair.
He seemed stupid, spoke with a stutter, with infinite difficulty, as if ideas could not form in his thick, brutish soul.

sentences: But, with all due respect, sir, Conseil pointed out, it's like a true isthmus that connects Europe to Africa.

--I would add, I continued, that a similar barrier exists between Gibraltar and Ceuta, which, in geological times, completely closed off the Mediterranean.
--Eh!
said Conseil, what if some volcanic push were to raise these two barriers above the waves one day!
--Finally, if you would allow me to finish, if this phenomenon were to occur, it would be unfortunate for Mr. de Lesseps, who is working so hard to cut through his isthmus!
--I agree, but I repeat, Conseil, this phenomenon will not happen.
The intensity of the underground forces is always decreasing.

The fatigue of the crossing, the dangers faced, everything had to start over!
We had gone backwards instead of moving forwards!
Ah!
Fate plays such tricks on me!
he exclaimed; the elements conspire against me!
Air, fire, and water are combining their efforts to oppose my passage!
Well!
we shall see what my will can do.

I will not yield, I will not back down an inch, and we will see who will prevail, man or nature!” Standing on the rock, irritated and threatening, Otto Lidenbrock, like the fierce Ajax, seemed to challenge the gods.
But I thought it wise to intervene and put a stop to this reckless fervor.
“Listen to me,” I said to him in a firm tone.

His exasperated hunger made him tremble like a feverish person: but a terror still held him back, paralyzing him.
He listened.
The whole house seemed to tremble; doors were closing, quick footsteps were running on the floor above.

This fossilized body was not the only one in the immense ossuary.
Other bodies were encountered with every step we took in this dust, and my uncle could choose the most wonderful of these samples to convince the skeptics.
In truth, it was an astonishing sight to see these generations of men and animals mingled in this cemetery.
But a serious question arose that we dared not resolve.
Had these living beings slipped through a convulsion of the earth to the shores of the Lidenbrock sea, while they were already reduced to dust?
Or did they rather live here, in this underground world, under this artificial sky, being born and dying like the inhabitants of the earth?
Until now, only the sea monsters, the fish, had appeared alive to us!
Was some man from the abyss still wandering on these deserted shores?
For another half hour, our feet trod on these layers of bones.
We moved forward, driven by an intense curiosity.
What other wonders did this cave hold, what treasures for science?
My gaze was prepared for all surprises, my imagination for all astonishments.
The shores of the sea had long since disappeared behind the hills of the ossuary.
The reckless professor, caring little about getting lost, was leading me far away.

By a phenomenon I cannot explain, and thanks to its complete diffusion at that time, the light illuminated the various faces of the objects uniformly.

All vapor had disappeared.
The rocks, the distant mountains, some confused masses of faraway forests, took on a strange appearance under the equal distribution of the luminous fluid.

sentences: Jasper Hobson's first task was to inform his companions that the hurricane did not seem to have yet reached its maximum intensity and that they should expect it to last for several days.
But the lieutenant announced this in a peculiar tone, as if he were bringing some good news, and the inhabitants of the trading post could not help but look at him with a certain sense of surprise.
Their leader really seemed to welcome this battle of the elements.
On the 30th, Jasper Hobson, once again braving the gusts, returned, if not to the summit of Cape Bathurst, at least to the edge of the coast.
There, on this steep shore, at the limit of the long waves that struck it at an angle, he spotted some long grasses unknown to the island's flora.
These grasses were still fresh!
They were long strands of seaweed that, there was no doubt about it, had recently been torn from the American continent!
So that continent was no longer far away!
The northeast wind had thus pushed the island out of the current that had been carrying it until then!
Ah!
Christopher Columbus did not feel any more joy in his heart when he encountered these drifting grasses that announced to him the proximity of land!

sentences: Finally, coming to himself as if from a deep sleep, he said to Mentor: I am determined to follow you, but I have not yet said goodbye to Eucharis.
I would rather die than abandon her like this with ingratitude.
Wait until I see her one last time to bid her an eternal farewell.
At least allow me to tell her: O nymph, the cruel gods, the gods jealous of my happiness, compel me to leave; but they will prevent me from living rather than from remembering you forever.
O my father, either grant me this last consolation, which is so just, or take my life at this moment.
No, I do not want to stay in this island, nor to surrender to love.
Love is not in my heart; I only feel friendship and gratitude for Eucharis.
It is enough for me to tell her one more time, and I will leave with you without delay.

While Mentor was speaking like this, he continued his way toward the sea; and Telemachus, who was not yet strong enough to follow him by himself, was already strong enough to let himself be led without resistance.

Minerva, always hidden under the guise of Mentor, invisibly covering Telemachus with her aegis, and spreading a divine ray around him, made him feel a courage he had not yet experienced since being on this island.
Finally, they arrived at a place on the island where the shoreline was steep; it was a rock constantly battered by the foaming waves.
They looked from this height to see if the ship that Mentor had prepared was still in the same place; but they saw a sad sight.

Then, seeing the downstairs room empty as usual and simply watched over by his dog, he called for his wife.
"Hey!"
Carconte, he said, that worthy priest didn't deceive us; the diamond is genuine.
A joyful exclamation was heard, and almost immediately the staircase creaked under a step weighed down by weakness and illness.
"I say the diamond is genuine; here is a gentleman, one of the top jewelers in Paris, who is ready to give us fifty thousand francs for it.
However, to be sure that the diamond truly belongs to us, he asks that you tell him, as I have already done, how the diamond miraculously came into our hands.
In the meantime, sir, please have a seat, and since the weather is heavy, I will go get something to refresh you.
The jeweler was carefully examining the interior of the inn and the visible poverty of those who were about to sell him a diamond that seemed to come from a prince's jewel box.
"Tell me, madam," he said, wanting no doubt to take advantage of the husband's absence so that no sign from him would influence the woman, and to see if the two stories would match up well.
"But how did he come to possess this diamond?"
the jeweler asked.
Did he have it before going to prison?

"No, sir," the woman replied, "but in prison he apparently made the acquaintance of a very wealthy Englishman; and since his cellmate fell ill, and Dantès took care of him as if he were his brother, the Englishman, upon leaving captivity, left the poor Dantès, who, less fortunate than him, died in prison, this diamond which he bequeathed to us in turn upon his death, and which he asked the worthy abbé who came this morning to deliver to us.

sentences: What is he going to do? Villefort wondered, a man whose high position required such restraint and who, moreover, could not guess what his father was aiming at.
He turned to send for the second notary designated by the first; but Barrois, who had heard everything and guessed his master's desire, had already left.
Then the public prosecutor had his wife called to come up.
After a quarter of an hour, everyone was gathered in the room of the paralytic, and the second notary had arrived.
In a few words, the two ministerial officers reached an agreement.
They read a vague, ordinary will formula to Noirtier; then, to begin, so to speak, the investigation of his intelligence, the first notary turned to him and said:
I will name several numbers that will increase successively; you will stop me when I reach the one you believe to be yours.

There was a kind of solemnity in this interrogation; moreover, the struggle of intelligence against matter had perhaps never been more visible; and if it wasn't sublime, as we were about to say, it was at least a curious spectacle.
They formed a circle around Villefort, the second notary was sitting at a table, ready to write; the first notary stood in front of him and was questioning.

sentences: Villefort said nothing; he simply lifted his head, which he had kept down until then, and looked at the doctor with wide eyes.
--Of course, replied the king's prosecutor; you whispered to me not to move away.
--Have you noticed the symptoms of the illness that Mrs. de Saint-Méran succumbed to?
--Certainly; Mrs. de Saint-Méran had three successive attacks just minutes apart, and each time they were closer together and more severe.

When you arrived, Mrs. de Saint-Méran had already been gasping for a few minutes; then she had a seizure that I mistook for a simple nervous attack; but I only truly began to panic when I saw her lift herself up on her bed, her limbs and neck tense.
Then, from your face, I understood that the situation was more serious than I had thought.
Once the seizure was over, I looked for your eyes, but I couldn't find them.
You were checking the pulse, counting the beats, and the second seizure appeared before you had even turned back to me.
This second seizure was more terrible than the first: the same nervous movements occurred again, and her mouth contracted and turned violet.
"Already, since the end of the first one, I had recognized tetanus; you confirmed this opinion for me.
--Yes, in front of everyone, the doctor replied; but now we are alone.
The symptoms of tetanus and poisoning from plant matter are absolutely the same," Mr.
de Villefort stood up; then, after a moment of stillness and silence, he sank back onto his bench.

sentences: Oh!
Valentine suddenly exclaimed, "I understand!"
"My marriage, right, dear father?"
"Yes, yes, yes," the paralytic repeated three times, throwing a glance each time his eyelid lifted.
"Excuse me, sir," said the notary, "on the contrary, all of this is very logical and seems to chain together perfectly."
"And you're disinheriting your granddaughter," the notary exclaimed, "because she's making a marriage against your wishes?"

The two notaries were consulting each other; Valentine, with her hands clasped, looked at her grandfather with a grateful smile; Villefort bit his thin lips; Mrs. de Villefort couldn't suppress a joyful feeling that, despite herself, blossomed on her face.
"But," Villefort finally said, breaking the silence first, "it seems to me that I am the sole judge of the proprieties that favor this union.
As the sole master of my daughter's hand, I want her to marry Mr.
Franz d'Épinay, and she will marry him." "Sir," said the notary, addressing the old man, "what do you plan to do with your fortune in the event that Miss Valentine marries Mr.
Franz?"
"But," said the notary, "you know that the law opposes you completely disinheriting your son?"
You will only have access to the part that the law allows you to withdraw.
My father knows me, sir, said Mr.
de Villefort, he knows that his will will be sacred to me; moreover, he understands that in my position I cannot argue against the poor.
Nothing, sir, it's a decision made in my father's mind, and I know that my father does not change his mind.

It's because he brought the cook tulip onions instead of edible onions." Seven dropped his brush and exclaimed, "Of all the injustices----" when his gaze accidentally fell on Alice, who was standing there watching them, and he suddenly held back.
The others turned around as well, and all gave a deep bow. "Would you be so kind as to tell me why you are painting these roses?" Alice asked a little timidly.
Five and Seven said nothing but looked at Two.
Two began in a low voice: "The fact is, you see, miss, that there should be a red rose bush here, and we mistakenly planted a white one.
If the Queen noticed, we would all have our heads chopped off, you understand.
So, miss, you see that we are doing our best before she comes to----" At that moment, Five, who had been anxiously watching from the other side of the garden, shouted, "The Queen!
The Queen!" and the three workers immediately threw themselves face down on the ground.
There was a great noise of footsteps, and Alice turned around, eager to see the Queen.
First came soldiers carrying pikes; they were all made like the gardeners, long and flat, with hands and feet at the corners; then came the ten courtiers.
They were all adorned with diamond patterns and walked two by two like the soldiers.
Behind them came the Queen's children; there were ten of them, and the little cherubs frolicked joyfully, holding hands two by two; they were all decorated with hearts.
After them came the guests, mostly kings and queens.
Among them, Alice recognized the White Rabbit.
He looked flustered and agitated while speaking, smiled at everything that was said, and passed by without paying attention to her.
Following him was the Knave of Hearts, carrying the crown on a velvet cushion; and bringing up the rear of this long procession were THE KING AND QUEEN OF HEARTS.

sentences: Edmond heard the noise of the bed on which the corpse was being shaken; he heard the governor's voice, who ordered that water be thrown in his face, and seeing that, despite this immersion, the prisoner was not coming back, sent for the doctor.
The governor left; and a few words of compassion reached Dantès's ears, mingled with mocking laughter.
"Come on, come on," said one, "the fool has gone to join his treasures, safe travels!"
"He won't have, with all his millions, enough to pay for his shroud," said the other.
"Oh!"
replied a third voice, "the shrouds from the Château d'If are not expensive."
Perhaps, one of the first speakers said, since he is a man of the Church, some expenses will be incurred in his favor.
Edmond was listening, not missing a word, but he didn't understand much of it all.
Soon the voices faded away, and it seemed to him that the attendees were leaving the room.
However, he did not dare to go back in: someone might have left a keyholder to watch over the dead.
After about an hour, the silence was stirred by a faint noise that grew louder.
It was the governor returning, followed by the doctor and several officers.
There was a moment of silence: it was clear that the doctor was approaching the bed and examining the corpse.
The doctor analyzed the illness that the prisoner had succumbed to and declared that he was dead.
Questions and answers were exchanged with a nonchalance that outraged Dantès; it seemed to him that everyone should feel some of the affection he had for the poor abbé.

"I am sorry for what you are telling me," said the governor, responding to the certainty expressed by the doctor that the old man was indeed dead; he was a gentle, harmless prisoner, amusing with his madness and especially easy to watch.

Diavolaccio continued to advance in the deepest silence and laid Rita at the captain's feet.
Then everyone could recognize the cause of the young girl's paleness and the bandit's paleness: Rita had a knife plunged to the hilt beneath her left breast.
All eyes turned to Carlini: the sheath was empty at his belt.
Ah!
Ah!
said the chief, I now understand why Carlini stayed behind.
Any wild nature is capable of appreciating a strong action; although perhaps none of the bandits would have done what Carlini just did, they all understood what he had done.

sentences: Doctor Fergusson, after taking in the whole scene at a glance, approached the wooden bed of the sovereign.
He saw there a man in his forties, completely stupefied by all sorts of orgies and beyond help.
This illness, which had been dragging on for years, was nothing but a perpetual drunkenness.

This royal drunkard had more or less lost consciousness, and not even all the ammonia in the world could have brought him back to his feet. The favorites and women, kneeling, bowed during this solemn visit.

With a few drops of a strong cordial, the doctor briefly revived this stupefied body; the sultan moved, and for a corpse that had shown no signs of life for several hours, this symptom was met with renewed cries in honor of the doctor.
The doctor, having had enough, quickly brushed aside his overly demonstrative admirers and left the palace.
He headed towards the Victoria.
It was six o'clock in the evening.
Joe, during his absence, was waiting calmly at the bottom of the ladder; the crowd was paying him the utmost respect.
As a true Son of the Moon, he let them do as they pleased.
For a deity, he looked like quite a decent man, not proud, even familiar with the young African women, who never tired of watching him.
He also spoke to them in friendly terms.
"Worship, ladies, worship," he told them; "I am a good fellow, though the son of a goddess!" He was presented with propitiatory gifts, usually placed in the 'mzimu' or fetish huts.
These consisted of ears of barley and 'pombé.' Joe felt obliged to taste this kind of strong beer; however, his palate, though accustomed to gin and whiskey, could not handle its strength.
He made a terrible grimace, which the audience took for a friendly smile.

sentences: Thus, the memory of that ball became an occupation for Emma.
Every Wednesday, when it came around, she would tell herself upon waking, "Ah!
it's been eight days...
it's been fifteen days...

it's been three weeks since I was there." And gradually, the faces blurred in her memory; she forgot the tune of the contradances, she no longer saw the livery and the rooms so clearly; some details faded away, but the regret remained.
Often, when Charles was out, she would go to the wardrobe, between the folds of the linen where she had left it, to take the green silk cigar holder.
She bought herself a map of Paris, and with the tip of her finger, on the map, she would plan trips in the capital.
She would walk up the boulevards, stopping at every corner, between the lines of the streets, in front of the white squares that represented the houses.

With tired eyes in the end, she would close her eyelids, and she would see in the darkness the gas lamps twisting in the wind, with the steps of carriages unfolding with a loud noise, in front of the theater's portico.
The post boy, every morning, who came to tend to the mare, would cross the corridor with his heavy hooves; his blouse had holes; his feet were bare in slippers.
That was the stable boy in short trousers that one had to make do with!

When his work was done, he wouldn't return for the rest of the day, because Charles, upon returning, would put his horse in the stable himself, remove the saddle, and put on the halter, while the maid brought a bundle of straw and tossed it, as best she could, into the manger.

This jailer Antoine was his jailer.

He had mostly forgotten his name and face; but, upon hearing his name spoken, he saw him again as he was, with his bearded face, his brown jacket, and his keyring, of which he still seemed to hear the jingling.
The count turned around and thought he saw him in the shadow of the corridor, made even darker by the light of the torch held by the concierge.
And he placed his hand on his chest to suppress a violent heartbeat, frightened to hear his own story being told.
This dungeon, the concierge continued, had been inhabited by a prisoner a long time ago, a man very dangerous, it seems, and all the more dangerous because he was full of cunning.
Another man lived in this castle at the same time as him; that one was not wicked; he was a poor priest who was mad.
Monte-Cristo looked up to the sky, but he did not see the sky: there was a stone veil between him and the firmament.

sentences: I pulled Benedetto aside and proposed that he follow me, surrounding this proposal with all the promises that could entice a twelve-year-old.
He let me go on until the end, and when I finished, bursting into laughter: "Are you crazy, my uncle?
he said (he called me that when he was in a good mood); me change the life I lead for the one you lead, my good and excellent laziness for the horrible work you have imposed on yourself!
spending the night in the cold, the day in the heat; constantly hiding; when you show yourself, getting shot at, and all that to earn a little money!
Money, I have as much as I want!
Mother Assunta gives me some whenever I ask her.
So you can see that I would be a fool if I accepted what you are proposing.
I was astonished by this audacity and this reasoning.
Benedetto went back to playing with his friends, and I saw him from a distance showing me to them as an idiot.
Oh!
If he had been mine, replied Bertuccio, if he had been my son, or at least my nephew, I would have brought him back to the right path, for conscience gives strength.
But the thought of beating a child whose father I had killed made any correction impossible for me.

I gave good advice to my sister, who, in our discussions, constantly defended the poor little boy, and when she confessed to me that she had often been short of considerable sums, I pointed out a place where she could hide our little treasure.
As for me, my mind was made up.
Benedetto could read, write, and count perfectly, for when he happened to want to work, he learned in one day what others learned in a week.

My mind was made up, I said; I had to hire him as a secretary on some long-distance ship, and, without warning him at all, have him taken one fine morning and transported on board; in this way, and by recommending him to the captain, his entire future would depend on him.
With this plan settled, I left for France.

sentences: The old Baron des Ravots had been the king of hunters in his province for forty years.
But for the past five or six years, paralysis in his legs had kept him confined to his chair, and he could only shoot pigeons from the window of his sitting room or from the top of his grand porch.
On sunny days, he would roll his large chair, which resembled a bed, in front of the door.

A servant, behind his back, held the guns, loaded them, and passed them to his master; another servant, hidden in a bush, would release a pigeon from time to time, at irregular intervals, so that the baron would not be alerted and would remain alert.

And from morning till evening, he shot at the fast-flying birds, lamenting when he was caught off guard, and laughing until he cried when the bird fell straight down or performed some unexpected and funny tumble.

He would then turn to the boy who loaded the guns and ask, gasping with joy: In the autumn, during the hunting season, he would invite his friends, just like in the old days, and he loved to hear the distant gunshots.
He counted them, happy when they came in quick succession.
And in the evening, he demanded a faithful account of each person's day.
And they would spend three hours at the table recounting their shooting exploits.
These were strange and improbable adventures, where the boastful nature of hunters reveled.
Some of them had become legendary and were recounted regularly.
The story of a rabbit that young Viscount de Bourril had missed in his hallway made them double over with laughter every year in the same way.
Every five minutes, a new speaker would take the floor:

sentences: These thoughts came back to me as I considered the coal riches accumulated in this part of the earth's massif.
These, no doubt, will never be uncovered.
The exploitation of these remote mines would require too considerable sacrifices.
What's the point, anyway, when coal is practically spread across the surface of the earth in many regions?
Thus, as I saw these untouched layers, so they would remain even when the world's last hour strikes.
However, we were walking, and only among my companions did I forget the length of the road to lose myself in geological considerations.
The temperature remained roughly what it was during our passage through the lavas and schists.
Only, my sense of smell was affected by a very strong odor of hydrogen proto-carbide.
I immediately recognized, in this gallery, the presence of a significant quantity of this dangerous gas that miners call firedamp, which has often caused terrible disasters.
Fortunately, we were illuminated by the ingenious devices of Ruhmkorff.
If, unfortunately, we had carelessly explored this gallery with a torch in hand, a terrible explosion would have ended the journey by eliminating the travelers.
This excursion into the coal mine lasted until evening.
My uncle could barely contain the impatience caused by the horizontal nature of the road.

The darkness, always deep twenty paces ahead, made it impossible to gauge the length of the gallery, and I began to believe it was endless when suddenly, at six o'clock, a wall unexpectedly appeared before us.
To the right, to the left, above, below, there was no passage.
We had reached the end of a dead end.

You understand these matters perfectly, and I have nothing to say in response to your observation,
unless, of course, there exists some unknown current that is not yet marked on this map.
Indeed, this uncertainty is dreadful.
I wish it were tomorrow so that I could be definitively settled on the situation of the island.
So there was nothing left to do but wait.
They parted ways.
Everyone returned to their usual activities.
Sergeant Long informed his companions that the departure for Fort Reliance, scheduled for the next day, would not take place.

He explained that, after further consideration, the season was too advanced to reach the trading post before the severe cold, that the astronomer had decided to endure another wintering to complete his meteorological observations, and that the resupply of Fort Esperance was not essential, etc.
These were all things that these brave people cared little about.

Lieutenant Hobson made a special recommendation to the hunters, advising them to spare the fur-bearing animals from now on, which he had no use for, and to focus on edible game in order to replenish the factory's supplies.

He also forbade them from straying more than two miles from the fort, not wanting Marbre, Sabine, or other hunters to unexpectedly find themselves facing a horizon of sea, where a few months ago, the isthmus connecting Victoria Peninsula to the American continent had developed.
The disappearance of this narrow strip of land would indeed have revealed the situation.
This day seemed endless to Lieutenant Hobson.
He returned several times to the summit of Cape Bathurst, either alone or accompanied by Mrs.
Paulina Barnett.
The traveler, a woman of strong spirit, was not at all frightened.
The future did not seem daunting to her.
She even joked with Jasper Hobson, saying that this drifting island they were on might be the true vehicle to reach the North Pole!

sentences: Captain Nemo was looking at me.
I didn't ask him anything, but he guessed my thoughts, and he answered the questions I was eager to ask all by himself.
"Most of these dishes are unknown to you," he said to me.
However, you can consume them without fear.
They are healthy and nourishing.
For a long time, I have given up on food from the land, and I am no worse for it.
My crew, who are strong, do not eat any differently than I do.
--Yes, professor, the sea provides for all my needs.
Sometimes, I drag my nets, and I pull them up, ready to break.
At other times, I go hunting in this element that seems inaccessible to man, and I catch the game that lies in my underwater forests.
My herds, like those of the old shepherd of Neptune, graze fearlessly on the vast meadows of the Ocean.

I have a vast property there that I manage myself and that is always seeded by the hand of the Creator of all things." I looked at Captain Nemo with some astonishment, and I replied to him: "I perfectly understand, sir, that your nets provide excellent fish for your table; I understand less that you pursue aquatic game in your underwater forests; but I do not understand at all how a piece of meat, however small, appears on your menu.
So, sir, Captain Nemo replied to me, I never make use of the flesh of land animals.
However, I said, pointing to a dish where a few slices of fillet still remained.
What you believe to be meat, professor, is nothing other than sea turtle fillet.
Here are also some dolphin livers that you would take for a pork stew.
My cook is a skilled preparer who excels at preserving these varied products of the Ocean.
Taste all these dishes.

Here is a can of sea cucumbers that a Malay would declare unrivaled in the world; here is a cream whose milk comes from the breast of cetaceans, and the sugar from the large seaweeds of the North Sea, and finally, allow me to offer you anemone jams that are as good as those made from the most delicious fruits.

sentences: In front of us stretched four marble steps, and at the bottom of the last step, a boat was gently swaying.
From where we were, we could see a dark mass rising in the middle of a lake; it was the kiosk we were heading to.
That kiosk seemed quite far away to me, perhaps because of the darkness.
We got into the boat.
I remember that the oars made no sound as they touched the water; I leaned over to look at them: they were wrapped with the sashes of our Palicares.
Besides the rowers, there were only women in the boat, my father, my mother, Sélim, and me.
The Palicares had remained on the shore of the lake, kneeling on the last step, forming a barrier with the other three in case they were pursued.
I didn’t understand.
Why was my father fleeing, he who was all-powerful, he before whom others usually fled, he who had taken as his motto: 'Indeed, it was a flight that my father was making across the lake.'

sentences: And this is what has emboldened you, Maximilien; this is what gives me both a sweet and a bitter life, to the point that I often wonder which is better for me: the sorrow that my stepmother's harshness and her blind preference for her child caused me in the past, or the happiness filled with dangers that I experience when I see you.
Danger!
Maximilien exclaimed; can you say such a harsh and unjust word?
Have you ever seen a more submissive slave than me?
You have allowed me to speak to you sometimes, Valentine, but you have forbidden me to follow you; I have obeyed.

Since I found a way to slip into this enclosure, to talk with you through this door, to be finally so close to you without seeing you, have I ever, tell me, asked to touch the hem of your dress through these bars?
Have I ever taken a step to cross this wall, a ridiculous obstacle for my youth and strength?
Never a reproach about your strictness, never a desire openly expressed; I have been bound to my word like a knight of old.
Admit at least this, so that I do not think you unjust.
It's true, said Valentine, as she passed between two boards the tip of one of her slender fingers on which Maximilien placed his lips; it's true, you are an honest friend.
But in the end, you acted only out of self-interest, my dear Maximilien; you knew very well that from the day the slave became demanding, he would have to lose everything.

You promised me the friendship of a brother, to me who has no friends, to me whom my father forgets, to me whom my stepmother persecutes, and who has for consolation only the old man who is motionless, mute, frozen, whose hand cannot hold mine, whose eye alone can speak to me, and whose heart undoubtedly still beats for me with a remnant of warmth.
Bitter mockery of fate that makes me an enemy and a victim of all those who are stronger than me, and gives me a corpse for support and for a friend!
Oh!
truly, Maximilien, I repeat it to you, I am very unhappy, and you are right to love me for who I am and not for yourself.

sentences: Soon, he spotted the tartan, which, with the wind almost directly against it, was tacking between the Château d'If and the Planier Tower.

For a moment, Dantès feared that instead of hugging the coast, the small vessel would head out to sea, as it would have done, for example, if its destination had been Corsica or Sardinia: but from the way it was maneuvering, the swimmer soon recognized that it intended to pass, as is customary for vessels heading to Italy, between the island of Jaros and the island of Calasereigne.
It was then that he congratulated himself on the precaution he had taken to lie down on a beam.

Weakened as he was, he might not have been able to stay afloat until he reached the tartan; and certainly, if the tartan, which was possible, passed by without seeing him, he wouldn't have been able to make it back to the shore.
Dantès, although he was fairly certain of the course the vessel was taking, followed it with his eyes with some anxiety, until he saw it make its turn and come back towards him.
Then he swam towards it; but before they could meet, the vessel began to change course.
This time, it was both seen and heard.
The tartan interrupted its maneuver and turned towards him.
At the same time, he saw that preparations were being made to launch a lifeboat.
A moment later, the lifeboat, manned by two men, headed in his direction, rowing vigorously with its double oars.
Dantès then let go of the beam he thought he no longer needed and swam vigorously to save half the distance for those coming to him.

sentences: Of course, replied the harpooner, and yet, in the three hours that I've been on this floating island, it hasn't shown any sign of life.
No, Mr. Aronnax.
It lets itself be rocked by the waves, but it doesn't move.
We know, without a doubt, however, that it is capable of great speed.
Now, since a machine is needed to produce this speed and a mechanic to operate this machine, I conclude...
that we are saved.
At that moment, and as if to support my argument, a bubbling sound came from the back of this strange device, whose propeller was obviously a screw, and it started to move.
We barely had time to cling to its upper part, which emerged about eighty centimeters.
Fortunately, its speed was not excessive.
"As long as it navigates horizontally," murmured Ned Land, "I have nothing to say.
But if it takes a notion to dive, I wouldn't give two dollars for my skin!" Even less, the Canadian could have said.
It was therefore becoming urgent to communicate with the beings contained within the sides of this machine.
I searched its surface for an opening, a hatch, "a manhole," to use the technical term; but the lines of bolts, securely fastened over the joints of the plates, were clear and uniform.
Moreover, the moon then disappeared, leaving us in deep darkness.
We had to wait for daylight to consider how to enter the interior of this submarine.
Thus, our salvation depended solely on the whims of the mysterious helmsmen who were steering this device, and if they dove, we were lost!
Except for this case, I had no doubt about the possibility of establishing contact with them.
And indeed, if they did not produce their own air, they necessarily had to return to the surface of the Ocean from time to time to replenish their supply of breathable molecules.
Therefore, there was a need for an opening that connected the interior of the boat with the atmosphere.

sentences: As long as I understand your treachery, sir, and manage to make you understand that I want to take my revenge, I will always be reasonable enough, said Albert furiously.
And Monte-Cristo showed Albert the door with an admirable gesture of command.
Well, well!
said Monte-Cristo phlegmatically; you are looking for a quarrel, sir; I see that; but a piece of advice, viscount, and remember it well: it is a bad custom to make noise when provoking.
Noise does not suit everyone, Mr. de Morcerf." At that name, a murmur of astonishment passed like a shiver among the spectators of this scene.
Since the day before, the name of Morcerf had been on everyone's lips.

Albert better than anyone, and first of all, understood the allusion, and made a gesture to throw his glove in the count's face; but Morrel seized his wrist, while Beauchamp and Château-Renaud, fearing that the scene would go beyond mere provocation, held him back from behind.

But Monte-Cristo, without getting up, merely leaned his chair, extended his hand, and grasping the damp and crushed glove between the young man's clenched fingers: Monte-Cristo took up his binoculars and resumed looking, as if nothing extraordinary had just happened.
This man had a heart of bronze and a face of marble.
Morrel leaned in to his ear.
It is through Haydée that the Chamber was informed of his father's betrayal.
Indeed, said Morrel, I was told, but I did not want to believe it, that this Greek slave I saw with you here, in this very box, was the daughter of Ali-Pacha.

sentences: I was about to take my usual place on the raft when my uncle stopped me with his hand.

"I mustn't overlook anything," he replied, "and since fate has brought me to this part of the coast, I won't leave without having explored it." This remark will be understood when one knows that we had returned to the northern shore, but not to the exact spot of our original departure.
Port-Graüben was supposed to be located further west.
It was therefore only reasonable to carefully examine the surroundings of this new landing.
And, leaving Hans to his tasks, we set off.
The space between the sea's edge and the foot of the foothills was quite wide; one could walk for half an hour before reaching the rock face.
Our feet crushed countless shells of all shapes and sizes, where the animals of the earliest epochs lived.
I also spotted enormous shells, whose diameter often exceeded fifteen feet.
They belonged to those gigantic glyptodonts from the Pliocene period, of which modern turtles are merely a small remnant.
Moreover, the ground was strewn with a large quantity of rocky debris, rounded pebbles shaped by the waves and arranged in successive lines.
I was thus led to make this observation, that the sea must have once occupied this space.
On the scattered rocks, now out of its reach, the waves had left clear traces of their passage.
This could explain to some extent the existence of this ocean, forty leagues below the surface of the globe.
But, in my view, this body of water must gradually be lost in the depths of the earth, and it obviously originated from the waters of the Ocean, which broke through some fissure.
However, it had to be acknowledged that this fissure was currently blocked, for this entire cavern, or rather this immense reservoir, would have filled up in a relatively short time.
Perhaps even this water, having had to battle against underground fires, had partially vaporized.
Hence the explanation for the clouds hanging above our heads and the release of this electricity that created storms within the earth's mass.

sentences: I took her hand, a bit confused, stammering: "Sorry, sorry, miss.
I hurt you; I was brutal!
Don't hold it against me.
If you only knew?..." I was vainly searching for an excuse.
After a moment, she said: "I have nothing to know, sir." But I had found it; I exclaimed: "Miss, I've loved you for a year!" She was truly surprised and looked up.
I continued: "Yes, miss, listen to me.
I don't know Morin and I don't care about him.
I couldn't care less if he goes to prison and faces the courts.
I saw you here last year, you were over there, by the gate.
I felt a jolt when I saw you and your image has never left me.
Believe me, or don't believe me, I couldn't care less.
I found you adorable; your memory possessed me; I wanted to see you again; I seized the pretext of that stupid Morin; and here I am.

Circumstances pushed me beyond my limits; forgive me, I beg you, forgive me." She was watching for the truth in my eyes, ready to smile again; and she murmured: "Joker." I raised my hand, and, in a sincere tone (I even believe I was sincere): "I swear to you I'm not lying." We were alone, completely alone, Rivet and the uncle having disappeared into the winding paths; and I made a real declaration to her, long, sweet, pressing and kissing her fingers.
She listened to this as something pleasant and new, not quite knowing what to believe about it.
I ended up feeling troubled; thinking about what I was saying; I was pale, oppressed, shivering; and gently, I took her waist.

The children in slippers ran around there as if on a floor made for them, and their voices could be heard ringing out through the buzzing of the bell.
It diminished with the swaying of the thick rope that, falling from the heights of the bell tower, dragged along the ground by its end.

sentences: So they had talked about the various dangers threatening childhood and the carelessness of the servants.
Madame Homais knew a thing or two about it, still bearing on her chest the marks of a burning dish that a cook had once dropped onto her apron.
Thus, these good parents took numerous precautions.
The knives were never sharpened, nor were the floors polished.
There were iron grilles on the windows and strong bars on the door frames.

The little Homais, despite their independence, could not move without a supervisor behind them; at the slightest cold, their father stuffed them with chest protectors, and until they were over four years old, they all wore, mercilessly, padded rolls.
It was, to be fair, a habit of Madame Homais; her husband was inwardly distressed, fearing for the intellectual organs the possible effects of such compression, and he even managed to say to her:
—I need to speak with you, he had whispered softly in the clerk's ear, who then started walking ahead of him up the stairs.

sentences: Autumn, that wonderful autumn, blended its gold and purple with the last vibrant greens, as if drops of melted sunshine had flowed from the sky into the depths of the woods.
We crossed Duclair, and then, instead of continuing towards Jumièges, my friend turned left and, taking a back road, plunged into the thicket.
And soon, from the top of a large hill, we once again discovered the magnificent Seine valley, with the winding river stretching out at our feet.
On the right, a tiny building covered with slate and topped with a steeple as high as a parasol leaned against a lovely house with green shutters, completely dressed in honeysuckle and roses.
A loud voice shouted, "Here are some friends!" And Mathieu appeared in the doorway.
He was a sixty-year-old man, thin, with a goatee and long white mustaches.
My companion shook his hand, introduced me, and Mathieu welcomed us into a cool kitchen that also served as his dining room.
He said, "I don’t have a fancy apartment, sir.
I really like not to stray far from the stew.
The pots and pans, you see, they provide company." "Why are you coming on a Thursday?
You know well that it’s my Patroness's consultation day.

I can’t go out this afternoon." And, running to the door, he let out a terrible bellow: "Mélie-e-e!" which must have made the sailors on the ships passing up and down the river, way down in the hollow valley, look up.
She's not happy with me, you see, because yesterday I found myself in the nineties." My neighbor started to laugh: "In the nineties, Mathieu!
How did you manage that?"

sentences: Albert couldn't make sense of the banker's gaze; so, turning to Monte-Cristo, who had understood perfectly:
--Yes, replied the count: but do you find anything particular in his gaze?
--I certainly do; but what does he mean with his news from Greece?
--Because, as I presume, you have connections in the country." Monte-Cristo smiled as one always smiles when they want to avoid answering.
"Look, said Albert, here he comes towards you, I'm going to compliment Mlle Danglars on her cameo; in the meantime, the father will have time to speak with you.
--If you compliment her, at least compliment her on her voice, said Monte-Cristo.
Albert approached Eugénie with a smile on his lips.
Meanwhile, Danglars leaned in to the count's ear.
"You gave me excellent advice, he said, and there is a whole horrible story behind those two words: Fernand and Janina.
--Yes, I'll tell you that; but take the young man away: I would be too embarrassed to stay with him now.
That's what I'm doing; he's accompanying me. Now, do I always have to send you the father?
The count signaled to Albert.

Both of them greeted the ladies and left: Albert with a perfectly indifferent air towards Mlle Danglars' disdain; Monte-Cristo reiterating to Mme Danglars his advice on the caution a banker’s wife should have to secure her future.
Hardly had the count's horses turned the corner of the boulevard when Albert turned to the count, bursting into a laugh that was too loud not to be somewhat forced.

sentences: Fifty-four hours!
he said to his companions.
Now, since I am determined not to travel at night, for fear of missing a stream, a spring, or a pond, we have three and a half days of travel left, during which we must find water at all costs.
I felt it necessary to warn you about this serious situation, my friends, because I am only reserving one gallon for our thirst, and we will have to stick to a strict ration.
--Ration us, replied the hunter; but it’s not yet time to despair; we have three days ahead of us, don’t you think?
Well!

Since our regrets won't change anything, in three days it will be time to make a decision; until then, let's remain extra vigilant." At dinner, the water was strictly measured; the amount of brandy in the grogs increased; but one had to be wary of this liquor, which was more likely to intoxicate than to refresh.

The peaceful night, with its starry magnificence, was followed by the unchanging day and the blazing rays of the sun; from its first light, the temperature became scorching.

sentences: She spent the night like that.
The lamp went out when there was no more oil: she saw neither the darkness nor the light, and day returned without her seeing the day.
The pain had placed a blindfold over her eyes that allowed her to see only Edmond.
Ah!
You are here!
she said at last, turning towards Fernand.
I haven't left you since yesterday," replied Fernand with a painful sigh.
On his part, Caderousse was very worried and very troubled: instead of going out like Mr.

Morrel had done, instead of trying something in favor of Dantès, for whom he could do nothing anyway, he had locked himself away with two bottles of cassis wine and had tried to drown his anxiety in drunkenness.

But in the state of mind he was in, two bottles were far too little to extinguish his judgment; he had therefore remained, too drunk to go get more wine, not drunk enough for the drunkenness to have erased his memories, leaning over his two empty bottles on a wobbly table, and seeing dance, in the reflection of his long-wicked candle, all those specters that Hoffmann scattered on his damp punch manuscripts like a black and fantastic dust.
Villefort, after receiving Mr.
de Salvieux's letter, kissed Renée on both cheeks, kissed the hand of Mrs. de Saint-Méran, and shook that of the marquis, was racing to the post on the road to Aix.

sentences: Indeed, my dear Albert, said Franz, you are as wise as Nestor and as prudent as Ulysses; and if your Circe manages to turn you into some beast, she must be very skillful or very powerful." Albert was right.

The beautiful unknown woman had undoubtedly decided not to pursue the intrigue any further that day; for although the young men took several more turns, they did not see the carriage they were looking for: it had probably disappeared down one of the adjacent streets.
Then they returned to the Rospoli palace, but the count had also vanished with the blue domino.
The two windows draped in yellow damask were still occupied by people he had undoubtedly invited.
At that moment, the same bell that had signaled the start of the masquerade rang for the retreat.
The line along the Corso immediately broke up, and in an instant all the carriages disappeared into the side streets.
Franz and Albert were then facing the via delle Maratte.
The coachman drove in without saying a word, and, making his way to the Plaza de España along the Poli palace, he stopped in front of the hotel.
Master Pastrini came to greet his guests at the threshold of the door.

Franz's first concern was to inquire about the count and to express his regret at not having picked him up in time, but Pastrini reassured him by saying that the Count of Monte Cristo had ordered a second carriage for him, and that this carriage had gone to fetch him at four o'clock at the Rospoli palace.
He was also tasked, on his behalf, with offering the two friends the key to his box at the Argentina theater.
