sentences: Immediately, Engineer Serkö and Captain Spade move closer to him, and fearing that he might fall into the sea, they hold him firmly and then bring him back onto the deck.
I also observe,
--for I have long experience,
--that Thomas Roch is in the grip of intense agitation.
He spins around, he gestures, incoherent phrases that are directed at no one come out of his mouth...
This is all too evident; a crisis is imminent,
He is experiencing a crisis similar to the one that seized him during his last evening at Healthful-House, the consequences of which were so dire.
We will have to take hold of him and bring him down to his cabin, where I may be called to give him the special care I'm used to...
In the meantime, Engineer Serkö and Captain Spade are keeping a close eye on him.

Presumably, their intention is to let him be, and here’s what he does: After heading towards the main mast, which his eyes have vainly searched for sails, he reaches it, wraps his arms around it, and tries to shake it as if he wants to bring it down...
And then, seeing his fruitless efforts with the main mast, he attempts the same with the foremast.
His nervousness grows gradually.
Inarticulate cries follow the vague words that escape him...
Suddenly, he rushes towards the port shrouds and clings to them.
I wonder if he’s going to leap onto the stays, climbing up to the bars of the topgallant...
If he isn’t stopped, he risks falling onto the deck or, in a sudden roll, being thrown into the sea...

sentences: Mme Danglars cast a quick, probing glance around her that only Monte-Cristo could understand, taking in the courtyard, the peristyle, and the facade of the house; then, suppressing a slight emotion that would certainly have shown on her face if it had been possible for her to pale, she ascended the steps while saying to Morrel, "Sir, if you were one of my friends, I would ask you if your horse is for sale." Morrel gave a smile that closely resembled a grimace and turned to Monte-Cristo, as if asking him to help him out of the embarrassment he was in.
"Ah!"
madame, he replied, "why is it that this request is not directed at me?"
"With you, sir," said the baroness, "one has no right to desire anything, as one is too sure of getting it.
So it was addressed to Mr.
Morrel.
"Unfortunately," the count replied, "I am a witness that Mr.
Morrel cannot part with his horse, as his honor is at stake in keeping it.
"You see, madame..."
Morrel said, while giving Monte-Cristo a grateful smile.

"It seems to me, moreover," said Danglars in a gruff tone poorly disguised by his thick smile, "that you have enough horses as it is." It was not Mme Danglars' habit to let such attacks go unanswered, and yet, to the great astonishment of the young people, she pretended not to hear and said nothing.

Monte-Cristo smiled at this silence, which revealed an unusual humility, while showing the baroness two enormous Chinese porcelain pots, on which marine vegetation wound in such size and craftsmanship that only nature can possess such richness, vitality, and spirit.

Oh!

You see, they had strongly advised me not to say anything to you; they hadn't told me anything myself, and I kind of overheard this secret by being indiscreet; that's why I've been so reserved with you.
Forgive me, dear father Noirtier.” Once again fixed and expressionless, his gaze seemed to reply: “It's not just your silence that troubles me.” “What is it then?
asked the young girl: you might think that I would abandon you, dear father, and that my marriage would make me forgetful?
They told you then that Mr. d'Épinay agreed to us staying together?
Well, listen, said Valentine as she knelt before Noirtier and put her arms around his neck, I too have a lot of sorrow, because I don't like Mr.

Franz d'Épinay. When I wanted to retire to the convent, you remember that you were very angry with me? Well, Valentine continued, it was to escape this marriage that brings me despair. So, this marriage makes you very sad, dear father?
Oh my God, if you could help me, if we could together break their plan!
But you are powerless against them, you whose mind is so sharp and whose will is so strong, yet when it comes to fighting, you are as weak and even weaker than I am.
Alas!
you would have been such a powerful protector for me in the days of your strength and health; but today you can only understand me and either rejoice or grieve with me.

sentences: Ah!

Well, in any case, said Caderousse, who was drinking while talking and on whom the smoky wine of La Malgue was starting to take effect, in any case, Fernand is not the only one disturbed by Dantès's fortunate arrival, is he, Danglars?
No, you're right, and I would almost dare say that this will bring him bad luck.

But anyway, Caderousse replied as he poured a glass of wine for Fernand and filled his own glass for the eighth or tenth time while Danglars had barely touched his; anyway, in the meantime he is marrying Mercédès, the beautiful Mercédès; at least he is coming back for that.

Meanwhile, Danglars flinched at this unexpected blow and turned to Caderousse, whose face he studied in turn to see if the strike was premeditated; but he read nothing but envy on that face, which was already almost dazed by drunkenness.

"Well then," he said while filling the glasses, "let's drink to Captain Edmond Dantès, husband of the beautiful Catalan!" Caderousse raised his glass to his mouth with a heavy hand and downed it in one go.
Fernand took his and smashed it on the ground.
"Eh!
eh!
eh!"
Caderousse said, "what do I see over there, at the top of the hill, in the direction of the Catalans?
Look, Fernand, you have better eyesight than I do; I think I'm starting to see double, and you know, wine is a traitor: it looks like two lovers walking side by side, hand in hand.
God forgive me!
they don't suspect that we see them, and there they are kissing!"

sentences: The garden, longer than it was wide, stretched between two walls of rammed earth covered with espaliered apricots, all the way to a hedge of thorns that separated it from the fields.
In the middle, there was a slate sundial on a masonry pedestal; four flowerbeds filled with thin wild roses symmetrically surrounded the more practical square of serious vegetation.
At the very back, under the small fir trees, a plaster priest was reading his breviary.
Emma went up to the bedrooms.
The first one was unfurnished; but the second, which was the marital bedroom, had a mahogany bed in a recess with red drapery.
A shell box decorated the dresser; and on the writing desk, near the window, there was, in a carafe, a bouquet of orange blossoms tied with white satin ribbons.
It was a bridal bouquet, the bouquet from the other!
She looked at it.

Charles noticed this, took it, and went to put it in the attic, while Emma, sitting in an armchair (her belongings were arranged around her), thought about her wedding bouquet, which was packed in a box, and wondered, daydreaming, what would happen to it if she happened to die.
In the first few days, she occupied herself with contemplating changes in her house.

She removed the globes from the candlesticks, had new wallpaper put up, repainted the staircase, and had benches made in the garden all around the sundial; she even asked how to go about having a water fountain with fish.
Finally, her husband, knowing that she liked to go for drives, found a second-hand carriage that, with once new lanterns and studded leather mudguards, almost resembled a tilbury.

sentences: This sentiment is worthy of the father of peoples, Mentor replied; it is to this kindness, and not to the vain magnificence of your city, that I recognize in you the heart of a true king.
But you must safeguard your honor, for the very interest of your kingdom.

Let me handle it; I will make these kings understand that you have committed to restoring Ulysses, if he is still alive, or at least his son, to royal power in Ithaca, and that you want to forcibly drive out all of Penelope's suitors.
They will have no trouble understanding that this war requires numerous troops.
Thus, they will agree that you should initially provide them only with a small support against the Daunians.
At these words, Idomeneus appeared like a man relieved of a heavy burden.
You save, dear friend, he said to Mentor, my honor, and the reputation of this fledgling city, whose exhaustion you will hide from all my neighbors.

But what appearance is there in saying that I want to send troops to Ithaca to restore Ulysses, or at least Telemachus his son, while Telemachus himself is engaged in going to war against the Daunians!
At these words, Idomeneus exclaimed: Happy is the king who is supported by wise counsel!
A wise and loyal friend is worth more to a king than victorious armies.
But doubly happy is the king who feels his happiness and knows how to benefit from it through the proper use of wise counsel!
For it often happens that one distances from his trust wise and virtuous men whose virtue he fears, to lend an ear to flatterers whom he does not fear for their treachery.
I myself have fallen into this fault, and I will tell you all the misfortunes that have come to me from a false friend, who flattered my passions in the hope that I would in turn flatter his.

sentences: I must admit that it's quite a great misfortune, said the sergeant, that we came to settle on this peninsula just as it was about to break away from the continent and sail the seas!
For indeed, my lieutenant, things had been this way for a long, long time!
Perhaps centuries!
--You could say thousands and thousands of years, Sergeant Long, replied Jasper Hobson.
Just think that the topsoil we are walking on right now was brought here by the winds piece by piece, that this sand has flown here grain by grain!
Consider the time it took for these seeds of firs, birches, and strawberry trees to multiply, to become shrubs and trees!
Perhaps this ice floe that carries us was formed and fused to the continent even before the appearance of man on earth!
Well, exclaimed Sergeant Long, he should have waited a few more centuries before drifting away, that fickle iceberg!
That would have spared us a lot of worries and perhaps many dangers!" This very valid observation from Sergeant Long ended the conversation, and we set off again.
From Cape Eskimo to Morse Bay, the coast ran roughly north and south, following the projection of the one hundred twenty-seventh meridian.

Behind us, at a distance of four to five miles, we could see the pointed end of the lagoon, which was reflecting the sun's rays, and a little beyond that, the last wooded slopes whose greenery framed its waters.
A few whistling eagles passed through the air with great wingbeats.
Numerous fur-bearing animals, martens, minks, and ermines, lay hidden behind some sandy outcroppings or concealed among the sparse bushes of arbutus and willows, watching the travelers.
They seemed to understand that they had nothing to fear from gunfire.
Jasper Hobson also caught sight of a few beavers, wandering aimlessly and likely very disoriented since the little river had disappeared.
Without huts for shelter, and without a watercourse to build their village, they were destined to perish from the cold as soon as the severe frosts set in.
Sergeant Long also recognized a pack of wolves running across the plain.

In my opinion, his madness is already incurable.
Even if all the money he asks for were made available to him, nothing could be gained from it...
"That's likely," replied Count d'Artigas, "and yet, even though his financial demands are absurd, he has nonetheless invented a device of virtually infinite power..."

sentences: Having made this resolution, the next step was to carry it out.
It was only after long searches that Passepartout discovered a local antique dealer, to whom he presented his request.
The European outfit pleased the dealer, and soon Passepartout emerged dressed in an old Japanese robe and wearing a kind of ribbed turban, faded by the passage of time.
But in return, a few coins jingled in his pocket.

The first thing Passepartout did, now 'Japanese', was to enter a modest-looking tea house, where he had lunch made from leftover poultry and a few handfuls of rice, as a man for whom dinner would still be a problem to solve.
'Now,' he said to himself when he was well-fed, 'I must not lose my head.
I can no longer sell this rag for another one that is even more Japanese.
So I need to find a way to leave this land of the Sun as quickly as possible, of which I will only keep a lamentable memory!' Passepartout then thought about visiting the ships departing for America.
He planned to offer himself as a cook or servant, asking for nothing in return but passage and food.
Once in San Francisco, he would figure out how to get by.
The important thing was to cross the four thousand seven hundred miles of the Pacific that stretch between Japan and the New World.
Passepartout, being not the kind of man to let an idea linger, headed towards the port of Yokohama.
But as he approached the docks, his plan, which had seemed so simple when he first thought of it, appeared increasingly unfeasible.
Why would anyone need a cook or servant on an American liner, and what trust would he inspire, dressed like that?
What recommendations could he present?
What references could he provide?
A question arose in my mind.
How did the commander of this floating dwelling operate?
Did he obtain air through chemical means, by releasing oxygen contained in potassium chlorate through heat, and absorbing carbon dioxide with caustic potash?
In that case, he must have maintained some connections with the continents to procure the materials necessary for this operation.
Was he only limited to storing air under high pressure in tanks, then releasing it according to the needs of his crew?
Perhaps.

Or, a more convenient, economical, and therefore more likely method, did he simply come back to the surface of the water to breathe, like a cetacean, renewing his supply of atmosphere for twenty-four hours?
In any case, whatever the method, it seemed prudent to employ it without delay.
Indeed, I was already forced to take multiple breaths to extract the little oxygen contained in this cell when suddenly I was refreshed by a current of pure air, fragrant with saline emanations.
It was indeed the sea breeze, invigorating and rich in iodine!
I opened my mouth wide, and my lungs filled with fresh molecules.
At the same time, I felt a gentle rocking, a roll of moderate amplitude, but perfectly discernible.
The boat, the metal monster, had obviously just surfaced in the Ocean to breathe like whales.
The ship's ventilation system was therefore perfectly recognized.
When I had inhaled this pure air deeply, I searched for the duct, the 'aeriferous' one, if you will, that allowed this beneficial breeze to reach us, and I soon found it.
Above the door, there was an air vent that let in a fresh column of air, thus renewing the depleted atmosphere of the cell.

sentences: She felt, moreover, more irritated with him.

He was taking on a heavier appearance with age; he was uncorking empty bottles at dessert; he was running his tongue over his teeth after eating; he made a gurgling sound with each sip of his soup, and as he began to gain weight, his already small eyes seemed to be lifted towards his temples by the swelling of his cheeks.

Sometimes, Emma would tuck the red trim of his sweaters into his vest, adjust his tie, or toss aside the faded gloves he was about to put on; and it wasn't, as he thought, for him; it was for herself, out of a burst of selfishness, a nervous irritation.

Sometimes too, she would talk to him about things she had read, like a passage from a novel, a new play, or the anecdotes of high society that were recounted in the newspaper; for, after all, Charles was someone, always a willing ear, always ready to approve.
She confided a lot in her little dog!
She would have done so with the logs in the fireplace and the pendulum of the clock.
Spring returned.
She experienced breathlessness in the early warmth when the pear trees bloomed.
At the beginning of July, she counted on her fingers how many weeks were left until October, thinking that the Marquis of Andervilliers might still give a ball at Vaubyessard.
But all of September passed without letters or visits.
After the boredom of this disappointment, her heart was once again empty, and then the series of the same days began again.
They were now going to follow one after the other, always the same, countless, and bringing nothing!
Other lives, however dull they might be, at least had the chance of an event.
An adventure sometimes brought endless twists and turns, and the scenery changed.
But for her, nothing happened; God had willed it!
The future was a completely dark corridor, with a tightly shut door at the end.

look.
And she went to the desk, rummaged through all the drawers, mixed up the papers, and ended up so confused that Charles strongly urged her not to go to so much trouble for those miserable receipts.

Indeed, the following Friday, Charles, while putting on one of his boots in the dark closet where his clothes were kept, felt a piece of paper between the leather and his sock; he picked it up and read: "Receipt, for three months of lessons, plus various supplies, the sum of sixty-five francs.--Félicie Lempereur, music teacher."
"It must have fallen, no doubt," she replied, "from the old box of invoices that's on the edge of the shelf."

sentences: The servant at our inn was no more than eighteen years old, with bright blue eyes, a pale blue pierced by the two small black dots of her pupils; and her short, tightly packed teeth, which she constantly showed while laughing, seemed made to crush granite.
She didn't know a word of French, only speaking Breton, like most of her fellow countrymen.
However, my friend wasn't doing much better, and although no illness had manifested, the doctor forbade him from leaving yet, ordering complete rest.
So I spent my days near him, and the little maid constantly came in, bringing either my dinner or herbal tea.
I teased her a little, which seemed to amuse her, but we didn't talk, of course, since we couldn't understand each other.
Finally exhausted, she fell; and I picked her up roughly from the ground, off the pavement.
As soon as she was up, she ran to the door, pulled the bolts, and fled.
I barely saw her in the following days.
She didn't let me get close to her.
Then, as my friend had recovered and we were to continue our journey, I saw her enter, the night before my departure, at midnight, barefoot, in her nightgown, into my room where I had just retired.

She threw herself into my arms, embraced me passionately, then, until dawn, kissed me, caressed me, crying, sobbing, finally giving me all the assurances of tenderness and despair that a woman can give when she doesn't know a word of our language.
Eight days later, I had forgotten this adventure, common and frequent when traveling, as inn maids are generally meant to entertain travelers in this way.

sentences: It was on May 17th, about five hundred miles from Heart's Content, at a depth of two thousand eight hundred meters, that I spotted the cable lying on the sea floor.
Conseil, whom I hadn't warned, initially mistook it for a gigantic sea serpent and was preparing to classify it according to his usual method.
But I disabused the worthy fellow, and to console him for his disappointment, I taught him various details about the laying of this cable.
The operation went smoothly.
However, an incident occurred.
Several times, while unrolling the cable, the electricians noticed that nails had recently been driven into it with the intent of damaging its core.
Captain Anderson, his officers, and his engineers gathered, deliberated, and announced that if the culprit was caught on board, he would be thrown overboard without further judgment.
Since then, the criminal attempt has not been repeated.
I did not expect to find the electric cable in its original state, just as it was when it left the manufacturing workshops.
The long cable, covered in shell debris and bristling with foraminifera, was encrusted in a rocky coating that protected it from boring mollusks.

It lay quietly, sheltered from the movements of the sea, and under pressure favorable for the transmission of the electric spark that travels from America to Europe in thirty-two hundredths of a second.
The lifespan of this cable will undoubtedly be infinite, as it has been observed that the gutta-percha sheath improves with its time in seawater.
Was Captain Nemo going to surface to land on the British Isles?
No.
To my great surprise, he descended south and returned towards the European seas.
As I rounded Emerald Isle, I caught a glimpse of Cape Clear and the Fastnet lighthouse, which lights up the thousands of ships coming from Glasgow or Liverpool.

sentences: I have kept this sad relic.
And I wish that our sons never see war again.

Mrs. Lefèvre was a country lady, a widow, one of those half-peasant women with ribbons and frilly hats, one of those people who speak with airs of grandeur, put on a show in public, and hide a pretentious brutish soul beneath comical and colorful exteriors, just as they conceal their large red hands under raw silk gloves.
The two women lived in a small house with green shutters, along a road in Normandy, in the heart of the Pays de Caux.
Since they had a narrow garden in front of the house, they grew some vegetables.
As soon as Rose noticed the theft, she ran to inform her mistress, who came down wearing a wool skirt.
It was a desolation and a terror.
They had stolen, stolen Mrs. Lefèvre!
So, theft was happening in the area, and they could come back.
And the two frightened women gazed at the footprints, chatted, and speculated: 'Look, they passed through here.
They put their feet on the wall; they jumped into the flowerbed.' The news of the theft spread.
The neighbors arrived, confirmed the situation, discussed it in turn; and the two women explained their observations and ideas to each newcomer.
A farmer from nearby offered them this advice: 'You should get a dog.' Once everyone had left, Mrs. Lefèvre pondered this idea of a dog for a long time.

After some thought, she raised a thousand objections, terrified by the image of a bowl full of dog food; for she belonged to that frugal breed of country ladies who always carry coins in their pockets to ostentatiously give alms to the poor on the roads and to contribute to Sunday collections.

sentences: The castle of Kronborg soon disappeared into the mist, as did the tower of Helsingborg, rising on the Swedish shore, and the schooner tilted slightly under the breezes of the Kattegat.
What will be the duration of the crossing?
my uncle asked the captain.
About ten days, replied the latter, if we don't encounter too many north-west gales across the Faroe Islands.
In the evening, the schooner rounded Cape Skagen at the northern tip of Denmark, crossed the Skager Rack during the night, passed the end of Norway by Cape Lindness, and entered the North Sea.
Soon our schooner was battered by the waves of the Atlantic; it had to beat against the north wind and did not reach the Faroe Islands without difficulty.
On the 3rd, the captain recognized Myganness, the easternmost of these islands, and from that moment on, he headed straight for Cape Portland, located on the southern coast of Iceland.
The crossing offered no remarkable incidents.
I handled the trials of the sea quite well; my uncle, to his great dismay, and even greater shame, remained constantly ill.

He therefore could not engage Captain Bjarne on the subject of Sneffels, on communication methods, on transport facilities; he had to postpone his explanations until his arrival and spent all his time lying in his cabin, whose walls creaked from the heavy pitching.
I must admit, he somewhat deserved his fate.
On the 11th, we sighted Cape Portland; the weather, clear at that time, allowed us to glimpse the Myrdalsjökull, which dominates it.
The cape consists of a large hill with steep slopes, standing alone on the beach.

sentences: I was called three months ago to the bedside of this old woman.
She had arrived the day before in the cart that served as her home, pulled by the nag you saw, and accompanied by her two large black dogs, her friends and guardians.
The priest was already there.
She made us her executors, and to reveal the meaning of her last wishes, she told us her whole life story.
I know nothing more singular and poignant.
Her father was a chair caner and her mother a chair caner as well.
She never had a home planted in the ground.
As a little girl, she wandered, ragged, verminous, and sordid.

They would stop at the entrance of villages, along the ditches; they would unhitch the cart; the horse would graze; the dog would sleep with its nose on its paws; and the little girl would roll in the grass while her parents repaired all the old seats of the community in the shade of the roadside elms.
They hardly spoke in that mobile home.
After a few necessary words to decide who would go around the houses shouting the well-known cry: 'Chair caner!', they would start twisting the straw, face to face or side by side.

When the child wandered too far or tried to make friends with some village urchin, her father's angry voice would call her back: 'Will you please come back here, you little rascal!' Those were the only words of tenderness she heard.
When she grew older, she was sent to collect the scraps of damaged seats.

Then she began to form some acquaintances here and there with the kids; but it was the parents of her new friends who would harshly call their children back: 'Will you please come here, you little scamp!'
'I want to see you talking to the ragamuffins!...'

sentences: In the evening, on his way back, Charles recalled one by one the phrases she had said, trying to remember them and to complete their meaning, in order to grasp the part of her life that she had lived during the time he did not yet know her.
But he could never picture her in his mind any differently than he had seen her the first time, or as he had just left her a moment ago.
Then he wondered what she would become, if she would marry, and to whom?
Alas!
Monsieur Rouault was quite wealthy, and she!...
So beautiful!
But Emma's image always returned to his mind, and something monotonous like the buzzing of a spinning top droned in his ears: "If only you would marry, though!

If only you would marry!" That night, he did not sleep, his throat was tight, he was thirsty; he got up to drink from his water jug and opened the window; the sky was covered with stars, a warm wind was blowing, and in the distance, dogs were barking.
He turned his head towards the Bertaux.

Thinking that after all there was nothing to lose, Charles promised himself he would propose when the opportunity arose; but every time it did, the fear of not finding the right words stuck to his lips.
Monsieur Rouault would not have been upset if someone had taken his daughter off his hands, as she was of little use to him in his home.
He excused her internally, thinking she had too much spirit for farming, a cursed profession from heaven, since one never saw a millionaire in it.

Far from having made a fortune, the old man lost money there every year; for while he excelled in the markets, where he enjoyed the tricks of the trade, the actual farming, with the internal management of the farm, suited him less than anyone.
He was reluctant to take his hands out of his pockets, and he did not spare expenses for anything concerning his life, wanting to be well-fed, well-heated, and well-rested.
He loved strong cider, rare leg of lamb, and long-beaten glorias.
He took his meals in the kitchen, alone, in front of the fire, at a small table that was brought to him fully set, like in a theater.

sentences: That's fine; then Mr. Bertuccio, you may leave, I no longer need you.
Just let us know when lunch is served.
These gentlemen, he continued, turning to his two friends, are they honoring me by having lunch with me?
No, on the contrary, you are doing me a great pleasure; you will repay me for all this one day in Paris, one or the other, and perhaps both.
Mr. Bertuccio, please set three places.
There are few, at least, that I haven't seen, the count replied coldly.
And you found pleasure in witnessing these horrible spectacles?
My first feeling was repulsion, the second indifference, the third curiosity.
Why?
There is hardly anything in life that is a serious concern; it is death, well!

Isn't it curious to study the different ways the soul can leave the body, and how, depending on characters, temperaments, and even the customs of the country, individuals endure this supreme passage from being to nothingness?
As for me, I can tell you one thing: the more one has seen die, the easier it becomes to die; thus, in my opinion, death may be a punishment, but it is not an atonement.
I don't quite understand you, said Franz; explain yourself, because I can't tell you how much what you're saying piques my curiosity.
Yes, I know, replied Franz, human justice is insufficient as a comfort: it can shed blood in exchange for blood, that's all; we must ask it for what it can do and nothing more.

sentences: One cannot respond with more logic and accuracy, said the president of the Gun Club.
The question then comes down to this: Are the worlds habitable?
I believe so, for my part.
--However, one of the assistants replied, there are arguments against the habitability of worlds.
It would obviously require that the principles of life be modified in most cases.
Thus, to speak only of the planets, one would have to be burned on some and frozen on others, depending on how far they are from the Sun.
Did the opponent of Michel Ardan's theories venture any other arguments?
It is impossible to say, as the frantic cries of the crowd would have prevented any opinion from emerging.
When silence was restored even in the most distant groups, the triumphant speaker contented himself with adding the following considerations:
Well!
a boisterous voice exclaimed, let's join our efforts, invent machines and straighten the axis of the Earth!
A thunderous applause erupted at this proposal, whose author was and could only be J.-T.
Maston.
It is likely that the impassioned secretary had been carried away by his engineering instincts to make this bold proposal.

But, it must be said—because it is the truth—many supported him with their shouts, and undoubtedly, if they had had the fulcrum called for by Archimedes, the Americans would have built a lever capable of lifting the world and straightening its axis.
But the fulcrum, that is what was missing for these reckless mechanics.

Nevertheless, this "eminently practical" idea had enormous success; the discussion was suspended for a good quarter of an hour, and for a long, long time afterward, people talked in the United States of America about the proposal so energetically put forward by the perpetual secretary of the Gun-Club.

In the same funeral carriage, Beauchamp, Albert, and Château-Renaud were discussing this almost sudden death.

I saw Madame de Saint-Méran just last year in Marseille, Château-Renaud said; I was returning from Algeria; she was a woman destined to live a hundred years, thanks to her perfect health, her ever-present mind, and her always prodigious activity.
How old was she?
--Sixty-six, Albert replied, at least according to what Franz assured me.
But it wasn't her age that killed her; it was the grief she felt over the marquis's death; apparently, since that death, which had shaken her violently, she hasn't completely regained her sanity.
--From a cerebral congestion, it seems, or from a sudden apoplexy.
Isn't that the same thing?
--From apoplexy?
Beauchamp said, it's hard to believe.

Madame de Saint-Méran, whom I also saw once or twice in my life, was small, slender in build, and of a constitution much more nervous than sanguine; apoplexies caused by grief are rare in a body with a constitution like that of Madame de Saint-Méran.

A devoted boy who accompanied me on all my travels; a brave Fleming whom I loved and who returned my affection, a phlegmatic being by nature, regular by principle, zealous by habit, rarely surprised by life's surprises, very skillful with his hands, capable of any service, and, despite his name, never giving advice.
—even when it wasn't asked of him.
By rubbing shoulders with the scholars of our little world at the Jardin des Plantes, Conseil had come to know something.

I had in him a specialist, very knowledgeable about classification in natural history, navigating with the agility of an acrobat through the entire hierarchy of groups, classes, subclasses, orders, families, genera, subgenera, species, and varieties.
But his knowledge stopped there.
Classifying was his life, and he didn't know any more than that.
Very well-versed in the theory of classification, but lacking in practice, he wouldn't have been able to distinguish, I believe, a sperm whale from a baleen whale!
And yet, what a brave and worthy young man!

sentences: One of these silver foxes was a magnificent animal, slightly larger than the common fox.
It had ears, shoulders, and a tail of smoky black, but the fine tip of its tail and the tops of its eyebrows were white.

The particular circumstances in which this fox was killed deserve to be recounted in detail, as they justified certain concerns of Lieutenant Hobson, as well as some defensive precautions he felt he had to take.
On the morning of September 24, two sleds had brought Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, the lieutenant, Sergeant Long, Marbre, and Sabine to Morse Bay.
Fox tracks had been spotted the day before by a few men from the detachment, among rocks where thin shrubs were growing, and certain undeniable signs had revealed their passage.
The hunters, eager for the chase, set out to find a trail that promised them a valuable prize, and indeed, their search was not in vain.
Two hours after their arrival, a rather fine silver fox lay dead on the ground.
Two or three other carnivores were also glimpsed.
The hunters then split up.
While Marbre and Sabine pursued the tracks of one fox, Lieutenant Hobson, Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, and Sergeant Long tried to cut off the retreat of another fine animal that was trying to hide behind the rocks.
It was necessary to be cunning with this fox, which, barely showing itself, exposed no part of its body to the impact of a bullet.
For half an hour, this pursuit continued without yielding any results.
However, the animal was surrounded on three sides, with the sea blocking the fourth.
It soon realized the disadvantage of its situation and decided to escape with a tremendous leap, leaving the hunter with no other chance than to shoot it in mid-air.

sentences: At nine o'clock in the evening, the Victoria remained motionless above Mséné, a vast gathering of barely distinct villages in the shadows; sometimes the reflection of a stray ray in the dull water indicated regularly spaced ditches, and, through a final clearing, the eye could catch the calm and dark shapes of palm trees, tamarinds, sycamores, and gigantic euphorbias.
"I'm suffocating!
said the Scot, taking in as much of the thin air as possible; we're not moving anymore!
Shall we descend?
--If you're afraid of being carried away by the wind, it seems to me you have no other option.
--The storm might not break tonight, Joe replied; the clouds are very high.

--That's a reason that makes me hesitate to go above them; we would need to rise to a great height, lose sight of the ground, and not know all night whether we are making progress and in which direction.
--It's unfortunate that the wind has died down, Joe replied; it would have carried us far from the storm.
--That's regrettable, my friends, because the clouds are a danger to us; they contain opposing currents that can entangle us in their whirlwinds, and lightning capable of setting us on fire.
On the other hand, the force of the gust could send us crashing to the ground if we drop anchor at the top of a tree.
The Victoria must be kept in a safe zone between the dangers of the earth and the dangers of the sky.
We have enough water for the burner, and our two hundred pounds of ballast are intact.
If necessary, I would use it.

sentences: Telemachus, having donned these divine arms, instead of taking his usual belt, took the terrible aegis that Minerva had sent him, entrusting it to Iris, the swift messenger of the gods.
Iris had removed his belt without him noticing, and had given him in its place this fearsome aegis even the gods dread.
In this state, he runs out of the camp to avoid the flames; he calls to all the army leaders in a loud voice, and this voice already revives all the panic-stricken allies.
A divine fire sparkles in the eyes of the young warrior.
He always appears gentle, always free and calm, always focused on giving orders, like a wise old man dedicated to managing his family and teaching his children.
But he is quick and swift in execution: like a raging river that not only rushes its foamy waves with speed but also carries along in its course the heaviest vessels it is laden with.
Adraste trembles with rage, seeing the death of his dear son, that of several captains, and the victory slipping from his grasp.
Phalante, almost brought down at his feet, is like a slaughtered victim that escapes the sacred knife and flees far from the altar.
Adraste needed only a moment to complete the downfall of the Lacedaemonian.
Phalante, drowning in his blood and that of the soldiers fighting alongside him, hears the cries of Telemachus coming to his aid.
At that moment, life is restored to him; a cloud that had already covered his eyes dissipates.
The Daunians, sensing this unexpected attack, abandon Phalante to go repel a more dangerous enemy.
Adraste is like a tiger from whom gathered shepherds snatch away the prey he was ready to devour.
Telemachus searches for him in the fray and wants to suddenly end the war by freeing the allies from their relentless enemy.

sentences: A ship was leaving for Algiers; the cargo, the passengers packed on the deck, the crowd of relatives and friends saying goodbye, shouting and crying, was always an emotional sight, even for those who witness it every day; this scene could not distract Maximilien from a thought that had seized him the moment he set foot on the wide slabs of the quay.
As he was saying this, and in the direction indicated by the count, a painful moan was heard, and a woman was seen signaling to a departing passenger.
This woman was veiled; Monte-Cristo followed her with his eyes, with an emotion that Morrel would have easily noticed if, unlike the count, his own eyes had not been fixed on the ship.
Oh!
my God!
exclaimed Morrel, I'm not mistaken!
that young man who is waving his hat, that young man in uniform, is Albert de Morcerf!
The count smiled, as he did when he didn't want to respond.
And his eyes returned to the veiled woman, who disappeared around the corner of the street.
Dear friend, he said to Maximilien, do you not have something to do in this country?
I have to weep at my father's grave, Morrel replied quietly.
Morrel let his hand drop into the hand that the count was offering him; then, with a nod that it would be impossible to express the melancholy of, he left the count and headed eastward in the city.

Monte-Cristo allowed Maximilien to walk away, remaining in the same spot until he had disappeared, then he made his way towards the Allées de Meilhan to find the little house that the beginnings of this story must have made familiar to our readers.

sentences: Thus does Captain Nemo, Conseil replied wisely.
That's why he would have been better off naming his ship the Argonaut." The next day, January 26, we crossed the Equator at the eighty-second meridian, and we entered the northern hemisphere.
On January 27, at the opening of the vast Bay of Bengal, we encountered several times, a sinister sight!
the corpses that were floating on the surface of the waves.
They were the dead from the Indian cities, carried by the Ganges out to the open sea, and which the vultures, the only undertakers in the country, had not finished devouring.
But the sharks were not lacking to assist them in their grim task.
Conseil could hardly believe his eyes, and he was asking me about the causes of this strange phenomenon.
Fortunately, I was able to answer him.
"This is what is called a milk sea, I said to him, a vast expanse of white waves that is frequently seen along the coasts of Ambon and in those areas.
"But, asked Conseil, can you tell me what causes such an effect, because this water hasn't turned into milk, I suppose!

"No, my boy, and this whiteness that surprises you is due only to the presence of myriads of microscopic creatures, a kind of small luminous worms, gelatinous and colorless in appearance, the thickness of a hair, and whose length does not exceed one-fifth of a millimeter.
Some of these creatures stick together over distances of several leagues.
Yes, my boy, and don't try to guess the number of these tiny creatures!
You wouldn't be able to do it, because, if I'm not mistaken, some sailors have floated on these seas of milk for over forty miles.

sentences: I must therefore dismiss any idea of escape until I can secure a serious chance of success on my side.
If a favorable circumstance arises, I won't let it slip away.
As I walked along the rows of cells, I was able to observe some of the companions of Count d'Artigas, who have accepted this monotonous existence in the depths of Back-Cup.
I repeat, their number can be estimated at around a hundred, based on the number of cells in Bee-Hive.
However, if these inhabitants of Back-Cup are not connected by a bond of race, they are certainly united by their instincts and appetites.
What disturbing faces, what fierce figures, what fundamentally wild types!
They are violent natures, as can be seen, who have never learned to restrain their passions or shy away from any excess.
And,
--this idea comes to me,

Why wouldn't it be following a long series of crimes, thefts, fires, murders, and attacks of all kinds committed together, that they would have thought to take refuge deep in this cave, where they can believe themselves assured of absolute impunity?...
The Count of Artigas would then be nothing more than the leader of a gang of criminals, with his two lieutenants Spade and Serkö, and Back-Cup a den of pirates...
Such is the thought that has firmly lodged itself in my mind.
I would be quite surprised if the future proves that I was wrong.
Moreover, what I notice during this first exploration is meant to confirm my opinion and allow for the most suspicious hypotheses.

In any case, whatever they may be and whatever the circumstances that brought them together in this place, the companions of the Count of Artigas seem to have accepted his all-powerful domination without reservation.
On the other hand, if a strict discipline keeps them under his iron hand, it is likely that certain advantages must compensate for this kind of servitude to which they have consented...
Which ones?...

sentences: Telemachus resumes the account of his adventures. He recounts that during his journey from Tyre to the island of Cyprus, he had a dream in which Venus and Cupid invited him to pleasure. Minerva also appeared to him, covering him with her aegis; finally, he saw Mentor urging him to flee from the island of Cyprus.

Upon waking, the Cypriots, drowned in wine, were caught by a dreadful storm. The ship would have perished if Telemachus had not taken the helm. Arrival on the island of Cyprus. A depiction of the voluptuous customs of the inhabitants, the worship given to Venus, and the ominous impressions that Telemachus receives from it. There he finds Mentor, whose advice saves him from such great danger. The Syrian Hazael, to whom Mentor had been sold, returns Telemachus his wise guide; Hazael embarks with them for the island of Crete. They see on this journey the beautiful sight of Amphitrite being drawn in her chariot by sea horses.
The goddess herself led Telemachus to this cave, separate from hers.
It was neither less rustic nor less pleasant.
A fountain, flowing in a corner, made a gentle murmur that called for sleep.
The nymphs had prepared two beds of soft greenery there, on which they had spread two large skins, one of lion for Telemachus, and the other of bear for Mentor.
What then!
Teledmachus replied, could I refuse Calypso the chance to tell her my misfortunes?
No, Mentor replied, you had to tell her: but you should do so by only saying what could evoke her compassion.
You could say that you had been, at times wandering, at times captive in Sicily, and then in Egypt.
That would be enough to tell her: and everything else only served to increase the poison that already burns in her heart.
May the gods grant that yours can be preserved from it!
But what shall I do then?
Telemachus continued, in a moderate and docile tone.

It is no longer time, Mentor replied, to hide from her what remains of your adventures: she knows enough not to be deceived about what she does not yet know; your reserve would only serve to irritate her.
So finish telling her tomorrow everything that the gods have done in your favor, and learn next time to speak more modestly about anything that might attract you some praise.
Telemachus received such good advice with friendship, and they went to bed.

sentences: And he counted fifteen thousand francs in gold and thirty thousand francs in banknotes on the table.
--Wait until I light the lamp, said the Carconte, it's getting dark, and we might make a mistake.
Indeed, night had fallen during this discussion, and with the night, the storm that had been threatening for half an hour.
Thunder could be heard rumbling in the distance; but neither the jeweler, nor Caderousse, nor the Carconte seemed to care, as they were all three possessed by the demon of greed.
I myself felt a strange fascination at the sight of all this gold and all these banknotes.
It seemed to me that I was dreaming, and, as often happens in a dream, I felt chained to my place.
Caderousse counted and recounted the gold and the banknotes, then he passed them to his wife, who counted and recounted them in turn.

Meanwhile, the jeweler was making the diamond sparkle under the lamp's rays, and the diamond was throwing flashes that made him forget those which, as precursors of the storm, were starting to ignite the windows.

The Carconte went to a cupboard and returned with an old leather wallet, from which they took out some greasy letters to replace them with the banknotes, and a bag that contained two or three six-livre coins, which probably made up the entire fortune of the miserable household.
--There, said Caderousse, although you may have raised about ten thousand francs for us, would you like to have dinner with us?
It's with good heart.
--Thank you, said the jeweler, it must be getting late, and I need to return to Beaucaire; my wife would be worried;” he pulled out his watch.
Morbleu!
he exclaimed, it's almost nine o'clock, I won't be in Beaucaire before midnight.
Goodbye, my little children; if by chance you hear from the abbés Busoni, think of me.

sentences: Thank you, sir, Monte-Cristo said with a smile; my steward has already been instructed to rent a box in each of them.
No, sir, he is simply a compatriot of yours, if a Corsican can be considered a compatriot of anyone: but you know him, Monsieur de Morcerf.
Could it be the brave Signor Bertuccio, who is so good at renting windows?
And you chose this honest citizen of the world as your steward, Count?
Debray asked, how much does he take from you each year?
Well, I swear, the count replied, no more than anyone else, I'm sure of that; but he suits my needs, knows no impossibilities, and I keep him.
Albert smiled, he was thinking of the beautiful Greek woman he had seen in the count's box at the Valle theater and the Argentina theater.
I have something better than that, Monte-Cristo said: I have a slave.

You rent your mistresses at the Opéra theater, at the Vaudeville theater, at the Variétés theater; I bought mine in Constantinople; it cost me more, but in that regard, I no longer need to worry about anything.
But you forget, Debray said with a laugh, that we are, as King Charles said, free by name, free by nature; that by stepping on French soil, your slave has become free?
But will we see her, at least?
Beauchamp asked, or, since you already have a mute, do you also have eunuchs?

Indeed not, said Monte-Cristo, I don't take orientalism that far: everything around me is free to leave me, and by leaving me will no longer need me or anyone else; perhaps that's why no one leaves me.

sentences: Around March 20, the hunters reported the first swans, which were migrating from the southern territories and flying north while making sharp whistles.
A few 'snow buntings' and 'wintering hawks' also made their appearance.
But a vast white layer still covered the ground, and the sun could not melt the solid surface of the sea and the lake.
The thaw did not occur until the first days of April.
The breaking of the ice happened with an extraordinary crash, sometimes comparable to artillery fire.
Sudden changes occurred in the pack ice.
More than one iceberg, damaged by the impacts and eroded at its base, toppled with a terrible noise due to the shift in its center of gravity.
This led to collapses that accelerated the breaking of the icefield.
At that time, the average temperature was thirty-two degrees above zero (0° Celsius).
Thus, the first ice along the shore quickly began to dissolve, and the pack ice, driven by the polar currents, gradually receded into the mists of the horizon.
By April 15, the sea was free, and certainly a ship coming from the Pacific Ocean, through the Bering Strait, after following the American coast, could have landed at Cape Bathurst.
At the same time as the Arctic Ocean, Lake Barnett freed itself from its icy shell, much to the delight of the thousands of ducks and other waterfowl that were swarming along its shores.
But, as Lieutenant Hobson had predicted, the perimeter of the lake had been altered by the new slope of the land.
The section of the shore that stretched in front of the fort, bordered to the east by wooded hills, widened considerably.
Jasper Hobson estimated the retreat of the lake's waters on its eastern shore to be one hundred and fifty paces.
Conversely, these waters must have moved equally westward, flooding the land, unless some natural barrier contained them.

sentences: The volcanic nature of this enormous excavation was evident from all sides.
I pointed it out to my companions.

Can you imagine, I asked them, what this funnel must have been like when it was filled with bubbling lava, and when the level of this incandescent liquid rose to the mouth of the mountain, like molten metal on the walls of a furnace?
--I can perfectly imagine it, replied Conseil.
But will you tell me why the great founder suspended his operation, and how it is that the furnace has been replaced by the calm waters of a lake?
--Very well, replied Ned Land.
I accept the explanation, but I regret, for our sake, that this opening mentioned by the professor is not located above sea level.
And I would add, Master Land, that the waters would not have rushed under the mountain and that the volcano would have remained a volcano.
So your regrets are unnecessary." Our ascent continued.
The slopes became increasingly steep and narrow.
Deep excavations sometimes cut across them, which had to be crossed.
Overhanging masses had to be navigated around.
We slid on our knees, crawling on our bellies.
But with Conseil's skill and the Canadian's strength, all obstacles were overcome.
At a height of about thirty meters, the nature of the terrain changed, though it did not become any more passable.

Black basalts succeeded the conglomerates and trachytes; the former spread in lumpy layers with bubbles; the latter formed regular prisms, arranged like a colonnade supporting the vast vault, an admirable specimen of natural architecture.
Then, between these basalts, long flows of cooled lava twisted, embedded with bituminous streaks, and in places, wide carpets of sulfur spread out.
A more powerful light, entering through the upper crater, flooded all these volcanic deposits with a wave of brightness, forever buried within the extinct mountain.

sentences: Ah!
Sir, the baroness said, you know very well that I have had the best coachman in Paris at my service for a month now, unless, of course, you sold him along with the horses.

My dear friend, I will find you similar ones, even prettier if there are any; but gentle, calm horses that no longer inspire me with such terror." The baroness shrugged her shoulders with a look of deep disdain.

Danglars didn’t seem to notice this gesture, which was more than just marital, and turning to Monte-Cristo, he said, "Indeed, I regret not having known you sooner, Mr. Count; are you managing your estate?
I would have offered them to you.
Can you imagine that I gave them away for nothing, but as I told you, I wanted to get rid of them: they are young men's horses.
Sir, the count said, thank you; I bought some quite good ones this morning and not too expensive.
Here, look, Mr. Debray, you are an enthusiast, I believe?" While Debray approached the window, Danglars moved closer to his wife.
"Can you imagine, madam, he said to her quietly, that someone came to offer me an exorbitant price for these horses.

I don’t know who the fool is that is ruining himself who sent me his steward this morning, but the fact is that I made sixteen thousand francs on them; don’t sulk, and I will give you four thousand, and two thousand to Eugénie."
But I’m not mistaken, these are your horses, your very own horses hitched to the count's carriage.
The baroness whispered a few words in Debray's ear, who then approached Monte-Cristo.

sentences: However, time passed; night fell; the sounds of the street quieted down; my uncle, still bent over his task, saw nothing, not even the good Marthe who slightly opened the door; he heard nothing, not even the voice of that worthy servant saying: So Marthe had to leave without a response: as for me, after resisting for a while, I was overcome by an irresistible sleep, and I fell asleep on a corner of the sofa, while my uncle Lidenbrock continued to calculate and cross out.
When I woke up the next day, the tireless digger was still at work.

His red eyes, pale complexion, tangled hair under his feverish hand, and flushed cheeks clearly indicated his terrible struggle with the impossible, and the mental fatigue and strain he must have endured for hours.
Truly, he inspired pity in me.
Despite the reproaches I thought I had the right to make, a certain emotion overcame me.

The poor man was so consumed by his idea that he forgot to get angry; all his vital energies were concentrated on a single point, and since they were not escaping through their usual outlet, one could fear that their tension would cause him to explode at any moment.
I could have loosened that iron vise that was tightening around his head with just a gesture, with just a word!

sentences: People admired the wisdom and vigilance of Idomeneus, who had founded such a beautiful kingdom; and everyone concluded that, with peace established with him, the allies would be quite powerful if he joined their league against the Daunians.
It was proposed to Idomeneus that he join; he could not reject such a fair proposal, and he promised troops.

But since Mentor knew everything necessary to make a state flourish, he understood that Idomeneus's forces could not be as great as they appeared; he took him aside and spoke to him this way: At these words, Idomeneus, already having recovered from his initial eagerness, seemed ashamed of his delicacy.
'You see,' he said to Mentor, 'what the habit of being flattered does.'

'I owe you the safety of my new kingdom; there is no truth that I would not be happy to hear from your lips; but have pity on a king whom flattery has poisoned, and who has not been able, even in his misfortunes, to find men generous enough to tell him the truth.'
'No, I have never found anyone who loved me enough to want to displease me by telling me the whole truth.'
As he said these words, tears came to his eyes, and he embraced Mentor tenderly.
Then this wise old man said to him: 'It is with pain that I find myself compelled to tell you hard things; but can I betray you by hiding the truth from you?'
'Put yourself in my place.'
'If you have been deceived until now, it is because you have willingly allowed it; it is because you have feared overly sincere advisors.'
'Have you sought out the most disinterested people, and those most likely to contradict you?'
'Have you taken care to make the least eager men to please you speak, those most disinterested in their conduct, the most capable of condemning your passions and unjust feelings?'
'When you found flatterers, did you cast them aside?'
'Did you distrust them?'
'No, no, you have not done what those who love the truth do, and who deserve to know it.'
'Let’s see if you now have the courage to allow yourself to be humbled by the truth that condemns you.'

sentences: This was where Sir Francis Cromarty was supposed to stop.
The troops he was joining were camped a few miles north of the city.
The brigadier general bid farewell to Phileas Fogg, wishing him every possible success and expressing the hope that he would undertake this journey again in a less original but more profitable way.
Mr.
Fogg gently squeezed his companion's fingers.
Mrs.
Aouda's compliments were more affectionate.
She would never forget what she owed to Sir Francis Cromarty.
As for Passepartout, he was honored with a real handshake from the brigadier general.
All moved, he wondered where and when he could devote himself to him.
Then they parted ways.
From Benares, the railway partly followed the valley of the Ganges.

Through the train windows, on a fairly clear day, the varied landscape of Behar appeared, then green-covered mountains, fields of barley, corn, and wheat, rivers and ponds populated by greenish alligators, well-maintained villages, and still lush forests.

A few elephants and humped zebu came to bathe in the waters of the sacred river, and also, despite the late season and already cold temperature, groups of Hindus of both sexes were piously performing their holy ablutions.

These faithful, fierce enemies of Buddhism, are fervent followers of the Brahmanic religion, which is embodied in these three figures: Vishnu, the solar deity, Shiva, the divine personification of natural forces, and Brahma, the supreme master of priests and lawmakers.

But how must Brahma, Shiva, and Vishnu view this now 'Britishized' India when some steam boat passed by, whistling and disturbing the sacred waters of the Ganges, startling the seagulls flying above, the turtles swarming on its banks, and the devotees stretched along its shores!

sentences: My child, my uncle said as he held me to his chest, you are safe now! At that moment, Hans arrived.
He saw my hand in my uncle's; I dare say that his eyes expressed great satisfaction.
Hello, Hans, hello, I murmured.
And now, my uncle, can you tell me where we are right now?
Tomorrow, Axel, tomorrow; today you are still too weak; I have wrapped your head in bandages that must not be disturbed; so sleep, my boy, and tomorrow you will know everything.
It's eleven o'clock in the evening; today is Sunday, August 9, and I no longer allow you to question me before the 10th of this month." In truth, I was quite weak; my eyes closed involuntarily.
I needed a night of rest; so I let myself doze off with the thought that my isolation had lasted four long days.
The next day, upon waking, I looked around me.
My cot, made of all the travel blankets, was set up in a lovely cave, adorned with magnificent stalagmites, and the floor was covered with fine sand.
There was a half-darkness prevailing.
No torch, no lamp was lit, and yet some inexplicable lights were coming from outside through a narrow opening in the cave.
I could also hear a vague and indefinite murmur, similar to that of waves breaking on a shore, and sometimes the whistling of the breeze.
I wondered if I was truly awake, if I was still dreaming, if my brain, cracked from my fall, was not perceiving purely imaginary sounds.
However, neither my eyes nor my ears could be mistaken to that extent.

sentences: He no longer had, as he used to, those sweet words that made her cry, nor those passionate caresses that drove her mad; so much so that their great love, in which she was immersed, seemed to diminish beneath her, like the water of a river that would be absorbed into its bed, and she caught sight of the mud.
She refused to believe it; she increased her tenderness; and Rodolphe, less and less, hid his indifference.
She didn't know if she regretted having given in to him, or if she actually wished to cherish him even more.
The humiliation of feeling weak turned into a resentment that the pleasures tempered.
It wasn't attachment; it was like a constant seduction.
He captivated her.
She was almost afraid of him.

The appearances, however, were calmer than ever, Rodolphe having managed to conduct the affair according to his whim; and, after six months, when spring arrived, they found themselves facing each other like two newlyweds quietly tending to a domestic flame.
It was the time when Father Rouault sent his turkey, in memory of his healed leg.

sentences: However, according to the lieutenant's orders, the final preparations for wintering were coming to an end.
They were busy ensuring food for the domestic animals for the entire duration of the long polar night.

The dogs were healthy and were getting fat doing nothing, but they couldn't be overly pampered, as the poor creatures would have to work terribly hard when they left Fort-Espérance to reach the continent across the ice field.
It was therefore important to keep them in perfect condition.
Thus, the fresh meat, especially the flesh of those reindeer that could be killed around the trading post, was not spared for them.
As for the domestic reindeer, they were thriving.
Their stable was properly set up, and a considerable harvest of moss had been stored for them in the fort's warehouses.
The females provided abundant milk to Mrs.
Joliffe, who used it daily in her cooking preparations.
The corporal and his little wife had also replanted their crops, which had done so well during the warm season.
The ground had been prepared before the snow for the sorrel, scurvy grass, and Labrador tea plants.
These precious anti-scurvy items were not to be lacking for the colony.
As for the wood, it filled the sheds up to the roof.

The harsh and icy winter could now come, and the mercury column could freeze in the thermometer's bowl, without them having to resort, as in the days of the last severe cold, to burning the furniture of the house.
The carpenter Mac Nap and his men had taken their measures accordingly, and the debris from the boat under construction even provided a significant increase in fuel.

sentences: It seemed to me that I was transported to a delightful garden, like the one depicted in the Champs-Élysées.
In that place, I recognized Mentor, who said to me: Flee this cruel land, this pestilent island, where one breathes only pleasure.
The most courageous virtue must tremble there, and can only be saved by fleeing.

As soon as I saw him, I wanted to throw myself into his arms to embrace him; but I felt that my feet could not move, that my knees were giving way beneath me, and that my hands, striving to grasp Mentor, were seeking a vain shadow that always eluded me.
In that effort, I awoke, and I felt that this mysterious dream was a divine warning.
I felt filled with courage against pleasures, and distrustful of myself for hating the soft life of the Cypriots.
But what pierced my heart was that I believed Mentor had lost his life, and that having crossed the waters of the Styx, he inhabited the happy abode of the just souls.
This thought made me shed a torrent of tears.
I was asked why I was crying.
The tears, I replied, are only too fitting for an unfortunate stranger who wanders without hope of seeing his homeland again.
However, all the Cypriots who were on the ship were giving themselves up to wild joy.

The rowers, enemies of work, were falling asleep on their oars; the pilot, crowned with flowers, let go of the helm, and held in his hand a large jug of wine that he had nearly emptied: he and all the others, disturbed by the fury of Bacchus, sang, in honor of Venus and Cupid, verses that would horrify all those who love virtue.

sentences: I believed, however, the traveler replied, that since it absorbed the old Northwest Company, the Hudson's Bay Company found itself without competitors on the American continent.
Madam, Jasper Hobson replied, while there is no longer any significant association engaged in the fur trade outside of ours, there are still perfectly independent private associations.
In general, these are American companies that have retained agents or descendants of French agents in their service.
So these agents were held in high regard?
asked Mrs.
Paulina Barnett.
Certainly, madam, and rightly so.
During the ninety-four years of French supremacy in Canada, these French agents consistently proved superior to ours.
One must know how to give credit, even to one's rivals.
Yes...
especially...
At that time, the French hunters, leaving Montreal, their main settlement, ventured further north than anyone else.
They lived for years among the Indian tribes.
They sometimes married there.
They were called 'coureurs des bois' or 'Canadian voyageurs', and they referred to each other as cousins and brothers.

They were bold men, skilled, very experienced in river navigation, very brave, very carefree, adapting to everything with that particular flexibility of their race, very loyal, very cheerful, and always ready, in any circumstance, to sing as well as to dance!
And you suppose that this group of voyageurs, whose traces we have just recognized, ventured so far only to hunt fur-bearing animals?
No other hypothesis can be accepted, madam, replied Lieutenant Hobson, and certainly, these people are in search of new hunting grounds.

The order of incarceration came from above, and the order of release must also come from above.
Now, Napoleon has only been back for barely fifteen days; the letters of abolition must have just been sent out.
--But, asked Morrel, is there no way to expedite the formalities now that we are triumphant?
I have some friends, some influence; I can obtain the lifting of the order.
--In political matters, there is no record of incarceration; sometimes governments have an interest in making a person disappear without leaving a trace: incarceration notes would guide the searches.
--It has always been like this, my dear Mr. Morrel; governments come and go, and they are all alike; the prison system established under Louis XIV is still functioning today, near the Bastille.

The Emperor has always been stricter about the management of his prisons than the Great King himself; and the number of incarcerated individuals whose records leave no trace is incalculable." So much goodwill could have diverted certainties, and Morrel had no suspicions at all.

Sir, we know what petitions are: the minister receives two hundred a day and reads only four of them.
I reassured him as best I could, glad to have come that very evening and to witness the spectacle of this superstitious terror.
I told stories, and I managed to calm almost everyone down.
By the hearth, an old, nearly blind, mustachioed dog—one of those dogs that resemble people we know—was sleeping with his nose tucked into his paws.

Outside, the fierce storm battered the little house, and through a narrow window, a sort of peephole near the door, I suddenly saw a jumble of trees being tossed by the wind in the light of bright flashes of lightning.
Despite my efforts, I could tell that a deep terror gripped these people, and every time I stopped speaking, all ears listened intently.

Tired of witnessing these foolish fears, I was about to ask to go to bed when the old gamekeeper suddenly jumped from his chair, grabbed his gun again, and stammered in a bewildered voice: "There it is!"
There it is!
I can hear it!" The two women fell to their knees in their corners, hiding their faces, while the sons picked up their axes.

I was about to try to calm them again when the sleeping dog suddenly woke up and, lifting his head, stretching his neck, looking toward the fire with his almost extinguished eye, let out one of those mournful howls that make travelers shudder in the countryside at night.
All eyes turned to him; he remained still, standing on his legs as if haunted by a vision, and he began to howl at something invisible, unknown, and surely terrifying, as all his fur bristled.
The gamekeeper, pale, shouted: "He senses it!"
He senses it!
He was there when I killed him." And the distraught women both began to howl along with the dog.

sentences: My uncle stomped his foot while the horses headed towards the ferry.
I fully understood the necessity of waiting for a certain moment of the tide to undertake the crossing of the fjord, the moment when the sea, having reached its highest point, is calm.
At that point, the ebb and flow have no noticeable effect, and the ferry is not at risk of being swept away, either to the bottom of the gulf or out into the open ocean.
The favorable moment only arrived at six o'clock in the evening; my uncle, I, the guide, two ferrymen, and the four horses had taken our places in a kind of rather fragile flat-bottomed boat.
Having been used to the steam ferries of the Elbe, I found the oars of the boatmen to be a sad mechanical device.
It took more than an hour to cross the fjord; but finally, the crossing was made without incident.
It should have been dark, but at the sixty-fifth parallel, the daylight of the polar regions should not have surprised me; in Iceland, during the months of June and July, the sun does not set.
Nevertheless, the temperature had dropped; I was cold, and especially hungry.
Welcoming was the 'böer' that opened hospitably to receive us.
It was the house of a peasant, but in terms of hospitality, it was worth that of a king.
Upon our arrival, the host came to shake our hands, and without further ceremony, he signaled for us to follow him.
To follow him, indeed, as accompanying him would have been impossible.

A long, narrow, dark passage led into this dwelling built of barely squared beams and allowed access to each of the rooms; there were four of them: the kitchen, the weaving workshop, the 'badstofa', the family's bedroom, and, the best of all, the guest room.
My uncle, whose height had not been considered when building the house, did not fail to bump his head three or four times against the protrusions of the ceiling.
We were shown into our room, a sort of large hall with a packed earth floor and lit by a window whose panes were made of rather opaque sheep membranes.
The bedding consisted of dry straw thrown into two wooden frames painted red and adorned with Icelandic proverbs.
I did not expect this comfort; however, there was a strong smell of dried fish, cured meat, and sour milk in this house that did not sit well with my sense of smell.

sentences: Ah!
If you do something like that, I will declare you the greatest scientist in the world." The doctor fell silent for a few moments; he was deep in thought.
His two companions looked at him with emotion; they were excited by this extraordinary situation.
Soon Fergusson spoke again: "Here is my plan," he said.
We have two hundred pounds of ballast left, since the bags we brought are still intact.
I admit that this prisoner, a man clearly exhausted by suffering, weighs as much as one of us; we will still have about sixty pounds to throw off in order to ascend more quickly.

"Look, Dick: you agree that if I manage to reach the prisoner, and throw off an amount of ballast equal to his weight, I won't have changed the balance of the balloon; but then, if I want to achieve a rapid ascent to escape from this tribe of blacks, I can use more energetic means than the blowpipe; thus, by dropping this excess ballast at the right moment, I am sure I can rise very quickly.
"Yes, but there is a drawback; that is, in order to descend later, I will have to lose a quantity of gas proportional to the extra ballast that I will have thrown off.
Now, this gas is a precious thing; but one cannot regret its loss when it concerns the salvation of a man.
"So let's act, and arrange these bags on the edge of the basket so that they can be dropped all at once.
It conceals our preparations and will only dissipate when they are complete. Be sure to keep all the weapons within our reach.
We may need to fire a shot; however, we have one shot for the rifle, four for the two guns, twelve for the two revolvers, making a total of seventeen, which can be fired in a quarter of a minute.
But perhaps we won't need to resort to all this noise.
Are you ready?
"Good," said the doctor.
Keep an eye on everything.
Joe will be responsible for dropping the ballast, and Dick for removing the prisoner; but nothing should be done before my orders.
Joe, go first; detach the anchor, and quickly come back up into the basket.

sentences: And over there, at the edge of the horizon, Corsica was sinking into the night, slowly entering the sea, erasing its large shadow that appeared as if to tell the story of the two humble lovers sheltered by its shore.
A warm autumn sun was setting in the farmyard, above the tall beeches by the ditches.

Under the grass trimmed by the cows, the earth, soaked from recent rain, was damp, sinking underfoot with a sound like water; and the apple trees, laden with apples, scattered their pale green fruits among the dark green of the pasture.

Four young heifers were grazing, tethered in a line, and occasionally mooed towards the house; the poultry added a splash of color to the manure in front of the stable, scratching, stirring, clucking, while the two roosters crowed incessantly, searching for worms for their hens, which they called with a lively clucking.
The wooden gate opened; a man entered, perhaps forty years old, but who looked sixty, wrinkled, bent, walking with slow, heavy steps weighed down by the load of heavy clogs full of straw.
His long arms hung down on either side of his body.
As he approached the farm, a small yellow dog, tied to the foot of a huge pear tree next to a barrel that served as his kennel, wagged his tail and then started barking in joy.
The man shouted: A peasant woman came out of the house.
Her bony, wide, flat body was outlined under a woolen bodice that cinched at the waist.
A grey skirt, too short, fell to mid-calf, covering legs hidden in blue stockings, and she also wore clogs filled with straw.
A white bonnet, now turned yellow, covered some hair plastered to her scalp, and her brown, thin, ugly, toothless face displayed that wild and rough look often seen in peasants.
The priest says it's the end, that he won't make it through the night.
After crossing the kitchen, they entered the low, dark room, barely lit by a window, in front of which hung a piece of Normandy fabric.
The thick beams of the ceiling, darkened by time, blackened and smoky, spanned the room from one side to the other, supporting the thin floor of the attic, where herds of rats ran day and night.

sentences: Immediately, Louise slipped through the slightly ajar door like a snake and lightly jumped outside.
Eugénie, seemingly calm, although her heart was probably beating faster than usual, followed her out.

A porter was passing by, and they loaded him with the trunk; then, after the two young girls indicated that their destination was 36 Rue de la Victoire, they walked behind him, whose presence reassured Louise; as for Eugénie, she was as strong as Judith or Delilah.
They arrived at the indicated number.
Eugénie ordered the porter to drop off the trunk, gave him some coins, and after knocking on the shutter, sent him away.
The shutter that Eugénie knocked on belonged to a small laundress who had been informed in advance: she was not yet in bed and opened the door.
"Miss," said Eugénie, "have the concierge bring the carriage from the shed, and send him to fetch horses at the Post Office."
"Here are five francs for the trouble we’re giving him."

"Indeed," said Louise, "I admire you, and I would almost say that I respect you." The laundress looked on in astonishment; but since it had been agreed that there would be twenty louis for her, she made no comment.

A quarter of an hour later, the concierge returned with the postilion and the horses, which were harnessed to the carriage in the blink of an eye, and the concierge secured the trunk with a rope and a winch.
"Here is the passport," said the postilion; "which route are we taking, our young gentleman?"

I'm being cautious, said Eugénie; this woman to whom we are giving twenty louis could betray us for forty: on the boulevard, we'll take another route." And the young girl leaped into the carriage, perfectly at ease, barely touching the step.
A quarter of an hour later, the postilion, back on the right path, crossed, cracking his whip, the gate of the Saint-Martin barrier.
"Yes, my dear, and the abduction is indeed accomplished," replied Eugénie.
These words were lost in the noise made by the carriage rolling over the cobblestones of Villette.
