sentences: Morcerf, usually so heavy, had instead adopted a cheerful and affable demeanor; consequently, being fairly certain that his opening would be well received, he made no attempt at diplomacy and got straight to the point: "Baron," he said, "here I am.

For a long time, we've been circling around our old words...." Morcerf expected, upon saying this, to see the banker’s expression brighten, which he attributed to the banker’s silence; but, on the contrary, that expression became, almost unbelievably, even more impassive and colder.
"What words, Monsieur le Comte?"
the banker asked, as if he were vainly searching his mind for an explanation of what the general meant.
"Oh!"
the count said, "you are a formalist, my dear sir, and you remind me that the ceremony must be conducted according to all the rites.
Very well!
my faith.

Forgive me, since I have only one son, and this is the first time I am thinking of marrying him, I am still learning: come now, I will proceed." And Morcerf, with a forced smile, stood up, made a deep bow to Danglars, and said to him: "Monsieur le Baron, I have the honor of asking for the hand of Mlle Eugénie Danglars, your daughter, for my son, the Vicomte Albert de Morcerf." But Danglars, instead of welcoming these words with the favor that Morcerf might have hoped for, frowned, and without inviting the count, who had remained standing, to sit down: "Monsieur le Comte," he said, "before I respond, I will need to think.
"To think!"
Morcerf replied, increasingly astonished, "haven't you had time to think since we first discussed this marriage eight years ago?
"Monsieur le Comte," said Danglars, "every day things happen that make the reflections one thought were settled need to be reconsidered.
Allow me, said Morcerf; is this or is it not a comedy that we are playing?
I see him very often, said Danglars, shaking his cravat; he is one of my friends.
Well, one of the last times you saw him, you told him that I seemed forgetful, indecisive, regarding this marriage.
Well, here I am.
I am neither forgetful nor indecisive, as you can see, since I have come to demand that you keep your promise.

sentences: Franz and the count entered the same path, which, after a hundred steps, led them down a sloping incline to the bottom of a small valley.
Indeed, one of these two men was Peppino, while the other was a bandit on lookout.
"Excellency," Peppino said to the count, "if you would like to follow me, the entrance to the catacombs is just a short distance from here.
In fact, behind a thicket of bushes and among some rocks, there was an opening through which a man could barely pass.
Peppino slipped through the crack first, but as soon as he took a few steps, the underground passage widened.
Then he stopped, lit his torch, and turned around to see if he was being followed.
The count had entered first through a kind of window, and Franz followed behind him.
At the same time, they saw in the darkness the reflection of their own torch shining on the barrel of a rifle.
He stepped forward alone and whispered a few words to this second sentinel, who, like the first, saluted and signaled to the nighttime visitors that they could continue on their way.
Behind the sentinel was a staircase of about twenty steps; Franz and the count descended the twenty steps and found themselves in a kind of mortuary intersection.
Five paths diverged like the rays of a star, and the walls, carved with stacked niches shaped like coffins, indicated that they had finally entered the catacombs.
In one of these cavities, the extent of which was impossible to distinguish, a few reflections of light could be seen during the day.

Peppino obeyed, and Franz and the count found themselves in complete darkness; only about fifty steps ahead of them, a few reddish glimmers continued to dance along the walls, becoming even more visible since Peppino had extinguished his torch.
They advanced silently, the count guiding Franz as if he had the peculiar ability to see in the dark.
Moreover, Franz himself found it easier to distinguish his path as he got closer to those reflections that served as their guides.
Three arches, of which the middle one served as a door, provided them passage.

The night was fairly calm and faded away around five in the morning, while a light wind urged the balloon westward, and even a bit to the south.
Fergusson hurried to seize this good fortune.
He quickly lifted off and fled in a long trail of sunlight.
Quick crossing.--Prudent resolutions.--Caravans.--Continuous showers.--Gao.--The Niger.--Golberry, Geoffroy, Gray.--Mungo-Park.--Laing.--René Caillié.--Clapperton.--John and Richard Lander.

The day of May 17 was calm and free of any incident; the desert was beginning again; a moderate wind was bringing the Victoria southwest; it did not deviate to the right or left; its shadow traced a perfectly straight line on the sand.
Before his departure, the doctor had prudently replenished his water supply; he feared he might not be able to land in these regions infested by the Aouelimminien Tuareg.
The plateau, elevated eighteen hundred feet above sea level, sloped down towards the south.

The travelers, having cut the route from Aghadès to Mourzouk, often trodden by camel feet, arrived in the evening at 16° latitude and 4° 55' longitude, after covering one hundred eighty miles of long monotony.
During this day, Joe prepared the last pieces of game, which had received only a cursory preparation; he served very appetizing snipe skewers for dinner.
The wind being favorable, the doctor decided to continue his journey during a night that the moon, still nearly full, made radiant.
The Victoria ascended to a height of five hundred feet, and during this nighttime crossing of about sixty miles, even a child's light sleep would not have been disturbed.

On Sunday morning, there was a new change in the direction of the wind; it shifted to the northwest; a few crows were flying in the air, and, on the horizon, a group of vultures, which fortunately kept their distance.
The sight of these birds led Joe to compliment his master on his idea of the two balloons.
"Where would we be, he said, with only one envelope?
This second balloon is like a ship's lifeboat; in case of shipwreck, you can always take it to save yourself.

sentences: And when he lay down on the ground at night, wrapped in his coat next to his snoring comrades, he thought long and hard about his loved ones left behind and the dangers scattered along his path: if he were killed, what would become of the little ones?
Who would feed and raise them?
At that very moment, they were not wealthy, despite the debts he had incurred when leaving to leave them some money.
And Walter Schnaffs sometimes cried.
At the beginning of battles, he felt such weakness in his legs that he would have collapsed if he hadn't thought that the entire army would pass over his body.
The whistling of the bullets made the hair on his skin stand on end.
For months, he had been living in terror and anxiety.
His army corps was advancing towards Normandy; and one day he was sent out on reconnaissance with a small detachment that was simply supposed to explore a part of the country and then fall back.
Everything seemed calm in the countryside; nothing indicated a prepared resistance.

However, the Prussians were quietly descending into a small valley cut by deep ravines when a violent gunfire suddenly stopped them, knocking down about twenty of their men; and a group of sharpshooters, suddenly emerging from a small wood the size of a hand, charged forward, bayonets fixed.
Walter Schnaffs initially remained motionless, so surprised and distraught that he didn't even think of fleeing.
Then a wild desire to run seized him; but he immediately thought that he ran like a turtle compared to the lean Frenchmen who were bounding in like a herd of goats.

Then, spotting a wide ditch full of underbrush covered with dry leaves six paces in front of him, he jumped in feet first, not even thinking about the depth, like one jumps from a bridge into a river.
He passed through a thick layer of vines and sharp thorns that tore at his face and hands, and he fell heavily, sitting down on a bed of stones.
Immediately lifting his eyes, he saw the sky through the hole he had made.

This revealing hole could betray him, and he crawled cautiously on all fours to the bottom of this rut, under the roof of intertwined branches, moving as quickly as possible, away from the scene of the battle.
Then he stopped and sat down again, crouched like a hare among the tall dry grasses.

sentences: There's nothing simpler, replied the consul.
Look at those islands located beyond the port; land your balloon on one of them, surround yourself with a circle of sailors, and you won't have any risks to run.
Perfect, said the doctor, and we will be comfortable finishing our preparations.
The commander attended this meeting.
The Resolute approached the island of Koumbeni.
On the morning of April 16, the balloon was secured in the middle of a clearing, between the tall woods with a rugged ground.

Two masts, each eighty feet tall and placed at an equal distance from each other, were erected; a system of pulleys fixed at their ends allowed the removal of the aerostat using a cross cable; it was then completely deflated.
The inner balloon was attached to the top of the outer balloon so that it could be lifted like it.
It was at the lower appendage of each balloon that the two hydrogen introduction pipes were fixed.

The day of the 17th was spent setting up the apparatus designed to produce the gas; it consisted of thirty barrels, in which the decomposition of water occurred using scrap iron and sulfuric acid mixed with a large quantity of water.
The hydrogen traveled to a large central barrel after being washed along the way, and from there it passed into each aerostat through the introduction pipes.
In this way, each of them was filled with a precisely determined amount of gas.

For this operation, it was necessary to use eighteen hundred sixty-six gallons [three thousand two hundred fifty liters] of sulfuric acid, sixteen thousand fifty pounds of iron [over eight tons of iron], and nine hundred sixty-six gallons of water [nearly forty-one thousand two hundred fifty liters].
This operation began the following night, around three in the morning; it lasted nearly eight hours.
The next day, the aerostat, covered with its net, was gracefully swaying above the nacelle, held down by a large number of sandbags.
The expansion apparatus was assembled with great care, and the pipes coming from the aerostat were connected to the cylindrical box.
The anchors, ropes, instruments, travel blankets, tent, provisions, and weapons had to take their assigned places in the nacelle; the water supply was arranged in Zanzibar.
The two hundred pounds of ballast were distributed in fifty bags placed at the bottom of the nacelle, but still within reach.

sentences: And God has bestowed upon you, as He does for everyone, comfort in your suffering?
asked Monte-Cristo.

Yes, sir, the count, said Julie; we can say this, for He has done for us what He only does for His chosen ones; He has sent us one of His angels." The color rose to the count's cheeks, and he coughed to find a way to hide his emotion by bringing his handkerchief to his mouth.

Those who are born in a cradle of purple and have never desired anything, said Emmanuel, do not know what it is to experience the joy of living; just as those who have never risked their lives to the mercy of four planks tossed on a raging sea do not know the value of a clear sky." Monte-Cristo stood up, and without responding, for the tremor in his voice would have revealed the emotion he was feeling, he began to pace the salon.
Our magnificence makes you smile, sir, the count, said Maximilien, who was following Monte-Cristo with his eyes.

No, no, replied Monte-Cristo, very pale and pressing one hand against his heart, while with the other he pointed out to the young man a crystal globe under which a silk purse lay precious and resting on a black velvet cushion.

I was just wondering what this purse is for, which seems to contain a paper on one side and a rather beautiful diamond on the other." "This, sir, the count, is the most precious of our family treasures.

my brother is not speaking to you about the value of the stone, although it is valued at a hundred thousand francs, sir, the count; he only wants to tell you that the items contained in this purse are the relics of the angel we were speaking about earlier.

Indiscreet, you say?

sentences: Peppino stopped in front of a rock topped with a thick bush; this rock, slightly open like an eyelid, allowed passage to the young man, who disappeared into it like the devils in our fairy tales vanish into their traps.
The voice and gesture of the one following Danglars prompted the banker to do the same.
There was no longer any doubt, the French bankrupt was dealing with Roman bandits.
Danglars complied like a man caught between two terrible dangers, and fear made him brave.
Despite his stomach being rather unsettled for navigating the crevices of the Roman countryside, he slipped in behind Peppino, and, closing his eyes and letting himself slide, he landed on his feet.

Two other men descended behind Danglars, forming the rear guard, and, pushing Danglars whenever he happened to stop, they guided him down a gentle slope to the center of a sinister-looking crossroads.
Indeed, the walls, carved into stacked coffins, seemed, amidst the white stones, to open those deep black eyes one notices in skulls.
A sentinel struck the cap of his rifle against his left hand.
There, said the sentinel, pointing over his shoulder to a large room carved into the rock, the light of which reflected into the corridor through large arched openings.
And taking Danglars by the collar of his coat, he led him to an opening that resembled a door, through which one entered the room that the captain seemed to have made his quarters.
At this rather impertinent order, Peppino brought his torch so abruptly to Danglars' face that he quickly recoiled to avoid burning his eyebrows.
This disturbed face showed all the signs of a pale and hideous terror.
"This man is tired," said the captain, "let him be taken to his bed.
"Oh!"

murmured Danglars, "that bed is probably one of the coffins that are being dug into the wall; that sleep is the death that one of the daggers I see glinting in the shadows will bring me." The banker let out a muffled groan and followed his guide: he neither tried to pray nor to scream.
He had no strength, no will, no power, no feeling left; he was going because he was being dragged along.

sentences: As a child, young Vampa had a strange character.
One day, at the age of seven, he went to see the priest of Palestrina and asked him to teach him how to read.
It was a difficult task; for the young shepherd could not leave his flock.
But the good priest went every day to say mass in a poor little village too insignificant to pay a priest, and which, not even having a name, was known as dell'Borgo.
He offered Luigi to meet him on his way back and give him his lesson, warning him that this lesson would be short and that he should therefore make the most of it.

Every day, Luigi led his flock to graze along the road from Palestrina to the Borgo; every day, at nine in the morning, the priest would pass by, and the priest and the child would sit on the edge of a ditch, while the little shepherd took his lesson from the priest's breviary.

The priest had a writing teacher from Rome make three alphabets for him: one in large letters, one in medium, and one in small, and he showed him that by following this alphabet on a slate, he could learn to write with the help of a metal point.
The next day, he had gathered a supply of slates and set to work.
The priest, amazed by this profound intelligence and touched by this aptitude, gifted him several notebooks, a pack of pens, and a pocketknife.
It was a new study to undertake, but it was nothing compared to the first.
Eight days later, he handled the pen as skillfully as he handled the stylus.

The priest told this anecdote to the Count of San-Felice, who wanted to see the little shepherd, had him read and write in front of him, ordered his steward to have him eat with the servants, and gave him two piastres a month.
Indeed, he had applied this ease of imitation he possessed to all objects, and, like a young Giotto, he drew on his slates his sheep, trees, and houses.
Then, with the point of his pocketknife, he began to carve wood and give it all sorts of shapes.
This is how Pinelli, the popular sculptor, had started.

sentences: We were two friends followed by eight spahis and four camels with their camel drivers.
We no longer spoke, overwhelmed by heat, fatigue, and parched with thirst like this burning desert.
Suddenly one of these men let out a sort of cry; everyone stopped; and we remained motionless, surprised by an inexplicable phenomenon known to travelers in these lost lands.

Somewhere near us, in an indeterminate direction, a drum was beating, the mysterious drum of the dunes; it beat distinctly, sometimes more vibrantly, sometimes weakened, stopping, then resuming its fantastic roll.

The Arabs, terrified, looked at each other; and one said, in his language: 'Death is upon us.' And then suddenly my companion, my friend, almost my brother, fell from his horse, headfirst, struck down by sunstroke.

And for two hours, while I tried in vain to save him, this elusive drum filled my ears with its monotonous, intermittent, and incomprehensible sound; and I felt fear, real fear, hideous fear, creeping into my bones, in front of that beloved corpse, in this hole scorched by the sun between four sand dunes, while the unknown echo cast upon us, two hundred leagues from any French village, the rapid beating of the drum.
That day, I understood what it meant to be afraid; I realized it even better another time...
I don't know anything.
No one knows.

The officers, often surprised by this strange noise, generally attribute it to an echo that is amplified, multiplied, and excessively inflated by the rolling dunes, of a hail of grains of sand carried by the wind and hitting a tuft of dry grass; for it has always been noted that the phenomenon occurs near small plants scorched by the sun, and as hard as parchment.
So this drum would just be a kind of sound mirage.
That's all.
But I only learned this later.
It was last winter, in a forest in the northeast of France.
Night fell two hours earlier, so dark was the sky.
I had a peasant as my guide who walked beside me, along a very narrow path, under an arch of fir trees that the raging wind made howl.
Between the treetops, I saw clouds in disarray, frantic clouds that seemed to flee in terror.
Sometimes, under a massive gust, the entire forest would bend in the same direction with a groan of suffering; and the cold would overwhelm me, despite my brisk pace and heavy clothing.

sentences: Hippolyte, the innkeeper's boy, came to take the reins of the coachman's horses, and while limping on his club foot, he led them under the porch of the Lion d'Or, where many peasants gathered to watch the carriage.
The drum beat, the cannon boomed, and the gentlemen in line climbed to sit on the platform, in the red Utrecht chairs that Madame Tuvache had lent.
All these people looked alike.
Their soft, blond faces, slightly tanned by the sun, had the color of sweet cider, and their puffy sideburns escaped from large stiff collars held up by wide white cravats.

All the vests were velvet with shawl collars; all the watches had some oval carnelian seal at the end of a long ribbon; and one rested both hands on their thighs, carefully spreading the fork of their trousers, whose unblemished fabric shone more brightly than the leather of their sturdy boots.
The ladies of society stood behind, under the vestibule, between the columns, while the common crowd was in front, either standing or sitting on chairs.

Indeed, Lestiboudois had brought all the chairs he had moved from the meadow, and he even ran every minute to fetch more from the church, causing such a congestion with his business that it was very difficult to reach the small staircase of the platform.
I think, said Mr.

Lheureux (addressing the pharmacist, who was passing by to take his seat), that they should have planted two Venetian masts there: with something a bit severe and rich as novelties, it would have been quite a sight.
Certainly, replied Homais.
But what do you want!
It's the mayor who has taken everything under his hat.
Poor Tuvache doesn't have much taste, and he's even completely devoid of what one might call the genius of the arts.

However, Rodolphe, with Madame Bovary, had gone up to the first floor of the town hall, to the deliberation room, and since it was empty, he declared that they would be comfortable there to enjoy the spectacle more at ease.
He took three stools around the oval table, under the bust of the monarch, and having moved them closer to one of the windows, they sat down next to each other.

sentences: Such was the succession of phenomena that formed Iceland; all of them resulted from the action of internal fires, and to suppose that the internal mass remained in a permanent state of incandescent liquidity was madness.
Madness, especially, to claim to reach the center of the globe!
I reassured myself about the outcome of our venture while climbing the Sneffels.
The path was becoming increasingly difficult; the ground was rising; rock fragments were shifting, and it required the utmost attention to avoid dangerous falls.

Hans advanced calmly as if on flat ground; sometimes he disappeared behind large boulders, and we would momentarily lose sight of him; then a sharp whistle escaping his lips indicated the direction to follow.
He often stopped, picked up some rock debris, arranged them in a recognizable way, and thus created landmarks to indicate the way back.
A precaution that was good in itself, but that future events rendered unnecessary.
Three exhausting hours of walking had brought us only to the base of the mountain.
There, Hans signaled to stop, and a simple lunch was shared among all.
My uncle ate double portions to go faster.
However, since this break for refreshment was also a rest stop, he had to wait for the guide's good pleasure, who signaled the departure an hour later.
The three Icelanders, as taciturn as their companion the hunter, did not utter a single word and ate modestly.

We were now beginning to ascend the slopes of the Sneffels; its snowy summit, due to a common optical illusion in the mountains, appeared very close to me, and yet, how many long hours before reaching it!
What fatigue, especially!
The stones that no earth cement or grass bound together crumbled under our feet and went tumbling into the plain with the speed of an avalanche.

In certain places, the slopes of the mountain formed an angle of at least thirty-six degrees with the horizon; it was impossible to climb them, and these rocky inclines had to be circumvented with difficulty.
We then helped each other using our sticks.
I must say that my uncle stayed as close to me as possible; he did not lose sight of me, and on many occasions, his arm provided me with solid support.
For his part, he undoubtedly had an innate sense of balance, for he did not falter.
The Icelanders, although loaded, climbed with the agility of mountaineers.

sentences: I took one last look at the slightly yellowish sea of the Japanese landings, and I went back down to the main salon.
There, the captain took his position and calculated his longitude with a stopwatch, which he verified using previous hourly angle observations.
Then he said to me, "Mr. Aronnax, we are at one hundred thirty-seven degrees and fifteen minutes west longitude...
--Which meridian?
I asked eagerly, hoping that the captain's answer might reveal his nationality.
--Sir, he replied, I have various chronometers set to the meridians of Paris, Greenwich, and Washington.

But, in your honor, I will use the one from Paris." "One hundred thirty-seven degrees and fifteen minutes west of the Paris meridian, and thirty degrees and seven minutes north latitude, which is about three hundred miles from the coast of Japan.
Today is November 8th, at noon, when our underwater exploration voyage begins.
And now, professor, the captain added, I will leave you to your studies.
I have set the course to east-northeast at a depth of fifty meters.
Here are some large-scale maps where you can follow it.
The lounge is at your disposal, and I ask for your permission to withdraw." For an entire hour, I remained immersed in these thoughts, trying to unravel this mystery that was so intriguing to me.
Then my gaze fixed on the vast world map spread out on the table, and I placed my finger on the exact point where the observed longitude and latitude intersected.
The sea has its rivers just like the continents.
These are special currents, identifiable by their temperature, their color, and the most notable of which is known as the Gulf Stream.

Science has determined the direction of five main currents on the globe: one in the North Atlantic, a second in the South Atlantic, a third in the North Pacific, a fourth in the South Pacific, and a fifth in the South Indian Ocean.
It is even likely that a sixth current once existed in the North Indian Ocean when the Caspian and Aral Seas, joined with the great lakes of Asia, formed a single body of water.
My two brave companions were left speechless at the sight of the wonders piled before their eyes.

sentences: Blacas, my friend, you don't understand anything; I told you that Villefort was ambitious: to succeed, Villefort will sacrifice everything, even his father.
The duke left with the vigor of a young man; the fervor of his sincere royalism gave him twenty extra years.
Louis XVIII remained alone, looking back at his open Horace and murmuring: Mr.
de Blacas returned with the same speed he had descended; but in the antechamber, he was forced to invoke the authority of the king.
Villefort's dusty outfit, his costume, which was entirely inappropriate for court attire, had aroused Mr.
de Brézé's sensitivity, who was quite astonished to find this young man so presumptuous as to appear dressed like that before the king.

But the duke resolved all difficulties with a single word: Order of His Majesty; and despite the remarks that the master of ceremonies continued to make, for the sake of principle, Villefort was introduced.
The king was seated in the same place where the duke had left him.
Upon opening the door, Villefort found himself directly in front of him: the first movement of the young magistrate was to stop.
Villefort bowed and took a few steps forward, waiting for the king to question him.
“Mr. de Villefort,” Louis XVIII continued, “here is the duke of Blacas, who claims that you have something important to tell us.
Your Majesty, Mr.
the duke is right, and I hope that Your Majesty will recognize it yourself.
First of all, and before anything else, sir, do you think the situation is as dire as they want me to believe?
Sire, I believe it is urgent; but, thanks to the diligence I have shown, I hope it is not irreparable.
Speak at length if you wish, sir, said the king, who was beginning to succumb to the emotion that had unsettled Mr.
de Blacas's face and was affecting Villefort's voice; speak, and above all start from the beginning: I like order in all things.

Sire, said Villefort, I will give Your Majesty a faithful report, but I will ask you to excuse me if the turmoil I am in casts some obscurity on my words." A glance cast at the king after this insinuating preamble assured Villefort of the goodwill of his august listener, and he continued:

sentences: Franz sincerely complimented Albert; he received them like a man who deserves them.
He had recognized, he said, by certain signs of inimitable elegance, that his beautiful unknown must belong to the highest aristocracy.
While receiving this confidence, Franz noticed that Albert seemed to have something to ask him, yet he hesitated to make that request.
He insisted, declaring in advance that he was ready to make any sacrifices within his power for Albert's happiness.
Albert took just enough time to be polite: then finally he confessed to Franz that he would do him a favor by leaving him the carriage all to himself for the next day.
Albert attributed the extreme kindness shown by the beautiful peasant girl in lifting her mask to the absence of his friend.
It is clear that Franz was not selfish enough to stop Albert in the midst of an adventure that promised to be both delightful for his curiosity and flattering for his self-esteem.

He knew his worthy friend's perfect indiscretion well enough to be sure that he would keep him updated on every detail of his good fortune; and since, for the past two or three years, he had been traveling all over Italy, he had never even had the chance to embark on such an intrigue for himself, so Franz was not displeased to learn how things unfolded in such cases.
He therefore promised Albert that he would content himself the next day with watching the spectacle from the windows of the Rospoli palace.
Indeed, the next day he saw Albert passing by again and again.
He had a huge bouquet that he had undoubtedly tasked with being the bearer of his love letter.
This probability became certainty when Franz saw the same bouquet, distinguished by a circle of white camellias, in the hands of a charming peasant girl dressed in pink satin.
So in the evening, it was no longer joy, it was delirium.
Albert had no doubt that the beautiful unknown would respond to him in the same way.
Franz anticipated his desires by telling him that all this noise was tiring him, and that he had decided to spend the next day reviewing his album and taking notes.

She untied her hat and they landed on their island.

They lay on the grass; they kissed in secret under the poplars; and they wished, like two Robinsons, to live forever in this little place, which seemed to them, in their bliss, the most magnificent spot on earth.

It wasn't the first time they had seen trees, blue sky, grass, or heard water flowing and the breeze blowing through the leaves; but they had probably never admired all of this as if nature hadn't existed before, or as if it had only begun to be beautiful since their desires had been fulfilled.

sentences: How is it, Ned, I asked him, that you can’t be convinced of the existence of the cetacean we are pursuing?

Do you have any particular reasons for being so skeptical?” The harpooner looked at me for a few moments before answering, struck his broad forehead with his hand in a habitual gesture, closed his eyes as if to collect his thoughts, and finally said:

--However, Ned, you, a professional whaler, you who are familiar with large marine mammals, you whose imagination should easily accept the hypothesis of enormous cetaceans, you should be the last to doubt under such circumstances!
--That’s where you’re mistaken, professor,” replied Ned.

Let the general public believe in extraordinary comets that traverse space, or in the existence of antediluvian monsters that populate the interior of the globe, that’s one thing, but neither astronomers nor geologists accept such fantasies.
Likewise, the whaler.

I have pursued many cetaceans, I have harpooned a great number of them, I have killed several, but however powerful and well-armed they may be, neither their tails nor their tusks could have penetrated the iron plates of a steamer.
--However, Ned, there are ships that have been pierced through and through by the tooth of a narwhal.
--Wooden ships, that’s possible,” replied the Canadian, “but still, I have never seen them.
So, until proven otherwise, I deny that whales, sperm whales, or unicorns could produce such an effect.
No, professor, no.
Anything you want except that.
A gigantic octopus, perhaps?...
So, naturalist, Ned Land replied in a rather mocking tone, you still insist on acknowledging the existence of a huge cetacean...?
Yes, Ned, I repeat this to you with a conviction based on the logic of facts.

I believe in the existence of a highly organized mammal, belonging to the vertebrate branch, like whales, sperm whales, or dolphins, and equipped with a horned tusk whose penetrating power is extreme.
Hum!
said the harpooner, shaking his head like a man who refuses to be convinced.

Note, my worthy Canadian, I said, that if such an animal exists, if it lives in the depths of the Ocean, if it frequents the liquid layers located a few miles below the surface of the waters, it necessarily possesses an organism whose solidity defies all comparison.

sentences: Common madness, when it is not incurable, can only be cured by moral means.
Medicine and therapy are powerless in this regard, and their ineffectiveness has long been recognized by specialists.
Were these moral means applicable to the case of Thomas Roch?
It was permissible to doubt it, even in the calm and healthy environment of Healthful-House.
Indeed, anxiety, mood swings, irritability, oddities of character, sadness, apathy, and a reluctance for serious work or pleasure—these various symptoms were clearly evident.
No doctor could have been mistaken about it; no treatment seemed capable of curing or alleviating them.

It is now appropriate to explain under what conditions this Frenchman left France, what motives drew him to the United States, and why the federal government deemed it prudent and necessary to confine him in this mental health facility, where everything he unconsciously revealed during his episodes would be meticulously noted.
Eighteen months earlier, the Minister of the Navy in Washington received a request for an audience regarding a communication that the aforementioned Thomas Roch wished to make.
Just from that name, the minister understood what it was about.
Although he knew what the nature of the communication would be and what claims would accompany it, he did not hesitate, and the audience was immediately granted.

Indeed, the notoriety of Thomas Roch was such that, concerned about the interests he was responsible for, the minister could not hesitate to meet with the petitioner and to learn about the proposals he wanted to personally present to him.
Thomas Roch was an inventor,
He was a brilliant inventor.
Significant discoveries had already brought his rather loud personality to light.
Thanks to him, problems that had previously been purely theoretical received practical applications.
His name was well-known in the field of science.
He held one of the top positions in the scholarly world.

We will see what troubles, setbacks, disappointments, and even outrages he faced from the jesters of the press that led him to this period of madness which necessitated his internment at Healthful-House.
His latest invention related to war machines was called the Fulgurateur Roch.
This device had, according to him, such superiority over all others that the state acquiring it would become the absolute master of the continents and the seas.

sentences: But Fergusson stopped him with a firm hand, and, rushing to the anchor rope, he cut it with a single blow of the axe.
The flames, stretching towards the balloon, were already licking its illuminated sides; but the Victoria, freed from its ties, rose more than a thousand feet into the air.
Terrible screams erupted beneath the forest, accompanied by violent gunfire; the balloon, caught by a current that was rising with the day, headed west.
"If we hadn't taken the precaution to lighten ourselves last night," said the doctor, "we would have been lost without resources.
That's what it means to do things on time," replied Joe; "then you save yourself, and nothing could be more natural.
What are you afraid of, then?
asked Dick.
The Victoria can't descend without your permission, and when would it even descend?

The edge of the forest had just been passed, and the travelers could see about thirty horsemen, dressed in baggy trousers and flowing burnouses; they were armed, some with lances, others with long muskets; they were following the direction of the Victoria at a brisk gallop on their lively and spirited horses, which was moving at a moderate speed.

At the sight of the travelers, they let out wild cries, brandishing their weapons; anger and threats were visible on their swarthy faces, made fiercer by a sparse but bristly beard; they crossed these lowered plateaus and softened slopes leading down to Senegal with ease.
"It's definitely them!
said the doctor, the cruel Talibas, the fierce marabouts of Al-Eladji!
I would rather find myself in the middle of a forest, surrounded by a circle of wild beasts, than fall into the hands of these bandits.
--They don't look very accommodating!
said Kennedy, and they are some strong fellows!
--Fortunately, those beasts don't fly, replied Joe; that's something.
Look, said Fergusson, these ruined villages, these burned huts!
That is their work; and where vast fields once stretched, they have brought barrenness and devastation.

sentences: After hearing these words, I exclaimed: O happy day, sweet light, you finally reveal yourself after so many years!
I obey you; I leave after bidding farewell to this place.
Farewell, dear cave.
Farewell, nymphs of these damp meadows.
I will no longer hear the muffled sound of the waves of this sea.
Farewell, shore where I have so often suffered the insults of the air.
Farewell, promontory where Echo repeated my groans so many times.
Farewell, sweet fountains that were so bitter to me.
Farewell, O land of Lemnos; let me depart happily, since I am going where the will of the gods and my friends calls me!
Thus we departed: we arrived at the siege of Troy.
Machaon and Podalyre, through the divine knowledge of their father Asclepius, healed me, or at least put me in the state you see me in.
I no longer suffer; I have regained all my strength: but I am a bit lame.
I brought down Paris like a timid fawn that a hunter pierces with his arrows.
Soon Ilion was reduced to ashes; you know the rest.

I still had some aversion towards the wise Ulysses, due to the memory of my sufferings; and his virtue could not soothe this resentment: but the sight of a son who resembles him, and whom I cannot help but love, softened my heart for the father himself.

A dispute arose between Telemachus and Phalante, leader of the Lacedaemonians, regarding some prisoners taken from the Daunians that each claimed belonged to him. --While the case was being discussed in the assembly of allied kings, Hippias, brother of Phalante, seized the prisoners to take them to Tarentum. --Irritated, Telemachus attacked Hippias with fury and brought him down in a single combat. --Adraste, king of the Daunians, taking advantage of the turmoil in the allied army due to the quarrel between Telemachus and Hippias, attacked them unexpectedly. --He surprised a hundred of their ships with which he transported his own troops into the camp of the allies. --He set fire to it and began the attack on Phalante's quarter. --He killed Hippias, brother of Phalante.

He himself was pierced with wounds. --Telemachus, having donned his divine armor, rushed out of the camp at the first sound of this disorder, gathered the army of allies around him, and directed their movements with such wisdom that he quickly repelled the victorious enemy. --A storm separated the two armies and ended the battle. --Telemachus had the wounded carried away and provided them with all the relief they needed. --He took special care of Phalante and the funeral of Hippias.

sentences: The soldiers immediately crossed their bayonets, believing that the prisoner was rushing towards the inspector with ill intentions.

Then, he gathered in his gaze all that the human heart can hold of gentleness and humility, and expressing himself with a kind of pious eloquence that astonished those present, he tried to touch the soul of his visitor.
The inspector listened to Dantès' speech until the end, then turning to the governor, he said in a low voice, "He will turn to devotion; he is already inclined to softer feelings.
See, fear is having its effect on him; he recoiled before the bayonets; now, a madman does not recoil before anything: I have made some very curious observations on this subject at Charenton."
--I ask what crime I have committed; I ask to be given judges; I ask for my trial to be conducted; I finally ask to be shot if I am guilty, but also to be set free if I am innocent.
--Yes, I believe it, I know nothing.

But that matters little; what should matter, not only to me, the unfortunate prisoner, but also to all the officials administering justice, and even to the king who governs us, is that an innocent person is not a victim of an infamous denunciation and does not die behind bars cursing his executioners.
--You are quite humble today, said the governor; you have not always been like this.
You spoke quite differently, my dear friend, on the day you wanted to assault your guard.
--That's true, sir, said Dantès, and I humbly apologize to that man who has always been good to me....
But, what do you want?
I was mad, I was furious.
No, sir, for captivity has bent, broken, and annihilated me....
I've been here for so long!
Seventeen months!
Dantès replied.
Ah!

Sir, you don't know what seventeen months in prison is like: seventeen years, seventeen centuries; especially for a man who, like me, was on the verge of happiness, for a man who, like me, was about to marry a beloved woman, for a man who saw an honorable career opening up before him, and who now lacks everything; who, from the middle of the most beautiful day, falls into the deepest night, who sees his career destroyed, who doesn't know if the one who loved him still loves him, who is unaware if his old father is dead or alive.
Seventeen months in prison, for a man used to the sea air, to the independence of a sailor, to space, to vastness, to infinity!
Sir, seventeen months in prison is more than all the crimes that the most odious names in human language could ever deserve.
So have pity on me, sir, and ask for me, not leniency, but severity; not a pardon, but a judgment; judges, sir, all I ask for are judges; one cannot refuse judges to an accused person.

sentences: However, what he had not been able to write to Albert, since the events we are about to recount occurred after his letter had been sent, is that on the same day, a great agitation had manifested itself and reigned in the groups that are usually so calm in the upper assembly.

Everyone had arrived almost before the hour, and was discussing the sinister event that was going to capture public attention and focus it on one of the most well-known members of the illustrious body.
There were low readings of the article, comments, and exchanges of memories that further clarified the facts.
The Count of Morcerf was not liked among his colleagues.
Like all social climbers, he had been forced, to maintain his rank, to adopt an excessive hauteur.
The great aristocrats laughed at him; the talented repudiated him; the pure glories instinctively despised him.
The count found himself in that unfortunate position of the scapegoat.
Once designated by the finger of God for sacrifice, everyone was preparing to shout 'haro'.
Only the Count of Morcerf knew nothing.
He did not receive the newspaper containing the defamatory news and had spent the morning writing letters and trying out a horse.

He therefore arrived at his usual time, head held high, proud eye, insolent gait, got out of the carriage, passed through the corridors, and entered the hall, without noticing the hesitations of the ushers and the half-salutes of his colleagues.
When Morcerf entered, the session had already been open for more than half an hour.

Although the count, as we have said, was ignorant of everything that had happened, he did not change his demeanor or gait, yet his demeanor and gait appeared to everyone more arrogant than usual, and his presence on this occasion seemed so aggressive to this assembly jealous of its honor that everyone saw it as inappropriate, several as a provocation, and a few as an insult.
It was evident that the entire Chamber was burning to start the debate.
The accusatory newspaper was visible in everyone's hands; but, as always, everyone hesitated to take on the responsibility for the attack.
Finally, one of the honorable peers, a declared enemy of the Count of Morcerf, ascended to the podium with a solemnity that announced the awaited moment had arrived.

sentences: When the various objects had been arranged in the projectile, the water intended to create the spring was introduced between its partitions, and the lighting gas was forced back into its container.
As for the potassium chlorate and caustic potash, Barbicane, fearing unforeseen delays on the way, took along a sufficient quantity to renew the oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide for two months.
An extremely ingenious device that operated automatically was responsible for restoring the air's life-giving qualities and completely purifying it.
The projectile was therefore ready, and all that remained was to lower it into the Columbiad.
This operation, moreover, was fraught with difficulties and dangers.
The enormous shell was brought to the top of Stone's Hill.
There, powerful cranes seized it and held it suspended above the metal well.
It was an exhilarating moment.
If the chains were to break under this enormous weight, the fall of such a mass would certainly have triggered the ignition of the fulmi-cotton.
Fortunately, that was not the case, and a few hours later, the projectile-carriage, gently lowered into the heart of the cannon, rested on its layer of pyroxyl, a true explosive duvet.
Its pressure had no other effect than to pack the Columbiad's charge more tightly.
"I lost," said the captain as he handed President Barbicane a sum of three thousand dollars.
Barbicane did not want to accept this money from a fellow traveler; but he had to yield to Nicholl's insistence, who was determined to fulfill all his commitments before leaving Earth.
"Then," said Michel Ardan, "I have only one thing left to wish you, my brave captain.
You're going to lose your other two bets!
This way, we'll be sure not to get stuck along the way.

The first day of December had arrived, a fateful day, because if the launch of the projectile didn't take place that very evening at ten forty-six minutes and forty seconds, more than eighteen years would pass before the Moon appeared again under the same simultaneous conditions of zenith and perigee.
The weather was magnificent; despite the approach of winter, the sun was shining and bathing this Earth, which three of its inhabitants were about to leave for a new world.

sentences: Rodolphe had moved closer to Emma, and he was speaking in a low voice, talking quickly.
Doesn't this conspiracy of the world revolt you?
Is there a single feeling that it does not condemn?
The noblest instincts, the purest sympathies are persecuted, slandered, and if by chance two poor souls meet, everything is arranged so that they cannot join together.
They will try, however, they will flap their wings, they will call to each other.
Oh!
No matter, sooner or later, in six months, ten years, they will reunite, they will love each other, because fate demands it and they were born for each other.
The sweetness of this sensation thus penetrated her former desires, and like grains of sand in a gust of wind, they swirled in the subtle waft of the perfume that spread over her soul.
She opened her nostrils several times, forcefully, to inhale the freshness of the ivy around the capitals.

She took off her gloves, wiped her hands; then with her handkerchief, she fanned her face, while through the throbbing of her temples she heard the murmur of the crowd and the voice of the counselor chanting his phrases.
"Continue!
Persevere!
Do not listen to the suggestions of routine or the hasty advice of reckless empiricism!
Focus especially on improving the soil, on good fertilizers, on the development of horse, cattle, sheep, and pig breeds!
May these fairs be for you like peaceful arenas where the victor, upon leaving, will extend his hand to the vanquished and will fraternize with him, in the hope of better success!

And you, venerable servants, humble domestics, whose hard labors no government has considered until now, come receive the reward for your silent virtues, and be assured that the State, from now on, has its eyes on you, that it encourages you, that it protects you, that it will address your just claims and lighten, as much as it can, the burden of your painful sacrifices!" Mr.
Lieuvain sat back down; and then Mr.
Derozerais stood up, beginning another speech.
His, perhaps, was not as flowery as that of the counselor; but it was distinguished by a more positive style, that is to say, by more specific knowledge and higher considerations.
Thus, the praise of the government took up less space; religion and agriculture occupied more.
One could see the relationship between the two, and how they had always contributed to civilization.
Rodolphe, with Madame Bovary, was discussing dreams, premonitions, magnetism.
Going back to the cradle of societies, the speaker depicted those savage times when men lived on acorns deep in the woods.
Then they had left the skins of beasts, donned cloth, plowed fields, planted vines.
Was it a good thing, and was there not in this discovery more disadvantages than advantages?
Mr.
Derozerais posed this problem.
From magnetism, gradually, Rodolphe had come to affinities, and while Mr.

the president cited Cincinnatus at his plow, Diocletian planting his cabbages, and the emperors of China inaugurating the year with sowing, the young man explained to the young woman that these irresistible attractions stemmed from some previous existence:

Amidst these living plants and under the canopies of hydrophytes, awkward legions of arthropods scurried about, particularly serrated frogs, whose shell resembles a slightly rounded triangle, special birgus found in these waters, and horrible parthenopes, whose appearance was repulsive to the eye.
An equally hideous creature that I encountered several times was this enormous crab observed by Mr.

Darwin, to which nature has given the instinct and strength necessary to feed on coconuts; it climbs the trees along the shore, knocks down the coconut which splits upon falling, and opens it with its powerful claws.
Here, beneath these clear waves, this crab moved with unparalleled agility, while free turtles of the species that frequents the coasts of Malabar slowly navigated between the shaken rocks.
Around seven o'clock, we finally walked across the bed of pintadines, where pearl oysters reproduce by the millions.
These precious mollusks clung to the rocks and were firmly attached by their brown byssus, which does not allow them to move.
In what way are these oysters inferior to the mussels themselves, to which nature has not denied any ability for locomotion?
Captain Nemo gestured towards this prodigious heap of pintadines, and I understood that this mine was truly inexhaustible, for the creative force of nature surpasses the destructive instinct of man.
Ned Land, true to this instinct, hurried to fill a net he carried at his side with the finest mollusks.
But we could not stop.
We had to follow the captain, who seemed to navigate by paths known only to him.
The ground rose noticeably, and at times my arm, which I raised, exceeded the surface of the sea.
Then the level of the bank dropped capriciously.
Often we turned around high, pointed rocks shaped like pyramids.

In their dark crevices, large crustaceans, perched on their long legs like war machines, stared at us with their fixed eyes, while beneath our feet crawled myriads, glycymeris, aricia, and annelids, stretching their antennae and tentacular cirri to an excessive length.
At that moment, a vast cave opened before our steps, carved into a picturesque pile of rocks covered with all the high-lifes of the underwater flora.
At first, this cave seemed profoundly dark to me.
The sun's rays appeared to fade away in successive degradations.
Its vague transparency was nothing more than drowned light.

So, I said, after examining each of the various hypotheses one by one, and rejecting any other assumption, we must necessarily admit the existence of a marine animal of excessive power.
The great depths of the Ocean are completely unknown to us.
The sounding line has been unable to reach them.
What happens in these remote abysses?
What beings inhabit and can inhabit twelve or fifteen miles below the surface of the waters?
What is the organism of these animals?
One would hardly be able to conjecture it.
However, the solution to the problem presented to me may affect the nature of the dilemma.
Either we know all the varieties of beings that populate our planet, or we do not know them.

If we do not know them all, if nature still has secrets for us in ichthyology, nothing is more acceptable than to admit the existence of fish or cetaceans, of species or even new genera, with an essentially 'bottom-dwelling' organization, that inhabit the layers inaccessible to the sounding line, and that some event, a whim, a caprice, if you will, brings back to the upper level of the Ocean at long intervals.
Indeed, the narwhal is armed with a kind of ivory sword, a halberd, according to the expression of certain naturalists.
It is a main tooth that has the hardness of steel.
Some of these teeth have been found embedded in the bodies of whales that the narwhal always successfully attacks.
Others have been pulled out, not without difficulty, from the hulls of ships that they had pierced through and through, like a drill bores into a barrel.
The museum of the Faculty of Medicine in Paris has one of these tusks that is two meters and twenty-five centimeters long, and forty-eight centimeters wide at its base!
Well!

Suppose the weapon is ten times stronger, and the animal ten times more powerful, launch it at a speed of twenty miles per hour, multiply its mass by its speed, and you get a shock capable of producing the requested catastrophe.

Therefore, until further information is available, I would lean towards a colossal sea unicorn, armed not with a halberd, but with a true spur like armored frigates or war 'rams', which would have both the mass and the driving power.

sentences: At these words, the entire assembly, moved, asked him how he dared to say that an action which would bring certain victory to the league could ruin it.
How, he replied, can you trust one another if you once break the unique bond of society and trust, which is good faith?

After you have established as a principle that one can violate the rules of honesty and loyalty for a great interest, which of you will be able to trust another, when that other can find a great advantage in breaking his word and deceiving him?
Where will you be?
Which of you will not want to outsmart his neighbor with his own tricks?
What becomes of a league of so many peoples when they agree among themselves, through a common deliberation, that it is permissible to surprise one's neighbor and to violate the given faith?
What will be your mutual distrust, your division, your eagerness to destroy one another!
Adraste will no longer need to attack you; you will tear each other apart enough; you will justify his treachery.
O wise and magnanimous kings, you who command with such experience over countless peoples, do not disdain to listen to the advice of a young man!

If you were to fall into the most dreadful extremes to which war sometimes drives men, you would need to rise again through your vigilance and the efforts of your virtue; for true courage is never brought low.

But if you once break the barrier of honor and good faith, that loss is irreparable; you could no longer restore either the trust necessary for the success of all important affairs, nor bring men back to the principles of virtue, after you have taught them to despise them.
What do you fear?
Do you not have enough courage to win without deceiving?
Does your virtue, combined with the strength of so many peoples, not suffice for you?
Let us fight, let us die if we must, rather than win so disgracefully.
Adraste, the impious Adraste is in our hands, provided that we abhor imitating his cowardice and bad faith.
When Télémaque finished this speech, he felt that sweet persuasion had flowed from his lips and had reached deep into their hearts.

He noticed a profound silence in the assembly; each person was thinking, not of him or the grace of his words, but of the strength of the truth that was felt in the course of his reasoning: astonishment was painted on their faces.

Finally, a low murmur was heard spreading gradually through the assembly; some looked at each other and did not dare to speak first; they were waiting for the army leaders to declare themselves; and each had difficulty holding back their feelings.
At last, the grave Nestor spoke these words:

sentences: I would add that this man was proud, that his firm and calm gaze seemed to reflect lofty thoughts, and that from this whole, from the homogeneity of expressions in the gestures of the body and face, according to the observation of physiognomists, resulted an undeniable frankness.
I felt "involuntarily" reassured in his presence, and I had high hopes for our meeting.
Whether this man was thirty-five or fifty years old, I couldn't say.

He was tall, with a broad forehead, a straight nose, a distinctly shaped mouth, magnificent teeth, and fine, elongated hands, eminently "psychic"—to use a term from chirology—meaning worthy of serving a noble and passionate soul.
This man certainly represented the most admirable type I had ever encountered.
A particular detail: his eyes, slightly spaced apart, could simultaneously take in nearly a quarter of the horizon.
I later verified that this ability was accompanied by a vision power even greater than that of Ned Land.

When this stranger focused on an object, the line of his eyebrows furrowed, his wide eyelids drew closer together to encircle the pupils of his eyes and thus narrow the extent of his field of vision, and he looked!
What a gaze!
How it magnified objects diminished by distance!
How it penetrated you to the soul!
How it pierced through those liquid layers, so opaque to our eyes, and how it read to the depths of the seas!...
The two strangers, wearing berets made of sea otter fur and sea boots made of seal skin, were dressed in a particular fabric that accentuated their waists and allowed for great freedom of movement.
The taller of the two, obviously the leader on board, examined us with extreme attention, without uttering a word.
Then, turning to his companion, he conversed with him in a language I could not recognize.
It was a sonorous, harmonious, flexible idiom, whose vowels seemed subject to very varied accentuation.
The other responded with a nod and added two or three perfectly incomprehensible words.
Then, with his gaze, he seemed to question me directly.
I replied, in good French, that I did not understand his language; but he did not seem to understand me, and the situation became quite awkward.

sentences: But what catches the eye the most is, opposite the Lion d'Or inn, Mr. Homais' pharmacy!
Homais!

In the evening, especially when his lamp is lit and the red and green jars that adorn his storefront cast their two colored lights far onto the ground; then, through them, like in Bengal fires, the shadow of the pharmacist can be seen, leaning on his desk.

His house, from top to bottom, is plastered with inscriptions written in English, in round, in molded: 'Vichy, Seltz, and Barèges waters, purifying herbs, Raspail medicine, Arab racahout, Darcet pastilles, Regnault paste, bandages, baths, health chocolates, etc.' And the sign, which spans the entire width of the shop, displays in gold letters: Homais, pharmacist.

Then, at the back of the shop, behind the large scales fixed to the counter, the word laboratory unfolds above a glass door which, halfway up, repeats once again Homais, in gold letters, on a black background.
There is nothing more to see in Yonville.
The street (the only one), a rifle shot long and lined with a few shops, ends abruptly at the bend in the road.
If you keep it on the right and follow the bottom of the Saint-Jean hill, you soon arrive at the cemetery.

During the cholera outbreak, to enlarge it, a section of wall was torn down and three acres of land were purchased next door; but this new portion is almost uninhabited, with the graves, as before, continuing to pile up towards the gate.
The caretaker, who is also the gravedigger and sexton at the church (thus drawing a double benefit from the parish corpses), has taken advantage of the empty land to plant potatoes.
Year after year, however, his small field shrinks, and when an epidemic occurs, he doesn't know whether to rejoice at the deaths or to mourn the burials.

sentences: Sir, said the inspector, Providence has fortunately brought some change to this gigantic plan of which you seem to be quite an enthusiastic supporter.
It's the only way to make Italy a strong, independent, and happy state, replied the abbe.

That is possible, replied the inspector, but I didn't come here to give you a lesson in ultramontane politics; I came to ask you what I've already done, if you have any complaints about how you are fed and housed.
The food is what it is in all prisons, replied the abbe, that is to say, very bad; as for the accommodation, you can see it is damp and unhealthy, but still fairly suitable for a cell.
Now, that's not what this is about, but rather revelations of the utmost importance and interest that I have to make to the government.
That's why I'm so happy to see you, continued the abbe, although you have interrupted me in a very important calculation, which, if successful, might change Newton's system.
Can you grant me the favor of a private meeting?
You know your worth, replied the latter with a smile.
Then, turning to Faria:
However, sir, the abbe resumed, if it were a matter of making the government a huge sum, a sum of five million, for example?
Indeed, said the inspector, turning back to the governor, you even predicted the amount.
Well, the abbé replied, noticing that the inspector was making a move to leave, it is not necessary for us to be completely alone; Mr.
the governor can attend our conversation.
My dear sir, the governor said, unfortunately we already know by heart what you will say.
It's about your treasures, isn't it?" Faria looked at this mocking man with eyes where an impartial observer would certainly have seen the spark of reason and truth.
"Of course, he said; what do you want me to talk about, if not that?
Inspector, the governor continued, I can tell you this story just as well as the abbé, because I have been hearing about it for four or five years.
That proves, Mr. Governor, the abbé said, that you are like those people spoken of in Scripture, who have eyes but do not see, who have ears but do not hear.

sentences: Master Mac Nap first went to choose the trees needed for his construction.
He found a large number of these pines on the hills that closely resemble Scots pine.
These trees were of medium height and very suitable for the house he was to build.
In these rough dwellings, indeed, walls, floors, ceilings, partition walls, beams, ridge beams, rafters, shingles, everything consists of planks, beams, and girders.
It is understandable that this type of construction requires only very basic labor, and Mac Nap was able to proceed quickly — which in no way affected the solidity of the dwelling.
Master Mac Nap chose straight trees, which were cut a foot above the ground.
These pines, stripped of branches, numbering around a hundred, neither barked nor squared, formed as many girders each twenty feet long.
The axe and the adze only touched their ends to carve the tenons and mortises that would fix them to one another.
This operation took only a few days to complete, and soon all these woods, dragged by dogs, were transported to the plateau where the main house was to be located.
Previously, this plateau had been carefully leveled.
The ground, mixed with soil and fine sand, was beaten and compacted with heavy pounding.

The short grasses and the sparse shrubs that covered it had been burned on the spot, and the ashes resulting from the incineration formed a thick layer on the surface, completely impermeable to any moisture.
In this way, Mac Nap obtained a clean and dry site on which he could safely establish his first interconnections.
With this first work completed, at each corner of the house and directly above the partition walls, the main beams rose vertically, which were to support the frame of the house.
They were driven a few feet into the ground after their ends had been hardened in the fire.
These beams, slightly hollowed out on their side faces, received the transverse girders of the actual wall, between which the openings for doors and windows had been previously made.
At their upper part, these beams were joined by ties that, being well fitted into the mortises, thus consolidated the entire structure.
These ties represented the entablature of the two facades, and it was at their ends that the high roof trusses rested, whose lower ends overhung the wall, like the roof of a chalet.
On the square of the entablature, the ceiling girders extended, and on the layer of ashes, those of the floor.

sentences: It was clear that hatred was driving the Englishman to speak, and that, not knowing what to accuse the count of, he was blaming him for his greed.
--I hold a grudge against him, replied Lord Wilmore, because when he was passing through England, he seduced the wife of one of my friends.
--But if you hold a grudge against him, why don't you seek revenge?
--I've already fought the count three times, said the Englishman: the first time with a pistol; the second time with a sword; the third time with a sabre.

--The first time, he broke my arm; the second time, he pierced my lung; and the third time, he gave me this wound.” The Englishman turned down a collar that was up to his ears and showed a scar whose redness indicated it was relatively recent.
So I hold a deep grudge against him, the Englishman repeated, and he will surely die by my hand.
But, said the envoy from the prefecture, it seems to me that you are not on the path to kill him.
That was what the visitor wanted to know, or rather, it was all that the Englishman seemed to know.
The agent then stood up, and after greeting Lord Wilmore, who responded with the stiffness and politeness typical of the English, he withdrew.

For his part, Lord Wilmore, after hearing the street door close behind him, returned to his bedroom, where, in the blink of an eye, he lost his blond hair, his red sideburns, his false jaw, and his scar to regain the black hair, dark complexion, and pearl-like teeth of the Count of Monte Cristo.
The king's prosecutor was somewhat reassured by this double visit, which, in any case, had not taught him anything comforting, but also had not taught him anything alarming.
As a result, for the first time since the dinner at Auteuil, he slept the following night with some peace of mind.
They had reached the hottest days of July when this Saturday, when Mr. de Morcerf's ball was to take place, finally arrived in due course.
of Morcerf.

It was ten o'clock in the evening: the tall trees in the garden of the count's hotel stood out against a sky where the last remnants of a storm that had threatened all day slid away, revealing a blue canopy dotted with golden stars.

sentences: The Betis River flows through a fertile land, under a gentle sky that is always serene.

The land takes its name from the river, which empties into the great Ocean, not far from the Pillars of Hercules, and from that place where the furious sea, breaking its banks, once separated the land of Tharsis from great Africa.
This land seems to have preserved the delights of the golden age.
The winters there are mild, and the harsh north winds never blow there.
The heat of summer is always tempered by refreshing zephyrs that soften the air around midday.
Thus, the whole year is nothing but a happy union of spring and autumn, which seem to hold hands.
The land, in the valleys and in the flat fields, produces a double harvest every year.
The roads are lined with laurels, pomegranates, jasmines, and other evergreens that are always in bloom.
The mountains are covered with flocks that provide fine wool sought after by all known nations.

There are several gold and silver mines in this beautiful land; but the inhabitants, simple and happy in their simplicity, do not even bother to count gold and silver among their riches; they value only what truly serves the needs of man.

The women spin this beautiful wool and make fine fabrics of wonderful whiteness; they bake bread, prepare meals; and this work is easy for them, as one lives in this land on fruits or milk, and rarely on meat.

They use the leather from their sheep to make light shoes for themselves, their husbands, and their children; they make tents, some from tanned hides and others from tree bark; they make and wash all the family's clothes, and keep the homes in an admirable order and cleanliness.

Their clothes are easy to make; for in this mild climate, one wears only a piece of fine, light fabric that is not tailored, and which everyone wraps in long folds around their body for modesty, giving it the shape they desire.

When they are told about the peoples who have the art of making splendid buildings, gold and silver furniture, fabrics adorned with embroidery and precious stones, exquisite perfumes, delicious dishes, and instruments whose harmony enchants, they respond in these terms: These peoples are very unfortunate to have spent so much labor and industry corrupting themselves!
This superfluity softens, intoxicates, and torments those who possess it: it tempts those who are deprived of it to seek to acquire it through injustice and violence.
Can one call good a superfluity that serves only to make men wicked?
Are the men of this land healthier and stronger than we are?
Do they live longer?
Are they more united among themselves?
Do they lead a life that is freer, more peaceful, and happier?

On the contrary, they must be envious of one another, consumed by a cowardly and dark envy, always agitated by ambition, fear, and greed, incapable of pure and simple pleasures, since they are slaves to so many false necessities upon which they depend for all their happiness.

sentences: He woke up sober, his mind calm and clear, able to assess the situation and foresee the outcome.
After an hour, he was running around the countryside asking everywhere for news of his soldier.
He went to find the officers to find out, as he said, why they had taken his man away.
Since they knew about their relationship, no one suspected him; he even directed the search, claiming that the Prussian went out every evening to dance the cotillon.
An old retired gendarme, who ran an inn in a nearby village and had a pretty daughter, was arrested and shot.
SINCE his entry into France with the invading army, Walter Schnaffs considered himself the most unfortunate man.
He was big, walked with difficulty, breathed heavily, and suffered terribly from his very flat and very fat feet.

He was also peaceful and kind-hearted, by no means magnanimous or bloodthirsty, a father of four children whom he adored and married to a young blonde woman, whose tenderness, little attentions, and kisses he desperately missed every evening.
He loved to get up late and go to bed early, eat good food slowly, and drink beer in the breweries.

He also thought that everything sweet in life disappears with death; and he harbored a terrible hatred, both instinctive and rational, in his heart for cannons, rifles, revolvers, and sabers, but especially for bayonets, feeling incapable of maneuvering that quick weapon well enough to defend his big belly.

And when he lay down on the ground at night, rolled up in his coat next to the comrades who were snoring, he thought long and hard about his loved ones left behind and the dangers scattered along his path:--If he were killed, what would happen to the little ones?
Who would feed and raise them?
At that very moment, they were not rich, despite the debts he had incurred when leaving to leave them some money.
And Walter Schnaffs sometimes cried.
At the beginning of battles, he felt such weakness in his legs that he would have fallen down if he hadn't thought that the entire army would pass over his body.
The whistling of the bullets made the hair on his skin stand on end.

sentences: Wintering thus began.
The sleds were unloaded, the provisions were brought into the office; the clothes, the weapons, the utensils, and the furs were stored away.
The dogs returned to their doghouse, and the domesticated reindeer went back to their stable.
Thomas Black also had to deal with his relocation, and what despair it brought!

The unfortunate astronomer moved his instruments, books, and notebooks back to his room, and, more irritated than ever by 'this fate that was relentless against him,' he remained, as before, completely detached from everything happening in the factory.

One day was enough for the general reinstallation, and then this life of the winterers began again, a life that was uneventful and would seem horrifically monotonous to the inhabitants of large cities.

Sewing work, mending clothes, and even maintaining the furs, part of which might be saved, then observing the weather, monitoring the ice field, and finally reading, these were the daily occupations and distractions.
Mrs.
Paulina Barnett oversaw everything, and her influence was felt in all matters.
If, at times, a slight disagreement arose among these soldiers, sometimes made difficult by the annoyances of the present and the worries of the future, it quickly dissipated at the words of Mrs.
Paulina Barnett.
The traveler had a great hold over this small world and never used it except for the common good.
Kalumah had become increasingly attached to her.
Everyone also loved the young Eskimo woman, who was gentle and helpful.
Mrs.
Paulina Barnett had taken on the task of educating her, and she was succeeding, as her student was truly intelligent and eager to learn.
She perfected her in the study of the English language, teaching her to read and write.

Moreover, in these subjects, Kalumah found ten teachers who vied for the pleasure of training her; for among all these soldiers, raised in English possessions or in England, there was not one who could not read, write, and count.
The construction of the boat was actively pushed forward, and it was to be completely planked and decked before the end of the month.
In the midst of this obscure atmosphere, Mac Nap and his men worked diligently in the light of burning resin, while the others took care of the rigging in the factory's stores.
The season, although already quite advanced, remained uncertain.
The cold, sometimes very sharp, did not hold.
This was obviously due to the persistent westerly winds.

sentences: A group of about fifteen men, aged between twenty-five and forty, scattered among the dancers or chatting at the entrance, stood out from the crowd by a familial air, despite their differences in age, attire, or appearance.
Their clothes, better tailored, seemed to be made of a softer fabric, and their hair, styled in curls at the temples, was slicked back with finer pomades.

They had the complexion of wealth, a white skin enhanced by the pallor of porcelain, the sheen of satin, the polish of fine furniture, and maintained in good health by a discreet diet of exquisite foods.

Their necks turned comfortably in low cravats; their long sideburns fell onto turned-down collars; they wiped their lips with handkerchiefs embroidered with a large monogram, from which a sweet fragrance emanated.
Those who were starting to age looked young, while something mature spread across the faces of the young.

In their indifferent gazes floated the tranquility of passions satisfied daily; and, beneath their gentle manners, there pierced a particular brutality that comes from the mastery of somewhat easy things, where strength is exercised and vanity is entertained, such as handling racehorses and associating with fallen women.
Three steps away from Emma, a man in a blue coat was discussing Italy with a pale young woman wearing a pearl necklace.
They praised the size of the pillars of Saint Peter's, Tivoli, Vesuvius, Castellamare and the Cassines, the roses of Genoa, and the Colosseum by moonlight.
Emma listened with one ear to a conversation full of words she did not understand.
They surrounded a very young man who had beaten Miss Arabelle and Romulus the week before, and won two thousand louis for jumping a ditch in England.
One complained about his horses getting fat; another about printing errors that had distorted the name of his horse.
The air of the ball was heavy; the lamps were dimming.
They were flowing back into the billiard room.
A servant climbed onto a chair and broke two windows; at the sound of the glass shattering, Madame Bovary turned her head and saw in the garden, against the panes, the faces of peasants watching.
Then the memory of the Bertaux came to her.
She saw again the farm, the muddy pond, her father in a smock under the apple trees, and she saw herself, as before, skimming the milk pans with her finger in the dairy.
But, amidst the flashes of the present moment, her past life, so clear until then, was completely fading away, and she almost doubted having lived it.
She was there; then around the ball, there was nothing but shadow, spread over everything else.
She was then eating a maraschino ice, which she held in her left hand in a vermeil shell, and half-closed her eyes, the spoon between her teeth.
