sentences: Thus it was that the future father-in-law and the future son-in-law got into the same carriage, and Morrel, seeing them pass by, understandably felt serious concerns.

"Mr. d'Épinay," he said, "I believe I should remind you, and perhaps the timing is not as poorly chosen as it might seem at first glance, for obedience to the dead is the first offering that must be placed on the coffin; I must therefore remind you of the wish that Mrs. de Saint-Méran expressed the day before yesterday on her deathbed, which is that Valentine’s marriage should not be delayed.

You know that the affairs of the deceased are perfectly in order; that her will ensures Valentine the entire fortune of the Saint-Mérans; the notary showed me yesterday the documents that allow us to draft the marriage contract definitively.
You can see the notary and have these documents communicated to you on my behalf.
The notary is Mr.
Deschamps, Place Beauveau, Faubourg Saint-Honoré.
"Sir," d'Épinay replied, "it may not be the right time for Miss Valentine, as she is deeply immersed in grief, to think about a husband; truly, I would be concerned....
"Valentine," interrupted Mr.
de Villefort, "will have no greater desire than to fulfill her grandmother's last wishes; thus, the obstacles will not come from that side, I assure you.
"In that case, sir," Franz replied, "since they will not come from my side either, you can proceed as you wish; my word is pledged, and I will fulfill it, not only with pleasure but with joy.
"Then," Villefort said, "nothing stops you now; the contract was supposed to be signed three days ago, we will find it all prepared: it can be signed today.
Rest assured, sir, Villefort replied; it is not in my house that propriety is neglected.
Mlle de Villefort will be able to withdraw for the required three months to her estate in Saint-Méran; I say her estate because this property belongs to her.
There, in eight days, if you agree, quietly, without fanfare, without ostentation, the civil marriage will be concluded.
It was Mme de Saint-Méran's wish that her granddaughter marry on this estate.
Once the marriage is concluded, sir, you will be able to return to Paris, while your wife spends her mourning period with her mother-in-law.

sentences: He belonged to the great surgical school that emerged from Bichat's apron, to that now-disappeared generation of philosopher-practitioners who, cherishing their art with a fanatical love, practiced it with exaltation and insight!

Everything trembled in his hospital when he got angry, and his students revered him so much that they tried, as soon as they were established, to imitate him as closely as possible; so that one could find them, in the surrounding towns, wearing his long merino dressing gown and his wide black coat, the unbuttoned lapels covering his fleshy hands—very beautiful hands that never wore gloves, as if to be quicker to dive into misery.

Disdainful of crosses, titles, and academies, hospitable, generous, paternal with the poor, and practicing virtue without believing in it, he could almost have passed for a saint if the sharpness of his mind hadn't made him feared like a demon.

His gaze, sharper than his scalpels, pierced right into the soul and dismantled every lie through allegations and modesties.—And he went about like this, full of that benevolent majesty that comes from the awareness of great talent, fortune, and forty years of a laborious and irreproachable existence.
He frowned as soon as he entered, upon seeing Emma's cadaverous face, lying on her back, her mouth open.
Then, while pretending to listen to Canivet, he rubbed his index finger under his nose and repeated, 'It's all right, it's all right.' But he made a slow gesture with his shoulders.
Bovary watched him: they looked at each other; and this man, so accustomed to the sight of suffering, could not hold back a tear that fell onto his jabot.
'She is very ill, isn't she?'
'If only we could apply some mustard plasters!'
'I don't know what!'

Charles wrapped his two arms around her body, and he looked at her in a startled, pleading way, half-fainting against her chest.

my poor boy, be brave!
there's nothing more to be done.--And Doctor Larivière turned away.

sentences: I was crossing the great dunes south of Ouargla.
It is one of the strangest countries in the world.
You know the smooth sand, the straight sand of the endless beaches of the Ocean.
Well!
Imagine the Ocean itself turned to sand in the midst of a hurricane; picture a silent storm of motionless waves in yellow dust.
These waves are as high as mountains, uneven, different, raised just like wild waves, but even larger, and streaked like watered silk.
On this furious, silent, and motionless sea, the scorching sun of the south pours down its relentless and direct flame.
One must climb these golden ash waves, descend, climb again, climb endlessly, without rest and without shade.
The horses are groaning, sinking to their knees, and sliding down the other side of the surprising hills.
We were two friends followed by eight spahis and four camels with their camel drivers.
We no longer spoke, overwhelmed by heat, fatigue, and parched with thirst like this burning desert.
Suddenly one of these men let out a sort of cry; everyone stopped; and we remained still, surprised by an inexplicable phenomenon known to travelers in these remote lands.

Somewhere near us, in an indeterminate direction, a drum was beating, the mysterious drum of the dunes; it beat distinctly, sometimes more vibrantly, sometimes weakened, stopping, then resuming its fantastic rolling.

The Arabs, terrified, looked at each other; and one said in his language, 'Death is upon us.' And suddenly my companion, my friend, almost my brother, fell from his horse, headfirst, struck down by sunstroke.

And for two hours, while I tried in vain to save him, this elusive drum continually filled my ears with its monotonous, intermittent, and incomprehensible sound; and I felt fear, true fear, hideous fear, creeping into my bones, in front of that beloved corpse, in this hole scorched by the sun between four mounds of sand, while the unknown echo threw at us, two hundred leagues from any French village, the rapid beating of the drum.
That day, I understood what it was to be afraid; I learned it even better another time...

At that moment, the sun was approaching the highest point of its course.
The two observers then aimed the telescope of their sextant at the star that was still rising.

By means of the inclined mirrors placed on the instrument, the sun was to be, apparently, brought back to the very horizon, and the moment when it would seem to touch it by the lower edge of its disk would be precisely the moment when it occupied the highest point of the daily arc, and therefore, the exact moment when it would pass the meridian, that is to say, noon at that location.
--Noon!" replied Thomas Black at that very moment.
The telescopes were immediately lowered.
The lieutenant and the astronomer read the values of the angles they had just obtained from the graduated limbs and immediately set to work calculating their observations.

A few minutes later, Lieutenant Hobson stood up and, addressing his companions, said to them, "My friends, from this day, July 6, the Hudson's Bay Company, committing by my word, doubles the salary that is assigned to you!
Hurrah!
Hurrah!
Hurrah for the Company!" shouted the worthy companions of Lieutenant Hobson in unison.
Indeed, Cape Bathurst and the surrounding territory were undoubtedly located above the seventieth parallel.

The midnight sun shone for the first time in their eyes.
The location of the fort was irrevocably decided.
No other place could be more favorable than this naturally flat land, situated at the back of Cape Bathurst, on the eastern shore of the lagoon.
Jasper Hobson therefore resolved to immediately begin construction of the main house.
In the meantime, everyone had to organize themselves a bit as they pleased, and the sleds were ingeniously used to form the temporary camp.

sentences: An old castle bathes the base of its towers in a large, sad pond, sad, with flocks of wild birds.
A river flows from there that coasters can navigate up to the town.

And in the narrow streets with antique houses, men wear tall hats, embroidered vests, and four layered jackets: the first, as large as a hand, covering at most the shoulder blades, and the last stopping just above the seat of their trousers.

The girls, tall, beautiful, fresh, have their chests compressed in a wool vest that forms a breastplate, hugging them tightly, not even allowing a hint of their powerful and tormented bosoms to show; and they are dressed in a strange way: on their temples, two embroidered patches frame their faces, holding their hair that falls like a curtain behind their heads, then rising to be tucked at the top of their skulls under a peculiar bonnet, often made of gold or silver fabric.

The servant at our inn was no more than eighteen, with bright blue eyes, a pale blue pierced by two little black dots of her pupils; and her short, tightly packed teeth, which she constantly showed while laughing, seemed made for crushing granite.
She didn't know a word of French, speaking only Breton, like most of her compatriots.
However, my friend was not doing much better, and although no illness had declared itself, the doctor forbade him to leave yet, ordering complete rest.
So I spent my days near him, and the little maid constantly came in, bringing either my dinner or herbal tea.
I teased her a bit, which seemed to amuse her, but we didn't talk, of course, since we couldn't understand each other.
Finally exhausted, she fell; and I caught her roughly, on the ground, on the pavement.
As soon as she was up, she ran to the door, pulled the bolts, and fled.
I barely saw her in the following days.
She didn't let me approach her.
Then, as my friend was healed and we were to resume our journey, I saw her enter, the night before my departure, at midnight, barefoot, in her nightgown, into my room where I had just retired.

She threw herself into my arms, embraced me passionately, then, until dawn, kissed me, caressed me, crying, sobbing, finally giving me all the assurances of tenderness and despair that a woman can give us when she doesn't know a word of our language.

sentences: Since Franz still had enough time to catch up with his companion, and he no longer had to worry about his accommodation in Rome, he accepted this proposal to make up for his first hunt.
Upon his affirmative response, the sailors exchanged a few low words among themselves.
--No, the captain replied; but we must inform Your Excellency that the island is in default.

--That means that, since Monte-Cristo is uninhabited and sometimes serves as a stopover for smugglers and pirates coming from Corsica, Sardinia, or Africa, if any sign reveals our stay on the island, we will be forced, upon our return to Livorno, to undergo a quarantine of six days.
--Devil!
That certainly changes the thesis!
Six days!
Just as long as it took God to create the world.
That's a bit long, my children.
The captain commanded the maneuver; they set course for the island, and the boat began to sail in that direction.

Franz let the operation finish, and when they had taken the new route, when the sail had filled with the breeze, and the four sailors had taken their places, three at the front and one at the helm, he resumed the conversation.
"My dear Gaetano," he said to the captain, "you just told me, I believe, that the island of Monte-Cristo served as a refuge for pirates, which seems to me to be quite a different game than goats.
I was well aware of the existence of smugglers, but I thought that since the capture of Algiers and the destruction of the Regency, pirates only existed in the novels of Cooper and Captain Marryat.
Well, Your Excellency is mistaken: pirates are like bandits, who are supposed to have been exterminated by Pope Leo XII, yet they still stop travelers every day at the gates of Rome.
Haven't you heard that barely six months ago, the French chargé d'affaires near the Holy See was robbed just five hundred paces from Velletri?

Well, if Your Excellency lived in Livorno like us, you would occasionally hear that a small vessel loaded with goods or a nice English yacht, which was expected in Bastia, Porto-Ferrajo, or Civita-Vecchia, has not arrived, that no one knows what has become of it, and that it has probably crashed against some rock.

Well, that rock it encountered is a low and narrow boat, manned by six or eight men, who surprised or plundered it on a dark and stormy night at the turn of some wild and uninhabited islet, just as bandits stop and rob a stagecoach at the edge of a wood.

sentences: The door opened.
Mélie appeared, and right away, before she had said hello to us: "...

You two really had the meter, you pigs." Then Mathieu got angry: "Don't say that, Mélie, don't say that, I've never been to the meter." They served us an exquisite lunch, in front of the door, under two linden trees, next to the small chapel of "Our Lady of the Big Belly" and facing the vast landscape.
And Mathieu told us, with a teasing tone mixed with unexpected credulity, incredible stories of miracles.

We had drunk a lot of that lovely, tangy, sweet, fresh, and intoxicating cider that he preferred to all other drinks; and we were smoking our pipes, perched on our chairs, when two old women showed up.
They were old, thin, and bent.
After greeting us, they asked for Saint Blanc.
Mathieu winked at us and replied: He stayed there for a good five minutes; then he came back with a dismayed look.
He raised his arms:
"I don't know where he is, I can't find him; I'm sure I had him though."
Then, making a megaphone with his hands, he bellowed again: "Mélie-e-e!" From the back of the yard, his wife replied:

Isn't that the one you took last week to plug the hole in the rabbit hutch? Indeed, Saint Blanc, stuck in the ground like a simple stake, covered in mud and filth, served as a corner for the rabbit hutch.
He went to get some straw and made them a prayer stool.

Then, considering his filthy saint and, no doubt fearing a loss of reputation for his business, he added: He took a bucket of water, a brush, and began to wash the wooden figure vigorously while the two old women continued to pray.
Then, when he had finished, he added: 'Now there's no more harm.' And he brought us back to have a drink.
As he was bringing the glass to his mouth, he stopped and, looking a bit embarrassed, said: 'Still, when I put Saint Blanc with the rabbits, I really thought he wouldn't make any money.
It had been two years since anyone had asked for him.
But saints, you see, never go out of fashion.'
Let's have another drink.
With friends, you shouldn't go in for less than fifty; and we're only at thirty-eight.

sentences: After a moment, she said, "I have nothing to know, sir." But I had found my words; I exclaimed, "Miss, I have loved you for a year!" She was truly surprised and looked up.
I continued, "Yes, miss, listen to me.
I don't know Morin and I couldn't care less about him.
I don't care if he goes to prison or to court.
I saw you here last year; you were over there, by the gate.
I felt a jolt when I saw you, and your image has never left me.
Believe me or not, I don't care.
I found you adorable; your memory possessed me; I wanted to see you again; I seized on the excuse of that idiot Morin; and here I am.

Circumstances pushed me beyond limits; forgive me, I beg you, forgive me." She was searching for the truth in my eyes, ready to smile again; and she murmured, "Joker." I raised my hand, and in a sincere tone (I even believe I was sincere): "I swear to you, I'm not lying." We were alone, completely alone, Rivet and my uncle having disappeared into the winding paths; and I made a real declaration to her, long and sweet, pressing and kissing her fingers.
She listened to this as something pleasant and new, not quite knowing what to believe.
I ended up feeling troubled; thinking about what I was saying; I was pale, oppressed, trembling; and gently, I took her waist.
I spoke softly to her in the little curly hair by her ear.
She seemed almost lifeless, so lost in thought she was.

Then her hand met mine and squeezed it; I slowly pressed her waist in a trembling and ever-growing embrace; she didn't move at all; I brushed my lips against her cheek; and suddenly, my lips, without searching, found hers.
It was a long, long kiss; and it would have lasted even longer if I hadn't heard a "hum, hum" a few steps behind me.
She fled through a thicket.
I turned around and saw Rivet coming up to me.
He planted himself in the middle of the path; and without laughing: "Well!
that's how you handle that pig Morin's affair."

sentences: Then, around six o'clock, the carriage stopped in a narrow street of the Beauvoisine district, and a woman got out, walking with her veil down, without turning her head.
Upon arriving at the inn, Madame Bovary was surprised not to see the stagecoach.
Hivert, who had waited for her for fifty-three minutes, had finally left.
Nothing, however, forced her to leave; but she had given her word that she would return that very evening.
Moreover, Charles was waiting for her; and already she felt in her heart that cowardly submissiveness which is, for many women, both the punishment and the ransom of adultery.

Quickly, she packed her trunk, paid the bill, took a cabriolet from the courtyard, and, urging the groom on, encouraging him, and asking every minute about the time and the kilometers traveled, managed to catch up with the Hirondelle near the first houses of Quincampoix.
Barely seated in her corner, she closed her eyes and reopened them at the bottom of the hill, where she recognized from afar Félicité, who was prominently standing in front of the marshal's house.
Hivert held back his horses, and the cook, raising herself to the window, said mysteriously: The village was as silent as usual.
At the corners of the streets, there were small pink piles that were steaming in the air; it was the time for making jams, and everyone in Yonville was preparing their supply on the same day.

But in front of the pharmacist's shop, they admired a much larger pile, which surpassed the others due to the superiority that a pharmacy must have over bourgeois kitchens, a general need over individual whims.
She entered.
The large armchair was overturned, and even the Fanal de Rouen lay on the ground, stretched out between the two pilons.

She pushed open the corridor door; and, in the middle of the kitchen, among the brown jars full of currants, grated sugar, lump sugar, scales on the table, and basins on the fire, she saw all the Homais, big and small, wearing aprons that came up to their chins and holding forks in their hands.
Justin, standing, was lowering his head, and the pharmacist was shouting:
What's going on?
the apothecary replied.
They're making jam: it's cooking; but it was about to overflow because the boil was too strong, so I'm ordering another pot.
Then, he, out of laziness, out of sloth, went to take the key to the mess, which was hanging on its hook in my lab!

sentences: However, as if crossing the ice fields had been feasible, preparations for departure were actively continuing at the trading post.

Nothing should be overlooked for the safety of the expedition; everything had to be anticipated, and one had to reckon not only with difficulties and fatigue, but also with the whims of this polar nature, which fiercely defends itself against human exploration.
The dog teams had received special attention.
They were allowed to run around the fort so that the exercise would restore their somewhat stiffened strength from a long rest.
Overall, these animals were all in satisfactory condition and could, if not overworked, manage a long trek.
The sleds were carefully inspected.
The rough surface of the icefield would inevitably expose them to violent shocks.
Thus, they had to be reinforced in their main parts, their lower chassis, their curved front runners, etc.
This task rightfully belonged to carpenter Mac Nap and his men, who made these vehicles as sturdy as possible.
In addition, two large sled-carts were constructed, one intended for transporting provisions and the other for transporting furs.
These carts were to be pulled by domestic reindeer, and they were perfectly suited for this purpose.
The furs were, it must be agreed, a luxury cargo that perhaps wasn't wise to carry.

But Jasper Hobson wanted, as much as possible, to safeguard the interests of the Hudson's Bay Company, being determined, moreover, to abandon these furs along the way if they compromised or hindered the caravan's progress.
There was no risk, moreover, since these precious furs, if left in the trading post's stores, would inevitably be lost.
As for the provisions, that was another matter.
The supplies had to be abundant and easily transportable.
One could not rely in any way on the products of the hunt.
Edible game, as soon as the passage became feasible, would take the lead and would soon have rallied to the southern regions.

Therefore, preserved meats, corned beef, hare pâtés, dried fish, biscuits, of which the supply was unfortunately quite limited, etc., ample reserves of sorrel and other provisions, brandy, spirits for making hot drinks, etc., were placed in a special cart.
Jasper Hobson would have liked to bring fuel, for during six hundred miles, he would find neither a tree, nor a bush, nor moss, and one could not count on wreckage or wood washed up by the sea.
But such a burden could not be accepted, and he had to give up on it.
Fortunately, warm clothing would not be lacking; there would be plenty, comfortable, and if necessary, they could draw furs from the cart.

sentences: Then, Dumont d'Urville wanted to leave; but his crews were weakened by the fevers of these unhealthy coasts, and, very ill himself, he could only set sail on March 17.
Such is the essence of the account I gave to Captain Nemo.
"Thus, he said to me, we still do not know where this third ship built by the shipwrecked people on the island of Vanikoro went to its doom?"

I rushed to the window, and beneath the coral formations, covered with fungi, siphonophores, alcyonarians, and coralline algae, amidst myriads of charming fish—wrasses, glyphidodon, pomacentrids, diacanthus, holocentrids—I recognized certain debris that the dredges had not been able to dislodge: iron stirrups, anchors, cannons, cannonballs, a capstan fitting, a bow, all objects from the shipwrecked vessels now carpeted with living flowers.
And while I was looking at these desolate wrecks, Captain Nemo said to me in a grave voice: The others, weakened and ill, left with La Pérouse.
They headed towards the Solomon Islands, and they perished, body and soul, on the western coast of the main island of the group, between Cape Deception and Cape Satisfaction!
Here is what I found at the very site of this last shipwreck!" Captain Nemo showed me a tin box, stamped with the arms of France, and completely corroded by the saltwater.
He opened it, and I saw a bundle of yellowed papers, but still legible.
These were the very instructions from the Minister of the Navy to Commander La Pérouse, annotated in the margins by the hand of Louis XVI!
"Ah!
it's a beautiful death for a sailor!
said Captain Nemo then.
This coral grave is a peaceful tomb, and may heaven grant that my companions and I never have another!" "Sir, this brave boy said to me, may I wish you a happy new year?
--Of course, Conseil, just as if I were in Paris, in my study at the Jardin des Plantes.
I accept your wishes and thank you for them.
However, I would like to ask you what you mean by "a happy new year," given the circumstances we find ourselves in.
Is it the year that will bring an end to our imprisonment, or the year that will see this strange journey continue?

sentences: The stars shone through the bare jasmine branches.
They could hear the river flowing behind them, and from time to time, the rustling of dry reeds on the bank.
Clumps of shadow, here and there, swelled in the darkness, and sometimes, all shivering in unison, they rose and bent like immense black waves that seemed to advance to cover them.

The cold of the night made them cling to each other more tightly; the sighs from their lips seemed louder to them; their eyes, which they could barely see, appeared larger, and in the midst of the silence, there were softly spoken words that fell upon their souls with a crystalline sound and reverberated within them in multiplied vibrations.
And Rodolphe finished his sentence with a gesture that meant: I would crush her with a flick of my finger.
She was astonished by his boldness, although she sensed a kind of naivety and coarseness in it that scandalized her.

If she had spoken seriously, it would have been quite ridiculous, he thought, even odious, since he had no reason to hate good Charles, not being what one would call consumed by jealousy;—and on that subject, Emma had given him quite a lecture, which he also found in poor taste.
But she was so beautiful!
He had possessed so little of such innocence!
This love without libertinism was something new for him, and it, pulling him out of his easy habits, simultaneously stroked his pride and his sensuality.
Emma's exaltation, which his bourgeois common sense dismissed, seemed to him, deep down, charming, since it was directed at him.
Then, sure of being loved, he did not hold back, and gradually his manner changed.

He no longer had, as before, those sweet words that made her cry, nor those passionate caresses that drove her wild;—so much so that their great love, in which she was immersed, seemed to diminish beneath her, like the water of a river being absorbed into its bed; and she caught sight of the mud.
She did not want to believe it; she increased her tenderness; Rodolphe, less and less, hid his indifference.
She did not know if she regretted having yielded to him, or if she wished, on the contrary, to cherish him even more.
The humiliation of feeling weak turned into a resentment that the pleasures tempered.
It was not attachment, but more like a permanent seduction.
He captivated her.
She was almost afraid of it.

sentences: Yes, I know that; I learned it from the servants I saw fleeing the house.
I found out that her name was Valentine; and I have already prayed for her.
Thank you, thank you, sir, said d'Avrigny, and since you have already begun to exercise your holy ministry, please continue it.
Come and sit by the deceased, and an entire family in mourning will be very grateful to you.

I'm going, sir, replied the abbé, and I dare say that never have prayers been more fervent than mine." D'Avrigny took the abbé by the hand, and without encountering Villefort, who was locked in his office, he led him to Valentine's room, which the undertakers were only to take possession of the following night.
Upon entering the room, Noirtier's gaze met that of the abbé, and he surely thought he read something particular in it, for he did not take his eyes off him.
D'Avrigny entrusted the priest not only with the deceased but also with the living, and the priest promised D'Avrigny to offer his prayers for Valentine and his care for Noirtier.

The undertakers had carried out their funeral duties during the night, and sewn the body laid on the bed into the shroud that mournfully drapes the deceased, lending them, as one says about equality in death, a final testament to the luxury they loved in life.
This shroud was nothing more than a piece of magnificent batiste that the young girl had purchased fifteen days earlier.

In the evening, men called for this purpose had transported Noirtier from Valentine's room to his own, and, against all expectations, the old man had shown no reluctance to distance himself from his child's body.
They found him in the large armchair that served as his bed, resting in a gentle and almost smiling sleep.

"Look, said D'Avrigny to Villefort, who was watching his father sleep; look, nature knows how to soothe the deepest pains; certainly, one cannot say that Mr. Noirtier did not love his granddaughter; he is sleeping, nonetheless.
Noirtier did not love his granddaughter; he is sleeping, nonetheless.
Yes, and you are right, Villefort replied with surprise; he is sleeping, and it's quite strange, because the slightest upset keeps him awake for entire nights.
Look, I haven't slept, Villefort said, pointing to his untouched bed; pain does not overwhelm me, I've not gone to bed for two nights; but in return, look at my desk; have I written, my God!
during these two days and two nights!...

sentences: The two men continued to play; from time to time, a stronger gust from the hurricane shook the door, made the walls tremble, and the two drinkers looked up as if someone were about to enter.
Then Mathurin took the liter and filled Jérémie's glass.
But suddenly, the clock hanging on the counter struck midnight.
Its hoarse chime sounded like a clash of pots and pans, and the strikes resonated for a long time, with a metallic sound.

Mathurin immediately got up, like a sailor whose shift is over: The other moved with more difficulty, steadied himself by leaning on the table; then he made his way to the door and opened it while his companion turned off the lamp.

When they were in the street, Mathurin locked up the shop; then he said: Jérémie took three steps, then swayed, stretched out his hands, found a wall that supported him upright, and started moving again, stumbling.

At times, a gust of wind, rushing into the narrow street, pushed him forward, made him run a few steps; then when the violence of the storm ceased, he stopped abruptly, having lost his prop, and began to wobble again on his drunken, unsteady legs.
He was instinctively heading towards his home, like birds returning to their nests.
Finally, he recognized his door and began to feel around for the lock to insert the key.
He couldn't find the hole and cursed under his breath.

Then he banged on it with his fists, calling for his wife to come help him: He was no longer moving, stunned with fear, bewildered, in a devilish terror, haunted by all the mysterious things of the darkness, and he waited a long time without daring to make a move.
But, as he saw that nothing was stirring anymore, a bit of reason returned to him, the muddled reasoning of a drunkard.
And he sat down, very quietly.
He waited a long time again, and finally gathering his courage, he spoke: Then, all of a sudden, a doubt crossed his clouded mind, an indecisive doubt, a vague suspicion.
He did not move; he remained there, sitting on the ground, in the dark, searching for his thoughts, clinging to incomplete and stumbling reflections like his feet.

sentences: It was high time for Thomas Black.
Five more minutes, and the astronomer would have been frozen in place!
On December 2nd, the intensity of the cold had decreased.
These parhelion phenomena were a symptom that a meteorologist could not have mistaken.

They noted the presence of a certain amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, and indeed, the barometer dropped slightly, while the thermometer rose to fifteen degrees above zero (–90 degrees Celsius).
Although this cold still seemed harsh in any region of the temperate zone, professional winterers were handling it easily.
Moreover, the atmosphere was calm.
Lieutenant Hobson, having observed that the upper layers of icy snow had softened, ordered the clearing of the outer surroundings of the enclosure.
Mac Nap and his men undertook this task with courage, and within a few days it was successfully completed.
At the same time, they uncovered the buried traps, and they were reset.
Numerous tracks proved that fur-bearing game was gathering around the cape, and with the ground offering no food, they would easily be lured into the traps.
Following the advice of the hunter Marbre, they also built a reindeer snare, using the method of the Eskimos.
It was a pit about ten feet wide in all directions and about twelve feet deep.
A board acting as a seesaw, which could lift itself by its own weight, covered it in such a way as to completely conceal it.
The animal, attracted by the grasses and branches placed at the end of the board, was inevitably plunged into the pit, from which it could no longer escape.
It is understood that, with this seesaw system, the snare reset automatically, and that once a reindeer was caught, others could fall into it in turn.
Marbre encountered no other difficulty in setting up his snare than drilling through very hard ground; but he was quite surprised.
and Jasper Hobson was no less so
when the pickaxe, after having gone through four to five feet of earth and sand, encountered below a layer of snow, as hard as rock, which seemed to be very thick.

"It is necessary, said Lieutenant Hobson, after observing this geological arrangement, that this part of the coastline must have been subjected, many years ago, to extreme cold for a very long period; then, the sands and earth must have gradually covered the ice mass, presumably spread over a bed of granite.

sentences: The plan for this double kidnapping was therefore set, and it seemed to have every chance of success.

Unless, during the remaining two hours of daylight, it was noticed that the key was missing from the park gate and that the locks had been drawn, Captain Spade and his men were assured of being able to enter the Healthful-House park.
It should be noted, moreover, that, with the exception of Thomas Roch, who was under special surveillance, the other residents of the establishment were not subject to any such measures.
They occupied the pavilions or the rooms of the main buildings located in the upper part of the park.

Everything suggested that Thomas Roch and the guard Gaydon, caught off guard and unable to mount any serious resistance or even call for help, would fall victim to the abduction that Captain Spade was about to attempt on behalf of Count d'Artigas.
Count d'Artigas and Captain Spade boarded the dinghy.
Four oars quickly took them to the schooner, where they climbed up the side ladder.
Count d'Artigas immediately returned to his cabin at the back, while Captain Spade went to the front to give his final orders.
Arriving near the forecastle, he leaned over the starboard rail and searched the water for an object that was floating a few fathoms away.
It was a small buoy, trembling in the ripples of the ebb tide of the Neuze.
Night was gradually falling.
Towards the left bank of the winding river, the indistinct silhouette of New-Berne began to blend into the background.
The houses stood out in black against a horizon still marked by a long streak of fire at the edge of the western clouds.
On the opposite side, the sky faded into some thick vapors.
But it did not seem that rain was to be feared, and these vapors remained in the higher regions of the sky.

Around seven o'clock, the first lights of New-Berne twinkled at various levels of the houses, while the glimmers from the lower quarters reflected in long zigzags, barely flickering just below the banks, as the breeze softened with the evening.

The fishing boats were gently making their way back to the port's coves, some seeking a last breath with their billowing sails, others propelled by their oars, whose sharp and rhythmic strokes spread out into the distance.

Two steamers passed by, shooting jets of sparks from their double smokestacks crowned with black smoke, beating the waters with their powerful paddles, while the machine's balance swung up and down above the spar deck, neighing like a sea monster.

sentences: Then you will be known to be abandoned, and you will be believed to be poor; for I alone know your financial situation and I am ready to give you my accounts as a loyal partner." The baroness, pale and horrified, listened to this speech with as much dread and despair as Debray had shown calmness and indifference in delivering it.
"Abandoned!
she repeated, oh!
so abandoned...
Yes, you are right, sir, and no one will doubt my abandonment." These were the only words that this woman, so proud and so violently in love, could respond to Debray.
"But rich, very rich indeed," Debray continued, pulling out some papers from his wallet and spreading them on the table.
"Madam," said Debray, "it has been about six months since we became partners.
"It was in April of this year that our partnership was formed.
"In July, we added one hundred seventy thousand francs; that is, as you know, the month of Spanish bonds.

"In August, we lost three hundred thousand francs at the beginning of the month; but by the 15th we had recovered, and by the end we had taken our revenge; for our accounts, settled from the day of our partnership until yesterday when I closed them, show an asset of two million four hundred thousand francs, which means one hundred twenty thousand francs for each of us.
"Now," Debray continued, consulting his notebook with the method and calmness of a stockbroker, "we find eighty thousand francs for the compound interest on this sum that has remained in my hands.
--But, interrupted the baroness, what do these interests mean, since you have never put this money to use?
I beg your pardon, madam, said Debray coldly; I had your authority to act on your behalf, and I made use of your powers.
So that's forty thousand francs in interest for your share, plus the one hundred thousand francs of initial investment, which means three hundred and forty thousand francs for your portion.

Now, madam, Debray continued, I took the precaution of mobilizing your money the day before yesterday, not long ago, as you can see, and it would seem that I suspected I would soon be called to render my accounts to you.
Your money is there, half in banknotes, half in bearer bonds.

sentences: Besides, Rodolphe added, perhaps, from the world's perspective, one is right?
Well then!
he said, don't you know that there are souls that are constantly tormented?
They need both dreams and action, the purest passions, the most intense pleasures, and thus one throws oneself into all sorts of fantasies and madness.
Then she looked at him as one gazes at a traveler who has passed through extraordinary lands, and she continued: "And that is what you have understood, the Counselor said.
You, farmers and workers of the countryside; you, peaceful pioneers of a work entirely of civilization!
you, men of progress and morality!
you have understood, I say, that political storms are indeed more fearsome than the disorders of the atmosphere..."
One day, he said again, all of a sudden, when one had almost given up hope.
Then horizons begin to open up; it's like a voice shouting, 'There he is!' You feel the need to confide your life to this person; to give them everything, to sacrifice everything for them!
You can't explain it; you just sense it.
You've glimpsed each other in your dreams.
(And he was looking at her.) Finally, there it is, the treasure you've searched for so long, right in front of you; it shines, it sparkles.
Yet you still have doubts; you don't dare to believe it; you're left dazzled, as if emerging from darkness into light.
And as he finished these words, Rodolphe added a gesture to his phrase.
He ran his hand over his face, like a man who is dizzy; then he let it fall onto Emma's.
She withdrew hers.
But the Counselor was still reading: 'And who would be surprised by this, gentlemen?
Only someone who would be blind enough, deeply immersed (I don't hesitate to say), deeply immersed in the prejudices of another age to still misunderstand the spirit of the agricultural populations.
Where, indeed, can one find more patriotism than in the countryside, more dedication to the public cause, more intelligence in a word?

And I don't mean, gentlemen, this superficial intelligence, a vain ornament of idle minds, but rather this deep and moderate intelligence, which above all else seeks to pursue useful goals, thereby contributing to the good of each individual, to the common improvement, and to the support of the states, the fruit of respect for the laws and the practice of duties...'

sentences: O Aceste, if the misfortune of young Télémaque, who has never fought against the Trojans, cannot touch you, at least let your own interest touch you.

The knowledge I have gained about omens and the will of the gods tells me that before three days have passed, you will be attacked by barbarian peoples, who come like a torrent from the heights of the mountains, to flood your city and ravage your entire land.
Hurry to prevent them; put your people under arms, and don't waste a moment bringing the rich herds you have in the countryside inside your walls.
If my prediction is false, you will be free to sacrifice us in three days; if, on the other hand, it is true, remember that one should not take the life of those from whom one receives it.
Aceste was astonished by these words, which Mentor spoke to him with a confidence he had never found in any man.
I see well, he replied, O stranger, that the gods, who have dealt so poorly with you in all the gifts of fortune, have granted you a wisdom that is more valuable than all prosperity.
At the same time, he delayed the sacrifice and quickly gave the necessary orders to prevent the attack that Mentor had threatened him with.
All around, there were only trembling women, bent old men, small children with tears in their eyes, retreating into the city.
The lowing cattle and bleating sheep came in droves, leaving the lush pastures, unable to find enough barns to take shelter.

It was a cacophony of people pushing against each other, who could not hear one another, mistaking a stranger for a friend in the chaos, and running without knowing where their steps were leading them.
But the leaders of the city, believing themselves wiser than the others, imagined that Mentor was an impostor who had made a false prediction to save his life.
Mentor displayed in his eyes a boldness that astonishes the proudest warriors.
He took a shield, a helmet, a sword, a spear; he organized Aceste's soldiers; he marched at their head and advanced in good order towards the enemies.
Aceste, although full of courage, could only follow him from a distance in his old age.
I follow him more closely, but I cannot match his valor.
His armor resembled, in battle, the immortal aegis.
Death ran from rank to rank everywhere under his blows.

Like a lion from Numidia, devoured by cruel hunger, who enters a flock of weak sheep, he tears apart, he slaughters, he swims in blood; and the shepherds, far from helping the flock, flee, trembling, to escape his fury.

sentences: And what does one die of in prison when one dies at thirty, if not from the prison itself? What's strange about all this, the abbé replied, is that Dantès, on his deathbed, while kissing the feet of Christ, always swore to me that he was unaware of the true cause of his captivity.
It's true, it's true, murmured Caderousse, he couldn't have known; no, Monsieur l'abbé, he wasn't lying, the poor little one.

That's why he entrusted me with clarifying his misfortune, which he had never been able to clarify himself, and to restore his memory, if that memory had been tarnished in any way.” And the abbé's gaze, becoming more and more fixed, devoured the almost dark expression that appeared on Caderousse's face.
A wealthy Englishman, the abbé continued, his companion in misfortune, who was released from prison during the second Restoration, possessed a diamond of great value.
Upon leaving prison, he wanted to leave Dantès, who had cared for him like a brother during an illness, a token of his gratitude by leaving him this diamond.

Dantès, instead of using it to seduce his jailers, who could have taken it and betrayed him afterward, always kept it safely for the case that he would be released from prison; for if he were released, his fortune was assured by the sale alone of this diamond.
So it was, as you say, asked Caderousse with eager eyes, a diamond of great value?
Everything is relative, the abbé replied; of great value to Edmond; this diamond was valued at fifty thousand francs.
Fifty thousand francs!
said Caderousse; but was it really as big as a walnut?
No, not quite, said the abbé, but you'll see for yourself, because I have it with me.
The abbé took a small black leather box from his pocket, opened it, and made the dazzling wonder set in a beautifully crafted ring shine before Caderousse's dazzled eyes.
And he closed the case and put the diamond back in his pocket, which continued to sparkle in Caderousse's mind.
But how do you find yourself in possession of this diamond, Monsieur l'abbé?
asked Caderousse.
So Edmond made you his heir?

sentences: A few moments later, the three travel companions were settled in the projectile, having securely fastened the opening plate from the inside, and the mouth of the Columbiad, completely cleared, opened freely to the sky.
Nicholl, Barbicane, and Michel Ardan were definitively sealed in their metal wagon.

The moon was advancing across a sky of crystal clarity, extinguishing the twinkling lights of the stars in its wake; it was then traversing the constellation of Gemini and was almost halfway between the horizon and the zenith.
Everyone could easily understand that they were aiming ahead of the target, just as a hunter aims ahead of the hare he wants to catch.
A terrifying silence hung over the entire scene.
Not a breath of wind on the earth!
Not a breath in their chests!
Their hearts dared not beat.
All the startled gazes were fixed on the gaping maw of the Columbiad.
Murchison was watching the needle of his chronometer.
There were barely forty seconds left before the moment of departure would sound, and each of those seconds felt like a century.
At the twentieth second, there was a universal tremor, and it occurred to the crowd that the daring travelers locked in the projectile were also counting those dreadful seconds!
Isolated cries escaped: Immediately, Murchison, pressing the switch of the device, restored the current and sent the electric spark to the bottom of the Columbiad.
An appalling, unheard-of, superhuman detonation occurred instantly, unlike anything that could be imagined, neither the flashes of lightning nor the roar of eruptions.
A massive jet of fire erupted from the bowels of the earth like from a crater.
The earth heaved, and only a few people could momentarily glimpse the projectile slicing triumphantly through the air amidst the blazing vapors.

At the moment when the incandescent jet rose to the sky to a prodigious height, this outburst of flames illuminated the entire state of Florida, and for an immeasurable instant, day replaced night over a vast expanse of land.
This immense plume of fire was seen from a hundred miles out at sea in the Gulf as well as in the Atlantic, and more than one ship captain noted the appearance of this gigantic meteor in his logbook.

sentences: In his name, adultery is stigmatized and condemned, not because it is a recklessness that leads to disillusionment and regret, but because it is a crime against the family.

You stigmatize and condemn suicide, not because it is madness — the madman is not responsible — nor because it is cowardice, as it sometimes requires a certain physical courage, but because it shows contempt for duty in a life that is ending, and is a cry of disbelief in a life that is beginning.

This morality stigmatizes realistic literature, not because it depicts passions — hatred, vengeance, love; the world revolves around these, and art must portray them — but when it depicts them without restraint or measure.
Art without rules is no longer art; it is like a woman who would shed all her clothing.
Imposing the sole rule of public decency on art does not enslave it, but honors it.
One only grows with a rule.
Here, gentlemen, are the principles we profess; here is a doctrine we defend with conviction.
Gentlemen, Mr.
Gustave Flaubert is accused before you of having written a bad book, of having, in this book, outraged public morality and religion.
Mr.

Gustave Flaubert is here with me; he asserts before you that he has written an honest book; he asserts before you that the thought of his book, from the first line to the last, is a moral and religious thought, and that if it were not distorted (we have seen for a moment what great talent can do to distort a thought), it would be (and it will soon become again) for you what it has already been for the readers of the book: an eminently moral and religious thought that can be expressed in these words: the encouragement of virtue through the horror of vice.
I bring you here the affirmation of Mr.

Gustave Flaubert, and I boldly place it alongside the indictment of the public prosecutor, for this affirmation is serious; it is serious because of the person who made it, and it is serious because of the circumstances that presided over the execution of the book that I am about to present to you.
I told you that Mr.
Gustave Flaubert was a serious and grave man.
His studies, in accordance with the nature of his mind, have been serious and broad.
They have encompassed not only all branches of literature but also law.
Mr.
Flaubert is a man who did not content himself with the observations that his environment could provide; he has inquired into other environments.

sentences: After conferring with Sergeant Long, Jasper Hobson decided to grant a day of rest to his companions at this location.
The actual exploration, which was supposed to allow the lieutenant to identify a suitable site for establishing a trading post, was truly about to begin.
The Company had instructed its agent to remain as far north as possible above the seventieth parallel, and along the shores of the Glacial Sea.
However, to fulfill his mandate, the lieutenant could only search to the west for a point that was equally high in latitude and belonged to the American continent.

To the east, in fact, all these fragmented lands are more part of the Arctic territories, except perhaps for Boothia, which is clearly cut by the seventieth parallel, but whose geographical configuration is still very uncertain.
Taking longitude and latitude into account, Jasper Hobson, after marking his position on the map, saw that he was still over a hundred miles below the seventieth degree.

But beyond Cape Kruzenstern, the coast, running northeast, sharply exceeded the seventieth parallel, roughly at the one hundred thirtieth meridian, and precisely at the height of Cape Bathurst, indicated as a meeting point by Captain Craventy.
So it was this point that needed to be reached, and that is where the new fort would be built, if the location offered the necessary resources for a trading post.
"There, Sergeant Long," said the lieutenant, pointing to the map of the polar regions, "there we will be in the conditions imposed on us by the Company.
In this location, the sea, free for a large part of the year, will allow ships from the Bering Strait to reach the fort, supply it, and export its products.
--Not to mention," added Sergeant Long, "that since they will have established themselves beyond the seventieth parallel, our men will be entitled to double pay!
--That goes without saying," replied the lieutenant, "and I believe they will accept it without complaint.
Well, my lieutenant, we only have to leave for Cape Bathurst now," the sergeant simply said.
However, since a day of rest was granted, the departure only took place the next day, June 6.
This second part of the journey was supposed to be and indeed turned out to be completely different from the first.
The arrangements that had governed the sleds' movement until now had not been maintained.
Each team went at its own pace.
We traveled short distances, stopped at every corner of the coast, and most often walked.
Only one recommendation had been made to his companions by Lieutenant Hobson,
the recommendation not to stray more than three miles from the shore and to regroup with the detachment twice a day, at noon and in the evening.
When night fell, we camped.
The weather at that time was consistently nice, and the temperature was quite high, as it averaged fifty-nine degrees Fahrenheit above zero (15° Celsius above zero).
above zero).
Two or three times, brief snowstorms occurred, but they did not last long, and the temperature was not significantly affected.

sentences: Protésilas listened to all these praises with a dry, distracted, and disdainful air, like a man who knows he deserves even greater ones and who is too gracious to allow himself to be praised.
There was a flatterer who took the liberty of speaking to him in his ear to say something amusing against the authority that Mentor was trying to establish.
Protésilas smiled; the whole assembly immediately burst into laughter, although most could not yet know what had been said.
But Protésilas soon resumed his severe and haughty demeanor, and everyone fell back into fear and silence.

Several nobles were looking for the moment when Protésilas might turn to them and listen: they appeared moved and embarrassed; they had favors to ask of him; their pleading posture spoke for them; they seemed as submissive as a mother at the feet of the altars when she asks the gods for the healing of her only son.
Everyone seemed pleased, touched, filled with admiration for Protésilas, although all harbored in their hearts an unrelenting rage against him.
At that moment, Hégésippe entered, seized Protésilas's sword, and declared to him, on behalf of the king, that he was going to take him to the island of Samos.
At these words, all the arrogance of this favorite fell away, like a rock detaching from the top of a steep mountain.

There he was, trembling and troubled, throwing himself at Hégésippe's feet; he cried, hesitated, stammered, trembled; he embraced the knees of this man whom he had not deigned to honor with a glance just an hour before.
All those who had been praising him, seeing him lost and without resources, turned their flattery into merciless insults.
Hégésippe did not want to give him time to say his last goodbyes to his family or to take certain secret writings.
Everything was seized and taken to the king.
Timocrate was arrested at the same time: and his surprise was extreme; for he believed that being at odds with Protésilas, he could not be caught up in his downfall.
They departed on a ship that had been prepared.
They arrived at Samos.
Hégésippe left these two unfortunate men there; and, to add to their misfortune, he left them together.

There, they furiously reproached each other for the crimes they had committed, which were the cause of their downfall: they found themselves without hope of seeing Salente again, condemned to live far from their wives and children; I do not mention their friends, for they had none.
They were being taken to an unknown land, where they would have no other means of living than their labor, they who had spent so many years in luxury and splendor.
Like two wild beasts, they were always ready to tear each other apart.

sentences: Indeed, just at the moment of this debacle, the temperature had dropped several degrees.
A thick fog soon enveloped all these areas of the Arctic Ocean, but it was not an ordinary fog.
The ground was covered, at its surface, with a white crust, very distinct from the frost.
This was nothing more than a water vapor that freezes after it precipitates.

The very fine particles that made up this fog clung to the trees, shrubs, and the walls of the fort, to everything that jutted out, and soon formed a thick layer, adorned with prismatic or pyramidal fibers, the tips of which pointed into the wind.
Jasper Hobson then recognized this meteorological phenomenon, which whalers and winterers have often noted appearing in the spring in polar regions.

"This is not fog," he said to his companions, "it's a frost-rime, a frozen mist, a dense vapor that remains in a state of complete freezing." However, whether it was fog or frozen mist, the appearance of this meteor was nonetheless regrettable, as it occupied a height of at least a hundred feet above sea level, and so complete was its opacity that, placed three steps apart, two people could not see each other.
The winterers' disappointment was great.
It seemed that nature wanted to spare them no trouble.

It was at the moment when the thaw was occurring, when the drifting island was about to break free from the bonds that had chained it for so many months, and finally when its movements were to be monitored more closely, that this fog came to obstruct all observation!
And it was like this for four days!
The frost-rime did not dissipate until April 15.
In the morning, a violent southerly breeze tore it apart and annihilated it.
The sun was shining.
Lieutenant Hobson threw himself on his instruments.
He took readings, and the result of his calculations for the current coordinates of the island was this: Kalumah was right.
The island of Victoria, caught by the Bering current, was drifting south.
The winterers were finally getting closer to the more frequented areas of the Bering Sea.
They no longer had to fear being swept north.
It was now just a matter of monitoring the island's movement and estimating its speed, which, due to obstacles, was likely to be quite uneven.
This was what Jasper Hobson meticulously occupied himself with, taking readings of the sun and stars in turn.

The very next day, April 16, after observation, he calculated that if the speed remained uniform, the island of Victoria would reach the Arctic Circle around the beginning of May, from which it was separated by no more than four degrees of latitude.

sentences: She couldn't bear the affront that this wretch caused us, and she asked me for permission to travel.
No, with a relative...
But we are no less losing her, dear Eugénie; for I doubt that with the character I know her to have, she will ever agree to return to France!
What do you want, my dear baron, said Monte-Cristo, family troubles, troubles that would be crushing for a poor devil whose child is his entire fortune, but bearable for a millionaire.

Philosophers may say what they want, practical men will always contradict them on this: money consoles for many things; and you, you must be consoled more quickly than anyone else, if you acknowledge the virtue of this sovereign balm: you, the king of finance, the intersection point of all powers.” Danglars cast a sidelong glance at the count to see if he was joking or speaking seriously.
Yes, he said, the fact is that if fortune consoles, I must be consoled: I am rich.

So rich, my dear baron, that your fortune resembles the Pyramids; even if one wanted to demolish them, one wouldn't dare; if one dared, one couldn't.” “That reminds me, he said, that when you entered, I was in the process of making five small bonds; I had already signed two; would you allow me to make the other three?
There was a moment of silence, during which the banker’s pen could be heard scratching, while Monte-Cristo looked at the gilded moldings on the ceiling.
Bonds from Spain, said Monte-Cristo, bonds from Haiti, bonds from Naples?
No, said Danglars, laughing his self-satisfied laugh, bearer bonds, bonds on the Bank of France.

Here, he added, Mr. Count, you who are the emperor of finance, just as I am the king, have you seen many pieces of paper of this size worth a million each?” Monte-Cristo took in his hand, as if to weigh them, the five pieces of paper that Danglars proudly presented to him, and read: “May it please Mr.
the Regent of the Bank to pay to my order, and on the funds deposited by me, the sum of one million, value in account.
One, two, three, four, five, said Monte-Cristo; five million!
Goodness!
Look at how you go on, Lord Crésus!

sentences: Indeed, the storm could be heard howling around the house.
The snow that was falling, already almost solidified, crackled against the frost on the windows.
High-pitched whistles, passing through the joints of the doors and windows, sometimes rose to the limit of audible sounds.
Then, a great silence fell.
Nature seemed to catch its breath, and once again, the gust unleashed itself with terrible force.
You could feel the house trembling on its stilts, the boards creaking, the beams groaning.
A stranger, less accustomed than the fort's inhabitants to these atmospheric convulsions, might have wondered if the storm would carry away this assembly of planks and beams.
But Captain Craventy's guests were little concerned about the gust, and even outside, they would not have been more frightened than those little birds that play in the midst of storms.
However, regarding these guests, a few observations need to be made.
The gathering included about a hundred individuals of both sexes; but only two
--two women
did not belong to the usual staff of Fort-Reliance.
This staff consisted of Captain Craventy, Lieutenant Jasper Hobson, Sergeant Long, Corporal Joliffe, and about sixty soldiers or employees of the Company.

Some of them were married, including Corporal Joliffe, a happy husband of a lively and alert Canadian woman, a certain Mac Nap, a Scot married to a Scottish woman, and John Raë, who had recently taken a wife from the local Indian women.
All these people, regardless of rank—officers, employees, or soldiers—were being entertained that evening by Captain Craventy.
It should be noted here that the Company's staff did not provide their contingent to the party alone.
The nearby forts,
and in these distant lands, one is neighbors at a hundred miles away,
had accepted Captain Craventy's invitation.
Many employees or factors had come from Fort-Provence or Fort-Resolution, which belonged to the Slave Lake district, and even from Fort-Chipewan and Fort-Liard located further south.
It was a rare entertainment, an unexpected distraction, that these recluses, these exiles, half-lost in the solitude of the hyperborean regions, eagerly sought.

sentences: After dinner, the Count of Monte Cristo was announced.
The young men hadn't seen him for two days.
A matter, Master Pastrini had said, had called him to Civita-Vecchia.
He had left the night before and had only just returned an hour ago.
He had learned that the two friends had wanted to get a box at the Argentina theater, and that he had told them everything was booked.
As a result, he was bringing them the key to his box; at least, that was the apparent reason for his visit.

Franz and Albert hesitated a bit, claiming they were afraid of depriving him of it, but the Count replied that since he was going to the Palli theater that evening, his box at the Argentina would be wasted if they didn't take advantage of it.
Franz had gradually gotten used to the Count's pallor, which had struck him so much the first time he saw him.
He couldn't help but acknowledge the beauty of his stern face, of which the pallor was the only flaw or perhaps the main quality.
A true hero of Byron, Franz could not, we won't say see him, but only think of him without picturing that dark face on Manfred's shoulders or under Lara's cap.

He had that furrow in his forehead which indicates the constant presence of a bitter thought; he had those burning eyes that read deeply into souls; he had that haughty and mocking lip that gives the words that escape it a particular character that makes them deeply engraved in the memory of those who listen.
The Count was no longer young; he was at least forty, and yet it was perfectly clear that he was destined to surpass the young men he would encounter.
In reality, it was that, by a final resemblance to the fantastic heroes of the English poet, the Count seemed to possess the gift of fascination.
Albert was overflowing with happiness about the joy he and Franz had experienced in meeting such a man.
Franz was less enthusiastic, yet he was still under the influence that any superior man exerts on the minds of those around him.

He was thinking about the plan that the Count had already expressed two or three times to go to Paris, and he had no doubt that with his eccentric character, his distinctive face, and his colossal fortune, the Count would make a great impression there.

sentences: Only a new element of noise and movement had mixed into this crowd: the sellers of moccoli had just entered the scene.
The moccoletto is like life: man has only found one way to pass it on; and this way he receives from God.
But he has discovered a thousand ways to take it away; it is true that for this supreme operation the devil has somewhat helped him.
But who will describe the thousand means invented to extinguish the moccoletto, the gigantic bellows, the monstrous extinguishers, the superhuman fans?
Everyone hurried to buy moccoletti, Franz and Albert like the others.
After ten minutes, fifty thousand lights sparkled, descending from the palace of Venice to the Place du Peuple, and rising from the Place du Peuple to the palace of Venice.
You cannot imagine this sight if you have not seen it.
Imagine all the stars detaching from the sky and mingling on earth in a crazy dance.
All of this accompanied by cries like no human ear has ever heard elsewhere on the surface of the globe.
It is especially at this moment that there is no longer any social distinction.
The facchino clings to the prince, the prince to the Trastevere, the Trastevere to the bourgeois, each one blowing, extinguishing, relighting.
If old Aeolus were to appear at this moment, he would be proclaimed king of the moccoli, and Aquilon the presumptive heir to the crown.

This crazy and flamboyant race lasted about two hours; the street of the Cours was lit up as if it were broad daylight, and you could make out the features of the spectators up to the third and fourth floors.
Every five minutes, Albert checked his watch; finally, it showed seven o'clock.
The two friends were just at the height of the via dei Pontefici; Albert jumped down from the carriage, his moccoletto in hand.

Two or three masks tried to approach him to extinguish it or snatch it away, but, like a skilled boxer, Albert sent them rolling ten paces away from him one after the other as he continued his way towards the church of San-Giacomo.
The steps were crowded with curious onlookers and masks who were struggling to snatch the torch from his hands.

Franz watched Albert closely and saw him place his foot on the first step; then almost immediately a mask, wearing the well-known costume of the peasant with a bouquet, reached out his arm and, without him resisting this time, took the moccoletto from him.

sentences: But what a detestable maxim it is to believe that one's safety can only be found in the oppression of one's people!

Not educating them, not guiding them towards virtue, never making them love you, pushing them through terror to despair, putting them in the dreadful position of either never being able to breathe freely or shaking off the yoke of your tyrannical domination; is that the true way to rule without trouble?
Is that the true path to glory?
After this speech, Idoménée, persuaded by Mentor, hurried to distribute the vacant lands, to fill them with all the useless artisans, and to execute everything that had been decided.
He reserved only for the masons the lands he had destined for them, which they could only cultivate after finishing their work in the city.
At the same time, the city and the surrounding villages were filled with beautiful youth who had long languished in misery and who had not dared to marry for fear of increasing their woes.
When they saw that Idoménée was taking on feelings of humanity and wanted to be their father, they no longer feared hunger and the other scourges with which heaven afflicts the earth.
All that could be heard were cries of joy, the songs of shepherds and laborers celebrating their weddings.
One would have thought to see the god Pan with a crowd of Satyrs and Fauns mingling among the nymphs, dancing to the sound of the flute in the shade of the woods.
Everything was calm and cheerful; but the joy was moderate, and the pleasures served only to relieve the long labors; they were more vivid and pure because of it.
The elders, astonished to see what they had not dared to hope for after such a long age, wept from an excess of joy mixed with tenderness; they raised their trembling hands to heaven.
'Bless, they said, oh great Jupiter, the king who resembles you, and who is the greatest gift you have given us.
He was born for the good of mankind; grant him all the blessings we receive from him.
Our descendants, born from these marriages he favors, will owe him everything, even their birth; and he will truly be the father of all his subjects.
The young men and young women they married only expressed their joy by singing the praises of the one from whom this sweet joy had come.
Their mouths, and even more their hearts, were constantly filled with his name.
They felt happy to see him; they feared losing him: his loss would have been the desolation of every family.

sentences: The two forbidden women looked at each other; and Mrs. Lefèvre said in a sour tone, "I can't possibly feed all the dogs that will be thrown in there.
We must give it up." And, suffocated by the thought of all those dogs living at her expense, she left, even taking what was left of the bread, which she started to eat as she walked.
Rose followed her, wiping her eyes with the corner of her blue apron.
"Great misfortunes hardly sadden me," said Jean Bridelle, an old bachelor who was considered a skeptic.
I have seen the war up close: I stepped over bodies without pity.

The harsh brutalities of nature or men can make us cry out in horror or indignation, but they do not give us that pang in the heart, that shiver that runs down your back at the sight of certain little distressing things.
The most violent pain one can feel, of course, is the loss of a child for a mother, and the loss of a mother for a man.
That is violent, terrible, it upsets and tears apart; but we heal from these catastrophes like from large bleeding wounds.

Now, certain encounters, certain glimpses, certain secret sorrows, certain treacheries of fate, which stir up in us a whole world of painful thoughts, which suddenly open before us the mysterious door of moral sufferings, complicated, incurable, all the deeper for seeming benign, all the more acute for seeming almost elusive, all the more tenacious for seeming artificial, leave us with a trail of sadness in our souls, a taste of bitterness, a sensation of disenchantment that takes us a long time to shake off.
I have always had before my eyes two or three things that others surely would not have noticed, and which have entered me like long, thin, incurable stings.
You might not understand the emotion that has remained with me from these fleeting impressions.
I will only tell you one.
It is very old, but as vivid as if it were yesterday.
It may be that only my imagination has borne the cost of my tenderness.
I am fifty years old.
I was young then and I was studying law.
A little sad, a little dreamy, steeped in a melancholic philosophy, I did not care much for noisy cafés, boisterous friends, or silly girls.
I would get up early; and one of my greatest pleasures was to stroll alone, around eight in the morning, in the Luxembourg nursery.

sentences: His intention was to settle in this last city, which he had been assured was a city of pleasures.

He had barely traveled three leagues into the Roman countryside when night began to fall; Danglars had not thought he would leave so late, otherwise he would have stayed; he asked the postilion how far it was to the next town.
Danglars still felt a remnant of the well-being he had experienced the day before, which had given him such a good night's sleep.
He was comfortably stretched out in a good English coach with double springs; he felt himself being carried along by the gallop of two fine horses; he knew the relay was seven leagues long.
What to do when you are a banker and have happily gone bankrupt?

Danglars thought for ten minutes about his wife who remained in Paris, another ten minutes about his daughter traveling the world with Mlle d'Armilly, he spent another ten minutes on his creditors and how he would use their money; then, having nothing left to think about, he closed his eyes and fell asleep.
Danglars continued to sleep, telling himself that he would have plenty of time to wake up at the relay.
The carriage stopped; Danglars thought he was finally reaching the long-desired destination.

He opened his eyes, looked through the window, expecting to find himself in the middle of some city, or at least some village; but he saw nothing but a kind of isolated hovel, and three or four men moving about like shadows.

Danglars waited a moment for the postilion who had finished his relay to come and ask him for the fare; he planned to take the opportunity to ask his new driver for some information, but the horses were unhitched and replaced without anyone coming to ask the traveler for money.
Danglars, surprised, opened the door; but a strong hand immediately pushed it back, and the carriage rolled on.
It was still some romantic Italian that Danglars had remembered when his daughter sang duets with Prince Cavalcanti.
"Hey, friend!
where are we going then?"
he said, sticking his head through the opening.

He obeyed, not without anxiety; and as this anxiety grew minute by minute, after a few moments his mind, instead of the emptiness we noted when he set out, which had led to his sleep, his mind, let us say, was filled with a multitude of thoughts more than capable of keeping a traveler awake, especially a traveler in Danglars' situation.

sentences: You have already understood, gentlemen: the device I am describing to you is simply a gas burner using oxygen and hydrogen, whose heat exceeds that of forge fires.
From the lower part of my balloon, which is hermetically sealed, two tubes emerge separated by a small gap.
One originates in the upper layers of hydrogen gas, the other in the lower layers.
These two pipes are equipped at intervals with strong rubber joints, which allow them to adapt to the oscillations of the aerostat.
They both descend to the basket and disappear into a cylindrical iron box, which is called a heat box.
It is closed at both ends by two strong disks made of the same metal.

The pipe coming from the lower region of the balloon enters this cylindrical box through the bottom disk; it penetrates there and then takes the form of a helical coil whose overlapping rings occupy almost the entire height of the box.
Before exiting, the coil goes into a small cone, whose concave base, shaped like a spherical cap, is directed downward.
It is through the top of this cone that the second pipe exits, and it goes, as I told you, into the upper layers of the balloon.
The spherical cap of the small cone is made of platinum.
This is to prevent it from melting under the action of the burner.
For the burner is placed on the bottom of the iron box, in the middle of the helical coil, and the tip of its flame will slightly touch this cap.
You know, gentlemen, what a radiator designed to heat rooms is.
You know how it works.
The air in the room is forced to pass through the pipes, and it is returned at a higher temperature.
Now, what I have just described to you is, in fact, just a radiator.
Indeed, what will happen?
Once the burner is lit, the hydrogen in the coil and the concave cone heats up and quickly rises through the pipe that leads it to the upper regions of the aerostat.

A vacuum forms below, and it draws the gas from the lower regions, which in turn heats up and is continuously replaced; thus, an extremely rapid current of gas is established in the pipes and the coil, exiting the balloon, returning to it, and constantly overheating.

sentences: Indeed, half a dozen of these animals had managed to breach the palisade, and, attracted by the smoke, they were approaching the house.
As soon as Jasper Hobson was alerted to the presence of these fearsome carnivores, he ordered the corridor window to be barricaded from the inside.
That was the only exit that was passable, and once that opening was blocked, it seemed impossible for the bears to enter the house.

The window was therefore closed with strong bars that the carpenter Mac Nap secured firmly, after having made, however, a narrow opening that allowed observation of the movements of these troublesome visitors outside.
"And now," said the master carpenter, "these gentlemen won't enter without our permission.
So we have plenty of time to hold a war council.
--Well, Mr. Hobson," said Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, "nothing has been lacking in our wintering!
After the cold, the bears.
--Not 'after,'" replied Lieutenant Hobson, "but, more seriously, 'during' the cold, and a cold that prevents us from venturing outside!
So I don't know how we can get rid of these wicked beasts.
But they will lose patience, I suppose, replied the traveler, and they will leave just as they came!" "You don't know these animals, madam," he replied.
This harsh winter has starved them, and they will not leave the place unless they are forced to!
Yes and no, replied the lieutenant.
I know these bears won't enter the house; but as for us, I don't know how we'll get out if it becomes necessary!” Having said this, Jasper Hobson returned to the window.
Meanwhile, Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, Madge, and the other women, gathered around the sergeant, were listening to this brave soldier, who was addressing the 'bear issue' as an experienced man.

Time and again, Sergeant Long had dealt with these carnivores, which are frequently encountered even in the southern territories, but it was under conditions where they could be successfully attacked.
Here, the besieged were trapped, and the cold prevented them from attempting any sortie.
All day long, they closely monitored the comings and goings of the bears.
From time to time, one of these animals would come and rest its large head near the window, and a dull growl of anger could be heard.
Lieutenant Hobson and Sergeant Long held a council, and they decided that if the bears did not leave the area, they would make some loopholes in the walls of the house to shoot them.

But it was also decided that they would wait a day or two before using this method of attack, as Jasper Hobson was not keen on establishing any communication between the outside temperature and the already low temperature inside the room.
The seal oil, which was being put into the stoves, had solidified into such hard ice blocks that they had to be broken with an axe.
