sentences: We used to throw our caps on the ground when we entered the classroom, so that we would have our hands freer afterward; as soon as we crossed the threshold, we had to launch them under the bench, so they would hit the wall and create a lot of dust; that was the way it was.
But whether he hadn’t noticed this maneuver or hadn’t dared to comply, by the time the prayer was over, the newcomer was still holding his cap on his knees.

It was one of those composite hats, where you can find elements of a fur cap, a chapska, a round hat, an otter cap, and a cotton bonnet, one of those poor things, in short, whose silent ugliness has depths of expression like the face of a fool.

Ovoid and bulging with whalebones, it started with three circular rolls; then, separated by a red band, there alternated diamonds of velvet and rabbit fur; next came a sort of bag that ended in a cardboard polygon, covered with a complicated soutache embroidery, from which hung, at the end of a long, too-thin cord, a small cross of golden threads, like a tassel.
It was new; the visor was shining.
He stood up; his cap fell.
The whole class burst out laughing.
He bent down to pick it up.
A classmate knocked it down with an elbow, and he picked it up once again.
Remove your cap, then, said the professor, who was a witty man.
There was a loud laugh from the schoolboys that flustered the poor boy, so much so that he didn't know whether to keep his cap in his hand, leave it on the ground, or put it on his head.
He sat back down and placed it on his knees.
The same mumbling of syllables was heard, drowned out by the jeers of the class.
The newcomer, then making an extreme decision, opened his mouth wide and shouted at the top of his lungs, as if to call someone, the word: Charbovari.
It was a racket that sprang up suddenly, rising in crescendo, with sharp bursts of voices (they were yelling, barking, stamping their feet, repeating: Charbovari!

Charbovari!), then rolling into isolated notes, calming down with great difficulty, and sometimes suddenly picking up again along the line of a bench where, like a poorly extinguished firecracker, some muffled laughter still popped up here and there.

sentences: Victoria Island was then floating in the largest part of the Bering Sea, six hundred miles from the first Aleutians and more than two hundred miles from the nearest coast to the east.
Its movement was still occurring at a relatively considerable speed.
However, assuming it did not suffer any decrease, it would still need at least three weeks to reach that southern barrier of the Bering Sea.

Could this island last until then, whose base was thinning each day under the action of the already tepid waters, and brought to an average temperature of fifty degrees Fahrenheit (10° centigrade above zero)?
above zero?
Could its ground open up at any moment?
Lieutenant Hobson was urging with all his might the construction of the raft, whose lower frame was already floating on the lagoon's waters.
Mac Nap wanted to give this device a great solidity, so that it could withstand for a long time, if necessary, the shocks of the sea.
Indeed, it was to be assumed that, if he did not encounter any whaling ship in the Bering area, he would drift to the Aleutian Islands, and a long stretch of sea remained to be crossed.
However, Victoria Island had not yet experienced any significant change in its general configuration.

Reconnaissances were being made daily, but the explorers ventured out only with extreme caution, as at any moment, a fracture of the ground or a fragmentation of the island could isolate them from the common center.
Those who departed in this way could always be feared to not be seen again.
The deep cut located at the approaches of Cape Michel, which the winter's cold had closed, had gradually reopened.
It now extended for a mile inland to the dried-up bed of the small river.
One could even fear that it would follow this bed, which, already dug, was thinning the ice crust even more.
In this case, the entire portion between Cape Michel and Barnett Port, limited to the west by the riverbed, would have disappeared.
that is to say, an enormous piece, covering several square miles.
Lieutenant Hobson therefore advised his companions not to venture there without necessity, as a strong movement of the sea was enough to detach this important part of the island's territory.

sentences: And how did this misfortune come about?
the shipowner continued, picking up the conversation where the young sailor had left off.

--My God, sir, in the most unexpected way: after a long conversation with the port commander, Captain Leclère left Naples very agitated; after twenty-four hours, he was struck by fever; three days later, he was dead....

sentences: The whole table was shaken with joy.
The ground trembled, the glasses vibrated.
Then there was a flurry of double entendres that made the bride blush a little, all a-quiver with anticipation.

Then, after they had drunk barrels of brandy, everyone went to bed; and the young couple entered their room, located on the ground floor, like all the farm rooms; and, since it was a bit warm, they opened the window and closed the awning.

A small, tasteless lamp, a gift from the woman's father, was burning on the dresser; and the bed was ready to receive the newlyweds, who did not observe the formalities of the bourgeois in the cities during their first embrace.
The young woman had already taken off her headdress and dress, and she remained in her petticoat, unlacing her boots, while Jean finished a cigar, glancing at his companion.
He watched her with a gleaming eye, more sensual than tender; for he desired her more than he loved her; and suddenly, with a brusque movement, like a man about to get to work, he took off his coat.
She had undone her boots, and now she was taking off her stockings, then she said to him, addressing him informally since childhood: 'Go hide over there, behind the curtains, so I can get into bed.'
He pretended to refuse, then he went over there with a sly look and hid himself, except for his head.
She was laughing, wanted to cover his eyes, and they were playing in a loving and cheerful way, without learned modesty and without embarrassment.
Finally, he gave in; then, in a second, she untied her last petticoat, which slid down her legs, fell around her feet, and lay flat on the ground.
She left it there, stepped over it, naked under the flowing shirt, and slipped into bed, which creaked under her weight.

Immediately he arrived, barefoot himself, in his trousers, and he bent towards his wife, searching for her lips that she was hiding in the pillow, when a gunshot echoed in the distance, in the direction of the Râpées woods, it seemed to him.
He straightened up, anxious, his heart clenched, and, running to the window, he unhooked the awning.

sentences: No, replied Monte-Cristo, and God grant that I haven't contributed too much to it! The events that had just taken place were on everyone's mind in Paris.

Emmanuel and his wife were recounting them, with quite natural surprise, in their small living room on rue Meslay; they were linking these three catastrophes, as sudden as they were unexpected, to Morcerf, Danglars, and Villefort.
Maximilien, who had come to pay them a visit, was listening to them or rather attending their conversation, lost in his usual insensitivity.

"Indeed, said Julie, wouldn't one say, Emmanuel, that all these rich people, so happy yesterday, had forgotten, in the calculations on which they based their fortune, happiness, and status, the role of the evil genius, and that this one, like the wicked fairies from Perrault's tales who were neglected at some wedding or baptism, suddenly appeared to take revenge for this fatal oversight?
"What suffering!"
said Julie, recalling Valentine, whom she instinctively did not want to name in front of her brother.

"If it is God who has struck them, said Emmanuel, it is because God, who is supreme goodness, found nothing in the past of these people that warranted a reduction of their punishment; it is because these people were cursed.
"Aren't you being rather rash in your judgment, Emmanuel?"
said Julie.
When my father, with the pistol in hand, was ready to blow his brains out, if someone had said, as you say now: 'This man deserved his punishment,' wouldn't that person have been mistaken?
Yes, but God did not allow our father to succumb, just as He did not allow Abraham to sacrifice his son.
To the patriarch, as to us, He sent an angel who cut halfway the wings of Death." He had barely finished speaking these words when the sound of the bell rang out.

I would gladly accept your offer, the host replied; but unfortunately, if I go, it might be incognito. However, the dinner was progressing and seemed to have been served solely for Franz, as the unknown had barely touched one or two dishes of the splendid feast he had offered him, to which his unexpected guest had paid such great honor.
Finally, Ali brought the dessert, or rather took the baskets from the hands of the statues and placed them on the table.
Between the two baskets, he placed a small cup of vermeil closed with a lid of the same metal.
The respect with which Ali had brought this cup piqued Franz's curiosity.
He lifted the lid and saw a kind of green paste that resembled angelica jam, but which was completely unknown to him.
He replaced the lid, just as ignorant of what the cup contained after putting the lid back on as he had been before lifting it, and, looking back at his host, he saw him smile at his disappointment.
"You can't guess, he said to him, what kind of edible this little vase contains, and it intrigues you, doesn't it?"
"Well, this kind of green jam is nothing less than the ambrosia that Hebe served at Jupiter's table."

"But this ambrosia, said Franz, has undoubtedly lost its celestial name in passing through human hands to take on a human name; in common language, what is this ingredient called, for which, by the way, I don't feel much sympathy?"
Ah!

This is precisely what reveals our material origin, exclaimed Sinbad; often we pass by happiness without seeing it, without looking at it, or, if we have seen and looked at it, without recognizing it.
Are you a practical man and is gold your god? Taste this, and the mines of Peru, Guzarat, and Golconda will be opened to you.

Are you an imaginative man, are you a poet? Taste this again, and the barriers of the possible will disappear; the fields of infinity will open up, and you will stroll, free of heart, free of mind, in the boundless realm of daydreaming.

Are you ambitious, do you chase after the greatness of the earth? Always taste this, and in an hour you will be king, not just king of a small kingdom hidden in a corner of Europe, like France, Spain, or England, but king of the world, king of the universe, king of creation.

Your throne will be set on the mountain where Satan took Jesus; and, without needing to pay homage to him, without being forced to kiss his claw, you will be the sovereign master of all the kingdoms of the earth.

Several hundred of these birds, belonging mainly to edible species, were killed during the first fifteen days, adding a welcome supplement to the usual corn beef and biscuits.
Thus, animals were certainly not lacking in this territory.
The Company could easily stock its stores, and the fort's personnel would not leave their kitchens empty.
However, these two conditions were not enough to ensure the future of the trading post.
One could not settle in a country so far north if it did not provide, and abundantly, the fuel necessary to combat the harshness of Arctic winters.
Fortunately, the coastline was wooded.
The hills, which rose behind the coast, were crowned with green trees, among which the pine predominated.
There were significant clusters of these resinous species, which could be referred to as forests in certain places.
Sometimes, too, in isolated groups, Jasper Hobson noticed willows, poplars, dwarf birches, and numerous arbutus bushes.
At this time of the warm season, all these trees were lush, and they somewhat surprised the eye, accustomed to the stark and bare profiles of polar landscapes.
The ground at the foot of the hills was covered with short grass, which the reindeer eagerly grazed on and which would sustain them during the winter.
As one can see, the lieutenant could only be pleased to have sought out the new site for exploitation in the northwest of the American continent.
It has also been said that while animals were not lacking in this territory, men seemed to be completely absent.
Neither Eskimos were seen, whose tribes prefer to roam the districts closer to Hudson Bay, nor Indians, who do not usually venture this far beyond the Arctic Circle.
And indeed, at this distance, hunters can be caught by continuous bad weather, by a sudden return of winter, and then be cut off from all communication.
One can well imagine that Lieutenant Hobson did not think to complain about the absence of his fellow men.
He could only have found rivals among them.
It was an unoccupied land he was seeking, a desert where fur-bearing animals would likely seek refuge, and in this regard, Jasper Hobson had the most sensible remarks for Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, who was keenly interested in the success of the venture.
The traveler did not forget that she was the guest of the Hudson's Bay Company, and she naturally wished for the lieutenant's plans to succeed.

sentences: A great misfortune; but allow me to leave, it concerns something far more precious than my life.
No questions, count, I beg you, just a horse!
My stables are at your service, viscount, said Monte-Cristo; but you will exhaust yourself with fatigue by riding hard; take a carriage, a cab, any vehicle.

No, that would take too long, and besides, I need this fatigue that you fear for me, it will do me good." Albert took a few steps, spinning like a man struck by a bullet, and fell into a chair near the door.
Monte-Cristo did not see this second weakness; he was at the window shouting, "Ali, a horse for Mr.
de Morcerf!
Hurry up!
He is in a hurry!" These words revived Albert; he rushed out of the room, the count followed him.
"Thank you!"
murmured the young man as he jumped into the saddle.
You will return as quickly as you can, Florentin.
Is there a password so that they will give me horses?
Nothing but to return the one you are riding; another one will be saddled for you immediately." "You may find my departure strange, foolish, said the young man.

You do not understand how a few lines written in a newspaper can drive a man to despair; well, he added, throwing the newspaper at him, read this, but only after I have left, so you do not see my embarrassment." And while the count picked up the newspaper, he drove the spurs, which had just been fastened to his boots, into the horse's belly, which, astonished that there existed a rider who believed he needed such a stimulant, took off like a bolt from a crossbow.

The count followed the young man with an infinite sense of compassion, and it was only when he had completely disappeared that, turning his gaze back to the newspaper, he read the following: "He is now called Mr. Count de Morcerf, and is a member of the House of Peers."

Thus, this terrible secret, which Beauchamp had buried with such generosity, reappeared like an armed ghost, and another newspaper, cruelly informed, had published, the day after Albert's departure for Normandy, the few lines that had nearly driven the unfortunate young man mad.

sentences: That horrifying sight had driven me nearly insane; from the moment I could no longer help anyone, I felt only one need: to flee.
I rushed down the stairs, burying my hands in my hair and letting out a roar of terror.
In the lower room, there were five or six customs officers and two or three gendarmes, a whole armed troop.
They seized me; I didn't even try to resist, I was no longer in control of my senses.
I tried to speak, I let out a few inarticulate cries, that was all.
I saw that the customs officers and gendarmes were pointing at me; I looked down at myself, I was covered in blood.
That warm rain I had felt falling on me through the stairs was the blood of the Carconte.
Then I understood that they were taking me for the murderer.
I regained my voice, I regained my strength; I broke free from the hands of the two men holding me, shouting: "You'll tell your little story to the judges of Nîmes," they replied.
In the meantime, follow us; and if we have one piece of advice for you, it's not to resist.
That was not my intention; I was shattered by astonishment and terror.
They put handcuffs on me, tied me to the tail of a horse, and took me to Nîmes.

I had been followed by a customs officer; he had lost sight of me around the house, suspected I would spend the night there; he had gone to warn his companions, and they arrived just in time to hear the gunshot and to catch me in the midst of such evidence of guilt that I immediately understood how difficult it would be to prove my innocence.
So, I focused on one thing: my first request to the investigating judge was to ask him to search everywhere for a certain Abbé Busoni, who had stopped at the Pont-du-Gard inn during the day.
If Caderousse had made up a story, if this abbé did not exist, it was clear that I was lost, unless Caderousse was caught in turn and confessed everything.
Two months passed during which, I must say in praise of my judge, all efforts were made to find the person I had requested.
I had already lost all hope.
Caderousse had not been caught.

I was about to be tried at the first session when, on September 8, that is, three months and five days after the event, Abbé Busoni, whom I no longer hoped to see, appeared at the jail, saying that he had learned that a prisoner wished to speak to him.
He had learned, he said, about the matter in Marseille, and he was eager to fulfill my request.

sentences: Well, said Andrea, you see, the situation would be for the best, assuming that my request is not rejected by Madame Baroness Danglars and by Mademoiselle Eugénie.
We are now in charge of a rental income of one hundred seventy-five thousand livres.

Let's suppose one thing, that I obtain from the marquis that instead of paying me the income he gives me the capital (it wouldn't be easy, I know that well, but still it is possible), you would make those two or three million work for us, and two or three million in skilled hands can always yield ten percent.
I never take less than four, said the banker, and even at three and a half.
But for my son-in-law, I would take five, and we would share the profits.

Well, splendid, father-in-law, said Cavalcanti, allowing himself to be carried away by the somewhat vulgar nature that, from time to time, despite his efforts, broke through the veneer of aristocracy he was trying to cover them with.
Oh!
excuse me, sir, he said, you see, just the hope alone drives me almost mad, what would reality be then?

But, said Danglars, who, on his side, did not realize how this conversation, initially disinterested, was quickly turning into a business deal, there is surely a portion of your fortune that your father cannot refuse you?
Faith, said Andrea, I assure you, sir, that I have never focused my mind on this subject, but I estimate it at two million at least.
Well, sir, said Andrea, bowing to the banker with tender respect, may I hope...
Mr. Andrea, said Danglars, hope, and rest assured that if there are no obstacles on your part to halt the progress of this matter, it is settled.
But, said Danglars, reflecting, how is it that Mr.
the Count of Monte-Cristo, your patron in this Parisian world, has not come with you to make this request?
Now, said Andrea with his most charming smile, I have finished speaking to my father-in-law and I am addressing the banker.

sentences: Ah, that's right, said Abbé Faria.
We are prisoners; there are moments when I forget it, and when, because my eyes pierce the walls that confine me, I believe I am free.

Dantès did not understand how a man could risk his life for such interests; it is true that while he knew Napoleon because he had seen and spoken to him, he was completely unaware, on the other hand, of who Clement VII and Alexander VI were.
"Aren't you, said Dantès, starting to share the opinion of his jailer, which was the general opinion at the Château d'If, the priest that people believe...
ill?"

--Yes, yes, continued Faria with a bitter laugh; yes, it is I who am considered mad; it is I who have entertained the inmates of this prison for so long, and I would bring joy to little children, if there were children in this place of hopeless suffering."
--I see the escape as impossible; it is to rebel against God to attempt what God does not want to happen.
--Why discourage yourself?
it would be too much to ask of Providence to want to succeed on the first try.
Can't you restart in another direction what you did in this one?
But do you know what I've done to speak like this about starting over?
Do you know that it took me four years to make the tools I have?
Do you know that for the past two years I've been scraping and digging earth as hard as granite?

Do you know that I had to unearth stones that I once would have thought impossible to move, that entire days have passed in this titanic labor, and that sometimes, in the evening, I felt happy when I had removed a square inch of that old cement, which has become as hard as the stone itself?

Do you know, do you know that to store all this earth and all these stones that I was burying, I had to pierce the vault of a staircase, in the drum of which all these debris have been buried in turn, so that today the drum is full, and I no longer know where to put a handful of dust?

Do you know, finally, that I believed I was close to the goal of all my work, that I felt I had just the strength to accomplish this task, and that now God not only pushes this goal further away but moves it I don't know where?
Ah!
I tell you, I repeat it to you, I will do nothing from now on to try to regain my freedom, since it is God's will that it be lost forever.

sentences: Soon she resumed: "What if I were to completely cross the earth?
How funny it would be to find myself among people who walk upside down.

In the Antipodes, I believe." (She wasn't upset this time that there was no one there to hear her, as that word didn't seem quite right to her.) "Oh, but I will have to ask them the name of the country.--Excuse me, madam, is this New Zealand or Australia?"--At the same time, she tried to curtsy.
(What an idea!
Curtsying in the air!
Tell me, how would you go about it?) 'What a little ignoramus!' the lady will think when I ask her this question.

No, I shouldn't ask that; perhaps I'll see it written somewhere." Falling, falling, falling!--So Alice, having nothing better to do, started talking to herself: "Dinah will notice my absence this evening, of course." (Dinah was her cat.) "I hope they don't forget to give her her bowl of milk at tea time.
Dinah, my dear, why aren't you here with me?
There are no mice in the air, I'm afraid; but you could catch a bat, and that looks a lot like a mouse, you know.
But do cats eat bats?" Here sleep began to overtake Alice.
She kept repeating, half asleep: "Do cats eat bats?
Do cats eat bats?" And sometimes: "Do bats eat cats?" Because you see, since she couldn't answer either of those questions, it didn't matter how she asked them.

She was dozing off and began to dream that she was walking along holding Dinah's hand, very seriously saying to her: "Come on, Dinah, tell me the truth, have you ever eaten bats?" When suddenly, poof!
there she was lying on a pile of sticks and dry leaves,--and she had finished falling.
Alice hadn't hurt herself at all.
Quickly she got back on her feet and looked up; but everything was dark up there.
She saw in front of her a long passage and the White Rabbit running at full speed.

There wasn't a moment to lose; Alice took off like the wind and just arrived in time to hear the Rabbit say, as he turned the corner: "By my whiskers and ears, how late it is!" She was only two steps away: but as soon as he turned the corner, the Rabbit had disappeared.
She then found herself in a long, low room, lit by a row of lamps hanging from the ceiling.
Never, my lord, never.
He has a guard with him at all times who speaks his language and whom we are absolutely sure of.

In the event that, in one way or another, he were to let slip any information regarding his discovery, that information would be immediately collected, and we would see what use should be made of it." At that moment, Count d'Artigas cast a quick glance at Captain Spade, who responded with a gesture that seemed to say: understood.

And indeed, anyone who had observed the captain during this visit would have noticed that he was examining with particular attention this part of the park surrounding Pavilion 17, the various openings that provided access to it,
probably in view of a prearranged plan.
The garden of this pavilion bordered the wall of Healthful-House.
On the outside, this wall enclosed the very base of the hill, whose slope gently extended down to the right bank of the Neuze.
This pavilion had only a ground floor, topped by an Italian terrace.
The ground floor included two bedrooms and an anteroom, with windows barred by iron grilles.
On each side of the dwelling stood beautiful trees, then in all the splendor of their foliage.
In front, lush, velvety lawns flourished, where there were plenty of varied shrubs and vibrant flowers.
The whole area covered about half an acre, for the exclusive use of Thomas Roch, free to wander through this garden under the watch of his keeper.
When Count d'Artigas, Captain Spade, and the director entered this enclosure, the one they saw at the door of the pavilion was the keeper Gaydon.
Immediately, Count d'Artigas's gaze fell on this keeper, whom he seemed to observe with a peculiar intensity that went unnoticed by the director.
'There,' replied the keeper, pointing with his hand to a man who was walking thoughtfully under the trees behind the pavilion.
Mr.
Count d'Artigas was granted permission to visit Healthful-House, and he did not want to leave without having seen Thomas Roch, about whom there has been far too much talk lately...
--And there would be even more talk, replied Count d'Artigas, if the federal government had not taken the precaution of locking him up in this facility...

sentences: Fortunately, a few years earlier, a scholar from the Institut de France, Léon Foucault, had just invented a process that made polishing lenses very easy and quick by replacing the metallic mirror with silvered mirrors.
It was enough to cast a piece of glass of the desired size and then coat it with a silver salt.
It was this process, whose results are excellent, that was followed for the manufacturing of the lens.
Moreover, it was arranged according to the method devised by Herschell for his telescopes.
In the large apparatus of the astronomer from Slough, the image of the objects, reflected by the inclined mirror at the bottom of the tube, formed at the other end where the eyepiece was located.
Thus, the observer, instead of being positioned at the lower part of the tube, was raised to its upper part, and there, equipped with his magnifying glass, he peered into the enormous cylinder.
This combination had the advantage of eliminating the small mirror intended to redirect the image to the eyepiece.
The image was now subjected to only one reflection instead of two.
Therefore, there was a smaller number of light rays extinguished.
Thus, the image was less weakened.
Finally, this meant that more clarity was achieved, a valuable advantage in the observation that was to be made.
With these resolutions made, the work began.
According to the calculations from the Cambridge Observatory, the tube of the new reflector was to be two hundred eighty feet long, and its mirror sixteen feet in diameter.

No matter how colossal such an instrument was, it could not be compared to the telescope measuring ten thousand feet (about 3.5 kilometers) that the astronomer Hooke proposed to build a few years ago.
Nevertheless, establishing such an apparatus presented great difficulties.
As for the question of location, it was quickly resolved.
It was a matter of choosing a high mountain, and there are not many high mountains in the States.

Indeed, the orographic system of this great country consists of two mountain ranges of moderate height, between which flows the magnificent Mississippi, which Americans would call 'the king of rivers' if they accepted any form of royalty.
To the east, there are the Appalachians, whose highest peak, in New Hampshire, does not exceed five thousand six hundred feet, which is quite modest.

sentences: Barbicane and his colleagues were staring intently at the intruder who boldly threw himself into the discussion.
None of them knew him, and the president, feeling uneasy about the outcome of such a straightforward conversation, looked at his new friend with some apprehension.
The assembly was attentive and seriously worried, as this debate had resulted in drawing their attention to the dangers or even the real impossibilities of the expedition.
--Oppose, sir, replied Michel Ardan with perfect gallantry, oppose as much as you like!
--You know, said the stranger, that when light rays pass through a medium like air, they are deflected from a straight line, or in other words, they undergo refraction.
Well!
when stars are obscured by the Moon, their rays, grazing the edges of the disc, have never experienced the slightest deflection nor given the faintest hint of refraction.
From this, it follows that the Moon is not surrounded by an atmosphere.
They looked at the Frenchman, for once the observation was accepted, the consequences were rigorous.

"Indeed, replied Michel Ardan, that is your best argument, if not the only one, and a scholar might be at a loss to respond; I will only tell you that this argument does not have absolute value, because it assumes the angular diameter of the Moon is perfectly determined, which it is not.
But let's move on, and tell me, my dear sir, if you accept the existence of volcanoes on the surface of the Moon.
--Let me believe, however, and without exceeding the bounds of logic, that these volcanoes were active for a certain period!
This is certain, but since they could provide the necessary oxygen for combustion themselves, the fact of their eruption does not prove the existence of a lunar atmosphere at all.
Let's move on then, replied Michel Ardan, and set aside this kind of argument to focus on direct observations.
But I warn you that I am going to name names.
No doubt; but without explaining the origin of these bright spots, Herschell himself did not conclude from their appearance that a lunar atmosphere was necessary.
Well said, said Michel Ardan, complimenting his opponent; I see that you are very knowledgeable in selenography.

sentences: But what was this portion of the globe engulfed by cataclysms?
Who had arranged these rocks and stones like dolmens from prehistoric times?
Where was I, where had the imagination of Captain Nemo taken me?
I would have liked to question him.
Not being able to do so, I stopped him.
I grabbed his arm.

But he, shaking his head and pointing to the last peak of the mountain, seemed to say to me: I followed him in one last surge, and in a few minutes, I had climbed the summit that rose about ten meters above this rocky mass.
I looked at the side we had just crossed.
The mountain rose only seven to eight hundred feet above the plain; but from its opposite slope, it dominated the depths below this part of the Atlantic at double that height.
My gaze extended far and encompassed a vast space illuminated by a violent flash.
Indeed, this mountain was a volcano.
Fifty feet below the peak, amidst a rain of stones and cinders, a large crater was spewing torrents of lava, which cascaded like fire within the liquid mass.
Thus positioned, this volcano, like an immense torch, illuminated the lower plain to the farthest limits of the horizon.
I said that the underwater crater expelled lava, but not flames.

Flames require oxygen from the air, and they cannot develop underwater; however, lava flows, which contain the principle of their incandescence, can turn white-hot, successfully battle against the liquid element, and vaporize upon contact.
Rapid currents carried all these gases into diffusion, and the lava torrents slid down the mountain like the debris from Vesuvius onto another Torre del Greco.

Indeed, there, before my eyes, ruined, sunken, thrown down, appeared a destroyed city, its roofs collapsed, its temples fallen, its arches dislocated, its columns lying on the ground, where one could still sense the solid proportions of a kind of Tuscan architecture; further on, some remnants of a gigantic aqueduct; here, the muddy elevation of an acropolis, with the floating forms of a Parthenon; there, remnants of a quay, as if some ancient port had once sheltered merchant ships and war triremes on the shores of a vanished ocean; even further on, long lines of crumbled walls, wide deserted streets, an entire Pompeii buried beneath the waters, which Captain Nemo was resurrecting before my eyes!

sentences: Indeed, once, I wanted to move forward to the base of the bowsprit, from where I could have leaned out and seen the bow of the schooner cutting through the waters.
But, as a result of obviously given orders, the on-duty sailors opposed my passage, and one of them spoke to me in a brusque tone in a harsh English: 'Around ten o'clock, the breeze picks up,'
--a very favorable north-west breeze,
Captain Spade is giving his instructions to the first mate.
Immediately, he, with the whistle to his lips, has the mainsail, the foresail, and the jibs hoisted.
One could not have operated with more regularity and discipline aboard a warship.
The sky is beautiful, the clouds from the west dissipate as soon as they reach the heights of the zenith, and the sea shines under the downpour of sunlight.
So here are the conditions under which we are sailing through this part of the Atlantic Ocean, limited to the west by the coastline of the United States of America.
I call upon my memories: what are the islands or groups of islands that are found in this direction, before the lands of the Old Continent?
Moreover, before the Azores, on the line of the thirty-fifth parallel, at a distance of only twelve hundred kilometers, lies the group of Bermuda, which belongs to England.

It seems less hypothetical to me that if Count d'Artigas was responsible for the abduction of Thomas Roch on behalf of a European power, that power would be the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
To be honest, there remains the possibility that this individual acted solely in his own interest.
During this day, three or four times, Count d'Artigas came to take his place at the stern.
From there, his gaze seemed to carefully examine the various points of the horizon.
When a sail or smoke appears offshore, he observes them for a long time, using a powerful marine telescope.
I add that he didn't even deign to acknowledge my presence on the deck.
From time to time, Captain Spade joins him, and the two exchange a few words in a language that I cannot understand or recognize.
As for Thomas Roch, I haven't seen him all morning, and he must be locked in his cabin, under the influence of the crisis from the day before that has not yet ended.

But three knocks were heard on the stage; a roll of timpani began, the brass instruments struck chords, and the curtain, rising, revealed a landscape.

Said Danglars, you see that while I don't share, in general terms, your sympathy for frankness, I submit to it when I believe the circumstances invite me to do so.
I will continue then.
I proposed a husband to you, not for you, because in truth I wasn't thinking of you at all at that moment.
You love frankness, there you go, I hope; but because I needed you to take this husband as soon as possible, for certain business arrangements that I am currently establishing.

"It's as I have the honor to tell you, my daughter, and you mustn't hold it against me, for it's you who force me into this; it's against my will, you understand, that I enter into these arithmetic explanations, with an artist like you, who fears to enter a banker’s office to perceive unpleasant and anti-poetic impressions or sensations.

"But in this banker’s office, which you were kind enough to enter the day before yesterday to ask me for the thousand francs that I grant you each month for your whims, know, my dear young lady, that one learns a lot about the very use of young people who do not wish to marry.

For example, one learns, and out of respect for your nervous sensitivity I will tell you this in this salon, that a banker's credit is his physical and moral life, that credit supports a man just as breath animates the body, and Mr.

One learns that as credit withdraws, the body becomes a corpse and that this will happen very soon to the banker who takes pride in being the father of such a good logician." But Eugénie, instead of bending, straightened up under the blow.

her first glance was directed towards the spot where she had seen the Count the day before, so she caught sight of Franz and Albert in the box of the man about whom she had expressed such a strange opinion to Franz twenty-four hours earlier.

Her lorgnette was aimed at him with such intensity that Franz realized it would be cruel to delay any longer in satisfying her curiosity; thus, taking advantage of the privilege granted to spectators in Italian theaters, which allows them to treat the performance halls as their own reception rooms, the two friends left their box to pay their respects to the Countess.
Hardly had they entered her box when she signaled for Franz to take the place of honor.
"Well," she said, barely giving Franz time to sit down, "it seems you couldn't wait to get to know the new Lord Ruthwen, and now you are the best of friends?"

sentences: The count advanced, accompanied by Maximilien and Emmanuel; his calm and serene face stood in stark contrast to Albert's troubled expression, who was approaching on his side, followed by the four young men.
"Gentlemen," said Albert, "come closer; I want to ensure that not a word of what I am about to have the honor of saying to Mr.
the count of Monte-Cristo is lost; for what I am about to have the honor of telling him must be repeated by you to anyone who wishes to hear it, no matter how strange my speech may seem to you.
Sir, Albert said, his voice initially trembling but growing more assured; sir, I reproached you for having revealed the actions of Mr. de Morcerf.
in Epirus; for, however guilty Mr. de Morcerf may have been,
I did not believe that it was you who had the right to punish him.
But today, sir, I know that this right belongs to you.

It is not the betrayal of Fernand Mondego against Ali-Pasha that makes me so quick to excuse you; it is the betrayal of the sinner Fernand against you, and the unimaginable misfortunes that followed from that betrayal.

So I say it, so I proclaim it aloud: yes, sir, you were right to take revenge on my father, and I, his son, thank you for not having done more!” The thunder that fell among the spectators of this unexpected scene would not have astonished them more than this declaration from Albert.

As for Monte-Cristo, his eyes had slowly turned to heaven with an expression of infinite gratitude, and he could not help but admire how this fiery nature of Albert, whose courage he had known well among the Roman bandits, had suddenly bent to this sudden humiliation.
He also recognized the influence of Mercédès and understood how this noble heart had not opposed the sacrifice that she had known in advance would be in vain.
“Now, sir,” Albert said, “if you find that the apologies I have just made to you are sufficient, your hand, please.
After the rare merit of infallibility that seems to be yours, the first of all merits, in my opinion, is to know how to admit one's faults.
But this admission concerns me alone.
I acted rightly according to men, but you, you acted rightly according to God.
Only an angel could save one of us from death, and the angel descended from heaven, if not to make us two friends, alas!
fate makes that impossible, but at least two men who respect each other.”

sentences: However, to know which tendon to cut on Hippolyte, it was necessary to first understand what kind of clubfoot he had.

He had a foot that formed an almost straight line with the leg, which did not prevent it from being turned inward, so it was a clubfoot mixed with a bit of varus, or a slight varus strongly marked by clubfoot.

But, with this clubfoot, indeed wide like a horse's hoof, with rough skin, dry tendons, large toes, and where the black nails resembled the nails of a shoe, the stréphopode galloped like a deer from morning until night.
He could be seen constantly in the square, hopping all around the carts, throwing forward his uneven support.
He even seemed more vigorous on that leg than on the other.
From having served so much, it had developed qualities of patience and energy, and when given some heavy work, he preferred to strain it.

Now, since it was a clubfoot, it was necessary to cut the Achilles tendon, with the intention of later addressing the anterior tibial muscle to get rid of the varus; for the doctor did not dare to risk two operations at once, and he was already trembling, afraid to attack some important area he did not know.
Come on, calm down, said the apothecary, you will show your gratitude to your benefactor later!
The evening was delightful, full of conversations and shared dreams.

They talked about their future fortune, about improvements to make in their household; he envisioned his status growing, his well-being increasing, his wife always loving him; and she felt happy to refresh herself with a new, healthier, better feeling, finally experiencing some tenderness for that poor boy who cherished her.

sentences: I turned my gaze towards the plain; an immense column of pumice stone, sand, and dust was swirling upwards like a whirlwind; the wind was pushing it down against the slope of Sneffels, to which we were clinging; this opaque curtain stretched out before the sun cast a large shadow over the mountain.
If this whirlwind tilted, it would inevitably wrap us in its spirals.
This phenomenon, quite common when the wind blows from the glaciers, is called 'mistour' in the Icelandic language.
Without knowing Danish, I understood that we needed to follow Hans as quickly as possible.

He began to circle the cone of the crater, but at an angle to make walking easier; soon, the whirlwind descended upon the mountain, which shuddered at its impact; the stones caught in the wind's eddies flew down like rain in an eruption.

Fortunately, we were on the opposite slope and sheltered from any danger; without the guide's precaution, our shredded bodies, reduced to dust, would have fallen far away like the remnants of some unknown meteor.
However, Hans did not consider it wise to spend the night on the slopes of the cone.
We continued our zigzag ascent; the fifteen hundred feet that remained took nearly five hours; the detours, angles, and backtracks measured at least three leagues.
I could go no further; I was succumbing to the cold and hunger.
The air, slightly thin, was not enough for my lungs to function properly.

Finally, at eleven o'clock in the evening, in complete darkness, the summit of Sneffels was reached, and before going to take shelter inside the crater, I had time to glimpse the 'midnight sun' at the lowest point of its path, casting its pale rays on the sleeping island at my feet.
Dinner was quickly devoured and the small group settled in as best as they could.
The bedding was hard, the shelter flimsy, and the situation quite uncomfortable, five thousand feet above sea level.
However, my sleep was particularly peaceful that night, one of the best I had had in a long time.
I didn't even dream.
The next day, we woke up half-frozen by a very brisk air, under the rays of a beautiful sun.
I left my granite bed and went to enjoy the magnificent spectacle that was unfolding before my eyes.

sentences: On the 10th, there was no change.
J.-T.
Maston was on the verge of going mad, and there were concerns for the brain of this worthy man, who had been so well preserved until then under his gutta-percha skull.
But on the 11th, one of those dreadful storms from the intertropical regions broke out in the atmosphere.
Strong east winds swept away the clouds that had been gathering for so long, and in the evening, the half-eaten disk of the night star majestically passed among the clear constellations of the sky.

That very night, the thrilling news that had been so eagerly awaited burst like a clap of thunder across the States of the Union, and from there, leaping across the Ocean, it raced along all the telegraph wires of the globe.
The projectile had been sighted, thanks to the gigantic reflector at Long's Peak.
Here is the note drafted by the director of the Cambridge Observatory.
It contains the scientific conclusion of this great experiment by the Gun Club.
This projectile did not reach its target.
It passed by, but close enough, however, to be captured by the lunar attraction.
There, its straight-line motion changed into a circular motion of dizzying speed, and it was drawn into an elliptical orbit around the Moon, of which it became the true satellite.
The elements of this new celestial body have not yet been determined.
Neither its translational speed nor its rotational speed is known.
The distance separating it from the surface of the Moon can be estimated at about two thousand eight hundred thirty-three miles (approximately 4,500 leagues).

Now, two hypotheses may arise and lead to a change in the state of affairs: either the attraction of the Moon will ultimately prevail, and the travelers will reach their destination; or, maintained in an immutable order, the projectile will orbit around the lunar disk until the end of time.
What questions this unexpected outcome raised!
What a situation full of mysteries the future held for scientific investigations!
Thanks to the courage and dedication of three men, this seemingly futile endeavor of sending a projectile to the Moon had just yielded an immense result, with incalculable consequences.

The travelers, imprisoned in a new satellite, if they had not reached their goal, were at least part of the lunar world; they were orbiting around the night star, and for the first time, the eye could penetrate all its mysteries.

The names of Nicholl, Barbicane, and Michel Ardan will therefore be forever famous in the annals of astronomy, for these bold explorers, eager to expand the circle of human knowledge, boldly launched themselves through space and risked their lives in the strangest attempt of modern times.

sentences: He found it lamentable to live in this village, with Homais as a friend and Mr.
Guillaumin as a master.

The latter, completely absorbed in business, wearing gold-rimmed glasses and sporting a red beard on a white cravat, understood nothing of the subtleties of the mind, although he affected a stiff and English manner that had dazzled the clerk in the early days.

As for the pharmacist's wife, she was the best wife in Normandy, gentle as a lamb, cherishing her children, her father, her mother, her cousins, weeping for the misfortunes of others, letting everything go in her household, and hating corsets;

—but so slow to move, so boring to listen to, with such a common appearance and such limited conversation, that he had never thought, even though she was thirty years old, that he was twenty, that they lived door to door, and that he spoke to her every day, that she could be a woman for someone, nor that she possessed anything of her sex other than the dress.
And then, what was there?
Binet, a few merchants, two or three innkeepers, the priest, and finally Mr.
Tuvache, the mayor, with his two sons, well-off people, gruff, obtuse, cultivating their own land, having family feasts, devout besides, and part of a completely unbearable society.
But against the common backdrop of all these human faces, Emma's figure stood out, isolated and yet more distant; for he felt between her and himself like vague abysses.
As soon as the first cold weather arrived, Emma left her room to inhabit the hall, a long room with a low ceiling where there was, on the mantelpiece, a dense polypore spreading against the mirror.
Sitting in her armchair, near the window, she saw the villagers passing by on the sidewalk.
Léon, twice a day, went from his study to the Lion d'Or.
Emma, from afar, heard him coming; she leaned in to listen, and the young man slipped behind the curtain, always dressed the same way and without turning his head.
But at dusk, when, with her chin in her left hand, she had abandoned her unfinished tapestry on her lap, she often started at the sudden appearance of that shadow gliding.
She would get up and order that the table be set.

she said, she wanted to see me, she wanted to talk to me, she feared or sensed something...
Oh!

I cannot leave without saying goodbye to her, I cannot die without entrusting her to someone.” And he gently returned to his place and wrote at the bottom of the first lines: “I bequeath to Maximilien Morrel, captain of spahis and son of my former employer, Pierre Morrel, shipowner in Marseille, the sum of twenty million, part of which he will offer to his sister Julie and to his brother-in-law Emmanuel, if he does not believe, however, that this surplus of fortune should harm their happiness.
These twenty million are buried in my cave of Monte-Cristo, of which Bertuccio knows the secret.

“If his heart is free and he wishes to marry Haydée, daughter of Ali, pasha of Janina, whom I raised with the love of a father and who has had for me the affection of a daughter, he will fulfill, I will not say my last will, but my last desire.

“This present will has already made Haydée the heir to the rest of my fortune, consisting of lands, rents in England, Austria, and Holland, furnishings in my various palaces and houses, and which, after deducting these twenty million, as well as the various legacies made to my servants, could still amount to sixty million.” He was finishing writing this last line when a cry from behind him made him drop the pen from his hands.
Indeed, the young woman, awakened by the daylight that had struck her eyelids, had risen and approached the count without her light steps, muffled by the carpet, being heard.
“Oh!
my lord, she said, joining her hands, why are you writing like this at such an hour?
Why do you bequeath me all your fortune, my lord?
Are you leaving me then?
I am going on a journey, dear angel, Monte-Cristo said with an expression of infinite melancholy and tenderness, and if something were to happen to me... "Well?...
the young girl asked with an authority in her voice that the count had never known in her and which made him start.
"Well, if something happens to me," Monte-Cristo replied, "I want my daughter to be happy."
"Well, if you die," she said, "bequeath your fortune to others, because if you die...
I won't need anything anymore."
